units.la: PRÆSTANTISSIMO VIRO D. NICOLAO BRVLARDO A SILERI, Henrici IIII. Francor. & Navar. Regis Christianissimi in sacro consistorio Consiliario, & apud Helvetios Rhætósque Legato,
units.tr: To the most excellent man, Nicolas Brulart de Sillery, Councillor of Henry IV, King of France and Navarre, Most Christian King, in the sacred council, and Ambassador to the Swiss and the Rhaetians,

units.la: OCTRINAM morum, quæ vel vtilissima philosophiæ pars est, Brvlarde præstantissime, non vna ratione veteres sapientes tradiderunt. Fuêre qui in recte constituenda vitæ summa,& inueniendo bono, vt putabant , summo , quærendisque & explicandis mediis ad beatitatem ducentibus , suam omnem operam ponerent. Fuëre qui ad singulas vitæ humanæ partes studium conferret suum, & quid cuique personæ , cuique ætati conueniret,queꝫ officia singulorum , docere laborarent. Illam priorem veteres δογματικὴν[?], hac posteriorem ἀρχιτεκτονικὴν[?] philosophiam nuncuparūt.Fuit vero & tertium quoddam tractandæ morum disciplinæ genus , é re χαρακτηριστικὸν[?] ab iisdem illis nominatum. Pulcherrimam hac philosophandi viam,primus, vt videtur,senex facundissimi oris,
units.tr: The doctrine of morals, which is indeed the most useful part of philosophy, most excellent Brulart, has been handed down by the ancient sages in more than one way. Some devoted all their effort to fixing rightly the highest aim of life and finding the good, which they thought was the highest good, and to seeking out and explaining the means that lead to happiness. Others applied their study to the individual parts of human life, and laboured to teach what suits each person and each age, and the duties of each. The ancients called the former philosophy dogmatic [δογματικὴν] and the latter architectonic [ἀρχιτεκτονικὴν]. There was also a third kind of treating the discipline of morals, which from its nature they named characteristic [χαρακτηριστικὸν]. This most beautiful way of philosophizing was first invented, it seems, by Theophrastus, an old man of most eloquent mouth.

units.la: Theophrastus inuenit: primus certè, quod ex antiquis monumentis constet nobis, in eo se, & elegantissimum illud ingenium suum exercuit. Neque abest cōiectura, summum virum cùm à Platone didicisset, Virtutem, si oculis cerneretur mirabiles sui amores excitaturam: rationem & vestigasse prudenter, & pervestigasse solerter, qua cùm virtutis speciem pulcherrimā, tum etiam vitiorum dedecus ac turpitudinem ipsis pene dixerim corporis oculis spectandam exhiberet. Magnum sanè ausum, & eo viro dignissimum, qui felici illo seculo viueret, quod tulit Socratem, Platonem vidit, Aristotelem generi humano dedit: III viros constituendæ philosophiæ, sine dubio diuinitus excitatos. Quorū in sinu & gremio cùm fuerit hic de quo loquimur educatus, nec dubium, nec mirum est eam ipsum scientiæ βαθύτητα esse consecutū, eam scribendi facultatem adeptum, vt nihil vnquam sit ab eo prosectum, quod nō visum sit studiosis sapientiæ omnibus numeris perfectum. Testes sunt huius tātæ illius præstātiæ, cùm alia hominis monumenta, quæ in studiosorū manibus, hodiéque versantur: tum hic quoque liber aut libri potiùs ἀπαταρμάτιον[?], quod me auctore atque interprete in tuam se clientelam, si pateris BRVLARDE clarissime, gestit tradere. Est autè hic ille Theophraftei ingenij fœtus, de quo paulò antè dicebam : liber, fine dolo dicam, aurum contra non carus. Nam quod ille integer ad nos non peruenerit, adeò non debet ea calamitas reliquiarum istarum pretium apud nos imminuere:ut cōtrà potius eò maiore cura ac studio, ceu tabulæ aliquæ ex ingenti naufragio superftites, colligendę nobis colligandæque videantur.Neque fanè vereri unquâ subiit, ne quas horas in emendando, vertendo, & explicando hoc Fragmento ponebamus, eas docti viri malè nos collocasse iudicarent. Et verò pręter grauisimorum virorum adhortationes,quibus exci-
units.tr: Theophrastus invented it. At any rate he was the first, as is known to us from ancient records, to exercise his own most elegant genius in it. Nor is it a far-fetched guess that this great man, having learned from Plato that Virtue, if it could be seen with the eyes, would arouse wonderful love for herself, carefully investigated and diligently searched out the method by which he might display the most beautiful form of virtue, and also the shame and ugliness of vices, so that they might almost, I would say, be viewed with the eyes of the body. A bold undertaking indeed, and worthy of that man who lived in that happy age which bore Socrates, saw Plato, and gave Aristotle to the human race: three men raised up without doubt by divine providence to establish philosophy. Since the man of whom we speak was educated in their bosom and lap, there is no doubt and no cause for wonder that he attained the very depth of learning and gained such skill in writing that nothing ever came from him which was not seen by all students of wisdom to be perfect in every respect. Witnesses to this great excellence are other monuments of the man, which are still handled in the hands of students; and also this book, or rather these books, a little fragment [ἀπαταρμάτιον], which, with me as its author and translator, is eager to deliver itself into your protection, if you allow it, most illustrious Brulart. This is indeed that offspring of Theophrastus's genius of which I spoke a little earlier: a book, to speak without guile, not a cheap treasure. For the fact that it has not come down to us whole does not in the least diminish the value of these remains in our eyes; rather, on the contrary, they seem to us to be gathered and bound together with all the greater care and zeal, like tablets surviving a huge shipwreck. Nor has it ever occurred to us to fear that learned men would judge that we had spent our hours badly in emending, translating and explaining this fragment. And indeed, besides the exhortations of most grave men, by which we were first roused to devote whatever effort we could to Theophrastus,

units.la: ā 4 tati primùm fumus adhāc qualemcunque operam Theophrasto commodandam : exemplo etiam fumus confirmati doctifsimorum hominum , quos ante nos in eădem descēdisse arenam videbamus. qui si tantum aut temporis aut diligentiæ huic negotio impendissent, quātum res postulabat : facilè mihi persuadeo potuisse illos & mihi & aliis omnibus occasionem præripere falcem in ipsorū messem iniiciēdi. Verùm quid inter illorum editionem & nostram hanc intersit, doctis candidisq; lectoribus æstimandum & iudicandum relinquimus. In primis autem te BRVLARDE sapientissime, arbitrum ferimus : cuius iudicio si stabit & probabitur nostra hæc opella, næ caussa[?] non erit, cur de cæterorum eruditorum calculis aut desperemus, aut multū simus solliciti. quod enim ille olim de Platone, id ego non minori iure nunc de te, Unus tu mihi instar omnium. Nam & is es tu, in quo uno cūctas habitare virtutes, quas in aliis mirari solemus singulas, uno omnes ore pridem fatentur. Te quondam in media patria, & in oculis tuorum civium Reipu. gubernacula integritate, iustitia, & moderatione summa inter præcipuos tractantem, laudibus in cœlum omnes ferebant. Te nunc legationis huius amplissimo munere difficillimis hisce & tantùmnon desperatis temporibus sapientissimè, prudentissimèque fungentem; omnes mirantur. Te denique fortissima Heluetiorum gens tanquam unicum, & coelo delapsum fidei,constantiæ, veritatis, grauitatis, &c, ut uno verbo dicam, veteris illius Fracicæ generositatis,quę pridem defecisse in nostra gente artibus corrupta exoticis,videbatur,exemplar intuetur, suspicitque. Quid ego nunc commemorem, non iuris ciuilis tantùm, sed plurimarum artium honestissimarum accuratam cognitionem? quid summum illum amorem, ardorémque in litteras, & cùm plurima teneas,plura in dies discendi desiderium ? quod cùm à puero maximum tibi naturæ auctor Deus inoleuisset, ne nunc quidem inter tantas, tam molestas, tam difficiles curas & occupationes relanguit,nedum exaruerit. Accedit ad has tantas virtutes tuas, ceu inferta pulcherrima, singularis morum comitas: quæ te omnibus bonis non minus reddit amabilem, quàm illa priora venerabilem. Et erit aliquis qui miretur tantum te gratia, tantum auctoritate apud omnes pollere ? mirarer potius, fi qui effet, qui cùm te vidisset, cùm loquentem audiffet, non stuperet. Equidem, vt primùm te vidi, & quæ antè fama de te acceperam, præfens maiora omnia in te agnoui : nunquam ab eo destiti silentio,atque ἐυφη-[?]μία animum istum tuum tam excelsum , & tot virtutibus exaggeratum venerari. cuius affectus, animíque in te mei patere obsecro te , vir maxime , extare hoc , cuicuimodi est , testimonium : meámque hanc sive temeritatem, sive audaciam æqui boni consule. Vale. à d.
units.tr: we were also encouraged by the example of the most learned men whom we saw had gone down into the same arena before us. If they had spent as much time or diligence on this business as the matter demanded, I am easily persuaded that they could have snatched from me and from everyone else the chance of casting the sickle into their harvest. But what difference there is between their edition and this one of ours we leave for learned and fair-minded readers to weigh and judge. Above all, most wise Brulart, we take you as our arbiter. If our little work stands and is approved by your judgement, there will be no reason for us to despair of, or to be much anxious about, the verdicts of the other scholars. For what that man once said of Plato, I say now with no less right of you: you alone are to me equal to all. For you are the one in whom all those virtues dwell which we are used to admiring singly in others, and all men have long acknowledged this with one voice. Once, in your native city and in the eyes of your fellow citizens, you handled the government of the commonwealth among its foremost men, in integrity, justice and the highest moderation, and everyone lifted you to heaven with praises. Now, discharging this most ample office of embassy with wisdom and prudence in these most difficult and almost desperate times, you are admired by all. Finally, the most valiant nation of the Swiss gazes upon you and looks up to you as a unique model, fallen from heaven, of faith, constancy, truth, gravity, and, to put it in one word, of that old French nobility which seemed long ago to have vanished from our nation, corrupted by foreign arts. What need I now mention: your accurate knowledge not only of civil law but of very many most honourable arts? Or that supreme love and ardour for letters, and that, though you already hold very much, you desire to learn more with each passing day? This desire, which God the author of nature implanted in you to the greatest degree from boyhood, has not waned even now amid such great, troublesome and difficult cares and occupations, let alone dried up. To these great virtues of yours is added, like a most beautiful dowry, a singular courtesy of manners, which makes you no less lovable to all good men than those earlier qualities make you venerable. And will anyone wonder that you are so powerful in favour and authority with everyone? I would rather wonder if there were anyone who, having seen you and heard you speak, did not marvel. Indeed, as soon as I saw you, and found present in you all the greater things that report had told me before, I never ceased to keep silent and to admire, with reverent praise, that spirit of yours so lofty and so enriched with virtues. I beg you, most excellent man, let this testimony of my affection and of my mind towards you, of whatever kind it is, stand; and take this boldness or rashness of mine in good part. Farewell.
Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.

units.la: PETRI MATTHÆI I. C. Lugdun. PRÆFATIO AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: Preface to the Reader, by Pierre Matthieu, Doctor of Laws of Lyon

units.la: ISAACVS CA-SAVBONVS, cui nec desunt vires, nec languent animi, ad studiorum fulciendas ruinas, Lugdunum venit, eo maxime tempore, quo tota ciuitas ob sal. publ. & restitutam pacem, post tot malorum maria e sagis ad togas redierat, & ingenti laetitia apparatu desudabat. Diuertit ad amplissi-mum D. de Vic, Regis ab intimis consiliis, Tholosani Senatus Præsi
units.tr: Isaac Casaubon, who still has the strength and whose spirit does not flag in propping up the ruins of learning, came to Lyon, at the very time when the whole city, after the public safety and the restored peace, after so many seas of troubles, had returned from military cloaks to the togas and was busy with great rejoicing and preparation. He lodged with the most distinguished D. de Vic, one of the king's privy councillors, first president of the Toulouse Senate

units.la: Præsidem integerrimum , cuius ædes nunquam clausæ ijs quos ingenuus bonarum artium color non fucus commendat, eóque nomine vt palam apud superstites , sic æternùm apud posteros laudabitur. Illi suscepti itineris causam nouus hospes aperuit , se Athenæum dum in Volcis Aremouicis per hos nimbos & æstus ciuilis procella sumptu & applausu publico doceret, ab innumeris plagis , ijsque Chironijs non solùm curasse , sed sanasse, optare eum in publicam lucem, cum plerisque alijs scriptis emittere, & omnium editioni adesse, quòd olim expertus esset non integrum rem omnem Typographorum operis fidere, Probauit & comprobauit hanc mentem , simúlque pro ea exequenda nouas faces adiecit. Inde prala feruere cœperunt ab opusculo quod Theophrastus Erefius, cum ad incultos & male dolatos mores instituendos, auerruncandam è mentibus amentiam, tum ad virtutum & vitiorum indagădas naturas H᾽ΘIKOYS XAPAKTHPAS, quasi ἤθων ἀ-χονισμὸς inscripsit. Sed ut varia & incerta sunt aulicorum vices & sedes, quos plerumque improuisus negotiorum vortex alio abducit, cum ad coronidem vergeret opus, allati sunt regij codicilli, quibus Illust. de VIC in aulam euocatur, ad praeclaram legationem in Britanniam suscipiendum. Is Casaubonum optauit comitem, & ut non solet pendere ex crastino, aut ἐς ἄνεμον τὰ ἀσθξαῖα reijcere, tam subitam profectionem repente adeo instituit, ut abeunti vix datum sit amicis & clientibus precari bene. Quod ergo supererat operis ad excudendum, illud auctor levi manu, tumultuaria opera, & iam induta chlamyde recensuit, cumq; de illius causis, ordine & ratione præfari non posset itineri accinctus, id muneris delegauit, ratus eam vicem me obire posse et velle. Recusanti propter forenses curas, quibus indies abstrahor & auellor è gratis illis studiorum umbris, sub quibus olim apricari licuit, literas addidit tanti asse-ctus & benevolentia ut animum subsilire fecerint ad parendum. Non potui itaque non suaderi, quin has succenturiatas, et veluti anteambulones paginas inculti et supini stili, in limine elegantissimi operis, (Casauboni nominis studiosis offerrem. Videbor autem obscura facis igniculis tam late patentem, sefeq; iamdudum per orbem nostrum diffundentem splendorem illustrare, aut ἡλίῳ τὸ Φῶς δανείζειν, sed non pudebit praestare quod tam liquentibus causis recusare non potui. Ignoscet facile qui noscit.
units.tr: most upright president, whose house is never closed to those whom the genuine colour of the liberal arts, not a counterfeit, commends. For this he will be praised openly by the living and forever by posterity. The new guest explained to him the reason for his journey: while he was teaching at the Athenaeum among the Volcae Arecomici, through these storms and this heat of civil tempest, at public expense and with public applause, he had not only tended but healed countless wounds with Chironian remedies. He wished to bring him into the public light, together with many other writings, and to be present at the edition of all of them, because he had once learned by experience that the whole work cannot be trusted to the hands of printers. He approved and confirmed this intention, and at the same time added new torches to carry it out. Thereupon the presses began to seethe, starting with the little work that Theophrastus of Eresus, as well as for investigating the natures of the virtues and vices [ΗΘΙΚΟΥΣ ΧΑΡΑΚΤΗΡΑΣ], as if [ἤθων ἀκονισμὸς] inscribed, for instructing manners that are rough and badly shaped, for scouring folly from the minds of men. But as the fortunes and seats of courtiers are varied and uncertain, which an unforeseen whirlwind of affairs usually carries away elsewhere, when the work was nearing its completion, royal letters arrived, by which the most illustrious de Vic is summoned to court to undertake a distinguished embassy to Britain. He chose Casaubon as his companion, and, not being accustomed to depend on tomorrow or to cast the weak things [εἰς ἄνεμον τὰ ἀσθενῆ] to the wind, he so suddenly arranged so hasty a departure that the departing man had scarcely time to bid farewell to friends and clients. Therefore the author, with a light hand and in hurried labour, revised what remained of the work for printing, already dressed in his cloak, and since, girded for the journey, he could not preface it with its reasons, order and plan, he delegated this duty to me, thinking that I could and would take his place. When I refused, because of the cares of the courts by which I am daily drawn and torn away from those pleasant shadows of study under which it was once permitted to bask, he added letters of such affection and goodwill that they made my spirit leap to obey. I could not therefore be persuaded otherwise than to offer these supplementary and, as it were, preliminary pages, written by a plain and careless pen, at the threshold of a most elegant work, to the admirers of Casaubon's name. I shall seem to illuminate with the small flame of a torch something so widely spread, and that light which has long been diffusing its splendour through our world, and to lend light to the sun [ἡλίῳ τὸ φῶς δανείζειν]. But I shall not be ashamed to render what I could not, for such clear reasons, refuse. He who knows him will readily pardon it.

units.la: Habes ergo, vel me tacente, Amice lector, librum multò quàm antea castigatiorem, innumeris mendis ita olim scatentem, ut de eo dicere liceret, quod Simonem de Homericis scriptis Arato dixisse ferunt, depravatum, scilicet ab his qui emendare volebant, ut imperiti Chirurgi vulnus faciunt dum medentur. Solius erat CASAVBONI tam altos errores ingenij acie eruere, tam foedos critica spongia elucere, & Philosophum quem post Stratonem Cicero omnium fui ævi eloquentissimum & eruditissimum appellat, sua lingua & Latina loquentem primæuo splendori restituere. Addidit aliquot capita quæ hactenus desiderabantur, eiusdem auctoris & eadem forma percussa, ex laceris reliquiis vetustissimi codicis quem nactus est ante aliquot annos ex locupletissima Principis Palatini Bibliotheca à Marquardo Frehero I. C. præstantissimo, viro utraq; lingua maximo, studiis iuuandis, & vindicandis ab interitu, situ & pulvere veterum monimentis nato. Promiserat equidem ea maturius edere, nec per eum stetit quòd citius hoc nomen in aspero & probo non expunxerit; sed cùm per Typographos & tempora commodum non posset, solo tempore lapsam fidem exoluit cum fœnore[?]. Nam singulis capitibus notas adiecit, ad lucem plurium scriptorum, in quorum sententiis semper caligassemus, nisi hac fax præluxisset, quæ glaucomam obsidentem oculos prohiberet. Vberiores autem & auctiores essent, nisi eorum librorum subsidio, in excutiendis variis locis qui ab his tantum qui multum & multa legerunt tractari volunt, caruisset. Sed de hoc Theophrasti interprete quod olim Aristoteles de Theophrasto pronunciauit fas erit dicere, eum καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ὀξύτητος cuncta facillimè sine libris, iudicio potius & ingenii præstantia, & ψυχῆς ἀλιτάτω[?], ut cum Hippocrate loquar, quàm librorum auctoritate & compedio assequutum. Nec est quod hic hallucineris hanc ab aliis perfectam glaciem. Nam ut natura comparatum est res non nasci simul & perfici, nec in lucem omnia prodire, non ita primi singulas res librarunt, aut libarunt, ut posteris omnem scribendi praripuerint facultatem. Verum iniuriam me tanti viri fama facere putarem, si ex uno opere, ut [?]ἐκ φῆς ὀνύχων τὸν λέοντα, ingenii magnitudinem existimarem. Dicam vere, & ut mos meus liberè, eum ἀπὸ τὸ μήνιγγα [?]τῷ ἐγχε-φάλῳ, quod de Jove fabulantur, tot edidisse Palladas, easq; adversus malum liuoris dentem armatas, quot libros conscripsit. In ea vero ætatis asta[?]te, qua in publicum literarum theatrum productus floret, neq; octavum agonem Olympicum numeravit, tam uberes protulit ingenii fructus, ut ipsis legendis & colligendis innumera vix sufficiat Olympiades. Suis enim auspicijs tuti orbem quadrivium perambulant Aristoteles, Theophrastus, Laertius, Polyaenus, Strabo, Tranquillus, Theocritus, & plerique alij classici scriptores, quibus olim per barbariem excusi oculi, excisa aures, fracta crura, secti humeri flagellis. Auidè expectamus Athenæum, quem post Iacobi Dalecampij Lugdunensis Medici editionem olim Illustrissimo Archiepiscop. Lugdun. Galliarum Primati, utpote rarum & felicem ingenij fœtum, votam & dicatam recudit, elimat, illustrat, & quod πάυρος [?] πράξασθαι εὐμαρῆς [?], intentatos calles nullo antea tritos pede aperit, & multa quæ prouauos latuerunt extricat. Ita sentit nobile illud Galliæ nostræ decus Iosephus Scaliger, qui nuperis literis ad Clariss. de Vic, Casaubonum eruditorum Phænicem appellat. Ita sentiunt suis eulogiis praeclara illa sydera Aug. Thuanus, Petrus Faber Saniorianus, Iustus Lipsius, quorum nomini totus literatorum concessus plaudit & assurgit. Sic sentient omnes quibus est purior sensus. Reliquos qui plus verborum quam animi habent, quibus innatum est, & veluti οἰκεῖον[?] πρῶτον magnis inuidere conatibus, homines dodrantales, ignauiones usquequaq; contemnendos non moramur. Sed ne diutius te detineam, candide Lector, his praeclaris ingenij deliciis plane, plane tuis diu fruere, & Vale.
units.tr: You have, then, dear reader, even without my speaking, a book far more purified than before, which was formerly so teeming with countless blemishes that one could say of it what they report Simonides said of the Homeric writings of Aratus, that they had been corrupted by those who wished to emend them, just as inexpert surgeons make wounds while they treat them. It was for Casaubon alone to bring up such deep errors by the keen edge of his intellect, to wipe away such foul stains with the critic's sponge, and to restore to its first splendour, speaking its own Latin tongue, the philosopher whom Cicero, after Strato, calls the most eloquent and learned of all his age. He added some chapters that had hitherto been lacking, of the same author and stamped in the same form, from the torn remains of a very ancient codex, which he obtained some years ago from the very rich library of the Count Palatine, through Marquard Freher, the most outstanding jurist, a man great in both tongues, born to aid studies and to rescue from oblivion, dust and decay the monuments of antiquity. He had indeed promised to publish these things sooner, and it was not through him that he did not sooner strike out this name from the rough and honest list; but since this could not be done in time and by the printers, he discharged the broken promise, with interest, only when time had passed. For he added notes to each chapter, to illuminate several writers, in whose opinions we would always have been in the dark had this torch not shone before us, which drives away the cataract that besieges the eyes. The notes would have been fuller and more ample, had he not lacked the help of those books which are usable only by those who have read much and widely, in examining various passages. But concerning this interpreter of Theophrastus, what Aristotle once pronounced about Theophrastus may rightly be said: that by extraordinary acuteness he attained everything most easily, without books, through judgement and the excellence of his intellect, and (to speak with Hippocrates) through the most subtle workings of the soul, rather than through the authority and resources of books. Nor should you be misled here by the notion that this ice was broken by others. For, as nature has ordained, things do not come into being and reach perfection all at once, nor do all things come forth into the light; and the first men who touched on single subjects did not so exhaust them, or so taste them, as to snatch from posterity every faculty of writing. Indeed I would think I did an injury to the fame of so great a man if I judged the greatness of his genius from a single work, as one judges the lion [ἐκ φῆς ὀνύχων τὸν λέοντα] from its claw. I shall speak truly, and freely as is my custom: Palladas produced from his brain, as they fable Jove did, so many things as he wrote books, and armed them against the tooth of envy. But in that stage of life in which, brought forth into the public theatre of letters, he flourishes, and has not yet counted his eighth Olympic contest, he has produced such abundant fruits of genius that Olympiads would scarcely suffice for reading and collecting them innumerably. For under his auspices Aristotle, Theophrastus, Laertius, Polyaenus, Strabo, Suetonius, Theocritus and many other classical writers now walk safely through the world's crossroads, though formerly, through barbarism, their eyes were put out, their ears cut off, their legs broken, their shoulders torn with whips. We eagerly await the Athenaeus, which, after the edition of Jacques Dalechamps, a physician of Lyon, he has revised, polished and illustrated, and, as a rare and happy offspring of genius, dedicated and reissued to the most illustrious Archbishop of Lyon, primate of the Gauls; and, what is easy to achieve [πάυρος πράξασθαι εὐμαρῆς] for one who has done so much, he opens untrodden paths that no foot has trod before, and disentangles many things that lay hidden from our forefathers. Thus thinks that noble ornament of our Gaul, Joseph Scaliger, who in his recent letters to the most distinguished de Vic calls Casaubon the Phoenix of scholars. Thus think those brilliant stars, Augustus Thuanus and Pierre Faber of Saint-Orens, and Justus Lipsius, in whose name the whole assembly of scholars applauds and rises. So will all think who have a purer judgement. The rest, who have more words than mind, and who are born to envy great endeavours as if these were their own first possession, I do not stop to consider: men of nine inches, to be despised in every way for their idleness. But, not to detain you longer, candid reader, enjoy these illustrious delights of genius fully, fully and for long, and farewell.

units.tr: Chapters of the Characters of Theophrastus [κεφάλαια τῆς Ἠθικῶν χαρακτήρων τῷ Θεοφράστῳ]
On Sordid and Foolish Love of Praise, 57.
On Oligarchy, or the Manners of the Optimates, 69.

units.la: ΘΕΟΦΡΑΣΤ καὶ χαρα THEOPHRA racteres sine Morum defc
units.tr: Theophrastus, The Characters, or Descriptions of Manners

units.la: ÆPE equidem iam ante quum hac de re attentius cogitare coepissem, miratus sum: sed nec mirari fortasse desinā, quid causę sit cur quum Graecia omnis eidem caelo subiecta sit, quum etiam Graeci omnes codem[?] modo instituantur, non omnes tamen iisdem moribus
units.tr: Indeed, when I had begun some time ago to think about this matter more carefully, I was amazed. Perhaps, however, I will not stop wondering why, although all Greece lies under the same sky and all Greeks are brought up in the same way, not all of them have the same character.

units.la: ΔΗ μὲν ἐω̂ πεσπεσὸν πολ-λάκις ἐπισή-σας τῷ Δήμοιαν, ἐ-θαύμασα, ἴσως ἢ ἐδὲ παύσομαι θαυμά-ζων, π δήποτε τῆς Ἑλ-λάδος ὑπὸ τὸν αὑτὸν ἀέρα κειμένης, ἢ πάν-των τῶν Ἑλλήνων ὁ-μοίως παιδευομένων, συμξέξηνεν ἡμῖν ἐ-τῷ αὐτῷ τάξιν τῶν τεόπωρ ἔχ[?]ω. ἐγὼ γ̓[?], ὦ Πολυκλεις, σω-τηρήσας ἐκ*πολλῶ̈[?] τ̓ ἀνθρωπίνῳ φύσιν, καὶ ἐβιωκῶς ἔτι ἐν- γενήνοντα ζυνέα, ἐπ' ἢ ὡμιληκῶς πολλαῖς τε καὶ ταντοδαπαῖς φύσεσι, καὶ ᾧδατε- θεραμμένῳ δὲ ἀκρι- βείας πολλῆς τὰς τε ἀγαθοὺς ἕ ἀνθρώπων ἢ τοῖς φαύλοις, ὑπέ- λαβον εἶν συνξεχ̓ναι ἃ ἑκάτεροι αὐτῶν διπ- ηδεύσαν ἐν τῷ βίῳ, ἐκθήσω δέ σοι καὶ γέ- νῳ ὅσα τε τυγχάνει ἃν τόπων τούτοις προσκείμενα, καὶ ὃν τέσπον τῇ οἰκονομίᾳ λεῶνται. ὑπολαμβά- νω γὰρ, ὦ *Πολύκλεις, τοὺς *ἡμῖς ἡμῖν βελ- τίονς ἔσεσθ̓, καταλει- φθέντων αὐτοῖς ὑπο- μνημάτων τοιούτων. utamur.Ego siquidem, mi Polycles,quū à multo tēpore hominum naturas cssem [?] cōtēplatus, (quippe qui annos nonaginta novem iam vixerim : & cum multis, atq; omnis generis naturæq; hominibus sim versatus) quum inquâ diligētia magna & probos simul & improbos homines cōsiderassem, atque inter sè comparassem, faciendum duxi, ut quæ sit vitæ degendæ utrorumque ratio, hoc scripto complecterer.Exponam autem tibi generatim, cùm omnes morū speciēs quibus illi sunt prædīti, tū quis sit illorum vitæ cotidianæ modus.Liberos enim nostros, mi Polycles, fore meliores existimo, si monumenta ipsis huiuscemodi reliquerimus, quæ sibi pro exemplo proponentes, optimè moratos quosque sint electuri quibuscum versentur & consucscant[?], vt in viros tâdè nihil illis deteriores euadat.Sed iam ad rem ipsam me accingâ.Tuũ erit, ad ea quæ dicam animũ aduertere, & an rectè dicam pernoscere. Igitur, missis præfationibus, & ijs quæ multa poterât de re afferri, initium dicédi faciam ab illis qui cauillationem amplexi sunt, viriumq; ipsum primò definiam: deinde cauillatorē hominē describā qualis sit, & qui eius mores. Postea verò alias quoq;, animi affectiones generatim, vt ante diximus, explicare conabimur. οἷς παραδείγμασι χρῶ μῆροι, αἱρήσονταί τοῖς δυσχημονεσταῖς συνεί- ναί τε ᾧ ὁμιλεῖν, ὅ- πως μὴ καταδέεσεσθαι ὧσιν αὐτῶν. τεέλομαι δὲ ἤδη ἔπὶ τὸν λόγον. σὸν δὲ, ἀκολου- θήσας τε καὶ εἰδήσας εἰ ὀρθῶς λέγω. πρῶτον μὲν οὖν ποιήσομαι τὸν λόγον ἀπὸ τῶν τῆς ἀ- ρωνείας ἐζηλωκότων, ἀφεὶς τὸ προοίμαζέ- ος, καὶ πολλὰ ᾧ ἐπὶ τῇ ῳεάγματι λέγειν. καὶ ἄρξομαι πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῆς εἰρωνείας, καὶ δείξωμαι αὐτῷ· εἶθ' οὕτως τὸν εἴρωνα διέ- ξειμι, ποῖός τις ἔξι, ᾧ ὡς πίνα τέρπτον κατέ- νλωέ σ κ. Ὢ τὰ ἄλλα δὴ τῶν παθημάτων, ὥσπερ * ἐσφεδέμεω, πιεράσομαι κ ἡμῶν. φανερὰ κατασῆσαι.
units.tr: I have often wondered at this, and I still wonder why, since Greece lies under one sky and all Greeks are educated alike, their characters are not all the same. For my part, Polycles, having lived a very long time among men of many natures, now ninety-nine years old, and having associated with people of every kind, I have observed the good and the bad with great care. I thought it right to set down in writing what kind of life each of them leads. I will explain to you, by kind, all the characters these men have and how each manages his daily life. I think our children, Polycles, will be better if we leave them such records, so that they may take them as examples, choose the best-mannered people to associate with, and so that they themselves will not turn out worse than men of good character. Now I will come to the matter itself. You will attend to what I say and judge whether I speak rightly. Setting aside prefaces and the many things that could be said on the subject, I will begin with those who have embraced irony, and first define irony itself. Then I will describe the ironical man: what sort of man he is and what his character is. Afterwards I will try to explain the other affections of the mind in general, as I said before, so that those who wish to choose examples may choose them, and so that they may avoid associating with the ill-natured, lest they be harmed by them. Now I turn to the argument. First I will speak of those who have pursued irony, leaving aside the preface and the many things that could be said on the subject.

units.la: ΗΜΕΝ οὖν εἰρωνεία δόξειεν[?] ἂν εἶναι ὡς τύπῳ λαλεῖν[?], προαιρούμενος[?] τὸ χεῖρον φεύξεων[?] καὶ λόγων. ὁ δ' ἀνήρ[?] τοιοῦτος τίς ἐστιν οἷος προσελθὼν τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἐθέλειν λαλεῖν, ὃ μισεῖν. καὶ ἐπαινεῖν παρόντας οἷς ἐπιτύχοι[?] λάθρα, καὶ τυχοῖς συλλυπεῖσθαι ἡδομένοις. καὶ συμφωνεῖν ἢ ἔχειν τοῖς κακῶς αὐτὸν λέγουσι· καὶ ὅτι τοῖς καθ' ἑαυτὸν λεγομένοις, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἀδικουμένους ἀγανακτοῦντας πράως διαλέγεσθαι[?]. καὶ τοῖς συνυ[?]ναι καὶ αὐτοῖς βελτ[?]μένοις, προσαξαι ἐπανελθεῖν· καὶ μηδὲν ἂν
units.tr: Irony would seem to be a kind of pretended speech, for one who chooses to avoid the worse course in word as well as deed. Such a man approaches his enemies and is willing to talk with those he hates; he secretly praises those he happens to meet, and sometimes grieves along with those who are glad; he agrees with, or takes the side of, those who speak ill of him; he speaks mildly to those who are discussing his own affairs and to those who are angry at injuries done to them; and to those who are... he is ready to return, and to say nothing [ἡ μὲν οὖν εἰρωνεία δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι ὡς τύπῳ λαλεῖν, προαιρούμενος τὸ χεῖρον φεύγειν καὶ λόγων. ὁ δ' ἀνὴρ τοιοῦτος τίς ἐστιν οἷος προσελθὼν τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἐθέλειν λαλεῖν, ὧν μισεῖ· καὶ ἐπαινεῖν παρόντας οἷς ἐπιτύχοι λάθρα, καὶ τυχὸν συλλυπεῖσθαι ἡδομένοις, καὶ συμφωνεῖν ἢ ἔχειν τοῖς κακῶς αὐτὸν λέγουσι, καὶ τοῖς καθ' ἑαυτὸν λεγομένοις καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἀδικουμένους ἀγανακτοῦντας πράως διαλέγεσθαι· καὶ μηδὲν ἂν].

units.la: CAvillatio igitur, si quis rudi definitione complecti velit, est cum factorum tum dictorum, in deterius fictio. Homo autem cavillator talis est, qui ad inimicos suos adeat, quasi alloqui eos velit, non amplius odisse: quique illos quibus clam struit infidias, præsentes laudet, & si victi fuerint, eorum vice doleat. Si quis ipsi maledicat, ei ignoscit: iactaque in se convitia negligit: cum iis etiam, qui quod iniuria ab ipso passi sint, quiritant, blandè, benignéque loquitur. Eos qui ipsum cōfestim conventum velint, iubebit redire iterum. Quicquid agit, claid habet, & fe adhuc deliberare dicit. Idé fe modò aducniffe fingit:aut fub vefperam veniffe,& è via lâguere. Pecuniâ mutuò rogatibus,aut eranum ab ipfo exigētibus,Nihil vēdo, inquit: è contrario quū nihil vendet, tum vendere fe affirmabit. Quū quid audiuerit, videri volet animum non aduertiffe.Quum quid viderit , negabit vidiffe. Paćtus aliquid, negabit fe meminiffe. De aliis dicit fe cogitaturū, alia nefcire, mirari alia : de quibufdā fe quoque iâ[?] ante fimiliter cogitaffe. Deniq; frequens omnino in eius ore huiufmodi eft oratio, Nō credo: Non puto:Obftupefco. Sefe etiā aliū fuiffe dicet.Itē,Atqui nō hęc e-περὶ τῆ ὁμολογήσαι, ἀλλὰ φῆσαι βελτίω· ἀξ· ἡ προασπίσαι ἀξ [?] ἀρπ ὡς ἀγαγόνεναι, ἡ ὀλὲ γενεαξ αὐτὸν ⁊ μαλακιδίων· ἡ πρὸς τοὺς διαλιζομένας ⁊ ἐραστιζονιας, ὡς οὐ πωλεῖ· ἡ μὴ πωλῶν, φησὶ πωλεῖν. ⁊ ἀκήσας π, δοξει μὴ προασπίσαξ· ἡ ἰδὼν, φῆσει μὴ ἑωρακέναι. ⁊ ὁμολογήσας, μὴ μεμνῆσθαι. ⁊ τὰ μὴν σκέ- [?] φασὶ φάσκει, ⁊ ἡ φῇ οὐκ εἰδέναι, ⁊ ἡ θαυμάζειν, ⁊ ἡ ἤδη ποτὲ ⁊ αὐτὸς οὕτω διαλεξάσαξ. ⁊ τὸ ὅλον, δλεινὸς τῷ τοιούτῳ τρόπῳ τὸ λόγῳ ξεῖ- ξαξ, ἃ πιστεύω, οὐχ ὑπολαμβάνω, ἐκπλήττομαι ⁊ λέγει ἑαυτὸν ἕτερον γεγονέναι. ⁊ νῦν οὐ ταῦτα πρὸς ἐμὲ διεξ[?] παραδέξον μοι θεᾶγμα, ἃ λῷ τ[?] λέγε· ὅπως ὃ σὶ ἀ[?] σήπω, ἢ σκευὴ καὶ γνῶ, ἀπορᾶμαι· ἀ[?] ὅρα μὴ σὺ θᾶττον σοῦ ἡς Ἰοιαύτας φω[?] ἢ πλοκὰς ἢ παλ[?] λοιδορίας· οὐ χεῖρον ὀδύρεῖν ἐδὲν. Ὧ δ' ἡ[?] ἡθῶν μὴ ἁπλᾶ, ἀ[?] ὅπλεια, φυλάπε[?] μᾶλλον δεῖ ἢ τ[?] ἔχεις.
units.tr: Cavillation, then, if one wishes to grasp it in a rough definition, is a distortion for the worse of both deeds and words. The cavillator is a man of this sort. He approaches his enemies as if he wanted to speak with them, and says he no longer hates them. He praises in their presence those whom he secretly plots against, and if they have been defeated, he grieves in their stead. If someone speaks ill of him, he forgives him and ignores the insults flung at him. He speaks kindly and gently even with those who complain that they have been wronged by him. He tells those who want to see him at once to come back another time. Whatever he does, he has a pretext, and says he is still deliberating. He pretends he has only just arrived, or that he came in the evening and was delayed on the road. When people ask him for a loan, or demand a debt from him, he says, "I am selling nothing." On the contrary, when he sells nothing, he will assert that he is selling. When he hears something, he will want it to seem he did not notice it. When he has seen something, he will deny having seen it. Having agreed to something, he will deny remembering it. He says he will consider other matters, that he does not know some, that he marvels at others, and about some he says he had thought the same before. In short, his speech is always of this kind: "I don't believe it; I don't think so; I am astonished." He will even say that he himself was once otherwise. Likewise, "But this is not..." and, in general, the cavillator is clever at this manner of speaking: "What I believe, I do not suppose; I am astonished," and he says he has become another man. Now, do not speak these things to me; accept my reply... Let the man of such manners, who is not simple but full of guile, be guarded against more than you would guard against him.

units.la: ΤΗΝ δὲ κο[?] κολ[?]είαν ἰσολ[?] ἂν προσόμιλίαν αἰρ[?] ἔ), συμφέρταν ἢ κολακεύοντ[?]. τὸν κόλακα τοιοῦτόν π[?] ὥστε πορ[?] rat ipsi apud me oratio. Res mihi videtur mira, & fidem omnem superare: Quære alium cui ista narres: Tibine credam, an illius damnem fidē, nescio. At tu caue fis vocibus istiusmodi & recătatis dictis credas: qua re deterior nulla queat reperiri. Enimuero mores huiusmodi hominum, non simplicium sed insidiosorum, magis quàm viperas fugere debemus.
units.tr: Flattery might perhaps be defined as a kind of familiar association, which people use for their own advantage. The flatterer is such that his speech is his own: "Ready to say anything to me." This seems to me a strange thing, and beyond all belief. Look for someone else to whom you may tell these things. Whether I should believe you or condemn that man's good faith, I do not know. But you must take care not to trust voices of this kind or flattering words, for nothing worse can be found. Indeed, we ought to avoid the ways of such men, who are not simple but treacherous, even more than we avoid vipers.

units.la: ADulationem vero putet aliquis esse turpem vitæ quotidianæ confuetudinem, sed quæ adulatori conducat. Adulator autem is est, qui si cum aliquo ambulet ei dicat, Viden' ut omnes in te oculos convertunt? Fit hoc nemini ex omnibus civibus praeterquā tibi. Heri in porticu magnum bonae exîstimationis tuq; fructum capiebas. Nam quî homines ibi plus quâ triginta sederent, sermóque incidisset, Ecquis civium esset optimus? & orsos ab ipso, & in eiusdem nomē simul omnes recidisse. Hæc ille loquitur, aliáque his similia. Idem ex illius vestimentis cui afsentatur floccos solet eximere. Quod si qua vel palea vel festuca à vento acta illius capillamento adhaeserit, tollit adulator & simul renidens, En, inquit, quia biduo hoc ego te nō vidi, ut canitie barba tibi est referta:
units.tr: One might think flattery is a shameful habit of everyday life, but it is one that suits the flatterer. The flatterer is the sort of man who, when he walks with someone, says to him, "Do you see how everyone turns their eyes to you? This happens to no one among all the citizens except you. Yesterday in the portico you were gaining great esteem. For when more than thirty men were sitting there and the talk turned to who was the best of the citizens, they all began with him and all came back to his name." He says these things and others like them. He also usually picks bits of fluff from the clothing of the man he flatters. If some straw or chaff blown by the wind has caught in his hair, the flatterer removes it and, smiling, says, "Look, because I haven't seen you for two days, your beard is full of grey:"
"But you, Lane, what age are you?"

units.la: ὡς ἀπολέπουσιν εἰς σὲ οἱ ἀνθρωποι ςπτὸ ὑδενὶ γίνεταῖ τῶν ἐν τῇ πόλει παλιὰ ἡ σοῦ νυ δοκίμεις χθὲς ἐν τῇ σοφ· πλειόνων γὰρ ἡ τελέκονϖ ἀνθρώπων καθημ[?]ένων, ἐμπεσόντος λόγου τινὸς εἰπ βέλτιστος, ἀπ' αὐτοῦ ἐξαρμάς πάντας, ὅτι τὸ ὁ ὁμοι αὐτοῦ κατενεχθῆναι. ἀλλα τοιαῦτα λέγων. ὅπο τῆς ἱματίου ἀφελεῖν κροκίδα· ἢ ἐάν τι ὠρὸς τὸ τρίχωματῆς κεφαλῆς ὅπο πνδύματ προσενεχθῆ ἄχυρον καρφολογῆσαι· καὶ ὅπηελάσας ἢ εἶπεῖν, ὁρᾷς ὅτι δύο σοι ἡμερῶν οὐκ ἐντετύχηκας, πόλιων ἔχηκας τὸν πώγωνα μεσόν. καὶ ὡς; εἴτις καὶ ἄλλος, ἐ-χεις πρὸς ᾧ ἔτι μέ-λλοντα τῷ τρ χα[?]. καὶ λέγοντος ἢ αὐτὸ τι, τὰς ἄλλας σωπᾶν κελεύσου, ἢ ἐπαιγε-σαι ἢ ἀκοντος. ἢ δῤῥισομύναθαι ἢ, εἰ παύσεσθαι, Ὀρθῶς.
units.tr: "As people flock to you, and nothing in the city happens without you; for yesterday in the portico, when more than thirty people were sitting there and some discussion arose about who was best, they all began from you and all returned to your name." He says such things. If a little down from his cloak or a piece of straw blown by the wind falls on the hair of his head, he picks it off. Then, laughing, he says, "You see, I haven't met you for two days, and your beard is half grey." If someone else speaks, he tells the others to be silent, laughs at the speaker loudly or without cause, and if the speaker stops, he says, "Rightly!"

units.la: ζ σιωπᾶντι*πικρῶς ἐπηγελάσει, τὸ τε ἱμάτιον ὥσαι εἰς τὸ σόμα, ὡς δὴ ἃ δυ-νάμενος καταχεῖν τὸν γέλωτα· ἢ τοὺς ἀπαντῶντας ὁπὴ-ναι μικρὸν κελεῦσαι ἕως ἂν Αὐτὸς πα-ξέλθῃ. ἢ τοῖς παι-δίοις μῆλα ζ ἀπὶς[?] ῳριάμενος, εἰσενεί-κας δοῦναι, ὁρῶν-τῶ αὐτῷ· ἢ φιλήν-σας ἢ εἶπεν, ᾧ παῖδες νεόπια[?]! ἢ συωωνεμένῳ[?] ἢ κρη-πίδας, τὸν ποδα homo sis, habes ut si quis alius capillos nigros. Iam siloquatur Ille, hic vero adulator silentium omnibus imperare, in os laudare, dicenti voce gestúque applaudere, & ubi finem dicendi fecerit, Dictum bene! acclamare. Quòd si quem Ille sale aliquo perstrinxerit, eundem ille acerbè irridebit, vestémque in os sibi indet [?], quasi risum tenere non queat. In via si qui siant obvij, sistere gradum iubet, donec Ille transierit. Mala etiam & pyra à se empta domum liberis Illius afferre, & spectante ipso dare moris habet: atque adeo ipsos osculatus, Probi patris pulliticm [?]! ait, exclamans. Crepidas ementi si comes affuerit, pedem dicet ipso calceo esse cōcinniorem. Adeunte Illo ad amicorū aliquem, curfu præire assentator, & huic quidē, Venit Ille, inquit, ad te: statimq; reuersus, Ego, ait, de tuo adventu præmonui. Sanè etiam quæcūq; ad muliebre forum pertinent, didicit iste omnia sedulò & diligenter ministrare: necnon ex omnibus convivis vinū primus laudare: & Illi assiduè assistens, dicere, Ut tu molliter comedis! & de iis quæ mēsæ sunt apposita, aliquid attollens, Hoc verò, ait, quàm bonum est! Quærere etiam amat, nūquid Ille frigeat: nunquid tegi adhuc & amplius amiciri velit: & quidem hæc dicens, ad aurem hominis se inclinat, eíque aliquid insusurrat: in eūdem etiam dum φῆσαι ἐῇ εὐρυθμότερον τὸ ὑποδήματα-τῷ. καὶ πορευομένῳ πρός τινα τῶν φίλων, προδραμὼν εἶπεῖν, ὅτι πρός σε ἔρχεται· καὶ ἀναστρέψας, ὅτι προσπέπληκα [?]. ἀμέλει δὲ καὶ ἐκ γυναικείας ἀρρᾶς [?] διακονησάμενος ἰλαρὸς ἀπέλυσί [?]. καὶ τῶν ἐσιωμένων, ὡσαύτως ἐπαινεσαι τὸν οἶνον. καὶ {*}δαιμονίων εἶπεῖν, ὡς μαλακῶς ἐϊδίζε! ἔ ἄρας τί τῶν ἀπὸ τεχνίζης, φῆσαι, ὅτι ἀεὶ ὡς ξένηνον ἐξιὼν ἐρωτῆσαι μὴ ῥίγοι, καὶ εἰ ὀπθαλέιαν βούλεται ἔτι ὠφειλαι αὐτόν. καὶ μὲν ταῦτα λέγων, πρὸς τὸ οὓς παραπίπτων, ἐυρίζειν, καὶ εἰς ἐκεῖνον ἀποβλέπων, τοῖς ἄλλοις λαλεῖν. καὶ τὸ παιδὸς ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ ἀφελόμενος τὰ προσκεφάλαια, αὐτὸς ὑποσφῆσαι [?] τὴν οἰκίαν φῆσαι δὲ ἡρ-χιτεκτονῆας [?], ἐ τὸν ἀγρὸν δὲ περιτοῦ-σας, καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα ὁμοίαν εἶ)[?]. καὶ τὸ κεφάλαιον, τὸν κόλακα ὅτι θεάσασθαι πάντα καὶ λέγοντα καὶ πράττοντα οἷς χαρι-εἰδὼς ὑπολαμβάνει.
units.tr: When the man is silent, he laughs bitterly, thrusts his cloak into his mouth as if he could not hold back his laughter, or tells those who meet them to stand aside until he has passed. He buys apples and pears, and when the great man is watching, he has the habit of carrying them home and giving them to his children; then, kissing the children, he cries out, "Children of a good father!" When the great man goes shoe-shopping with him, he says the foot looks more elegant in the shoe. When the great man goes to visit one of his friends, the flatterer runs ahead and tells the friend, "He is coming to you," and then, returning, says, "I announced your visit beforehand." He also takes care to serve in all the matters that belong to a woman's market, and he is the first to praise the wine among all the guests; standing constantly at the great man's side, he says, "How delicately you eat!" Lifting something from the dishes set on the table, he says, "But this, how good it is!" He also likes to ask whether the great man feels cold, whether he wants to be covered or wrapped more, and while saying these things he leans toward the man's ear and whispers something to him, while looking at others and talking to them. He takes the cushions from a slave in the theatre and puts them under him himself; he says the house is well designed, and walking round the field, he praises the statue. In sum, the flatterer thinks he is admired in everything he says and does by the man he pleases.

units.la: Ἡ δὲ ἀδολεσχία, ὅτι μὲν λήξη-σις λόγων μακρῶν καὶ ἀπροσλαβόντων[?]· ὁ ᾧ ἀδολέσχης, τοιοῦτός ἐστιν οἷος ὃν μὴ γι-νώσκῃ, τούτῳ ὥσ-περ καινὸν κατεζομένῳ[?] πλη-alios alloquitur, oculos defixos habet. Puluinos in theatro puero ademptos, ipse substernit. Domum ait benè & ingeniosè fuisse dimensam; & ædificatam: agrum diligenter confitum: imaginem per esse similem. In summa, assentatorem semper videbis omnia sua dicta, factaque ad voluntatem aliorum referre & conformare.
units.tr: Tedious talking is a long-winded, drawn-out way of speaking. The tedious man is such that, when he meets someone he does not know, he sits down beside him as if he were an old acquaintance, and while talking to others he keeps his eyes fixed on that stranger. At the theatre he takes the cushions away from the slave boy and arranges them under himself. He says that the house was measured out well and cleverly and was built with skill; that the field was carefully planted; and that the statue is a good likeness. In short, you will always see the flatterer refer and shape everything he says and does to the wishes of others.

units.la: GArrulitas est longorum & inconsideratorum sermonum effutitio. Garrulus autem eiusmodi est, qui vel apud ignotum iuxtim ei assidens, uxoris fuæ laudes prædicare instituat : deinde quod præcedenti nocte somniauerit, id narret : tum quæcunque in cœna sibi fuerint apposita, omnia sigillatim recenseat. Mox vero vbi incaluerit, homines huius sæculi dicet esse antiquis deteriores : frumenta in foro vili vænisse pretio : peregrinos esse in vrbe quàm plurimos : mare statim à Dionysiis patere nauibus : & si Iupiter pluerit, eorum quæ terra conduntur meliorem forè prouentum : seque agrum suum in sequentem annum esse culturum : ait etiam viuendi rationes esse perdifficiles : & quum Mysteria agitarentur Damippum facem omnium maximam statuisse. Quærit σὸν, ὥςπερ τὸν μὲν τῆς ἑαυτῆ γυναικὸς εἰπεῖν ἐγκώμιον[?]. εἶτα ὁ τῆς νυκτὸς εἶδεν ἐνύπνιον, τοῦτο ἀληθὴς[?] σας[?]· εἶθ' ὣν εἶχεν ὅτι τῷ δείπνῳ ᾷ καθέκαςα[?] διεξελθεῖν· εἶτα δὴ προχωροῦντωξ[?] ᾧεάγματ[?] ῷ, λέγειν ὡς πολὺ πονηρότεροί εἰσιν οἱ νῦν ἀνθρωποι τ[?] ἐχαίων[?]· ἡ ὡς ἀξιοι γεγόνασιν οἱ πυροὶ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ· καὶ ὡς φολλοὶ ὑπὸ δημῶσι ξένοι· καὶ τὴν Θάλαττὰν ἐκ Διονυσίων πλωΐμον ἔξ[?]). καὶ, εἰ ποιήσειεν ὁ Ζεὺς ὑσωρ[?], ᾶ ἐν τῇ γῇ βελτίω ἔσεσθ[?]. καὶ, ὁ ἀχρὸς εἰς νέωσα γεωργήσῃ. ἔ, ὡς χαλεπὸν ἔσι τὸ ζῆν. ἡ, ὡς Δάμπω μυσπρίοις μεγίςην ἁδάκ ἔσηοτ[?]. ἔ, πό[?] Ε, πόσοι εἰσὶ κίονες ἕ[?] Ωἰσθεία. Ἓ, χθὲς ἡμέ-σα. ἡ, τίς ὅστιν ἡμέρα σήμερον ἡ καὶ ἐμουμένη τις ἀὐτὴν, μὴ ἀφίσαν. ἡ ὡς Βοσδρομῶν ἡ μὴ ὅτι τὰ μυστήρια, Πυαισφιῶν δὲ ἀπατηρία, Ποσφδιῶν. ἡ κατ' ἀρχοῖς Διονύσια. παρεσίσαν[?] ἂ δὲ χρὴ τοῖς τοιούτοις τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἡ ἀλλαχοῦ μὲν ἀπαλλάττεσθαι, ὅστις ἀτυρσῆ[?] ἐκλεῖαι ἐῇ. ἔγον γὰρ συναρχεῖαν τοῖς μήτε χολὴν[?], μήτε αὐδλὼ διαχινώσκεσιν.
units.tr: Garrulity is the pouring out of long and thoughtless talk. A garrulous man is one who, even when he sits beside a stranger he has only just met, starts to sing his wife's praises. Then he tells what he dreamed the night before, and goes through everything that was set before him at dinner, one dish at a time. Once he has warmed to his subject, he says that the people of this age are worse than those of old; that grain has sold cheaply in the market; that there are very many foreigners in the city; that the sea is already open to the Dionysian ships; that if Jupiter sends rain, the crops stored in the ground will likely yield better; and that he will be tilling his field next year. He also says that the ways of living are extremely hard, and that when the Mysteries were being celebrated, Damippus set up the greatest torch of all. He asks how many pillars there are, and whether it was yesterday or the day before. He asks what day today is, or whether it is some other day he is being told about, and that the Mysteries fall in Boedromion, the Apaturia in Pyanepsion, the Dionysia at the beginning of Posideon. One should keep away from such people, and avoid them wherever one can, since they will not let anyone else get a word in.

units.la: ΗΔΕ ἀγροικία δέξειεν ἂν εἴη ἁμαρτία ἀχήμων[?]· ὁ At rufticus is cft , qui haufto pharmaco in concionem nihilominus prodeat : quique vnguenta non fuauius fragrare thymo dicat: calceos gestat pede grādiores : voce etiam alta loqui fucuit. Amicis neceffariifque fuis parum fidens , de rebus maximis ad famulos refert : quaecunque in concione audiuit, omnia mercenariis fuis, qui ruri apud ipfum opus faciunt , enuntiat. Sæpe etiam velte ita fupra genu fubducta fedct[?], vt denudatæ corporis partes confpici queant. In via aliorum quidem nihil admiratur , neque vlla re obftupefcit : fed fi bouem, afinum, aut hir-δὲ ἀρχοικῷ, τοιῶ-τὸς τῆς οἵῳ κυνεῶ-να πιὼν εἰς ἐκκλη-σιαν πορδευξ. Ϛ τὸ μύρον φάσκειν ἰδὲν ἔ- Ὑμᾶς ἥλιον ὁζειν. ἢ μείζω τῇ ὡσοδὸς ἃ ὑποδήματα φορεῖν.
units.tr: Rusticity may be described as a clumsy kind of error. The rustic is the sort of man who, after taking a purgative, goes to the assembly all the same; who says that perfume smells no sweeter than thyme; who wears shoes larger than his feet; and who is also in the habit of speaking in a loud voice. He has little confidence before his friends and acquaintances, yet he reports matters of the greatest importance to his servants, and whatever he has heard in the assembly he passes on to the hired men who work on his farm in the country. He often sits with his cloak drawn so far up above his knees that the bare parts of his body can be seen. On the road he is astonished at nothing belonging to others and is amazed by nothing at all; but if he sees an ox, a donkey, or a goat,
or to speak in a loud voice.

units.la: ἢ τοῖς μὲν φί-λοις καὶ οἰκείοις ἀπ-σεῖν, πρὸς ἢ τοὺς αὐτῇ οἰκέτας ἀνακοινᾶσθαι ὠεὶ τῶν μεγίστων.
units.tr: He keeps little faith with his friends and relatives, and discusses matters of the greatest importance with his servants.

units.la: καὶ τοῖς παρ' αὐτῷ ἐργα-ζομένοις μισθωτοῖς ἐν ἀγρῷ, πάντα τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας διη-γεῖσθαι. καὶ ἀναςεβλη-{*}μμῷ ἄνω τῇ γόνα-τῷ, καθιζάνειν, ὥστε τὰ γυμνὰ αὐτῇ{*}φαί-νεσθαι. καὶ ἐπ' ἄλλῳ μήτε θαυμάζειν, μήτε ἐκπλήτεσθαι ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς· ὅταν δὲ ἴδῃ βοῦν, ἢ ὄνον, ἢ
units.tr: He reports to the hired men who work for him in the fields everything he heard in the assembly. He often sits with his tunic drawn up above the knee, so that his bare body shows. On the road he wonders at nothing and is never astonished by anything; but when he sees an ox, an ass or a runner, he stops, stands still and stares at it.

Quumq; aliquid è proptuaria cella depromit, decerptū inde frustū vorat:& vinū meracius potat : diligēter interim ne hoc ancilla panifica refcifcat[?],cauēs[?].Deinde verò cū illa molere, & quę sunt ad victū neceffaria, tū fibi tū vniuersę familię parare solet.Inter prādendū iumentis pabulū obiicit : & si quis fores pulset,ipse aufcultat.Vocato etiā cane,& eius stro manu prehēso,Hic, inquit,& agrū & domū quique in ea sunt oēs cūstodit. Argentū quod ab aliquo acceperit , quasi tenue aut nimis asperū solet reiicere , & vt alio id sibi mutetur postulare. Aratrum si cui forte vtēdum dederit, aut cophinum,aut falcem, aut faccum , nocte intempefta illa repetet , si per infomniam fuerit corū recordatus. In urbē cum venit,obuium quemque interrogans , Quāti, ait, pelles & salsamenta vænibāt ? &, Nūquid hodie ludi nouam lunam adducunt? Dicit etiam , se simul ac descenderit, tōdere velle. Idem cantare in balneo , & clauis calceos suffigere , &, quia eadem via erat , ab Archia salsamenta accipere, ac portare ipse,moris habet.
units.tr: When he chooses to take something from the storeroom, he bites off a piece and eats it, and drinks his wine neat, all the while taking care that the bakeress does not notice. Then, when he is grinding with her and preparing the food they need, he provides for himself and the whole household. At dinner he throws fodder to the beasts of burden, and if anyone knocks at the door he answers it himself. He calls the dog, takes hold of its muzzle and says: "Guard the field, the house and those inside." When he is given money, he rejects it as too thin or too rough and asks for it to be exchanged for another coin. If he lends someone a plough, a basket, a sickle or a sack, he will ask for it back in the dead of night, if he happens to remember it in a dream. When he comes into the city, he asks everyone he meets: "How much are hides and salted fish selling for?" and "Do the games bring in the new moon today?" He says that as soon as he comes down he wants a haircut. It is his habit to sing in the bath, to nail his shoes together with pegs, and, because it is the same road, to take salted fish from Archias and carry it home himself.

units.tr: Flattery, if one wishes to define it, is a companionship of rather dishonourable pleasure, having the allurements of pleasure. It is the habit of one who, when he has been remembered in a dream during the night, or when he has been awake, goes down to the bath, asks the attendant about the leather sacks and the salt-fish, and says whether the games are bringing in a new moon. He also says he will shave as soon as he has come down, sings in the bath, drives nails into his shoes, and, because the road is the same, takes the salt-fish from Archias and carries them himself as is his custom.

units.tr: Obsequiousness, as I see it, is a kind of seeking to please, not so much for the sake of pleasure as for the sake of gain.

units.la: νῆς ᾧ Διδασκαλικὴ[?]· ὁ ᾧ ἀρεσκῷ, ἀμέλει τοιοῦτός τις οἷ πόρ-ρώθεν προσαπορίζου-σας, καὶ ἄνδρα κεκτ-σον εἰπὼν, καὶ θαυμά-σας ἱκανῶς, ἀμφοτέ-ρας ταῖς χερσὶ μὴ ἀ-φιέναι, καὶ μικρὸν προ-πέμψας, καὶ ἐρωτήσας ποτε αὐτὸν ὄφελος, ἐπ ἐπαινῶν ἀπαλλάτε-ὅς. καὶ ὁ Δακληθεὶς[?] ἢ πρὸς δίαιταν, μὴ μόνον ᾧ πάρεσι βάλεωσι δεξέ-σθαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἀν-τιδίκῳ, ἵνα κοινὸς εἴ) δοκῇ· καὶ τοὺς ξένους ὦ εἰπεῖν ὡς δικαιότερα λέγοντι τ' πολιτῶν. καὶ κεκλημένος δὲ ὅτι δεῖπνον, κελεύσας κα-λέσαι τὰ παιδία τὸν ἑαυτῶν ἁ, καὶ εἰσελθὰ, φησι σὺν ὁμοιότερα τῷ πατρί· ὦ πρὸ-σαγορεύω, φιλῆ-bens. Blandus verò is est, qui procul aliquem salutare, & virum appellare præstantissimum, fortunámque eius admirari soleat, & utraque manu prehendens, non dimittat: sed aliquan-tisper comitatus, quærens quādo fit illum visurus, vix tandem domum revertatur simul eius laudes prædicans. Idem captus arbiter, non ei tantùm cui adest, sed adversæ etiam parti, ut communis utriusque amicus habeatur, gratificari studebit.
units.tr: The obsequious man is one who, from a distance, will greet someone and call him a most excellent man, and will marvel greatly at his good fortune. Taking him by both hands, he does not let go, but escorts him for a little way, asks when he will see him again, and at last scarcely returns home, while still praising him. The same man, when he is acting as arbiter, will be eager to oblige not only the party he is with but also the opposing party, so that he may be thought a common friend of both. He also says that foreigners speak more justly than citizens.

units.la: Peregrinos iustiora quā civeis loqui dicit. Ad cœnam invitatus, convivij dominum ut liberos suos vocet rogabit: atq; illis ingredictibus negabit ficum ficui tam esse similem, quàm illi sint parentibus: deinde eos ad se vocabit, osculatúfque, sibi afsidere jubebit: & cum aliis jocans, En utrem, inquiet, En securim: alios in sinum recubere dormientes, quamuis oncre grauetur, sinet. Comam sæpius solet tōdere: dentes nitidos habere: vestes quæ usui adhuc esse possint, mutare: unguéto uti. Ac fori quidem in eã maximè partem ventitat, ubi sunt argentariorum menfæ: gymnafia verò illa frequentat, in quibus se ephebi exercent: in theatro autem & spectaculis iuxta ipsos prætores sedet. Idé in foro sibi quidé nihil: sed amicis qui Byzantij sunt mittenda munera emtitat: necnon Laconicas canes quas Cyzicü: & mel Hymettium quod [illegible, ~3 letters] Rhodum mittat: atque σαγ, ⁊ παρ αὐτὸν κα-ϑίσαι[?]· ⁊ τοῖς μὲ συμ-παιζειν αὐτὸς, λέγων, ἀσπὸς,πέλεκις· ⁊ ἅ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς γαστρὸς ἐὰν καθεύδειν, ἅμα θλι-βόμενον. καὶ πλήσα-κις ἢ ἀποκιέσθαι[?], ⁊ τοῖς ὀδόντας λευκοὺς ἔχειν. ἢ τὰ ἱμάτια ἢ ζέησα μεταβάλλεσθαι, ⁊ χρίσματα ἀλείφε-σϑαι. ἢ τῆς μὴ ἀρορᾶς πρὸς τὰς τραπέζας προσφοιτᾶν. τῶν δὲ γυμνασίων ἐν τόποις διατρίβειν οὐ ἂν ἐρη-θοι γυμνάζωνται. τὸ ἢ θεάτρῳ καθῆσθαι, ὅ-ταν ἡ θέα, πλησίον τῶν θεατῶν· ἢ ἀρορᾶζειν αὐτὰ μὴ μηδὲν ξένοις ἢ εἰς Βυζάντιον ὀπισάλμαῖα[?]· ⁊ Λα-κωνικὰς κύνας εἰς Κύ-ζικον. ἢ μέλι[?] μήτ-τον, εἰς Ῥόδον. ἢ ταῦτα πιῶν, τοῖς ἐν τῇ πό-λῃ ἀπηγεάζ.[?] ἀμέλης[?] ἢ ϲ πίθηκον θρεψαμένοις[?] νὸς, ἢ πύτρον, ἢ Ἰπσα-θης, ἢ Σικελικὰς ᾶδε-σεράς, ϲ ἀλορκαδ.ιους ἀσεχαλλοις[?], ἢ {*}Θυ-ειακὰς τῶν σεγγῶ-λων ληκύθους, ἢ ἐαπ-ιήρίας τῶν σωλιῶν ἐν Λακεδαίμονϑ, ἢ αὐλαίαν ἔχοσαν Πέρσας ἐνυφασμένας, ἢ αὐλίδιον παλαι-σεικὸν κόινν ἔχον, ἢ σφαιεισήειον· καὶ τοῦτο ϑεῖων χρῆν ἀεὶ τοῖς φιλοσόφοις, τοῖς σοφισταῖς, τοῖς ὁπλομαχοῖς, τοῖς ἀρ-μονικοῖς ὑπολαμβάνυ-σαι. ἢ αὐτὸς ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήξεσιν ὑστερον ἐᾶσιν, ὅτι τῶν ϑεω-μύων, ὡς ἔτερον, ὅτι τοῦτο ὄζὴμ ἡ πα-λαίσεα. hæc se facere suis ciuibnatrat. Præterea solet idem, simiā domi alere, satyrū emere, & colūbas Siculas, necnon dorcadios talos, & Thyriacas ampullas ex iis quę forma sunt rotūda: itē baculos ex obliquis Lacedæmone aduectos, necnō aulæū vbi sint Persae intexti. Habet etiam idē paruulū atrium puluere palaestrico refpersum, & sphæristerium: atq; has ædium suarū partes solet ille obuio cuique vel è philosophorū grege, vel sophistarum, vel corū qui se armis, aut musico cantu exercent, cōmodare, vt ibi artis suæ periculum faciant: quod quidem dum illi faciūt, ipse de aliquo è spectatoribus alij dicit, Eccū tibi cuius est hæc palaestra.
units.tr: When invited to dinner, he will ask the host to call his children; and when they come in, he will say that a fig is not so like a fig as they are like their parents. Then he will call them to him, kiss them, and bid them sit beside him. Joking with the others, he will say, "Look, a wineskin! Look, an axe!" He will let the children who fall asleep lie on his lap or on his stomach, even though they weigh heavily upon him. He often has his hair cut, keeps his teeth white, changes his clothes while they can still be worn, and anoints himself with perfume. He frequents the marketplace chiefly where the bankers' tables are, and frequents the gymnasia where the young men exercise; in the theatre and at spectacles he sits next to the magistrates themselves. In the market he buys nothing for himself, but he buys gifts to send to his friends at Byzantium, Laconian dogs to send to Cyzicus, and Hymettian honey to send to Rhodes. He says these things are done by him as favours to his fellow citizens. Moreover, he is in the habit of keeping a monkey at home, buying a satyr, and keeping Sicilian doves, Dorcadian knucklebones, and Thyriacan flasks of the round shape; also staves brought from Lacedaemon, and a hanging with Persians woven into it. He also has a small courtyard sprinkled with wrestling dust, and a ball-court. He is accustomed to lend these parts of his house to whoever he meets, whether a philosopher, a sophist, or one who exercises himself in arms or in music, so that they may try out their skill there. While they do this, he himself says to another of the spectators, "Look, there is the owner of this wrestling-ground for you."

units.la: DEfperatio eft per quâ aliquis & facere quiduis & loqui cōtra honeftatem fuftinet.
units.tr: Desperation is that through which a person endures both doing anything whatever and speaking against decency.

units.la: Homo autē defperatus & ad omnem audaciam proiectus, is eft qui iusiurandū facilè fufcipiat: qui malè audire ac conuitiis proscindi, fúsque, déque habeat. Moribus eft veteratoris calidi improbiqúe, & hominis spurci, ac quiduis audētis. Atquè adeo non pudebit eū, saltare cordacem etiam sobrium, & in comico choro personatum: & quum præstigiæ spectâtur, ad quémque spectâtium adire & stipem æream exigere: ac si quis tesseram asserens, gratis spectare postulet, cum eo rixabitur. Cauponā q
units.tr: A desperate man, thrown headlong into every kind of boldness, is one who readily takes an oath, who bears being abused and torn apart with insults as if it were nothing to him, and cares not a whit. He has the manners of a crafty, wicked old hand, a filthy fellow, ready to dare anything. And so he will not be ashamed to dance the cordax even when sober, or to appear masked in the comic chorus. When conjurers' tricks are on show, he will go up to each of the spectators and demand a copper coin for the collection; and if someone holding up a ticket asks to watch for nothing, he will quarrel with him. Cauponā q

When a juggling show is on, he goes up to each spectator and collects a contribution in bronze coins. If someone shows a ticket and asks to watch for nothing, he will quarrel with him.

Ϲ μετα- ξὺ οἱ μὲν προσία- σιν, οἱ δὲ ἀπίαστι πὴν ἀχθῶσαν αὐτῷ· ἀλλὰ τοῖς μὲν ἡχλῳ, τοῖς δὲ συλλαλῷ, τοῖς δὲ μέρῳ τῷ πεάγματῷ λέγ· οὐκ ἄλλως θεωρεῖᾳς cere, leno ac portitor coactórque esse folet: ac qui à nullo turpi artificio se abstineat, præco erit : coquus erit : aleator erit : matri suæ alimenta denegabit: furiti[?] etiam conuictus obtorto collo rapictur[?], atque in carcere diutius quàm in suis ædibus habitabit. Est etiam iste ex iis qui turbam circa se fistunt, & obuios ad se vocant quibuscum voce magna & præfracta loquuntur, iisque maledicta ingerunt: atque interea partim accedunt, partim discedunt, priusquam quid sibi ille velit audierint: dum ille aliis principium, aliis vix syllabam, aliis partem aliquam de re tota refert: non aliter quàm in celebri hominum conuentu profligatum ac perditū ingeniun̄ suum spectari postulas. Litibus etiam partim quæ ipsi intedūtur[?], partimquas ipse aliis intendit, solet esse implicitus: atq; in aliis absentiam suam iureiurando interposito excusare: ad alias iudicio se sistere, in sinu quidem scriniū, præ manibus vero forensium[?] libellorum fasciculū habens. Quin etiam, quæ eius est insignita impudentia, ducem se rabulis forensibus præbet: ac mox illis pecunia fenori data, pro usura drachmæ cuiusque ternos semiobolos in dies exigit: sæpe etiam popinas & macella ubi pisces ac fallamēta venundunt[?], per-
units.tr: He is also wont to be a pimp, a tax-collector and a debt-collector, and he is compelled to do so. Whoever abstains from no dishonourable trade will be a herald, a cook, a gambler. He will deny alimony to his own mother. Even when he is a thief's accomplice, he is dragged off by the collar and lives in prison longer than in his own house. This is also the sort of man who gathers a crowd around himself and calls passers-by to him, with whom he talks in a loud, brash voice and heaps abuse upon them. Meanwhile some come up to him and some walk away before they have heard what he wants. He tells one man the beginning, another scarcely a syllable, another some part of the whole business. You would think you were watching a shameless and ruined character put on display before a crowded gathering of people. He is also usually caught up in lawsuits, some that are brought against him and some that he brings against others. He excuses his absence from others on oath, and he appears in court before others, carrying the writings in his bosom and a bundle of legal documents in his hands. Indeed, marked by his peculiar impudence, he sets himself up as the leader of the legal pettifoggers. Once they have lent out money at interest, he collects for the loan three half-obols per drachma each day. Often he also goes to the taverns and the meat markets where fish and salted goods are sold, and...
itself, or whenever he is of all things
some to pursue, some to deny under oath, some merely to be present

units.tr: holding that one in his bosom and a bundle of documents in his hands; not rejecting, but leading the market-men, lending money to them, or exacting three half-obols a day of interest on the drachma, or frequenting the wrestling-schools, fish-markets and grain-markets; and taking his interest from the sales into his cheek. They are troublesome, having a tongue unloosed for abuse, speaking so loudly that the market and the workshops ring with it. ## On Garrulity

units.tr: Garrulity, if one wished to define it, would be an intemperance of speech. The talker is such a person that, whoever meets him, he will say to him whatever he likes; he says it in this way, and that he knows everything, so that even if you listen to him you will learn it all.

units.la: Sút sanè istiusmodi homines admodum difficiles: quorum quidem os ad convitiandum facilè solvitur: atque id voce ita contenta, ut eorum clamoribus & forum, & omnes tabernæ personent.
units.tr: Such men are indeed very troublesome: their mouths are quick to abuse, and they speak so loudly that the forum and all the shops resound with them.

Loquax verò is est, qui solet ei qui cum verba facit, dicere, quicquid ille narrare inceperit, Nihil dicis: se rem omnem probè tenere: illum, si operam sibi dare velit, intellecturum. Deinde refpondětem interpellans, Tu, ait, ne obliuiscaris eorum quæ dicturus eras : &, Factum bene quod in memoriam revocasti : &, Quàm iuuat interdum sermones mutuos serere!&, Quod præterij : &, Celeriter tu quidem rem percepisti : &, Pridem expectabam an eodem mecum recideres : aliasq; huiusmodi occasiones loquendi captās, ne respirare quidem eos sinit, quibuscum loquitur. Ac postquā singuli sunt ab eo ita enecti, tum ad eos accedere non veretur, qui plures vna coierunt, eosque de rebus seriis agentes, in fugam vertere. units.tr: Garrulity, if anyone wishes to define it, would seem to be an intemperance of speech. The garrulous man is one who, whenever someone is speaking, is sure to say, whatever the other has begun to relate: "You say nothing; I know the whole matter well; if you wish to give me your attention, I will understand it." Then, interrupting the one who answers, he says: "Do not forget what you were about to say"; "Well done for reminding me"; "How pleasant it is sometimes to exchange conversation!"; "What you passed over"; "You have grasped the matter quickly"; "I was waiting a long time to see whether you would fall into the same thing as I did." He seizes other such occasions for talking, so that he does not even let those he is speaking with draw breath. And when he has worn out each one singly, he does not hesitate to approach those who have gathered in a group and are discussing serious matters, and to put them to flight. Moreover, when he enters the games and the wrestling-grounds, he so far from restraining the boys that he even urges them on to learn so much; he talks to the trainers and the teachers; and those who say they are leaving he escorts out and brings back home. And when he has learned of the assemblies, he reports them; he also recounts the story, which is commonly told, of the rhetorician Aristophon's brawl, and of the Lacedaemonians' battle under Lysander; and whatever speech he himself once made in the assembly, and rejected there, he recites. While narrating these things he is at the same time pouring himself out upon the crowd, and with such weariness of the hearers that one forgets at once what he says, another dozes off, another leaves while he is still speaking. In short, if he sits beside someone to judge, he will hinder him from judging; if he sits to watch, from watching; if he sits down to eat, he will prevent the one reclining beside him from eating. For, he says, it is hard for the garrulous man to be silent: he has his tongue as it were in water, and so he would rather seem more chattering than any swallow, and he endures being mocked, even by his little servants, who, when they want to sleep, bid him tell them something and talk on, so that, as they say, sleep may creep upon them.

units.la: verba interea cū corporum exercitatoribus seu pædotribis,& ludimagiftris funditās. Si quis discedere se velle dicat,comitari ille,& domū vsq; deducere ac persequi. Si forte quid fit in cōcione actum refcierit, id aliis postea narrabit:tū de eo prælio quod prætore Aristophonte nobili illo oratore commissum est, longā narratione contexitē, de ea pugna quæ à Lacedæmoniis duce Lysandro est pugnata: & si quid ipse vnquā pro cōcione cum aliqua sua laude dixerit. Atque hæc narrans, simul in vulgus inuehetur:idq; tāto cum audiētium tædio, vt corū alius quæ ab ipso dicuntur obliuioni statim mandet, alius dormitet, alius loquentem adhuc deferat, discedatque. Denique siue ad iudicandum cum alio sedeat, iudicare: siue ad spectandū, spectare:siue ad cibum sumēdum, cibum sumere cōsessorem impediet. Quippe, inquit, loquaci durum est tacere:linguam enim tāquam in udo habet:atq; adeo præ quauis hirundine garrulus videri malit,quàm tacere: adeo se irrideri fert patiētur:idq; vel à puerulis suis, qui somnū petituri iubeant ipsum aliquid sibi narrantem, verba facere:vt ita nobis,inquiunt,somnus obrepat.
units.tr: Such a man's speech, when he is with the trainers of bodies or with the schoolmasters, is poured out in the same way. If anyone says he wishes to leave, he follows him, escorts him home, and pursues him. If he happens to learn what was done in the assembly, he will afterwards tell it to others, weaving in a long narrative of the battle fought under the praetor Aristophon, the noble orator, and of the battle the Lacedaemonians fought under their commander Lysander, and of whatever speech he himself once made in the assembly with some credit to himself. In telling these things he at the same time rails at the common people, to the great weariness of his hearers, so that one of them at once forgets what he is saying, another dozes off, and another, still addressed, takes his leave and goes away. Finally, if he sits beside someone to judge, he judges; if to watch, he watches; if to eat, he hinders his fellow-diner from eating. For, he says, it is hard for a talkative man to keep silent: his tongue is, as it were, always wet, and so he would rather be thought more garrulous than any swallow than hold his peace; he suffers himself to be laughed at, even by his little boys, who, when they are about to sleep, bid him say something to them, so that, as they put it, sleep may creep upon us.
ON RUMOUR-MONGERING, or the fabrication of rumours.

units.la: ΗΔΕ λογοποιία, ἔστι σύνθεσις ψευδῶν λόγων καὶ πραξέων, ὧν ἐβάλ-[?] ταχ ὁ λογοποιῶν. ὁ ἡ λογοποιὸς, τοιοῦτός τις οἷ ὑπωπτήσας τῷ φίλῳ, ἀδὺς καταξαλῶν τὸ ἦθ[?] καὶ μεισλάσας, ἐρωτήσας, πόθεν σὺ, καὶ πῶ λέγεις; καὶ ἔχεις ὥδε τῆδε εἰπεῖν καινόν; καὶ ὑπεξαλῶν ἐρωτᾶν, μὴ λέγεταί τι καινότερον; καὶ μὲν ἀγαθὸ ὡς ὅτι τὰ λεγόμενα. καὶ οὐκ ἐάσας ἀποκρίνασθαι, εἶπεν, τί λέγεις; οὐδὲν ἀκήκοας; ἀδικῶ μοι σὲ ἀδωχήσθην καινῶν λόγων. καὶ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ ἡ σεαπωτὴς, ἡ παῖς Ασέως τῇ αὐλητῇ, ἡ Λύκων ὁ ἐργολάβος ωθαγοροῦς ἐξ αὐτῆς τ' μάχης, οὗ φησὶν ἀκηκοέναι. αἱ μὲν οὖν ἀναφοραὶ τῶν λόγων τοιαῦταί εἰσιν gentis constitio. Famigrator autem is est qui obuius amico factus, statim mutato vultu ac renidens, interroget, Vnde tu, & quid ais? &, Habésne super hoc noui quicquâ? & pergens interrogare, Nihilne, inquit, noui dicitur? atqui fausta fanè sunt & læta, quæ vulgò narrantur: tum autem prius quàm ille respondeat, Quid ais, inquit, nihilaudiuisti? Ergo ego te, sicut video, rerũ nouarum epulis lautè excipiam. Ac statim est illi aut miles aliquis, aut Astei [?] tibicinis puer, aut manceps Lyco qui ex ipso prælio sit reuersus, à quo se dicat audiisse: autores siquidē ille tales eorumque dictitat profert, quos nemo queat arguere.Refert autē accepisse se ab illis, Polysperchontem cum rege hostes prælio fudisse, & superasse: Cassandrúmque vivum in hostium potestatē venisse. Quod si quis ei dicat, Tu autē hæc credis? Imò,inquiet: rē enim clarissima omniū voce tota urbe ferri: rumorem crescere: omnes congruere: eadem enim de prælio ab omnibus narrari: magnum nimirum ea pugna fartū[?] esse factum. Idque se ex eorum etiam vultu, qui rem gerunt publicā,colligere:quem viderit ipsis penitus immutatū. Addit deinde se inaudisse quendam qui ex Macedonia aduenerit,quíque omnibus quæ gesta sunt interfuerit , quintū iam diem ab illis domi ocαὐτ᾽, ὧν ᾔδεις ἂν ἐ-χοι ὅπλα θέσθαι. διη-γῆται ἢ τούτοις φά-σκων λέγην[?], ὡς Πολυ-ἀπέρχων καὶ ὁ Βασι-λεὺς μάχῃ νενίκη-κε, καὶ Κασανδρος ἐ-ζώγρηνταη. καὶ εἴπῃ τὶς αὐτῷ, σὺ ἢ ταῦτα πιστεύῃς; φήσῃ· τὸ πεῖσμα ἐόαδς[?] ἢ ἐν τῇ πόλει, ἢ τὸν λόγον ἐπευλεῖνειν[?], καὶ πάντα ἢ συμφωνεῖν. ταῦτα λέγειν ὡς ἢ μάχης, ἢ πολιῶ τ᾽ ζωμὸν γεγονέναι. εἴ ἢ αὐ-τῷ ⊂ σημεῖον τὰ πρό-σωπα τ᾽ ἐν τοῖς πεφ-γμασιν· ὁρᾶν ἢ αὐτ[?] πάντων μεταξελλη-κοτα. λέγα δ᾽ ὡς καὶ ἀπ[?]ηκοε παρὰ τὸ τοῖς κρυπτομένων πινα ἐν οἰκία, ἡ δηπάμπλω ἡμέρας ἤκουλα ἐκ Μακεδονίας, ὃς πάντα ταῦτα εἶδε. καὶ πάντα διεξιὼν, πῶς οἴεσθε; πιθανῶς ξειλιάζει. λέγων, Δυσυχὴς Κάσανδρος! ὦ ἀλαίπω- ρῷ! ἐνθυμὴ τὸ τῆς τύχης· ἀλλ' οὐ ὡς ἰχυ- ες ἡ γυρόμεθα. Ἐ, δεῖ δὲ {*}αὐτὸ σε μό- νον εἰδέναι. πᾶσι δὲ τοῖς ἐν τῇ πόλει πρὸς- δεδραμηκὸς λέγων. τῶν τοιούτων ἀνθρώ- πων τεθαύμακα ἡ ποτε βάλλονται λο- γοποιοῦντες. ἐ γὰ μό- νον Ψοδονταις, ἀλ- λὰ Ἐ ἀλυσιπελῶς ἀ- παλλάττεσι. πολλάκις γὰρ αὐτῶν οἱ μὲν ἐν τοῖς βαλανείοις ὠφελ- σάσης πεπιμῳοι, Τὰ ἱμάτια ἀποβεβλήκα- [illegible, ~12 letters] cultari. Atque vbi hæc commemoravit, miserationes adiicit: at scin quomodo? sanè quā persuasibiliter. O infelicem, inquiens, Cassandrũ! O virum ærumnosum! En Fortuna quid possit. at fuit certè Cassander præpotens. Tu verò, ait, tacitus hoc tecũ habeto: ipse autem ad civium unumquemque accurrit, ut ei omnia narret. Equidem mirari soleo quid sibi homines hoc genus falsis rumoribus fingendis spargendisq; velint: quæ res, ut taceam medacij turpitudinem, non raro ipsis incommoda cuenit. Factum enim sæpe, ut dum isti in balneis cocursus facerent, vestes interea suas furto amitterēt: alij dum in porticu aut pedestri aut nauali prælio vincunt, quòd vadimonium non stitissent, graviter multati sunt. Quibusdam etiam, dum urbes verbis suis fortiter caperent, cœna interea loci periit. Enim vero misera est istorum vita & conditio: nā quæ porticus est, quæ officina, quæ fori pars, in qua dies non traducant integros, magno cum audientium quos falsis suis narrationibus obtundunt, tædio?
units.tr: Rumour-mongering is the invention of false reports and stories. The rumour-monger is the sort of man who, meeting a friend, puts on a sly and sudden look and asks: "Where have you come from? Where are you going? Have you got any fresh news about this?" Then, pressing on, he asks: "Nothing new is being said? Yet what is commonly reported is surely good and cheerful." Before the other can answer, he cries: "What do you mean? Have you heard nothing? I'm sorry for you; I can see you've been left out of the feast of new tidings, and I'll give you a good dinner of it." At once he has some soldier, or the boy of Asteius the flute-player, or Lyco the contractor, who has just come back from the battle itself, and from whom he says he heard it. He always produces such authorities, the sort nobody can refute. He reports that he had it from them that Polysperchon and the king had routed the enemy in battle and won the day, and that Cassander had been taken alive into enemy hands. If someone says to him, "Do you really believe this?" he replies: "Of course! It is the most certain thing in the world; the whole city is saying it in one voice. The rumour grows, everyone agrees, for everyone tells the same story of the battle. It must have been a great victory indeed. I can tell it from the faces of those who run the public business: they are utterly changed, as anyone can see." Then he adds that he heard from a man who has just arrived from Macedonia, who was present at everything that happened, and who has been hidden at home these five days. Going through it all, how do you think he behaves? He is wonderfully persuasive. "Unlucky Cassander!" he says, "Poor fellow! Think of the turn of fortune! But you must keep this to yourself alone." Then he runs off to all the people in the city to tell each of them. I have often marvelled at what such men want with inventing and spreading these lies. Not to mention the shamefulness of the falsehood, it often does them no small harm. It has often happened that while these men were busy with their crowds at the baths, their clothes were stolen in the meantime; others, while they were winning battles by land or sea in the colonnade, failed to appear in court and were heavily fined. Some, while they were storming cities with their words, lost their dinner in the meantime. Indeed, the life and condition of such people is wretched: what colonnade, what workshop, what part of the forum is there in which they do not spend whole days, to the great weariness of the hearers whom they wear out with their false tales?
