Quando obsonatur, laniū meminisse iubet, si ulla unquam in re fuerit de eo bene meritus: deinde autē trutinæ assistens, principio quidem carnes: sed si id nō possit, os saltem aliquod in lancem iniiciet: quod si auferre queat, id optimè: si non, tum ille è mensa vel aliquod intestinorum frustum rapiet, & cum risu discedet. Jam si peregrinis apud se diuertētibus locū in theatro ad spectandum standū emerit,ipse quoque nullo pro capite suo dato ære spectatum venict. quinctiam liberos suos cū pædagogo cōdem secum postero die ducere non dubitabit.
units.tr: ...going to him to borrow. Then, after sacrificing to the gods, he himself dines at another man's house. He calls his attendant over and, with everyone listening, takes a piece of meat and bread from the table and says, "Eat heartily, my good man." When he buys provisions, he tells the butcher to remember him if ever he has done him a good turn. Then, standing by the scales, he first tries to slip in some meat, or if he cannot, at least a bone, into the pan; and if he can carry it off, all the better. If not, he takes a piece of entrails from the table and leaves laughing. When he has bought a seat in the theatre to watch the show, though visitors are staying with him, he comes to the performance without paying anything for his own head. Moreover, he does not hesitate to bring his children, with their tutor, along with him the next day.

units.la: Quæcūque autem paruo empta ferentem aliquem viderit,sibi quoq; cōmunicari iubebit. Et vbi ad ædes alienas venerit, vel ordeum, vel si vsus ita tulerit paleam mutuaturus,cos coget à quibus acceperit , id quod dederint domum sibi apportare. Sæpe etiā in balneis ad æna accedens postquam arytænā mersam repleuit, sese ipse,nō sine magno bal-ἀγὰν ἢ ἑ τοὺς εἰς τὴν ὑσεραίαν, ἡ τὸν παιδαγωγόν. ἡ ὅστις ἐωνημένῳ· ἀξιά τις φέρει, μεταδοῦναι πελεῦσαι ἔ αὐτ᾽. ἔ ὅτι ἡ ἀλλοτρίαν οἰκίαν ἐλθὼν, δανείσας κείθας, ᾧ τοῖ ἀχρεῖον ἐ ταῦτα χρήσας, ἀναγκάσαι ἀποφέρειν πρὸς αὐτόν. ἁμνὸς ἢ ἐ πρὸς τὰ χαλκία ἃ ἐν τῷ βαλανέῳ προσελθὼν, καὶ βάψας ἀρύταιναν, βοῶντ᾽ τῷ βαλανέως, {*}αὐτὸς * αὐτῇ καταχέασαι, ἐ εἰπεῖν, ὅτι λέλουταί ἀπὼν· χάρει, ἡδέα σοι χαρεῖς.
units.tr: Whatever he sees someone carrying home after buying it cheaply, he orders to be shared with himself too. And when he goes to other people's houses to borrow barley, or chaff if that is what he needs, he makes those from whom he borrowed carry what they gave him to his own house. Often too, in the baths, he goes up to the cauldrons, dips in a ladle, and fills it, and then, not without great shouting from the bath attendant, pours it over himself.

units.la: neatoris clamore, perfundit: dein discedens, Laui, inquit: & ad balneatorem conversus, Ego verò, ait, gratiam tibi nullam.
units.tr: ...the bath attendant's shouting; then, as he leaves, he says, "I have bathed," and turning to the bath attendant, he says, "I give you no thanks at all."

units.la: Ἡ δὲ μικρολογία ὅτι φειδωλία ἢ δυσφόρως [?] τὸν καιρόν. ὁ ἢ μικρολόγος, τοιοῦτός τις οἰ ἐν τῷ μέλλει ἡμωξεόλιον ἀπαγῆρ ὅτι τὸν οἰκίαν, καὶ συσιπῶν ἀειθμεῖν πόσας κύλικας ἐκα-στον {*}πέπωκε.
units.tr: Pettiness is a kind of stinginess, or a grudging spending on trifles. The petty man is the sort who, when he is about to entertain, goes to the market and buys a half-obol's worth of something for the house, and sits there counting how many cups each of his guests has drunk.

units.la: ἀπαρχέας ἐλάχισον τῇ Ἀρτέμιδι τῶν σωδλειπωνουμένων. καὶ ὅσα μικρὰ τῆς ψειά-μίμυ λογίζεται, πᾶν τὰ φάσκειν ἐᾶν. καὶ οἰκέτης χύτεαν ἢ λοπάδα καταξαύλος, εἰς ψεαξαι ἀπὸ τῶν ὀπτηδείων.
units.tr: He makes a small offering of first-fruits to Artemis from what is left over, and whatever is trivial he reckons up, forbidding anyone to say that it is nothing. When a slave breaks a jug or a dish, he deducts it from the cost of the food.

units.la: Sordida parsimonia est studium parcēdi sumptibus ultra modū. [illegible, ~8 letters] Sordidè parcus is erit[?], qui à sodalibus apud se coniuia agitare solitis tanquam pro menstrua domus pensione semiobolum exigat: & in conuiuio quot quisque calices educat, numeret: qui etiam ex omnibus conuiuis Dianæ minima libamenta offerat. Iam quæcunque ei quispiam fert impensa, etsi paruo empta, nimio tamen constare dicet. Si famulus ollam aut patinam fregerit, de eius demenso tantum detrahet, quanti erat quod fractum est. Quòd si vxor trichalcum amiserit, ille verò omnem suppelle[?] supellectilem, lectos etiam, atque capsas loco mouebit, & omnia stragula scrutabitur. Quicquid vendit tanti vendit, vt ea res emptori cedere bono non queat. Ficum de suo horto neminē gustare siuerit: neminē per fundum suum trāsire:aut vllam cadivam oliuam, palmulāve auferre. quotidie terminos inspectat suos, ecquid immoti eodem loco iidem maneāt. Porrò autem debitum si quis die praestituta non soluerit, poenā pro mora,atque adeo vsurae vsuram solet exigere. Populares conuiuio accipiens, minutas apponet carnes: quumque ad obsonandum exierit,sæpe vacuus domū reuertetur. Vxori iolet[?] edicere ne cuiquam salem[?] aut ellychnium, ἐὰν τι πωλῇ, τοσά-τε ἀποδόσῳ ὥσπε μὴ λυσιτελεῖν τῷ πεια-μένῳ. ἢ οὐκ ἂν ἐά-σαι ἢ τε συνοτεραγή-σαι ὀν τῇ αὐτῇ κή-πῳ, ἢ τε ἀλλὰ δ' αὐ-τῆς ἀργῆς φορουθῆ-ναι, ἢ τε ἐλάαν ἡ φοί-νικα τῶν χαμαὶ πε-πτωκότων ἀνελέσθ. ἢ τοὺς ὄρους ἢ ὅπι-σκοπεῖσθαι ὀσημέραι, εἰ ἀχμώνυσιν οἱ αὐ-τοί. ὀξνὸς ἢ ἢ ὑπερ-μερίαν πράξαι, καὶ τόκον τόκῳ· ἢ ἐσιῶν δημότας, μικρὰ ἂ κρέα κόψας ὠμὰ ἀθεί-ναι· ἢ ὀψωνῶν, μηδὲν πειράμενος εἰσελθεῖν. ἢ ἀπορρόσαι τὴν γυ-ναικὶ μήτε ἄλας ἔχων νύξ, μήτε ἐλλύχνιον, μήτε κύμινον, μήτε ὀρίγανον, μήτε λὰς, μήτε σέμμα[?] μήτε Θυνλήμα[?] ἀλλὰ λέγλν ὅτι μικρὰ ζῶντα πολ[?] ὃξι τῦ ἑαυτῦ. τὸ ὅλον δὲ, τῶν μ[?] κρολόγων καὶ τ[?] ἀγυροθήκας ὅξι[?] δεῖν σὐρωπώσας [?] κλεῖς ἰωμῦας. αὐτοὺς δὲ φορουῶ[?] ἰλάττω τῶν μικρ[?] τὰ ἰμάπα, ἢ ἐκ [?] ξυδίων μικρῶν π[?] ἀλειφομύοις, καὶ [?] χεῶ χειρομύοις, τὸ μέσον τῆς ἡμέ[?] ὑπολυομύοις, πρὸς τοὺς γναφεῖς [?] τεινομύοις, ὅπως ἱμάπιον αὐτοῖς ἐ[?] πολλὰ γλῶ, ἵνα ῥυπαίνηται ζαχ[?]. τε ῖ- [?] ᾶ [?] ῖ, [?] ᾧ [?] λά [?] ται [?] ῶ- [?] ἀς [?] ῖ- [?] ται [?] ῶς [?] ῶν [?] λῶ- [?] ἴνυ [?] ἐν [?] ᾧ [?] ας [?] καὶ [?] ἄξ [?] τὸ [?] ἔξει [?] μὴ [?] aut cyminum, aut origanum, vel etiam farris quicquam, vel corollam ullam, vel libum ullum commodet: Magnam enim, inquit, parua hæc tandem in anno summam efficiunt. In summa, fordidorum iftorum hominum loculos videas fitu obfitos, claues ferrugine illitas. Ipfos quinetiam videre licet veftes geftare intra quâ modicas: guttulos ex quibus unguantur paruulos habere: capite effe, ad cutem vsque attonfo: calceos medio die exuere: &cum fullonibus obnixè agere, vt ad poliendam fuam veftem, cretæ multum adhibeant, ne fordes facilè contrahat.
units.tr: Sordid parsimony is an eagerness to save expense beyond what is reasonable. The sordidly thrifty man is one who demands half an obol from his companions, who are accustomed to hold dinner parties at his house, as if it were a monthly rent for the house. At the dinner he counts how many cups each man drinks. He also offers the smallest possible portions to Diana from every dinner. Whatever expense anyone incurs for him, he says it costs too much, even if it was bought cheaply. If a servant breaks a pot or a dish, he deducts from the servant's allowance the exact price of what was broken. If his wife loses a bronze coin, he moves all the furniture, even the beds and the chests, and searches every blanket. Whatever he sells, he sells at such a price that the buyer cannot profit from it. He will not allow anyone to taste a fig from his garden, or to pass through his land, or to take away a single fallen olive or date. Every day he inspects his boundary stones to see whether they still stand in the same place. If anyone fails to pay a debt on the day set, he usually exacts a penalty for the delay, and even interest on the interest. When he entertains his fellow citizens at dinner, he serves meat cut into tiny pieces. When he has gone out to buy provisions, he often returns home empty-handed. He instructs his wife not to lend salt, or a lamp wick, to anyone. "If she sells anything," he says, "let her sell it at such a price that the buyer gets no profit." Or he forbids her to let anyone gather up a fallen olive or a date from under the tree in the same garden, or to lend cumin, or marjoram, or any flour, or any garland, or any cake. "For these small things," he says, "add up to a large sum over a year." In short, you may see the purses of such sordid men mouldy and their keys smeared with rust. You may also see them wearing clothes that are only moderately good, keeping small flasks of ointment for their children, going with their heads shaved close to the skin, taking off their shoes in the middle of the day, and hard at work with the fullers, insisting that they use a great deal of chalk to polish their clothes, so that they do not easily collect dirt.

units.la: Impuritatem vero definire non est difficile: Est siquidem iocus ludúsve evidens nimis ac flagitiosus. Impurus vero is est qui si in liberas mulieres incidat, veste subducta pudenda illis ostendat. In theatro reliquis tacentibus, ipse plaudit: & quos alij libenter spectant, ipse sibilis consectatur: & toto theatro ad spectandum intento, ipse resupinato corpore ruɶtat[?], ut qui sedent oculos avertere necesse habeant. Ac quando maximè frequens est forum, ad nuces, mala, & [illegible, ~10 letters]
units.tr: It is not difficult to define impurity: it is a joke or a game that is too plainly shameful and disgraceful. The impure man is one who, if he meets free women, lifts his clothing and shows them his private parts. In the theatre, when the others are silent, he claps; and whatever others gladly watch, he hisses at. And when the whole theatre is intent on the spectacle, he lies back and stretches himself, so that those seated must avert their eyes. And when the marketplace is most crowded, he goes to the stalls of nuts, apples, and [illegible].

units.la: Οὐ χαλεπὸν ἢ[?] ὅξι[?] τ' ἐλλυ-ρίαν ὁρίσασθαι, ἔσ[illegible, ~8 letters] & reliquos omnis generis fructus accedens, ibíque stans, de iis comeπαιδία ἐπιφανὴς καὶ ἐπονείδιστος. ὁ δὲ ἐδελ-λυερὸς, τοιοῦτ[?] οἷος ὑπαντήσας γνωαξειν ἐλευθέρας, ἀναου-ειαμψῷ[?] δεῖξαι τὸ αἰδῶον. καὶ ἐν θεάτρῳ κεοῖεῖν, ὅταν οἱ ἄλ-λοι παυωνται,
units.tr: It is not difficult to define offensiveness: it is a conspicuous and reproachful buffoonery. The offensive man is such that, when he meets a free woman, he lifts his clothing and shows her his private parts. And in the theatre, when the others fall silent,
he belches, to the annoyance of those who gladly watch the spectacle.

units.la: ὅταν σιωπήσῃ τὸ θέα-τρον, ἀναχυψας ἐρυ-γεῖν, ἵνα τοῖς καθη-μένοις ποιήσῃ μετα-σεαφῶν.
units.tr: When the theatre falls silent, he leans back and belches, so that those who are seated are put to shame.

units.la: πληθύ-σης ἢ ἀγορᾶς προσ-ελθὼν πρὸς ἃ πά-ρυα, ἢ ἃ μῆλα, ἢ τὰ ἀκεόδρυα, ἐσηκὼς τεαχημαπίζεσ[?] ἅμα τὰ πωλούντων πρὸς[?] λαλῶν.¶ καλέσαι ἢ τῶν παιδίοντων[?] ὀνομα-σί τινα, ᾧ μὴ σωνήθης ὄσί.¶ ἀποδόντα δὲ πᾶν ὁρῶν, ἔφη μεῖναι[?] κελοῦσαι.¶ ἡπλαμέ-νῳ ᾧ μεγάλῳ δίκῃ ἀπόντ᾽ ἀπὸ τὴν δικα-στηρίου περιστελθεῖν,¶ συνηθλιῶαι,¶ ὀφω-νεῖν ἑαυτὸν,¶ ὠλη-τσίδας μισθᾶς.¶ δεικνύειν ᾧ τοῖς ἅπαν-τῶν τε ὠφωνημένα, καὶ ἀπαγαλὸν ὅπ ταῦτα.¶ διηγέας προσάς προς κυρέων, ἡμυρπώλιον, ὅπ με-θύσκεως μέλλ.¶ οἱ-νοπωλῶν, κεκραμέ-νον ἡ οἶνον τῷ φίλῳ ἀποδόας.¶ ὅπ δὲαν ἡνίκα ἀν δὴ πορδε-δαι, ἀπῶν τοὺς ἡμεῖς, dit, fermones interea cū eorum venditore ferens.
units.tr: When the market is crowded, he goes up to the stalls of pears, apples, or wild fruits, and stands there chattering with the sellers. He calls some of the boys by names they do not know. Seeing someone sell something, he orders him to wait. When he has lost a great lawsuit and is coming back from the court, he goes round to his friends; he hires flute-girls for a dinner; he shows the fine things he has bought to everyone; he gives away a cake to a friend who is out walking; he sells wine, and gives his friend it mixed with water. Whenever he is ready to go somewhere, he leaves behind those who are with him and carries on conversations with the wine-seller.

units.la: Non etiam dubitat prætereuntium aliquem, nulla sibi familiaritate iunctum, nominatim cōpellare: & si quē aliquo properantem videat, iubebit expectare. Solet etiam ad eum qui in grādis pecuniæ iudicio causa ceciderit, redeuntem è iudicio accedere, & ei gratulari: quūq; [?] sibi opsonia emerit, & tibicinas cōduxerit, vt cuiq; obuius fuerit fastus, obsonia illi oftēdere, & ad ea inuitare. idemq; ad tonstrinam aut tabernam vnguentariā astans, narrat velle se mox ad ebrietatem vsq; bibere. Vinum vendens, etiam amico dilutum dabit. Ad ludos, quādo maxime spectandum est, liberos suos ire non finit: tunc finit, quando gratis per theatrorum redemptores licet spectare. Cū legatus peregrè proficiscitur,relicto domi viatico quod publicè accepit,à legationis sociis mutuò rogabit. Moris etiam habet famulum itineris comitē, onerare quidem sarcinis supra modum,victū verò ei suppeditare angustè nimis & infra modū. Lautia si cum aliis acceperit, suam portionem petet,vt eam statim vēdat. In balneis lauans , puerulo appellato , Nam hercule tu , inquit, oleum nimis rancidum mercatus es : & simul alieno se inūgit. Quòd si quos pueri nummos æreos, vt fit, in via repererint , partē inde sibi poscet, illud vsurpās, Mercurium esse commu[illegible, ~12 letters] ne. Eiusdem[?] hominis sunt hæc quoque. Phidonia
units.tr: He does not hesitate to call out to some passer-by, with whom he has no acquaintance, by name; and if he sees someone hurrying somewhere, he tells him to wait. He is also accustomed to approach a man who has lost a large sum of money in a lawsuit as he returns from court, and to congratulate him. When he has bought provisions and hired flute-girls, he shows the provisions to whoever he meets, and invites them to the feast. Likewise, standing at the barber's or at the perfumer's shop, he says that he means to drink until he is drunk. When he sells wine, he gives even his friend a diluted measure. He does not let his children go to the games when the crowd is most eager to watch, but he allows it when they may watch free of charge through the contractors of the theatres. When he travels abroad on an embassy, he leaves at home the travel allowance he received from the state, and borrows from his fellow envoys. He also makes a habit of loading his servant who accompanies him on the journey with baggage beyond his strength, while giving him food that is far too meagre and below what is sufficient. If he receives a share of the public dinners with others, he asks for his portion so that he can sell it at once. When he bathes, he calls to a little slave boy, "By Hercules, you have bought oil that is far too rancid," and at the same time he anoints himself with another man's oil. If boys find some bronze coins on the road, as happens, he demands a share of them, claiming them as if they were offerings to Mercury. Of the same man are also these things: when the theatre-contractors release the crowd, he gives his slave a ticket... and when he is abroad on public business, he leaves the travel money from the city at home, and borrows from his fellow envoys. He also places on his servants a load greater than they can carry, and gives them too little food for their needs. He sells whatever he receives from the guest-hospitality. When he anoints himself in the bath and says, "You have bought rancid oil," to the slave boy, he anoints himself with another's oil. When he carries coins on the road, the slaves who come upon them demand a share, and he calls it common property of Hermes. Of the same kind are these: he measures out for the boy, in a Pheidonian measure, the food for the household, and is greatly concerned. If he gives back thirty minas of a debt, he pays back less than four drachmas. When he enters the theatre, he asks everyone for a share of the common meal. He also takes under the table half the radishes, so that the serving boys do not get them.

units.la: ἡνίκα πεζῇκα ἀφια- σιν οἱ θεατρῶναι. καὶ ἀποδημῶν δημοσίᾳ, τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἐφόδιον οἴκοι καταλιπεῖν, ὥσπερ ἡ τῶν συμπρεσβευτῶν δανείζειν. καὶ τὰς ἀκολάσθω δῶπιθεῖναι μείζον φορτίον ἢ δυνάμει φέρειν, καὶ ἐλάσσω δῶπιδεία τ' ἱκανῶν. καὶ ὅπο τ' ξενίων τὸ μέρ[?]ος. Τὸ ὠπὶ ἀπαντήσας ἀποδόσθω. καὶ ἀλειφόμενος ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ, καὶ εἰπὼν, σαπρόν τὸ ἔλαιον ἐπρίω, τῷ παιδαρίῳ· τῷ ἀλλοτρίῳ ἀλείφεσθω. καὶ τὸ δὲ εισκομιζῶν χαλκῶν ἐν τ' ὁδοῖς ὑπὸ τ' οἰκετῶν δύνος ἀπαντήσας τὸ μέρος, κοινὸν εἴφησας τὸν Ἑρμῆν. τὰ δὲ ἢ τοιαῦτα· Φειδωνίῳ μέτρῳ τὸν παῖδα [?] ἐκκεκομψμένῳ με-τρεῖν αὐτὸς τοῖς ἔνδον ἀδηδείᾳ, σφόδρα [?] ὑπολῶν, ὑποωρία-ας. ἀμέλη ὃ ἢ χρέος ὑποδιδῷς τριακοντα μῶν, ἐλάττον τέτρα-σι δραχμαὶς ὑποδι-δόναι. Ὁ φεάτορας ἐσιῶν, αἰτεῖν τοῖς αὐ-τ πασὶν ἐκ τῆς κοι-νῆς ὄψον. τὰ ἡ κατα-λεπέμβυα ὑπὸ τῆς τεαπέζης ἡμίσον τῶν ῥαφανίδων ὑπογρά-φειαν, ἵνα οἱ διάκο-νοιοῦντες παῖδες μὴ λάβωσιν.
units.tr: When the theatre is emptied, he... (Greek passage garbled in the scan; the sense: when the spectacle is over he leaves the money for the public ... and when abroad on public business he keeps the travel allowance from the city at home, and borrows from his fellow envoys; he loads his servants beyond their strength and feeds them too meagrely; when he bathes he tells the slave that the oil is rancid and anoints himself with another man's oil; he claims for Hermes the coins found on the road.)

units.la: ΗΜΕΝ οὖν ἀ-καιρία, ἔστιν ἐmenfura si quid metiatur,eam adhibet,cuiius fit fundum collisum & introrsus adactum: domesticis suis demensum ipse per quàm studiosè radès metitur ..... & si triginta minas folucre habeat, vt quatuor tamen drachmæ de solido desiderentur, operam dabit. quando etiam tribuleis conuiuio accipit, solet pueris suis obsonia è communi postulare: dimidiatos verò raphanos, si qui forte de mensa tollantur, annotat, ne eos pueri ministrantes capiant.
units.tr: Untimeliness is, if he measures anything out, to use the measure that has been bored through and driven inward. He measures out for his household himself, and most diligently. If he has thirty minas to pay and four drachmas are still wanting to make the full sum, he will take the trouble to find them. When he receives friends at a dinner, he usually asks his slaves for side dishes from the common supply. Any half radishes that happen to be taken from the table he notes down, so that the serving boys do not get them.
On Intempestivity, or Ignorance of Timing.

units.la: Intempestivitas est congressio molesta iis quibuscum congrediaris.
units.tr: Intempestivity is an unwelcome intrusion upon those with whom you are dealing.

units.la: Homo autem intempestiuus is est, qui ad amicũ occupatum accedēs, velit rē cōmunicata cum illo deliberare: quíq; ad amicam suam febri laborantem veniat comessatum. Solet etiam cum qui jam ante fuerit ex sponsu cōdemnatus adire, rogas ut pro se quoque intercedere velit. & ad dicendum testimonium tunc venit quum res est iudicata: ad nuptias vocatus, in mulierum genus invehitur. Eos qui e longinquo itinere modō advenerint, ad deambulandum secum invitat: rē jam vēdita emptorem adducit qui pluris sit empturus. Sepe etiam e medio hominum sibi affidentium surgit, ut rē illis orsus a capite exponat, qua omnes jam audiverint ac pernorint: & ὁ δ [illegible, ~12 letters] τόξ [illegible, ~12 letters] λε [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀν [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀρ [illegible, ~12 letters] μὴ [illegible, ~12 letters] ρέ [illegible, ~12 letters] ὥφ [illegible, ~12 letters] ὡς [illegible, ~12 letters] ᾳ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐκ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐπ [illegible, ~12 letters] δὲ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐξ [illegible, ~12 letters] πρ [illegible, ~12 letters] κα [illegible, ~12 letters] νπ [illegible, ~12 letters] τα [illegible, ~12 letters] η. units.tr: The intempestive man is one who, going to a friend who is busy, wants to discuss business with him, or who goes to his girlfriend while she is ill with fever in order to join a drinking party. He is also in the habit of approaching someone already condemned in a suit over a surety, and asking him to intercede for him as well. He comes to give evidence when the case has already been decided. Invited to a wedding, he rails against the female sex. To those who have just arrived from a long journey he proposes a walk. When the goods are already sold, he brings along a buyer who would have paid more. Often, too, he gets up from among people who are sitting with him, to set out the matter from the beginning, though everyone has already heard it and knows it by heart. He goes to someone who is in a hurry and holds him up with long talk.

units.la: 4 προθύμῳ· δὲ ἐπι- μελη̃θῆναι ἃ μὴ βέ- λεταί τις ἡδέως, ἀι- χώεται[?] ἢ ἀπειπα- ϑαι. καὶ ϑύοντας καὶ ἀναλίσκοντας, ἥκων τόμον ἀπαιτήσων. ἐ- μαστιγουμένῳ οἰκέτου παρέσεως, ἀλλ' ἡγεῖ[?] ὅτι καὶ ὧς ποτε ταῖς οὕτω πληγὰς λαβὼν ἀπήγξατο. καὶ παρὼν διαίτῃ, συγκρύψῃ[?], ἀμφοτέ- ρων βουλομένων διαλύεσθαι. καὶ ὀρχησά- μενος ἀφαλλὰ[?] ἐ-ταῖς μηδὲ πω μυ-θούντων.
units.tr: Being eager to take up matters that someone would gladly not have touched, he is annoyed or refuses. When people are feasting and spending, he comes to demand back a debt. When a slave is being whipped, he is present, and says that the man who once received such blows also hanged himself. He is present at a dispute and tries to settle it, while both parties wish to have done with it. He dances and ... among those who have not yet begun to drink.

units.la: ἈΜΕΛΕΙ περι-εργία δ᾽ ἔξει ἐν περισποιήσεις τις λόγων καὶ πράξεων, quæ nollet quidem aliquis, sed denegare tamen erubescit, ad illa curanda, promptus est. Ad eos qui sacra faciunt & epulas concelebrant, accedit, vt aliquam inde partem auferat. Quòd si præsente eo famulus cædatur: sibi quoque puerum aliquando fuisse narrabit, qui similiter virgis cæsus se suspederit. Idé captus arbiter, duos litigantes quorū vterque rem transfigi optat, inter se cōmittet. Denique saltaturus socium manu prehendit, qui nōdum sit vino madidus.
units.tr: Officiousness is a kind of busy interest in words and deeds, which a man would not want, yet he is too ashamed to refuse and is quick to take them up. He approaches those who are offering sacrifices and holding feasts, so that he may carry off some portion from them. If a slave is beaten in his presence, he will say that he too once had a boy who, beaten in the same way with rods, hanged himself. Appointed as arbiter between two litigants, each of whom wishes the matter to be settled in his own favour, he will bring them together to settle it between themselves. Finally, when about to dance, he takes by the hand a companion who is not yet drunk with wine.

units.la: Περιεργία, (quâ liceat sedulitatem ineptâ dicere) est dictorū factorumq; simulatio cū significatione beneuolentiæ.
units.tr: Officiousness (which may be called foolish zeal) is the pretence of words and deeds with a show of goodwill.

units.la: Mores eiusmodi hominis ita sunt. Facilè surgēs è medio,in se recipit,quibus præstandis par nō sit: rem quæ omnium cōfessione iusta est, pluribus verbis,in aliquo inhærēs, docere instituit,nullo modo posse argui. Puerum vini amplius miscere cogitquàm quàtum omnes qui adsunt cōviuæ queat ebibere.Contendētes pugnantesq; invicem instigat. Solet etiam viâ præ-ire,quam ignoret ipse:cuius quidem exitum mox invenire nequeat: & ad ductorem exercitus accedens,rogare, ecquādo sit aciem ad dimicādum instructurus:necnō quid in perendinum diem imperet:& ad patrem veniens, En,inquit, mater in cubiculo jam dormit. Ac μετ' ἀνοίας. ὁ ἢ περίεργος, τοιοῦτός πις, οἷ ὦ ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι ἀνασὰς ἃ μὴ δυνήσεται. καὶ ὁμολογουμένως τῆς πραγματος δίκαιος εἴη ἐν τινι σὰς ἐλεγχθῆναι. καὶ πλέον ἐπαναλήψασθαι τὸν παῖδα κεφάσαι ἢ ὅσα δύνανται οἱ παιζοντες σκπιεῖν. καὶ λεγείρειν τοῖς μαχομένοις, καὶ ἢς ἃ γινώσκει ἀτεαῶς ἡ-γήσασθαι, εἶτα μὴ ἀδυνάσθαι δρεῖν ἔ παρδύεταί. ¶ τὸν ἑαυτὸν ὃ προσελθὼν ἐρωτῆσαι, ποτὲ μέλλει ἀποξαστεῖν, καὶ πὶ μὴ τῷ αὔριον ἀποξηλά.
units.tr: Such a man's habits are these. He readily gets up from the company and takes on tasks which he is not equal to performing. A matter which everyone agrees is just, he sets about explaining at great length, clinging to some point, and cannot be persuaded that he can be refuted. He orders the boy to mix more wine than all the guests at the banquet could drink. He stirs up those who are quarrelling and fighting. He is accustomed to go ahead on a road whose way he does not know himself, and cannot soon find its end. Approaching the commander of the army, he asks when he will draw up the battle line, and what he orders for the day after tomorrow. Coming to the father, he says, "Look, mother is already asleep in her room."

units.la: ¶ προσελθὼν τῷ πατρὶ εἰπεῖν, ὅτι ἡ μήτηρ ἤδη καθεύδει ἐν τῷ δωματίῳ. καὶ ἀπαγορεύοντῳ τῷ ἰατρῷ, ὅπως μὴ δύ-σῃ οἷον τῷ καλλω-πιζομένῳ[?], φήσας ἐκ-λεῖδαι[?] ἀφ᾽ [illegible, ~4 letters] λαμβάνειν, ὥστε-πίσαι τὸν κακῶς ἔ-χοντα. ἢ γυναικὸς ἢ πλουτήσαιο[?], ὅτι-ἱρεάλαι[?] ὅτι τὸ μυῆ-μα, τῆτε ἀνδρὸς αὐ-τῆς ἢ τῆ πατρὸς καὶ τῆς μητρὸς ἢ αὐτῆς τῆς γυναικὸς τοῦ-νομα, ᾧ ποταπὴ ὄζι.
units.tr: And when the doctor forbids the sick man wine, he invites him to drink, saying he wants to test him. If his wife has died, he inscribes on her monument the names of her husband, her father and mother, and of herself, together with her nationality, and adds that all of them were of excellent character.

units.la: καὶ προσεπιφέραι ὅτι ἢ τοι πάντες ζεν-σοί ἦσαν. καὶ ὁμύ-ναι μέλλων, εἰ φεῖν πρὸς τοὺς ᾧλεσηκό-τας, ὅτι καὶ πρότε-ρον πολλάκις ὁμώ-μοκα. quum vini vsum ægroto medicus interdixerit, solet hic illum quasi periculi faciendi causa ad bibendum cõponere. Quòd si vxor obierit, monumento eius & mariti & patris & matris, nomina inscriber,itémque cuias ipsa fit: tum hoc elogium insuper adiiciet, SINGVLARI OMNES ISTI PROBITATE ERANT. Idem si iusiurandum adigatur, conuersus ad circunstantem turbam, Ego verò, inquit, iam antè sæpius iuraui.
units.tr: And when the physician has forbidden a sick man the use of wine, he is wont to urge him to drink, as though to put it to the test. If his wife has died, he inscribes on her monument the names of her husband, her father and mother, and her own name, and of what country she is, and then adds this inscription: "ALL THESE WERE MEN OF SINGULAR UPRIGHTNESS." And if he is to be made to swear an oath, he turns to the bystanders and says, "But I have sworn many times before."

units.la: STupiditatem quoque definire, possis vt sit animi tarditas, seu dicendum, seu faciendum sit aliquid. Stupidus verò is est, qui sedens ad calculos postquam rationes putauit, & summâ subduxit, roget eū qui sibi assidet, Summa quāta est? Ac quū ei litem aliquis intenderit, vbi ad diem illum vētum est, quo disceptari causa debet, eius oblitus, in agrum proficiscitur. Sæpe etiam sedens in theatro ad spectandum, discedētibus aliis somno obrutus ibi relinquitur: quippe qui se ad multa noctem cibis ingurgitarit: ac tandem sede sua exsurgēs, in vicini canē incidit, à quo mordetur. Idem quod ac-
units.tr: Stupidity too may be defined as a slowness of mind, whether in speaking or in doing something. The stupid man is one who, sitting down to his counters, after he has reckoned up the accounts and totted up the sum, asks the man sitting beside him, "What is the total?" When someone has brought a lawsuit against him, and the day has come on which the case must be argued, he forgets it and goes off into the country. Often, too, when he is sitting in the theatre to watch a play, he is left behind there, overcome by sleep, while the others leave; for he has spent the night stuffing himself with food. And finally, rising from his seat, he runs into a neighbour's dog, by which he is bitten. He does the same thing also...

units.la: ΕΣΤΙ ἡ ἀ-ναισθησία, ὡς ὁ-ρῳ εἰπεῖν, βεβαρυτὴς ψυχῆς ἐν λόγοις καὶ πράξεσιν. ὁ δὲ ἀ-ναίσθητος, τοιοῦτός τις οἷον λογισμῷ ὁ-ταῖς ψήφοις ἢ πε-φάλαιον ποιήσας, ἐ-ρωτᾶν [?]ἅ ΣΔ ἀκαθη-[?]μένον, τί γίνεται ἢ καὶ δίκην φόβων, καὶ ταύτῳ εἰσιέναι μέλ-λων, [?]ὅτι ἀπλαδόμενος εἰς ἀρχὴν πορεύεσθαι. ἢ θεωρῶν ἐν τῷ θεά-τρῳ, μόνος καταλεί-πεται καθεύδων.
units.tr: Insensibility, as I would define it, is a dullness of soul in words and deeds. The insensible man is of such a kind that, when he has added up a sum with counters, he asks what the total is; or, when about to go to court to answer charges, he sits down, forgets, and goes off to the country; or, watching in the theatre, he is left behind alone, asleep.

units.la: ὡς πολλὰ φαίνων ἢ νυκ-τὸς, ἢ ὅτι θάκης ἀνι-σάμενος, [?]ὑπὸ κινοῦς τῆς τῷ γέγονεν ἀν-ηθλιώσαι. καὶ λαβὼν καὶ ὑποθεὶς αὐτὸς, τ[?]το ζῆν, ἢ μὴ δύ-ναδς ὁρᾶν. ἢ ἀ-παγγέλλοντός τινος αὐτῷ ὅτι τετελευ-τήκε τις αὐτὸς τ[?] φί-λων, ἵνα ὠδ[?]αχθῶ-[?]τας, συνθ[?]πάσας ἢ δακρύσας, εἰπεῖν, ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ. δεινὸς ὢ ἢ, ἀπολαμβά-νων ἀργύριον ὀφειλό-μενον, μαρτύρας πα-ρακαλεῖν· ἢ χειμῶ-νῳ ὄντος μάχεσθ[?] τῷ παιδί, ὅτι σικύους οὐκ ἠρόεασε[?]· ἢ τὰ παιδία ἑαυτῷ πα-λαιδν ἀναλκάζων, ἢ τροχάζειν, © εἰς κό-ποις ἐμβάλλειν. ἢ ἐν ἀγρῷ αὐτοῖς φανῆν ἵππων, ὡς ἀλας ἐς τὰν χύτραν[?] ἐμβάλ-λων, ἀθέωτον[?] ποιῆ-σαι. ἢ ὕονλος τῆ δίδε, εἰπεῖν, ἡδύγε τῶν ἀ-
units.tr: Since he has eaten heavily at night, he rises from his seat and is bitten by a neighbour's dog. Taking something and handing it over, he says that he cannot see it. When someone reports that one of his friends has died, he says, "Good luck!" instead of joining in the mourning or weeping with the rest. When he recovers a debt, he calls witnesses to it. In winter he quarrels with his servant because he has not bought cucumbers. He makes his little children wrestle and race until they are exhausted. In the country, when he cooks lentils, he puts salt in the pot twice, so that the dish cannot be eaten. When it rains, he says how pleasant the water of the stars is. Asked how many dead are carried out through the Sacred Gate, he replies, "I wish you and I had as many."

units.la: ceperit ipse ac recondiderit, id ipsum quaerere solet, reperire autem non potest. Quúmque nunciatur illi obiisse aliquem ex familiaribus ipsius, ut veniat exequias, tum ille vultu ad mœstitiam composito, lacrymas etiam fundens, Bene, inquit, eveniat. Debitas autem pecunias recipiens, testes sibi asciscit: & vigente hyeme, cum famulo quod cucumeres non emerit, iurgatur. Puerulos quinetiam suos, ut lucta se exerceant, cursu contendant, usque ad fatigationem cogere solet. In agro lentem ipse coquens, sale bis in ollam iniecto, ut mâdi nequeat efficit. cumque à Ioue pluit, Sane quàm, inquit, siderum aqua suauis mihi videtur. ...... Rogatus ab aliquo, Ecquot putet Sacra porta elatos mortuos: Quot utinam, respondens ait, ego & tu haberemus.
units.tr: He takes what he has himself received and hides it away, and then he looks for it, but cannot find it. When he is told that one of his acquaintances has died, and he is asked to come to the funeral, he composes his face to sorrow and even sheds tears, and says, "Well, may it turn out well." When he receives money owed to him, he takes witnesses. In winter, when his servant has not bought cucumbers, he scolds him. He even makes his little children exercise at wrestling and race until they are worn out. In the country, cooking lentils himself, he puts salt into the pot twice, so that it cannot be eaten. When it rains from Jupiter, he says, "Surely the water of the stars is much sweeter to me." Asked by someone how many dead are carried out through the Sacred Gate, he answers, "I wish you and I had as many."

units.la: ARrogantia est verborum sæuitia in congressionibus & vitæ quotidianæ usu. Homo arrogans ita est comparatus, ut si quis ex ipso sciscitetur, Ubi est ille? respondeat, Ne sis mihi molestus. salutatus, salutare invicem negligit. cumque aliquid vendit, indicare quidem merces suas,interrogatus Quanti? non dignatur: verùm ipse potius emptorem interrogat, Ecquid in-καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι λέγουσι {*}πίστης, ἢ λέγοντός τὴν Θ, πόσοις οἱ κῆ[?] ὡς ἱερὰς πύλας ἐξε-νηνεχθαι νεκροὺς; πρὸς τοῦτον εἰπεῖν, ὅσοι ἐ-μοὶ ἢ σοὶ ψοῖντο[?].
units.tr: Arrogance is savagery of words in dealings and in the everyday conduct of life. The arrogant man is of such a kind that, if someone asks him, "Where is so-and-so?" he replies, "Don't bother me." When he is greeted, he neglects to greet in return. When he is selling something, he does not deign to tell the buyer the price when asked, "How much?" but instead asks the buyer, "Do you want anything else?" And when others say "faith," or when someone says "Theta," he asks how many dead have been carried out through the sacred gate. To this he answers, "As many as you and I may wish."

units.la: Ἡ δὲ αὐθάδεια, ἔστιν ἀπαιδευσία ὁ-μιλίας ἐν λόγοις. ὁ δ᾽ αὐθάδης, τοιοῦτός τις οἷος ἐρωτηθεὶς, ὁ δεῖ-να πε[?] ὅξιν, εἰπεῖν, θεάματα[?] μοι μὴ πάρεχε. ἢ προσαγορευθεὶς, μὴ ἀνθρωπος[?] εἰπεῖν. ἢ πωλῶν τι, μὴ λέγειν τοῖς ὠνη-μένοις, πόσου ἂν ἀπο-δοῖτο, ἀλλ᾽ ἐρωτᾶν τι ἀπορήσει[?] καὶ τοῖς π-μῶσι, μῶσι, ἢ πέμπασιν[?] εἰς τὰς ἑορτὰς, εἰπεῖν ὅτι οὐκ ἂν ἡδύοιτο διδόμενα. καὶ οὐκ ἔ-χων[?] συγγνώμων οὔ-τε τῷ ἀπώσαντί αὐ-τὸν ἀκυσίως, οὔτε τῷ ὠσαντι, οὔτε τῷ ἐμβάντι. ἢ φίλῳ ἤ[?] ἔρανον καλοῦσαντί εἰσ-ενεγκεῖν, εἰπὼν ὅτι οὐκ ἂν δοίη, ὕστερον ἥκειν φέρων, καὶ λέγειν ὅτι ἀπολύσει[?] καὶ τοῦτο τὸ ἀργύριον. καὶ προς-παίσας ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ, δῖνος[?] καταράσασθαι τῷ λίθῳ. καὶ ἂν ὑπο-μένειν, οὐκ ἂν προ-μένειν πολλῷ χρόνον ἐδένα[?]. καὶ οὔτε ἀ-σαι, οὔτε ῥῆσιν εἰ-πεῖν, οὔτε ὀρχήσα-σθαι ἂν ἐθελήσαι. δη-[illegible, ~6 letters] ueniat damnandum. Religiosis quoque hominibus, & qui ad festa solennia diis dona mittunt, dicere solet minimè gratis datum ipsis iri, si quid divino acceperint munere. Si quis illum vel inuitus, aut expulerit, aut pepulerit aut pede prefferit, nõ est exorabilis. Et cum amico dixerit collectâ ab ipso petenti, nihil se largiturum, poftea ipse vltro afferet, dicetque, Velle se hanc quoque pecuniam perdere. In via si ad lapidem offenderit, maledicet illi. Et vt aliquando subsistat alicuius expectâ di causa: nũquam tamen diutius cuiquam præstolabitur. Idem vt cantet in cõuiuiis, aut vice sua recitet, aut saltet, adduci non poteft. Postremò diis ipsis vota facere non curat.
units.tr: Churlishness is a lack of training in social intercourse in speech. The churlish man is of such a kind that, when asked, "How is so-and-so?" he replies, "Don't put on a show for me." When greeted, he does not answer, "Hello, friend." When selling something, he does not tell the buyers what he would take for it, but asks them what they want to pay. When he sends gifts to friends at the festivals, he says that they would not be pleased to receive them. He is unforgiving toward anyone who pushes him by accident, toward one who shoves him, and toward one who tramples on him. When a friend who is collecting a club contribution asks him to pay in, he says he will not give anything, and later comes bringing it, and says he is losing this money too. If he stumbles on a stone in the road, he curses the stone. If he stops to wait for someone, he will never wait long for anyone. He will not sing at a party, recite in his turn, or dance, no matter how he is pressed. Religious people too, and those who send gifts to the gods at solemn festivals, he is wont to tell that nothing will be given to them free, if they have received any divine gift. If anyone pushes him, even against his will, or drives him away, or strikes him with a foot, he cannot be appeased. When a friend who has asked him for a collection says he will give nothing, he later brings it of his own accord and says he is willing to lose this money as well. Finally, he does not care to make vows to the gods themselves.

units.la: Superstitionē sanè definire possumus, meriulosum erga numen affectū. Superstitiosus veros est qui elotis manibus, c aqua lustrali aspersus templo, foliū lauri ore rehensum tenens, interum diem ita ambulet. i via mustela ingrediēte transcurrerit, non ante rogredietur quàm alius rior trăsierit, aut ipse tres pides trans via miserit. erpentes si viderit in æbus, sacellum eo loco struet. Lapides vnctos ii sunt in triviis solet oo ex ampulla perfunre: nec prius discedere àm pofito genu eos erit veneratus. Quòd si
units.tr: We may define superstition as a fearful attitude toward the divine power. The superstitious man is of such a kind that, having washed his hands and sprinkled himself with lustral water from the temple, holding a laurel leaf in his mouth, he spends the whole day walking about like this. If a weasel runs across his path, he will not go on until someone else has passed by or he himself has thrown three stones across the road. If he sees snakes in his house, he builds a shrine on that spot. He is accustomed to anoint the stones at crossroads with oil from a flask, and he does not leave until he has knelt and venerated them. But if

units.tr: ...from the flask of olive oil, having fallen down and worshipped...

units.la: ΑΜΕΛΕΙ ἡ δει-σιδαιμονία δὲ ξύλον ἐστὶ[?] δειλία πρὸς τὸ δαιμόνιον. ὁ δὲ δεισιδαίμων, τοιοῦτός τις οἷος ὑπονιψάμενος ὡς χεῖρας ἢ περιῤῥανάμενος ὑπὸ ἱερεῦς δάφνης εἰς τὸ στόμα λαβὼν, οὕτω τὴν ἡμέραν διαπατῆσαι, ἢ τῶν ὁδῶν ἐὰν ἀπει-δράμῃ γαλῆ, μὴ πρὸ-πεσὸν περιοδεύειν, ἕως διεξέλθῃ τῆς, ἢ λίθος τῆς ὁδοῦ ἀλαλάξῃ. ἢ ἐὰν ἴδῃ σοφῷ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ, ἱερὸν ἐνταῦθα ἱδρύσασθαι. καὶ τῶν λιπαρῶν λίθων τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἐρείοδοις[?] κατα[illegible, ~4 letters]ὅτι ἡ ἀπαλλάττεσθαι. ἢ ἐὰν μῆς Φύλακον ἀλφι-τῶν ἐλφάγη, πρὸς [?] ἐξηγητὴν ἐλθὼν, ἐ-ρωτᾶν τί χρὴ ποιεῖν. ἢ ἐὰν ἀποκρινῆ αὐτῷ ἐκδοῦναι τῷ σκυτο-δέψῃ, ἀπογράφαι μὴ προσέχων τούτοις, ἀλλ' ἀποτροπαῖς [?] ἐκ-δύσασθαι. ἢ πυκνὰ ἢ τ' οἰκίαν καθαρίειν.
units.tr: Superstition is a kind of cowardice before the divine. The superstitious man is one who, after washing his hands or sprinkling himself with water from the priest's laurel and putting a leaf of it in his mouth, spends the whole day that way. If a weasel runs across his path, he will not go on until someone else has crossed it or he has thrown stones across the road. If he sees a snake in his house, he sets up a shrine there. He anoints the stones at the crossroads with oil and, when he has done so, leaves without finishing his business. If a mouse gnaws a sack of meal, he goes to an interpreter and asks what he must do. If the answer is that the bag must be taken to the leather-worker to be patched, he disregards the advice, has the sack emptied, and considers it a matter of religious duty to rid himself of it. He is also in the habit of purifying his house often, and he will not set foot on a tomb, nor go near any funeral rites, nor approach any woman who has just given birth.

units.la: ℭ ὅτε ὀπιθλῶν [?] μνή-μαλι, ὅτε ὅτι νεκρὸν ἐλθεῖν, ὅτε ὅτι λέ-γει.
units.tr: Whenever he hears a muttering or a sound, whenever he is told that someone has died, whenever someone speaks of it, he is alarmed and takes it as an omen.

units.la: ℭ ὅταν ἐνύπνιον ἴδῃ, πορεύεσθαι πρὸς τοὺς ὀνειροκρίτας, πρὸς τὰς μάντεις, πρὸς τοὺς ὀρνιθοσκό-πους, ἐρωτῶν τίνι θεῷ ἢ θεᾷ προσεύ-χεσθαι δεῖ. ἢ τελεσ-θησόμενον, πρὸς τοὺς ὀρφεοτελεστὰς καὶ μη-να πορεύεσθαι μὴ τῆς γυναικός. ἐὰν ἢ μὴ mus fortè farinæ follé arroscrit,adit ad interpretē, & quid facto fit opus eū percontatur:qui si respōdeat, cerdoni nimirū tradendum esse illum follem, vt farciatur : superstitiosus iste neglecto arioli responso, religioni rem habens, exinanitum saccum à se amolietur. Solet etiam domum crebrò purificare:sepulcrum nullû infistere: ad defunctorum iusta nullus accedere : neq; item ad vllam vnquam puerperam. Insomnium porrò si viderit, pergere ille ad somniorû interpretes,ad diuinos, ad augures, scifcitaturus, cui deo, cui dæ vota sint facienda. Et vt sacris initietur, ad Orpheotelestas quot mensibus cum vxore: aut si vxori non vacet, cum nutrice & filiolis suis,itat. Præterea in compitis ante quàm inde discedat, aqua in caput aspersa se lustrat. Patricibus quinetiā ascitis [?], iubet se squillæ aut calculi circumlatione purgari. Quòd si quem mẽte raptum aut comitialem viderit, solet inhorrescēs in sinum sibi despuere.
units.tr: Whenever he has a dream, he goes to the dream interpreters, to the seers and to the bird-watchers, asking to which god or goddess he ought to pray. Or, if he is to be initiated into the mysteries, he goes to the Orpheotelestae every month, and not alone: with his wife, or if his wife is busy, with his nurse and children. Moreover, at the crossroads, before he leaves, he sprinkles water on his head to purify himself. If he has been assigned a Patrician office, he orders himself to be purified by the swinging of a squill or a pebble. If he sees a man seized by a fit or an epileptic, he shudders and spits into his own bosom.

units.la: Querela iniqua est expostulatio nullo iure facta. Hominis autē queruli mores istiusmodi sunt, vt si ad eum amicus portionem aliquam è communio miserit, dicat ei qui afferat, Hoc illud est quòd ego ad cœnam non vocatus: invidisti nimirum mihi iusculum & villum tuum. & cum illū τῆς πτήσης ἡ τ̓ πυ- δίων. ἡ ὅτι τοῖς τρι- ὁδοῖς ἀπελθὼν κ̓ κεφαλῆς λάσας. ἐ ἱερείας καλέσας, σκύλλῃ ἢ σκύλακι κελεύσαν αὐτὸν πε- εἰκαθᾶραι. μαινό- μενον [?]Τείδων ἢ ὅπί- λαπίτον [?], φρίξας εἰς κόλπον πῦσαν.
units.tr: An unjust complaint is a remonstrance made without any right. The querulous man behaves like this: if a friend sends him a portion from a shared meal, he says to the one who brings it, "So this is why I was not invited to dinner! You have grudged me your broth and your little dish," and so on. Likewise, as for superstition, he washes himself with water in the crossroads before leaving, has himself purified by a priestess, or has a dog or puppy led round him, and when he sees someone seized by madness or a fit, he shudders and spits into his bosom. [τῆς πτήσης ἢ τῶν πυδίων. ἢ ὅτι τοῖς τριόδοις ἀπελθὼν κατὰ κεφαλῆς λούσας. ἢ ἱερείας καλέσας, σκύλλῃ ἢ σκύλακι κελεῦσαν αὐτὸν περιελαυνῆσαι... μαινόμενον ἢ ἐπίληπτον, φρίξας εἰς κόλπον πτύσαι.]

units.la: ἘΣΤΙ ἡ μνη- μοιρία, ὅπ- τίμησις ὥσπερ τὸ πεφυκὸς ἀδυνην. ὁ δὲ μνημοίρ[?]ων, τοιόσδε τις οἷος, ἀ- ποξείλα[?]ν μερί- δα τῆ̃ φίλᾳ, εἰ̓ῶ̃ν πρὸς τὸν φέροντα, ἐφθόνησάς μοι τῆ̃ ζωμῆ̃, καὶ τῆ̃ οἰνα- ρίᾳ, οὐκ ὅτι δεῖπνον καλέσας· ἡ ὑπὸ τῆς ἑταίρας καὶ φιλή-μῳ, εἶπεν, Θαυ-μάζω εἰ σὺ ἢ ἀπὸ ψυχῆς με φιλεῖς. ἢ τῷ δὴ ἀγανακτῶν ἃ δι' ὅτι ὑξ, ἀλλὰ διὰ ὅτι ὕστερον. Ϲ ὁρῶν τι Ϲ ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ ἐαλάν-τιον, εἶπεῖν, ἀλλ' ἢ ἀποσαρὸν εὕρηκα ἐ-δέσωλε. Ϲ ἀφιάμε-νῷ ἀνδρόποδον ἄ-ξιον, ἢ πολλὰ δεν-θεὶς τὸ πωλοῦντος, θαυμάζω, εἶπεν, ὅ τι ὑμῖς ἔτω ἄξιον ἐώ-νημαι, ἢ πρὸς τὸ ἐυαγ-γελιζομένον ὅτι υὸς σοι γέγονεν, εἶπεν, ὅ-τι ἂν προσθῆς, ἢ τῆς οὐσίας τὸ ἡμίου ἀπε-σιν, ἀληθῆ ἐρεῖς. καὶ νίκλω νίκησας ἢ λα-βὼν πάσας τὰς ψή-φως, {*}ἐκαλεῖν τῷ χράψαντί τὸν λόγον, ὡς πολλὰ παραλε- amica etiam & etiam fua-uiatur, Miror, inquit, si tu ex animo ista mihi des-bafia. Ioui succenset, non modò si nō pluat: sed etiam si serius. cúmque in via crumenam inuenit, Ego verò, ait, thesaurum nullus vnquam reperi. Similiter quum paruo mācipium emerit, vtpote exorato multis precibus venditore, Mirum fanè, inquit, si tantulo quicquā emerim quod sit alicuius pretii. Iam si quis lætum illum nuntium ipsi affe-rat, Filiolo, inquiens, au-&tus es: Adiice, ait ille, Et dimidia bonorum pars tibi periit, tum quod res est dixeris. Idem postquam in iudicio omnium cal-culis vicit, nihilominus tamen de eo conqueritur, qui oratione scripsit quā pro se habuit, vt qui mul-ta ipsius iusta omiserit. m si ad subleuandam ius egestatē amici pe-nias contulerint: & di-t deinde aliquis, Nunc o hilaris: Quo pacto e possum? inquiet:cùm singulis sua sit pecunia ldenda:& hocamplius atiæ cuique tanquam accepto beneficio ha idæ?
units.tr: Forgetfulness is a kind of habitual weakness of memory. The forgetful man is one who, having sent a portion of a meal to a friend, says to the bearer, "You begrudged me the broth and the wine, not that you invited me to dinner." When a female friend calls him dear and says she loves him, he replies, "I wonder whether you really love me from the heart." Finding a stone on the road, he says, "I have found a stone I had lost long ago." When he is offered a slave for sale, and the seller praises him at length, he says, "I wonder what on earth I have bought, since the seller praised it so much." When someone tells him that a son has been born to him, he says, "Whatever you add, you will tell the truth"; and when he is told that half his property has been lost, he says, "You are telling the truth." After winning a case by a unanimous vote, he calls for the man who wrote his speech, as though many points had been left out.

units.la: Diffidentia[?] est per quam omnes frau-suspectos habemus. ffidens autem is est, si ad emenda obso-puerum miserit, aliū X mittat, qui percōte-quanti emerit. Si ferat : pecunias, solet eas sulis stadiis numerare.
units.tr: Distrust is the habit by which we regard everyone as a cheat. A distrustful man, when he has sent a slave to buy something, sends another to ask how much he paid. If he is handed money, he is in the habit of counting it again at the stalls.

units.tr: The money that remains from the dues, or when money has been collected for a contribution from wealthy friends, and someone says, "Are you cheerful now, or how is it?" he replies that the money must be paid back to each of them, or else, apart from these, that he owes thanks to those who have done him the service.

units.la: ΕΣΤΙΝ ἀμέλῃ ἀπιστία, ὑπόληψίς τις ἀδικίας κατὰ πάντων. ὁ γὰρ ἀπιστῶν, τοιοῦτός τις οἷος, ἀποσείλας τὸν παῖδα ὀψωνήσοντα, ἕτερον παῖδα πέμπειν. ςωσόμυον πόσον ἔτ[?]ωρίατο. ἔφερων αὐ[?]τὸν ἀεληθμεῖν πόσον ἔςι. § τὴν γυναῖκα τὴν αὐ-τῆς ἐρωτᾶν κατακεί-μένου, εἰ κέκληκε τὸν κιβωτόν, ἢ εἰ σεσήμανταί τὸ κοι-λιώχον, ἢ εἰ ὁ μο-χλὸς εἰς τὴν θύραν τοῦ αὐλαίαν ἐμβέ-ζληται. § ἐὰν σκεί-νῃ φῇ, μηδὲν ἦπον αὐτὸς ἀνασὰς γυμ-νὸς ἐκ τῶν ςρωμά-των, § ἀνυπόδη-τος, τὸν λύχνον ἀ-ψας, ταῦτα πάντα [?]ωειϑραμῶν ὁπηνέ-ψασθ, ἢ οὕτως μόλις ὕπνῳ τυγχάνῃ. καὶ τοῖς ὀφείλουσας αὐ-τῷ ἀργύριον, μὴ μάρτυρων ἀπαντῶν τοῖς τόκοις, ὅπως μὴ δώασιν ἔξαρνοι γε-[illegible, ~5 letters] Cubans in lecto, vxorem interrogat an capsam bene clauserit : an probè fit arca obsignata : an vestibuli foribus pessulus fit obdicus : ac licet affirmet illa, nihilo tamen fecius[?], nudus ac discalceatus è lecto surgens, accensa lucerna,obire singula & inspicere pergit , ac vix ita tandem somno se dedere.
units.tr: Mistrust is a careless distrust, a suspicion of injustice toward everyone. The mistrustful man, after sending his slave to shop, sends another to ask how much it cost. Once he has brought the thing home, he calculates again how much it is worth. As he lies in bed he asks his wife whether she has locked the chest, whether the cupboard is sealed, or whether the bolt has been shot home in the door of the vestibule. Even if she says that it has, he nevertheless gets up naked and barefoot from the bed, lights the lamp, and goes on checking each thing and looking it over, and only with difficulty does he finally manage to sleep. He also goes with witnesses to collect the interest from those who owe him money, so that they cannot deny it.

units.la: Ad debitores suos fœnus fortis exacturus , cum testibus accedit : ne inficias videlicet ire possint. Vestem poliendam dealbandámque , non ei dare solet qui fullo sit optimus: sed ei qui fideiussorem det idoneum. Quòd si quis pocula ab ipso commodato roget, solet ille ma-
units.tr: When he means to exact interest from his debtors, he goes with witnesses, so that they cannot deny it. He does not give his clothes to be cleaned and whitened to the best fuller, but only to one who will provide a reliable surety. If someone asks to borrow cups from him, he is most inclined to refuse outright, and if he does give them, he demands them back at once.

units.la: νέος.[?] τὸ ἱμάτιον[?] ἐνδῶαι[?] δ̓νός[?], οὐχ ὡς ἐέλτισα ἐρχόεται[?], ἀλλ' ὅταν ἢ ἀξιῷ ἐγξυντὴς τῆ ναφέως[?]. ¶ ὅταν ἦκη τὰς αἰτησομένῳ ἐπιπώματα[?], μάλισα μὲν μὴ δουῶαι. ximè quidem, non dare: ut si quando det, continuò repetere. Puerum à pedibus iubet non à tergo fequi,sed ante se ambulare: e posit ille inter eundū ugam capeffere, hac raione cauens. Poftremò is qui cum aliquid ab ipo fumferint, dicunt illi, Lefer in rationes : Imò, it,deponc:non enim vaat mittere flagitatum.
units.tr: He orders the boy to follow at his feet, not at his back, but to walk ahead of him, so that while they walk he can seize the boy's cloak, thus guarding himself. Lastly, when people have taken something from him, he says, "Put it down in the accounts!" No, rather, "Pay it up now, for I have no time to send for what is owed."

units.tr: Foulness is neglect of the body and uncleanness, which is troublesome to other people. The foul man is one who, suffering from leprosy and scabies, with his nails overgrown, walks about among people and says that these diseases are a family inheritance, since his father and grandfather were subject to them too.

units.tr: He is also in the habit of not letting his animals (or his household) alone, and of refusing to leave off, and on the road and among those around him, he goes on in a way that is hard to bear.

units.tr: There is a kind of churlishness that, in the way it treats others, is harsh and unkind. The churlish man is one who, when his slave is ill, does not attend to him but leaves him to fend for himself, so that he may not run off. When he has received something, he speaks and sends for others, to his own advantage.

units.tr: Surliness is a harsh and unpleasant disposition in body and manner. The surly man is one who is so forbidding that people cannot approach him, and who keeps his nails long and dirty.

units.la: τὸν πατέρα ἔχειν καὶ τὸν πάππον. ἀμέλει δεινὸς ¶ ἕλκη ἔχειν ἐν τοῖς ἀντιχνη-μίοις, ¶ φρόςπαίσματα ἐν τοῖς δακτύλοις, ἢ ταῦτα μὴ ἀπεσπόσυ, ἀλλ' ἑαυτὴν ἀπειωνῆμα. ¶ τὰς μαχάλας ἀπειῳδεις ἢ δυσεία ἔχὴν ἄχεις ὅπ πολὺ τῶν πλουρῶν. ἢ τοὺς ὀδόντας μελανὰς ¶ ἐθιομψύοις. ὥστε δυσ-ἐντυχὴς ἐῇ καὶ ἀνδρὸς, ¶ τὰ τοιαῦτα. ἐθίων ἀπομύπ-ᾳν. ῥύειν ἐξάμε-ῳ, ὠροσλαλεῖν, ¶ [illegible, ~12 letters] & patrem & auum fuiffe eis obnoxios. Solet etiam ulcera in tibiis, & in manibus tubercula habens, nullam iis medicinam facere: sed finere donec incurabilia reddantur. Axillas ferarum more hirsutas,pilis magnam laterum partem occupantibus, habet. Dentes verò nigros atque exesos, ut molestus sit & infvavis cum eo congressus. Eidē hæc quoque conveniunt: nares inter comedendum mungere: & quum edere inceperit colloqui: & ex ore quædam emittere:inter bibendum eructare: oleo in balneis uti rancido: idemq; in forum veste amictus quæ sit maculis inquinata, prodibit: quúmque ad arufpi-
units.tr: He has ulcers on his shins and sores on his fingers, and he does not treat them but lets them fester, and his father and grandfather had the same. His armpits are hairy, with hair covering a large part of his sides, and his teeth are black and decayed, so that anyone who meets him finds him unpleasant. He also has these habits: he blows his nose while eating, starts talking as soon as he begins to eat, spits things out of his mouth, belches while drinking, uses rancid oil in the baths, and goes out into the forum in a cloak stained with spots. When his mother has gone to the diviner, he keeps talking all the while and does not hold his tongue, and he is in the habit of not refraining from abusive words.

units.la: ἀπορριπτεῖν δὲ τὸ σῶμα. ἅμα πεῖν, προσερυγγάνειν. ἐ-λαίῳ σαπρῷ ἐν βα-λανείῳ χεῖρας. ἡμά-τιον κηλίδων μεσὸν ἀναβαλόμενον, εἰς ἀγορὰν ἐξῆλθεν. ἢ εἰς ὀρνιθοσπό-σπόπ[?] em mater exierit , lingua interea non fauere, eque à malis verbis fe bstinere moris habet. Sæpe etiam dum vota liationésque fiunt , pateam fibi è manibus clabi init,& simul rifuma tollit, uasi aliquid fecerit porentofum. Tibicines fi auiat , vnus inter omnes ianibus plaudere, atque orum etiam modulos iepta imitatione effinere : dein tibicine quod itò finem non fecerit inrepare:& dum vltra mém vult exspucre, eum ui pocula in conuiuio inistrat, confpuit.
units.tr: He throws his body about carelessly and, at the same time, spits. He anoints his hands with rancid oil in the bath. Often, too, while vows are being made and libations poured, he begins to pick at the garland in his hands and then laughs out loud, as though he had done something clever. When flute-players are playing, he alone among everyone claps his hands and mimics their tunes in a clumsy imitation. Then, when the flute-player has not stopped at the proper time, he joins in again, and while wanting to spit beyond the wine, he spits on the cups that the waiters bring round at the banquet.

units.la: TÆdium , si definire velis , est molestus bsque damno congrefis. Homo tædiosus est σκόῳ τῆς μητρὸς ἐξελθέσης, βλασφημῆσαι. καὶ δυσχολῶν καὶ ἀπογνωσθέντων [?] ἐμβαλεῖν τὸ ποτήριον, καὶ γελάσαι ὡς τεταπινότι [?] πεποιηκώς. καὶ αὐλήμως δὲ κεχτῆσθαι τὰς χεῖρας μόνων τῶν ἄλλων. ὁ σωτερεῖζειν δ᾽ ὅπ[illegible, ~3 letters]μπᾶν τῇ αὐληςίδι μὴ ἔχων ἐπαυσαμένη [?]. καὶ ἀποπνῦσαι δὲ βελόμενον ὑπὲρ τῆς τραπέζης, ἀποπνῦσαι τῷ οἰνοχόῳ.
units.tr: Tediousness, if you wish to define it, is an annoying encounter that causes no harm. The tedious man is one who, when his mother has gone out, breaks into abuse; who is sullen and ill-humoured, flings down the cup and laughs as though he had done something clever; who keeps his hands busy with nothing else; who, unable to hold back from the flute-girl, wants to spit out over the table and spits at the cupbearer.

units.la: ΕΣΤΙ ἡ ἀηδία, ὡς ὅρῳ ὠφελαξεῖν, ἐντεύξις λύπης ποιητικὴ ἀδολ[?] βλάβης. ὁ ἀηδὴς, τοιοῦτός τις οἷ[?] ἐ-γείρειν ἀξίᾳ[?] καθόλ-δον[?]ζα εἰσελθὼν, ἵνα αὐτῷ λαλῇ. ἀνά-γκαθαι[?] δὲ μέλλοντας κωλύειν. προσελ-θὼν, δὲς[?] ὅπως ἐᾶν, ἕως ἂν ἐπιπατήσῃ[?].
units.tr: Unpleasantness [ἀηδία] is, as I would define it, an encounter that produces distress without any harm. The unpleasant man is the sort who, when he comes in to someone who is about to get up, sits down beside him so that he can talk at him. When people are about to leave, he detains them; he approaches as they are setting off and tells them to wait until he has finished speaking.

units.la: τὸ παιδίον τῆς πίτης ἀφελόμ[?]ενον μασσώμυνον[?], σπίζειν αὐτὸς, ὑποκορίζε-σθαι ὡς ποπαύζων[?]. καὶ ἐδίων δ᾽ ἅμα δι-ηγεῖας ὡς ἐλέξογν[?] πιῶν, ἄνω καὶ κάτω καθαρθεῖν. ὁ ζωμὸν[?] τὰ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐν τοῖς ὑποχωρήμασιν αὐτῷ μελαντέρα ἡ χολή. ἐρωτῆσαι δὲ δεινὸς ἐναντίον τῶν οἰκείων, ὡς ποία ἡ-μέρα μεταπίπτει καὶ ὅτι ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ δῶ παρ᾽ αὐτῷ λακκαῖον.
units.tr: He takes the child from its nurse, chews its food for it, feeds it himself, and coos over it with pet names as though he were a baby-talker. While he talks, he makes a show of having drunk a purge and of having been emptied out, top and bottom. He says that in his stools the bile was darker than the broth. He is clever at asking, in front of his family, what day the weather is changing, and at saying that the water in his house is cold and that his cistern is full of it.

units.la: ὡς κἂπ[?]ῳ λάχα-qui vix incipientem dormire,excitet, ingressus vt cum eo colloquatur : & qui ad eum accedens qui inibi eft,vt nauim foluat, moram ei afferat, & expectare iubeat,donec aliquot secum spatia confecerit. Infantem etiá puerum nutrici suæ admens, ipse mansum ei cibum in os inferet, & blandiculè compellans , poppysmis permulcebit. Inter edendum narrat se helleboro accepto , quæ in vifceribus hærerent, eiecisse deiecisseque : tum addit, in effusis bilem fuisse iure appolito magis atram. A matre præsentibus amicis & familiaribus. quærere amat,Ecqua me die, mater,peperisti ? Aquam ait sibi esse in cisterna frigidam : olera in horto multa & tenera : domum suam hospitibus ita patere, quasi esset publicum diuersorium: & quū peregrinos hospitio excipit, parasitum suū producit, ut videant illi qualis sit: atq; in cōuiuio ad ipsum cōuersus, Heus tu, parasite, inquit, ut iis qui hîc adsunt, sis oblectamento.
units.tr: He is the sort who wakes someone who has only just begun to fall asleep, comes in to talk with him, and who, when someone is about to set sail, comes up and delays him, telling him to wait until he has gone some distance with him. He takes an infant from its nurse and puts chewed food into its mouth himself, coaxing it with endearments and smacking kisses. While eating, he tells how he took hellebore and purged what was lodged in his bowels, and then adds that in what he brought up the bile was blacker than the sauce. He likes to ask his mother, in front of friends and relations, "On what day did you give birth to me, Mother?" He says the water in his cistern is cold, and that the vegetables in his garden are many and tender. His house is open to guests as if it were a public inn; when he receives strangers, he brings out his parasite to show them what sort he is; and turning to him at dinner he says, "Hey, you parasite, be a delight to those who are here."
On Sordid and Foolish Desire for Praise.

units.la: Μικροφιλοτιμία[?], quā possis Latinè dicere ineptam ac circa res paruas versantem ambitionem: ea est honorum ac gloriæ cupido illiberalis. Homo verò ineptè ambitiosus is est, qui ad cœnam vocatus, conti[?]atori ipsi studeat asside-[?]e : qui filium Delphos [?]bducat, vbi comam poνα πολλὰ ἔχων καὶ ἀπαλά, ¶ ὅτι ἡ οἰκία αὐτοῦ πανδοχεῖον ὅς. ¶ ξενίζων δὲ δείξας τὸν ὠδάσιτον αὐτοῦ ποῖός τις. καὶ παρακαλῶν δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ ποτηρίᾳ ὅτι τέρψον τοὺς παρόντας.
units.tr: Petty ambition, which in Latin you might call a foolish ambition concerned with trivial matters, is an illiberal desire for honours and glory. The foolishly ambitious man is one who, when invited to dinner, takes pains to sit beside the host; who, when he takes his son to Delphi, sees to it that the boy has many soft locks of hair; who makes sure he has an Ethiopian slave as his attendant; who, if he must pay a mina of silver, labours to hand it over in small, grudging coin. If he has sacrificed an ox, he is in the habit of nailing its forehead, wreathed with great garlands, above the doorway at the entrance, so that everyone who comes in can see that he has sacrificed it. When he has led a procession with the other horsemen, he gives all the rest to a boy to carry home, while he himself walks about in the forum wearing his robe.

units.la: Ἡ δὲ μικροφιλοτιμία ὄρεξίς ἐστι τιμῆς ἀνελεύθερος. ὁ δὲ μικροφιλότιμος τοιοῦτός τίς ἐστιν οἷος ἀποδύσασθαι, ὅτι δεῖπνον κληθεὶς, παρὰ αὐτὸν τὸν καλέσαντα καταπέμψας ἀφωνῆσαι. ¶ τὸν γὰρ ἀποκέρδαν ἀπαζαλῶν εἰς Δελφοὺς, ἢ δὲ ἐπιμεληθῶν
units.tr: Petty ambition is an ungenerous desire for honour. The petty-ambitious man is the sort who, when invited to dinner, sends a messenger back to the very man who invited him, to make excuses. [Ἡ δὲ μικροφιλοτιμία ὄρεξίς ἐστι τιμῆς ἀνελεύθερος.] For him, the one who sends the bill to Delphi, or who looks after...

units.la: ἀλλ' ὅπως αὐτῷ ὁ ἀ-κόλουθ© ΑΓΙΟΙ ἐ-σαι. Ϛ ἀποδοὺς μνᾶν[?] ἀργυρίου, καὶ τὸν ποιή-σαι ἀποδοῶ. καὶ βοῦν θύσας, τὸ ἀρο-μετωπίδιον ἀσπαλί-κευ̂ τῆς εἰσόδε πρὸς-παλαλύσαι, ἐμ-μάσι μεγάλους ἀξι-δήσας, ὅπως οἱ εἰσι-όντες ἴδωσιν ὅτι ἔσω̃ ἔθυσε. Ϛ πομπεύσας ὃ μὴ τῶν ἱππεῶν, Ϛ μὴ ἄλλα πάντα ἀπο-δοῦναι τῷ παιδὶ ἀ-πενεγκεῖν οἴκαδε, ἀ-ναξαλόμενος ἢ ἀοι-μάπον εἰς τὸ ἀγρο-ὰν ἀφεῖπαλεῖν. καὶ κυναρίσ ἢ τελουτή-σαντ. ὁ, αὐτὸ μνή-μα ποιῆσαι. Ϛ σηλί-σιον ποιῆσας, ὅπ-γραψαι, ΚΑΛΛΟΣ ΜΕΛΙΤΑΙΟΣ. ἡ ἀναδεὶς δακτύλιον nat: qui operam det ut pedissequum habeat genere Æthiopem: qui et-iam, si minam argenti velit soluere, laboret ut reddat in aspero. Et si bouem sacrificarit, solet anteriorem capitis eius partem magnis redimitā sertis pro foribus in ipso introitu figere: ut intelligant quicunque ingredietur, esse ab ipso boucm [?] mactatum. Atque ubi pōpam cum aliis equitibus duxit, reliquis omnibus puero traditis, qui ea domum referat, ipse trabeatus in forum pergit, & ibi deambulat. quūmq; illi paruulus aliquis canis fuerit mortuus, monumentum ei faciet, ascriptis etiam in columella his verbis, SOBOLES MELITENSIS. Iam cum aereū annulū Æscu-lapio la pio confecrarit, appensis fubinde nouis coronis totum atteret: atq; adeo ipse quotidie unguentis oblinitur. Sanè ctiam, quæ pertinent ad curam magistratus quos prytaneos vocant, ipse diligenter curare solet: quò pofsit, ubi litatum fuerit, rem populo renuntiare. Itaque candidatus & coronatus in cōcionem prodit, & infit, Nos prytanei, ô Athenieses, Matri Deûm sacra recte fecimus, & litauimus: vos igitur omnia faufta exspectate. His ita renuntiatis, domum revertitur: deinde uxori narrat sibi prosperè supra modum res succedere. χαλκοῦ ἐν σκληπτῷ, τε τειβξιν σεφα[?] ἀλείφεως ὀσ[?] ἀμίλει ἢ ᾧ σ[?] κίνσας ως[?] ῳρυζάνεων ὅ[?] παγείλη τῳ[?] ᾧ ἰεφ. ᾧ σιδυασαμένῳ[?] φρὸν ἱμαπον[?] φανωμένῳ, τ[?] θεὼν εἰσεῖν, ω[?] Ἀθηναῖοι, ἐ[?] οἱ ῳρυταγὲς[?] τῇ μητρὶ τῶν[?] ἀξια ᾧ καλὰ[?] μεῖς ἐδιξεσθ[?] χαθά. ᾧ ζ[?] παγείλας, ἀπ[?] ηησας οἴκ[?] ἑαυτὸ γυναι[?] καθ' ἑαρξολ[?] ἡμερᾶι. τὰ Α- ἵστορ ἐκ ποιοῦντα. ἡμέρᾳ. ωσδοι- ἀ τῶν ὡς ἀ- δήμῳ ὥσδα- λαμ- ἐστε- παρελ- ἄνδρες ὑόμῳ ἰσεᾷ θεῶν ὁ υ- τὰ ἀ- ὅτα ἀ- τῶν δι- ἀδὲ τῇ ὡς λῶ δι-
units.tr: ...so that his own servant is an Ethiopian. He also takes care that, if he has to pay a mina of silver, he pays it in small and worn coins. When he sacrifices an ox, he has the forehead, wreathed with large garlands, nailed up beside the door at the entrance, so that everyone who comes in can see that he sacrificed there. When he leads a procession among the horsemen, he hands over everything else to a boy to carry home, while he himself walks about the forum in his fine robe. If some small dog of his dies, he sets up a monument to it and has an inscription cut on the pillar: "Beautiful, Melitean." When he has dedicated a bronze ring to Asclepius, he wears it down by constantly hanging new garlands on it, and he himself is anointed with perfume every day. He also takes care to look after the business of the magistrates called prytaneis, so that when a sacrifice has been properly made he can report it to the people. So, crowned and garlanded, he comes forward to the assembly and says: "We prytaneis, Athenians, have rightly performed the sacrifice to the Mother of the Gods, and the omens are favourable; so you may expect every good thing." Having made this announcement, he goes home and tells his wife that things are going far better for him than he could have hoped.

units.la: Ἡ δὲ ἀνελευθε-ρία, ὅτι ὠφελ[?]ία τῆς ἀπὸ φιλοπ-μίας δαπάνλω[?] ἔχε-σα. ὁ δὲ ἀνελευθε-ρῶν, τοιοῦτός τις οἷ-ος νικῆσαι προαγω-γοῖς, ταινίαν ἀνα-θεῖναι ξυλίνην τῷ Διονύσῳ, ἐπιγρά-ψας αὐτὸς τὸ ὄνομα. καὶ ἀπιδόσεων γνω-μῶν, ἐκ τῆς δη-μου ἀνασὰς, σιωπᾷν, ἢ ἐκ τῆς μέσης ἀ-πελθῶν. καὶ ἐνδι-δοὺς αὐτὸς θυγατέρα, τῇ μὲν ἱερείᾳ, πλὴν τῶν ἱερείων, τὰ κρέα ἀποδίδοσθαι· τοὺς δὲ διακονοῦντας ἐν τοῖς γάμοις οἰκο-
units.tr: Illiberality is a deficiency of expense that ought to come from love of honour [ἀνελευθερία ... ἀπὸ φιλοτιμίας δαπάνης]. The illiberal man is the sort of person who, after winning a victory with his chorus, dedicates to Dionysus a wooden ribbon and inscribes his own name on it. When contributions are proposed in the assembly, he keeps silent or gets up and leaves in the middle of the proceedings. When he gives his daughter in marriage, he sells the meat of the sacrifices to the priestess, except for the portions of the priests, and he requires the servants who wait at the wedding to be household slaves [οἰκοτρόφοι]...

units.la: Illiberalitas est nimius quidā præ studio parcendi sumtibus, gloriæ contemtus. Illiberalis autem is est, qui si e tragico certamine victoriam reportarit, tæniam Libero patri ligneam confecret, in qua nomen ipsius sit inscriptum: qui etiam cū necessario Reip. tempore pecuniæ à civibus extra ordinem conferuntur, in concione surgens, silentio utatur, aut è medio se proripiat. Filiam suam nuptum collocans, mactatq; victimę carnes omnes, iis exceptis quæ ad sacrificulos pertinent, vedit: & ad ministrandum in nuptiis, mercede conductos adhibet, qui suo quisque cibo vescantur. Triremi præfectus quam instruxit, gubernatoris stragulis tabulata sternet, suis interea uti parcens.
units.tr: Illiberality is a certain excessive zeal for sparing expenses and a contempt for glory. The illiberal man, if he has won the victory in a tragic contest, dedicates to Father Liber a wooden ribbon bearing his own name inscribed on it. When public contributions are levied from the citizens beyond the ordinary in a time of necessity, he rises in the assembly and keeps silent, or slips away from the middle of the crowd. When he gives his daughter in marriage, he sells the meat of all the sacrificial victims, except the parts that belong to the priests. For the servants who wait at the wedding, he hires men for a fee, and each of them brings his own food. When he is in charge of a trireme he has equipped, he spreads the decks with the helmsman's coverlets, sparing his own.

units.la: E foro postquã opsona-tus est, rediens, carnes ipse gestat, atque olera etiam in sinu. Vestem quando à sordibus purgandam locauit, domi tantisper se continet. Quòd si quis amicorum eius fortuna usus adversa, eranum à suis familiaribus exigat, ídq; ipse sciat, deflectens ex itinere, domum tendit.
units.tr: After he has bought provisions in the market, he carries the meat home himself on the way back, and vegetables too, in the fold of his cloak. When he has hired someone to have his clothes cleaned of dirt, he stays indoors meanwhile. And if one of his friends, being fallen on hard times, asks him for a loan from his own circle, and he knows it, he turns aside from the road and heads home.

units.la: Vxori ancillas emit ille quidem nullas: sed quę in publicum prodeunte comitentur, conducit. Ma-ne vbi surrexit, domum ipse mundare, lectósque [illegible, ~20 letters] purgare solet: & ledens, obsoletum & tritum quod gestat pallium inuertere.
units.tr: He buys no maidservants for his wife, but hires some to attend her when she goes out in public. When he rises in the morning, he himself sweeps the house and usually cleans the couches [illegible]. And when he sits down to dinner, he turns inside out the worn and threadbare cloak he is wearing.

units.la: ϲ τειπεαρχῶν, τὰ τῆ κυβερνήτῃ στρώματα ὑπὸ τῆς καταστρώμα-τῶν ὑποσορέννυσθαι, τὰ ἢ ἄνπε δὲ πολιθέναι. ἢ ἐξ ἀγορᾶς ἢ ὀφω-νήσας, τὰ κρέα αὐτὸς φέρειν. ϲ τὰ λαχανα ἐν τῇ προκολπίῳ. ϲ ἔνδοθ μιᾶν ὅταν ἐκ-λήῳ ἱματίου ἐκπλυναι. ϲ φιλὸς ἐςα-νον συλλέγοντος, προ-εισδύμῳ, ἀποκάμ-ψας ἐκ τῆς ὁλῆς, οἱ-κάδε πορεύθλῶναι. ϲ μὴ ὡριαῖς ἀρεα-παάνας, ἀλλὰ μιαδ-θαι εἰς ἐαϲ ἐξόδους. ϲ ἀνασᾶς, τῶ οἰκίαν καλύναι, ϲ τὰς ηλί-νας ἐκκορῆσαι. καὶ καθεζόμμῳ πα-εασρέψαι τὸν τέί-βωνα ὃν αὐτὸς φο-ρεῖ.
units.tr: As trierarch, he has the helmsman's bedding spread under the decks, and he keeps his own in the hold. When he has bought meat in the market and is carrying it home, he carries it himself. He carries the vegetables in his bosom. When he has a single garment to be washed, he has it washed himself. When friends are gathering contributions, he slips in unnoticed, turns back from the whole business, and goes home. He does not hire helpers for his own errands, but has them done by himself. When he has to sweep the house, he does it himself, and he scrapes the lamps clean. And when he sits down, he turns inside out the cloak he wears.

units.la: ΑΜΕΛΕΙ δὲ ἡ ἀλαζονεία δόξειν ἔξ προσδο-κία τινῶν ἀγαθῶν οὐκ ὄντων. ὁ δὲ ἀλα-ζὼν, τοιοῦτός τις οἷος ἐν τῷ διαζόγματι [?] ἐσπουδῶς διηγεῖσθαι ξε-νοις ὡς πολλὰ χρή-ματα, αὐτοῖς ὅσον ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ. ἢ ὥσε τῆς ἐργασίας τῆς ἀ-νεισικῆς διεξιέναι, ἡλίκη, καὶ αὐτὸς ὅ-σα ἐλαφε. ὁ σωσο-δοιπορού ἀπολαύσας ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ, λέγην ὡς μὴ ἘΥ' ἀνδρὶ ἐ-σεατόν σωτο· καὶ ὅ-σα λιθοκόλλητα πο-τήρια ἐκόμισε, καὶ ἔτι τῶν τεχνιτῶν τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, ὅτι βελπους εἰσὶ τῶν ἐν [?]
units.tr: Arrogance seems to be the expectation of good things that do not exist. The arrogant man is such a person as, at a dinner, eagerly tells the guests how much money he has, as much as there is in the sea. Or he recounts the scale of his shipping business and how much he has spent on it. When he has been saved from danger on the road, he says that no one is more fortunate than he is. He also boasts of how many jewelled cups he has brought home, and that the craftsmen in Asia are inferior to those who [illegible].

units.la: Ostentatio dici queat, inanis bonorū quorundam quæ non adsint prædicatio. Ostentator autem ciusmodi est, qui in Digmate [?] Piraei stans, peregrinis narret multam se pecuniam traiectitiā habere: & de toto fœnebri quæstu longos sermones habeat, quantus ille fit, explicans, & quæ lucra inde fecerit. Inter eundū viæ comitem nactus, se sub Alexandro in illa nobili expeditione meruisse narrabit: & quàm multa inde gemmata potoria reportarit: Asiaticos etiā artifices Europeis esse præstantiores, dissen-tientibus aliis contendet.
units.tr: Ostentation may be defined as the vain boasting of certain goods that one does not in fact possess. The ostentatious man is one who, standing in the [...] of the Piraeus, tells foreigners that he has a great deal of money out at sea, and holds forth at length about his whole moneylending business, explaining how large it is and what profits he has made from it. If he meets a travelling companion, he will tell how he served under Alexander in that famous expedition, and how many jewelled drinking cups he brought back from it. He will also insist that Asian craftsmen surpass European ones, and when others disagree, he will argue the point.

units.la: τῇ Εὐρώπῃ, ἀμφισβητήσου-[?] einde literas ab Antitro esse allatas memoit,quæ ipsum vix duos comitatum in Maceniam venisse dicant. ,cùm esset sibi mate-e concessa immunis exertatio, oblato benefiut noluisse, ut omnes [?]nnium calumnias effuret. Eundem se, in ca[?]ite annonæ amplius [?]inque talenta pauperis ciuibus largientem [?]umsisse. Quod si ignoassideat, eos iubebit [?]nere calculos, & illon quibus aliquid erorit numerum inire : qui sexcenti reperiantur, [?]culis figillatim multicatis, probabilibus et-[?]n cuique eorum nonibus additis, efficiet: o ut decem talenton summa tandem col-
units.tr: He will then mention letters brought to him from Antipater, saying that they state he had scarcely arrived in Macedonia with two attendants. Although the export of timber had been freely granted to him, he says he refused the offered favour, so that no one could bring a charge against him. He claims that in a year of dear grain he gave the citizens more than a thousand talents for the poor. If someone doubts this, he will order them to bring counters and to reckon up the people to whom he gave anything. He will show that six hundred such persons turn up, each one's counter marked separately, with plausible names added for each of them, so that in the end the sum comes to ten talents.

units.la: καὶ [?]χρέμματα ἀ-πεῖν ὡς [?]παρέσῃ παρ[?] Ἀντιπάτρῳ, τρίτον δὴ λέγοντα ἐπιδη-μέως αὐτὸν εἰς Μα-κεδονίαν· ἐ διδοῦ-
units.tr: He also says that he had been present with Antipater, and that he had come to Macedonia for the third time as an official envoy [...].

units.la: tur : quam omnem νης αὐτῷ ἐξαγωγῆς ξύλων ἀτελὲς, εἰ-πεῖν ὅτι ἀπείρητα ὅ-πως μηδὲ ὑφ' ἑνὸς συκοφαντηθῇ. ἢ ἐν τῇ αποδίᾳ ὡς πλείω ἢ πέντε τάλαντα χρύοιτο[?] αὐτῷ τὰ ἀ-ναλώματα διαδίν-τι τοῖς ἀποδόχεις[?] τῶν πολιτῶν. ἢ ἀγωνώ-σαμ δὲ ἀσβεκαθη-μένων[?], κελεῦσαι θεῖ-ναι τὰς ψήφους, καὶ ποσοσῦ αὐτὰς καθ' ἑξακοσίοις, κατὰ μίαν. καὶ προστι-θεὶς πιθανὰ[?] ἑκάστοις τέτωρ[?] ὀνόματα, καὶ ποιῆσαι δέκα τάλαντα. ἢ τέτο φήσας εἰσενεγκεῖν. εἰσενηλωχέναι εἰς ἐρά-νοις αὐτὸν. ἡ ὡς τὴν ἀρχίας[?] εἰπεῖν ὅτι ὁ πίθησιν, ὁ δὲ τὰς λειτουργίας ὅσας λελει-τουργηκε. ἡ προσελ-θὼν δ' εἰς τοὺς ἵππους τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς πωλέ-σι, περιποιήσασθαι[?] ὠνητιᾶν. ἡ δὲ τὰς κλίνας ἐλθὼν, ἱμα-τισμὸν ζητῆσαι εἰς δύο τάλαντα. ἡ τῷ παιδὶ μάχεσθαι οὐκ ἔχων χρυσοῦν νῦν τῷ ἀκολουθεῖν. ἡ μισθω-τῇ οἰκίᾳ οἰκῶν, φῆσαι ταύτῳ ἐν τῷ πα-τρῴαν, περὶ τ μὴ εἰ-σιόντας. διότι μέλλει πωλεῖν αὐτῷ ἀφ᾽ τὸ ἐλάττῳ ἐν ὡς τὰς ξενοδυχίας.
units.tr: ...the whole sum, saying that he was exempt from duty on exporting timber, so that he could not be accused even by one man. Or, when at the trading port, he says that his expenses have cost him more than five talents, which he distributes among the citizens who are needy. Or, having entered a contest and being seated, he orders the votes to be cast, and has them counted at six hundred, one for each; adding plausible names to each of them, he makes it ten talents, and saying this, he brings it in. Or he claims to have been taken captive by the enemy at sea. Or, as in the magistracy, he says he [did such-and-such], and he recounts all the public services he has performed. Or, going up to the fine horses that are for sale, he pretends to want to buy them. Or, going to the couch makers, he asks for a purple cloak worth two talents. Or, not having money to pay the boy, he has him follow him wearing gold. Or, living in a rented house, he says to someone that this is his father's house, and that he wants to sell it because it is too small for receiving guests, so that they will not come in.

units.la: [illegible, ~25 letters] summā, se inopibus subleuādis impēdisse affirmabit:& tamē,inquit, in hac ratione non duco,instruētas à me triremes,quibus prēfui:& alia quib⁹ Reip. causa sum functus,munia sumtuosa. Idē ad eos accedens, qui generosos equos vēdūt, velle se emere simulat: & in nundinis ad tentoria eorū qui mercēs vænum exponūt, appropinquans[?], vestem sibi ostendi iubet duūm talētorum. Pucrū quòd se sine auro sequatur, grauiter obiurgat. Denique in cōducto habitans,si cum aliquo sermonem habeat, qui id ignoret, paternas esse has ædes dicet: quas ipse, quòd sint ad hospites excipiendos angustiores, vendere cogitet.
units.tr: He will declare that he has spent [...] talents in total on relieving the poor; and yet, he says, he does not count among this the triremes he equipped and commanded, nor the other costly public duties he discharged for the state. When he approaches those who sell well-bred horses, he pretends he wants to buy one. At the fairs, approaching the tents of those who put their wares on sale, he orders a garment worth two talents to be shown to him. He sharply rebukes a slave boy for following him without gold. Finally, when living in a rented house, if he is talking with someone who does not know this, he will say that these are his family's ancestral house, which he is thinking of selling because it is too cramped for entertaining guests.

units.la: SUperbia est, aliorum omnium praeter quam ui, contemtus. Homo uperbus talis est. Si quis cum properè conventum velit, à cœna se illum cōveniturum dicet inter ambulandum. Si fuerit de quoquam bene meritus, neminisse beneficij etiam n viis iubebit, atq; adeo oget. Prior ad quemquā accedere nolet. Eos qui emūt aliquid ab ipso, vel aliquid rerum illius conduxerunt, iubere non eretur, vt prima luce ad e veniant. Dum per vias ingreditur, caput semper demittens, obviorum neminem alloquitur. Si viùm aliquando ei fuerit, amicos convivio excipe-Ἔστι ἡ ὑπερφανία καὶ καταφρόνησις τῆς πλὴν αὐτοῦ τῶν ἄλλων. Ὁ δὲ ὑπερήφανος τοὺς δὲ τὰς, οἷος τῷ ἀσθενοῦντι ὑπὸ δείπνε ἐν ἰδ[?] φάγειν ἐν τῷ ὠφελι- παίειν. ἡ δὲ ποιήσας, μεμνῆσθαι φάσκειν ἐν τῇ ὁδοῖς, ἡ βιάζειν. ἡ περιελθεῖν πρότερον ἐδενὶ ζελήσας. καὶ τὲς πολεῖτας ἡ μεμιδωμένους δέ- νος κελόσαν ἡκειν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀμὶ ἡμέρα. ἡ ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς προδύμου μὴ λα- λεῖν τοῖς ἐντυγχάνε- σι, ἡ ἀπὸ κεκυφώς. ὅταν δὲ αὐτῷ δόξῃ ἐσᾶν τὰς φίλας, ἀυ- τὸς μὴ σωφρονεῖν,
units.tr: Arrogance is contempt for all others except oneself. The arrogant man is such that, if he wishes to meet someone quickly, he says he will meet him after dinner, while walking. If he has done someone a favour, he bids that person remember it even on the road, and indeed presses him for it. He will not be the first to approach anyone. Those who buy something from him or rent some of his property he does not deign to order to come to him at first light. As he walks through the streets, he always keeps his head bowed and speaks to none of those he meets. If at some point it suits him, he entertains his friends at a banquet, but he himself does not dine with them. [Greek, as printed: Ἔστι ἡ ὑπερφανία καὶ καταφρόνησις τῆς πλὴν αὐτοῦ τῶν ἄλλων. Ὁ δὲ ὑπερήφανος τοὺς δὲ τὰς, οἷος τῷ ἀσθενοῦντι ὑπὸ δείπνε ἐν ἰδ[?] φάγειν ἐν τῷ ὠφελι- παίειν. ἡ δὲ ποιήσας, μεμνῆσθαι φάσκειν ἐν τῇ ὁδοῖς, ἡ βιάζειν. ἡ περιελθεῖν πρότερον ἐδενὶ ζελήσας. καὶ τὲς πολεῖτας ἡ μεμιδωμένους δέ- νος κελόσαν ἡκειν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀμὶ ἡμέρα. ἡ ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς προδύμου μὴ λα- λεῖν τοῖς ἐντυγχάνε- σι, ἡ ἀπὸ κεκυφώς. ὅταν δὲ αὐτῷ δόξῃ ἐσᾶν τὰς φίλας, ἀυ- τὸς μὴ σωφρονεῖν,]

units.tr: But he gives instructions to one of those under his power to look after the guests. When he goes to visit someone, he sends ahead a man to announce, "He is coming." When he is having a massage or taking food, he allows no one to come in to him. Moreover, if he is settling accounts with someone, he tells a boy to move the counters, and when he has reached the total, he has it carried over to another account as an expense. In letters he never writes, "You will do me a favour," but "I want this done," and "I have sent someone to take it," and "See that it is not done otherwise," and "as soon as possible."

units.la: ENimuero timiditas videri queat, deiectio animi meticulosa. Homo timidus eiusmodi est: navigans, dicet promontoria esse hemiolias navicis. Ad minimam fluctuum agitationem, quaeret, sintne qui navigant omneis initiati. Gubernatore nauim inhibentem interrogat, an medium cursum teneat navis: &, quid a Deo speret aut metuat. Se ex infomnio terreri, narrat assidenti: indufium deinde exuit, & puero tradit. nautas ut se ad terram admoveant, orat. Militiae vero solet idem omnes ad se comilitones vocare: & vbi
units.tr: Timidity may be thought to be a fearful, cowardly depression of the spirit. The timid man is of this kind: when sailing, he says the headlands are as far off as a voyage of a day and a half. At the slightest rocking of the waves, he asks whether any of those sailing are unaware of it. When the helmsman checks the ship, he asks him whether the ship is holding a middle course, and what he hopes or fears from God. He tells his neighbour that he is frightened by a dream; then he takes off his tunic, gives it to a boy, and begs the sailors to bring the ship to land. In military service he is accustomed to summon all his fellow soldiers to himself, and when
