units.tr: Cowardice would seem to be a fearful shrinking of the soul. The coward is of this kind: when sailing, he says the headlands are a day and a half away; at the slightest rocking of the waves he asks whether anyone among the passengers is not aware of it, and when the wind drops he asks whether they are making any progress. What does he think of the things of God? He says to Adamantus that he has heard them from a dream. He takes off his tunic and gives it to the fire. The coward, falling to the ground, calls his slave first to come near, and

units.la: λέγειν ὡς ἔργον ἀγ-γνῶναι δῆι[?] πότερόν εἰσιν οἱ πολέμιοι. καὶ ἀκαιωνχρασυῆς[?], ὁρῶν πλουτίας[?], εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὰς παρεισηκότας, ὅτι τὴν ἀπάθην λαβεῖν ὑπὸ ἡ ἀσθενῆς ἐπελά-θετο. καὶ τέγεεν ὑπὸ τὴν σκηνὴν, τὸν παιδα ἐκπέμψας, κελεύων προσποπεῖας[?] τὸ ἐ-σιν οἱ πολέμιοι, καὶ ἀποκρύψας αὐτὴν ὑ-πὸ τὸ προσεφά-λαιον, εἶτα δήτερίζειν πολὺν χρόνον. καὶ ἐν τῇ σκηνῇ ὁρῶν τεαυ-μαχίαν προσφεύ-μένον τῶν φίλων, προσδραμεῖν, καὶ θεωρεῖν κελεύειν. Ὁ τῆτον ἐξεπόδιζν[?] καὶ προσαπολυίζειν[?], μίας σοβεῖν, καὶ πᾶν μᾶλλον ἢ μά-χεσθαι τοῖς πολε-μίοις. ἢ τὸ σάλπιγξ[?] stantes diligéter respexit, difficile, inquit, est cognitu, sint hostes, an non. Clamore audito, & visis qui caderent, astantibus dicit se præ festinatione, oblitum esse spatham sumere. & postquâ in tentorium curriculo se recepit, puerum inde mittit, iussum ubi sint hostes diligenter speculari. Interea spatham sub pulvino abscondit: deinde ea quærenda longum tempus terit. Tum si vulneratum aliquem in castra ab amicis deferri videat, accurrit, & habere bonum animum iubet: hunc curat, & saniem spogia effingit, necnon muscas abigit: quidvis denique potius facit, quàm ut cum hostibus pugnet. Aeneatore classicum canēte, sedens ipse
units.tr: says it is a task to find out which side the enemy are on. When he sees the soldiers sitting idle, he tells those who are standing by that he has caught a chill from being unwell. He crawls under the tent, sends out the boy with orders to look carefully whether the enemy are at hand, hides his sword under the pillow, and then spends a long time searching for it. When he sees a comrade wounded in the camp, he runs to him and urges him to take heart; he tends him, wipes away the pus, and brushes off the flies. In short, he does anything rather than fight with the enemy. When the trumpeter sounds the call to arms, he sits himself down

Amat etiam sanguinis de alieno vulnere plenus, ad reversos è pugna accedere, narras, se cum suo periculo unū ex amicis servasse. ad jacentem etiam tribules & populares introducit, qui cum visant: simul horum singulis narrat, se illum suis ipsius manibus in tētorium portasse.
units.tr: in the tent. "Go to the devil," he says, "this fellow won't let me get any sleep, sounding the signal so often." He is also fond of visiting those returning from battle, and when they have been wounded he tells them, with pride, that he saved one of his friends at the risk of his own life. He even brings in fallen fellow tribesmen and countrymen, and to each of those who see them he says that he carried that man into the tent with his own hands.

units.la: DE OLIGAR- CHIA, sive moribus optimatium.
units.tr: On Oligarchy, or the Manners of the Nobles.

units.la: Videri posit oligarchia, vehemens esse honorum cupiditas absque ullo lucri studio. Oligarchi sive optimatis hi sunt οὐκ ἐάσεις τὸν ἀν-θρωπον ὕπνῳ λαβεῖν πυκνὰ σημαίνων. ¶ αἵματος ἢ ἀνάπλεως ἀπὸ ἕ ἀλλοτρείας τραύ-μάτῳ[?], ἐπιλυγχάνειν τοῖς ἐκ τῆς μάχης ἐ-πανιέσι, ¶ διηγεῖσθαι ὡς κινδυνεύσας ὡς σέσωσε τῶν φίλων. ¶ εἰσάγων πρὸς τὸν κατακείμενον σιφλό-μυρῷ τὰς φιλέτας, τὸν δῆμον· ἐκ τέτων ἅμα ἑκάσῳ διηγεῖ-σθαι ὡς αὐτὸς αὐτὸν τῇ αὐτῆς χερσὶν ὅπι σκη-νὴν ἐκόμισεν.
units.tr: Oligarchy might seem to be a vehement desire for honours with no pursuit of gain. Oligarchs, or nobles, are the sort who "do not let a man get any sleep, constantly signalling" [οὐκ ἐάσεις τὸν ἄνθρωπον ὕπνῳ λαβεῖν πυκνὰ σημαίνων]. Full of blood from another's wound, they approach those returning from battle and boast that they saved one of their friends at their own risk. They also bring in their fellow-tribesmen and fellow-citizens to the man lying down, and to each of them they tell how they carried him into the tent with their own hands.

Deliberante populo ecquis magistratui in curatione pompæ fit comes adiiciedus, prodit ipse & eo se honore dignum pronuntiat. Homeri versuum tenet solum hûc unum, Non multos regnare bonum est: rex unicus esto. aliorum omniû nihil scit.
units.tr: Oligarchy might be defined as a kind of love of rule that craves strong gain. Such an oligarch, when the people are deliberating whether someone should be assigned as companion to the magistrate in charge of a procession, comes forward himself and declares that he is worthy of that honour. He holds on to only one of Homer's verses, "Many rulers is not good; let there be one ruler," and knows nothing of all the rest. He does not hesitate to use such words as: "We ought to gather together and deliberate, and get free of this crowd in the marketplace." He keeps on approaching the magistrates, and when someone insults him, he says: "I and they cannot live in this city together."

units.tr: He is also accustomed to use this kind of talk: "We must gather together and deliberate, free ourselves from this forensic crowd, and close the approach to the magistrates against him." If some have wronged him, he says, "We cannot, I and they, live in this city." At midday he comes out in public, shaved in a medium style, with his nails carefully pared, strutting through the forum and saying, "There is no living

units.tr: in this city!" And in the courts, where many are in litigation, he makes trouble for people. Likewise, he says he is made to blush with shame whenever someone shabby and squalid sits beside him in the assembly; and that the whole class of orators who engage in public affairs deserves hatred. He claims that Theseus was the first author of these evils for the city. He also has similar talk with foreigners, and with those citizens who follow the same faction.

Annos natus sexaginta poëtarum versus memoriæ mandat: hos ad pocula canere incipiës obliuiscitur. Discit à filio quomodo fiat in acie conversio ad dextra, quomodo itē ad finistra. Dum rus pergit, alieno equo vehens simul obvios salutare meditatur: cadēs verò caput deturpat. Solet etiā ad statuam ludens se exercere:&c cum pedisequo arcu & iaculis certare: ac simul discere ab alio, & eundem docere velle, ac si esset is quoque artis imperitus. Idem lustans & in balneo Lavans nateis subinde agitat indecenter.
units.tr: Such a man, having reached sixty years, learns speeches by heart. Taking this as if he had learned everything, ... At sixty he commits the verses of the poets to memory; but when he begins to sing them over his cups, he forgets them. He learns from his son how to make a wheel to the right in battle formation, and likewise to the left. While going into the country on another's horse, he practises greeting passers-by at the same time; but when he falls, he disfigures his head. He is also accustomed to exercise himself by playing at a statue, and to compete with his footman with bow and javelins; and at the same time he tries to learn from another and to teach the same man, as if he too were unskilled in the art. Likewise, when he goes round the sights and bathes, he keeps wiggling his buttocks indecently.

units.tr: Evil-speaking is a disposition of the mind inclined toward the worse part in speech. The evil-speaker is characterised thus. If you ask, "Who is so-and-so?", he begins, like those who recount a pedigree, with the founder of the family: "His father, he says, was first called Sophias; enrolled among the numbers, he began to be called Sophistratus; then he became one of the common people enrolled among the dependants. His mother, indeed, is a noble Thracian woman, for they say that women of that kind are nobles at home. But he himself, born of such parents, is a worthless scoundrel." He goes on and says, "These are the women who snatch at passers-by from the road. ... Others also ..."

units.la: ΕΣΤΙ ἡ κακο-λογία ἀγὼν τῆς ψυχῆς εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐν λόγοις{*}. ὁ ἡ κακο-λόγῳ τοῖοσδέ τις ὅζιν, οἵῳ ἐρωτηθεὶς, ὁ δεῖνα τί ὅζις; καθάπερ οἱ ἡυεαλογῆν-τες πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῆς ἡύσης ὡτ ἀρξασ[?].
units.tr: Evil-speaking is a contest of the soul toward the worse in words. The evil-speaker is of such a kind that, when asked, "What sort of man is so-and-so?", he begins, like those who trace a pedigree, from the first ancestor.

units.la: Ὁ μὲν πατὴρ Σωσίας ἐξ ἐρχῆς ἐκαλεῖτο· ἐγίνετο δ' ἐν τοῖς σεαλιώταις Σωσίσεκτ[?]. ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐς τοὺς δημότας ἐνεγράφη. ἡ μὲν τοι μήτηρ Θεαίτα ὅςι. τὰς ἢ τοιαύτας ἐν τῇ παρθένῳ δύηρες ἐξ φασίν. αὐτὸς ἢ ἔτ' ὡς ἐκ τούτων γεγονὼς κακὸς μασιγίας. καὶ ἐ[?]ς {*}τούτοις διεξιών, αὐτὰ αἱ γυναῖκες ἐκ τῆς ὁδῷ τὰς παριόντας ἁρπάζεσι· ἢ κακῶς λεγόντων ἑτέρων σω-ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι ἢ αὐ-{*}τὸς, λέγων, ἢ ἐγὼ Τε-τὸν τὸν ἄνθρωπον πάντων μεμίσηκα, ἢ ὃ εἰδεχθής τις ὑπὸ τῷ προσώπῳ ὄψιν ἢ δὲ πονηρία ὑδὲν ὁ-μοιον. σημεῖον ᾧ, τῇ ἢ ἑαυτῆ γυναικὶ τρεῖς χαλκὰς εἰς ὀ-λον δίδωσι. καὶ τὰ ψυχρὰ λέγεσθαι[?] ἀναγ-κάζει τὸ Ποσειδῶνος {*}ἡμέρα. ἡ συγκαθή-μενος δεινὸς ᾧσεὶ {*}τὸ ἀνασάντος εἰπεῖν. ἢ ἄλλα πλεῖστα ᾧσεὶ τῶν φίλων ἢ οἰκείων τελευτηκότων κακῶς
units.tr: His father was at first called Sosias; he became Sosistratus among the enrolled, and then was entered among the demesmen. His mother is Theaita. Such women, they say, are noble at home. He himself, though born of such parents, is a worthless scoundrel. Going on through these matters, the women snatch the passers-by from the road. Others, when people speak ill of someone, take up the matter and say, "I too hate this man above all others; if you look at his face he is an ugly, hateful sight, and by his wickedness he is nothing like it." As proof, he gives his own wife only three coppers for the marketing, and he forces the cold water on the day of Poseidon. Sitting among others, he is clever at saying something against the absent, and he speaks ill of many other dead friends and relatives.

units.la: Τέλος de absente detrahentibus, idem facit ipse quoque, & ait, Ego etiam hunc hominem omnium odi maxime. Etenim si faciem spectes, turpis est & quem merito oderis: si improbitatem, nihil ei simile. Scias ita esse, cum uxori tres aeris nummulos in opsonium dare soleat: & ut Posidone mèse frigida lauet, cogere. Moris etiam habet, sedens inter plures, furgere ut aliquē accuset: plurimáque alia de amicis & familiaribus suis male loqui:& de ipsis etiam mortuis detrahere.
units.tr: Finally, he does the same with absent persons who are being disparaged, and says, "I too hate this man above all others." For if you look at his face he is ugly and deserves to be hated; if you look at his wickedness, he is nothing like that. You may know this is so, since he is accustomed to give his wife only three coppers for provisions, and to compel the washing in cold water on the day of Poseidon. He also has the habit, when sitting among several people, of rising to accuse someone; and he says many other evil things about his friends and acquaintances, and even disparages the dead.

The character of the ostentatious rich man.

units.la: ORATIO est, cùm alicuius natura certis describitur signis, quae sicuti notae quaedam naturae sunt attributa. Vt si velis non diuitem, sed ostentatorem pecuniosum describere: Iste, inquies, iudices, qui se dici diuitem putat esse praeclarum, primùm nunc videte, quo vultu vos intueatur. nónne vobis videtur dicere, darem si mihi molesti non essetis? cùm vero sinistra mentum subleuat, existimat se gemmae nitore, & auri splendore aspectus omnium perstringere. Cùm puerum respicit hunc vnum, quem ego noui (vos non arbitror nouisse) alio nomine appellat, deinde alio atque alio: Heus tu, inquit, veni Sannio, ne quid isti barbari perturbent: vt ignoti qui audiunt, vnum putent eligi de multis: ei dicit in aurem, aut vt domi lectuli sternantur, aut ab annunculo rogetur Æthiops, qui ad balneas veniat, aut asturconi locus ante ostium suum detur, aut aliquod fragile fulfa [?] choragium gloriae comparetur. Deinde exclamat, vt omnes audiant, Videto, vt diligenter enumeretur, si potest amitte noctem. Puer qui iam bene hominis naturam nouit, Tu illo plures mittas oportet, inquit, si hodie vis transnumerari. Age, inquit, duc tecum Libanum, & Sofiam. Sane.
units.tr: A description is when a person's nature is portrayed by certain signs, which are attached to it as marks of that nature. For example, if you want to describe not a rich man but a showy moneyed man, you might say: "That man, judges, who thinks it a fine thing to be called rich, look first at the expression with which he regards you. Does he not seem to you to say, 'I would give, if you were not a nuisance to me'? But when he props up his chin with his left hand, he thinks he dazzles everyone's eyes with the gleam of his gem and the glitter of his gold. When he glances at the one slave whom I know (I do not think you know him), he calls him by one name, then by another and another: 'Hey you, come here, Sannio, lest those barbarians make any mess!' so that the strangers who hear think he is picking one out from many. Then he whispers in his ear that either the couches are to be spread at home, or that his little uncle is to be asked to send the Ethiopian to the baths, or that a place is to be given before his door for the little Spanish horse, or that some fragile stage-prop of glory is to be got ready. Then he calls out, so that everyone can hear: 'See that it is counted carefully; if you can, let the night slip away.' The slave, who already knows the man's nature well, says: 'You ought to send more than that, if you want to be counted in today.' 'Come,' he says, 'take Libanus and Sophia with you. Very well.'

units.la: Deinde casu veniunt hospites homini, qui istum splendidè, dum peregrinaretur, receperunt: ex ea re homo hercle sane conturbatur: sed tamen à vitio natura non recedit. Bene, inquit, facitis cùm venitis: sed rectius fecissetis, si ad me domum recta abiissetis. Id fecissemus, inquiunt illi, si domum nouissemus. At istud quidem, inquit, facile fuit undelibet inuenire. Verum ite mecum: sequuntur illi: sermo interea huius consumitur omnis in ostentatione. § Quaerit in agris cuiusmodi frumenta sint: negat se, quia villa incensa sint, accedere posse, nec aedificare etiam nunc audere: tametsi in Tusculano quidem coepi insanire, et in isdem fundamentis aedificare. Dum haec loquitur, venit in aedes quasdam, in quibus sodalitium erat eodem die futurum: quo ipse pro notitia domini adium ingreditur cum hospi-tibus. Hic, inquit, habito. perspicit argentum quod erat expositum, visit triclinium stratum, probat: accedit servulus, dicit homini clare dominum iam venturum, si velit exire. Itane, inquit? Eamus hospites, frater venit ex Salerno, ego illi obuiam pergam: huc vos decima venitote. hospites discedunt. Ille se raptim domum suam coniecit: illi decima, quo iuserat, veniunt. quaerunt hunc. reperiunt domus cuius sit: in diuersorium deriti conferunt se. Vident hominem postera die: narrant, expostulant, accusant. ait ipse eos similitudine loci deceptos, angiporto toto deerrasse: contra valetudinem suam se ad multam noctem expectasse. Sannioni puero negocium dederat, ut vasa, vestimenta, pueros corrogaret. servulus non inurbanus, satis strenue et concinne comparat. ipse hospites domum deducit. Ait se aedes maximas quasdam amico ad nuptias commodasse. Nunciat interea puer argentum repeti: (pertinuerat enim, qui commodarat) Apage te, inquit: aedes commodaui, familiam dedi, argentum quoque vult? tametsi hospites habeo, tamen utitur licet, nos Samiis delectabimur. Quid ego qua deinde efficiat, narrem? eiusmodi est hominis natura, ut qua singulis diebus efficiat gloria atque ostentatione, ea vix anno sermone enarrare possim. Huiusmodi notationes, quae describunt quid consentaneum sit uniuscuiusque iuscuiusque natura, vehementer habent magnas destationem: totam enim naturam cuiuspiam ponunt anoculos: aut gloriosi, ut nos exempli causa coeperamus, [?]t inuidi, aut timidi, aut auari, ambitiosi, amatoris, luriosi, furis, quadruplatoris: denique cuiusfis studium [?]otrahi potest in medium tali notatione.
units.tr: Then by chance some guests arrive, who had entertained him splendidly while he was travelling. The man is thoroughly disconcerted by this, yet his nature does not depart from its vice. "It's good of you to come," he says, "but you would have done better to come straight to my house." "We would have done so," they reply, "if we had known the house." "But that," he says, "was easy to find anywhere. Come with me." They follow, and meanwhile his whole talk is spent on show. § He asks what sort of crops are in the fields; he says he cannot go near, since his farmhouse has been burned, nor does he yet dare to build again, though at Tusculum I have indeed begun to be mad and to build on the same foundations. While he is talking, he comes into certain buildings in which a club was to meet that same day; there, on the strength of his acquaintance with the owner, he goes in with the guests. "Here," he says, "I live." He looks over the silver that has been laid out, inspects the dining room laid with couches, and approves. A little slave comes up and tells the man plainly that the owner is now coming, if he wishes to go out. "So?" he says. "Let us go, guests; my brother is coming from Salerno, and I will go to meet him. Come to me at the tenth hour." The guests depart. He hurries home; they come at the tenth hour, as he had ordered. They look for him, find out whose house it is, and turn aside to an inn to take themselves off. They see the man the next day; they complain, remonstrate, and accuse. He says they were deceived by the likeness of the place and wandered through the whole alley; for his part, he had waited for them until late in the night, though his health was poor. He had given the slave Sannio a task: to gather vessels, clothes and boys. The slave, not unrefined, prepares them quite briskly and neatly. He himself leads the guests home. He says he has lent some very grand houses to a friend for a wedding. Meanwhile the slave announces that the silver is being demanded back, for the lender had been pressed. "Go away!" he says. "I lent the houses, I gave the household; does he want the silver too? Although I have guests, still, let him use it; we will enjoy the Samian ware." Why should I tell what he does after that? The man's nature is such that the things he does every day through show and ostentation I could hardly recount in a year's talk. Descriptions of this kind, which set out what is fitting to each person's nature, are of very great use, for they put the whole nature of someone before our eyes: whether a boastful man, as we began by way of example, or an envious, timid, avaricious, ambitious, amorous, luxurious, thieving or informing man. In short, any pursuit whatever can be brought into the open by such a characterization.

units.la: UTILIUS LUPUS DE FIGURIS SENTENTIA- RUM LIBRO II.
units.tr: UTILIUS LUPUS ON THE FIGURES OF SENTENCES, BOOK II.
The character of a drunken man.

units.la: CHARACTERISMOS[?]. Quemadmodum pictor coloribus figuras describit: sic orator hoc schemate, aut vitas, aut virtutes eorum de quibus loquitur, deformat. LYONIS. Quid in hoc arbitrer bona spei reliquum re[?]lere, qui omne vitae tempus una, ac desperatissima constitudine produxit? Nam simul atque ex primis horis ei, nimia cibi ac vini satietate, vix meridiano tempore, enus[?] crapula est experrectus: primum oculis mero madidis, humore obcaecatis, visu grauidis, lucem constanter tueri non potest: deinde confectis viribus, utpote cuius vena non sanguine, sed vino sunt repleta, se ipse erigere in valet: tandem duobus innixus languidus, qui cubanfit defatigatus tunicatus sine pallio, soleatus pre[?] lectulo palliolo frigus a capite defendens, flexa ceruice, summissis[?] genibus, colore exangui, protinus ex cubiculari lectulo excitatus, in triclinium trahitur: ibi praesto sunt cotidiani pauci eodem studio excitati conuiua. hic vero prinps[?] paulum illud reliquum quod habet mentis ac sensus, poculis extrudere festinat,& eos bibendo prouocat, & lacessit perinde ac si in hostium prælio quàm plurimos superarit, atque adflixerit, amplissimam sibi victoriam paratam existimans. Interea procedit simul & illud tempus, & potatio: oculi vinum lacrymantes caligant; ebriosum ipsi vix ebrij cognoscunt: alius sine caussa iurgio proximum lacessit: alius somno deditus, vt cogitur vigilare: alius rixari parat: alium turbas vitantem, ac domum reuerti cupientem retinet ianitor, pulsat, exire prohibet domum, interdictum demonstrans. Interim alium contumeliose extra ianuam eiectum, vacillantem puer sustentat, ac ducit pallium per lutum trahentem. Nouissime solus in triclinio relictus, non prius poculum ex manibus emittit, quàm somnus oppressit bibentem, ac dissolutis artubus, ipsum poculum suapte natura dormienti excidit.
units.tr: CHARACTERISMOS. Just as a painter depicts figures with colours, so the orator, by this figure, distorts either the lives or the virtues of those about whom he speaks. LYCO. What hope of good remains for a man who has spent his whole life in one desperate state of mind? For as soon as he wakes, at about midday, from the excessive gorging of food and wine and the morning's drunken sleep, first, his eyes, soaked with wine, blinded by moisture and heavy with sleep, cannot keep steady gaze on the light. Then, his strength spent, since his veins are filled not with blood but with wine, he is unable to raise himself. At last, leaning on two attendants, he is dragged, pale and limp, from his bedroom couch into the dining room. He is tired out, wearing only a tunic without a cloak, with sandals on his feet and a little cap on his head to ward off the cold, his neck bent and his knees weak, his face bloodless. There the few daily companions, roused to the same eagerness, are waiting. Here, first of all, he hurries to use the little reason and sense he still has left: he pushes the cups along, urges his companions to drink and provokes them, as if he were winning a great victory in a battle with enemies, thinking that a splendid triumph has been prepared for him. Meanwhile, both the hour and the drinking advance. His eyes, weeping over the wine, grow dim; the drinkers can scarcely recognise the drunkard. One man, without any cause, picks a quarrel with his neighbour; another, overcome with sleep, is forced to stay awake; another prepares to brawl; another, trying to avoid the disturbances and wishing to go home, is held back by the doorkeeper, who pushes him and forbids him to leave, pointing to the ban. Meanwhile, a boy supports another man who has been shamefully thrown out of the door and staggers, while he drags his cloak through the mud. Last of all, left alone in the dining room, he does not let go of the cup from his hands until sleep overcomes the drinker, and with his limbs slack, the cup itself, by its very nature, falls from the sleeping man. Characterismus.

units.la: Characterismus. In vulgatis editionibus legitur Chresterismus. absque dubio mendose.
units.tr: Characterismus. In the common editions it is read as Chresterismus, which is undoubtedly a mistake.
Aut vitas, read aut vitia; the sentences that follow confirm this.

units.la: Visu granidis. Prior vox mendum continet. Scrib. vino gr. οἰνοζαρέστ[?].
units.tr: Visu granidis. The first word contains an error. Write vino gravidis [οἰνοβαρές], heavy with wine.

units.la: Soleatus pro lectulo. Fortean, vt è lectulo. κρηπῖδας ἔ-χων ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς κλινῆς. Sed videtur qui Lyconis locū è Graeco vertit, reperisse in suo codice, ἐπὶ pro ἀπὸ: neque de menda esse suspicatus.
units.tr: Soleatus pro lectulo. Perhaps it should read ut è lectulo, "as from the couch." The Greek is κρηπῖδας ἔχων ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς κλινῆς [wearing sandals, as from the couch]. But the man who translated Lyco's passage from the Greek seems to have found ἐπὶ in his manuscript in place of ἀπὸ, and does not appear to have suspected an error.

units.la: Palliolo frigus a capite defendens. Rectè palliolo sic alibi: quia tamē Græcè scripserat Lyco, fortasse pileolo scribendum. πιλίδιον ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ ἔχων πρὸς τὸ ψῦχος.
units.tr: Warding off the cold from his head with a little cap. Palliolo is correct as used elsewhere; but since Lyco wrote in Greek, perhaps it should be written pileolo [πιλίδιον ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ ἔχων πρὸς τὸ ψῦχος], "with a little cap on his head against the cold."
He provokes his neighbour to a quarrel [τὸν πλησίον ἐρεθίζει].

units.la: Ex Q. Horatij Flacci Satyr. lib. 1. Sat. 1 x.
units.tr: From Q. Horatius Flaccus, Satires, Book 1, Satire 1.9

units.la: Bam forte via Sacra, sicut meus est mos, Nescio quid meditans nugarum, totus in illis. Occurrit quidam notus mihi nomine tantum, Arreptaq; manu, Quid agis dulcissime rerum? Suauiter, ut nunc est, inquam: & cupio omnia, quae vis. Cum assectaretur, Nunquid vis? occupo: at ille Noris nos, inquit: doctì sumus. hic ego, Pluris Hoc, inquam, mihi eris. miserè discedere quaerens Ire modo ocyus, interdum consistere, in aurem Dicere nescio quid puero. cum sudor ad imos Manaret talos: ô te Bollane cerebri Felicem, aiebam tacitus: cum quidlibet ille Garriret, vicos, urbem laudaret, ut illi Nil respondebam: Miserè cupis, inquit, abire, Iamdudum video: sed nil agis: usque tenebo: Persequar. Hinc quò nunc iter est tibi? Nil opus est te Circumagi: quendam volo visere, non tibi notum: Trans Tiberim longè cubat is prope Caesaris hortos. Nil habeo quod agam, & non sum piger: usque sequar te. Demitto auriculas, ut iniqua mentis asellus, Cum gravius dorso subiit onus. Incipit ille: Si bene me novi, non Viscum pluris amicum, Non Varium facies. nam quis me scribere plureis, Aut citius possit versus? quis membra movere Mollius? inuideat quod & Hermogenes, ego canto. Interpellandi locus hic erat. Est tibi mater,
units.tr: Just by chance, as is my habit, I was walking along the Sacred Way, lost in some trifling thought, my whole mind taken up with it. A certain man came up, known to me by name only, and seizing my hand said, "How are you, dearest of men?" "Very well, as things go," I said, "and I wish you everything you desire." When he kept following me, he asked, "Is there anything you want?" I pressed on, and he said, "You know me, I am a learned man." Here I said, "You will be worth more to me for that." Trying miserably to get away, I hurried, then stopped, then whispered something in my slave's ear, while sweat ran down to my ankles. "O Bolanus, happy in your brain!" I muttered to myself. While he chattered on about anything at all, praising the streets and the city, I answered him nothing. "You are miserably eager to leave," he said, "I have seen it these many minutes; but you won't get anywhere. I'll hold on; I'll follow you. Where is your route from here? There's no need to go around: I want to visit a certain man, not known to you, who lies sick far across the Tiber, near Caesar's gardens. I have nothing to do, and I am not busy: I'll follow you all the way." I drooped my ears, like a donkey that is unwilling when a heavier load has been put on its back. He began: "If I know myself well, you will not make Viscus a friend above me, nor Varius. For who could write more verses than I, or faster? Who could move his limbs more gracefully? Even Hermogenes would envy me when I sing." Here was the place to interrupt. "Have you a mother, relatives, anyone who needs you alive?" "No one: all are dead. Happy them! Now I alone remain. Finish me off, for a sad fate threatens me, which an old woman from the Sabine country foretold when I was a boy, shaking the divining urn: that neither bitter poisons nor an enemy's sword will carry him off, nor pain in the side, nor cough, nor slow gout. A chatterbox will destroy him at last; if he has any sense, let him avoid talkative people as soon as he grows up." We had come to the Temple of Vesta, the fourth hour of the day already past, and I had to answer in court to a man who had given bail, or else lose the case. "If you love me," he said, "stay here a little. Meanwhile, if I am able to stand, or if I know the civil law, I am hurrying to where you know." "I am uncertain what to do," I said. "Shall I leave you, or the case? Please let me go." "I won't do it," he said, and began to walk ahead. Since it is hard to resist, I followed along with the winner.

units.la: Cognati: quis te saluo est opus? Haud Mihi[?] quisquam: Omnes compositi. Felices: nunc ego resto: Confice: namque instat fatum mihi triste, Sabella Quod puero cecinit, divina mota anus urna. Hunc neque dira venena, nec hosticus auferet ensis. Nec laterum dolor, aut tussis, nec tarda podagra. Garrulus hunc quando consumet cunque: loquaceis, Si sapiat, vitet, simulatque adoleverit aetas. Ventum erat ad Vesta quarta jam parte diei Praterita, & casu tunc respondere vadato Debebat: quod ni fecisset, perdere litem. Si me amas, inquit, paullum hic ades. Interea si Aut valeo stare, aut novi civilia jura: Et propero quo scis. Dubius sum quid faciam, inquit: Tene relinquam, an rem. Me sodes. Non faciam, ille: Et pracedere coepit. ego, ut contendere durum est, Cum victore sequor.
units.tr: Relatives: who needs you alive? No one: all are laid to rest, happy in their lot. Now I alone remain. Finish me off, for a sad fate is upon me, which an old woman from Sabina foretold when I was a boy, shaking the divining urn: that neither bitter poisons nor an enemy's sword will carry him off, nor pain in the side, nor cough, nor slow gout; a chatterbox will be his undoing, so let him, if he has sense, avoid talkative people as soon as he grows up. We had come to the Temple of Vesta, the fourth hour of the day already past, and I had to answer in court to a man who had given bail, or else lose the case. "If you love me," he said, "stay here a little. Meanwhile, if I am able to stand, or know the civil law, I am hurrying to where you know." "I am uncertain what to do," I said. "Shall I leave you, or the case? Please let me go." "I won't do it," he said, and began to walk ahead. Since it is hard to resist, I followed along with the winner.

units.la: ISAACI CASAVBONI IN THEOPHRASTI CHA-racteres Ethicos Prolegomena.
units.tr: Isaac Casaubon's Prolegomena to the Ethical Characters of Theophrastus.

units.la: NScRIPTIO huius libelli, quæ in omnibus codicibus hæc est, Θεοφράστε[?] Ηθικοὶ χαρακτῆρες, tribus verbis triadeclarat: auctore scripti istius: materiam eius, siue subiectum: formam siue tractandi modum: de quibus omnibus aliquid est nobis hoc loco dicendum. Auctorem esse verè aureoli libelli istius Theophrastum Eresium, magnum illum maximi Aristotelis discipulum, verum censeo. Nam & Diogenes Laertius inter Theophrasti librorum indices, Ηθικὸς χαρακτῆρας[?] recensèt: & Suidas qui paucissimos eius philosophi libros commemorat, huius tamen meminit: quod etiam indicio esse possit, in pretio olim apud doctos Theophrasti hoc opus fuisse. Deinde quum certum omnino sit, prodiisse hæc ex eruditissimi & elegantissimi alicuius viri officina, qui Athenis eo ipso tempore quo claruit Theophrastus, & vixerit (id quod non vno loco annotatum à nobis demonstratúmque est) & scripserit, non video quid caussæ esse queat, cur aut veterum codicum, qui omnes in Theophrafti nomine consentiunt, fidem in dubium vocemus: aut si de illorum fide non dubitetur, quid opus sit Theophraftum alium ab Erefio illo quærere, omnibus seculis inauditum, omnibus priscis scriptoribus illaudatum, cui hæc tribuantur. Accedit huc Euftathii testimonium, qui in rhapfodiam Iliadis v, non hoc solum docet, scriptos esse à Theophrasto (Erefium absque dubio intelligit,) Characteres: sed illud etiam manifestò indicat, ita planè illos fuisse scriptos, vt factum videmus in his reliquiis. Quare non assentior doctis quibusdam viris, qui ab Ariftotelis discipulo hunc librum abiudicarunt: qui præter illud vnicum argumentum de quo mox dicemus, nihil penitus habent quo suam fententiam tueri possint. An enim illud dicent? parum tanto scriptore dignum hoc esse scriptum. Ita video doctissimum Victorium exiftimaffe. Mihi vero contrarium prorsus viderur: nam & opus hoc, efset modo integrum, & quale auctor ediderat, diligentiffimum iudico quod tanto viro tribuatur: & vicissim, eo fuisse comperior Theophraftum ingenio, vt nemo aptior huic argumento isto modo tractando inueniri potuerit. Fuisse enim illum politiffimi, elegantiffimi & amoenissimi ingenii virum (talem omnino hæc opera desiderabat) cum alia arguunt quæ de eo, & ex eo apud veteres fcriptores leguntur: tum illud in primis quod de illo Hermippus ipsius æqualis apud Athenæum testatur: singularem quandam fuisse hominis venustatem & industriam in exprimendis effingendisque hominum moribus: quod quàm belle auctori huic conueniat, nemo non intelligit. Ideo videtur M. Tullius Theophrasti scriptis vnicè capi delecctarique solitus, & vt auctor est Plutarchus, delicias suas eum appellitate : amicum etiam suum,ad Atticum scribens, vocat, sæpéque dilaudat. quin Aristoteles quoque apud A. Gellium lib. xiii[?], suauitatem huius sui discipuli linguæ pariter ac vitæ commendat. Nihil dicam de stylo : nam quæ magna adeo similitudo aut dissimilitudo in his tam paucis chartis, cum reliquis Theophrasti scriptis, in tanta præsertim argumentorum dissimilitudine, notari posset ? & tamen qui illa legerit aliquando, non dubito quin etiam in his Theophrastei characteris notas saltem aliquas mecum sit agniturus. Atque illud quidem in primis : quòd & hæc & illa cùm legas, scias facile ab Aristotelis discipulo vtraq; esse profecta. Sed nimirum doctos-homines qui aliter existimarunt, monuit locus ille in epistola προσφωνητικῇ[?], vbi ait auctor, se hæc scripsisse, cum annum ætatis iam absoluisset vndecentesimum: id enim Eresio Theophrasto conuenire non posse: quippe cuius vitæ terminum statuat diligentissimus auctor, Diogenes Laertius, annum octuagesimum quintum. Nos quoque olim impulit hæc ratio, vt de menda suspectum Theophrasti locum haberemus : nam vt propter hoc vnum argumentum negemus Aristotelei Theophrasti librum hùc esse, adduci nunquam potuimus. Putabamus igitur scribendum esse in libelli huius initio, non ἐννήκοινῷ ἐννέα[?], vt omnes libri habent : sed vt ait Laertius, ἐξ ὁμωνύμου[?] ἐννέα[?]. Neque enim verisimile nobis videbatur, aut Laertij codices hic falsos esse, aut ipsum. Nam si ita esset, aiebamus, & ad centesimum vsque annum Theophrastus vitam produxisset, nō videtur M. Tullius quo loco querelam Theophrasti morientis de breuitate vitæ humanæ refert, tacituros fuisse, quàm longam nactus ille vitam, de natura tamen quæreretur. videtur etiá Censorinus vir vndecunque doctissimus, cum plerosque veteres philosophos longæuos in libro De die natali, cap. x v. nominaret, Theophrastum non fuisse omissurus. Multo verò minùs Lucianus qui ex professo omnes pene μακροβίους[?] philosophos libro singulari collegit, hunc tanti præsertim nominis virum, omisisset. Hæc igitur nos olim, vt arbitramur etiam nunc, non sine aliqua ratione. etsi de emendatione verborum Theophrasti, propter eas causas, quæ ibi exponentur, sententiam mutauimus. Atque ex iis quæ eo loco scripsimus satis paret illorum error, qui aut Theophrastum aliquem aliū à discipulo Aristotelis comminiscuntur, aut omnino Theophrastum fuisse huius libri patrem negāt. Verum de auctore quidem satis superque.
units.tr: The title of this little book, which is the same in all the manuscripts, Θεοφράστου Ηθικοὶ χαρακτῆρες [Theophrastou Ēthikoi charaktēres], declares three things in three words: the author of the work, its matter or subject, and its form or manner of treatment. I must say something about each of these here. I hold that the author of this truly golden little book is Theophrastus of Eresus, the great pupil of the great Aristotle. Diogenes Laertius, in his catalogue of Theophrastus' books, lists the Ethical Characters [Ηθικὸς χαρακτῆρας], and Suidas, who mentions very few of this philosopher's books, also records this one. That may itself be a sign that this work was once highly prized by learned men. Furthermore, since it is quite certain that these pieces came from the workshop of some very learned and elegant man who lived at Athens at the same time as Theophrastus, flourished then, and wrote (as I have noted and shown in more than one place), I do not see what reason there can be either to doubt the testimony of the old manuscripts, which all agree in ascribing the work to Theophrastus, or, if their testimony is not doubted, why we should look for some other Theophrastus, different from the Eresian, to whom these pieces could be assigned, a man unknown in every age and unmentioned by all the older writers. To this is added the testimony of Eustathius, who, in his commentary on the fifth rhapsody of the Iliad, not only teaches that the Characters were written by Theophrastus (he undoubtedly means the Eresian), but also plainly indicates that they were written in just the way we see in these surviving fragments. So I do not agree with certain learned men who have denied this book to the pupil of Aristotle. Apart from that one argument, which I shall mention shortly, they have nothing at all to support their opinion. Will they say this: that the work is too unworthy of so great an author? That, I see, is what the most learned Victorius thought. But to me the opposite seems entirely true. I judge this work, were it complete and in the form its author gave it, to be so painstaking that it deserves to be ascribed to so great a man. And conversely, I find that Theophrastus had such a talent that no one more suited to treating this subject in this way could have been found. For that he was a man of most polished, elegant and charming talent (and such a talent this kind of work absolutely requires), we may learn both from other things read about him and from his writings among the ancient authors, and above all from what Hermippus, his contemporary, bears witness to in Athenaeus: that he had a singular charm and diligence in portraying and depicting human manners. How well this suits the author of this work, everyone understands. For this reason Marcus Tullius seems to have been accustomed to take delight in the writings of Theophrastus alone, and, as Plutarch reports, he called him his darling; and in writing to Atticus he calls him his friend and often praises him highly. Indeed Aristotle too, in Aulus Gellius (book 13), commends the sweetness of this pupil's language and of his life alike. I say nothing about the style: for what great likeness or unlikeness could be noted between these few pages and Theophrastus' other writings, especially given such great dissimilarity of subject? Yet whoever has read both, I do not doubt, will at some point recognise with me at least some marks of Theophrastus' character even in these pages. And above all this: when you read these and those, you will easily know that both came from the pupil of Aristotle. But the learned men who thought otherwise were certainly moved by that passage in the dedicatory letter, where the author says that he wrote these things when he had already completed his ninety-ninth year. For this, he says, cannot suit Theophrastus of Eresus, whose end of life the most careful writer Diogenes Laertius sets at his eighty-fifth year. This same reasoning once moved me too to suspect the text of Theophrastus of corruption. For I could never bring myself, on account of this one argument alone, to deny that this little book is by the pupil of Aristotle. So I thought that in the opening of this little book one should read, not "ninety-nine" as all the books have [ἐννήκοντα ἐννέα], but, as Laertius says, "ninety-nine" in the other sense [ἐξ ὁμωνύμου ἐννέα]. For it did not seem likely to me that either the manuscripts of Laertius or he himself were in error here. For if it were so, I argued, and Theophrastus had lived on to his hundredth year, Marcus Tullius would not, in the place where he reports Theophrastus' lament on dying about the brevity of human life, have failed to say how long a life he had attained, though he still complained about nature. Censorinus too, a most learned man in every respect, when in his book On the Birthday, chapter 15, he named most of the long-lived ancient philosophers, would not have omitted Theophrastus. And much less would Lucian, who in a single book deliberately gathered almost all the long-lived philosophers, have left out a man of such great name. These were my views then, and I still think them not without some reason, although, for the reasons that will be set out there, I have changed my opinion about the correction of the words of Theophrastus. From what I wrote in that place it is sufficiently clear how wrong those are who either invent some other Theophrastus, not the pupil of Aristotle, or deny altogether that Theophrastus was the father of this book. But enough and more than enough about the author.

units.la: Argumentum autem & subiectum scripti istius philosophicum plané est: de moribus enim hominum hic agitur, & ad bene honesteque vitam degendam nobis hoc scripto præire Theophrastus voluit: quo nihil est φιλοζωικώτερον, nihil philosopho dignius. Enimuero morum conformandorum quod ethicus philosophus prærogatiuæ iure quodam, quasi proprium sibi assumit, non vna est à veteribus sapientibus inuenta & exculta ratio. Nā idem hic, si propius attendimus, & ethici philosophi, & historici, & poetæ finis est: verum illius quidem ἁπλῶς[?] : horum non ἁπλῶς[?] : habent enim hoc amplius & historicus & poëta suos peculiares fines : ille, ut rerum gestarum memoriam conferuet: & ut lectorem suum iis maximè præceptis quæ ad Remp. bene gerendam necessaria sunt, instruat: hic ut τὸν ἀκροατὴν[?] iuvando simul etiam delectet.
units.tr: The argument and subject of this work is entirely philosophical. For it deals with the manners of men, and Theophrastus wished by this writing to guide us toward living a good and honourable life. Nothing is more life-loving (φιλοζωικώτερον [philozōikōteron]) than this, and nothing is more worthy of a philosopher. Indeed, the forming of morals, which the ethical philosopher takes to himself as if by a certain right of precedence, as his own, has been discovered and cultivated by the ancient sages in more than one way. For if we look more closely, the same end belongs to the ethical philosopher, the historian and the poet, though in the case of the philosopher it is the end simply (ἁπλῶς [haplōs]), while theirs is not simply so. For the historian and the poet each have further and peculiar ends of their own. The historian aims to preserve the memory of deeds done, and to instruct his reader in those precepts above all that are needed for the good conduct of the commonwealth. The poet aims to delight the listener (τὸν ἀκροατήν [ton akroatēn]) while also helping him.

units.la: Quare tendunt quidem eôdem omnes quodammodo : sed diuersis tamen itineribus. Philosophi ratio simplex est, & ut sic dicam, recta directáque via : de virtute enim & vitio disputans, illam fequendam, hoc fugiendum nos docet: & ad eam rem præcepta nobis suggerit. Historicus & poëta, non virtutes nec vitia in abstracto (ut loquuntur) nec eorum caussas naturámve, quod philosophorum est: sed his præditos homines confiderant: factáque nobis & mores utrorumque explicantes, imitandorum atque fugiendorum exempla suppeditant: & tacitè quodammodo nos inspicere in vitas hominum iubent, atque ex aliis fumere exemplum nobis. Rursus autem magna est latáque inter historicum & poëtam differentia: ille res gestas, uti gestæ sunt, simpliciter narrat: hic & gestas, (non enim omnia fingunt, sed multa affingunt tantùm poëtæ, ait verissimè scriptor eruditiffimus Strabo) & quæ geri potuerunt, cum decenti imitatione exequitur: unde illi ϑοιητὴς[?], ut Plato docet, nomen inditum: quia rerum quas refert, non narrator solùm ut historicus: sed quasi fabricator est & auctor: quod ille imitandi artificio præstat. Omnis enim poëta μιμητὴς[?], ait idem Plato. Ipsorum quinetiam poëtarum, multiplex est inter ipsos discrimen: differunt enim, ut docet Ariftoteles, τῷ ἑτέρως, τῳ ἑτέρως, τῳ ἑτέροις μιμεῖσθαι. Quorsum hæc? vt appareret libellum hunc, medii cuiusdam esse inter philosophorum & poëtarum scripta generis. Subiectum quidem est de moribus: quos emendare, vnicus est auctori in hoc opere finis propositus: atque hoc saltem illi cum ethico philosopho commune est, & ambobus proprium. Cæterum tractatur hoc subiectum, non more philosophorum: sed novo quodam docendi genere, quod descriptione constat eorum quæ homines aut hac aut illa virtute vitióve præditi, facere ἢ ζωῆς εἴσι consueuerunt: διαφέρει δ' ὡδὲν (inquit philosophus, quarto Nicomacheorum) τῶ ἐξιν ἢ τ κῇ τῶ ἐξιν σκο-πεῖν. Fit autem hoc à Theophrasto magna ex parte μιμητικῶς: quod poëtarum esse, supra posuimus. Itaque plurima inuenias in his breuibus reliquiis, quæ veluti tabulæ e naufragio superstites vtcunque remanserunt, ex quibus huius operis cum poëtis, scenicis maximè & comicis, quos esse optimos exprimendorum morum artifices scimus, affinitas percipi queat: vt suis locis cum cura est à nobis indicatum. Mores igitur hominum ita hicolim erant descripti, vt liceret tanquam in speculo hinc virtutis splendorem & pulcherrimam intueri faciem: illinc verò vitiorum turpitudinem & dedecus animadvertere. Nunc, melior eius pars, proh dolor! intercidit: nam & ea pars quæ erat de virtutibus tota hodie desideratur: & illius quæ de viriis, haud, scio an portio saltem ἀξιόλογος fuerit, quantumcunque est quod ad nos peruenit. Quota enim est obscero vitiorum pars quæ hîc continetur?
units.tr: So all of them tend, in a way, to the same goal, but by different roads. The philosopher's method is simple, and, if I may put it so, straight and direct. For in disputing about virtue and vice, he teaches us to follow the one and flee the other, and he furnishes us with precepts for this purpose. The historian and the poet do not consider virtues or vices in the abstract (as the phrase goes), nor their causes and nature, which is the business of philosophers. Rather, they consider men endowed with these qualities. In setting forth their deeds and manners, both supply us with examples to imitate or to avoid, and they urge us, in a manner of speaking, to look silently into the lives of men and to take example from others for ourselves. Again, however, there is a great and wide difference between the historian and the poet. The historian narrates deeds simply as they were done. The poet, though he too narrates deeds that were done (for poets do not invent everything, but only add many things, as the most learned writer Strabo says very truly), also presents what could have been done, with a fitting imitation. Hence, as Plato teaches, the name ποιητής [poiētēs] was given to the poet, because of the things he relates he is not merely a narrator, as the historian is, but is, as it were, a maker and author. This the poet achieves by the art of imitation. For, as the same Plato says, every poet is an imitator (μιμητής [mimētēs]). Even among the poets themselves there is a manifold difference, for, as Aristotle teaches, they differ in their means, their objects and their manner of imitation (τῷ ἑτέρῳ, τῷ ἑτέρῳ, τῷ ἑτέρως μιμεῖσθαι [tō heterō, tō heterō, tō heterōs mimeisthai]). Why do I say all this? To make clear that this little book belongs to a certain middle kind of writing, between the writings of philosophers and those of poets. Its subject is manners, and the only end the author has set himself in this work is to correct them. This at least he shares with the ethical philosopher, and it is proper to both. But this subject is treated not in the manner of philosophers, but by a new kind of teaching, which consists in a description of those things which men, endowed with this or that virtue or vice, are accustomed to do in the course of their lives. As the philosopher says in the fourth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, it makes no difference whether one considers the state (ἕξις [hexis]) or what is done in accordance with the state (κατὰ τὴν ἕξιν [kata tēn hexin]). Theophrastus does this largely in a mimetic way (μιμητικῶς [mimētikōs]), which, as we have said above, belongs to poets. Thus in these brief remains, which have survived in some form like planks saved from a shipwreck, you will find much that lets one perceive the affinity of this work with the poets, especially the dramatic and comic poets, whom we know to be the best artists in representing manners. I have noted this with care in the appropriate places. The manners of men were described here in such a way that one could see, as in a mirror, the splendour and the most beautiful face of virtue on one side, and on the other the baseness and disgrace of vice. Now, alas, the better part of it has perished. For the whole part that dealt with the virtues is wholly lost to us today, and of the part on the vices, I do not know whether even a worthwhile portion would have been left, however much has come down to us. For how small a part of the vices is contained here!

units.la: Nomen porrò χαρακτῆρες quo suum hoc opus Theophraftus appellauit, à re impositum est, itaque argumento libri conuenit vt nihil supra. Erat namque hoc tanquam exemplar & speculum quoddam morum,vbi virtutis & vitij cuiusque expressæ notæ cernebantur. Itaque titulus hic Ἠθικοὶ χαρακτῆρες tantundem ferme valet, ac fi dixisset Εἰκόνες ἠθῶν (fiue εἰκονισμοί,vt appellat Seneca) hoc est, Imagines morum: sicut Cicero comicos appellat imaginem vitæ quotidianæ: & magnus Bafilius vitas sanctorum virorum,εἰκόνας ἐμψύχως τῆς χ̄ρ Θεὸν πολι- τείας.Εἰκὼν & χαρακτὴρ atque εἰσοπτρον sæpe eandem vim habent:Quare etiam , quod D. Paulus ad Colofl. dixit, Christum esse εἰκόνα τὰ ἀοράτυ Θεῦ, in ea ad Hebræos voce χαρακτὴρ est expressum. In libro autem Sapientiæ in eadem sententia vtitur auctor vocibus ἐξοπτρον & εἰκών. Porrò is verus est cuiufque rei χαρακτήρ,ea vera imago, quæ illius naturam optimè exprimit. Ideo Hebræi sapientes naturam vocant טבע , quasi dicas χαρακτῆρα, aut σφραγίδα. nam illis טבע sigillum significat. Veteres verò quidam qui post Theophraftum idem argumentum tractarunt, μικρὸν παρεκλίνοντες, vt diceret Ariftoteles, χαρακτηρισμὸς vocarunt , quos ille χαρα- κτῆρας : quidam longiùs abierunt,& similium fcriptorum titulos dissimiles (vti fere fieri videas ) sunt commenti. Seneca ad Lucilium,epistola xcvi.Ait vtilem futuram esse descriptionem cuiusque virtutis.Hac Pofidonius Aetiologiam ( malim Ethologiam, vide Quintilianum. )vocat:quidam χαρακτηρισμὸν appellant, signa cuiusque virtutis & vitij ac notas reddèntem, quibus inter se similia discriminentur.Hæc res eandem vim habet quam pracipere. Nam qui praecipit dicit, Illa facies, si voles temperans esse. Qui describit, aut Temperans est, qui facit illa, qui illis abstinet. Quaeris quid interfit? Alter praecepta virtutis dat: alter exemplar. Descriptiones has, & vt publicanorum vtar verbo εἰκονισμὸς, ex vsu esse confiteor. Pulcherrime ista Senecae explicat nostri huiusce libri Θεοφράστου: quaeris potius cum Seneca vertere De signis ac notis morum. Simplicius tamen nos, & vt in inscriptione, breuius, Morum descriptiones au Ctore Cicerone: qui in Topicis descriptiones Latine dicit, quos Graeci, inquit, χαρακτῆρας: alij rhetores χαρακτηρισμὸς dixerunt, vt Rutilius Lupus. nam pessime hodie in eius libris chrestlerifmus editum est, pro characterismus. eius locum infra describemus. Poteramus & Notationes morum: idque fortasse rectius: nisi M. Tullium sequi libitum fuisset. Auctor ad Herennium, Notatio est, cum alicuius natura certis describitur signis, quae sicuti nota quaedam, natura sunt attributa. quo loco extat sane quam elegans & graphica oftetatoris pecuniosi descriptio. Atque haec quidem ita: nunc illud vice corollarij adiiciemus. Et apud Graecos Satyrus antiquissimus Peripateticus, & apud Romanos doctissimus Varro, libros non dissimilis, vt videtur, argumenti ediderunt: quos tamen non χαρακτῆρας, sed χαρακτῆρων inscripserant. Varronis librum laudatum aliquoties apud Latinos grammaticos reperimus: verùm ita, vt de eius argumento pro certo quicquam pronuntiare non possimus. ac fieri potest, vt fit is ipse quem Nonius De proprietate scriptorum vocat. quod si est, nihil hûc scilicet facit. Satyri verò librum affinè huic Theophrasteo fuisse argumenti similitudine, fermè mihi perfuasit aliquando hic ex illo locus, ab Athenaeo prolatus, quem apponam: dignum profecto ubique, non ibi tantum legi. Est autem character hominis asoti. Οἱ πολέμιοι ἢ οὐσίας ὑπάρχοντες, καὶ κατα-θέχοντες τὸν ἀγρὸν, διαπράζοντες τὴν οἰκίαν, λαφυροπωλοῦντες [?] ὑπάρχον, σκοπούμενοι τί δεδαπάνηκε, ἀλλὰ τί ἀπέσεσαι, ἀλλὰ τί ἀ̓ πέσεσαι· ἐν τῇ νεότητι καὶ τῷ γήρως ἐφόδια προσκαταλιπόντες, χαίροντες τῇ ἑταίρᾳ, ὦ τοῖς ἑταίροις· καὶ πρὸ οἴνῳ, ὦ τοῖς συμπότας.
units.tr: The name χαρακτῆρες [charaktēres], which Theophrastus gave to his work, was taken from its subject, so it fits the content of the book exactly and nothing more could be asked of it. The book was, as it were, a model and mirror of morals, in which the distinct marks of each virtue and vice were seen clearly drawn. Hence the title Ἠθικοὶ χαρακτῆρες [Ēthikoi charaktēres] means almost the same as if he had written Εἰκόνες ἠθῶν [Eikones ēthōn], or εἰκονισμοί [eikonismoi], as Seneca calls them, that is, Images of manners. Cicero likewise calls comedy an image of everyday life, and the great Basil calls the lives of holy men living images of the life lived toward God [εἰκόνας ἐμψύχους τῆς πρὸς Θεὸν πολιτείας]. Eikon [εἰκών], charaktēr [χαρακτήρ] and esoptron [εἴσοπτρον] often have the same force. For this reason, when St Paul says in Colossians that Christ is the image [εἰκὼν] of the invisible God, the Epistle to the Hebrews expresses the same idea with the word charaktēr. In the book of Wisdom the author uses the words esoptron [ἔσοπτρον] and eikon [εἰκών] for the same thing. Moreover, the true charaktēr of any thing is that true image which best expresses its nature. So the wise Hebrews call nature teba [טבע], as if you were to say charaktēr or sphragis [σφραγίς], a seal, for teba among them means a seal. Some ancient writers who handled the same subject after Theophrastus, departing a little, as Aristotle puts it, called the genre charaktērismos [χαρακτηρισμός], and the works they wrote, which he called charaktēres. Others went further away and invented titles for similar writings that differ (as you may often see), Seneca to Lucilius, letter 96: he says that a description of each virtue will be useful. Posidonius calls this aetiologia (I would rather say ethologia; see Quintilian), while some call it charaktērismos, giving the signs and marks of each virtue and vice, by which like things are distinguished from one another. This procedure has the same force as giving precepts. For he who gives a precept says: "Do this, if you wish to be temperate." He who describes says: "He is temperate who does these things and abstains from those." You ask what the difference is? The one gives the rules of virtue, the other a model. I admit that such descriptions, or, to use the word of the tax-collectors, eikonismos [εἰκονισμός], are useful. Seneca explains this very well for our Theophrastus. You would rather render it with Seneca as On the signs and marks of manners, but we shall be simpler and, as in the title, briefer: Descriptions of manners. Cicero, in the Topics, calls descriptions in Latin what the Greeks call charaktēres, and other rhetoricians called them charaktērismos, as Rutilius Lupus does. For today, in his books, the word is very badly printed as chrestlerismus for characterismus; we shall describe its place below. We could also have said Notationes morum, and perhaps this would be more correct, were it not that we preferred to follow Marcus Tullius. The author to Herennius says: A notation is when the nature of someone is described by certain signs, which are attributed to it as if they were a kind of mark. In that passage there is indeed a very elegant and vivid description of a rich miser. So much for that; now we shall add something by way of a corollary. Among the Greeks Satyrus, the most ancient Peripatetic, and among the Romans the most learned Varro published books of a similar subject, as it seems; yet they entitled them not charaktēres but charaktērōn [χαρακτήρων]. We often find Varro's book cited by the Latin grammarians, but in such a way that we cannot state anything for certain about its subject. It may well be the very book Nonius calls On the Propriety of Writers; if so, it has nothing to do with this matter. As for Satyrus's book being close to this Theophrastean one in its subject, a passage from Athenaeus, which I shall set out, has at some time almost persuaded me of it. It is worth reading anywhere, not only there. It is the character of a dissolute man: His enemies are the owners of his estate; they seize his fields and pull down his house; they sell off his plunder, looking not at what he has spent but at what he will spend; leaving provisions behind for his youth and old age; rejoicing with the courtesan, with his companions and with his drinking-partners. [Οἱ πολέμιοι ἢ οὐσίας ὑπάρχοντες, καὶ κατα-θέχοντες τὸν ἀγρὸν, διαπράζοντες τὴν οἰκίαν, λαφυροπωλοῦντες [?] ὑπάρχον, σκοπούμενοι τί δεδαπάνηκε, ἀλλὰ τί ἀπέσεσαι, ἀλλὰ τί ἀ̓ πέσεσαι· ἐν τῇ νεότητι καὶ τῷ γήρως ἐφόδια προσκαταλιπόντες, χαίροντες τῇ ἑταίρᾳ, ὦ τοῖς ἑταίροις· καὶ πρὸ οἴνῳ, ὦ τοῖς συμπότας.]

units.la: Postremò neillud quidem prætermittam quod est à veteribus criticis probè, vt mea sententia fert, obseruatum. Aiunt illi, Homerum fontem illum ingeniorum, huiusmodi descriptionum primum auctorem esse: eundemque suo exemplo cum aliis præiuisse, tum etiam nostro huic auctori, quādo isti operi manum admoueret. Nam similem esse fortis & ignaui characterē hūc apud poëtā Iliad. lib.xiii.
units.tr: Last of all, I will pass over one point which the ancient critics have, in my judgement rightly, observed. They say that Homer, that fountain of talents, was the first author of descriptions of this kind, and that by his example he went before others, and also before our author here, when the latter set his hand to that work. For in the thirteenth book of the Iliad there is a similar character of the brave man and the coward.

units.la: Ἐνθ᾽ ὅ, τε δ᾽ ἁλὸς ἀνὴρ ὅςτ᾽ ἀλκιμῷ ἐξεφαάνθη. Τῇ μὲν γάρ τε κακῇ τρέπτει χερὸς ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ, Οὐδέ οἱ ἀπέμας ἤδη ἐρητύετ᾽ ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός. Ἀλλὰ μεσχαλάζει, καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀμφοτέρῃς πόδας ἴζε. Ἐν δέ τέ οἱ κραδίη, μεγάλα στέρνοισι παλλομένη Κῆρας οἰομένῳ· πάσχῳ δέ τε γίνετ᾽ ὀδόντων. Τῷ δ᾽ ἀγαθός, ὅτ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἐπέμπει χερὸς, ὅτέ τι λίλω Ταρβεῖ, ἐπεὶ δὲν παρὼν ἴσιζη λόχον ἀνδρῶν. Ἀρχῇ ὃ ᾿Ϛχισα μιγήμεναι ἐν δαὶ λυγρῇ.
units.tr: There the man of the sea, who has shown himself a man of courage ... For the coward, his hands shift now this way, now that; his spirit is no longer steady in his breast, but he is in anguish and sits down on both feet. His heart beats mightily in his chest, as he expects death, and his teeth chatter. But the brave man, when he is about to ... and he is not afraid, since he stands among the ranks of men. [Ἐνθ᾽ ὅ, τε δ᾽ ἁλὸς ἀνὴρ ὅςτ᾽ ἀλκιμῷ ἐξεφαάνθη. Τῇ μὲν γάρ τε κακῇ τρέπτει χερὸς ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ, Οὐδέ οἱ ἀπέμας ἤδη ἐρητύετ᾽ ἐν φρεσὶ θυμός. Ἀλλὰ μεσχαλάζει, καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀμφοτέρῃς πόδας ἴζε. Ἐν δέ τέ οἱ κραδίη, μεγάλα στέρνοισι παλλομένη Κῆρας οἰομένῳ· πάσχῳ δέ τε γίνετ᾽ ὀδόντων. Τῷ δ᾽ ἀγαθός, ὅτ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἐπέμπει χερὸς, ὅτέ τι λίλω Ταρβεῖ, ἐπεὶ δὲν παρὼν ἴσιζη λόχον ἀνδρῶν.]

units.la: [?]ccuratæ descriptiones: quas diligenter obseruasse, non ad eloquētię solūm studia, sed (quod antiquius esse debet) ad naturam virtutum & vitiorum penitus cognoscendam, utile fuerit & conducibile.
units.tr: Accurate descriptions, which it would be useful and profitable to observe diligently, not only for the study of eloquence but (which ought to come first) for a thorough knowledge of the nature of virtues and vices.

units.la: ISAACI CASAVBONI AD THEOPHRASTI CHARA- CTERES ETHICOS
units.tr: Isaac Casaubon on the Ethical Characters of Theophrastus

units.la: [?]ΔΗ μὲν καὶ πρότερον πολλάκις.] Ostendit Theophrastus, non imparatum se ad huius operis scriptionem accedere: sed re saepius secum considerata, expensaque. Ideo ait ὅτι σημαίνας τὸν διά-νοιαν[?]: familiari Aristoteli, & aliis philosophis loquendi genere. simplicius Xenophon initio Παι-δείας[?], Ἔννοια ποτὲ ἡμῖν ἐγχωρεῖ[?]. & initio Commentariorum, Πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα[?]. At noster mox quoque verbis significantissimis vtitur, σωθεωρήσας[?], & ἀπαγγελτικῶ[?]: quae dictiones, Θεάσαι inquam, & Θεωρῶν[?], à rebus diuinis originem habentes, de quibus dum attentius meditamur, fimus ipsi quodammodo diuini, & vt philosophus ait in decimo Nicomacheorum, nos ipsos ἀπαθανατίζομεν[?]: postea ad eas res sunt translatae, quas cum magna voluptate, vel magna cum attentione contemplamur. Eôdem spectat & quod ait, ὁμοιωθῆναι πανταχῶς ἀνθρώ-πων φύσειν[?]: fuit enim necesse vt qui describere hominum mores cogitaret, cum diuersæ naturæ & ingenij hominibus versaretur. Sic Plato 111. De Republica dicebat, eum qui futurus sit bonus iudex, debere τασ αυ[?]ταῖς φύσεσιν ὡμιλκέναι[?]. Horatius ad Pisones,
units.tr: "Indeed, I have often before..." [Δὴ μὲν καὶ πρότερον πολλάκις.] Theophrastus shows that he does not approach the writing of this work unprepared, but after having often considered and weighed the matter with himself. So he says that he has "signified the thought" [ὅτι σημαίνας τὴν διάνοιαν], a manner of speaking familiar to Aristotle and other philosophers. More simply, Xenophon at the beginning of the Education of Cyrus says, "It occurs to us at some time" [Ἔννοια ποτὲ ἡμῖν ἐγχωρεῖ], and at the beginning of his Memorabilia, "I have often wondered" [Πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα]. Our author soon also uses very expressive words, "having contemplated together" [συνθεωρήσας] and "in a way that reports" [ἀπαγγελτικῶς]. These expressions, I mean "to behold" [θεᾶσθαι] and "contemplating" [θεωρῶν], derive their origin from divine things; while we meditate on these attentively, we become in some measure divine ourselves, and, as the philosopher says in the tenth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, we "make ourselves immortal" [ἀθανατίζομεν]. Afterwards these words were transferred to those things which we contemplate with great pleasure or great attention. To the same point belongs what he says, "to be made like the natures of men in every way" [ὁμοιωθῆναι πανταχῶς ἀνθρώπων φύσεσιν]. For it was necessary that one who meant to describe the manners of men should associate with people of diverse nature and disposition. So Plato, in the third book of the Republic, said that he who is to be a good judge ought to have dealt with "the various natures" [τὰς αὐταῖς φύσεσιν ὁμιλεῖν]. Horace, in the Art of Poetry:

units.la: Respicere exemplar vitæ morumq;, iubebo Doctum imitatorem, & vivas hinc ducere voces.
units.tr: "I will bid the learned imitator look to the model of life and manners, and draw living words from there."

units.la: Ita, locum habet hîc quoque familiaris ille naturæ rerum circulus: Nam ex diligenti vitæ hominum obseruatione, confecta est hæc morum depictio: ex huius veluti tabulæ contemplatione non otiosa, vitæ & morum nascetur emendatio.
units.tr: Thus that familiar circle of the nature of things has its place here too. For this description of manners has been drawn up from a careful observation of human life; and from the attentive contemplation of this, as it were, picture, the amendment of life and manners will arise.

units.la: Τί γὰρ δὴ πρὸς τὴν Ἑλλάδα[?]; ] Legi malim, τί δὴ πρὸς τὴν [?]Ἑλλάδος: sicut mox, πάντων τῶν Ἑλλήνων[?].
units.tr: "What then, with regard to Greece?" [Τί γὰρ δὴ πρὸς τὴν Ἑλλάδα;] I would rather read "What then, with regard to Greece?" [τί δὴ πρὸς τὴν Ἑλλάδος], as shortly after "of all the Greeks" [πάντων τῶν Ἑλλήνων].

units.la: Duas hîc notat causas varietatis illius quæ in hominum moribus atque institutis cernitur: locorû positionem, & institutionem à pueris. Illud quàm magnum ad eam momentum sit, & experientia arguit, & philosophi, geographi, astronomiqué, vel docent, vel docere conantur: tangit etiam Hippocrates in libro de aëre, aquis, & locis: & Galenus multis locis. mitto quæ Polybius, Seneca, Cicero, aliúque multi super hoc non vno loco. Ingenia hominû, ait Curtius lib.v 111. vbique locorum situs format. In institutione autem puerili, nô dicam multum momenti: sed pene dixerim, ὅλον καὶ τὸ πᾶν[?] esse positum. Quod ait, Græciam totam eidem subiectam esse cæli regioni, Græcosque omnes eadem disciplina solitos imbui, accipiendum est vt dictum τὰχυμερέστερον[?], ac minus ἀκριβῶς[?]. Nam vt demus in eadem inclinatione cæli Græciam totam (non enim hîc loquimur de magna Græcia, aut Græcis Asiaticis, sed de ea tantum Græcia quæ velut matrix omnium Græcarum coloniarum erat) fuisse: tamen si eiusdem partes inter se compares, reperies differetiam fuisse & in aeribus regionum & in habitantium ingeniis mirum quantam. Ne longe abierim, quis nescit in Boeotia alium longe cæli haustum fuisse, alium in continenti Attica? longeque crassiore aëre usos quàm ipsorum vicinos Athenienses? Notum illud, Boeotum in crasso inrares aëre natum. Itaque etiam ingenia longe diuersa, ut ex Græca historia cuiusvis notum. Idem de reliquis terræ Græciæ regionibus dici potest. Quid autem de institutione? An putamus similiter suos liberos instituisse Athenienses & Lacedæmonios? Imò verò ita diuersa erat educatio, ut difficilius sit reperire in quo convenirent, quàm in quo differrent. Quare ut modò diximus commoda interpretatione iuvandum hoc Theophrasti dictum: deque iis tantùm accipiendum quæ Græcis solis propria, iisque omnibus communia erant: barbaris autem, aut eorum plerisque non item. Putavimus aliquando locum totum sic esse legendum: τί δὴ ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως ἁπάσης, ἔατο τὸν αὐτὸν αἰθέρα κλίμενος καὶ πάντων τῆς πολιτῆς ὁμοίως παιδί. Monebat hoc etiam, quod Theophrastus toto hoc libello de Atheniensibus tantùm videtur agere: omnia enim ad mores Athenienfium & ea quæ fieri in ea urbe solebant, referuntur. Veruntamen nunc placet magis ut nihil mutemus: sed locum ita ut supra exposui accipiamus. Nam quod de Athenis ita quasi de tota Græcia loquitur, hæc quoque causa esse potest: quòd illa urbs dum floruit, ocellus Græciæ, & ἙλλάδἙλλὰς fuit : vt non fine ratione, ficuti Roma δῆμος τῆς οἰκουμένης,& pop. Rom. δῆμος τῆς οἰκουμένης à Polemone oratore,vt referunt Galenus & Athenæus, vocatus est : ita Athenæ Ἑλλάδ[?] δήμῳ Ἀθηναίων[?] populus Athenienfis δῆμος τῆς Ἑλλάδος dici potuerit.
units.tr: Here he notes two causes of the variety that is seen in the manners and customs of men: the position of places, and training from boyhood. How great a weight the former has for this, both experience proves, and philosophers, geographers and astronomers either teach or try to teach. Hippocrates also touches on it in his book On Airs, Waters and Places, and Galen in many places. I pass over what Polybius, Seneca, Cicero and many others have said on this in more than one place. "The natures of men," says Curtius in book eight, "are shaped by the situation of places everywhere." As for childhood training, I will not say it has much weight, but I would almost say that the whole matter rests on it. As for his saying that all Greece lay under the same region of the sky, and that all Greeks were accustomed to be imbued with the same discipline, this must be taken as said roughly and less than exactly. For even if we grant that all Greece (for here we are not speaking of Magna Graecia, or of the Greeks of Asia, but only of that Greece which was, as it were, the mother of all the Greek colonies) lay under the same inclination of the sky, yet if you compare its parts with one another you will find a remarkable difference both in the air of the regions and in the dispositions of the inhabitants. Not to go far afield, who does not know that in Boeotia the air was quite different from that in Attica on the mainland, and that the Boeotians breathed a far thicker air than their neighbours the Athenians? That saying is well known: "born in thick Boeotian air". So too their dispositions were very different, as anyone knows from Greek history. The same can be said of the other regions of Greece. But what of training? Do we think that the Athenians and the Spartans brought up their children in the same way? Indeed the education was so different that it is harder to find where they agreed than where they differed. Therefore, as we have just said, this saying of Theophrastus should be helped by a fair interpretation, and taken only of those things which were peculiar to the Greeks alone and common to all of them, but not of the barbarians, or of most of them. We once thought the whole passage should be read thus: "why, from the whole city, they were under the same sky and were similarly brought up in the same way..." [τί δὴ ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως ἁπάσης, ἔατο τὸν αὐτὸν αἰθέρα κλίμενος καὶ πάντων τῆς πολιτῆς ὁμοίως παιδί]. What also warned us was that Theophrastus seems to treat only of the Athenians throughout this little book, for everything is referred to the manners of the Athenians and to what was customary in that city. Nevertheless we now prefer not to change anything, but to take the passage as I have explained above. For his speaking of Athens as if of all Greece may have this cause too: that while it flourished that city was the eye of Greece, and was Hellas itself; so that, not without reason, just as Rome was called by the orator Polemo "the people of the world" [δῆμος τῆς οἰκουμένης], and the Roman people "the people of the world", as Galen and Athenaeus report, so Athens could be called "the people of Greece" [δῆμος τῆς Ἑλλάδος], the Athenian people.

units.la: Propterea ait Menáder apud Alciphronem in epistola ad Glycerâ,videre fe ἐν ταῖς Ἀθήναις τὴν Ἑλλάδα ὅλην, τῷ Ἰωνίᾳ,ἕως Κυκλάδας πάσας[?]. Rectéque meo iudicio & verè Philo Iudæus, ὥσπερ ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ κόρη ἢ ἐν ψυχῇ λογισμὸς, τὸ ἐν Ἑλλάδι Ἀθῆναι[?]. Cæterum περὶ τῆς τῶν τρόπων οὐσίας[?] egregius est Theophrasti noftri locus,quem defcripfit & nobis cóferuauit Porphyrius in libro ii[?] περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων[?]. Diligens lector ibi requirat:nobis enim is liber nunc ad manum non eft:qui ista recenfemus non per otium in museo,fed ὁδὸς παρέργων ἐν ἀπορίᾳ[?], omnibus studiorum præsidiis destituti.
units.tr: For this reason Menander, in Alciphron's letter to Glycera, says that he sees "in Athens all Greece, Ionia, and all the Cyclades" [ἐν ταῖς Ἀθήναις τὴν Ἑλλάδα ὅλην, τὴν Ἰωνίαν, ἕως Κυκλάδας πάσας]. And rightly and truly, in my judgement, Philo the Jew says that "as the pupil is in the eye, or reason in the soul, so Athens is in Greece" [ὥσπερ ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ κόρη ἢ ἐν ψυχῇ λογισμὸς, τὸ ἐν Ἑλλάδι Ἀθῆναι]. But the passage of our Theophrastus concerning the substance of manners [περὶ τῆς τῶν τρόπων οὐσίας] is an excellent one, which Porphyry copied out and has preserved for us in the second book On Abstinence from Animals [περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων]. The diligent reader should look for it there; for that book is not now at hand for us, who are making these remarks not at leisure in a museum, but on the way, in difficulty, deprived of all the resources of study.

units.la: Pag. 2. καὶ βιβλιοκῶς.] Malim , ἄτε βιβ. vel ἄτε καί. Locum subobscurum dedimus operam vt planum versio redderet.
units.tr: "Page 2. And bibliokos [καὶ βιβλιοκῶς]." I would prefer "since he was a bibliophile" [ἄτε βιβ.], or "since also" [ἄτε καί]. We have taken pains to make this rather obscure passage clear in translation.

units.la: Ἔτη ἐννενήκοντα ἐννέα[?].] Ita legitur etiam in antiquis quatuor codicibus Palatinæ bibliothecæ. memini etiam in Ioannis Tzetzæ Chiliadibus hunc locum ita defcriptum reperire, & fimiliter annos centum vno dempto attribui Theophrafto hunc librum fcribenti.Quod etfi mirum eft, propter tot auctorum filentium, qui longæuos philofophos recenfuerunt: poteft tamen vnius faltem teftis, eiufque admodum ἀξιοπιστίᾳ[?], auctoritate defendi. Ait enim Hieronymus in epiftola ad Nepotianum, Vnde & sapiens vir Graciæ Theophrastus,(ita omnino fcribendum, non Themistocles) cum expletis centum & septem quadragesimum ait fuisse: vt necesse sit annum ei proximum qui habuit archonta Praxibulum, esse annum V. C. quadringentesimum trigesimum nonum. Sic autem Plinius libro tertio, Theophrastus qui primus externorum aliqua de Romanis diligentius scripsit, Circeiorum insulae & mensuram posuit, stadia LXXX. in eo volumine quod scripsit Nicodoro Atheniensium magistratu: qui fuit vrbis nostrae CCCCXL. annus. Ita scribi debuit hic locus, foedè in omnibus quas hactenus vidi editionibus corruptus. magistratu, inquam, legendum non magistratui. non enim ἄρχοντι Νικοδώρῳ, sed ἀρχοντος Νικοδώρου[?], Plinius dicere voluit. Iam diximus Plinium saepe illud ἄρχοντος Graecorum in historia Attica, vertere magistratu. Sic & Seneca epistola xviii. Hoc certè in his epistolis ait, quas scripsit Charino magistratu ad Polyænum. At in vulgatis Senecae editionibus scriptum inuenias Charino de magistratu. falsò: nam χαίρειν[?] ἄρ-χοντι dicere auctor voluit: & in meo scripto codice non extat illud de. Fuit Charinus hic archon anno primo olympiadis cxviii[?]. auctor Diodorus libro xx. Agebat Epicurus tunc temporis annum xxxv. siquidem natus est ille tertio anno olympiadis centesimae nonae: denatus autem anno altero olympiadis cxxviii. quod noto, vt obitet[?] Laertij vulgatas editiones emendem, in quibus malè scribitur obiisse Epicurum [illegible, ~25 letters]. vera lectio est, [illegible, ~30 letters]. Sed vt ad Plinium redeam, falsissimè sanè legunt vulgò cccclx. in superiore loco: legendum enim vt nos emendavimus, & quidam etiam veteres codd. habent, cccccxl. Mitto rationes chronologicas, quas de facili possim afferre. Plinium ipsum malo: cuius hæc sunt libro xiii. cap. xvi. Theophrastus qui primus à Magni Alexandri ætate scribit quæ circa urbis Romæ quadringentesimum quadragesimum gesta sunt annum. Non alia iam confirmatione opus habent superiores emendationes: & alioqui res eiusmodi est quæ inspectione magis fastorum Græcorum, Latinorumque indigeat, quàm longiore probatione.
units.tr: "Ninety-nine years" [Ἔτη ἐννενήκοντα ἐννέα]. This is read so also in the four ancient manuscripts of the Palatine library. I remember also finding this passage described thus in the Chiliads of John Tzetzes, and similarly ascribing to Theophrastus, writing this book, one hundred years less one. Although this is surprising, given the silence of so many authors who have listed long-lived philosophers, it can nevertheless be defended by the authority of at least one witness, and a very trustworthy one. For Jerome, in his letter to Nepotianus, says: "Hence also Theophrastus, the wise man of Greece" (it must be written thus, not Themistocles), "is said to have been in his forty-seventh year when he had completed one hundred and seven," so that the year next after him, which had Praxibulus as archon, must be the year of Rome 439. Pliny, in book three, writes: "Theophrastus, who first wrote somewhat more carefully among foreign authors about the Romans, set down the measure of the island of Circeii as eighty stadia, in the volume he wrote to Nicodorus in the magistracy of the Athenians, which was the four hundred and fortieth year of our city." This passage ought to have been written thus, and in all the editions I have seen so far it is shamefully corrupted. "In the magistracy," I say, must be read, not "in the magistrate." For Pliny wished to say not "to the archon Nicodorus" [ἄρχοντι Νικοδώρῳ], but "of the archon Nicodorus" [ἀρχοντος Νικοδώρου]. We have already said that Pliny often renders that Greek ἄρχοντος in Attic history as "magistracy". So too Seneca, in letter eighteen: "Certainly in these letters, he says, which he wrote in the magistracy of Charinus to Polyaenus..." But in the common editions of Seneca you will find written "Charinus de magistratu" falsely; for the author wished to say "greetings to the archon Charinus" [χαίρειν ἄρχοντι], and that "de" is not in my manuscript. This Charinus was archon in the first year of the hundred and eighteenth Olympiad, as Diodorus reports in book twenty. Epicurus was then thirty-five years old, since he was born in the third year of the hundred and ninth Olympiad, and died in the second year of the hundred and twenty-eighth Olympiad. I note this so that I may correct the common editions of Diogenes Laertius, in which it is wrongly written that Epicurus died [illegible, about 25 letters]. The true reading is [illegible, about 30 letters]. But to return to Pliny: the common editions read "four hundred and sixty" in the earlier passage, which is quite falsely read; it must be read as we have emended it, and some old manuscripts also have "four hundred and forty". I pass over the chronological arguments which I could easily bring forward. I prefer Pliny himself, whose words are in book thirteen, chapter sixteen: "Theophrastus, who first wrote from the age of Alexander the Great, of the events that happened around the four hundred and fortieth year of the city of Rome." The earlier emendations need no further confirmation; and in any case a matter of this kind requires more the inspection of the Greek and Latin calendars than a lengthy proof.

units.la: Καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ [?] τυγχάνει ψυχή. ] Ita accipe: exponam tibi: quid? ἐὰν ψυχὴ [?]. quomodo autem; καὶ ψυχή [?]. Illis declaratur subiectum: his modus & ratio eius tractandi. Legimus vero προσκείμενα non προκείμενα, ut vulgò: nam mores sunt accidentia quædam, quæ nobis προστίκει [?] & inhærent, atque habitus per quos dicimur ἦθοι [?]. M. Tullius mores comparat unguentis quibus corpus extrinsecus oblinitur, cùm ait in Bruto, Ita peregrinata eloquentia tota Asia est, ut se externis oblineret moribus.
units.tr: "And the soul [?] happens to be soul." Understand it thus: I shall explain to you. What? "If soul [?]." How? "And soul [?]." The first clause sets out the subject, the second the mode and method of treating it. We read proskeimena [προσκείμενα], not prokeimena, as the common text has it. For manners are certain accidents which attach to us and cling to us, and habits through which we are called ēthoi [ἦθοι]. Marcus Tullius compares manners to the unguents with which the body is smeared from outside, when in the Brutus he says: Thus eloquence, having wandered abroad, has covered all of Asia, so that it smeared itself with foreign manners.

units.la: οὐ τρόπον τὴν οἰκονομίαν χρῶντο [?]. ] Verba sonant, quomodo rem administrarent familiarem. Maluimus tamen aliter vertere: quia in plerisque capitibus de familiæ administratione nihil legas. Cæterū quod generaliter his verbis dicitur, cautè accipiendum, cùm hac restrictione, quod ad illa attinet quæ faciunt, ἢ ζωῆς εἰσιν, ἢ ζωῆς [?].
units.tr: "How they managed their economy" [οὐ τρόπον τὴν οἰκονομίαν χρῶντο]. The words sound as if they meant how they managed their household affairs. We preferred, however, to translate it otherwise, since in most of the chapters you will find nothing about the management of a household. As for what is said here in general terms, it must be taken with caution, with this restriction: as regards those things which they do, they either belong to life or to the life of others [?].

units.la: Τὰς ὑμῶν ἡμῶν. ] Videtur Theophrastus cùm hæc scribebat, vel natura vel adoptione liberos habuisse: quorum tamen neque Laertius meminit: neque ulla eorum in testamento Theophrasti mentio. Mouerit hoc fortasse aliquem: sed enim multi casus interuenire potuerunt post scriptum hunc librum, qui liberis illum orbum facerent. Quid si vero συλλογιστικὸν[?] ἀξίωμα esse dicamus, & in scribendo & in loquendo valde vsitatam figuram? Adde quod olim senes à iuuentute patres salutari solebant.
