units.tr: "Your and our" [Τὰς ὑμῶν ἡμῶν]. Theophrastus seems, when he was writing this, to have had children, either by nature or by adoption. Yet neither Laertius mentions them, nor is there any mention of them in Theophrastus' will. This may perhaps trouble someone; but many accidents could have intervened after this book was written to leave him bereft of children. What if we say that it is a syllogistic assumption [συλλογιστικὸν ἀξίωμα], and a figure of speech very common both in writing and in speaking? Add that in former times old men were customarily greeted as fathers by the young.

units.la: Πρῶτον μὲν οὖν π.] Pertinet hoc ad ordinem quem toto libro erat secutus: primum, inquit, de εἰρωνείᾳ verba faciam: deinde reliqua animi παθήματα σιγλατim describam. Quod sequitur, καὶ ἀρξόμαι πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῆς εἰρωνείας, non eodem referendum, sed ad methodum quam in singulis capitibus est seruaturus: quae ea est, vt vitium ipsum rudi descriptione initio statim adumbret: deinde vitiosum hominem suis coloribus depingat, iis commemorandis quae facere solet, quatenus talis est: puta, ὁ εἴρων, quà est εἴρων. Nonnunquam etiam breuem monitionem, velut ὑπομύθιόν[?] quoddam, & epicitharisma post fabulam adiicit.
units.tr: "First, then, ..." [Πρῶτον μὲν οὖν]. This pertains to the order which he followed throughout the book. First, he says, I shall speak about irony [εἰρωνεία]; then I shall describe the remaining passions of the mind one by one. What follows, "and I shall begin first from irony" [καὶ ἀρξόμαι πρῶτον ἀπὸ τῆς εἰρωνείας], is not to be referred to the same thing, but to the method he will keep in each chapter. This is: first, he sketches the vice itself in a rough description at the outset; then he paints the vicious man in his own colours, recalling the things such a man is accustomed to do, insofar as he is such. For example, the ironist, as far as he is an ironist. Sometimes, too, after the story he adds a brief admonition, a sort of moral tag [ὑπομύθιον], and an epicharisma [ἐπικιθάρισμα].

units.la: ὥσπερ ὑπερθέμβλω.[?] ] Quidam ὑπερθέμβλον[?]. quod est vsitatius, sed nihil mutandum. Sic in Rhetorica ad Alexandrum συλλήβδην ἢ τὰς πάσας πίστεις καθάπερ ὑπερθέμβλα[?] δεξιλαλύσαμεν[?]. Scripta lectio ὑπερθέμβλων[?]. vitiosè, pro ὑπερθέμβλω.
units.tr: "As if a hyperthemblos" [ὥσπερ ὑπερθέμβλω]. Some read hyperthemblon [ὑπερθέμβλον], which is more usual, but nothing should be changed. So in the Rhetoric to Alexander, "having briefly set out all the proofs like hyperthembla" [καθάπερ ὑπερθέμβλα]. The reading hyperthemblōn is written, faultily, for hyperthemblō.
On the chapter concerning irony [περὶ εἰρωνείας].

units.la: Ηὐλὴ οὖν εἰρωνείας.[?] ] Ante omnia sciendum est in vocibus εἴρων & εἰρωνεία latere homonymiam. Aliàs enim εἴρωνα cum vocant Graeci, qui ita fit factus, vt de se semper intra modum loquens, potius sibi ea bona demat quibus est praeditus, quàm alieni quicquam tribuat. Talis olim Socrates fuit, & postea Africanus teste Fannio apud M. Tullium; quos nemo propterea vituperauit, inquit ille. etsi, vt ex eodem Tullio discimus, reperti sunt etiam philosofophi quibus Socratis εἰρωνεία adeo non probaretur, vt non dubitarent, eum scurram Atticum nominare, vt est in primo De natura deorum. Hæc εἰρωνεία & iocandi ratio admodum olim familiaris Atheniensibus fuit: ideo ait Anacharsis apud Lucianum, [?]τῷ ἐκείνῳ λῶ ἄρα, ὁ ἐγὼ ἀεὶ ὑμῖν ὑπνου τῆς Ἀθηναίων, ὡς εἶπε εἰρωνεῖς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις[?]. & alibi idem εἰρωνείαν καὶ μυκτῆρα Ἀτ-τικὸν commemorat: Seneca nasum Atticum. eandem ob causam Epicurus homo non aptissimus ad iocandum, Ciceroni dicitur minimè respipiens patriam, fecundo De natura deorũ. sic enim omnino legendum non respiciens. Aliàs verò non cum laude hæc vox dicitur; sed summo potius cum probro: de eo enim vsurpatur, qui fimulare & dissimulare quiduis didicit non per iocum nec modestiâ vlla, sed fui commodi causa, & vt alteri incommodet. Sic apud comicos εἰρων inter grauissima conuitia ponitur, vt apud Ariftophanem. In sacris autem literis εἰρων hic, & εἰρωνεία nominari solent, ὑπόκεισις & ὑποκεῖσθαι, vocibus fignificantiffimis: quas Themiftius sua ætate ea notione solitas vsurpari in oratione quadam notat. Atque hæc est ea εἰρωνεία, isque εἰρων de quo Theophraftus hoc toto capite. Ariftoteles contra in Nicomachheis priorem illam intelligit, non hanc posteriorem: quod moneo, quia video doctos viros aliter hæc accepisse: in quo sanè eos ratio fugit, vt ex sequentibus apparebit. Porrò εἰρωνείαν de qua hic, non placuit dissimulationem dicere: nimis enim angusta augusta est ea vox, ut etiam Quintiliano visum: cùm hîc non de dissimulatione agatur, qualis fuit illa Socratica: sed longè ut diximus alia, cum dissimulatione, tum etiam simulatione: eorum nimirum qui ob turpem aliquam causam, tam simulant se habere aut agere quod non habent, aut non agunt: quàm de iis qui quod habent agúntve dissimulant. Cicero de hac ironia loquens, utramque vocem solet coniungere. Officiorum libro tertio, Quod si Aquiliana definitio est vera, ex omni vita simulatio dissimulatióque tollenda est. Et mox, Ita nec ut emat melius, nec ut vendat, quicquam simulabit dissimulabitve vir bonus. Saluftius Catilin. cuiuslibet rei simulator ac dissimulator. Idem auctor falsum vocat hominem εἴρωνα. & re vera, εἰρωνεία hic descripta, fallacia est. Nos malumus tamen vel ironiam (quàdo eam vocem ciuitate Romana Tullius ipse donauit) vel cauillationem, vitiú hoc Latinè dicere. vix enim aliam dictionem Latinam reperias quae Graecae fit magis ἀλίσχρῳ[?] similis enim in ea later homonymia. Gloffarium Cauillatio, κακοήθεια[?], εἰρωνεία. Sic accipitur verbum Cauillari apud Liuium, aliosque. Plutarchus hominem εἴρωνα, qualis hic describitur, vocat ἀλαζόνα καὶ ἀναλγῆ[?] in comparatione Alcibiadis cum Coriolano.
units.tr: "Then, therefore, of irony" [Ηὐλὴ οὖν εἰρωνείας]. Before all things it must be understood that the words eirōn [εἴρων] and eirōneia [εἰρωνεία] carry an ambiguity. For otherwise the Greeks call a man eirōn who has been so made that, always speaking within measure about himself, he rather takes away from himself those goods with which he is endowed than attributes anything to another. Socrates was once such a man, and afterwards Africanus, as Fannius testifies in Marcus Tullius; no one blamed them for it, says he. Yet, as we learn from the same Tullius, there were even philosophers to whom the irony of Socrates was so far from pleasing that they did not hesitate to call him an Attic buffoon, as is said in the first book On the Nature of the Gods. This irony and manner of jesting was very familiar to the Athenians of old. Hence Anacharsis, in Lucian, says that he was sorry for the Athenians, as if they were ironical in their speeches; and elsewhere the same man mentions Attic irony and sneer [εἰρωνείαν καὶ μυκτῆρα Ἀττικόν]; Seneca speaks of the Attic nose. For the same reason Epicurus, a man not very apt for jesting, is said by Cicero to be by no means looking back on his country, in the second book On the Nature of the Gods; for so it must be read entirely, not respiciens. Elsewhere, however, the word is not used with praise but rather with the greatest reproach. For it is applied to a man who has learned to feign and dissemble anything, not in jest nor with any modesty, but for his own advantage and to injure another. Thus among the comic poets eirōn is placed among the gravest insults, as in Aristophanes. In sacred literature, however, the ironist and irony are commonly called hypokesis [ὑπόκεισις] and hypokeisthai [ὑποκεῖσθαι], very significant words, which Themistius, in a certain speech, notes were customarily used in that sense in his own time. And this is that irony, and that ironist, of whom Theophrastus treats in this whole chapter. Aristotle, on the contrary, in the Nicomachean Ethics understands the former sense, not this latter one. I note this because I see that learned men have understood these things differently; in which they have certainly missed the reasoning, as will appear from what follows. Moreover, we did not think fit to render the irony of which we speak here as dissimulation; for that word is too narrow, as it seemed also to Quintilian, since here we are not treating of dissimulation of the kind Socrates practised, but, as we have said, of something quite different: both dissimulation and also pretence, namely of those who, for some base reason, pretend to have or to do what they do not have or do, or who conceal what they have or do. Cicero, speaking of this irony, is accustomed to join both words. In the third book of the Offices: But if the definition of Aquilius is true, pretence and dissimulation must be removed from all of life. And soon after: So neither in order to buy better, nor to sell, will a good man pretend or dissemble anything. Sallust in the Catiline: a pretender and dissembler of anything whatever. The same author calls a man eirōn a deceiver; and indeed the irony described here is deceit. We prefer, however, to express this vice in Latin either as ironia (since Tullius himself gave that word citizenship in the Roman tongue) or as cavillatio. For you could hardly find another Latin term that is more like the Greek one in this respect, since in it too the ambiguity lies. The glossary has cavillatio: malice [κακοήθεια], irony [εἰρωνεία]. The verb cavillari is understood in this way in Livy and others. Plutarch, comparing Alcibiades with Coriolanus, calls a man eirōn of the kind described here boastful and unfeeling [ἀλαζόνα καὶ ἀναλγῆ].

units.la: προσποίησις[?] ὅτι χεῖρον πράξεων καὶ λόγων. ] Hæc Theophrasti definitio, siue descriptio. Aristoteles vero sic, προσποιητὴς[?] ὅτι ὁ ἔλαττον ὁμοίως ἐν λόγοις καὶ ἐν πράξει[?]. Hanc definitionem hausimus partim ex libro quarto, partim ex fecundo Nicomacheoum. Differentia in vnica voce posita est. Aristotees[?] ait, ὅτι ὁ ἔλαττον in minus: de eo enim irone intelligebat,qui omnia minora fingeret : Theophraftus ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον [?] in peiorem partem : quia de eo loquebatur qui non deteriora tantùm sua fingeret : sed omnia etiam ad malum aliquem finem referret : quod perpetuò obseruabis in omnibus notis quibus suum εἴρωνα insignit. Tantum igitur commune est inter vtrunque, quod simulatione vterque vtitur,& à vero vterque discedit : finis verò longè diuersus. Si quis dicat, etiam eum de quo Ariftoteles sentit & loquitur, qualis nempe fuit Socrates, posse quiduis ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον [?] fingere. Respondemus ex Ariftotele, ὡς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει ἔστιν ὁ εἴρων : sed ἐν τῇ προαιρέσει. Non enim fi quis ea facultate praeditus fit,vt quiduis simulare,dissimulareque fui commodi causa queat, statim εἴρων & hypocrita fuerit dicendus : sed fi ad facultatem eam voluntas accefferit. Solitus olim gloriari imperator Titus,fe vel maximum falsarium esse potuisse:imitari enim norat omnium manus & chirographa. nemo tamen propterea falsarium eum merito dixerit. Sic sophiftam non iure dixeris eum qui omnia sophistarum περισσὰ [?], omnes περιφρείας [?] & praestigias norit : sed qui nouit simul & vtitur. Sic solo fine feparantur ἀπέρια [?] & κολακεία. Sunt alia fexcenta de genere hoc. Solet autem Theophraftus suas defcriptiones cum excusatione quadam proferre, ne quis hic exquisitas requirat definitiones. Air igitur ὡς τύπῳ λαβεῖν : quod loquendi genus ex Ariftotele aliisq, Theophrafti libris, & Platone ipso notum est. Apud eundem in 1 1 1. De republica opponūtur ἐν τύπῳ & δι' ἀκριβείας.quin ipsæ defcriptiones huiufcemodi minus accuratæ, τύποι vocantur, & ἐπογραφαί[?] in philosophorum scholis.
units.tr: "A pretence of worse deeds and words" [προσποίησις ὅτι χεῖρον πράξεων καὶ λόγων]. This is Theophrastus' definition, or description. Aristotle, however, puts it thus: "pretence is that the ironist makes things less, equally in words and in deed" [προσποιητὴς ὅτι ὁ ἔλαττον ὁμοίως ἐν λόγοις καὶ ἐν πράξει]. We have drawn this definition partly from the fourth book, partly from the second book of the Nicomachean Ethics. The difference lies in a single word. Aristotle says ho elatton [ὅτι ὁ ἔλαττον], "making things less": for he was thinking of the ironist who would make everything smaller. Theophrastus says epi to cheiron [ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον], "toward the worse part", because he was speaking of the man who not only feigns his own things as worse, but refers everything to some evil end; this you will observe constantly in all the marks with which he distinguishes his ironist. So the only thing common to both is that each uses pretence and each departs from the truth; the end is quite different. If someone says that the man of whom Aristotle thinks and speaks, such as Socrates indeed was, could also feign anything toward the worse, we reply from Aristotle that the ironist is so in capacity [ἐν τῇ δυνάμει], but not in purpose [ἐν τῇ προαιρέσει]. For if someone is endowed with the faculty to feign anything and to dissemble for his own advantage, he is not at once to be called an ironist and a hypocrite; but only if will is added to that faculty. The Emperor Titus was once accustomed to boast that he could have been the greatest forger of all, for he knew how to imitate everyone's hand and handwriting. Yet no one would rightly for that reason call him a forger. So too you would not rightly call a man a sophist who knows all the sophists' tricks, all their fallacies and sleights of hand, but one who both knows them and uses them. Thus apereia [ἀπέρια] and flattery [κολακεία] are distinguished by purpose alone. There are six hundred other things of this kind. Theophrastus, moreover, is accustomed to set forth his descriptions with a certain apology, so that no one may here look for exact definitions. He says, therefore, that they are given as it were in outline [ὡς τύπῳ λαβεῖν]; this manner of speaking is known from Aristotle and from other books of Theophrastus, and from Plato himself. In the same author, in the third book On the Republic, in outline [ἐν τύπῳ] is opposed to with precision [δι' ἀκριβείας]. Indeed, descriptions of this kind, being less exact, are called typoi [τύποι] and epographai [ἐπογραφαί] in the schools of the philosophers.

units.la: οἷς ἐωίθεὶς λάξρα[?] ] Non est ἐπιβλέπειν[?], innuebi in aliquem: sed tanquam ex insidiis & superiore loco adoriri. Significat & ἐπιχειρεῖν[?], accingere se ad aliquid faciendum. Vnde est [illegible, ~9 letters] apud philosophum in Physiognomonicis, pro cunctatore. Hos homines de quibus hic Theophrastus, Græci [illegible, ~7 letters] & [illegible, ~9 letters] siue [illegible, ~9 letters] vocant: quibus conuenit prouerbium Plautinum,
units.tr: The Greek verb here does not mean to look at someone or hint at them [ἐπιβλέπειν], but to attack as from an ambush and from higher ground. It also means to undertake something, to gird oneself to do it [ἐπιχειρεῖν]. Whence the philosopher in the Physiognomonics uses the word for a dawdler. The Greeks call the men of whom Theophrastus speaks [illegible], and [illegible], or [illegible]. The Plautine proverb suits them:

units.la: Palam inquit blandiuntur: clam si occasio usquam est Aquam frigidam subdole suffundunt. item illud Sophocleum,
units.tr: "Openly," he says, "they flatter; but secretly, if ever there is an opportunity, they slyly pour cold water over you." So too the line of Sophocles:

units.la: Σαίνεις δ' ἄνδρες, καὶ κύων λαβάρψ ἔι[?].
units.tr: You fawn upon men, as a dog does when it has something in its jaws [Σαίνεις δ' ἄνδρες, καὶ κύων λαβάρψ ἔι].

units.la: Συλλυπεῖσθαι ἠπλωμένοις.] Puta, in iudicio, si litem perdiderint: aut ex aliquo certamine (qualia erant apud veteres multa) inferiores recesserint: aut denique clade belli sint affecti. Late patet Græcorum vox ἵππ[?], cui parem Latini non habent. Talis εἰρωνεία[?] Polymestoris apud Euripidem. cum enim per summum nefas impurus ille filium Hecubæ Polydorum occidisset, & domus Priamicæ casu totus exultaret, ita tamen ibi Hecubam alloquitur,
units.tr: To condole with those who have been stretched out [Συλλυπεῖσθαι ἠπλωμένοις]. For instance, in a court, if they have lost their suit; or if they have come off worse in some contest (of which the ancients had many); or if they have been struck by defeat in war. The Greek word [ἵππ...] has a wide range, and Latin has no equal to it. Such is the irony of Polymestor in Euripides. When that impure man had, by the most unholy crime, killed Polydorus, the son of Hecuba, and the house of Priam was altogether rejoicing at the chance, he nevertheless addresses Hecuba thus:

units.la: Ὦ φίλταθ' ἀνδρῶν Πείαμε, φίλτατη [?] ἐν, Ἑκάβη, δ' ἀκρύω τ' εἰσορῶν, καὶ δὴ τοῖς καὶ ἑαυτὸν λεγομένοις.] Est ὑπερβολὴ quaedam: bis enim idem dicit. Nam cum superioribus ista malo coniungere & repetere συγχωρῶ[?] ἔχειν, quàm cum sequentibus, vt vulgò interpretes.
units.tr: "O dearest of men, Priam, dearest... Hecuba, seeing you weep..." [Ὦ φίλταθ' ἀνδρῶν Πείαμε, φίλτατη ἐν, Ἑκάβη, δ' ἀκρύω τ' εἰσορῶν]. This is a kind of hyperbole, for he says the same thing twice. I prefer to join these words and repeat "I agree to have" [συγχωρῶ ἔχειν] with what precedes, rather than with what follows, as the interpreters commonly do.

units.la: Pag.5. ἀπὸ τῆς δαιδαλμένης ἐπανιζοντας.] hoc est, siue quis δάνειον[?] ab ipso petat, siue ἔρανος. quid sit δάνειον[?], nemo ignorat: ἔρανος vero quid esset in toto isto libello, nescierunt priores interpretes. vide ad caput de arrogantia. Huc pertinent illa Horatii,
units.tr: Page 5: "from the embroidered..." [ἀπὸ τῆς δαιδαλμένης ἐπανιζοντας]. That is, whether someone asks for a loan [δάνειον] from him or for a shared contribution [ἔρανος]. No one is ignorant of what a loan is; but what an eranos was in this whole little book, the earlier interpreters did not know. See the chapter on arrogance. To this belong those lines of Horace:

units.la: Sed metui mea ne finxisse minora putarer, Dissimulator opus propria, mihi commodus uni.
units.tr: "But I feared that I would be thought to have made up lesser things, a dissembler of my own affairs, useful to myself alone."

units.la: καὶ μὴ πωλῶν φάσει πωλεῖν.[?] Quorsum hoc? nempe vt eo pacto manum illi adeat apud quem ista loquitur: itaque pecunia illam emungat, aut aliam fraudem faciat. Noui ego non paucos qui has artes probè callerent: quos cum videas holosericis indutos ambulare, aut cum audias magnificè se & suos quæstus prædicare, meros Crassos Croesófve esse censeas. hac ratione homines simplices & parum cati inducuntur vt putent si quid habeant nūmorum, non id melius vsquam collocari, quàm apud istos posse, quos tantis opibus esse præditos audiunt. Vt enim fama est homini, exinde pecuniam solet inuenire. Sic misellis os sublinitur.
units.tr: And, though not selling, to say that he is selling [καὶ μὴ πωλῶν φάσει πωλεῖν]. Why so? Clearly, so that by this method he may get into the hand of the one to whom he speaks, and so squeeze money out of him, or work some other fraud. I know not a few who understand these arts well. When you see them walking about clothed in silk, or hear them boasting grandly of themselves and their gains, you would think them mere Crassuses or Croesuses. By this method simple and not very wary people are led to think that if they have any money, it could be placed nowhere better than with those whom they hear are so richly endowed. For, as the saying goes, a man usually finds money afterwards. Thus the poor fellows have mud smeared on their mouths.

units.la: καὶ ἀκούσας τι δόξῃ μὴ προσποιεῖσθαι.[?] Planè mirorcur hac lectione quisquam offendatur. δόξει, hoc est, videri volet. est autem pro, μὴ δόξει προσποιεῖσθαι. vt apud Plutarchum in re fere eadem, ὑ δοκῶν ἀκούειν. Euripides Medea, Ἡ κεντᾷ τὰ λέγοντα ὑ δοκῶν κλύειν.[?] Aristophanes Pluto, ὡς ἐδόκουν μ' ὁρᾶν ἔτι,[?] hoc est, dissimulabant se videre me. Scribitur & δείξει fortasse pro λέξει.[?] sed nihil mutandum.
units.tr: And having heard something, he seems not to pretend [καὶ ἀκούσας τι δόξῃ μὴ προσποιεῖσθαι]. I am truly amazed that anyone takes offence at this reading. δόξει means "will wish to appear"; it stands for "will not wish to appear to pretend" [μὴ δόξει προσποιεῖσθαι], as in Plutarch in nearly the same matter, "seeming not to hear" [ὑ δοκῶν ἀκούειν]. In Euripides' Medea: "he stings the words, seeming not to hear" [Ἡ κεντᾷ τὰ λέγοντα ὑ δοκῶν κλύειν]. In Aristophanes' Plutus: "as they seemed to see me still" [ὡς ἐδόκουν μ' ὁρᾶν ἔτι], that is, they pretended not to see me. Perhaps δείξει is written for λέξει, but nothing need be changed.

units.la: καὶ ὁμολογήσας, μὴ μεμνῆσθαι.[?] Ecce ait se εἴρωνα cum intelligere, qui pactus aliquid (sic, non fassus vertimus) dicat se non meminisse: hoc est, pactis non stet. Hoc planè alienum est ab eo quem Aristoteles εἴρωνα vocat: diserte enim philosophus admonet, se non tractare eo loco de ea veritate aut falsitate quę spectatur in contractibus & commerciis: sed de ea quæ in colloquiis ac familiari consuetudine. [?] γὰρ, περὶ τῆς ἐν [?] ὁμολογίας ἀληθῶς λέ-γομεν, ὡς [?] ὁ εἰς ἀδικίαν [?] ἀκαρασωσίως συλλέγει [?] ἄλλης γὰρ ἂν ἐν ᾧ ὦτ' ἀρετῆς. Sunt autem hoc hominū genere omnia referta quibuscum nisi è syngrapha semper agas, nihil agas. Talis ille leno Cappadox in Curculione Plautina.
units.tr: And having agreed, to say that he does not remember [καὶ ὁμολογήσας, μὴ μεμνῆσθαι]. See, he says that he understands the ironist, who, having made some agreement (we render "agreed," not "confessed"), says that he does not remember; that is, he does not abide by his agreements. This is plainly foreign to the one whom Aristotle calls the ironist. For the philosopher expressly warns that there he is not treating of that truth or falsehood which concerns contracts and dealings, but of that which concerns conversation and familiar intercourse. Men of this kind are full of such things, and unless you deal with them from a written bond, you accomplish nothing. Such is that Cappadocian pimp in Plautus' Curculio:

units.la: Mil. Quando vir bonus es, responde quod rogo.
units.tr: Mil. Since you are an honest man, answer what I ask.

units.la: Mil. Promisistin' si liberali hanc quisquam assereret manu,
units.tr: Mil. Did you promise, if anyone should claim this with a free hand,

units.la: Te omne argentum redditurum? Ca. non commemini.
units.tr: that you would return all the silver to him? Ca. I don't remember.

units.la: κἀγὼ μὲν σκέψασθαι. ] Lego σκέψασθαι. Hoc nostri εἴρωνες dicere solent, l'y penseray. Menander lepidis verbis eos exagitat, qui rogati aliquid ab amico egeno, dicunt Σκέψομαι: quod hodie nimis multi faciunt, amici nomine tenus, & vt ille ait, Factiosi lingua, inertes opera, sublesta fide. Sic Menander,
units.tr: And I will consider [κἀγὼ μὲν σκέψασθαι]. I read σκέψασθαι. Our ironists are wont to say "I'll think about it" (l'y penseray). Menander lashes with witty words those who, when asked for something by a needy friend, say "I will consider" [Σκέψομαι]. Many do this today, in name only; and, as he says, "factious in the tongue, idle in deed, weak in good faith." So Menander:
[Illegible in the scan; the Greek lines cannot be recovered.]
[Illegible in the scan; the Greek lines cannot be recovered.]
[Illegible in the scan; the Greek lines cannot be recovered.]

units.la: Potest & ἐσκέφθαι, quod quidam codices habent, ferri: optimeque cum sequentibus conueniret: vertes, se iam cogitasse.
units.tr: The reading ἐσκέφθαι, which some manuscripts have, may also be accepted, and it would agree best with what follows: render it "that he has already considered."

units.la: Καὶ λέγει ἑαυτὸν ἕτερον γεγονέναι.] Sensus est, cùm ipsemet fuerit qui id quo de quæritur dixerit secerítve, non se tamen, sed alium fuisse dicet, à quo id fit dictum factúmve. Nostri homines hoc dixerint, Vous me prenez pour vn autre. Possis hoc & ad verbum ἐκπλήττομαι referre. nam qui ἐκπλήττομαι (est autem ἔκπληξις siue stupor, aut horror, vehemens quædam admiratio, id est, θαυμαστότης ὑπερβάλλως ait philosophus Topicorum quarto) ij quodammodo de statu mentis deiiciuntur, eáque ecstasi alij à se ipsis fiunt. Sæpe etiam accidit, vt quis opinioni suæ & expectationi contrarium quid audiēs, in stuporem simul detur,& sententiam mutare cogatur:& ita quoque alius à seipso fiat:sicut Megaronides ille Plautinus in Trinummo qui cum Calliclem eo consilio adiisset vt eum concastigaret pro commerita noxia, vbi tamen eum loquentem audit, repente mutat animum, & exclamans, ait :
units.tr: And he says that he himself has become another [Καὶ λέγει ἑαυτὸν ἕτερον γεγονέναι]. The sense is that, although he himself was the one who said or did the thing in question, he will say that he was not himself but another, by whom it was said or done. Our people would say "You take me for someone else" (Vous me prenez pour vn autre). One may also refer this to the verb ἐκπλήττομαι. For those who are struck (ἔκπληξις means stupor or horror, a vehement kind of wonder, that is, θαυμαστότης ὑπερβάλλως, as the philosopher says in the fourth book of the Topics) are in some way thrown out of their state of mind, and by this ecstasy others are made other than themselves. It often also happens that someone, hearing what is contrary to his opinion and expectation, is at once struck with stupor and forced to change his mind, and so too becomes another than himself. So Megaronides in Plautus' Trinummus, who had gone to Callicles with the purpose of rebuking him for his deserved offence, but when he hears him speaking, suddenly changes his mind and, exclaiming, says:

units.la: Proh di immortales verbis paucis quàm citò
units.tr: "Good immortal gods, how quickly with few words..."

units.la: Alium feci sti me, alius ad te veneram. Sic apud Demosthenem in ea πρὸς Φορμίωνα, de eo qui sententiam mutauerat, ἑτέρῳ ἤδη λῶ καὶ ὁ αὐτός. Prima interpretatio magis mihi probatur, estque simplicior.
units.tr: "...I have made myself another than I was; I had come to you as another." So too in Demosthenes, in the speech against Phormio, about one who had changed his opinion: "now he wishes to be another, and yet the same" [ἑτέρῳ ἤδη λῶ καὶ ὁ αὐτός]. The first interpretation seems more probable to me, and it is the simpler.

units.la: Pag. 6. ἀλλ᾽ ἔρα μὴ τὸν Ζάτλον. ] Ζάτλον, hoc est, citiùs & nimis ἀλύως [?] atque ἀλαζονικῶς [?], simplicium hominum more, qui fere subitò credunt. vel ζᾶτζῶν [?] accipe pro ἀδρόως [?] & repente: quod de iis vsurpatur qui impetu quodam animi magis quàm consilio aliquid faciunt. Sic apud philosophum opponuntur ζᾶτλον [?] & ἐκ προϐαγωγῆς. Seneca eleganter impetu placere pro ζᾶτλον [?] καὶ ἀλαζονικῶς [?], epistola c 1. Notabis illud ϊσέλεν φωνᾶς [?]: erat vsitatius φωνᾶς [?], vt πισζέιν λόγως [?]: sed φωνᾶς omnes etiam scripti Palatini.
units.tr: Page 6: "But beware lest he be Zatlon" [ἀλλ᾽ ἔρα μὴ τὸν Ζάτλον]. Zatlon means too quickly and excessively, rashly and boastfully, in the manner of simple people, who often believe on the spot. Or take the word as meaning "impetuously" and "suddenly" [ἀδρόως], which is used of those who do something by a certain impulse of mind rather than by deliberation. So in the philosopher the terms "Zatlon" and "from forethought" are opposed. Seneca elegantly uses impetu placere for the Greek, in letter c 1. You will note the phrase ϊσέλεν φωνᾶς: the more usual form was φωνᾶς, as in πισζέιν λόγως; but all the Palatine manuscripts also have φωνᾶς.

units.la: καὶ πλοκὰς καὶ παλιλλογίας. ] Vocat πλοκὰς quæ Cicero inuolucra & integumenta dissimulationis: siue subdolos & ad fallendum compositos sermones, tanquam retia aut laqueos. Has poëta vetus apud M. Tullium versutiloquus malitias dicit. Possis vertere orationem intortam cum Plauto in Ciftellaria: vbi festiuissimus poëta istiusmodi homines (alterplices veteribus Latinis dictos, Graecis στρεφλιμάλλης[?]) inuoluolo similes ait bestiae damnificae, quae in pampini folio implicat se. Sic πλήσσειν μυχανὰς[?] saepe apud Graecos poëtas. Παλιλλογίας vertimus dicta recantata. Cantare enim est, idem saepius dicere, vt & ὑμνεῖν apud Graecos. Videtur autem Theophrastus ista voce sermones ancipites, & qui diuerso aut etiam contrario modo accipi queant, intelligere. πάλιν utrunque significat, & iterum, & contra. Hic igitur significat non iterum, sed contra: sic apud poëtam πάλιν εἰπεῖν, non est iterum dicere, sed contrarium. & παλινωδία est, non tam iterata cantio, quàm priori contraria: & sic apud Horatium, recantata opprobria. apud Pindarum παλίλλωσος & πόλις χρὴ βάρβαρος, Vrbs quae diuersa lingua vtitur ab aliarum gentium linguis. Idem poëta Nemeonicarum, oda prima, παλιγλωσσον δὲ οἱ ἀθάνατοι θέαν, hoc est, contrariam. Ita alia multa dicuntur.
units.tr: And crafty turns and recantations [καὶ πλοκὰς καὶ παλιλλογίας]. He calls πλοκὰς what Cicero calls wrappings and coverings of dissimulation: sly speeches composed for deceiving, like nets or snares. An old poet in Cicero calls these crafty-tongued wickednesses. One might render it a twisted speech, with Plautus in the Cistellaria, where that most witty poet compares men of this sort (called alterplices by the old Latins, and στρεφλιμάλλης by the Greeks) to a harmful beast that wraps itself in a vine leaf. So too πλήσσειν μυχανάς is often used by Greek poets. We render παλιλλογίας as recanted sayings. For to sing again [cantare] is to say the same thing repeatedly, as ὑμνεῖν does among the Greeks. Theophrastus seems to mean by this word speeches that are ambiguous and can be taken in a different or even opposite way. πάλιν means both "again" and "back/against." Here it means not "again" but "against." So in the poet, πάλιν εἰπεῖν means not to say again but to say the contrary, and παλινωδία is not so much a repeated song as one opposed to an earlier one; and so in Horace, recanted reproaches. In Pindar, παλίλλωσος and "a city that uses a barbarous tongue" mean a city that uses a language different from the languages of other peoples. The same poet, in the first Nemean ode, has παλιγλωσσον δὲ οἱ ἀθάνατοι θέαν, that is, "contrary." Many other things are so named.

units.la: ὃ χείρον ἔστ' ἂν εἰπεῖν οὐδέν[?]. Præclarè maximus poëtarum.
units.tr: "What is worse than nothing to say" [ὃ χείρον ἔστ' ἂν εἰπεῖν οὐδέν]. Most admirably said by the greatest of the poets.

units.la: Ἐχθρῷ γάρ μοι κεῖνῳ ἔμως ἀΐδαο πύλησιν[?]Ὅς χ' ἕτερον μὲν κἀδ' ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, ἄλλο δ' βάζει[?].
units.tr: "For I hate that man as much as the gates of Hades, who hides one thing in his mind and speaks another" [Ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν, ὅς χ' ἕτερον μὲν κεύθῃ ἐνὶ φρεσίν, ἄλλο δὲ βάζῃ].

units.la: Haud minus ille mihi exosus quàm ianua Ditis, Mens aliud cui tecta tegit, quàm lingua loquatur.
units.tr: I hate him no less than the gate of Dis, the man whose mind conceals one thing while his tongue says another.

units.la: THN ἡ κολακείαν. ] Inter virtutes quæ ad ὁμιλίας & vitæ quotidianæ consuetudinem proprie pertinent, ideoque ἐξῆς ὁμιλητικῆς [?] à Platone vocantur, Aristoteles quarto Nicomacheorum primam numerat illam, qua qui fuerit prædictus, is & facta & dicta omnia sua ita temperabit, vt eius conuictus omnibus sit futurus gratus, suauis atque etiam iucundus: omni enim asperitate morum, & morositate, quæ est ἀηδίας ξυνοίκῳ [?], carebit: imò è contrario in eo elaborabit vt, quantum honestas & virtutis amor permittent, voluptati sit iis quibuscum versatur. Hanc virtutem quia proprio nomine carebat, Aristoteles in Nicomacheis φιλίαν nuncupauit, explicatione adiecta, quomodo eam vocem vellet hic intelligi: at in Eudemiis σεμνότητα vocauerat. & vt in nominibus virtutis variauit, ita etiam in vitiorum ei oppositorum, vt capite περὶ αὐθαδείας dicemus. Habet enim hæc quoque virtus sibi opposita vitia hinc καὶ ἔλλειψιν, illinc καὶ ὑπερβολήν. ac de iis quidem qui defectu humanitatis peccant hac in parte, est caput illud περὶ αὐθαδείας. De iis vero qui modum excedunt, & nimis suaues ac dulces esse volunt, sunt hæc duo capita: περὶ κολακείας alterum, alterum περὶ ἀρεσκείας. nulla enim re admodum hæc duo vitia differunt, nisi fine qui diuersus est. quo quidem ita discriminantur, vt cum vitium sit vtrumque, tamen comparata blanditia ad adulationem pene virtus videatur, non vitium: verùm de blanditia infrà suo loco. Adulationis autem finis est, priuatum commodum. Eam definit Theophrastus ὁμιλίαν αἰχρὰν, συμφέρυσαν ἢ τῷ κολα-κεύοντι[?]. In Theæteto Platonis κολακεία definitur breuiter, τέχνη ἡδωλικὴ[?] ars suauitatis conciliatrix. In eiusdem Definitionibus (non enim iis assentiri debemus, qui temerè & contra auctoritatem vetustissimorum scriptorum illum librum à Platone abiudicant) ita definitur. Κολακεία ὁμιλία ἡ πρὸς ἡδονὴν ἀνὰ τὸ βέλτιστον[?], quam definitionem tribuit Theophrastus blanditiæ: meliori sanè consilio, & conuenientiùs iis quæ ante ex Aristotele diximus: addit verò Plato etiam aliam, ἔξις ὁμιλητικὴ πρὸς ἡδο-νὴν ὑπερβάλλων τὸ μέτριον. quæ etiam blanditiæ melius conueniat. quare prudenter Theophrastus ex Aristotele illa adiecit, συμφέρυσαν ἢ τῷ κολακεύοντι, vt à blanditia separaret. Quod autem ait αἰχρὰν, mallem ἐπαινῶ[?] dixisset: aut potius simul vtrumque posuisset. Nam & indecora adulatio est, vt vocatur Suetonio, rectéque Tacitus adulationi fœdum crimen seruitutis inesse pronunciat: & proprium hoc est adulatoris, abiectè & demissè loqui & in omnibus regi suo supparasitari ac secundas agere: ideo dicebat philosophus Politicorum libro quinto, ἔρ-γον κολακείας εἶναι, ὑπευθῦς[?] ὁμιλεῖν. & verè Clear-chus Solensis Aristotelis discipulus proprium hoc adulatoribus esse dixit, vt suos sibi ipsi animos frágerent, & spiritum generosum qui ingenuos decet, demerent, ὑπεναὶ ποιουῦτις τὰ ἡ ὑμ αὐτοῦ[?]: eos verò quibus seruirent, tumore inflarent, & redderét vanos & χαυνῶς ἐχ κενοὺς[?], atq; vt loquitur Seneca, infatuarent. Vertimus autem αἰχρὰν turpem, nō indecoram: nā αἰχρὸν opponitur τῷ καλῷ, id est honesto: aliud verò vero est τὸ ἀρέϊον, aliud τὸ κάλον, si proprie loqui volumus. Porrò vocis κόλαξ notatione varie explicant Graeci grammatici, quos te reicio. Veteres Romani grassari, ἀντὶ τῆς κολακείας vsurpant, vt Festus docet: & ita dixit Horatius, Obsequio grassare. inde grassator, ὁ κόλαξ: quem etiam stlatarium à stlata quod fuit navigij genus, vt puto ὑπηρέτης dixerunt. Glossarium, Stlatarius, ἐργόμωκος. quid autem sit ἐργόμωκος, in altero Glossario declaratur: ἐργόμωκος, adulator, ambitiosus. Ἐργομωνία, adulatio. Ἐργομωκεύω, ancillor, adseclo, adulor. vbi etiam vides ancillor, idem esse cum adulor. quod probatur altero Glossario, vbi haec scribuntur, Ancillor, κολακεύω. Ancillula ἐργόμωκος, παιδίσκη. Adiiciam & haec ex eodem libro, Adsentio, ἐργομωκῶ. συνκαθίζομαι. & alibi, Fuco, ἐργόμωκος. Puto autem ex eo dici ἐργόμωκον adulatorem, quia fere solent adsentatores eos quibus palam adulantur à tergo pinsare, vt verissimè Persius ait. Hesychius sanè aliter, ἐργομωκῶν, ἐμπαίζων.
units.tr: Among the virtues that properly belong to social intercourse and the ordinary conduct of daily life, and which for that reason Plato calls "sociable," Aristotle in the fourth book of the Nicomachean Ethics lists first the one possessed by a man who so governs all his deeds and words that his company will find him agreeable, pleasant and even delightful. Such a man will be free of all harshness and surliness, which is [ἀηδία] unpleasantness to one's companions. On the contrary, he will work to give pleasure to those with whom he lives, as far as honour and the love of virtue allow. Because this virtue had no proper name, Aristotle called it friendliness [φιλία] in the Nicomachean Ethics, adding an explanation of how he wished the word to be understood there, but in the Eudemian Ethics he had called it courtesy [σεμνότης]. As he varied the names of the virtue, so he also varied the names of the vices opposed to it, as I shall say in the chapter On Surliness [περὶ αὐθαδείας]. For this virtue too has opposed vices, one on the side of deficiency and one on the side of excess. The chapter On Surliness deals with those who fall short of civility in this respect. Those who go beyond the mean and want to be too agreeable and sweet are the subjects of two chapters: one On Flattery [περὶ κολακείας] and the other On Obsequiousness [περὶ ἀρεσκείας]. These two vices differ in almost nothing except in their end, which is different. They are distinguished in such a way that, although both are vices, the courtship of favour, compared with flattery, seems almost a virtue and not a vice. But I will speak of courtship of favour in its proper place below. The end of flattery is private advantage. Theophrastus defines it as a shameful association, profitable to the flatterer [ὁμιλίαν αἰσχράν, συμφέρουσαν τῷ κολακεύοντι]. In Plato's Theaetetus flattery is briefly defined as a knack of pleasing, an art that wins favour through agreeableness. In the Definitions attributed to Plato (for we should not agree with those who rashly, and against the authority of the most ancient writers, deny that book to Plato), it is defined thus: flattery is an association aimed at pleasure at the expense of what is best. Theophrastus attributes this definition to courtship of favour, and with better judgment and more fittingly with what we said earlier from Aristotle. Plato, however, adds another definition: a sociable habit that goes beyond the mean in pursuit of pleasure, which fits courtship of favour even better. So Theophrastus wisely added from Aristotle the words "profitable to the flatterer," in order to separate it from courtship of favour. But I would have preferred him to say "praiseworthy" [ἐπαινῶ] instead of "shameful," or else to have put both words together. For flattery is also unseemly, as Suetonius calls it, and Tacitus rightly declares that a foul crime of servitude lies in flattery. It is also the mark of a flatterer to speak abjectly and submissively, and to play the parasite and the second fiddle to his lord in everything. So the philosopher in the fifth book of the Politics said that it is the business of flattery to converse with a man in a servile way [ὑπευθύς]. And truly Clearchus of Soli, a disciple of Aristotle, said that it is characteristic of flatterers to break their own spirits and to strip away the noble spirit that becomes free men, making themselves abject; and to puff up those whom they serve with swelling, making them vain and empty, and, as Seneca says, to make them fools. We have translated αἰσχρόν as "shameful," not "unseemly," for αἰσχρόν is opposed to καλόν, that is, to the honourable; the seemly [ἀρέσκον] is one thing, and the beautiful [κάλον] is another, if we want to speak precisely. The Greek grammarians explain the etymology of the word κόλαξ in various ways, which I pass over. The ancient Romans used the verb grassari to mean flattery, as Festus teaches, and so Horace said "to grassari by obsequiousness." Hence grassator, the flatterer, whom they also called stlatarius, from stlata, which was a kind of boat, a servant as I think [ὑπηρέτης]. The Glossary has: stlatarius, [ἐργόμωκος]. What ἐργόμωκος means is explained in another Glossary: ἐργόμωκος, a flatterer, a fawner. ἐργομωνία, flattery. ἐργομωκεύω, I play the handmaid, I follow, I flatter. Here you also see that ancillor is the same as adulor, which is confirmed by another Glossary where these are written: ancillor, [κολακεύω]. Ancillula, [ἐργόμωκος], [παιδίσκη]. I will add these from the same book: adsentio, [ἐργομωκῶ], [συγκαθίζομαι]. And elsewhere: fuco, [ἐργόμωκος]. I think ἐργόμωκος was used for a flatterer because flatterers usually pinch from behind those whom they flatter to their faces, as Persius very truly says. Hesychius, however, has something different: ἐργομωκῶν, mocking.

units.la: ὑπολάζοι ἀντὶς ὁμιλίαν.] Late patet vox ὁμιλία, & ea omnia fermè complectitur quae in vitae quotidianae vsu solent accidere. Latini ferè pluribus verbis huius Graeci vim exprimunt: sicut & Graeci quoque interdum coniungunt ἡ ὁμιλία & τὸ συζῆν, vt in quarto Nicomacheorum. Eruditissimus Apuleius τὸ ὁμιλεῖν voce fabulari expressit in apophthegmate quodam Aristippi. iterum dico, parum commodè. Scio, erunt etiam hic qui exclament: sed nos istos exclamatores alibi σὺν θεῷ χάρις μέσως compescemus. Latissimè sanè patet vt diximus vox Graeca: quare etiam Aristoteles ὁμιλίας
units.tr: The word ὁμιλία has a wide range, and it covers nearly everything that usually happens in daily life. Latin writers mostly express the force of this Greek word with several words; the Greeks too sometimes join ἡ ὁμιλία and τὸ συζῆν, as in the fourth book of the Nicomachean Ethics. The very learned Apuleius rendered τὸ ὁμιλεῖν by the word fabulari in a certain saying of Aristippus, though I say again that it was not very apt. I know there will be some here who will cry out, but we will silence those clamourers elsewhere, with God's help. The Greek word certainly has a very wide range, as I have said. For this reason Aristotle, in the seventh book of the Nicomachean Ethics, spoke of the associations [ὁμιλίας] of men and affairs.

units.la: ἀνθρώπων & πραγμάτων dixit in septimo Nicomacheorum,& ante eum Isocrates in priore ad Nicoclem, & Hippocrates περὶ ψυχῆς ἐν τῷ θαλάττῃ ὁμιλεῖν, in Prorrhetico maiore. & in lib. Περὶ ἰητρῶν,de instrumentis medicorum loquens, εἰ μέλλει ὁμιλεῖν περὶ τῶν [?] ὠνῶτι μέρει. Vide Erotianum. Apud Plutarchum leges ὁμιλεῖν ἡδονὰς: apud historicos sæpe ὁμιλεῖν καιροῖς: quod Plutarchus in Mario dixit ὁμιλεῖν τύ-χαις. quem locum deprauat Muretus in Variis suis: nam prorsus est ὑσλ@ ἡ ἐλλώφ@, quod ille somniat ὁμιλήσαι. per inquam hoc est ineptum. cum & in Sylla iterum sic loquatur idem auctor: & quod Muretus non est ἰδὲ ὄναρ suspicatus, Bœotus à Bœoto fœnerarit loquendi id genus. Ita enim Pindarus Nemeonicarum ode prima, — ὁ δ' οἱ φράξει ἡ ἀσυῖ σπραπ Ποίαις ὁμιλήσ τύχαις. Sic vsurpatur vox ἀποδομιλεῖν in Platonis Lachete. Sic etiam dixit Athenæus καθομιλεῖν καιρὸς, libro xii. Porro est hæc dictio militaris propriè, & in castris nata. vide Eustathium. Apud Latinos Cicerone inferiores, non minus latè patet verbum connersatri. maximè apud Senecam : vt, conuersari tristitia. ὁμιλεῖν λύπῃ epistola c.
units.tr: and before him Isocrates in the first oration To Nicocles, and Hippocrates in On the Soul, when he says that one should associate [ὁμιλεῖν] with the sea, in the greater Prorrhetic. And in the book On Physicians, speaking of the instruments of doctors, he says: if he is going to deal [ὁμιλεῖν] with the … part. See Erotianus. In Plutarch you will read ὁμιλεῖν ἡδοναῖς, to converse with pleasures; in historians often ὁμιλεῖν καιροῖς, to deal with occasions; which Plutarch in the Life of Marius called ὁμιλεῖν τύχαις, to deal with fortunes. Muretus corrupts this passage in his Variae Lectiones, for it is certainly the reading ἐλλώφ..., which he imagines to be ὁμιλῆσαι. I say that this is absurd, since the same author speaks so again in the Life of Sulla. And although Muretus did not suspect that it was a dream, the Boeotian borrowed this kind of expression from a Boeotian. Thus Pindar, in the first Nemean ode: "Which fortunes you deal with." So the word ἀποδομιλεῖν is used in Plato's Laches. Athenaeus also said καθομιλεῖν καιρός, in book twelve. Moreover, this word is properly a military term, born in the camp; see Eustathius. Among the Latins after Cicero the verb conversari is no less wide in its range, especially in Seneca, as conversari with sadness, ὁμιλεῖν λύπῃ, in epistle [c.].

units.la: τὸν ὁ κόλακα Ϭιστ.] Habes perpulchram adulatoris descriptionem apud Plutarchum, De discrimine amici & adulatoris, ibi, Τοιαῦτ' ὁ κό-λαξ, οἱ φιλ. &c. Galenus in libro de dignoscendis curandisque animi affectibus adulatorem tribus notis insignit, ποιῶν προσομαρ ... ποιῶ ... σωμάτ ... ἐν τοῖς πολὺ δυναμένοις ἢ πλείστοις. [?]
units.tr: On the flatterer, you have a most beautiful description in Plutarch, On the Difference between a Friend and a Flatterer, where he says, "Such is the flatterer, the friends…" etc. Galen, in the book On Recognising and Curing the Affections of the Soul, marks the flatterer with three signs: he makes himself agreeable … he makes himself … among those who have the greatest power or the most.

units.la: Pag. 7. ἐνθυμῇ ὡς ἀντολέπεσιν εἰς σε οἱ ἀνδρ. ] Si-milia hic Artotrogus regi suo apud Plautum initio
units.tr: Page 7: "Consider how the men set themselves against you." Artotrogus says something similar to his king at the beginning of Plautus's

units.la: ἀυδοκιμεῖς χθὲς ἐν τῇ σοφ.] Non assentior interpretibus quibus videntur hæc Latinè efferenda, dignitatis tuæ splendorem magno omnium assensu obti-[illegible, ~4 letters]. Aliud enim est ἀδοκιμεῖν ibi loco, aliud apud M. Tullium dignitatis splendorem obtinere: quod potius convenit τῆς ἐν τέλει. at ἀδοκιμεῖν id est, bene audire, siue bona fama, etiam mediocris fortunæ & pauperi, quorum est magna passim indignitas, convenire potest: ex sequentibus enim apparet ad laudem probitatis & integræ vitæ esse hoc referendum, non ad dignitatis splendore. Quare existimo ἀδοκιμεῖν hic esse quod dixit Cicero, fructum virtutis suæ capere, in Miloniana. & alibi idē τὸ ἀδοκιμεῖν vocat fructum bonæ existimationis. Est autem mirè emphatica translatio verbi καταχρῶσθαι[?], quod mox sequitur. Nam voluit indicare, sicuti sua sponte grauia deorsum feruntur, ita omnes qui aderant, non quod eius qui laudabatur gratiam captarent, sed tanquam ὑπὸ αὐτῆς ἀληθείας ἐκλαμπόμενοι, vt loquitur philosophus, in eius nomen incidisse: quasi videlicet ita sit omnibus perspecta eius probitas, vt iam illius nomen non hominis, sed virtutis ipsius proprium videatur. Parem elegantiam obseruabamus apud Plinum Secundum in sententia non dissimili: vbi reddi nomina tanquam debitum dicuntur, eo sensu quo hic καταφέρεσθαι εἰς τὸ ὄνομα epistola xxiii. libri ix. Vtitur hanc vocem Theophrastus iterum Περὶ λαλιᾶς.
units.tr: "You were well thought of yesterday in the assembly" [ἀδοκιμεῖς χθὲς ἐν τῇ σοφ...]. I do not agree with those interpreters who think these words should be rendered in Latin as "to obtain, by the general assent of all, the splendour of your dignity". For ἀδοκιμεῖν here means something different from obtaining the splendour of dignity in Cicero's sense, which would better suit one in high office. But ἀδοκιμεῖν, that is, to be well spoken of, or to have a good reputation, can also suit a man of modest fortune and a poor man, of whom there is widespread indignity. For it appears from what follows that this refers to praise of probity and an upright life, not to the splendour of dignity. Hence I think ἀδοκιμεῖν here means what Cicero, in the Pro Milone, called "to take the fruit of one's virtue"; and elsewhere he calls the same thing "the fruit of good esteem". The word καταχρῶσθαι, which immediately follows, is a remarkably emphatic metaphor. Theophrastus meant to indicate that, just as heavy things fall downward of their own accord, so all who were present, not to win the favour of the man being praised, but as if illumined by truth itself, as the philosopher says, fell upon his name: as if his probity were so evident to all that his name now seemed the property not of a man but of virtue itself. We observed a similar elegance in Pliny the Younger, in a not dissimilar sentiment, where names are said to be "paid back" as a debt, in the sense in which here καταφέρεσθαι εἰς τὸ ὄνομα, in letter 23 of book 9. Theophrastus uses this word again in On Talkativeness.

units.la: ἀπὸ τὸ ἰματίῳ ἀφελεῖν χροχίδα.] Hippocrates dixit ἀπὸ τῶν ἰματίων χροχίδας ἀποληλύθαι magis proprie: sed & idem alibi ἀφιλεῖν χροχίδα. dicitur & λέγειν χροχίδα, vt apud Celsum in veste floccos legere. Vocarunt autem Graeci κροκύλεγμον genus hoc adulationis. Hesychius, Κροκύλεγμα, τὸ κολακευτικῶς τὰς κροκίδας ὑπολέγειν τῆς ἱματίων [?]. Adeo autem frequens fuit haec adulatio, vt inde natum sit prouerbium, quod ita explicant Graeci. Suidas Ἀφαυρὴν κροκίδας. ὅτι τῶν πάντα ποιούντων ἐνεκεν κολακείας. ἄλλως τε Αεισοφάνης ἐν τῇ κολακευτικῇ πάρων καὶ τὰς κροκίδας ἀ-φαυρῶν [?]. In Plutarchi Sylla, Valeria soror Hortensij de veste Syllę floccum vellens, lepidissimè illi adulatur. Non solùm autem floccos vel fratillos tollere olim adulatores solebant: sed & alias omne genus sordes abstergere: neque omisit hoc praeceptū nequitiarum magister in Arte. & in Amoribus ait idem poëta, Dum loquor, alba nigro sparsa est tibi pulvere vestis: Sordida de nitido corpore puluis, abi. In Vespis Aristophanis Euphemius κόλαξ dicitur spogia calceos mundare. τὸν σπόγγον ἔχων, ait, ἐκ τῆς λεκάνης [?] ἡμῖν [?] ἀψηκωρεῖ [?]. Videntur & caudas leporum soliti secum gestare, vt praesto esset quo oculos fenum lippientium κολακευτικῶς abstergerent. Aristophanes in Equitibus.
units.tr: To pick the nap off the cloak [ἀπὸ τὸ ἰματίῳ ἀφελεῖν χροχίδα]. Hippocrates said more properly ἀπὸ τῶν ἰματίων χροχίδας ἀποληλύθαι, "to have the flocks removed from the garments," but elsewhere he also says ἀφιλεῖν χροχίδα. People also say λέγειν χροχίδα, as in Celsus, "to gather flocks from a garment." The Greeks called this kind of flattery κροκύλεγμον. Hesychius: Κροκύλεγμα, "the flattering picking up of the flocks of a garment" [?]. This flattery was so common that a proverb arose from it, which the Greeks explain. Suidas: Ἀφαυρὴν κροκίδας, "because of those who do everything for the sake of flattery." And elsewhere Aristophanes, in the Flatterer, says: "picking the flocks and wiping away..." [?]. In Plutarch's Sulla, Valeria, the sister of Hortensius, plucks a flock from Sulla's robe and flatters him most wittily. Flatterers were accustomed to remove not only flocks or bits of lint but every kind of dirt. The master of wantonness did not omit this precept in his Art of Love, and the same poet says in the Amores: "While I talk, your white dress is sprinkled with black dust; go away, filthy dust from a shining body." In Aristophanes' Wasps, the flatterer Euphemius is said to clean shoes with a sponge: "holding the sponge," he says, "out of the basin..." [?]. It seems they also customarily carried hares' tails with them, so that there would be something at hand with which to wipe the eyes of those with sore eyes, in a flattering manner. Aristophanes in the Knights.

units.la: Ἰδὲ δ' ἔχω κέρκον λαγῷ τὰ Φαλαμῶ [?] ἀφέλῃν [?].
units.tr: "Look, I have a hare's tail for you to wipe..." [?]

units.la: Similiter in Lysistrata mulier nequam marito suo adulatur. Turpissimum verò illud apud eundem poëtam adulationis genus, Ασομυξάμψῳ [?] ὦ ἥμ', ἐμὲ πρὸς τὸ κεφαλὴ ὑπολῶ [?]. Spurcum hoc & foedum: sed longè turpiora his apud Athenaeum legas, & Suetonium in Vitellio, capite secundo.
units.tr: Similarly in Lysistrata a wicked wife flatters her husband. The most shameful kind of flattery in the same poet is... [?]: a filthy and foul thing. But you will find far more disgraceful things in Athenaeus, and in Suetonius, Vitellius, chapter two.

units.la: Προσυεχθῆ ἄχυρον.] Secuti sumus Palatina exemplaria. In quibusdam editis olim est, προσεχθῆ.
units.tr: "Having been brought up to the chaff" [προσυεχθῆ ἄχυρον]. We have followed the Palatine manuscripts. In some printed editions of the past it reads προσεχθῆ.

units.la: Ἔχεις πρὸς ἔτη μέλλουσαν τῷ τρίχα.] Serò canescere, vegetæ senectutis & viridis argumentum: qualis est eorum quos Græci ἀωσγέροντας [?] vocant: qualis etiam ille Plautinus Periplectomenes, qui negat se propter ætatem exaruisse ex amœnis rebus. Ideo olim soliti homines molles, quos-ne longa quidem ætas ad frugem bonam reuocarat, canitiem occultare, non secus ac mulieres. Testimonia de utrisque passim sunt obvia in Græcorum epigrammatis, Martiale, aliisque poëtis. sed & pharmaco usos constat viros molles & effœminatos, ad celandam capitis nivem: eius fuci compositione docet elegas poëta Serenus Sammonicus, & meminere Tertulliani, Iosephus, alij. Clemens Alex. χρίσματα [?] πολιῶν vocat lib. 1 1 1. Pædag. Aristophanes Concionantibus,
units.tr: "You have hair which is going to turn white in time" [Ἔχεις πρὸς ἔτη μέλλουσαν τῷ τρίχα]. To turn grey late is a sign of a vigorous old age and of greenness, like that of those whom the Greeks call ἀωσγέροντας [?]; like also Plautus' Periplectomenes, who says that he has not dried up from pleasant things because of his age. So in former times soft men, whom even a long life had not brought back to good sense, were accustomed to hide their greyness, just as women did. Testimonies to both are found everywhere in Greek epigrams, in Martial and in other poets. It is also established that soft and effeminate men used a drug to conceal the snow on their heads; the poet Serenus Sammonicus teaches the preparation of this dye in his elegies, and Tertullian, Josephus and others make mention of it. Clement of Alexandria calls it χρίσματα πολιῶν, "anointings of grey hair," in Book III of the Paedagogus. Aristophanes, in the Ecclesiazusae [?]:

units.la: ἐδ᾽ ἂν εἰ τὸ φάρμακον [?] Ἐψεσ᾽ ἔτυχες ᾧ Ἀυσικράτης μελαινῇ [?].
units.tr: "...you would not have found the drug, with which Ephesian... black..." [?]

units.la: Adulatores quoque moris habuisse suo regi canos vellere, testatur idem poëta Equitibus, ubi sic loquitur adulator,
units.tr: The same poet, in the Knights, testifies that flatterers also had the custom of plucking grey hairs from their king; the flatterer speaks thus:

units.la: Ἐγὼ ὃ ὡς σωλιάς γέ σύ 'κλέγων, υἱὸν ποιήσω [?].
units.tr: "I, as a flatterer, will make you a..." [?]

units.la: Καὶ λέγοντοῦ αὐτέ τι.] [?] Puta in declamationibus, aut recitationibus, quibus olim docti homines impensè delectabantur. In iis igitur, aut similibus συλλυπήσεσιν [?], adulator ei quem obseruat audientiam facit, ac reliquis ad laudandum recitatorem quamuis ineptum, & præsit exemplo, & celeusmafin hortatur. Variis autem modis solebant veteres in istiusmodi cœtibus (Græci ἐπιδείξεις [?] & ἀκροάσεις vocant: Cicero quoque acroases) approbationis signum dare: maximè verò his tribus: silentio attento, gestu corporis aliquo (vel manibus plaudentes, vel assurgentes, exultantesque, vel certo quodam modo vultum componentes) & secunda acclamatione. Plinius Secundus lib. quinto de recitationibus loquens: Multa enim a multis admonetur: & si non admoneatur, quid quisque sentiat, perspicit ex vultu, oculis, nutu, manuum motu, murmure, silentio: quae satis apertis notis indicium ab humanitate discernunt. Idem libro sexto, Non labra diduxerunt, non monuerunt manum, non denique assurrexerunt saltem lassitudine sedendi. Libanius in epistola ad magnum Basilium, ἔτω καλὴν ἐ ταύτλυ ἡν λέγεις κακῶς εἰρη- σω τὸ ὄμισολὴν, ὡς δ' οἱ παρόντες ἡμῖν ἐν ἔχον μὴ πη- δὲν ἀναγιγνωσκομένης[?]. De silentio attento locus est egregius apud Platonem tertio, de Legibus, pessime vulgò, ut alia fexcenta, acceptus, quem veluti in transcursu proferam atque interpretabor. Ibi igitur cum hospitis Atheniensis sermonem exciperet Clinias Cretensis, vellet-que illi significare sibi & sodali suo Megillo vehementer probari quę modo dixisset, sic ait: Λόγῳ μὲν ζῶν σε, ὦ ξένε, ἐπαι- νεῖν ἐπαχθέστερον· ἔργῳ δ' ὁ σφόδρα ἐπαινεσόμεθα. προοῦ- μως γὰρ τοῖς λεγομένοις ἐπακολουθήσομεν. ἐν οἷς ὅγε ἐλλ- όεῳ ἐπαινῶν καὶ μὴ, μάλιστα δὲ καταφανής[?]. hoc est, Verbis quidem te, hospes, laudare, grave & odiosum sit: at nos reipsa te vehementer laudabimus. Ad singula enim tua verba summo studio animos mentesque nostras admonebimus: quo maxime pacto homo liber laudetne an non declarare solet. Plinius secundo epistolarum, Imaginor qui concursus, quae admiratione, qui clamor, quod etiam silentium maneat. quo ego cum dico vel recito non minus quam clamore delector, sit modo silentium acre & intentum & cupidum vlteriora audiendi. De acclamationibus dicemus mox: quæ quàm crebræ fieri solerent, apparet ex his Senecæ, Controuersiarum libro 1x. loquitur de declamatoribus: Quid, ait, quod laudationibus crebris sustinentur, & memoria illorum assuemit certis interuallis quiescere?
units.tr: "And he speaks something..." [?] Think of declamations or recitations, in which learned men of old took the greatest delight. In these, or in similar gatherings [?], the flatterer makes a hearing for the one he is courting, and urges the others, by his example, to praise the reciter, however inept, and cries out in praise. The ancients, in such assemblies (the Greeks call them ἐπιδείξεις and ἀκροάσεις; Cicero too calls them acroases), used various ways of showing approval, but chiefly these three: attentive silence, some bodily gesture (either clapping the hands, or rising and leaping up, or composing the face in a certain way), and a second acclamation. Pliny the Elder, speaking in Book V on recitations: For many things are prompted by many; and if no one prompts, what each person thinks is perceived from the face, the eyes, a nod, a movement of the hands, a murmur, silence; these, by quite plain signs, show the difference from civility. The same, in Book VI: They did not part their lips, they did not move a hand, they did not even rise at least from weariness of sitting. Libanius, in a letter to Basil the Great: "...so fine a thing as you say I have said badly... and those present with us did not read..." There is an excellent passage about attentive silence in Plato's third book of the Laws, which is very badly taken by most people, as are countless other things; I will cite and interpret it as I pass. There, when Clinias the Cretan was receiving the speech of the Athenian guest, and wished to signify to him and to his companion Megillus that what he had just said was greatly approved, he speaks thus: "To praise you, stranger, in words would be rather burdensome; but we will praise you vehemently in deed. For we shall attend to each of your sayings with the greatest eagerness; in which way a free man usually shows whether he praises or not." Pliny, in Book II of the Letters: I picture to myself what a crowd there is, with what admiration, what shouting, and even what silence remains. When I speak or recite, I am delighted no less by silence than by shouting, provided the silence is keen and attentive and eager to hear more. We shall speak of acclamations shortly; how frequent these were is clear from Seneca, Controversiae Book IX, where he speaks of declaimers: What, he says, of the fact that they are sustained by frequent praises, and that their memory, accustomed to them, has to rest at certain intervals?

units.la: Καὶ ἐπαινέσαι δὲ ἀκονῶ.[?] ) Ambigo scripseritne Theophrastus ἀκονῶ[?], vel ἀκούοντα[?], vt sit is sensus quem expressimus, assentatori haud malè conueniens: an potius ἀκοῦσαι[?], vt iubeat auditores auris suas commodare recitatori, & tacitè eum laudare: quod quomodo fieri soleret, modò diximus: Sententia quàm probauimus sic expressa est ab Eupolide in Adulatoribus, ἐπ' ἄνδρα ἠλίθιον ἀλλ' ἀντὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ[?] ἀλλ' ἔτι ... ἐαυτῷ[?] τῶν εἰμί[?] χάρ τι τύχῃ λέγων ὁ ἀλαζών, πάνυ τοῦτ' ἐπαινῶ, καὶ καταπλήξομαι, δοκῶν τοῖς λόγοισι χαίρειν.
units.tr: "And to praise, I hear..." [?] I am unsure whether Theophrastus wrote ἀκονῶ [?] or ἀκούοντα [?], so that the sense is what we have expressed, fitting well enough for a sycophant; or rather ἀκοῦσαι [?], so that he bids the hearers lend their ears to the reciter and praise him silently; how this was customarily done we have just said. The sense, which we have approved, is so expressed by Eupolis in the Flatterers: Against a foolish man, but instead of his own... For if the boaster happens to say something, I will praise it greatly and be struck with amazement, seeming to rejoice in his words.

units.la: Καὶ ὑπομιμνήσκει ἡ, εἰ παύσεται ὁρᾷς.[?] ) Legimus, καὶ εἰ παύσεται[?]. Interpretes non erant hæc assecuti. notum quid sit apud Græcos oratores ὑπομονή[?], & ὑπομαίνεσθαι[?] ἐπαινῶ. Illud autem Ὀρᾷς, est visitata in recitationibus acclamatio, sicut & Εὖ, vel Υπέρ[?], Horatius in arte.
units.tr: "And he reminds him, if you see that he will stop" [?] We read, "and if he will stop" [?]. The interpreters had not grasped these words. It is known what among the Greek orators is ὑπομονή [?] and ὑπομαίνεσθαι [?] praise. But that ὌΡᾶς, "look," is an acclamation customary in recitations, just as Εὖ, "well," or Ὑπέρ, "beyond," Horace says in the Art of Poetry:
—for he will cry out finely, well, rightly.

units.la: Cicero tertio de Oratore, Quare Bene & Præclarè, quamuis nobis sæpe dicatur: Belle & Festiùe nimiùm sæpe nolo. quanquam illa ipsa exclamatio, Non potest melius, sit velim crebra Persius.
units.tr: Cicero, in Book III of the De Oratore: Therefore "Well and excellently," though often said to us, "Nicely and wittily" I do not want said too often; although that very exclamation, "It cannot be better," I would gladly have frequent, says Persius.

units.la: Euge tuum & Belle: nam belle hoc excute totum, item, —quin lepidum hoc optes audire Decenter.
units.tr: "Bravo, your fine!" and "Nicely": for take this whole thing nicely, likewise, —indeed you would wish to hear this charming thing decently.

units.la: Talis quoque illa in Actis exclamatio adulatorum, Vox Dei, non hominis. Sic Plutarchus, De se ipso sine inuidia laudando, οἱ δ' ἐπαινοῦντες[?], τὸ Θεὸς καὶ τὸ Δαιμονίως, καὶ τὸ Μεγάλως, ἐν ταῖς ὁπὸ εἰξεσι προσ-ἐχόμενοι, καὶ τὸ Μετρίως καὶ τὸ Ἀντιφρώπινος ἀποσαπολ-λύωσι. Frequentissima vero etiam Romae illa fuit acclamatio Σοφῶς. unde est toties apud Martialem grande sophos. Sidonius Apollinaris libro primo, Ad sophos meum non modo laticlavi, sed tribulium quoque fragor concitaretur. Idem libro primo, Ob hoc illi maximum sophos non eloquentia prius quam verecundia dedit. Ætas Quintiliani humanitatem vocauit hunc morem. ipse appellat vere indecoram & theatralem licentiam, studiorum perniciosissimam hostem. libro 11. cap. 11. Nos alibi demonstramus irrepsisse postea hanc consuetudinem è scholis in veteris Ecclesiae ritus.
units.tr: Such also is that acclamation of flatterers in the Acts: "The voice of God, not of man." So Plutarch, On Praising Oneself Without Envy: "Those who praise cling to 'God,' and 'Demonically,' and 'Greatly,' in their own ways, and they pronounce 'Moderately' and 'Humanly' from the heart..." But the acclamation "Wisely" [Σοφῶς] was extremely frequent even at Rome; hence the so often repeated "great wise" in Martial. Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I: At my wisdom not only the clapping of the broad-striped senators but the rattle of the lower ranks was roused. The same, Book I: For this reason he gave him the greatest "wise," not before eloquence but before modesty. The age of Quintilian called this custom humanitas; he himself rightly calls it an indecorous and theatrical licence, the most pernicious enemy of studies, Book XI, chapter 11. We show elsewhere that this custom later crept from the schools into the rites of the early Church.

units.la: καὶ σκωψαντι πικρῶς, ὑπηχλάσαι. ] Mutata distinctione sensum longè acutiorem reddidimus. Nam adulator vt indicet quàm probet scomma amici magni sui, quasi parum sit, si ridenti arrideat, in effusiorem risum & cachinnationem soluitur: ac quo magis rem videri sibi ridiculam ostendat, vestem in os inserit, & se risu penè enectum dicit. Tale illud omnino apud Plutarchum, in elegantissimo libro de discrimine adulatoris & amici, σὺ μὲν ..., inquit adulator, ἐ ἐλαϊ· ἐγὼ δ' ἐξιδύνασκον γελῶι. Tu quidem ridebas: ego vero risu penitus moriebar. Iuuenalis de adulationibus Graeculorum,
units.tr: And when he has mocked bitterly, he gives a little cough. I have changed the punctuation, which makes the sense much sharper. For the flatterer, to show how much he admires his great friend's jest, is not content simply to smile with him when he smiles; he breaks into a louder laugh and guffaw. To show how ridiculous he finds the thing, he stuffs his garment into his mouth and says he is almost dead with laughing. Plutarch has something quite like this in his most elegant book on the difference between the flatterer and the friend, where the flatterer says: You were laughing; but I was dying of laughter altogether. [σὺ μὲν ... ἐ ἐλαϊ· ἐγὼ δ' ἐξιδύνασκον γελῶι]. Juvenal, on the flattery of the Greeklings: The nation is a comedian: you laugh? He is shaken by a louder guffaw.

units.la: Natio comœda est: rides? maiore cachinno concutitur. Sed est & alia lectio, καὶ σκωψαντι ψυχρῶς, ὑπηχλάσαι. pulchrè sanè. Plurarchus περὶ δυσωπίας Periclis dictum illud, Amicum esse se ad aras vsque, reprehendens quòd hoc esset nimis prope ad grauissima peccata accedere, subiicit, ὁ ἢ π ῥῳδεν ἑαυτὸν ἰδίας μήτε λέγον[?] ἐπαινεῖν ἀσφ[?] γνώμης, μήτε ἀδοῦλ[?] κρίνειν, μήτε σκώπτειν ἀφυῶς[?] ὑπηλάν ἐν ἐάσει μέχρι τότε φροντιδεῖν: qui locus hanc lectionem vehementer aftruit atque exponit.
units.tr: The nation is a comedian: you laugh? He is shaken by a louder guffaw. There is also another reading, "and when he has mocked coldly, he gives a little cough" [καὶ σκωψαντι ψυχρῶς, ὑπηχλάσαι], which is quite fine. In his essay on how to avoid shame, Plutarch, rebuking Pericles' saying that he was a friend "even to the altars", adds that a man should not praise himself too much in his own opinion, nor be ready to judge things by his own taste, nor mock clumsily, nor cough at the right moment, nor wait for others to speak first. That passage strongly supports this reading and explains it.

units.la: ἕως ἂν αὐτὸς παρέλθῃ.] Αὐτὸς, hoc eft, Ille, & vt hodie loquuntur homines κολακικοί[?], Dominus fine adiectione. Ita semper in hoc capite designatur ὁ κολακοδούλος[?], qui eft adulatori inftar domini. Sunt enim αὐτὸς & ἐκεῖνοι, voces feruorum, quas honoris caussa proprio rum nominum loco vsurpabant. Ariftophanes Ranis,
units.tr: Until he himself has passed by. "Himself" here means that man, and, as the flatterers of today would say, the Master without any addition. In this chapter the flatterer's slave is always marked in this way, since he stands to the flatterer as a master. For autos and ekeinoi are the words slaves used, which they employed in place of proper names out of respect. Aristophanes, in the Frogs:

units.la: ἰδοῦ νῦν φράζον πρώτισα τὰς αὐλητρίας Τὰς ἔνδον ἔσω, αὐτὸς ὡς εἰσέρχομαι.
units.tr: Look now, first of all, the flute-girls inside, as I come in, "the master himself". [ἰδοῦ νῦν φράζον πρώτισα τὰς αὐλητρίας Τὰς ἔνδον ἔσω, αὐτὸς ὡς εἰσέρχομαι.]

units.la: scholiastes, αὐτὸς ἀλλ' τὸ ὁ δεσπότης. Sic apud Latinos. Plautus Cafina, ybi Stalino & ancilla colloquuntur.
units.tr: The scholiast: "autos, but in the sense of the master." It is the same among the Latins. Plautus, in the Casina, where Stalino and a maidservant are talking:

units.la: St. Quid tu hic agis? An. Ego eo quo me Ipfa misit. Ipfa. hoc eft, Hera mea. Terentius Hecyra,
units.tr: St. What are you doing here? An. I am going where my mistress has sent me. "Mistress" here means my lady.

units.la: Sed Pamphilum ipsum video stare ante ades.
units.tr: Terence, in the Hecyra: But I see Pamphilus himself standing before the house.

units.la: Donatus, Ipsum, à quo missus sum: vel dominum, vt Graeci αὐτόν. Idem notat Asconius in quendam Verrinarum locum. Erat & discipulorum vox, cum de praeceptore loquerentur: vnde illud Αὐτὸς ἔφα. Ariftophanes Nebulis,
units.tr: Donatus: "Ipsum, the one by whom I was sent; or master, as the Greeks say autos." Asconius makes the same note on a passage in the Verrines. It was also the word of pupils when they spoke of their teacher, whence the saying Autos epha, "the master himself said". Aristophanes, in the Clouds:

units.la: Στ. Φέρε, τίς γὰρ ἔσθ' οὗτος σὺν τῇ κρεμαστρᾷ ἀνὴρ; Μα. Αὐτός. Στ. τίς αὐτός; Μ. Σωκράτης.
units.tr: St. Come, who is this man with the hanging basket? Ma. Autos. St. Who is autos? M. Socrates.

units.la: Scholiastes ibi, Honoris caussa, inquit, non statim Socratis nomen profert. Idem notatur ab eodem etiam alibi, & à Donato non vno loco. Apud Platonem in Protagora pulsantibus fores Calliae sophistae, respondet ianitor, 'Οὐ χολὴ αὐτῷ, id eft, Doctori non vacat. Cum igitur vox κόλαξ ad aliud referatur, & fit τὸ πρὸς τι, vt herus & seruus, patronus & libertus, itémque patronus & cliens. Theophrastus τὸν κολακεδόμψυχον [?], id est, eum qui se fi suit adulari, vt Cicero loquitur, αὐτὸν appellat, pulchrè loquendi genus ipsum quo adulatores vtuntur, retinens. Nos aliquando αὐτὸν regem diximus: Nam apud Latinos ὁ κολακεδόρχος [?], Rex dicitur: & vt docet Donatus rex & parasitus ita sunt τῆ πρὸς τι, vt patronus & libertus. Dicitur & dominus: vnde illud Iuuenalis,
units.tr: The scholiast there: "Out of respect, he says, he does not at once utter Socrates' name." The same thing is noted by the same scholiast elsewhere, and by Donatus in more than one place. In Plato's Protagoras, when people knock at the door of the sophist Callias, the doorkeeper replies, "Autos is not free", that is, the teacher is not at leisure. Since the word kolax is used in relation to something else, and is a relative term, like master and slave, patron and freedman, and likewise patron and client, Theophrastus calls the man who wishes to be flattered autos, the flatterer's own term, keeping the elegant form of speech that flatterers themselves use. Sometimes we have called autos "the king". For among the Latins the flatterer's king is called rex, and, as Donatus teaches, the king and the parasite are related to each other as patron and freedman are. He is also called dominus, whence Juvenal's line:
—master, yet also the king of masters

units.la: Si vis tu fieri, nullus tibi parvulus aula Luserit Aeneas.
units.tr: If you want to be, no little Aeneas will play in your hall.

units.la: Apud Graecos ὁ τυφῶν & ὁ κόλαξ similem saepe relationem habent: quare ὁ τυφῶν est rex. vt cum scribit scholiastes Aristoph. Ὅτι τῷ εἰώθασι τῆς τυφῶν οἱ κόλακες λέγειν [?]. & apud Demosthenem saepe τυφῶν & κολακεύειν pro eodem ponuntur. Interdum vero ad deos refertur κόλαξ & appellatio: & ita dicti sunt οἱ Διονυσιακοὶ τεχνῖται, qui vitam tolerarent artes Baccho sacras exercentes, vt comoedi & tragoedi, & natio illa tota, histriones, praestigiatores siue θαυματοποιοί, rhapsodi, citharoedi, λιθοχιθαρισταί [?], tibicines, ἀλεσκέται [?]: hi inquam omnes dicti sunt Δορυφοροκόλακες [?]: itémque μυσοκόλακες: nam ita eos vocat Dionysius Halicarn. libro septimo.
units.tr: Among the Greeks, typhōn and kolax often have a similar relation, so that typhōn means king, as the scholiast on Aristophanes writes: "because flatterers are accustomed to say typhōn of the king". And in Demosthenes typhōn and kolakeuein are often used for the same thing. Sometimes too the term kolax is applied to the gods. In this way the Dionysiac artists were so called, those who earned their living by practising the arts sacred to Bacchus, such as comic and tragic actors, and that whole tribe of stage performers, conjurers or thaumatopoioi, rhapsodes, lyre-players, stone-lyre players, pipers, and aleskētai. All of these, I say, were called doryphorokolakes, and likewise musokolakes*; for so Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls them in his seventh book.

units.la: χρηστὸς πατρὸς νεότης [?]. ] Etiam hic seruat idioma adulatorum. Νεότης autem maluimus pullitiem, quam pullos vertere, aut pullastros: quia fere in his vocibus latet obscoenitas, vt Festus docet. Iuuenalis de adulatoribus,
units.tr: The youth of a good father. Here too he keeps the idiom of the flatterers. I have preferred to render neotēs as "chickenhood" rather than "chicks" or "young birds", because a certain obscenity lies hidden in these words, as Festus teaches. Juvenal on flatterers:
—he himself, chattering, will rejoice together with the nest.

units.la: καὶ πορευόμενος[?] πρὸς τινα τῶν φίλων. Mos fuit Græcis Romanisque cum ad aliquem amicorum viserent, nuncio misso suum aduentum significare. Plinius Secundus epistolarum libro primo, Enigilaueram. Nuntius à Spurina: venio ad te: Imo ego ad te: Coimus in porticum Liuia, cum alter ad alterum tenderemus. Apud Romanos verò etiam maritus rure domum reuertens, mittebat qui aduentum significaret vxori, vt auctor est Plutarchus in Quæstionibus Romanis: ac videtur fuisse hoc munus eorum seruorum, quos anteambulones vocat Martialis. Epiphanius [illegible, ~12 letters] Mox legendum [illegible, ~10 letters], non προσαγορεύσα[?]. Sic Terentius, Abi Geta pranuntia.
units.tr: And going to one of his friends. It was the custom among Greeks and Romans, when they were going to visit one of their friends, to announce their coming by sending a messenger. Pliny the Younger, in the first book of his letters: I had woken up. A message from Spurinna: I am coming to you. No, I am coming to you. We met in the Livian portico, as each of us was hastening to the other. Among the Romans, a husband returning home from the country also sent someone to announce his arrival to his wife, as Plutarch records in his Roman Questions; and this office seems to have belonged to those slaves whom Martial calls anteambulones. Epiphanius [illegible]. Presently [illegible] should be read, not prosagoreusa. So Terence: Go, Geta, and announce me beforehand.

units.la: Ἐν τῆς γυναικείας ἀγορᾶς διακονήσας ξωνητός. De muliebri foro tantùm docent hos veteres: fuisse apud Athenienses locum in foro, qui γυναικεῖα ἀγορὰ vocaretur: vbi minuta vasa, atque vt puto ἐπιτράπεζα & escaria in primis, vænirent. Auctor Pollux libro decimo, capite secundo. Atque hoc etsi à doctis viris rectè est isto loco adnotatum: iidem tamen sensum horum verborum nescio an peruiderint: certè non aperuerunt. Voluit enim Theophrastus hisce verbis declarare, quod Plutarchus ait esse adulatoris proprium: circa minuta quædam & sordida officia, quæ verus & ingenuus amicus, vt se indigna spernit, versari, ea obire atque exequi: at scin quomodo? tanta diligentia, vt cum cernas illis rebus occupatum, putes in eo quod agat, opes Græciæ positas. Idco ait ἀπρόσι[?], hoc eft, fedulò, properè, & quasi vno fpiritu. fic Latini vim vocis Græcæ exprimunt. Seneca Clitum iftum vno fi potes fpiritu exupera, hoc eft,ἀπνάςι. Plin. dixit pro eo, raptim & fine interspiratione. D. Hieronymus, in epiftola quadam, vna falua non diffimili fenfu.Plato in Theæteto,ὅρως καὶ ὀξέως ἀπνέειν in fimili fententia dixit. Plutarchus vero fignificantiffimis verbis τὸ ἀπνάςι expreffit, συνεχῶς, καὶ ἐνδελεχῶς, καὶ ἀσφαλῶς. Eius locum apponam, qui ifti erit pro amplo commentario.
units.tr: Serving in the women's market, a hireling. The ancient writers teach us only this about the women's market: at Athens there was a place in the marketplace called the gynaikeia agora, where small vessels were sold, and, I think, especially epitrapezia and food. Pollux, book ten, chapter two, is the authority. Although learned men have rightly noted this passage, I do not know whether they have grasped the sense of these words, for certainly they have not explained it. Theophrastus meant by these words to set out what Plutarch says is proper to the flatterer: he busies himself with certain petty and sordid duties, which a true and well-born friend, scorning them as beneath him, will not do; the flatterer performs and carries them out. And how? With such diligence that when you see him occupied with those things, you would think the wealth of Greece depended on what he is doing. Therefore he says apros[?], that is, diligently, hastily, and as if in one breath. So the Latins express the force of the Greek word. Seneca: If you can, outdo that Clitus in one breath, that is, apnastí. Pliny used for it hastily and without drawing breath. St Jerome, in a certain letter, in one breath, with much the same sense. Plato, in the Theaetetus, used "to breathe quickly and sharply" in a similar sense. Plutarch expressed apnastí in very meaningful words: continually, unceasingly, and assiduously. I shall quote his passage, which will serve here in place of a full commentary.

units.la: Ἐν ταῖς [illegible, ~6 letters] πολλὰ [?] οἱ φίλοι τῶν μικρῶν, [illegible, ~10 letters] ἐξακριβῶν [?] τεςςάρες, ἑαυτὸς εἰς τὰ ὑπερ- [illegible, ~8 letters] ἀλλ᾽ ἐκεῖνο (ὁ κόλαξ) ἐπαινῶν συνεχῶς, καὶ ἐνδελεχῶς, καὶ ἀσφαλῶς, ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ τόπον τινὰ χώραν διαχωρίας, ἀλλὰ βελόμενος κελεύειν, κἂν μὴ κελεύσῃ ἀνοήτως, μᾶλλον ὅλως ἐξαδυμῶν καὶ πολυ- ψύμενος. id eft, Si quid faciendum fit, multa minuta prætermittunt veri amici, haudquaquam follicitè inquirentes, neque fatagentes, neque fe ad omnia minifteria vltrò ingerentes. Adulator contra affiduum in his, fedulum, atque indefeffum fe præbet: nullum aliū locum, nullas partes obeundas relinquens: fed fibi optans imperari: agrè etiam, ni id fiat, ferens: aut animum potius despondens, & miserè quiritans. alludit huc Horatius illis verbis fecundo Satyrarum,
units.tr: [The Greek text here is too corrupted to give with confidence.] "Among ... friends of small matters ... [illegible] ... but he, flattering him continually, and unceasingly, and assiduously; while the other, not wishing to be told the place or part to be taken, but wishing to be ordered, and if not ordered, foolishly ... rather altogether sweetening and making much of him." That is: If something needs doing, true friends neglect many small things, not very anxiously seeking them out, nor busying themselves, nor thrusting themselves forward to every service. The flatterer, on the contrary, presents himself constantly in these things, eagerly and tirelessly, leaving no other place and no other part to be performed, but wishing to be commanded; and bearing it badly if it is not done; or rather losing heart and whining wretchedly. Horace alludes to this in those words of the second book of the Satires:

units.la: —nec non vernaliter ipfis Fungitur officijs. Nam vernaliter eft, adulatorum in morem. Non eft autem arbitrandum ad vafa tantum nefcio quæ hæc pertinere, quia Pollux dicat in foro mulicbri vafa væniffe: quin potius generaliter ad ea omnia referendum, quæ ad epulas & inftruendam menfam pertineát. Erat autem obsonari officium olim, alias feruorum ἀγοραςῶν siue obsonatorum, quorum Athenæus libro III. & Seneca epistola quadragesima septima meminerunt: & in Θεοφίλει[?] suo Theodoretus, in vita Petri Galli eremitæ: alias adulatorum ac parasitorum: quod illa Ergasili parasiti Plautini querela de sui temporis iuuentute declarat.
units.tr: —nor does he perform the duties with a slave's springtime zeal. For vernaliter means in the manner of flatterers. Nor should we think that these things pertain only to some vessels, because Pollux says that vessels were sold in the women's market; rather they should be referred generally to everything that pertains to feasts and the furnishing of the table. Procuring provisions was once a separate duty, that of the slaves called agorastai or purveyors, whom Athenaeus in book III and Seneca in letter forty-seven mention; and Theodoret in his Theophilus, in the life of Peter the Gaulish hermit. It was also the duty of flatterers and parasites, as the complaint of Ergasilus, the parasite in Plautus, about the youth of his own time makes clear.

units.la: Ipsi obsonant, quæ parasitorum ante erat prouincia.
units.tr: They do the marketing themselves, which used to be the job of parasites.

units.la: Ipsi de foro tam aperto capite ad lenones eunt.
units.tr: They themselves go openly to the pimps in the forum, heads uncovered.

units.la: In tribu quàm aperto capite sontes condemnant reos.
units.tr: In the tribal court they openly condemn the accused, heads uncovered.

units.la: & in Milite sic de se Periplectomenes,
units.tr: And in the Miles Gloriosus, Periplectomenes says of himself:

units.la: Vel hilarissimum conuiuam hinc indidem expromam tibi,
units.tr: Either I will produce for you from here and there the most cheerful dinner guest,
or a leading parasite and an excellent marketer.

units.la: Gnatho quoque Terentianus ideo se charum ait esse cupedinariis, coquis, laniis, cetariis, sartoribus piscatoribus & aucupibus, quia & olim sibi re sua salua. & nunc perdita, suo regi obsonans sæpe illis profuisset. In Adelphis autem indicat Demea obsonare itidem ac scortum ducere, hominis nihili esse officium.
