Hinc nomen habuit apud Apollodorum ex quo Phormionem suam Terentius transtulit, parasitus Phormio: id enim nomen poëta parasito tribuit, alludens ad φορμίδα[?]: erat autem φορμὶς vas vimineum ut sportula, quod ad macellū & forum cum irent, secum ferebant: quale est quod Galli vocant rabas. unde est φορμὶς καρύων[?] & φορμὶς σύκων apud Athenæum: quod Cicero pro Flacco fiscinam ficorum dixit: Plutarchus περὶ φιλοπλουτίας[?] ἀρρίχον ἰχάδων[?]. Xiphilinus ex Dione ἀεῖχον[?] (nam & ita scribitur) ἐπάρχαι[?] ἐχ(ε)ῖν. Aristoteles III. Rhet. ἄλαρον συκαμίνων[?]. Fuisse autem in Τωμακεία[?] ἀγορᾷ non tantùm vasa, sed omne fermè genus obsoniorum vendi solita, vel ipso Polluce teste probare possumus:qui Κύκλον, & γευμαχείαν[?] ἀγορὰ, pro eodé accipere videtur. In Cyclo autem omnia id genus exceptis carnibus proftabant. Scholiastes Ariftoph. Ὁ κύκλῳ & Ἀθλώνιον[?] ὅτι καθάπερ μακέλλῳ, ἐκ τῆς καθα- σκευῆς τῶν προσηγορίαν[?] λαβὼν ἐ. ἔα δὲ ἡ ὁ πραστικὸς[?] χωρεῖς κρεῶν & ἄλλα ὡς ἰα ἐξαιρέτως οἱ ἰχθύες. Quod ait à forma hoc forum Circuli nomen esse nactum, quippe quod esset rotundum, verum est: constat enim pleraque antiquorum fora fuisse eius formae. propterea Homerus, vt notant veteres, τὴν ἀγορὰν[?] vocat ἱερὸν κύκλον. & Sophocles, κυκλόεις[?] (in editis libris hodie, Φρόνοι[?]) ἀγορᾶς dixit. Euripides quoque ἀγορᾶς χρυσέων κύκλον. Sic apud Dionem Prusensem, τὸν τῆς Εὐδοξίης ἀγερᾶς κύκλοι legas.
units.tr: Terence's Gnatho also says he is dear to the dainty-sellers, cooks, butchers, fishmongers, tailors, fishermen and fowlers, because in the past, while his own property was safe, and now that it is lost, he often served them by doing the marketing for his master. In the Adelphi, Demea indicates that doing the marketing is just like leading a prostitute, the office of a worthless man. Hence Terence took the name Phormio, which he transferred from Apollodorus, and called the parasite "Phormio," alluding to the basket [φορμίς]. A phormis was a wicker basket, like a sportula, which people carried with them when they went to the market and the forum. It is what the Gauls call a rabas. Hence the "basket of nuts" [φορμὶς καρύων] and "basket of figs" [φορμὶς σύκων] in Athenaeus. Cicero in the Pro Flacco called it a basket of figs (fiscina). Plutarch, in his work on the love of wealth, speaks of a basket of figs. Xiphilinus, from Dio, has a basket of ... (for so it is also written). Aristotle in the third book of the Rhetoric mentions a basket of mulberries. That not only containers but almost every kind of delicacy was usually sold in the market, we can show from Pollux's own testimony, who seems to take the "Cyclus" and the "market for delicacies" as the same thing. In the Cyclus almost all such things were on sale, except meats. The scholiast on Aristophanes says that the name "Cyclus" (circle) was given to the market from its shape, and that is true, since most ancient markets were of that shape. For this reason Homer, as the ancients note, calls the agora a "sacred circle." Sophocles speaks of the "circle of the agora" (in the printed books today, "Phronoi"). Euripides too speaks of the "golden circle of the agora." So in Dio of Prusa you may read of "the circles of the agora of Eudoxia."

units.la: ὡς μάλακως ἐθέλεις[?]!) Simillimę voces adulatorum Dionysij tyranni, quas refert Diogenes Cynicus in epistola ad ipsum. Σὺ δ', inquit, ὥσπερ & παιδία πάππως τινὲς καὶ τίτθας εἰσηγάγυ[?]· καὶ (οἱ φασί[?], Δέξαι τέκνον. Ἔγχεαι εἴ τι μὲ φιλεῖς μικρὸν ἔτι μόνον τῆς προσφέρε[?]. id est, Tu vero inflar puerorum asciniisi tibi nescio quos paterculos & nutrices, qui tibi aiunt, Accipe hoc, fili: Infunde si quid me amas adhuc parum: Tantum hoc amplius ede.
units.tr: "How softly you want it!" These are very similar words of the flatterers of the tyrant Dionysius, which Diogenes the Cynic reports in his letter to him. "You," he says, "like the grandfathers and nurses of children, bring in certain people who say, 'Take this, son. Pour in, if you love me at all, just a little more of what is offered.'" That is: "You, like the fathers and nurses of little children, bring in I know not who, who say to you, 'Take this, son. Pour in a little more, if you love me at all. Eat this too.'"

units.la: Da Trebio: pone ad Trebium; vis, frater, ab illis Iibus?
units.tr: Give to Trebius; set it before Trebius; do you wish, brother, some of those cakes?

units.la: & προσοχεφάλαια.) Solebant enim potentiores & delicatiores spectare sedentes in puluinis: cuius moris etiam in Æschinis & Demosthenis orationibus est mentio. χαὶ τῷ εἰκόνα ὁμοίαν ἔχῃ). ) Intelligendum hoc est de imagine quam artifex pulchriorem multo fecerit eo quem refert. Nam hoc quoque adulationis genus olim vsitatum fuit : Lucianus ὑπὲρ τῆς εἰκόνων. Sunt, ait, qui non ἐν ἐπαίνοις tantùm, sed etiam ἐν γραφαῖς & ὁμοία κολακευόμενοι τε καὶ ἐξαπατᾶσθαι θέλοντι [?] vide reliqua. Seneca loquens de philosopho rebus non artificiis, epistola cxii. Non exurgit in plantas, nec in summis ambulat digitis, eorum more qui mendacio statuam (scrib. staturam) adiuuant, longiorésque quam sunt, videri volunt.
units.tr: And "with the pillows" (prosokephalaia): for the more powerful and more luxurious were accustomed to look on from couches with cushions, and mention of this custom is also found in the speeches of Aeschines and Demosthenes. And "with an image like him" (tēn eikona homoian): this must be understood of a portrait that the artist made much more handsome than the person it represents. For this kind of flattery was also used in former times. Lucian, in his work on portraits, says: "There are those who are flattered and want to be deceived not only in praises but also in paintings and likenesses." See the rest. Seneca, speaking of the philosopher in regard to things, not arts, in letter 112: He does not rise up on his toes, nor walk on the tips of his fingers, like those who help out their stature with a lie and want to seem taller than they are.

units.la: Atque hæc de adulatione Theophrastus in isto libello. Nam alibi plura de fœditate eius vitij fuisse ab illo scripta, edito etiam Περὶ κολακείας libro integro, testantur veteres: & laudat eum librū Athenæus in sexto Deipnosophistarum. Docuerat & Eupolis eodem argumento fabulam Κόλακες inscriptam: cuius meminit Pollux lib. vii.cap. vltimo. & Menander item Κόλακα, teste Athenæo.
units.tr: And this is what Theophrastus says about flattery in this little book. For the ancients testify that he wrote much more about the foulness of this vice elsewhere, and even a whole book, On Flattery. Athenaeus praises that book in the sixth book of the Deipnosophists. Eupolis, too, had produced a play on the same subject entitled The Flatterers (Kolakes), which Pollux mentions in the last chapter of book seven. Menander likewise wrote a Flatterer, according to Athenaeus.

units.la: Περὶ ἀδολεσχίας.) Et hoc caput & duo item alia, quorum alterum inscribitur Περὶ λαλιᾶς, alterum Περὶ λογοποιίας, ad vitæ quotidianæ confuctudine, m& eas quas superiore capite ὁμιλητικὰς ἕξεις, vocari à Platone dicebamus, pertinent. Nam cum vt docet Aristoteles vita humana duabus quasi partibus continetur, otio & negotio, siue vt loquitur Theophrastus hoc capite σχολὴ καὶ ἀσχολία, (Cicero & Salustius inca & feria vocant) virtus & vitium etiam in remissione hac & ἀναπαύσει vt philosophus appellat, locum habent:ipséque in quatto Nicomacheorum quasdam virtutes & vitia recenset huius generis. Non est autem inter ὁμιλίλι[?]κὰς[?] virtutes postrema censenda illa quæ opponitur tribus supra nominatis vitiis: quæ virtus nomine proprio cum apud Græcos tum apud Latinos caret. Ambrosius quidem in Officiis loquendi modum appellat, & primum officium esse statuit: sed nos latius patentem virtutem quandam quærimus: quæ nihil aliud est quàm mediocritas quædam circa congressiones & colloquia familiarium, & quando, & quandiu, & quomodo iis debeamus indulgere præscribens. Hanc ἀνώνυμον virtutem notam facient quæ ei sicut reliquis virtutibus opponuntur vitia, & κῆ[?] τὸ ἐλλείπον[?], & κῆ[?] τὸ ὑπερβάλ-λον. Nam & austeritate ea sunt quidam, ut ab istiusmodi congressionibus abhorreant, aut in iis tanquam lapides conticescant: quos merito reprehendas: & contrà alij sunt qui istis σωφρόσυς[?] nimis delectentur, aut modum in iis tenere nesciant. Hi posteriores modum excedunt & ὑπερβολὴ peccant: illi priores ἐλλεί̈ψει[?]: de quibus nihil amplius dicemus hoc loco, nisi quòd Theophrastus αὐθαδείας nomine hoc quoque vitium est complexus, de quo infrà. At eorum qui ὑπερβολὴ hac in re peccant, multiplex est differentia: latissimè enim id vitium patet, quodque in multas quasi species dividi queat. Ex iis sunt illæ tres quas totidem capitibus Theophrastus describit, ἀδολεσχία, λαλιά[?], λογοφιλία[?]: quæ vitia etsi affinia sunt (quippe quasi species eiusdem generis) differunt tamen inter se non parum. Nam ut de ἀδολεσχία primùm dicamus: qui congressionibus id genus ita delectantur, vt voluptati illi quam ex colloquiis mutuis & confabulationibus persæpe nugatoriis quibus solent homines otio dediti & garruli senes se oblectare, omnia postponant, faciléque vel dies integros de lana caprina aut gerris Siculis cum sui similibus colloquentes traducant: hos Græci ἀδολέσχης[?] quasi auidos confabulandi ἐπὶ τὸ ἀδολεσχεῖν[?] τῇ λέξῃ[?] nuncuparunt. Est autem λέξη[?] (ea vox pura puta est Hebraea vel Syriaca) cum istiusmodi confabulatio: tum locus ipse vbi ea fine otiosi homines coire solet, apud Homerum & Hesiodum. fuitque ea d[?]ctio diu in vsu apud Ionés & Dores in ea notione. Ἀδολεσχίαν hanc definit Theophrastus διήγησιν λόγων μακρῶν[?] & ἀπρος[?]. λόγων: sic eius præceptor τῆς ἀδολέσχης definiebat tertio Nicomacheorum, ὅτις φιλομύθης[?] καὶ διηγηματικὸς[?], καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν τυχόντων καταταξίοντας[?] τῆς ἡμέρας[?]. Similiter etiam Dion Chrysostomus in oratione quadam τοῖς ἀδολέσχοις tribuit λόγως ἀπλοῦντας[?] καὶ μακρὰς, sermones sine mente & longos. & in optimo Glossario ἀδολεσχὴς vertitur fabulosus, hoc est, φιλόμυθος, vt dixit Aristoteles. Themistius oratione septima, φιλόμυθον ἀληθῶς ὅτι ἐς μέλλον, ἀδολεσχεῖν τε & πολλὰ δοκιμῶν[?]. Veteres Latini fatuum dixerunt: est enim fatuus à fando, & inepta loquentem notat: quanquam potest origo vocis esse Hebraica, à dictione 'פתי', quæ significat hominem ἀφρων & fatuum. Sed & fabulatorem & nugatorem Latini τὸν ἀδολέσχον vocant: & ἀδολεσχίαν nugas: vt apud Terétium nugas dicere, pro ἀδολεσχεῖν. Nos autem ἀδολέσχω garrulum diximus, & ἀδολεσχεῖν garrire. Cicero Attico libro x 1 1. Nouì nihil. quid ergo opus erat epistola? quid cum coram fumus & garrimu[?] quicquid in buccam? Est profecto quiddam λέγειν, quae habet etiam, si nihil subest, collocutione ipsa suauitatem. Λαλιά vero vitium est quo tenentur ij qui non solum confabulationibus iis nimis sunt dediti, quae erat ἀδολεσχίαν[?] nota: sed hoc amplius, modum in congressibus tenere nescientes, perpetuò loqui, tacere nunquam, neque vllas aliis loquendi vices tradere solent: sed γλωσσαλγία[?] & loquendi morbo, vt Cato vocabat, laborant: quam αἰσχύνην[?] νόσον verissimè Euripides appellauit. Haec est quam Theophrastus λαλιὰν vocat. Reperiuntur verò quidam minimi pretij & male feriati homines, quibus mos est falsa quaedam confingere quae aliis narrent: iis maximè qui nouorum nunciorum audiendorum desiderio ducuntur: qua prurigine teneri multos videas. Graeci fictores istos nouorum rumorum λογοποιούς dixerút, & vitiũ ipsum λογοποιίαν[?]: de quibus infrà pluribus. Ex his quae diximus intelligi potest, & quid commune habeant haec tria, ἀδολεσχία, λαλιά, & λογοποιία, & quid differant: subtiliter enim & ingeniosè ea Theophrastus distinxit. At à scriptoribus vulgò istae distinctiones non obseruantur: quare etiam Plutarchus in eo commentario quem scripsit Περὶ ἀδολεσχίας, tres has species vnica illa voce complectitur.
units.tr: Concerning garrulity. This chapter, and two others, one of which is entitled On Chattering and the other On Gossip-mongering, belong to the everyday customs of life, and to those dispositions which, as we said in the previous chapter, Plato called sociable [homilētikai hexeis]. For since, as Aristotle teaches, human life is contained in two parts, as it were, leisure and business, or, as Theophrastus says in this chapter, scholē and ascholia (Cicero and Sallust call these otium and feriae), virtue and vice also find a place in this relaxation and recreation, which the philosopher calls anapausis. Aristotle himself, in the fourth book of the Nicomachean Ethics, lists some virtues and vices of this kind. Now among the sociable virtues, that one which is opposed to the three vices named above should not be counted last. It has no proper name, either among the Greeks or among the Latins. Ambrose, in his On the Duties, calls it a manner of speaking and holds it the first duty. But we are looking for a virtue of wider scope, which is nothing other than a certain moderation in the meetings and conversations of friends, prescribing when, how long, and in what manner we ought to indulge in them. The vices that are opposed to this nameless virtue, as to the other virtues, will make it known, both kata to elleipon [by deficiency] and kata to hyperballon [by excess]. For some, from a kind of austerity, shrink from such gatherings, or fall silent in them like stones; and these deserve to be rebuked. On the other hand, there are others who take too much delight in such pleasant company, or do not know how to keep moderation in it. The latter exceed the measure and sin by excess; the former by deficiency. We will say nothing more about these here, except that Theophrastus included this vice too under the name of authadeia (self-will), of which more below. But among those who sin by excess in this matter there is a manifold variety, for this vice extends very widely and can be divided into many kinds, as it were. Among these are the three which Theophrastus describes in as many chapters: garrulity (adoleschia), chatter (lalia), and gossip-mongering (logopoiia). These vices, although they are related (being as it were species of the same genus), nevertheless differ from one another not a little. To speak first of garrulity: those who take such delight in these meetings that they put everything else after the pleasure they get from mutual conversations and chats, which are very often trifling, in which idle men and talkative old people like to amuse themselves, and who can easily spend whole days talking with their like about goat's wool or Sicilian trifles, these the Greeks call adolesches, as being eager for chatter, from adoleschein [to chatter] in speech [lexē]. Now lexē (a word which is purely, as they say, Hebrew or Syriac) means both such a conversation and also the very place where idle men are accustomed to meet for it, in Homer and Hesiod. This word was long in use among the Ionians and Dorians in this sense. Theophrastus defines this garrulity as "a narration of long and pointless speeches" [diēgēsis logōn makrōn kai apsophōn]. So too his teacher defined the garrulous man in the third book of the Nicomachean Ethics: he is one who is fond of stories and narration, and who spends the whole day on whatever happens to come along. Similarly, Dio Chrysostom in a certain speech attributes to garrulous persons simple and long speeches [logous aplousntas kai makras], that is, "discourses without sense and long." And in the excellent glossary adolesches is rendered as fabulosus, that is, philomythos, as Aristotle said. Themistius, in his seventh oration, says that the one who is truly a lover of stories is the one who chatters and gives many opinions. The old Latins called it fatuus, for fatuus comes from fari (to speak), and denotes one who speaks foolishly, although the origin of the word may be Hebrew, from the word pāti, which means a fool without wisdom. But the Latins also call a teller of tales and a trifler adolescho, and garrulity they call nugae (trifles), as in Terence, nugas dicere, for adoleschein. We have said that adolesches is talkative and adoleschein is to chatter. Cicero, in book eleven of the letters to Atticus: "I know nothing. Why then was there need of a letter? Why, when we are together, do we chatter whatever comes to our mouths?" There is indeed a certain kind of talk which has a charm of its own in conversation even when there is nothing in it. But lalia (chatter) is a vice by which those are seized who not only are too devoted to those conversations which marked adoleschia, but also, not knowing how to keep measure in company, are accustomed to talk perpetually, never to be silent, and never to yield turns of speaking to others. They suffer from glōssalgia and the disease of talking, as Cato called it, which Euripides most truly called a shameful disease. This is what Theophrastus calls lalia. Moreover, there are certain men of little worth and idle, who are accustomed to invent false stories to tell others, especially those who are driven by a desire to hear new reports; many of whom you may see gripped by this itch. The Greeks called these inventors of new rumours logopoioi, and the vice itself logopoiia; more on these below. From what we have said, it can be understood both what these three, garrulity, chatter and gossip-mongering, have in common, and how they differ, for Theophrastus distinguished them subtly and ingeniously. But writers commonly do not observe these distinctions; hence Plutarch, in the commentary he wrote On Garrulity, embraces all three species under that single word.

units.la: ξὴ ἐπροσωπολήπτων[?].) Sapientis est, è corde intimo, non è labris tantùm summis vocem mittere: quod faciunt homines vani, qui quodcunque in solum venit, vt dicitur, temerè effutiunt. Plutarchus perelegantèr, ἐσὴν ἀτεχνῶς[?], inquit, ἡ λάλη ςάθμη πρὸς τὰς λόγος ὁ ἀδολέσχης[?]. Imitatur autem Platonem illo loco ( vt obiter hoc dicam ) non insolens Plutarchus. Ait de se Socrates in Charmide, ἀλκὴ σάθμη εἰμὶ πρὸς τὰς καλάς[?]. Prouerbium est ἀλκὴ σάθμη[?], de eo qui omnia indiscriminatim probat. Tale est apud A.Gellium ex Lucillio alba linea. Fere enim minio aut rubrica utuntur fabri, non creta. Platonis interpretes quid inter σάθμη & σαθμῷ interesset nescierunt: & ut cum Platone dicam, πρὸς τ' νοῦν τῷ Φιλοσόφῳ ἀποδαχῶς ἀλκὴ σάθμη ἐχρῶντο[?]. In contrarium sensum usurpatur vox σάθμη, ut cum ait Iulius Pollux, ἀλλ' ἐδ' ἐν Θεοπόμπῳ σάθμη τῷ εἰς ἐμφυλείας κείσιν[?]. Sic legendum apud Pollucem lib. IIII. cap. XII.
units.tr: It is the mark of a wise man to send forth his voice from the innermost heart, not merely from the outer lips; vain men do the opposite, rashly blurting out whatever comes into their mouths, as the saying goes. Plutarch puts it elegantly: the chatterer is simply a touchstone for words, testing everything indiscriminately. Plutarch, not unusually, imitates Plato in this passage. Socrates says of himself in the Charmides, I am a touchstone for beautiful things. Touchstone is a proverb for one who approves everything without distinction. Similar is the white line in Aulus Gellius, quoted from Lucilius. Workmen use red ochre or chalk for marking, not white. The interpreters of Plato did not know the difference between the two words for touchstone, and, to put it in Plato's words, they used them without discrimination [ἀλκὴ σάθμη]. The word is used in the opposite sense when Julius Pollux says: "But in Theopompus too the touchstone is used for the setting of a dispute." This is how the passage in Pollux, book 4, chapter 12, should be read.

units.la: Οἶ(& ὃν μὴ γινώσκει, τύτῳ.) Ita orditur descriptionem garruli & Horatius:
units.tr: [Greek phrase, corrupt in the scan, ending "whom he does not know, this one"]. Horace also begins his description of the chatterer in this way:

units.la: Accurrit quidam, notus mihi nomine tantum,Arreptaq; manu, Quid agis dulcissime rerum?
units.tr: A certain man runs up to me, known to me by name only, and, seizing my hand, says: "How are you, dearest of men?"

units.la: Pag. II. καὶ ὡς ἄξιοι οἱ πυροὶ ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ.) Intellige hic πυρῶν ἀγοράν, qualis Romæ erat Minutia frumentaria. Similis Daui ἀπολογία apud Terentium in contraria sententia.
units.tr: Page 2: and how dear the wheat is in the market. Understand here the wheat market, such as the grain dole (Minutia frumentaria) at Rome. Similar is Davus's apology in Terence, though in the opposite sense.

units.la: —di vestram fidem, Quid turbæ est apud forum! quid illic hominū litigāt! Tum annona cara est: quid dicam aliud nescio.
units.tr: Good heavens, what a crowd there is in the forum! What quarrelling men there are there! And then the grain is dear; I know not what else to say.

units.la: ἡμῖν τὸ Σαλαμίνα ἐν Διονυσίων πελώριον ἂν ἐκ(?).) Notum est plura fuisse celebrata ab hominibus Atticis Dionysia siue Liberalia: nam & in urbe sub initium veris quæ vocabant ἐν κατ' ἄγυ Διονύσια: & in agris autumni tempore, quæ & Λήναια, & ἐν κατ' ἀγρὸς Διονύσια, itemque minora: erat enim ea tanquam præparatio ad altera Bacchanalia maiora & antiquiora. quare etiam Διονύσια solùm quoties dicunt, Attici scriptores verna Dionysia intelligunt: ut hic Theophrastus. Nam hyeme maria olim fuisse clausa, & ineunte vere solita aperiri, parumque in vsu hybernam nauigationem fuisse nemo ignorat, ex Horatio, Vegetio, aliis sexcentis. Aristoteles libro primo De generatione animalium docens varie τῷ ἐκ accipi, cum dicitur aliquid ἐκ τῶν δὲ ἡμέρας [?], vel ἔτι [?], ita scribit, ἢ γὰρ δὲ ὡς τόδε μὴ τοῦτο [?] ἐκ τῆς Πλαταιῶν ὁ ἄλς [?], qui locus non erat praetermittendus.
units.tr: [Greek phrase, corrupt in the scan, about the Dionysia at Salamis]. It is well known that the Attic people celebrated several Dionysia, or Liberalia. In the city, at the beginning of spring, they kept what they called the Dionysia in the town; in the countryside, at the time of autumn, they kept the Lenaea and the Dionysia in the fields, and also smaller festivals. These were a preparation for the other Bacchanalia, which were greater and older. For this reason, when Attic writers say simply "the Dionysia," they mean the spring festival, as Theophrastus does here. That in olden times the seas were closed in winter and opened again at the start of spring, and that winter navigation was little practised, no one is unaware, from Horace, Vegetius and countless others. Aristotle, in book 1 of On the Generation of Animals, teaching the various senses in which from (ἐκ) is used, when something is said to be from the days or from the year, writes thus about the Plataean... This passage should not be passed over.

units.la: καὶ εἰ ποιήσειν ὁ Ζεὺς ὕδωρ.] In Aristophanis Vespis chorus senum inter eundum ad Pnycem curiam ita blaterat.
units.tr: "And if Zeus should make water." In Aristophanes' Wasps the chorus of old men, walking to the Pnyx, chatters in this way.

units.la: ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ ἐδ᾽ ὅπως ὑχ ἡμερῶν τετλάρων τὸ ἀλέσσον. ὕδωρ ἀναγκαίως ἔχει τὴν Ζεὺς ποιῆσαι [?].
units.tr: "But I do not know how, for four days now, the bread... It is necessary for Zeus to make water."

units.la: δᾶ ὁ καὶ τῆς καρπίμων ἀτὰ μὴ εἰ πρώϊμα [?] ὕδωρ ψυέσθω [?].
units.tr: "...and may the water not fall early upon the fruits of the field."

units.la: Vbi etiam vides locutionem Atticæ plebis ποιεῖ Ζεὺς ὕδωρ, pro pluit: quod loquendi genus eleganter hic Theophr. retinuit. Sanè ὕδωρ, pro cælesti aqua apud scriptores Atticos translatitium est.
units.tr: Here you also see the expression of the Attic common people, "Zeus makes water," meaning "it rains." Theophrastus has kept this way of speaking elegantly. Indeed, the use of water for heavenly water is a transferred usage among Attic writers.

units.la: καὶ ὁ ἀγρὸς εἰς νέωσι γεωργήσι [?]. ) Legimus καὶ ὅτι τὸν ἀγρὸν εἰς νέωσι γεωργήσι [?]. Græcum est prouerbium, Ἀεὶ γεωργῶν εἰς νέωσι πλάσσω [?].
units.tr: "...and the field to be tilled for a new..." We read: "and that the field is to be tilled for a new..." There is a Greek proverb: "always tilling the field for a new [crop]."

units.la: ὡς χαλεπὸν ἐστι τὸ ζῆν. ) Danus Terentianus, Tum annona cara est. eadem planè sententia. sic autem ut Theophrastus loquitur scholiastes vetus Aristophanis in Ranas. Possumus etiam τὸ ζῆν exponere ἀφορμὴ εἰς τὸ ζῆν. sic vocabant Attici quod Gallicè dicimus moyen de viure. vulgò φροϊλίν [?]. Scholiastes Euripidis Medea, Ἡν ἡμεῖς περιοχολῶ κλαπέρ [?] εἰς τὸ ζὴν Ἀτλικοὶ ἀφορμλὼ καλῶσι. Artemidorus lib. v.cap. LXXXIX. ἀφορμλὼ βιωλικὼ: Tertullianus exhibitionem, nota voce lurisconsultorum. Cassiodorus, Quale fuit rogo tunc miseris viuere? hoc est, οἷον λῶ τὶς Καμπώρῳ τότε τὸ ζῆν.
units.tr: "How hard it is to live." Terence's Davus says the same thing: Then the grain is dear. An old scholiast on Aristophanes' Frogs uses the phrase in just this way. We may also explain "to live" (τὸ ζῆν) as "the means of living" (ἀφορμὴ εἰς τὸ ζῆν). The Attic writers called by this name what we in French call moyen de vivre, commonly the means of subsistence. The scholiast on Euripides' Medea says that the Attics call this a means of living. Artemidorus, book 5, chapter 89, speaks of a means of living. Tertullian uses exhibitio, a term familiar to the lawyers. Cassiodorus has: What kind of life was it then for wretched folk? That is, "what kind of life was it then for the wretched in Campania?"

units.la: μυστηρίοις μεγίστην ἀᾶδα ἐσπεν.) Mysteria noctu peragebantur: videtur ergo aemulatio quaedam fuisse, quis maximam facem accederet: quod Graeci dicunt ἀᾶδα ἱστάναι. quasi statuere & defigere ad lucendum. Plutarchus in Cicerone & ὁ φῶς πολλὰ καλέλαμπε τὲς ἑνωπὰς, λαμπάδια καὶ ἀᾶδας ἱσώλων ἐπὶ τῆ Σύρας. inde apud scriptores saepe ἀᾶδυχεῖν & μυσηρία. & placet veteribus Grammaticis ἀᾶδυχεῖν proprie dici de eo qui fit daduchus in Eleusiniis initiis. Fuerunt & alia λαμπαδυχίας certamina varia Athenis, ut praeter Platonem, Paufaniam in Atticis, & Suidam, scholiastes Aristophanis docet: sed id aliud, ut puto, erat. Quanquam quod ait μεγίςλω, putauimus aliquando eo pertinere, quod videtur in eiusmodi agonibus fuisse aliquod virium corporis specimen. Ait enim Comicus in Ranis, λαμπάδα δ' ἐδεῖς οἵος τε φέρειν ὑπ' ἀγυμνασίας ἔτι νῦν. & Andocides in oratione quadam inter καταφρώματα fua numerat, quòd λαμπαδῆν εἴχνοτε. Sed de mysteriorum facibus passim veteres.
units.tr: He set a very great torch for the mysteries. The mysteries were performed at night, so there seems to have been a certain rivalry over who would set up the greatest torch. The Greeks call this "to set up a torch," as if to fix and plant it so that it would shine. Plutarch, in his Life of Cicero, says that a great light shone from the torches and lamps set up in the Syracusan... Hence in the writers one often finds "to be torch-bearer" and "the mysteries." The ancient grammarians hold that the word for torch-bearing properly refers to the man who acts as torch-bearer in the Eleusinian initiations. There were also various other torch-races at Athens, as Plato, Pausanias in his Attica, Suidas and the scholiast on Aristophanes teach; but that, I think, was something different. Although when the text says "the greatest," I once thought it referred to a display of physical strength in such contests. For the comic poet in the Frogs says that no one is now able to carry the torch because of lack of exercise. Andocides, too, among his boasts, mentions that he once carried the torch. But the ancients write about the torches of the mysteries everywhere.

units.la: Pag. 12. ἆϕ͂ε εἰσὶ κιόρες τὰ Ὠιδεῖα.) Eius generis illi fermones apud Horatium, —cum quidlibet ille Garriret, vicos, vrbem, laudaret. Fuit autem Odeum, vt auctor est Plutarchus in Pericle, τῇ ἐλέξ ϑεάτρου ἀϑεέφ τολὺ μέγιστον τὴ πολύς ἐστο. Vide Vitruuium. Eo in loco musici aliisque id genus in arte sua se exercebant, & spectatores oblectabant, maximè ante extructum theatrum, vt annotat Hesychius. Sed & frumenta ibi solita vendi, & tempore caritatis pauperioribus diuidi, ex Demosthenis oratione contra Phormionem didicimus: quare etiam controuersiæ omnes ad rem frumentariam, itemque ad debita quacunque ex causa alimenta pertinentes, ibidem disceptabantur. Pollux, libro v iii. Ὡς ὃ ὅπ τῷ σίτῳ δίκας ἐν τῷ Ωιδείῳ ἐδίκαζον. οἱ τὸς δὲ ὅπ ὃν, αἱ ὀφειλόμεναι προσφαί[?]. Inde est apud Demosthenem, δίκας σίτυ εἰς ᾠδεῖον δικάζεσθαι. in ea contra Neæram.
units.tr: Page 12: These are the odeum-talkers. Horace's chatterers are of this kind: when he chattered about whatever, praised the streets, the city. The Odeum, as Plutarch says in Pericles, was a building next to the theatre, with a great many columns. See Vitruvius. In that place musicians and others of this sort practised their art and entertained spectators, especially before the theatre was built, as Hesychius notes. We learn from Demosthenes' speech against Phormio that grain was also regularly sold there and, in times of dearth, distributed to the poorer people. For this reason all lawsuits concerning the grain supply, and likewise concerning debts of any kind arising from maintenance, were also heard there. Pollux, book 8: "Lawsuits about grain were heard in the Odeum, and those about debts..." Hence in Demosthenes: "to bring lawsuits about grain to the Odeum," in his speech against Neaera.

units.la: Βουδρομιῶνος μὲν τὰ μυστήρια. ) Intellige de maioribus initiis: nam minora mysteria Pyanepsione celebrabantur. Testis Demosthenes, Plutarchus & alij.
units.tr: In Boedromion the mysteries. Understand this of the greater initiations; for the lesser mysteries were celebrated in Pyanepsion. Demosthenes, Plutarch and others bear witness.

units.la: Πυανεψιῶνος ὁ ἀπαλήρια.) Testantur scholia Aristophanis in Acharnenses,aliiq; grammatici.
units.tr: In Pyanepsion the Apaturia. The scholia on Aristophanes' Acharnians and other grammarians attest this.

units.la: Ποσιδεῶνος ὁ τὰ κατ' ἀγρὸς Διονύσια.) Hæc sunt quæ minora Dionysia dicebantur: nam maiora mense Anthesterione peragebantur. Sed de his consulat lector vnicum illud seculi decus, Iosephum Scaligerum, in operis magni libro primo.
units.tr: In Poseideon the Dionysia in the countryside. These are what were called the lesser Dionysia; the greater were celebrated in the month of Anthesterion. On these matters the reader should consult that unique glory of our age, Joseph Scaliger, in the first book of his great work.

units.la: Μεριστεὸς ὁ γὰρ τὰς Θιώτας τὴν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ διαρπάζειν ἀπαλλάττεσθαι.) Merito semper nobis de mendo fuit hic locus suspectus. Nam quis eorum qui purius locuti sunt ἀπαλλάττειν τινά vnquam dixit, pro fugere procul ab aliquo? postulabat sanè loquendi consuetudo τινός: vel absolutè ἀπαλλάττεσθαι. vtrumque passim vsurpant scriptores antiqui: vt & ἀπαλλάττειν τινά, pro, à se remouere aliquem. illud autem primum, quod sciam, nunquâ. Quare non dubito quin isti loco culpæ nota sit apponenda:culpæ autem, librarij : qui vocem omisit ex perpetuo usu scriptorum Atticorum nobis restituendam ita ergo legimus, ἀφροσείᾳ ᾧ χ[?] [?] Ϛ̣ῶς ζῶντας τὴν [?] ἀνθρώπων φύγειν, ὁ διαρρίψιον ἀπαλ[?] λάττεσθαι[?]. Qui Aristotelicæ dictioni assuefactas aures habent, agnoscunt hic illud philosopho familiare φεύγειν ἀφροσείας[?]: vel ἀφροσείας [?] ἃς χεῖρας: quod Plautus dixerit fugere demissis manibus. Origo inde, quod contentiùs currimus manus demissas habentes, & circum latera iactantes. Nicomacheorum lib. IIII. ἐδαμῶς τ' ἂν ὁμμοῖοι σὺ μεγαλοψύχῳ φέγειν ἀφροσείας[?]. De incessu animalium, capite III. ἡ οἱ θεοὶ ἡ δαίτην ἡ[?] ἀφροσείαις[?]. deinde causam explicat: necnon Problematum, sect. quinta. Διαρρίψιον autem dixit Theophrastus pro eo quod Plautus non uno loco grandi gradu. Nam qui cursu contendunt, ut gradum grandiant, crura vehementer aperiunt, quod est διαίρεσθαι : sicut διαίρειν σῶμα, os aperire est. At qui cruribus apertis stant, ut qui parant se ad hostilem impetum excipiendum, διαγάβ ἐν proprie dicuntur: unde est apud Platonem ex Tyrtæo δ' διαγάβτα μάχεσθαι. Artemidorus libro I. ὡς ἀνλάσα συμεῖςνες, διαγάβειν μὴ ὡς βαδίζειν, ἀεὶ ὁ μένων ἐν τῷ ἀπὸ ζῷα. Aliud est quod Latini dicunt suris apertis ambulare: id enim vel naturæ vitium est, vel stultæ ambitionis. Varro Meleagro, Non modo suris apertis, sed pane natibus apertis ambulans. Turpilius Demiurgo, Aperta sura, brachia autem procera, horrorem mihi ex corde exsuscitabant. Fallitur vero Nonius infigniter qui apertum in hoc Turpilij loco pro nudato positum putat. Atque hinc possunt intelligi Cassiodori verba male accepta doctissimis viris, lib. IIII. Superbus quinetiam varicatis gressibus patet. Affine est apud Ouidium varicitas ambulare, Μαζωλεχίας[?], vel potius Καχωλεχίας[?] lib. III.
units.tr: "Meristeus; for he wishes to escape the... of men and to go away plundering." This passage has always seemed corrupt to me. For which of the purer writers ever said apallattein tina, meaning to flee far from someone? Ordinary usage would require tinos, or the absolute apallattesthai. Ancient writers use both forms everywhere, as well as apallattein tina in the sense of removing someone from oneself; but the first form, so far as I know, never occurs. So I do not doubt that a mark of fault should be placed against this passage; the fault is the copyist's, who omitted a word that we must restore from the constant usage of the Attic writers. Thus we read: "...to flee from the crowd of men and go away from the plunder." Those whose ears are used to Aristotle's diction will recognise here the phrase familiar to the philosopher, phugein aphroseias [to flee from folly], or aphroseias has cheiras, which Plautus rendered as to flee with hands hanging down [fugere demissis manibus]. The origin of the phrase is that men who run hard do so with their hands hanging down and swinging at their sides. In the Nicomachean Ethics, book 4, the great-souled man will never run with hasty steps... In On the Gait of Animals, chapter 3, the gods... and then he explains the cause; likewise in the Problems, section 5. Theophrastus used diarrhipsion for what Plautus often calls with a grand stride [grandi gradu]. Those who race, in order to lengthen their stride, open their legs wide, which is called diaireisthai, just as diairein sōma means to open the mouth. But those who stand with their legs spread apart, as those who prepare to receive a hostile attack, are properly said diabebēkenai; hence in Plato's quotation from Tyrtaeus: to fight with legs apart. Artemidorus, book 1: "as those who strike out their legs wide, to walk apart, not as those who go, always standing in the same place." The Latins also have a different expression, to walk with the calves exposed [suris apertis ambulare]; this is either a natural defect or a sign of foolish vanity. Varro, in his Meleager: walking not only with calves exposed, but with buttocks bared too. Turpilius, in his Demiurgus: An exposed calf, and arms long, stirred up horror in my heart. But Nonius is grievously mistaken when he thinks that apertum in this passage of Turpilius means naked. From this we can also understand the words of Cassiodorus, which have been wrongly taken by very learned men, in book 4: Pride even stands open with bow-legged steps [Superbus quinetiam varicatis gressibus patet]. Close to this is Ovid's to walk bow-legged, in book 3, which the Greeks call makholekhia or rather kakholekhia.

units.la: Illa velut coniunx Vmbri rubicunda mariti Ambulat, ingentes varica fertque gradus.
units.tr: So, like the ruddy wife of an Umbrian husband, she walks, and bowlegged, she carries her huge strides.

units.la: verùm quæsiuerim ego hîc libenter, quomodo varica mulier ingentes gradus facere possit. id enim planè contra rerum naturam est: nisi si ingentes gradus improprie dixit, gradus paruos quidem & lentos, sed quos efficiant multùm hiantia crura: id enim est varicus. sed hæc in transcursu.
units.tr: But I would gladly ask here how a bowlegged woman can make huge strides, for that is plainly contrary to nature. Unless he meant "huge strides" improperly, that is, small and slow steps, but ones made with the legs spread wide, since that is what varicus means. But these points in passing.

units.la: ὅςις ἀπαυρ[illegible, ~6 letters] βέλτ[?]ιον ἔ[?]ϊ[?]. ] Facetè & suauiter. Est autem hoc è vulgi sermone petitum: &, vt Donatus diceret, est ἰδιωτισμός[?] hominis ab aliqua re abhorrentis. cum enim molestam sibi fuisse alicuius garrulitatem volebant indicare, dicebant se ab eo fuisse enectos. Sic Horatius metuit ne à garrulo illo suo enecetur. Eadem mens illius quæ in Milite Plautina hoc pronuntiat.
units.tr: [ὅστις ... βέλτιον ἐστί] Wittily and pleasantly put. This expression is taken from common speech, and, as Donatus would say, it is an idiom of a man who is put off by something. When they wished to show that someone's chatter had been a nuisance to them, they said they had been killed by him. So Horace fears lest he be killed by that talkative fellow of his. The same idea is in the Miles of Plautus, where he says this.

units.la: Iam iam sat amabo est: finite abeam si possum viua à vobis.
units.tr: Now, now, I have had enough of loving. Let me go, if I can, alive from you.

units.la: item illius qui sic loquitur in quinto Theocriti idyllio,
units.tr: Likewise of the speaker in the fifth idyll of Theocritus:

units.la: —τὸν ξένον ἐς πόλιν αὖθις ζῶ᾽ ἀφῖξ.
units.tr: [τὸν ξένον ἐς πόλιν αὖθις ζῶ᾽ ἀφῖξ] "...the stranger, I shall come back alive to the city."

units.la: Simili ratione ϑάνατον[?] siue mortem aut morbum sibi esse dicebant rem auditu molestam. Sophocles, ὤμοι, ϑάνατος[?] [illegible, ~8 letters] ἀκούειν. Tale illud Epicharmi ἀλλ' ἔστ[?]ιν[?] ἰδοὺς νῦν, ἀποθανοῖς[?]. Cicero sæpe, mortis instar putare. Cæterum videtur Theophrastus cum hæc scriberet præceptoris sui meminisse: Aristotelem enim aiunt, cùm fortè in locutulcium quendam & μα[?]λ[?]ακ[?]ὸν[?] incidisset, qui longos illi sermones quosdam & ineptos narrans, subinde diceret, Nunquid hoc mirum ô Aristoteles? respondisse: Minimè id quidem: verùm illud mirum, si quis pedibus praeditus te & garrulitatè tuam ferat.auctor Plutarchus.
units.tr: In a similar way they said that death, or illness, was itself an unpleasant thing to hear. Sophocles: "Alas, death ... to hear." Such is that saying of Epicharmus: "But if you see him now, you will die." Cicero often: to think it like death. But Theophrastus seems, in writing this, to be recalling his own teacher. For they say that Aristotle, when he happened to meet a certain chatterer and a [?] who, telling him long and pointless stories, kept saying, "Isn't this amazing, Aristotle?", replied: "Certainly not. But it would be amazing if someone with feet carried you and your chatter." Author: Plutarch.
On the chapter concerning rusticity [περὶ ἀγροικίας].

units.la: Ἡ δὲ ἀγροικία δόξειεν ἂν τῇ ἀμαθίᾳ ἀχρήμων.) Contraria est rusticitas hæc elegantiæ illi quæ spectatur in gestu, habitu, ac sermonibus familiaribus: quam Græci κοσμιότητα dixerunt, atque ita definierunt, Κοσμιότης, ὅταν μὲν περὶ τὸ σχῆμα ἐν κινήσει καὶ ῥήματι σώματος[?]. ἢ ἀξία περὶ τὸ σχῆμα καὶ κίνησιν σώματος[?]. extant hæ definitiones in libello qui est penes nos Περὶ παθῶν ψυχῆς Andronici philosophi: quem de affectionibus animi scripsisse accuratè ex Galeni aliquot locis satis constat. Plato in Ὅροις, sic, κοσμιότης, ἀξίωσις καὶ κίνησιν σώματος[?]. Opponitur igitur rusticitas ei quod vocant philosophi τὸ πρέπον & decorum in cultu & motu corporis: de quo egregiè multa M. Tullius Officiorum libro primo. Stoici rusticitatem definiebant ignorationè & morum & legum siue institutorum vrbanorum.
units.tr: Rusticity would seem to be a kind of uselessness that comes from ignorance. This rusticity is the opposite of that refinement which is seen in gesture, dress and everyday conversation, which the Greeks called kosmiotes (seemliness) and defined thus: seemliness is when the movement of the body and the speech are in order, or worth concerning the posture and movement of the body. These definitions are found in the little book we have, On the Affections of the Soul by the philosopher Andronicus, which is generally agreed to have been written on the affections of the mind, accurately, from several passages of Galen. Plato in his Definitions says thus: seemliness is dignity and movement of the body. Rusticity is therefore opposed to what the philosophers call to prepon, propriety, in dress and bodily motion, about which Marcus Tullius writes excellently in the first book of De Officiis. The Stoics defined rusticity as ignorance of manners and of laws, or of urban customs.

units.la: Ἡ ἀγροικία, inquit Stobæus in Excerptis ethicis ex libris Stoicorum, ἔστιν ἀπειρία τῶν κατὰ πόλιν ἐθῶν καὶ νόμων[?]: aut potius νομίμων. Grammatici ita distinguunt: Ἀγροῖκος (aiunt illi) ὁ ἐν ἀγρῷ κατοικῶν, is est qui rure habitat. qui etiam ἀγροῖκος dicitur. ἀγροικος vero, ὁ σκαιὸς τὸν τρόπον, homo scævis moribus & molestis: ἀγριος vero crudelis. Aristoteles tamen quo nemo caftius vnquam locutus, quem ἀχρεῖον vocauit in fecundo Nicomacheorum, in quarto extremo ἄχρειον appellat. & ita alios quoque optimos auctores loqui obferuatum nobis. Longè autem anguftius accipit ille ibi ἀχρειότητος nomen, quàm hîc accipiatur. eum vide.
units.tr: "Rusticity," says Stobaeus in his Ethical Excerpts from the books of the Stoics, "is inexperience of the customs and laws of the city": or rather of its lawful institutions. The grammarians distinguish thus: agroikos (they say) is one who lives in the fields, who dwells in the country, and is also called agroikos. But agroikos, one who is rough in character, a man of harsh and troublesome manners; agrios means cruel. Yet Aristotle, than whom no one has ever spoken more chastely, whom he called achreion in the second book of the Nicomachean Ethics, in the last part of book four calls it achreion. We have observed that other excellent authors also speak thus. But he takes the term achreiotes there far more narrowly than it is taken here. See him.

units.la: Pag. 13. κυκεῶνα πιῶν.) Notum quid foleat iis accidere qui pharmacum fumpferint. Κυκεῶνα vertimus pharmacum : nam potum medicamentorum fignificari putamus hoc loco. Veteres Latini κυκεῶνα cocetum dixêre. hinc eft apud Tertullianum in libro Aduerfus Valentinianos Neftoris cocetum. fruftra enim funt docti viri qui torquent fe tantopere in expofitione illius loci. Atqui Tertullianus fine dubio ad Νέστορ κυκεῶνα refpicit: de quo Homerus Illiadis lib. λ.
units.tr: p. 13. [κυκεῶνα πιῶν] It is known what usually happens to those who have taken a drug. We translate kykeona as "drug," for we think a drink of medicines is meant here. The old Latins said cocetum for kykeon. Hence in Tertullian, in the book Against the Valentinians, we find "Nestor's cocetum." Learned men are wasting their effort in torturing themselves so much over the explanation of that passage. And yet Tertullian undoubtedly refers to [Νέστορ κυκεῶνα], "Nestor's kykeon," about which Homer speaks in the eleventh book of the Iliad.

units.la: κὴ μείζω τὰ ποδὸς τὰ ἐπιδήματα φορεῖν. [?] ) Horatius.
—acutisNaribus horum hominum rideri poffit, eo quodRufticus tonfo toga defluit,& male laxusIn pede calceus haret. Similis rusticitas
units.tr: ...by the sharp noses of these men, it can be laughed at, because the rustic's toga slips from his shoulders, and a loose shoe clings to his foot. A similar rusticity

units.la: apud eundem epiftola prima, Si toga diffidet impar. Ouidius, Sit bene conueniens & fine labe toga. Fuiffe autem vehementer irrideri folitos qui nimis laxos calceos geftarent, oftendit locus hic Ariftophanis in Equitibus,
units.tr: appears in the same author's first epistle: If the toga does not fit well. Ovid: Let the toga be well fitting and without stain. That those who wore overly loose shoes were greatly mocked is shown by this passage of Aristophanes in the Knights:

units.la: Καὶ νὴ Δία, κάμε τῆτ' ἔδρασε ταυτὶ ὥστε κατα-γέλων
units.tr: [Καὶ νὴ Δία, κάμε τῆτ' ἔδρασε ταυτὶ ὥστε κατα-γέλων] "Yes, by Zeus, and he did this so that he was ridiculed..."

units.la: Παμπόλλων [?] ἡμῖν δημόταισι καὶ τὰς φίλοις καταγέλ-ᾶσθαι [?]
units.tr: [Παμπόλλων ἡμῖν δημόταισι καὶ τὰς φίλοις καταγέλ-ᾶσθαι] "by many of us common people, and by his friends."

units.la: Πεὶν γὰρ ἢ Περγασῆσιν, ἐνεὸν ἐν ταῖς ἐμβάσιν. [?] vbi notabis obiter, eos quibus male laxus calceus hæreret in pede,dici solitos ἐὶν ἐν ταῖς ἱμάσι [?], hoc est, natare in soccis: quod hodie quoque vulgo vsurpatur. Similirer Ouidius inter munditiarum praecepta,
units.tr: [Πεὶν γὰρ ἢ Περγασῆσιν, ἐνεὸν ἐν ταῖς ἐμβάσιν.] Where you will note in passing that those whose loose shoe hung on the foot were said to be [ἐν ταῖς ἱμάσι], that is, "to swim in socks," a phrase still used commonly today. Similarly Ovid, among his precepts on personal elegance: Nor let your foot wander and swim in a loose leather.

units.la: Nec vagus in laxa pes tibi pelle natet.& post hunc Sidonius Apollinaris, Laxo pes natet altus in coturno. D. Hieronymus non dissimilem sententiam in dissimili more verbo fidere vsus extulit. si pes, ait, laxa pelle non fileat [?]. Porrò ab hac rusticitate natum apud Græcos prouerbium, de re quauis parum conueniente: id enim dicebant esse ὑπὲρ τὸν πόδα [?]: vt contra ἐπὶ πόδα dicebant ἀπροπμιαρικῶς [?] de omnibus quæ apta erant & conueniebant. Plato comicus ὡς ἔγε μοι τὸ ἐμμέτρα τοῦ ἐπὶ πόδα [?]. Lucianus de conscribenda historia ridens scriptorem historiæ ineptum, ὁρᾶς ὡς ἐμμελὴς ἡ ἀρ-χὴ καὶ ἐπὶ πόδα ἡ ἱστορία, ὁ τῇ ῥύσῳ εἴδεις τῆ λό-γων ἀρπίνει [?]; sic legendum est, non ἐπὶ πόδα: in quo mirè cæcutierûr doctissimi homines:sed & τῇ ἱστορία malim. Hesychius, ἐπὶ πόδα, ὅτως ἐπάλουν τὸ ἀρχαῖον, μεταφορικῶς τῶν τοῖς ποσὶν ἐξηρμένων [?]; ἢ ἀκριβῶς [?]. Idem Lucianus in apologia ἐπὶ τῆς ἰδίου μισθῷ σώ [?]. Περὶ πόδα ζῶν [?] καὶ σὲ τὸν Σαλαμὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀ [?]. merito te aliquis & conuenienter fidis tuis Salathum appellarit. Vtitur & alibi, itemque scriptores alij, vt dicemus, faciente Deo breui, in editione Prouerbiorum. Dixerunt & ἀρειτες pro eodem: nam idem Hesychius ita annotat, Περὶ ἐπὶ τῶ ἀρμόζου. καὶ πόδα. Pollux quoque libro septimo ἀρεῖπόδα ἢ ἐνοδιμαῖα [?], ἀρμόζου. Apud Plautum in Truculento, non tufticitatis tantùm, fed etiam impudentię nota eft, calceis inconcinnis vti.
units.tr: After him, Sidonius Apollinaris: Let the foot swim deep in a loose buskin. Jerome, using a similar idea in a different manner, with the verb fidere, said: if the foot does not stick in loose leather. Further, from this rusticity came a Greek proverb about anything rather unsuited: they said it was [ὑπὲρ τὸν πόδα], "above the foot," just as, conversely, they said [ἐπὶ πόδα] of all things that were apt and suitable. The comic poet Plato: [ὡς ἔγε μοι τὸ ἐμμέτρα τοῦ ἐπὶ πόδα]. Lucian, in his essay on writing history, ridicules an inept historian: [ὁρᾶς ὡς ἐμμελὴς ἡ ἀρχὴ καὶ ἐπὶ πόδα ἡ ἱστορία...]: "See how the beginning is harmonious and the history fits the foot..." So it must be read thus, not [ἐπὶ πόδα]; in this most learned men have been strangely blind. I would also prefer [τῇ ἱστορία]. Hesychius: [ἐπὶ πόδα], "thus the ancients used to say, metaphorically, of things raised to the feet," or [ἀκριβῶς], "exactly." The same Lucian, in his Apology, [ἐπὶ τῆς ἰδίου μισθῷ ...] and [Περὶ πόδα ζῶν καὶ σὲ τὸν Σαλαμὸν ...]: "someone has rightly and suitably called you Salathus, with your sandals." He uses it elsewhere, and other writers too, as we shall say, God willing, shortly, in the edition of the Proverbs. They also said [ἀρειτες] for the same thing; for Hesychius again notes: [Περὶ ἐπὶ τῶ ἀρμόζου. καὶ πόδα], "suitable, and for the foot." Pollux too, in book seven, has [ἀρεῖπόδα ἢ ἐνοδιμαῖα], "suitable." In Plautus' Truculentus the wearing of ill-fitting shoes is a mark not only of rusticity but also of impudence.

units.la: Nihili me ! perdidi omne quod fuit : fio impudens:
units.tr: Nothing to me! I have lost everything I had: I am becoming shameless.

units.la: Nec mihi adeft ad illu penfi ta quos capiam calceos. Ita legitur hic locus non in editione folùm doctiffimi Camerarii : fed etiam in Lambiniana, & nouiffima quoque Plantiniana,quam eruditiffimi viri curarunt.mendofiffimè fané.Lego ex veftigiis ipfis deprauatæ lectionis:
units.tr: Nor do I have even enough money for those shoes I would buy. So this passage is read not only in the edition of the most learned Camerarius, but also in the Lambinian and in the newest Plantinian edition, which learned men prepared. It is very faulty indeed. I read it from the traces of the corrupted reading itself:

units.la: Nee mihi adeft tantillum penfi iam, quos capiam calceos.
units.tr: Nor have I even a little money now, which shoes I might take.

units.la: Senfus eft quem dixi : vide huc A. Gellium libro xiii. cap. xx.
units.tr: The sense is what I have said. See Aulus Gellius, book 13, chapter 20.

units.la: μεγάλη τὴ φωνὴ λαλεῖν.) Vt Stratyllax in Truculento Plautina, & initio Moftellariæ Grumio : cuius fermonem ita excipit Tranio,
units.tr: [μεγάλη τὴ φωνὴ λαλεῖν] "to speak with a loud voice." Like Stratyllax in Plautus' Truculentus, and Grumio at the beginning of the Mostellaria, whose speech Tranio takes up thus:

units.la: Quid tibi malum hic ante ædes clamatio eft?
units.tr: What is this shouting in front of the house for you?

units.la: An rure cenfes te effe? abfcede ab ædibus,
units.tr: Do you think you are in the country? Go away from the house,

units.la: Abi rus, abi directe. Bafilius in epiftola ad Gregorium, vbi pleraque ethica præcepta continentur, τὸ ⊙, ait, φωνῆς ὁ μέγας φρολιμπλέος, ὡς μήτε σφόδρα γὰρ τῷ ἀκολῷ ἐαν σμικρότατος, μήτε φορλικὸν τῇ μεγέθει τῆς ἀγλαΐας[?] appellat vir fanctiffimus φορλικότητα[?], quam Theophraftus ἀγροικίαν.
units.tr: Go to the country, go straight there. Basil, in his letter to Gregory, where most of the ethical precepts are contained, says of the loud voice that one should be neither too much (?) nor rustic by the greatness of the display; this most holy man calls such a fault [φορλικότητα], which Theophrastus calls rusticity [ἀγροικίαν].

units.la: ἐ ἀναβλέπμενος ἄνω τῇ γόνατ© καθιζάνων.) Meminit huius rusticitatis & ineptitudinis vetus poëta Philetærus, siue Amphis Ἀμφίδαλλε σέφρος φάρος[?] ἢ καθήμενος (vel καθίσας) ἔλαν ; μὴ δ᾽ ἀρχαίως ἄνω γόνατος ἀμφιέσ̣ην[?]. Ita legi debet hic locus apud Athenaeum libro primo ex veteribus membranis. Sappho quoque similem rusticitatem in æmula & ἀντιλύχῳ Andromeda ridebat, vt eft apud eúdem Athenæu.
units.tr: "Looking up, sitting with his knees drawn up.)" The old poet Philetaerus, or perhaps Amphis, mentions this rusticity and awkwardness: "...sitting (or having sat) ... and not lifting his knees up in the old way." This passage ought to be read so in Athenaeus, book 1, from the old manuscripts. Sappho too ridiculed a similar rusticity in her rival Andromeda, as Athenaeus also reports.

units.la: Τίς δ' ἀχρείωτις Φέλγει νόον[?], ἐπισαμένη [?] ἐρᾶσα [?] ἔλκεν ὅπ' τῆς σφυρῶν[?];
units.tr: "Who, with her ... and ..., has drawn Andromeda by the ankles?" [Τίς δ' ἀχρείωτις Φέλγει νόον, ἐπισαμένη ἐρᾶσα ἔλκεν ὅπ' τῆς σφυρῶν;]

units.la: Negat Sappho posse cuiquam placere Andromedam, quae rusticarum more vestem subductam gestet. Quod prorsus hodie mulieribus rusticanis nostratibus conuenit: quas saepe videas, non rure tantum subducta indecore veste opus facere: sed etiam urbem ita ingredi cum ad nundinas venitant. Notum est autem veteres subligaculis, quibus nos hodie vtimur, extra stadium aut scenam non esse vsos: itaque & Romani veteres togam ad calceos demittebant, & Graeci pallium quod si quid illis diligentius esset faciendum, vel pallium ponebant: vel in humeros retrorsum reiiciebant: quod Athenis facitabant quando in publicum aut in concionem prodibant, homines qui naui & actuosi haberi volebant, vt indicat Aristophanes Concionantibus. Atque hic est fere seruorum habitus in comoediis Graecis & Latinis palliatis. Apud Plautum Capteiueis ait ille
units.tr: Sappho denies that Andromeda can please anyone, since she wears her dress tucked up in the manner of country women. This fits our own country women today, whom you often see working with their clothes hitched up indecently, not only in the fields but also when they enter the town to go to market. It is well known that the ancients did not wear the undergarments we use today outside the racecourse or the stage. So the old Romans let their togas hang down to their heels, and the Greeks either laid aside their cloak, if they had some task to do that required care, or threw it back over their shoulders. The Athenians did this when they came into public or to the assembly, men who wished to be thought refined and active, as Aristophanes shows in the Ecclesiazusae. This is almost the dress of slaves in Greek and Latin comedies, the palliatae. In Plautus' Captivi the character says:

units.la: Nunc certa res est: est: eodem pacto ut comici serui solent,
units.tr: "Now the matter is settled: just as comic slaves are wont to do,

units.la: Coniiciam in collum pallium, primo ex me hanc rem ut audiat.
units.tr: I shall throw my cloak around my neck, first to hear this business from me."

units.la: Age nunc iam orna te Epidice, & palliolum in collum coniice,
units.tr: "Come now, Epidicus, adorn yourself and throw the little cloak around your neck,

units.la: Atque dissimulato, quasi per urbem totam hominem quasi fueris.
units.tr: and, pretending, become a man running about the whole city as if you were a slave."

units.la: Dicitur & colligere pallium pro eodem. Capteiueis.
units.tr: The same is also said of gathering up the cloak. In the Captivi:

units.la: Collecto quidem est pallio: quidnam acturus est?
units.tr: "Indeed he has gathered up his cloak. What is he about to do?"

units.la: Sic Geta apud Terentium vt Antiphonem properet inuenire, humerum sibi onerat pallio. Propterea Oppianus poëta fummus, in venatoris institutione eum admonet, vt venatum iturus pallium sibi in humeros coniiciat. Nam hic est sensus horum versuum quos interpretes non intellexerunt, ne Græci quidem,
units.tr: So too Geta in Terence, hurrying to find Antipho, loads his shoulder with his cloak. For this reason the excellent poet Oppian, in his instruction on hunting, advises the hunter who is about to go hunting to throw his cloak over his shoulders. For this is the sense of the following verses, which the interpreters did not understand, not even the Greeks:

units.la: Αὐχένῳ δ' αὖ ἑκάτερθε παρήορον ἐκ πταλαμάων [?] / Βύμα ἀμείς ἐλλοιτ' ὄψιν [?], ἀνταρῶν ὑπὲρ ὤμων [?], / Ῥίπτον ἐς κάμαξιν [?].
units.tr: "And on each side of the neck, hanging down from the shoulders, ... throw it on the ..." [Αὐχένῳ δ' αὖ ἑκάτερθε παρήορον ἐκ πταλαμάων ...]

units.la: subiicit deinde Μήδ' ἄρα λῶπα ἔχειν [?] μάλα λώϊον, quæ verba de pallio non minus quàm superiora sunt accipienda.Nam est perinde ac fi diceret: Imò fi me audias, non solum in humeros pallium coniiiicies: sed etiam omnino depones. id enim esse non tantùm expeditius, sed etiam tutius propter eam quàm affert caussam. λῶπ@ fiue λώπιον idem est atque ἱμάτιον, & vt ait Aristoteles primo Topico ζῶν ἀεὶ ἀνδρῶν [?]. Pallium sanè Græci hanc ipsam ob caussam belli tempore deponebant, vt Romani togam. erántque milites Græcorum magnam partem μονοχίτωνες, vt eos vocat Plutarchus. apud quem ὁ ἐν ἱματίῳ βίῳ, est vita togata, & opponitur bellicæ: vt in vita Pompeii. & in eiusdem Camillo bis, εἰ ἐν ἱματίῳ est altæ pacis indicium. Xylander tunicatos vertit. non rectè. nam vel de toga Romanorum, vel de pallio Græcorum omnino intelligendum. Porrò autem, maxima semper fuit hominibus liberis nec ineptis cura, quoties in publicum esset prodeundum, vt decenti essent habitu, quod Græci vocant εὐχημονεῖν [?], Plautus eufche me adstare in Trinummo & Milite. In hoc qui es-sent sent negligentiores, rustici habebantur, vt hîc.Horatius,
units.tr: He then adds: "And it is much better not to wear a cloak at all" [Μήδ' ἄρα λῶπα ἔχειν μάλα λώϊον], and these words must be taken of the cloak no less than the preceding ones. For it is as if he said: "Indeed, if you listen to me, you will not only throw the cloak over your shoulders but put it off altogether, since this is not only more convenient but also safer, for the reason he gives." Lōpos, or lōpion, is the same as himation, and, as Aristotle says in the first book of the Topics, ... The Greeks indeed put aside the cloak for this very reason in time of war, as the Romans did the toga, and most of the Greek soldiers were monochitōnes, as Plutarch calls them. In Plutarch the "life in a cloak" [ἐν ἱματίῳ βίος] is the civil life, the life of the toga, opposed to the military life, as in his life of Pompey, and twice in his Camillus, where "in a cloak" is a sign of deep peace. Xylander translates tunicatos, which is not right, for it must be understood of the Roman toga or the Greek cloak alike. Furthermore, free men who were not foolish always took the greatest care, whenever they had to go out in public, to be decently dressed, which the Greeks call eukhēmonein. Plautus has eusche me adstare in the Trinummus and the Miles. Those who were more careless in this were regarded as rustics, as here in Horace:

units.la: Rusticius tonso toga defluit. Defluere enim dicitur vestis cum negligentius habetur: dicitur & trahi, vt in Cistellaria Plauti, & apud Græcos σρεδρυ. quanquam alio sensu interdum & σύρεδρυ & ἐλκεδρυ & trahi, de syrmate sive delicata veste dicuntur, quæ propendente lacinia trahitur potius quàm gestatur. Athenæus de hoc κοσμιότητι studio antiquorum loquens libro primo, Ευελεν, inquit, αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ κοσμίως ἀ ἀλαμβάνειν τῶν ἐδῆ· καὶ τοὺς μὴ πεσωμένας τὴν ἐπωμένην. Plato vero in Theeteto inter hominis non ingenui nec liberaliter educati notas hanc quoque ponit, quòd nesciat ἀναλλάττεσθαι ἐνδείξια ἐλλόγως. hoc est, vestem dextrè decenterque hominum liberorum more componere. hic enim est sensus illorum verborum Platonis: vt pluribus aliàs Deo dante sumus demonstraturi.
units.tr: "The rustic's toga slips down from his unshaven ... " For the dress is said to defluere ("slip down") when it is worn carelessly; it is also said to be dragged, as in Plautus' Cistellaria, and among the Greeks syrredu. Yet in another sense syrredu, elkedru and "dragged" are sometimes said of the syrma, or fine delicate dress, which is dragged along by its trailing hem rather than worn. Athenaeus, speaking of the ancients' concern for decorum in book 1, says: "They also took care to put on their clothes properly, and those who did not ..." Plato, in the Theaetetus, counts among the marks of a man who is not well-born or liberally educated that he does not know how to arrange his garments eulogōs, that is, to dress properly and decently in the manner of free men. For this is the sense of those words of Plato, which, God willing, I shall explain at more length elsewhere.

units.la: ὥσπερ δὲ γυναικὶ αὐτοῖς φαίνεσθαι. ] Video doctos viros ita hunc locum vertisse quasi legeretur ὥσπερ καὶ γυναικὶ δὲ αἰδοῖα αὐτοῖς φαίνεσθαι. & profectò id videtur voluisse dicere Theophrastus: neque aliter accidere potest, si quis vel si qua adducta supra genu veste sedeat. Sic apud comicum dicitur mulier ἀναλλομένη ἑφλύειν τὸ φορμίον. hoc est, τὸ αἰδοῖον: in Concionantibus. Veruntamen cum hanc lectionem habeant omnes codd. generalius accipiatur hic locus de aliis quoque corporis partibus. Ita enim est: præter caput & manus nulla alia pars est quàm denudatam habere honestum sit. Quare etiam auctor libri Περὶ ἐυχημοσύνης sive is est Hippocrates sive alius, hoc præceptum non præteremi-fit. sic. Τπρεῖν ἢ χὴ, inquit, ἐωΰλον ὅτι μάλισα, μὴ πολλὰ φαίνονζ τῇ τὰ σώματ ἀ μερίων. Apud Hebraeos vox ערוה quae nuditatem significat, interdum etiam partes eas corporis notat quae neque ostendi neque nominari honeste possunt. An igitur & plebs Attica sic locuta? Nam haec quidem lectio in qua omnes mss. consentiunt manifesto ἐςράιζει.
units.tr: "But as for a woman, they appear to them..." [ὥσπερ δὲ γυναικὶ αὐτοῖς φαίνεσθαι.] I see that learned men have translated this passage as if it read "just as, for a woman, their private parts appear to them." And this is certainly what Theophrastus seems to have meant; nor can it happen otherwise if a woman sits with her dress drawn up above the knee. So in the comic poet a woman is described as "leaping up and showing her phormion," that is, her private part, in the Ecclesiazusae. Yet since all the manuscripts have this reading, the passage should be taken more generally, of other parts of the body too. For the rule is this: apart from the head and hands, no other part may honourably be left bare. Hence the author of the book On Decorum, whether it is Hippocrates or another, does not omit this precept either: "Take care above all, he says, that the parts of the body are not too much exposed." Among the Hebrews the word ervah, which means nakedness, sometimes also denotes those parts of the body which can be neither shown nor named decently. Did the Attic common people also speak so? For this reading, in which all the manuscripts agree, plainly suits the context.

units.la: Pag. 14. καὶ προαιρῶν δέ τι.] Signatum verbum προαιρεῖν, è pinn aliquid promere. Aristophanes Thesmophoriazusis —λῶ ἡμῖν πρὸ τὰ αὐτὰς ζαμιεῖς προαιρεῖσας λαβεῖν ἀλφιτον, ἔλαιον, οἶνον. est & apud Thucydidem in octaua προαιρεῖν pro ex horreo promere, siue deripere horreo, vt loquitur Horatius. Clemens Alex. προκομίζειν ἐν τῇ ζαμιείᾳ. Male autem vulgò scribitur προαιρῶν: quod manifestissimè declarant illa Diogenis Laertii in Lacyde, ἐπιδὰν γάρ τι προίληται τῆ ζαμιείᾳ. Saepe in hac voce peccatum offendes à librariis: saepe ab interpretibus. Sic in Lyside Platonis ἀσπαγάλυς ἐν τῷ φορμίσκῳ προαιρεῖσθαι, est, promere & educere, non autem seligere: vt vertunt. δῆμος φυγεῖν.] Fortasse δῆμος scribendum.
units.tr: Page 14. "And taking something out..." [καὶ προαιρῶν δέ τι]. The word proairein is used in the sense of "to bring something forth from a store." Aristophanes in the Thesmophoriazusae: "I want you to take from the store-room the barley meal, the oil, and the wine..." It is also found in Thucydides, book 8, proairein for "to take out of a granary," or "to draw from a granary," as Horace puts it. Clement of Alexandria has prokomizein en tē tamieiā. The common reading proairōn is wrong, as Diogenes Laertius in the life of Lacydes plainly shows: "for whenever he takes something from the store-room." Mistakes in this word are often made by copyists and often by translators. So in Plato's Lysis, "to take out the knucklebones from the little basket" means to take out and bring forth, not to choose, as the translators render it. "The people fled." Perhaps dēmos should be written.

units.la: καὶ ζωρότερον οἶνον.] Vertimus meracium, neque tamen nos fugit quàm variae fuerint veterum criticorum sententiae super illo Homeri Ζωρότερον ἢ κέρασαι. vide grammaticos & Plutarchi Symposiaca. Aristotelem vero si sequimur auctorem in libro De poetica, vertemus auidius. Sanè apud Graecos olim & meraca potio, & grandia pocula hominis parum politi notae erant: Barbarorum enim id esse existimabant, non Graecorum: quod declarant antiqua prouerbia, Ἐπιτυδίζειν [?], & ὀφελις ἀμυσις apud Callimachum : apud Horatium Threicia amyflis. Sic & gulofitatem vitium barbarorum appellarunt, & prouerbio notarunt quod apud Seruium obseruauimus, Ἡ πλησμονὴ τῆς βαρβάρων.
units.tr: "And wine more undiluted." We have translated it neat, though we are not unaware how varied the opinions of the ancient critics were about Homer's zōroteron ē kerasai. See the grammarians and Plutarch's Symposiaca. If we follow Aristotle, however, the author in his book On Poetics, we shall translate it more boldly. Indeed among the Greeks of old, both neat drinking and large cups were known as the mark of a man of little refinement. For they thought these belonged to the barbarians, not to the Greeks. Ancient proverbs show this, such as epitydizein and the "ophelis of undiluted drinking" in Callimachus, and Threicia amystis in Horace. So they also called gluttony a vice of barbarians, and marked it with a proverb which we have noted in Servius: "the satiety of the barbarians."

units.la: κἀτ' ἀλέ(ας μετ' αὐτῆς.] Lego ἀλέσαι. vel defit aliquid necesse est. ac fortasse ita legi debet : κἀτ' ἀλέ-(ας μετ' αὐτῆς, μετρεῖν ὡς ἔνδον πάσῃ ἡμέρᾳ [?], & ἐπ. hoc est, & postquam cum ancilla sua molsit, tum alys omnibus domesticis, tum sibi etiam ipsi victum metitur. Mera enim rusticitas est, patremfamilias tanquam unum è feruis è demenso vivere.
units.tr: "And grinding with her..." [κἀτ' ἀλέ(ας μετ' αὐτῆς]. I read aleesai, or something must be missing. Perhaps it should be read thus: "and, after she has ground with her maidservant, ... measures out food for every day ..." That is, "after she has ground with her maid, she then measures out the provision for all the other household, and for herself too." For it is sheer rusticity for the head of a family to live on a measured ration like one of the slaves.

units.la: Ὡς ὑποζυγίοις ἐμβαλεῖν τὸν χόρτον.] Hæc vera lectio: sic dixit Plutarchus in Eumene ὡς ἵπποις χυλὸν ἐμ-βαλεῖν. Iuuenalis, infundere iumentis ordea. alij scri-ptores χόρτον ἐβάλλοντο [?].
units.tr: To throw the fodder to the beasts of burden. [Ὡς ὑποζυγίοις ἐμβαλεῖν τὸν χόρτον.] This is the true reading. Plutarch in the Life of Eumenes says in the same way "to throw the juice to the horses" [ὡς ἵπποις χυλὸν ἐμβαλεῖν]. Juvenal has "to pour barley into the beasts of burden" (infundere iumentis ordea). Other writers read "they were pelted with fodder."

units.la: ἐπαυχύσαι υἱός.] Scribendum ὑπακοῦσαι. sic semper Graeci κόπτειν τῷ θύρᾳ & ὑπακούειν iungunt, non ἐπακούειν. Plautus in Trinummo auscultare, in Moftellaria, respondere. Refero autem hoc quoque ad ἀεὶ σῶν : in eo enim rusticitas praecipua.
units.tr: "To hear the son" should be read as "to answer the door" [ὑπακοῦσαι]. The Greeks always join knocking at the door (κόπτειν τῷ θύρᾳ) with answering (ὑπακούειν), never with hearing (ἐπακούειν). Plautus uses "to listen" (auscultare) in the Trinummus and "to answer" (respondere) in the Mostellaria. I refer this also to "always at home" [ἀεὶ σῶν], for in that the rusticity is most marked.

units.la: ἐὰς φυλάσσει ὁ χύ.] Præclarè ista homini rustico conueniunt: nam vulgò rustici canes appellabant custodes mutos. Columella libro septimo capite XII. Nunc ut exordio priore sum pollicitus, de mutis custodibus loquar: quanquam canis falso dicitur mutus custos. Neque solùm rustici eorum custodia utebantur: sed & urbani homines: quos constat ad fores vel seruum ostiarium, vel canem cathenarium habere solitos, aut utrunque. De Romanis pridem notarunt docti viri: de Græcis verò non sinunt nos dubitare infiniti auctorum loci. Eustathius Iliadis libro χ. ΕΘ&ῶ ὡς αὐλείας θύρας τηρεῖσθαι ἐαυτὸν κυ-νῶν[?]. Aristophanes Lysistrata,
units.tr: These words suit a rustic man very well, for country people commonly called dogs "mute guardians." Columella, book 7, chapter 12: "Now, as I promised at the beginning, I shall speak of the mute guardians, although a dog is wrongly called a mute guardian." Nor did only country people use their guardianship; city folk too, who, as is well known, were accustomed to keep at their doors either a doorkeeping slave or a chained dog, or both. Learned men have long noted this for the Romans, and for the Greeks countless passages of authors leave no room for doubt. Eustathius, on Iliad book 10, says that he kept himself as a dog to guard the courtyard door [ὡς αὐλείας θύρας τηρεῖσθαι ἑαυτὸν κυνῶν]. Aristophanes in the Lysistrata:

units.la: —πρὸς γέ μὴ τῷ Θύραν Προαγορεύω μὴ βαδίζειν τῷ ἐμῷ.
units.tr: "I forbid anyone to walk up to my door..." [πρὸς γέ μὴ τῷ Θύραν Προαγορεύω μὴ βαδίζειν τῷ ἐμῷ.]

units.la: Ἠν μὲν γὰρ τὸ χάραγμα φέρῃς φίλῳ, ὥτε θυρωρὸς Ἐν σποδῷ, ὥτε κύων ἐν ἀποθύροις δίεταί[?].
units.tr: "For if you bring a brand to a friend, you are like a doorkeeper among the ashes, or like a dog that runs about among the outer doors." [Ἠν μὲν γὰρ τὸ χάραγμα φέρῃς φίλῳ, ὥτε θυρωρὸς ἐν σποδῷ, ὥτε κύων ἐν ἀποθύροις δίεταί.]

units.la: Idem Antiphanes poëta alius eiusdem generis, canes vocat Φρεροδόμους[?]. Sed testium ἄλις[?], tanquam ἑρύος[?]. Plutarchus in libro De curiositate, notat seruos ianitores succeßisse in locum θυρωρῶν[?] siue marmulorum quibus antiquiores utebantur.
units.tr: Antiphanes, another poet of the same kind, calls dogs by a similar name. But of the witnesses there is enough, as one might say. Plutarch, in his book On Curiosity, observes that household servants took over the place of the doorkeepers, or of the little guard-dogs, which the older generation used.

units.la: λίαν μὲν λυπρὸν ἔϊ[?].) Scribe, λέγων λυπρὸν ἔϊ[?]) : vel λίαν λέγων λυπρὸν εἰ[?]. pro λέγων ἔϊ[?]) λίαν λυ[?]. Est autem ambigua vox λυπρὸς, quae & asperum numerum, utpote recens percussum significare potest: & veterem atque usu tritum, aut aliàs minus probatum: quale est quod vocatur à Iuuenale tenue argentum, venaeq; fecunda. Deinde lego, ἡ γὰρ ὥρα ἕτερον ἅμα ἀλλάττεσθαι[?]. aut αὐτὴν ἀλλάττεσθαι[?]. Nemo autem nescit quàm sit plerunque difficile rusticis hominibus hac in parte satisfacere: qui quòd sint τῆς ἀργυρογνωμονικῆς imperiti, fraudem undique suspectant, omnia tuta timentes. Ex hac re natum apud Graecos proverbium, de iis qui iudicio & penitus singula examinant, ἐξεταζὼν ἀργυρομονικῶς[?]. extat apud Lucianum, & Maximum Tyrium.
units.tr: "Very harsh it is..." Read "saying, it is very harsh," or "saying very harsh, it is." The word λυπρὸς is ambiguous: it can mean rough (of a coin, freshly struck and sharp-edged) or old and worn, or something less approved by use, such as what Juvenal calls "thin silver, productive of veins." Then I read: "for the hour to change itself" or "to change it." No one fails to see how hard it usually is for rustic people to be satisfied in this matter. Being unskilled in assaying silver, they suspect fraud on every side, fearing all things as unsafe. From this came the Greek proverb about those who judge and examine each thing carefully: "examining like a silver assayer" [ἐξεταζὼν ἀργυρομονικῶς]. It is found in Lucian and in Maximus of Tyre.

units.la: ἡ ὁ ἀπορέον ἐγένετο[?].) Scribendum est, ἐγένετο absque litera subscripta: non enim est ἐγενίζω[?], sed ἀγὰρ[?]: in quo graviter sunt lapsi interpretes, cùm hìc, tum capite De impudentia, ubi vox ἀγενίζω[?] cum subscripto vitiosè posita in fœdum errorem cos impulit. Neque verò divinare possum quid iisdem in mentem fuerit, cum θύλακον verterent reticulum panis. Atqui ne tum quidem cum θύλακον ἀλφίτων dicunt Græci, id significare volunt:nedum cum θύλακον tantùm. vide ad caput De superstiti-tione.
units.tr: "Became doubtful" [ἡ ὁ ἀπορέον ἐγένετο]. It must be written ἐγένετο without the subscript letter. For it is not ἐγενίζω but ἀγὰρ, in which the interpreters have badly slipped, both here and in the chapter On Impudence, where the word ἀγενίζω, wrongly written with the subscript, led them into a shameful error. Nor can I guess what came into their minds when they rendered θύλακον as "bread-basket." Yet not even when the Greeks say θύλακον ἀλφίτων do they mean that, much less when they say θύλακον alone. See the chapter On Superstition.

units.la: Pag. 15. ταῦτα τῆς γυναικὸς καὶ ἀξυνίαν ἀναμιμνη-σκόμεθα.[?] Deesse aliquid, nemo tam cæcus quin videre queat: lego ἀπαλλεῖν ταῦτα τ. ν.[?] in quo sanè magna est rusticitas & diffidentia, quæ sæpe conjuncta videas.
units.tr: Page 15: "we remember these things of the woman and of her lack of understanding" [ταῦτα τῆς γυναικὸς καὶ ἀξυνίαν ἀναμιμνησκόμεθα]. That something is missing, no one is so blind that he cannot see. I read "to put away these things," and in this there is indeed great rusticity and distrust, which you often see joined together.

units.la: πόρς ἢ(ἂν αἱ διφθέραι.) Διφθέραι sunt, non pelles, sed vestes è pellibus, hoc est, rhenones: sicut & pelles Latinis pro vestibus è pelle: unde apud rei rusticæ scriptores inter familiæ vestes sunt pelles manicatæ, & passim. Pellibus autem Attici rustici, (imò ut arbitror omnes operæ viliores) vestiti esse solebant, ut notum est ex Aristophanis multis locis & eius Scholiaste: qui in Nebulas διφθέραν ait fuisse σαιμρυικὸν ἐπιβόλαιον,[?] sicut Ouidius in Metamorphosi pastoritiam pellem vocat. Theophylactus in epistolis, ὁ ἢ τῷ διφθέραν ἀγεῖς ὁ τῷ ἰδίω πρὸς ἄγυ χωρεῖ.[?] hinc dicti sunt in fabulis Græcorum διφθεῖαι vt præter Græcos auctor est Varro. & hic est quem pastoralem habitum vocat Livius, Florus in eadem historia pastorium. Posteriori ætas, vt comici Scholiastes annotat, ἰσάλλω appellabat: quæ est vox depravata ab antiqua ἰξαλλή, quæ etiam apud Hippocratem legitur, & proprie caprae pellem significat. nam ἰξαι olim pro αἴξαι quod est impetuosè ferri, & salire. unde ἰξαλῶν proprium cius animalis epithetum. Caprarũ autem pellibus in hanc rem vsos veteres etiam Varro ait libro secundo extremo rei rusticæ. Simylus in Moreto, cinctus villosa tergore capra.
units.tr: "The hides, if..." The διφθέραι are not skins but garments made of skins, that is, cloaks, just as the Latins also used "skins" for garments made of hide. Hence in the writers on farming the family clothing includes sleeved skins, and so on in many places. Attic country people, indeed (I think all the lower-paid workers), used to wear skins, as is known from many passages of Aristophanes and his scholiast, who says that the diphthera in the Clouds was a shaggy covering [σαιμρυικὸν ἐπιβόλαιον]; Ovid in the Metamorphoses calls it a "shepherd's skin" (pastoritiam pellem). Theophylact in his letters: "he who leads the diphthera leads the one who goes to the field." Hence the Diphtheiai were named in the Greek fables, as Varro, besides the Greeks, is authority for. This is the garment Livy calls "pastoral dress," and Florus in the same history calls "shepherd's dress." The later age, as the scholiast of the comic poet notes, called it isallo, a word corrupted from the old ixalle, which is also read in Hippocrates and properly means a goat's skin, for ixai was once used for aixai, meaning to rush forward violently and leap; whence ixalon is the proper epithet of that animal. That the ancients used goatskins for this purpose Varro too says in the last part of book 2 of On Farming. Simylus in the Moretum: "girt with a shaggy goat's hide."

units.la: καὶ τὸ Θεῖχος.[?] ] Cur rusticus de salsamentorum pretio potissimum quærit? Quia salsamenta erant tenuiorum & rusticorum cibus. Testes infiniti: vel lege Lucianum De conscribenda historia. Ideo etiam de re vili & abiecta dicebat Θεῖχος ἀξιώτερον,[?] Vilius est salsamento. eo proverbio vsus Aristophanes in Vespis.
units.tr: "And the salted fish?" Why does the rustic ask especially about the price of salted fish? Because salted fish was the food of the poorer sort and of country people. Witnesses are without number; or read Lucian's On How to Write History. For this reason he also called a cheap and despised thing "worth more than salt fish," for it is cheaper than salt fish. Aristophanes used this proverb in the Wasps.

units.la: καὶ εἰ σήμερον ὁ ἀγὼν ῥυμνίαν ἄγει.[?] ] Sanè rusticis-simè hoc quidem: saltem enim dicere debuerat iste, ἡ ῥυμνία ἄγει τὸν ἀγῶνα: quo fere modo loquitur homo & ipse ἀγὲς πλέως Strepsiades apud Aristophanem.
units.tr: "And if today the contest brings a ..." Certainly this is most rustic, for he ought at least to have said "the contest brings the ..." in the way that the man himself, Strepsiades in Aristophanes, speaks in a nearly similar manner.

units.la: —ἐγὼ δ' ἀπόλλυμαιὉρῶν ἀγχᾶν[?] τὼ σελίνω ὡς εἰκάδας.
units.tr: "But I perish, gazing at the ... celery as ... " [ἐγὼ δ' ἀπόλλυμαι ὁρῶν ἀγχᾶν τὼ σελίνω ὡς εἰκάδας.]

units.la: Non multum abest ab hac rusticitate mulier illa in comici Concionantibus, quæ sic loquitur.
units.tr: Not far from this rusticity is that woman in Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae, who speaks thus.

units.la: Λέγοι δ' ὅπως καὶ τ' ἀεὶ τάξις δράξομαι[?]Εως ἔτ' ἔστιν ἄστρα κ[αὶ] τ[ὴν] οὐρανόν.[?] Dicite nobis, inquit, quid facto sit opus dum adhuc in cælo sunt stellæ. nam qui ita loquitur, nónne existimare is videtur noctu tantùm esse in cælo astra, non autem interdiu, quia tum nulla cernantur? qua opinione ne ipsum quidem rus magis rusticum: etsi scio similia fuisse Epicuri & aliorum quorundam morosophorum deliramenta. Romani quoque rustici soliti dicere Cælum esse fine Luna, in cius syderis coitu. vt refert Plinius libro xiv. cap. xxi.
units.tr: "Tell us," she says, "what must be done while the stars are still in the sky" [Λέγοι δ' ὅπως καὶ τ' ἀεὶ τάξις δράξομαι, Εως ἔτ' ἔστιν ἄστρα καὶ τὸν οὐρανόν]. For does not one who speaks so seem to think that the stars are in the heavens only at night, and not by day, because then none are seen? Not even the countryside holds this opinion so rustically, though I know that similar were the ravings of Epicurus and certain other babbling philosophers. Roman country people too used to say that "the sky is there until the moon," at her conjunction with that star, as Pliny reports in book 14, chapter 21.

units.la: καὶ εἰπὼν[?] δὲ ὅτι βούλεται καταβὰς ἀποκείρασθαι.[?] ) Traiectio notanda. rectum erat, ὁ εἰπὼν ἔτι βούλεται[?] [illegible, ~8 letters] familiaris hæc figura loquendi Aristoteli & nostro huic auctori, vt infrà quodam loco annotauimus. Intelligendum est autem rufticũ ista dicere qui habeat barbam & comam incultam atque horridam. Ferè enim fit vt rustici homines huic elegantiæ alia negotia magis [?] facientia anteuertant,& diu intonsi maneát. Quare Suidas rusticitatis notam facit, [?] barbam promittere. [?] autem vel [?], vt mox, [?] vel [?] [?] ἡ [?].
units.tr: "And having said that he wishes, going down, to have his hair cut" [καὶ εἰπὼν δὲ ὅτι βούλεται καταβὰς ἀποκείρασθαι]. The inversion should be noted: the correct order would be "the one who said he still wishes..." This figure of speech is familiar to Aristotle and to this author, as I have noted elsewhere. One should understand that the rustic says these things who has an uncared-for and bristly beard and hair. For it usually happens that country men put other business, which takes up their time, before this kind of neatness, and remain unshorn for a long while. Hence Suidas makes it a mark of rusticity to let the beard grow.

units.la: ἐν βαλανείῳ ἄπαγ.) Seneca ad Lucilium epistola LVII. 1. de balnei tumultu & clamoribus loquens, Adiyce nunc Scordalum, & furem deprehensum, & eum cui vox sua in balneo placet. hoc est, [?] ἐν βαλανείῳ ᾄδοντα. Lege Artemidorum Ὀνειροκριτικῶν libro primo, capite LXXVIII. Similis rusticitas & [?] eorum qui lauantes recitabant, quos notat Horatius libro primo Sermonum. Græci eos qui indecenter se gererent in balneis, Triballos vocabant ab immani & inhumana gente Illyrica. Etymologici auctor, Τρίβαλλοι, οἱ ἐν τοῖς βαλανείοις ἀναγώγως [?] ἀσχημονοῦντες. alij paulo aliter apud Demosthenem & Isocratem interpretantur. vide Hesychium.
units.tr: "In the bath, sing" [ἐν βαλανείῳ ἄπαγ.]. Seneca, in letter 57 to Lucilius, section 1, speaking of the tumult and shouting in the baths: "Add now Scordalus, and the thief caught in the act, and the man whose voice pleases him in the bath." That is, singing in the bath [ἐν βαλανείῳ ᾄδοντα]. Read Artemidorus, Oneirocritica, book 1, chapter 78. A similar rusticity belongs to those who recited while bathing, which Horace notes in book 1 of the Satires. The Greeks called those who behaved indecently in the baths "Triballi," from the savage and inhuman Illyrian people. The author of the Etymologicon: "Triballoi, those who behave indecently in the baths unseemly" [Τρίβαλλοι, οἱ ἐν τοῖς βαλανείοις ἀναγώγως ἀσχημονοῦντες]. Others explain it somewhat differently, in Demosthenes and Isocrates. See Hesychius.

units.la: [?] εἰς τὰ [?] ἡ Ἅλυς [?].)
