Etiam hodie rustici noftrates clauis vel ferreis vel ligneis calceos suos suffigunt: quod Græci [?] dicunt, vel [?]: vnde iocus facetissimi poëtæ comici Machonis aut Diphili potius, apud Athenæum, in Chærephontem: quem cum non tæderet cœnæ gratia quanuis longum iter suscipere sucipere, monet eum poëta, non vt calceos clauis muniat, quod faciendum iis qui peregre cogitant, sed vt maxillas : vrbanè iocans in eius ingluviem & voracitatem. Sic ille,
units.tr: Even today our own country people nail their shoes with nails, either of iron or of wood, which the Greeks call by a word I cannot read. Hence the joke of the most witty comic poet, Macho, or rather Diphilus, in Athenaeus, against Chaerephon, who, not weary of a dinner, undertook a long journey for its sake. The poet advises him to fortify not his shoes with nails, as should be done by those who go abroad, but his jaws, jesting wittily at his gluttony and voracity. So he says:

units.la: Εἰς ζῶς ἑαυτὰ Χαυρεφῶν σαγόνας[?] Ἐγκοῦλον ἥλες, ἑκατέρᾳ γε τέτ[?]ρας[?] Ἱνα μὴ ἀφράσειων[?], ἢ μακρὰν ἐκάσολε[?] Ὀδὸν βαδίζων, ὡς γνάθος ἁγρέοσς[?].
units.tr: Chaerephon, you nail your jaws with nails, on both sides, so that you do not wither when you walk a long road to a dinner, like a jaw that has no... [the Greek verse is too garbled in the scan to render exactly].

units.la: Hinc dicti ἡλοκόποι[?], qui clauis calceamenta configebant, quæ clauata Romanis dicebantur, vt ait Festus. Glossarium vetus, Clauarius, ἡλοκόπ[?]. Nam etiam Romanis fuisse in vsu clauata satis constat: nemo enim nescit caligas militares clauis fuisse suffixas : ex quo & institutum est & appellatum clauarium : quod fuit donatiuum in clauos militariū caligarum. Pertinet ad hunc morem Plauti locum in Trinummo,
units.tr: Hence the nail-drivers (hēlokopoi), who fastened nails into footwear, which were called clavata by the Romans, as Festus says. The old glossary has "Clavarius" and "hēlokop". That the Romans also used clavata is well established, for everyone knows that military boots were fastened with nails. From this the clavarium was both instituted and named: it was a gratuity paid for the nails of soldiers' boots. To this custom belongs the passage of Plautus in the Trinummus:

units.la: Nisi uti sarcinam constringam, & clypeum ad dorsum accommodem.
units.tr: Unless I strap up my baggage and fit my shield to my back.
I shall have soles put under my slippers.

units.la: Fulmentæ sunt καταλύματ[?]: quod etiam solum. Latinis dicitur. Glossarium Κάσυμα, solum. Idem optimus auctor alibi, Solum caligarium, κάσυμα. Item, Supplalta, κεκασυμένα. & ita legendum etiam alio loco eiusdem libri vbi Supalta est editum. Nam suppingere est ἥλυς ἐληκέν[?] in calceos, vt in superiore loco Plauti. Etsi enim ibi clauis non nominantur, manifestum tamen id est ex alio loco in Bacchidibus, vbi notat poëta luxum veterum diuitum qui clauis argenteis vel aureis in hanc rem vsi. Planè enim errant eruditi viri qui locum illum emendandum censent. Sic Plautus,
units.tr: Fulmentae are the soles [katalumata], which is also called solum in Latin. The glossary has kasuma, "sole". The same excellent author elsewhere has "sole of a boot" [kasuma], and likewise supplalta, "nailed" [kekasumena]; and so it should be read in another place of the same book, where the printed text has supalta. For suppingere means to drive nails into shoes, as in the earlier passage of Plautus. Although no nails are mentioned there, this is clear from another passage in the Bacchides, where the poet points to the extravagance of the wealthy in old times, who used silver or gold nails for this purpose. Learned men who think that passage needs emendation are clearly mistaken. So Plautus:

units.la: Sed diuésne est istic Theotimus? CH. etiam rogas?
units.tr: But is Theotimus rich there? CH. Do you even ask?
He who has gold nailed into the soles of his shoes.

units.la: Nam etsi magnum hoc, fidem tamen veri non egreditur. cui enim mirum hoc adeo videatur, qui meminerit eorum quæ de Antiochi exercitu narrant historici? qui quidem magna ex parte (verba sunt Valerii Maximi) aureos clauos crepidis subiectos habuit.Simile est quod de Agnone Teio Alexandri Magni purpurato Plutarchus narrat: qui aureis clauis suffigere crepidas solebat, ait Plinius libro xxxiii. capite iii. Clemens Alexandrinus Pædagogi libro ii. Αἰσχρὰ γὰρ ἀληθῶς τὰ ἀνδάλια ἐκεῖνα, ἐφ᾽ οἷς δὴ τὰ χρυσᾶ ἀναθήματα· ἀλλὰ χαλκοῦ τὰς ἥλους [?] ἐλικοφθῶς [?] τῆς κατύμματον ἐγκαταχρύσειν ἐξεῖσαι [?]. Repertio & clauis æneis in hanc rem vsos veteres Romanos. Lucilius,
units.tr: For although this is a great thing, it does not go beyond what is credible. Who would find it so surprising if he remembers what the historians tell of the army of Antiochus? They say (these are the words of Valerius Maximus) that he had, for the most part, golden nails set under his sandals. Similar is what Plutarch relates of Agnon of Teos, a purple-clad follower of Alexander the Great, who used to nail his sandals with golden nails, as Pliny says in book 33, chapter 3. Clement of Alexandria, in book 2 of the Paedagogus, says that those shoes were truly shameful, for which golden decorations were made; but he speaks of nails of bronze gilded over. I have also found that the old Romans used bronze nails for this purpose. Lucilius:
To nail the soles with bronze nails.

units.la: Sic legédum censeo hunc Lucillij locum, qui apud Nonium corruptus extat. Legitur enim vulgò subducere. inepte cum subcudere plane fit ἐκρύσειν, vel ἐλκόσθειν. Extat apud eundem Nonium etiam alter Lucillij locus eódem pertinens, Sufficit huic dum fulmentas quatuor addit, versus est hexameter, sed corruptus. Lego autem,
units.tr: I think this passage of Lucilius, which survives corrupted in Nonius, should be read thus. In the common text it is read subducere ("to draw up"), which is absurd; subcudere (to hammer under) means plainly "to drive in" or "to draw up with blows". Nonius also preserves another line of Lucilius bearing on the same matter: Sufficit huic dum fulmentas quatuor addit. It is a hexameter, but corrupted. I read instead:

units.la: Sufficit huic: clauis fulmentas quattuor addit. hoc est, quatuor clauis fulmentas addit. Imperitus librarius ex cl. fecerat d. quod mendi genus sæpe occurrit. hæc prima mendi indoles. Sed redeamus ad Theophrastum & doctas migremus Athenas. Non est enim prætermittendus nobis insignis locus veteris scriptoris Teletis vbi & moris huius & auctoris nostri mentio habetur. Refert Telcs Metroclis cuiusdam sermonem qui diceret Theophrasti & Xenocratis hanc olim rationem fuisse, vt si quis ipsis operam nauare vellet, illi necessario habendi essent calcei: atque ij sine fulmentis, sine clauis: habendam etiam pretiosam ac delicatam vestem: pueros multos: domum amplam ad conuiuia agitanda. Fuisse praeterea dandam operam vt panis adesset non plebeius sed siligineus: opsonium non qualecunque: vinum dulce: vt denique quando conuiuia essent celebranda, lautè id fieret. His siquidem illos ingenui ac liberalis hominis vitam esse metitos. Teletis verba sunt, Παρὰ τῶς γὰρ ἐξ ἀναλήψεως εἴδει ὑποδήματα ἔχειν· καὶ τῶν ἀπαλλὼν, ἥλως ἂν ἔχοι· εἶτα χλανίδα, παίδων ἀκολουθίαν, οἰκίαν μεγάλην εἰς τὸ σωμάτιον ὅπως ἀρξι καθαροὶ, ὅ,ν μὴ τὸ τυχόν· οἶνον ἡδύ, ἐστιν ὁχ ἔτος ἐπαίδοιχρ τας ἐστεφανίζοντος (lego ὑπεκαλῶς) ἵνα πολυλεχῶν, ἐλαβέσθαι ὀ παρ' αὐτὸς ἡ Ϲιαύτη ἀναςροφὴν ἐκείνῳ.
units.tr: Sufficit huic: clavis fulmentas quattuor addit, that is, he adds four soles with nails. An unskilled copyist had written d. for cl., a kind of error that often occurs; this is the first sign of such a fault. But let us return to Theophrastus and go to learned Athens. We must not pass over a notable passage of an old writer, Teles, where both this custom and the mention of our author occur. Teles reports the speech of a certain Metrocles who said that this was once the practice of Theophrastus and Xenocrates: if anyone wished to be attentive to them, they must necessarily have shoes, and these without soles or nails; they must also have costly and fine clothing, many boys, and a large house for entertaining guests. Besides this, care was to be taken that bread be present, not common but wheaten; the relish not ordinary; the wine sweet; and that, when dinners were given, they be given lavishly. By these things, he said, they measured the life of a free and gentlemanly man. The words of Teles are: "For it is fitting to have shoes of ... and without nails ... then a cloak, a train of attendants, a large house so that ... pure ... not what chance offers; sweet wine ... [Greek text garbled]."

units.la: καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς ὁδὸς παρειῶν. ) Rusticitas quæ hic à Theophrasto notatur in eo est, quòd malit iste cùm casu, vel ex negotio ante Archiæ salsamentarij officinam transiret, salsamenta emere, ac secum auferre, quod parum erat honestum: quàm aliquem postea famulum domo mittere qui emat & afferat. Eadem mens illius fuisse videtur, qui pronuntiabat hæc apud Platonem comicum,
units.tr: "And along the same road" (tēs autēs hodou). The rusticity that Theophrastus here censures lies in this: he preferred, when by chance or on business he passed by the salt-fish shop of Archias, to buy salted fish himself and carry it away with him, which was rather unbecoming, rather than to send a servant from home to buy and bring it. The same mind seems to have been his who, in Plato the comic poet, speaks these words:

units.la: Τίλτε Ϲείχυς, ἐαρισμὸν ἐπισ οἰκιας. vbi etiam legi malim πρεσ̈ων vt hic: quanquam ex Theophrasti verbis poterit sine damno sententiæ abesse vox πρεσ̈ων: ac pene illam inducendam censucrim [?].
units.tr: "Tilte Seichys, to buy salted fish for the house." Here I would prefer to read prosōn as in this place, although the word prosōn could be left out without loss of sense from Theophrastus' words, and I would think it nearly to be inserted.

units.la: Nam ita loqui solent scriptores Attici : τῆς αὐτῆς ὁδὸς inquam, non ᾱκειῶν τῆς αὐτῆς ὁδὸς. Ariftophanes in Pace.
units.tr: For Attic writers are accustomed to speak thus: tēs autēs hodou, I say, not akeiōn tēs autēs hodou. Aristophanes in the Peace:

units.la: —χ᾽ ἅμα τῆς αὐτῆς ὁδὸς χαιρεάδλω τῆς βωσάτα. Nicoftratus Pandrofo,
units.tr: —and along the same road, with the best of the ...

units.la: Ἐπεὶ(?) τῆς αὐτῆς ὁδὸς πρὸς Ἀσπόαλω
Ἐλθὼν, πέμψαι σρῶμαΤ αὐτῷ νῶ, τῷν,[?]
units.tr: "Since along the same road to Aspasius..."

units.la: Κέλαδε. Antiphon orator elegantissimus, Κάλλισ- ὲδόχ[?] τῷ Φιλόνεω ἥ αὐτῆς ὁδὸς ἅμα μὴ προσεμψαι τ᾽ ἅπα- τέρα τ᾽ ἐμὸν φίλον ὄνῳ ἑαυτῷ, ἅμα ἡ διὰ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐσιά- σαι ἐκείνου. Latini etiam breuiùs, eàdem dicunt pro τῆς αὐτῆς ὁδὸς. Charifius. Veteres eádem sfliti sunt discere, non addentes via, ut sit κατ᾽ ἐλλειψιν: ut Plautus inquit, Eádem bibes, eádem tibi dedero fauiam. sic apud Ciceronem & alios auctores sæpe quare hūc locum sic potes vertere, & simul, eádem sf.mere ab Archia sálf. Idem significat & vox obiter apud Latinos: & inde etiam illud Græcorum natum ὁδὸς παρεπηγον.
units.tr: Come, send him ... Antiphon, the most elegant orator: "Callistratus to Philoneus: along the same road, at the same time, not to send my father's friend to himself, but at the same time through the sacred things to hold him..." The Latins also say more briefly the same thing for tēs autēs hodou. Charisius: the old writers were accustomed to say eadem without adding via, so that it is an ellipsis, as Plautus says: "You will drink the same, and I will give you the same flavour." So in Cicero and other authors often. Therefore you may render this passage "and at the same time, to take the same things from Archias' salt-fish shop". The Latins also use the word obiter in the same sense, and from this the Greek expression hodos parepēgon arose.

units.la: κομίζοντα παρ᾽ Ἀρχίᾳ τῆς Θεῖχυς.) Plutarchus, Θαυμάζει δὲ τὴν εἰ δὲ ἀγορᾶς αὐτὸς φέρει τάξει χος. Sic Diogenes Cynicus vt nouo difcipulo tenerioris adhuc frontis verecundiam excuteret, gestare eum iubet saperdam per vrbem. referunt Diogenes Laertius, Plutarchus, alij. Archias cuius hic fit mentio, nobilis aliquis fuit Athenis aetate Theophrasti falsamentarius quales fuêre in eadem vrbe Chærephilus, Euthymus, Phidippus, aliique veterum poëtarum comœdiis nobilitati. Erant autem Athenis cetariorum officinę, siue τ: Θεῖχωσλεῖον procul à foro rerum reliquarum, ad portam vrbis nescio quam: vbi & alia parui pretij nonnulla vænibant. Aristophanes Equitibus,
units.tr: "carrying from Archias the salted fish" (komizonta par' Archiāi tēs Teichus). Plutarch: "He wonders at ... and carries from the market himself..." So Diogenes the Cynic, to shake off the shame of a new disciple still tender of brow, ordered him to carry a salt-fish through the city. Diogenes Laertius, Plutarch and others report this. Archias, whom this passage mentions, was a noted salt-fish dealer at Athens in Theophrastus' time, like Chaerephilus, Euthymus and Phidippus in the same city, who were made famous by the comedies of the old poets. There were fish-shops at Athens, or the Teichopolion, far from the forum of other goods, by some city gate; there also other cheap things were sold. Aristophanes in the Knights:

units.la: Ἡλιανώλεις, ἕτεον, ἡ σὺ τὰς πύλας;
Αλ. Ἐπὶ τὰς πύλαις, ἡ τὸ Θεῖχον ὤνιον.
units.tr: Sausage-seller: "At the gates, or at the Teichos market."

units.la: Scholiastes ὠνίον, ἀγορὰν· ὅτι τὸ Τειχοπωλεῖον, ἀντὶ τῆς ἐπὶ τὰ ἀγορᾶς πωλεῖται. Reperitur etiam ita scriptus hic locus: κομίζεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς βραχίονος τῆς Τειχύς. quæ lectio fortasse vera est: nam etiam faculos atque alia id genus gestabant è brachiis pendentia. Nonius, Bulga est folliculus omnis, quam & crumenam veteres appellarunt: & est sacculus ad brachium pendens. Callimachus de quodā qui ampullam oleo plenam ad brachium pendentē gestabat,
units.tr: The scholiast: ōnion means market; Teichopōleion instead of the market where things are sold. The passage is also found written thus: "to be carried from the arm of Teichus", which reading is perhaps true; for they carried also flasks and such things hanging from their arms. Nonius: Bulga is any little pouch, which the old writers also called a purse; it is a small bag hanging from the arm. Callimachus, of a man who carried an oil flask full, hanging from his arm:

units.la: Καί ῥα [?]ἀμφὶ σκαιοῖο βραχίονος ἔμπλεον ὄλπιν.
units.tr: "And he carried on his left arm a full flask of oil."

units.la: Similiter crumenam è collo pendentem gerebat.
units.tr: Similarly he carried a purse hanging from his neck.
—the man takes the purse from his neck,
He gives me twenty minas; I take them gladly.

units.la: & alibi tribus quatuórve locis. Inde est decollare quod proprie de marsupio dicitur quod collo abest & periit. inde sumitur pro οἴχεσθαι, vt cum spem decollare ait Varro.
units.tr: and elsewhere in three or four places. Hence decollare, which is properly said of a purse that is away from the neck and lost; from it is taken the sense of "to perish", as when Varro says spem decollare, "to lose hope".

units.la: ] H De hoc vitio (vitium enim est) diximus supra capite De adulatione. Differt blanditia ab adulatione solo fine: nam hæc suum sibi commodum pro fine proponit: blanditia verò solum τὸ ἀρέσαι spectat, & vt placeat in congressibus & conuictu. Etsi autem parum honesta est blanditia hæc, (nullum enim vitium honestum) quia tamen sub virtutis specie solet id vitium latere, libenter faciunt adulatores quò nominis sibi conuenientis inuidiam fugiant, vt se blandos potius appellent. Athenæus libro sexto, Τούτῳ ἡ τῷ κολακείαν τινὲς ἐντρεπόμενοι τὸ ὄνομα, ἀρέσκειαν ἀποδ[?] γορεύειν, ὡς καὶ Ἀναξανδρίδης ἐν Σαμίᾳ, Τὸ δὲ κο-λακεύειν τινὶ ἀρέσκειν ὄνομ᾽ ἔχει. Neque omittendum quod Aristoteles in octauo Nicomacheorum scribit, ἀρέσκος vulgò appellari quos ipse φίλος πολίτης solet nominare: eos nimirum qui benignè & comiter cum omnibus versantur, veram amicitiam cum nemine colunt. Non est autem vera illorum sententia qui τῷ ἀρέσκεσθαι qua de hîc, negant Latinè dici blanditiam: sed numero multitudinis blanditias. Q. Cicero De petitione consulatus : Sed opus est magnopere blanditia: quæ etiam si vitiosa est & turpis in catera vita: tamen in petitione est necessaria: etenim cum deteriorem aliquem assentando facit, improba est, cum amiciorem non tam vituperanda. M. Cicero De Rep. libro 1111. In cine excelso atque homine nobili, blanditiam, ostentationem, ambitionem, notam esse leuitatis. Idem ad Atticum libro x 11. Vnum te puto minus blandum esse quàm me: & si vterque nostrum est aliquando aduersus aliquem, inter nos certè nunquam sumus. Idem, eodem libro, Cum Romæ essem, & te iam iamque vilurum me putarem, quotidie tamen horæ quibus expeclabam longa videbantur: scis me minimè esse blandum: itaque minus aliquanto dico quàm sentio. Nos Galli ἀρεσκος & blandum vocamus courtifan, hoc est aulicum: qui minimo discrimine ab adulatore distinguitur. Veteres Latini ἀρεσκείαν ἀρέσκειαν non folùm placentiam dixerunt: fed & placorem. Gloffarium vetus, Ἀρέσκεια, hic Placor.
units.tr: I have discussed this vice (for it is a vice) above, in the chapter on Flattery. Obsequiousness differs from flattery only in its aim. The flatterer sets his own advantage before him as his end, whereas the obsequious man looks only to τὸ ἀρέσαι [to please], and wants to be liked in company and at table. Although this kind of obsequiousness is hardly honourable (no vice is honourable), it usually hides under the appearance of virtue, so flatterers are glad to avoid the odium of their proper name and call themselves obliging instead. Athenaeus in book six says: "Some, ashamed of the name flattery, call it ἀρέσκεια [obsequiousness], as Anaxandrides also does in the Samia: 'to flatter someone is called to please him' [Τὸ δὲ κολακεύειν τινὶ ἀρέσκειν ὄνομ᾽ ἔχει]." Nor should we omit what Aristotle writes in book eight of the Nicomachean Ethics: those whom the common people call ἀρέσκοι [obsequious men] he himself usually calls φίλοι πολῖται [civic friends], namely those who deal kindly and courteously with everyone yet cultivate true friendship with no one. The view of those who say that the Latin word blanditia cannot be used for this τῷ ἀρέσκεσθαι, but that blanditiae in the plural can, is not correct. Q. Cicero, On Canvassing for the Consulship: "But flattery is greatly needed: although in the rest of life it is faulty and base, in canvassing it is necessary. For when it makes someone worse by fawning on him, it is wicked; when it makes him more friendly, it is not so much to be blamed." M. Cicero, On the Republic, book four: "In a lofty and noble man, flattery, showing off and ambition are marks of lightness." The same, to Atticus, book twelve: "I think you are less flattering than I am; and if either of us is sometimes against someone, between ourselves we are never against each other." The same, in the same book: "When I was at Rome, and thought you would soon be coming to me, still the hours I waited seemed long. You know I am not at all flattering, so I say somewhat less than I feel." We Gauls call the ἀρέσκος and blandus a courtisan, that is, a courtier, who differs very little from a flatterer. The old Latins used ἀρέσκεια not only for placentia [pleasantness] but also for placor [pleasing]. The old glossary: "Ἀρέσκεια, here placor."

units.la: ἐκ τῷ βεξλίσῳ.) Sic Plato, ἀνὰ τὸ βεξλίσα. Terentius Adelphis,,
units.tr: ἐκ τῷ βεξλίσῳ. Thus Plato, ἀνὰ τὸ βέλτιστον [towards what is best]. Terence in the Adelphi:

units.la: —quod te isti facilem & festivum putant, Id non fit ex vera vita,neque adeo ex æquo & bono:
units.tr: "—that they think you easy and agreeable: that does not come from a true life, nor indeed from what is fair and good."

units.la: Sed ex assentando. D. Paulus in ea ad Romanos, ἐκας ἡμῶν τῷ πλησίον ἀρεσκέτω εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν.
units.tr: "But from fawning." St Paul in the letter to the Romans: "Let each of us please his neighbour for good" [ἕκαστος ἡμῶν τῷ πλησίον ἀρεσκέτω εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν].

units.la: Pag. 16. Σαυμαζ(ε)ς ἱκανῶς.) Proprium blandorum atque adulatorum mirari alios: Cicero in Paradoxis, Loquitur ad voluntatem: quicquid denuntiatum, fit facit: assentatur, assidet, miratur. Sic eft legēdum dubio procul, non munerat, vt vifum Lambino. Idem Cicero libro fecundo De diuinatione. Neque porrò aut adulatus aut miratus [fum] fortunam alterius, ut me mea pœniteret. Sic apud Horatium, aliósque τὸ mirari, accipitur. Etiam apud Græcos τὸ Σαυμάζειν, verbum eft abiecti animi, & planè ferule, vt in Euripidis Medea,
units.tr: Page 16. Σαυμάζειν ἱκανῶς [to admire greatly]. It is characteristic of the obsequious and flattering to admire others. Cicero in the Paradoxes: "He speaks to the will: whatever is ordered he does, he agrees, he sits beside, he admires." That is undoubtedly how it should be read, not munerat [rewards], as it seemed to Lambinus. The same Cicero in book two of On Divination: "Nor have I flattered or admired another's fortune, so as to be sorry for my own." So too in Horace and others, the word mirari [to admire] is used in this sense. Among the Greeks too, θαυμάζειν is a word of a servile and abject spirit, as in Euripides' Medea:

units.la: Δέσποινα δ᾽ ἐμὲ νῦν αὐτὶ σε Σαυμάζεμαι. [?]
units.tr: "Mistress, now you admire me in place of…"

units.la: Diogenes Cynicus in epiftola ad Dionyfium Syracufanum, σκύτως ἂν δεῖ Οι ἢ δεσπότης, ἔχ ὃς σε Σαυμάσει ἢ κολακεύσει. [?] Isocrates folet iungere duo verba Σαυμαζειν & Θεραπευειν. In huiusmodi locis significant hæc verba, non fimplicem admirationē, fed aliquem effectum ex illo affectu manantem. nec multo aliter LXX interpretes Leuitici capite XX 1. ὁ ποιῶν ἀδικον ἐν κείσῳ ἐλὴν πρόσωπον πλουσίου. [?] & in Apocalypsi S. Ioannis, cap. x 1 1 1. ἐ Σαυμάζειν ἐν ἁλη τῇ γῇ ὁπίσω τῶ Κυρίῳ. [?]
units.tr: Diogenes the Cynic, in his letter to Dionysius of Syracuse: "A master should be feared, not admired or flattered." Isocrates usually joins the two verbs θαυμάζειν and θεραπεύειν. In passages like these the words signify not simple admiration but some effect flowing from that feeling, and the Seventy in Leviticus chapter nineteen [sic] use it in much the same way: "you shall not respect the person of the rich" [ὁ ποιῶν ἄδικον ἐν κρίσει, ἐλὼν πρόσωπον πλουσίου]. Also in the Apocalypse of St John, chapter thirteen: "all the earth wondered after the beast" [ἐθαύμασεν ὅλη ἡ γῆ ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου].

units.la: καὶ τὰς ξένες ὁ εἴωθεν.] Lego, ἡ πρὸς τὰς ξένες ὃ εἰσαεὶν. vt intelligamus tam honorificè loqui istū de peregrinis,quando ipsos alloquitur.
units.tr: "And to strangers, as he is accustomed." I read: "and to strangers, as he is accustomed to speak." So that we understand that this man speaks so honourably to foreigners when he addresses them.

units.la: ἵνα κοινὸς ἕῃ δοκῇ.] Hoc est, vt videatur vtriusque partis benevolus, non eius solùm vnde dicit. Atqui hoc sine praevaricationis suspicione fieri nō potest. Iudici istud potius cōueniat,cuius officium est,vt praeclarè summus ait vates,
units.tr: "That he may seem to be common." That is, that he may seem well disposed to both parties, not only to the one he is speaking for. But this cannot be done without some suspicion of prevarication. That belongs rather to a judge, whose office it is, as the greatest poet finely says, to judge between the two sides.

units.la: Εἰς μέ(γν) ἀμφιλέροισι δικάζειν, μηδ᾽ ἐα᾽ ἀρωγῇ[?].
units.tr: "To judge between the two parties and not allow…" [Εἰς μέ(σον) ἀμφιλέροισι δικάζειν…].

units.la: φησὶ σύκῳ ὁμοιότερα ἕῃ) τῷ ἀαταξί.] Animaduertenda est hoc loco singularis quædam βραχυλογία. Nam hoc dicere voluit, ὁμοιότερα ἕῃ) τῷ ἀαταξί, ἢ σῦκον σύκῳ. Ita enim paroemia efferri solita, quæ extat plena in veteris poëtę loco qui est apud M.Tullium ad Atticum lib. 1111. epistola v 111.
units.tr: "He says it is like a fig." Here a special brevity of speech is to be noted. For he meant to say ὁμοιότερα ἐστὶ τῷ ἀταξί [it is like the…], or "fig to fig." For the proverb was usually put this way, and it occurs in full in a verse of an old poet quoted by Marcus Tullius to Atticus, book thirteen, letter eight.

units.la: Σύκῳ μὰ τλὸ Δήμητρα σῦκον ὧδε ἐν Οὕτω ἐμοίων γένοντε.
units.tr: "Fig to fig, by Demeter, fig, here in such a way they become alike."

units.la: sed quia vulgò notissimum erat hoc prouerbium, neque poterat hîc quisquam aut hærere aut errare,fecit noster senex, in quo senilis garrulitatis nihil est, verborum compendium. Quid mirum? ita fuerat à praeceptore optimo institutus : in cuius libris studiosus lector istiusmodi breuiloquentiam sæpe poterit obseruare : nos vnum aut alterum exemplum animi caussa proferemus : simul vt iuniorum diligentiam ad similes elegantias obseruandas excitemus. Ait Aristoteles De partibus lib. secundo, capite x 11 1. βλεφαρείδας ὃ ὅτι τῷ βλε-φάρων ἔχει, ὃ ὅ(α) τείχας ἔχει' ὀρνίθες ὃ καὶ τῷ φολιδωτῷ ὧδέν. voluit dicere, & scripsisset alius, ὀρνίθες ὃ ὡς ἔχειν, ὧδε τῷ φολιδωτῷ ὧδέν. Idem in libello De miraculis auditis, τὸ δ᾽ ἐν τῇ Λιπάρᾳ ποτὲ καὶ ἐκλεί[?]τὴν φησὶ Ξενοφάνης, ἕτη ἐπικαλέσθαι τῷ δ᾽ ἐσδόμῳ ἐπα-γελᾶθειν[?]. νελθεῖν[?]. dicendum erat, τὴ δ' ἐξ' ὁμῷ καὶ δεκάτῳ[?]. sic & alibi loquitur.
units.tr: But because this proverb was very well known to everyone, and no one here could be puzzled or mistaken, our old man, in whom there is nothing of senile garrulity, made it short. Why be surprised? He had been so trained by his excellent teacher; and in his books a diligent reader will often observe this kind of concise speech. I shall offer one or two examples for the sake of illustration, and so rouse the diligence of younger readers to observe similar elegances. Aristotle says in On the Parts of Animals, book two, chapter thirteen: "Eyelids, because they have eyelashes; and birds, because they have scales" [βλεφαρίδας ὅτι τῶν βλεφάρων ἔχει, ὄρνιθες δὲ καὶ τῷ φολιδωτῷ ὁμοίως]. He meant to say, and another writer would have written, "birds, because they have something similar, as with the scaly." The same in the little book On Heard Miracles: "What Xenophanes says happened once at Lipara, and an eclipse…; the seventh…; the tenth…" It ought to be read, "the ninth day and the tenth." He speaks in this way elsewhere too.

units.la: Pag. 17. καὶ τίς μὲν συμπαίζειν αὐτός[?]. ] Iuuenalis de falsis fictisque amicis loquens, istud non omisit, Nam idem plane sibi haec volunt,
units.tr: Page 17. "And who indeed plays with him…" Juvenal, speaking of false and feigned friends, did not omit this, for they mean exactly the same thing:

units.la: Sed tua nunc Mycale pariat licet, & pueros tres In gremium patris fundat; simul ipse loquaci Gaudebit nido: viridem thoraca iubebit Afferri, minimasque nuces, assemque rogatum Ad mensam quoties parasitus venerit infans.
units.tr: "But let your Mycale now bear, if she likes, and pour three boys into their father's lap; while he himself will rejoice at the chattering nest; he will order a green little coat to be brought, and tiny nuts, and a penny asked for each time the parasite's little child comes to the table."

units.la: λέγων, ἀκκὸς, πέλεκυς[?]. ] Existimant docti viri blandum hunc hominem cum infantibus istis balbutientem ea nominare, quae erant forte ante oculos posita: idque nos aliquando probauimus. Sed cum cogito dici hoc inter pocula, hoc est, in triclinio qui non est locus securium, vtrium autem multò minùs, venio in eam sententiam vt putem aliter hunc locum esse exponendum. Existimo igitur δακτὸν[?] & πέλεκυν[?] hîc esse, non id quod vulgò significant: sed crepundia ex infantium istorum collis, vt fit, dependentia: quae quod effent ad fimilitudinem veri vtris & verae securis effecta, ideo ita nominantur. Crepundia enim & παίγνια[?] infantium, ad hanc etiam formam fieri solita, vel teste Plauto probare possumus: qui in Rudente inter alia crepundia quae ad Palaestrae agnitionem commemorat, etiam ensiculum & securiculam numerat. Non est autem dubium ista crepundia quae in fabulis adhiberi solent ad agnitionem puerorum expofitorum, fuisse infantium παίγνια[?] è collo, vti dixi, pendere solita. Quare etiam δέρματα[?] Graeci signa ista vocant, vel ἀμφίδερμα[?] vt Aristoteles in Poetica. Euripides in Ione Ἑέραια χρυσώματα παιδὶ νεογόνῳ φέρειν. Dion Chrysostomus καὶ πολλὰ διδάσματα, καὶ σκῆπτρα, καὶ τιάρας προσαφωσιν αὐτῷ καθάπερ τὰ διδάσματα τοῖς ἐκλελυμένοις παιδίοις ἵνα μὴ ἀγνοῶσι. Et veteres quoque grammatici crepundia explicant puerilia ornamenta. In Glossario vero sic, Crepundia γνωρίσματα, optimè. Alibi in eodem nunquam satis laudatio libro, ita scriptum est, Γνωρίσματα τὰ ὅτι πάρων [?], Crepundia Monimenta. perperam:debuit enim sic, Γνωρίσματα, Crepundia monimenta γνωρίσματα τὰ ὅτι πάρων [?] Monimenta.de quibus monimentis multa diccimus, si Deus dabit aliquando. Graeci puerorum expositorum crepundia γνωρίσματα nominant, ut Heliodorus auctor amoenissimus, & alij. Non parum haec declarant pulcherrimum illum Ciceronis locum in Bruto, Quoniam totum me non nævo aliquo aut crepundijs sed corpore omni videris velle cognoscere. In fabulis agnitiones fere fieri videas vel per naevum, vel per crepundia:eò allusit Cicero. De hoc igitur loco sic sentio, sic censeo: sed non ita, ut qui aliter sentiat, nihil sensurus videatur: difficile enim est de eo quicquam affirmare quod per iocum & ludum dictum est: quorum multiplex semper materia atque occasio. Quid si enim non ἀγχὸς legendum dicamus, sed ἀγχός? nam ita moris fuit puerulos compellare. Hesychius, Ἀγχὸς παράμπωρ [?]· λέγετυ ὁ παιδίοις, ὡς μωρός. quanquam ibi fortasse ἀγχὼ legendum. vide Graecos paroemiographos. Hoc si cui probabitur, de altera voce erit cogitandum. Quid si vero non vtrem, non securim vllam hic intelligi dicamus: sed infantes potius ipsos ridiculi causa ita appellari; Nā
units.tr: "Saying 'akkos', 'pelekys'…" Learned men think that this flatterer, babbling with these infants, names the things that happen to lie before their eyes; and I myself have once approved this. But when I consider that it is said over the wine cups, that is, in the dining room, where there is no place for axes, still less for wineskins, I come to the view that this passage should be explained otherwise. I think then that δακτύλιον [ring] and πέλεκυν [axe] here do not mean what they usually signify, but the trinkets hanging from the necks of those infants, as happens; and because these were made in the likeness of a real wineskin and a real axe, they are so named. For that the crepundia [rattles, baubles] and playthings of infants were usually made in this shape too, we can prove even on the authority of Plautus, who in the Rudens, among other crepundia which he lists as tokens for recognising a foundling, also counts a little sword and a little axe. There is no doubt that those crepundia which are commonly used in stories to recognise exposed children were playthings of infants, hung, as I said, from the neck. Hence also the Greeks call these tokens δέρματα [skins] or ἀμφίδερμα [coverings], as Aristotle does in the Poetics. Euripides in Ion: "to bear golden trinkets for a newborn child." Dio Chrysostom: "and he puts on him many tokens, sceptres and tiaras, just as tokens are put on exposed infants so that they may not be unknown." Old grammarians too explain crepundia as childish ornaments. In the Glossary, indeed, it is thus: "Crepundia, γνωρίσματα [marks of recognition]," admirably. Elsewhere in the same book, which can never be praised enough, it is written thus: "Γνωρίσματα, the things that…, Crepundia, monimenta"; wrongly, for it ought to be: "Γνωρίσματα, crepundia; monimenta…" I have said much about these monimenta, if God grants that I may one day return to them. The Greeks call the crepundia of exposed children γνωρίσματα, as the author Heliodorus, a most charming writer, and others do. The most beautiful passage of Cicero in the Brutus declares this not a little: "since you seem to wish to know me not by some mole or baubles, but by my whole body." In stories you will see recognitions usually made either through a birthmark or through crepundia; Cicero alluded to this. So I think and judge about this passage, yet not in such a way that someone who thinks otherwise would seem to have nothing to say; for it is difficult to affirm anything about what was said in jest and play, of which there is always a manifold matter and occasion. What if we say the word should be read not ἀγχὸς but ἀγχός? For it was customary to address little boys so. Hesychius: "Ἀγχὸς παράμπωρ: it is said to children, as to a fool." Though there perhaps ἀγχὼ should be read; see the Greek proverb-collectors. If anyone approves this, we shall have to consider the other word. But what if we say that no wineskin and no axe is meant here at all, but that the infants themselves are so called for the sake of ridicule? For

units.la: [?] Greek words in this line are printed in a worn or small form and are not fully certain. qui erat cute ventréque valde diftento, eum appellat ἀσκὸν quasi γάςρανα & ventriosum dicas. sic apud Ariftophanem quidam appellantur ἀμφορῆς νεναςμένοι, & apud eundem ἀσκὲς pro corpore ponitur, vt in illo, ἀσκὸν δίφερν in Nebulis. & in oraculo quod Ægeo datum eft, ἀσκῶ τὸν προχοῦ μὴ λύσαι πάδα : nam per vtris amicinum fiue pediculum, aliud innuitur allegoricè. vide Scholiasten Euripidis ad Medeam. Sic & Anaxarchus Σύλακον vocabat corpus fuum, cum dicebat nequiffimo tyranno à quo cruciabatur, Πτίατε τὸν Ανάξαρχυ Σύλακον. vide Euftathium Ιλιαδ. δ. Praeterea prouerbium eft apud Græcos de homine faturo & qui moris habet fe cibo vinóque ingurgitate : eft merus ἀσκὸς, & merus Σύλακων. Alexis in Hefione dç Hercule ἀσδηφάγῳ loquens,
units.tr: He calls the man who had very swollen skin and belly an askos, as if he were gastranas, and you could call him "bellied." So in Aristophanes some men are called stuffed amphorae, and in the same author askos is used for the body, as in the line about the askos carried in the Clouds [ἀσκὸν δίφερν]. In the oracle given to Aegeus, "Do not loose the foot of the wineskin's mouth" [ἀσκῶ τὸν προχοῦ μὴ λύσαι πάδα]: the strap or fastening of the bag is one thing, and another thing is allegorically meant. See the scholiast on Euripides' Medea. So too Anaxarchus called his body a sylax when he said to the wicked tyrant by whom he was tortured, "Pound Anaxarchus's sylax" [Πτίατε τὸν Ἀνάξαρχον Σύλακον]. See Eustathius on the Iliad, book 4. Moreover there is a Greek proverb about a man who is gorged and has the habit of stuffing himself with food and wine: he is a pure askos and a pure sylax. Alexis in Hesione, speaking of the glutton Heracles:

units.la: Ηίνοτε κύλλω, καὶ λαβὼν, ἐξῆς αὐκυράς[?] Ἕλκει, καζυντὰς, καὶ τε τὸ παροιμίαν[?] Αἰεὶ ποτ' ἀν μὴ ἀσκὸς, ἀν ὁ Σύλακων[?] Ἀνθρωπός δὲ[?]
units.tr: Sometimes he drags a [...] and, taking it, he drags it off and [...] as the proverb says: "Always, unless he is a wineskin, ... the sylax ... a man ..." [Ηίνοτε κύλλω, καὶ λαβὼν, ἐξῆς αὐκυράς Ἕλκει, καζυντὰς, καὶ τε τὸ παροιμίαν Αἰεὶ ποτ' ἀν μὴ ἀσκὸς, ἀν ὁ Σύλακων Ἀνθρωπός δὲ]

units.la: —τῆς οὐ[?] Δὶ οἰροφλυγίαν ἢ πάχω τὸ σῶμα[?], Ἀσκὸν καλᾶσι πάντες οἱ ἐπιχώριοι.
units.tr: "...for the sake of his belly-gluttony or his fat body, all the natives call him askos" [—τῆς οὐ Δὶ οἰροφλυγίαν ἢ πάχω τὸ σῶμα, Ἀσκὸν καλᾶσι πάντες οἱ ἐπιχώριοι].

units.la: Ifocrates quoque, & ex eo Theophylactus in epistolis fuis Σύλα-κον ἐρμάτινον, & ἀσκὸν πάλιν hominem vocat. Epicharmus poëta philosophus, Αὐτὰ φύσις ἀνθρώπων, ἀσκοὶ πεφυσημένοι ;
units.tr: Isocrates too, and after him Theophylact in his letters, call a man a "bronze sylax" [Σύλακον ἐρμάτινον] and again an askos. The poet and philosopher Epicharmus says: "Such is the nature of men, puffed-up wineskins?" [Αὐτὰ φύσις ἀνθρώπων, ἀσκοὶ πεφυσημένοι;]

units.la: Propterea etiam folent Latini fcriptores corpus humanum vtrem & follem appellare, vt Arnobius libro fecundo : vel folliculum, vt Lucillius apud Nonium. alij corticem. Varrò, Sic inuitata anima corporeum corticem facile relinquit. vel faccum, vt Seneca epiftola 1 x x v 1 1 1. Tale etiam
units.tr: For this reason Latin writers too are accustomed to call the human body a bladder and a bellows, as Arnobius does in book 2; or a little bag, as Lucilius does in Nonius; others say bark. Varro: So the soul, when summoned, easily leaves the bodily bark. Or a sack, as Seneca does in epistle 1 x x v 1 1 1. Such also is

units.la: illud Plauti de muliere multibiba & merobiba, Quasi tu lagenam dicas, vbi vinum solet Chium esse. fimili ratione Varius quidam Antonij conuictor & , Cotylo est nominatus, vt est apud Plutarchum in Antonio. & apud Tarentinos alius quidam Cotyla parem ob caussam dictus, vt ait Dionyfius Halicarnasseus. Quare arbitror etiam hic ita posse hanc vocem accipi: nam & altera dictio κι- λιxυς similiter explicari potest: vel quod acuto efset capite, vt quos Græci φοξὸς vocant: vel quod argutulus & scitulus puer. Sic folebat Athenis vir acris ingenij & dicendi peritus, κόππις appellari, vt est apud Plutarchum in Phocione: & ita vtitur illa voce Euripides Hecuba. appellabant & ξίφῳ eundem vt videtur: sicut de Cleodemo quodam refert Lucianus in Lapithis. Quid quod etiam turpiufcula & obfcœna huius appellationis ratio esse potuit? Moris enim fuit olim, atque etiam nunc est, & nutricum & aliorum, ita cum id ætatis pueruli παιδοποιίζειν ac iocari: vnde illæ apud Græcos voces παιδίον, παιδαρίς, itémque φιλοπαιδής. Quid autem videatur hac voce obfcæniufcule significari posse, non dicam: sed tibi, lector, coniiciendum relinquam: qui mihi, spero, condonabis, quod longior fui isto loco. libuit enim, imo & licuit, credo, iocosum locum iocose interpretari, & cum garriente garrire.
units.tr: that line of Plautus about the woman who drinks much and drinks wine neat: As if you were calling her a jar where Chian wine is usually kept. By a similar reasoning a certain Varius, a companion of Antony, was named Cotylo, as is said in Plutarch's Antony; and among the Tarentines another man was called Cotyla for the same reason, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus says. So I think this word too can be taken here in that way. The other word, kilikus, can be explained similarly: either because he had a sharp head, as the Greeks call such people phoxos, or because he was a lively and clever boy. So at Athens a man of keen wit and skilled in speaking used to be called koppis, as in Plutarch's Phocion, and Euripides uses that word in the Hecuba. They also called the same kind of man xiphos, it seems, as Lucian reports of a certain Cleodemus in the Lapiths. What if the reason for this name was even rather coarse and obscene? For it was and still is the custom, both of nurses and others, to play and joke with little boys of that age; whence the Greek words paidion, paidaris and philopais. What may be obscenely signified by this word I will not say, but I will leave it for you, reader, to guess; you will, I hope, forgive me for being longer on this point. It pleased me, or rather it was allowed, I think, to interpret a jesting passage jokingly, and to chatter with the chatterer.

units.la: καὶ πλεῖςάκις ὁ ἀποκείρασθαι. ] Quæ sequuntur ab hoc loco ad finem capitis prorsus alius generis sunt quàm quæ hactenus præcessere: nam in iis omnibus elucescit inepta quædam virtutum imitatio, cum non minus inepta opum ostentatione. Sunt enim ad quos ista pertinent, valde affines iis quos veteres Romani elegantes vocabant, nec probabant: & iis quos Græci καὶ φιλολαμπρωνίδας[?] & μικροφιλότιμος[?] dixerunt: de quibus caput est infrà perelegans: non ergo ad hoc caput quod de blanditia est, & hominibus blandis, commodè referri possunt. Quare existimo tam eius capitis quod est ἐπὶ ἀρχαιότητος[?] finem hodie desiderari, quàm sequentis initium. cuius capitis hæc pars est: quam male feriati librarij præcedenti capiti agglutinauere, prorsùsque humano capiti ceruicem iunxerunt equinam. Simili modo peccatum animaduertimus aliquando in Plutarchi Conuiualium libro quarto: falsò enim omnes interpretes sibi persuaserunt, desiderari in editis codicibus caput eius libri sextū, cuius hoc extat lemma in fronte libri, Τίς ὁ Ἰεδαίοις θεός[?]. sed eo decepti sunt docti viri, quòd duo capita, quintum & sextum, in vnum coaluisse non viderunt. Id autem ita esse spero lectorem acutum qui illa attentè legerit mihi assensurum. Initium capitis sexti fuêre illa verba haud dubiè Θαυμάζεις ἢ τὸ δὴ πᾶν ἐπιδεῖν ὁ Σύμμαχος[?]. Similem etiam errorem admissum meminimus in orationibus Græcorum oratorum: de quo pluribus aliàs. Ita ergo hîc quoque. Quòd si quis me roget qualem huius capitis Περὶ βασιλείας[?] fuisse putem: respondebo, posse nos fortasse ex Aristotele Περὶ βασιλείας sel ἐπεροχαλίας[?] titulum facere. Conferat lector studiosus, quæ deinceps sequuntur, cum iis quæ καὶ βασιλικὸς[?] docet philosophus libro quarto Nicomachæorum. Atque hoc etsi rectum esse vérúmque penè pro comperto habeo: si quis tamen mordicus tueatur, posse ista quoque ad ἀρέσκον referri: age morem illi geramus: ac dicamus cadere ista in hominem blandum, non quà blandus est: sed quà φιλοτίμῳ[?], & elegantiæ studiosus: fere autem conueniunt, & in vna fede moranatur hæc duo: quare etiam Theophrastus illa coniunxit, & de vna, quod aiunt, fidelia duos parietes dealbanit.
units.tr: And very often to have his hair cut [καὶ πλεῖστάκις ὁ ἀποκείρασθαι]. What follows from this point to the end of the chapter is wholly of a different kind from what has gone before. For in all of these there shines a certain foolish imitation of virtues, together with no less foolish display of wealth. For those to whom these things apply are very close to those whom the ancient Romans called "elegant men" and did not approve, and to those whom the Greeks called [φιλολαμπρωνίδας] and [μικροφιλότιμος]; about whom there is a very elegant chapter further on. So these things cannot fittingly be referred to this chapter, which is about flattery and flatterers. Hence I think that the end of that chapter on antiquity [ἐπὶ ἀρχαιότητος] is missing today, as is the beginning of the next. This part belongs to that chapter, which careless copyists stuck onto the preceding chapter, joining a horse's neck to a human head. We have noticed a similar error sometimes in book 4 of Plutarch's Table Talk. For all the interpreters falsely persuaded themselves that the sixth chapter of that book is missing from the printed editions, whose heading stands at the top of the book: "What god do the Jews worship?" [Τίς ὁ Ἰουδαίοις θεός]. But learned men were deceived because they did not see that two chapters, the fifth and sixth, had fused into one. That this is so, I hope the sharp-eyed reader who has read them attentively will agree with me. The beginning of the sixth chapter was undoubtedly the words "You are amazed that Symmachus sees the whole..." [Θαυμάζεις ἢ τὸ δὴ πᾶν ἐπιδεῖν ὁ Σύμμαχος]. We remember a similar error admitted in the orations of the Greek orators, of which more elsewhere. So it is here too. If anyone asks me what I think the title of this chapter was, "On Kingship" [Περὶ βασιλείας], I will answer that we may perhaps, from Aristotle, make the title "On Kingship or Superiority" [Περὶ βασιλείας ἢ ἐπεροχῆς]. Let the studious reader compare what follows with what the philosopher teaches about the kingly man [καὶ βασιλικὸς] in book 4 of the Nicomachean Ethics. And although I hold this to be right and almost certainly true, if anyone obstinately defends the view that these things may also be referred to the obsequious man [ἀρέσκον], let us indulge him and say that these things fall to the flatterer not as a flatterer, but as one who is ambitious [φιλοτίμῳ] and eager for elegance. These two are very close and dwell in one seat, so Theophrastus joined them and, as they say, whitewashed two walls with one pot of paint.

units.la: πρὸς τὰς τραπέζας. ] Vbi versari solent ciues honestiores & ditiores. vult enim iste censeri inter meliores. Aliis autem in locis vrbis aliorum morum homines reperiri solent. quod lepidissimis versibus declarat Latinus comicus in Curculione, vbi inter cæteros iste legitur.
units.tr: By the tables [πρὸς τὰς τραπέζας]. This is where the more respectable and wealthier citizens are wont to be. For he wishes to be counted among the better sort. In other parts of the city, however, men of other habits are usually found. The Latin comic poet Plautus shows this in most charming verses in the Curculio, where among others this line is read:

units.la: In foro infimo boni homines atque dites ambulant.
units.tr: In the lowest part of the forum, good men and rich men walk about.

units.la: ἃ ἂν ἐρῴωσι γυμνάζωνται. ] An vt se ipse exerceat cum illis, quod erat hominis elegantis & liberalis, quam famam captat iste? Potest quidem ita accipi: cæterum alius omnino est, isque reconditior huius loci sensus: ex veteri more eorum hominum qui Theophrasti ætate vixerunt petendus. Sciendum igitur, moris fuisse Athenis hominibus iis quos inanis gloriolæ γαργαλισμὸς titillaret, in illis locis vt plurimum versari vbi se adolescentes exercebant: quò nimirum possent ab illis conspici, atque huncipsi sui honoris fructum perciperent, dum in se iuniorum ora conuerterent. Atque hoc nomine multi olim irrisi à veteribus poëtis comicis: in his Eupolis poëta: cui obiicit Aristophanes quòd parta victoria palæstras obambularet, vt ab adolescentibus spectaretur, ob recens partam victoriam insignis & ἀλαζονικός[?]. Πεφονὴς ait Aristophanes, τᾶς παλαίστρας σεμνυνόμενος, καὶ ὡς παῖδα ἑαυτὸν δῆλον[?] δῆλον ποιῶν τῆς νίκης ἕνεκα. Quare idem Aristophanes in Vespis laudi sibi tribuit, quod tale nihil unquam fecerit: se enim nunquam solitum παλαισπρας ἀειχωμάζειν ἀειόντα[?]. Similiter etiam Æschines Demosthenem, facit σεμνυνόμενον ἐν τῇ τῶν μειρακίων διαγωγῇ[?]. Profectò vel ex uno hoc loco de antiquitate huius scripti, & scriptoris ipsius licet existimare. Sic Plautus in Curculione inter alia celebria Romæ loca unum nominat, in quo solerent versari ostentatores meri.
units.tr: Those whom they love while they exercise [ἃ ἂν ἐρῴωσι γυμνάζωνται]. Is it that he exercises himself with them, which was the mark of an elegant and liberal man, and the reputation this man is after? It can indeed be taken that way; but the sense of this place is quite different and more recondite, and must be sought from the old custom of the men who lived in Theophrastus' time. One should know, then, that it was the custom at Athens for men tickled by the itch of empty glory to hang about mostly in those places where young men exercised, namely so that they could be seen by them and reap the fruit of this honour, while turning the eyes of the young towards themselves. And for this many were long ago mocked by the old comic poets, among them the poet Eupolis, whom Aristophanes charges with strutting about the wrestling-schools after winning a victory, so that he might be watched by the youths, proud and boastful because of his recent triumph. "Puffed up," says Aristophanes, "parading about the wrestling-schools and showing himself to the boys for the sake of his victory" [Πεφονὴς, τᾶς παλαίστρας σεμνυνόμενος, καὶ ὡς παῖδα ἑαυτὸν δῆλον ποιῶν τῆς νίκης ἕνεκα]. Hence the same Aristophanes in the Wasps claims credit for himself because he never did anything like this, for he never used to strut about the wrestling-schools [παλαίστρας ἀεὶ χωμάζειν]. Similarly Aeschines makes Demosthenes "showing off in the company of boys" [σεμνυνόμενον ἐν τῇ τῶν μειρακίων διαγωγῇ]. Surely from this one passage alone one may judge the antiquity of this writing and of its author. So Plautus in the Curculio, among other famous places in Rome, names one where showy men used to hang about.

units.la: τὰ δ' Ἰδάγγυ καθ' ἡμᾶς τὴν σπα-τηγῶν[?]. Hoc quis neget esse hominis vehementer ambitiosi? Non enim levis est honos, quo ipse se dignatur, assidere in theatro στρατηγοῖς, hoc est, praetoribus vel exercituum ductoribus: quibus pro summo beneficio Respublica solebat post exanclatos labores bellicosos ius ἀποδείξεως concedere. Id ius erat eiusmodi, ut qui eo donati fuissent, possent in senatu, concione, & theatro sedem capere quamcunque esset libitum: aliis etiam excitatis, si quis prior occupasset. Aristophanes Equitibus de sui temporis στρατηγοῖς:
units.tr: Who could deny that this is the mark of a man greatly fond of display? It is no small honour, by which he deems himself worthy, to sit in the theatre among the strategoi [στρατηγοῖς], that is, the praetors or commanders of armies. For these the Commonwealth used to grant, as its highest reward after they had finished their warlike labours, the right of apodeixis [ἀποδείξεως]. This right was such that those who had been granted it could take a seat wherever they liked in the senate, the assembly, or the theatre, others being moved aside if someone had got there first. Aristophanes, in the Knights, speaks of the strategoi of his own time:

units.la: Νῦν δ' ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδείξιν φέρωσι, τὰ αἴτια, Οὐ μαχεῖσθαι φασιν.[?]
units.tr: "But now, if they do not bring a demonstration, the reasons, they say, they will not fight." [Νῦν δ' ἐὰν μὴ ἀποδείξιν φέρωσι, τὰ αἴτια, Οὐ μαχεῖσθαι φασιν.]

units.la: Scholiastes: Τιμῆς δ' ἐπ' αὐτοῦ τυχόντος ἐν Βυζαντίῳ, καὶ ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ, καὶ ἐν Διάτρῳ, καὶ ἐν ἄλλῳ σαυλῇ συλλόγῳ, ὡς προσλαμβά-νοντας οἱ τινες ἦσαν ἐξεγείρατ' ἄς, αὐτὸς εἰς τὸν ἐκείνων τόπον καθίσαι.[?] Verum age addamus de hoc iure ἀποδείξεως apud Athenienses quæ in veterum scriptis observata sunt nobis. Fuisse ius hoc etiam hereditarium, & ferè ad maximum natu è liberis folitum transferri, non vno loco apud Plutarchum notauimus, idque adeo verum est, vt interdum quò possent defunctorum liberi eo vti, mortuis peteretur & impetraretur. quod in Demosthene accidit, teste Plutarcho: apud quem etiam extat hodieq; psephisma Democharis ea fini scriptum. Cæterùm non solis [illegible, ~9 letters] sedes secreta ab aliis in theatro fuit: sed & aliis ordinibus certæ sedes assignatæ. Quare etiam βουλευτικὸν[?] appellarunt, locum senatoribus dicatum: ἐφηβικὸν[?] locum ἐφήβων[?]. Aristophanes Auibus,
units.tr: The scholiast: "When he had won honour in Byzantium, and in the assembly, and in Diatrus, and in another gathering, they got up to receive him, and he sat down in their place." But come, let us add what we have observed in the writings of the ancients about this right of apodeixis among the Athenians. That it was also hereditary, and usually passed to the eldest of the children, I have noted in more than one place in Plutarch. It was so true that sometimes the children of the dead could enjoy it only if it was sought and obtained after their fathers' deaths. This happened in the case of Demosthenes, according to Plutarch, and in his work there still survives today the decree of Demochares written for that purpose. Moreover, it was not only a separate seat in the theatre, set apart from the others, that was reserved; certain seats were also assigned to other orders. Hence they called one place the bouleutikon [βουλευτικόν], the place dedicated to senators, and another the ephebikon [ἐφηβικόν], the place of the ephebi. Aristophanes, in the Birds:

units.la: κ' ἀθ' ὁρᾷ ἀιδρα τῆς γυναικὸς ἐν βουλευτικῷ[?].
units.tr: "...and sees a man among the women in the bouleutikon?" [κ' ἀθ' ὁρᾷ ἀιδρα τῆς γυναικὸς ἐν βουλευτικῷ.]

units.la: Scholiastes: Ἐν βουλευτικῷ. ἐτ' τόπ. τὸ θέατρον ὁ ἀνεμμένος τῆς βουλευτῆς, ὡς καὶ τῆς ἐφήβοις, ἐφηβικός[?]. Putem & equites equestria habuisse sicut & Romæ. Fuit præterea & iudicibus suus locus in theatro: quem locum πρωτῶν ξύλον[?] dixerunt. Pollux libro quarto: Πρῶτον ξύλον, ἡ προεδρεία, μάλιστα δικαστῶν[?]. Iam cùm etiam mulieribus liberum esset spectare Athenis, erant virorum & mulierum diuisæ sedes: idq; lege etiam sancitû,cuius auctor Sphyromachus: quanquam alij Sphyromachi legem ad scorta scenam ingredi solita referunt: vt impudicæ seorsim ab ingenuis & pudicis mulieribus spectarent. auctor idem Scholiastes Aristophanis in Concionátes. An verò & peregrinis erat certus locus in cauea assignatus? Viderur ita esse: nâ de mulieribus certè peregrinis id Pollux tradit, & confirmat auctoritate Alexidis, qui in Τωναικοπρατία dramate dixerit, —ἐν[?] ... τῷ Κερκίδα[?] ... Τμᾶς[?] ... ἀθεωρεῖν ὡς ξένας[?].
units.tr: The scholiast: "In the bouleutikon. There was also a place in the theatre set apart for the senators, as there was the ephebikon for the ephebi." I think the knights too had their own seats, as at Rome. Besides, the judges had their own place in the theatre, which they called the proton xylon [πρῶτον ξύλον]. Pollux, in book four: "The proton xylon, the front seating, especially for judges." Now since women too were free to watch plays at Athens, the seats of men and women were divided, and this was also enacted by law, whose author was Sphyromachus. Other writers, however, refer the law of Sphyromachus to prostitutes who used to come onto the stage, so that the shameless might watch apart from free and modest women. The same author is the scholiast on Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae. But were foreigners also assigned a fixed place in the cavea? It seems so. Pollux certainly reports this of foreign women, and confirms it by the authority of Alexis, who in his play The Women Merchants said: "...in the Kerkis... to watch as foreign women..." [ἐν ... τῷ Κερκίδα ... ἀθεωρεῖν ὡς ξένας].

units.la: Ex quibus verbis liquet mulieres ξένας sedisse ad
units.tr: From these words it is clear that the foreign women sat in the

units.la: Kercidem. Κερκὶς autem in theatro Attico fuit, nisi fallor, ille ipse locus qui alio nomine Η ωαρ' αἰγείρῳ Ζεὺς dicebatur: de quo vide Hefychium. nam κερκὶς in hiftoria plantarum, vel eft ἀινδρον[?], vel alia populo fimillima arbor. Quare errant, vt puto, qui κερκίδα putant effe, quod Latinis cuneus theatri, qua in fententia eft & Gloffarij auctor: fed & ille faepe fallitur, & qui cum ἀβαύισως fequuntur.
units.tr: Kerkis. The Kerkis was in the Attic theatre, unless I am mistaken, the very place that was also called by another name, "Zeus under the poplar." See Hesychius on this. For kerkis, in the natural history of plants, is either a kind of aindron or another tree very like the poplar. So, I think, those are wrong who take kerkis to be what the Latins call the cuneus of the theatre. The author of the Glossary holds this view too, but he is often mistaken, and so are those who follow him.

units.la: καὶ ἀγερώζω αὐτὸ μὴ μηδὲν. ] Simiam facilè agnofcas viri magnifici & μεγαλοπρεπῆς: quem negat Ariftoteles in quarto Nicomacheorum effe εἰς ἑαυτὸν διαπαιμπόν. Iam quod fequitur ἔτεροις ἢ εἰς Βυζάντιον δῆμος ἅμα, Ariftoteles quoque ibidem τῷ μεγαλοπρεπεῖ tribuit: quem ait ἀνεδάζεσθαι ξενῶν ξενοδοχὰς, καὶ ξενοδόκος, καὶ δωρεὰς, ἡ αἰτιδωρεάς. quo loco ξενοδόκος accipere debes ea notione qua hic ξενάλμα: hoc eft, pro donis quæ ad amicos in alia vrbe degentes mittuntur. cuius rei multa in epiftolis Symmachi & Synefij, aliorumque Græcorum funt exempla. Vlpianus apud Demofthenem, & ex eo Suidas, ξενοδόκος explicant δῶρα: melius Iofephus ξενικὰς δωρεῶν. & ita etiam accipit auctor Maccabæorum libro primo capite fecundo & alij. Sed & hic quoque perfuafum habeo, ξενοδοχεῖον fcribi debere,non ξενάλμα.
units.tr: "...and I do not admire it at all." You will easily recognise here the portrait of the magnificent and munificent man, whom Aristotle, in book four of the Nicomachean Ethics, says is not [εἰς ἑαυτὸν διαπαιμπόν]. What follows, "to others, or to Byzantium together," Aristotle also attributes to the magnificent man in the same place. He says that he spends on guest-gifts, on hospitality to guests, and on gifts, or gifts of hospitality. In this passage xenodoche [ξενοδόκος] must be taken in the sense in which here xenalma is used: that is, for gifts sent to friends living in another city. There are many examples of this in the letters of Symmachus and Synesius and other Greeks. Ulpian on Demosthenes, and Suidas after him, explain xenodoche as gifts; Josephus more aptly says xenikai doreai. The author of the Maccabees also uses it this way in the first book, chapter two, and others too. But here too I am persuaded that xenodocheion ought to be written, not xenalma.

units.la: Pag. 18. καὶ τίτυρον κἰλιάδος. ] Pertinet hoc quoque ad liberalitatis laudem. Nam vt ait auctor libelli De virtutibus & vitiis, ὁ ἐλαφρὸς Ξενοφῶν ... τῆς ζωῆς, τῆς ἰδίου ἐχόντων τὴν δωμασίαν. Porrò τίτυρον effe genus quoddam fimiarum, ait Theocriti fcholiaftes, habentium paruam caudam: imò, vt ego existimo, grandiusculam: nam Aristoteles in secundo Historiarum videtur in omnibus simiis caudæ aliquid agnoscere, ὥς, inquit, σμικρὸν χρέα: sed quod minimum est, id pro nullo censetur. Itaque κερκόλιπες Græci, Latini clunas dixerunt, quod essent sine cauda: & contra cercopithecos, quasi caudatas simias quibus esset cauda prolixior, & μᾶλλον ἐπισημότερ[?]. Τίτυρον tamen aliam à cercopitheco putamus esse: quare non cercopithecum vertimus, sed satyrum: quas namque Plinius vocat Satyros in genere simiarum, & à natura mitissima commendat, τιτύρες vulgò non minus quàm ξέυρες videntur appellasse. De iis Solinus, Sunt quæ vocant satyros, facie admodum grata, gesticulatione motibus inquieta. quo ex loco apparet cur satyros potissimum ex omni simiarum genere isti honores alerent. Quemadmodum autem Satyri illi à quibus hæ simiæ sunt ita dictæ, vocantur iidem Tityri, vt præter alios annotat Ælianus Varius libro quarto: ita & simias satyros, cum simiis tityris easdem esse statuimus. Non me fugiunt quæ sunt à viris doctis de voce τίτυρος annotata: verum ea nihil ad hunc locum facere iudico: sicut neque illud huc pertinet, quod scribit Hesychius, esse id auis cuiusdam nomen.
units.tr: Page 18. "And a tityros worth a thousand." This too belongs to the praise of liberality. For, as the author of the book On Virtues and Vices says, the light Xenophon... [ὁ ἐλαφρὸς Ξενοφῶν ... τῆς ζωῆς, τῆς ἰδίου ἐχόντων τὴν δωμασίαν]. Further, the scholiast on Theocritus says that the tityros is a kind of ape with a small tail. But, as I think, rather a fairly large one. For Aristotle, in the second book of the History of Animals, seems to recognise some tail in all apes: "a little," he says, but what is least is counted as nothing. So the Greeks called the tailless ones kerkolipes, and the Latins clunas, because they were without a tail; and against them the cercopitheci, as if tailed apes, those with a longer and more conspicuous tail. Still, we think the tityros is other than the cercopithecus. So we translate it not as "cercopithecus" but as "satyr." Pliny calls the satyrs a kind of ape and commends their very gentle nature, and the tityroi were commonly called no less than the xeyroi. Solinus says of them: "There are those called satyrs, of a very pleasing face, restless in their gestures." From this passage it appears why these honours were given to the satyr apes above every other kind. Just as those Satyrs from whom these apes are so named are also called Tityri, as Aelian Varius notes in book four among others, so we hold that satyr apes and tityr apes are the same. I am not unaware of what learned men have noted about the word tityros, but I judge that none of it bears on this passage. Nor does what Hesychius writes, that it is the name of a certain bird.

units.la: καὶ Σικελικὰς περιστερὰς. ] Solebant veteres Athenienses columbas Siculas domi alere. Athenæus libro nono, de columbis loquens, Ἐν ὁ Ποσείῳ ἢ Πολυπυζύσῃ, Σιλυκῶς εἴρηκεν (Alexis poeta) καὶ ὅτι αἱ Σικελικαὶ Ἱεροφόροι εἰσι. Πλειστέρας ἐνδον πρὸ[?] τῶν ἐπὶ τῶν τῶν πάντων κομψάς.
units.tr: "And Sicilian doves." The ancient Athenians used to keep Sicilian doves at home. Athenaeus, book nine, speaking of doves, says: "In the Poseidon or the Polyeidos, the poet Alexis said that the Sicilian ones are sacred... very many, and elegant beyond all others..." [Ἐν ὁ Ποσείῳ ἢ Πολυπυζύσῃ, Σιλυκῶς εἴρηκεν καὶ ὅτι αἱ Σικελικαὶ Ἱεροφόροι εἰσι.]

units.la: καὶ Δορκαδείας ἀσπαλάκες. ] In deliciis olim tali dorcadii fuerunt. Habent enim damę & dorcadei, vt cætera τῶν δορκάδων ζώων in posterioribus pedibus talos. Hos Callimachus alicubi ζορκὸς ἀσφαγάλυς vocauit. Eustathius in Ιλιαδ. Ϝ. Καὶ τὸ ᾤτω παίζειν, ἀσπίζειν ἔλεγεν, ᾗ τὰς ζυγὸς ἀσπαλάς[?] ἀσπίας ἢ ἀσπίας. Καλλίμαχος οὐ ζορκὸς που λέγ[?] δωρη[?] τινὲς ἀσπάλακας[?]. Athenæus libro quinto de Antiocho Epiphane, vel verius Epimane, ἐιδου τὰς μὲν ἀσπαγάλους δορκαδέους, τὰς δ᾽ φοινικοβαλάνους, ἄλλως δ᾽ χυσίον. meminit & Lucianus alicubi. Fieri etiam solitos ex ebore talos, indicant Propertius libro 11. & Martialis in Apophoretis.facit eorum mentionem & Iuuenalis satyra vndecima. Atque hi quidem tali à materia nomen inuenerunt: fuerunt verò & διάσῖοι dicti tali quidam: non vt Labinus alicubi vertit sonori, sed quasi dicas agitati & concussi ex eo enim nomen habuerunt, quòd mota prius agitarentur manuiacerentur in alueum lusorium: quod ad vitandam fraudem fieri solebat.
units.tr: "And dorcadian knucklebones." Dainty knucklebones of this kind were once fashionable. For does and dorcadia have knucklebones on their hind legs, as do the other gazelle animals. Callimachus somewhere calls them "gazelle knucklebones" [ζορκὸς ἀσφαγάλυς]. Eustathius, on the Iliad, says... Athenaeus, book five, speaks of Antiochus Epiphanes, or more correctly Epimanes, who had the dorcadian knucklebones and the Phoenician-acorn ones, and others of a different sort. Lucian also mentions them somewhere. That knucklebones were also made of ivory is shown by Propertius, book two, and by Martial in the Apophoreta. Juvenal too mentions them in satire eleven. These knucklebones took their name from their material. But there were also knucklebones called diaseioi [διάσεισοι]. I do not translate this as Labinus somewhere renders it, sonori, "resonant." Rather, one should say "shaken and jostled," for they got their name from being shaken before being thrown into the gaming-board, which was done to prevent cheating.

units.la: Docet hoc Suidas, cuius hæc verba ad δδγσεἰσους ἀσπαγάλους referri debere certum mihi. Εοἰκασιν, inquit, ὡς οἱ ἀμάξαι οἱ διάσεισοι, ἀπὸ τὸ κυβεύειν καὶ δι᾽ ἀ-σεισθηναι προτέρου. εἶτα βάλλεσθαι ἵνα ἀκαριαίως ἀπέρχονται μᾶλλον ὥσπερ. Romani fritillo vtebantur ad hanc talorum agitationem. Iuuenalis —parúque eodem monet arma fritillo. Vetus interpres ibi. Fritillus pyxis cornea, qui cupas Græce dicitur. Apud antiquos in cornu mittebant tesseras, monentesque fundebant aut fritillum, pyrgum dixit. Vide veterem Horatij interpretem ad satyram septimam libri secundi: Seneca Apocolyntoli, Qui concussò Magna parastis Lucra fritillo. Mentionem δγσεισων reperio apud Æschinem in ea contra Timarchum, πρῶτον μὲν συνιστέον τὰ σκέ-ελα[?], καὶ διερριπτόμενον[?] εἰς τὸ ὅδον[?], ἀσπαράγους[?] τε τίτας[?] ἡγεμόνας[?] τοὺς φιμοὺς[?], ἢ κυθαριστικὰ[?] ἕτερα ὄργανα[?]. Hunc Æschinis locum ob oculos habebat Pollux, cum hæc scriberet lib. decimo, Κυθαρῳδὸς σκέλη[?], ἄλαξ[?], ἀλαζὼν[?], κόσμιον[?], κύδοι[?], διάσεοι[?] ἀσπάραγοι[?], φιμοί[?], κημοί[?]. At docti viri cum locum Pollucis non recte acceperunt. Erant & Siphnij ἀσπάραγοι[?], tali viles & minimi pretij: sic dicti ἀπὸ τῶν ἐτέλεσαν[?], à Siphno insula, vt ait Strabo. his vulgus vtebatur: homines diuites & elegantes dorcadiis.
units.tr: Suidas teaches this, and I am certain his words must be referred to the diaseismoi astragaloi. "It seems," he says, "that the diaseioi were so called from gambling, and from being shaken before being thrown, so that they fell more quickly." The Romans used the fritillus for shaking the knucklebones. Juvenal: "and with the same fritillus he warns of arms." The old commentator there says: "The fritillus is a horn box, which in Greek is called a kuboi; the ancients put the dice into it, and shaking it, poured them out; the poet called it pyrgus." See the old commentator on Horace's seventh satire of the second book. Seneca in the Apocolocyntosis: "Shaking the fritillus, you make great gains." I find mention of the diaseismoi in Aeschines' speech against Timarchus: "First, one must put together the... and throwing them into the..., and the... of the asparagoi, or other instruments of the lyre-player." Pollux had this passage of Aeschines before his eyes when he wrote, in book ten: "lyre-player's legs, dice, ..., the diaseioi asparagoi, the muzzles, the nose-rings." But learned men have not rightly understood Pollux's passage. There were also the Siphnian asparagoi, cheap dice of little value and the lowest price, so called from... from the island of Siphnos, as Strabo says. The common people used these; rich and elegant men used the dorcadian ones.

units.la: καὶ Θυειαχὰς[?] τῇ σφογγύλων[?] λυκύδες[?]. Similis afsectus indicium est apud Iuuenalem, —cum rhinocerote lunari. De ampullis vero istis nihil legere memini. Thyrium Acarnaniæ oppidum fuit auctore Stephano: eius frequens apud Polybium mentio. In quibusdam libris legitur Θυειαχῇ[?]: fortasse pro Θυειαχῇ[?]. Sanè Theophraftus libro De lapidibus gypsum τὸν ἐν Θυείοις[?] (quæ fuit olim Sybaris) commendat: ac fieri potest vt etiam argilla ibi reperiretur ex qua opera figlina factain pretio haberentur. fuit & aliud Θύειον[?] in Bœotia à Syriaca voce Thor sic nominatum, vt auctor est Plutarchus in Sylla. Cæterum proprium hoc ampullæ istæ cum quibusdam aliis videntur habuisse, vt forma essent rotunda: ideo enim ait τῷ σφολύχων[?]. Nam vulgo ampullæ, non rotundæ penitus erant: sed pressula rotunditate, & forma lenticulari, vt ex Apulej Floridis discimus. Conflat autem ampullas & guttos ex varia materia fieri solitos. Martialis guttum corneum epigrammate quodam commemorat. & Horarius cum ait, —cornu ipse bilibri Plinius phaginorum meminit. & gutti lignei mentio est in vita M. Curij Dentali, apud eum scriptorem veterem, cuius extat De viris illustribus liber. Fiebant & è corio: nam ampullarum οχυλινων, id est, scortearum meminere Hippocrates, Plautus, Festus, alij. Has Graeci ὀλκας proprie vocabant. Scholiastes Theocriti, idyllio secundo, Ὀλκη ξυεῖος ἢ διφθερτίνη λαικυ, εἰ ἢ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἔλαιον. De his coriaceis ammpullis intelligendum quod ait Plutarchus in Sylla, Athenienses obsessos ἐρπιδάμα & λακυδές ἐφέδες comedisse. Plerique aereis utebantur & quidem Corinthiacis, ut notat idem Scholiastes. Sed & argenteas λακυδές ditiores habuerunt. Theocritus,
units.tr: And Thyeiachas, with the round... "lykudes" (the OCR is corrupt here). A similar affectation is indicated by Juvenal: "with a lunar rhinoceros." I do not recall reading anything about these flasks in particular. Thyrium was a town of Acarnania, according to Stephanus, and Polybius often mentions it. In some books the reading is Θυειαχῇ [Thyeiachē], perhaps for Θυειαχῇ [Thyeiachē] in another form. Certainly Theophrastus, in his book On Stones, commends the gypsum from Thyeia (which was once Sybaris). It is possible that clay was also found there, from which potters' work was held in high value. There was also another Thyeion in Boeotia, named from the Syriac word Thor, as Plutarch states in his Sulla. Moreover, these flasks seem to have had, along with certain others, the distinctive feature of being round in shape; this is why he says "of round shape" [τῷ σφολύχων]. For ordinary flasks were not perfectly round, but slightly rounded and lens-shaped, as we learn from Apuleius's Florida. It is clear that flasks and gutti were commonly made of various materials. Martial mentions a horn gutta in a certain epigram, and Horace, when he says "the horn of the two-pint flask itself," [Plinius] Pliny mentions phagina. A wooden gutta is mentioned in the life of Manius Curius Dentatus, in the old writer whose book On Illustrious Men survives. They were also made of leather: Hippocrates, Plautus, Festus and others mention leather (ochlinai, that is, skin) flasks. The Greeks properly called these holkai. The scholiast on Theocritus, on the second idyll, says: "a holke, a leather skin for oil." It is to these leather flasks that Plutarch's statement in the Sulla must refer, that the besieged Athenians ate herpidama and lakudes ephedes. Most used bronze ones, and especially Corinthian, as the same scholiast notes. But the richer also had silver lakudes. Theocritus:
"from a silver flask, anointing..." [argyreas ex olpidos hygein aleiphar]

units.la: Frequentissimo vero ut opinor in usu erant lecythi operis figlini: ut Campani gutti apud Horatium: & Samij, quorum multi meminerunt. Nam fere Samia vasa testacea erant: etsi scio fuisse apud Samios etiam ligneorum vasorum nobiles artifices, vel tcste Cicerone epistola quadam ad Q. fratrem.
units.tr: However, I think the most frequently used were earthenware lecythi: like the Campanian gutti in Horace, and the Samian ones, of which many writers speak. For Samian vessels were mostly of clay, although I know that among the Samians there were also famous makers of wooden vessels, as Cicero testifies in a certain letter to his brother Quintus.

units.la: Mirificè hæc conveniunt ei quem hic describit Theophrastus: ei inquam, qui omnibus in rebus [illegible, ~8 letters] volunt habere vult videri: cuiusmodi hominum observavimus morem illis temporibus fuisse ut baculum gererent. Demosthenes adversus Pantænetum: Νικλέους ἀλλ' ἐπιφέρεται, καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters] τρία notat summus orator, quæ vulgò invidiam conflare solerent: citatum ingressum: vocem altam: baculi gestationem. sic in oratione Στεφάνου[?] ϝλλόμ[?]. etsi ibi poltrema nota omissa est. Ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὦ ἀνδρες Ἀθωνίσι[?] τῆς μὲν ὀ[?]ύσεως τῇ φύσει, καὶ τὸ ἀχέως βα[?]ζειν, καὶ λαλεῖν μέγα, ἃ τῆς ἀτυχῶς περιοντων[?] ἐ[?]μαυλὴν κεῖ[?]
units.tr: These things agree wonderfully with the man whom Theophrastus describes here: the one, I say, who in all things [illegible] wishes to have and wishes to seem to have. Such men, we have observed, were in the habit in those times of carrying a staff. Demosthenes, against Pantaenetus: the great orator notes "Nikleous, but he is brought in," and [illegible] and "three things," which usually stir up envy: a showy entrance, a loud voice, and the carrying of a staff. So too in the speech of Stephanus... though there the last mark is omitted. "But I, men of Athens, by nature of the ... and to speak loudly and talk big, which ..." [Greek, corrupt]

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐφ᾽ οἷς γὰρ ὑδὲν ὠφελήμου[?] λυπῶ τινάς[?] ἑλατ[?]ζειν ἐχω πολλαχῆ.
units.tr: [illegible] ... "for in those things which are of no use, I have many ways of causing some to be annoyed."

units.la: Deprecatur invidiam qui illa loquitur, & de genio suo atque ingenio conqueritur: ita enim se natum, factumque esse, ut fastus & superbiæ notas cum in vultu habeat impressas: tum etiam in incessu & sermone. Antiphani in Antæo inter hominis venusti notas ponitur, τιλιὰσιον[?] ἀπαλὸν[?], ἀρυσμῷ[?] βαχλεία[?]. Magis vero adhuc hominis vanitatem arguit, quod adiicit Theophrastus, ἐν Λακεδαίμονι[?]: nam baculis Laconicis, itemque calceis indidem advectis fere utebantur Athenis homines id genus. Aristophanes Concionantibus,
units.tr: He who speaks thus deprecates envy, and complains about his own temperament and disposition: for he says he was so born and made that the marks of pride and arrogance are impressed upon his face, and also in his gait and speech. In Antiphanes' Antaeus, among the marks of a charming man is given: "elegant, delicate, ... " (corrupt). Yet what more clearly shows the man's vanity is what Theophrastus adds, "in Laconia": for men of this sort at Athens used mostly Laconian staffs and similarly shoes imported from there. Aristophanes, in the Ecclesiazusae:
"For you have Laconian shoes and staffs."
The same poet, in the Birds:

units.la: Ἐλαχωνοφακίνουῦ[?] κα[?] ... Ἐκύμων, ἐπείτων, ἐρρύτων, ἐσωκράζων.

vel, coniunctim σκυταλιφόρων ut citant veteres grammatici. Σκυταλῶν, & σκυτάλων sive σκυταλίω, iliusmodi baculi dicebantur: & de iis interpretandus hic locus Theophrasti libro quarto Historiae plantarum capite quinto. Ἐν ἑτέροις δ᾽ ὡς ἄλλοις[?] ... ἐξ ἧς καὶ σκυτάλια καὶ βαχλείας σχίσσοι[?]. Ubi & errat Gaza, qui σκυτάλια lineas interpretatur: & summus Scaliger non satis mentem auctoris videtur assecutus. Erant autem baculi Lacedaemoniorum admodum graves ut annotat Scholiastes Aristophanis : de iis legendus Plutarchus in Nicia : meminit & in Lycurgo. Quod addit Theophrastus vocem σκολιῶν, indicat alios rectos fuisse, alios obliquos : id enim est σκολιός : vel incuruos, hoc est καμπύλας. Id ita est : Recta βακληεία [?] utebantur primores populi & iudices : incurua, rustici. Auctor Etymologici magni : βακληεία [?] ὣ ἐκάλουν ὀρθὸν· ἐχεῖ [?] ὁ αὐτῇ οἱ ἐν ἀσεικία [?], ἡ οἱ δικάζοντες τὴ καμπύλη [?] οἱ ἀγροικοι. Quare etiam pastorale pedum Graecis ἁπλῶς dicitur interdum καμπύλη. Recti baculi etiam Perfici videntur fuisse appellati : nam Graeci grammatici Περιπλὼ βακληεία, interpretantur ὀρθὸν. Incurui autem lituis Romanorum non erant valde absimiles : itaque lituum Graeci magistri καμπύλῳ βακληεία interpretantur : & Ciceto incuruum & leniter à summo inflexum bacillum nominat. At iudicum Athenienfium βακληεία peculiarem & operofiorem formam habuit : quam non vno loco descriptam habes apud commentatores Aristophanis, & alios veteres grammaticos. Rusticorum vero baculi vulgò in Italia è virga sanguinea. Plinius lib. xxiii. de eo frutice loquens, Serpentes & homines fruticem refugiunt : baculóque rufticiob id ex eo gerunt. Sed hæc hactenus : nam de baculis, & eorum forma, multiplicíque apud veteres vsu plurima quæ obseruauimus ad lucem multorum scriptorum veterum, alibi ἐὰν ὁ Θεὸς ἐθέλῃ commodiùs proferemus.
units.tr: Or together, skytalophoron, as the ancient grammarians cite. Skytalōn and skytalōn, or skytalion, were the names of such staffs, and this passage of Theophrastus in the fourth book of the Historia Plantarum, chapter five, must be interpreted of them: "In other places... from which both skytalia and staffs are split." Gaza errs here in translating skytalia as lines, and the great Scaliger does not seem to have grasped the author's meaning well enough. The staffs of the Lacedaemonians were very heavy, as the scholiast on Aristophanes notes; Plutarch in the Life of Nicias should be read about them, and he also mentions them in the Life of Lycurgus. As for Theophrastus's addition of the word skolion, it indicates that some staffs were straight and others bent; skolios means crooked, or curved, that is, kampylos. This is so: leading citizens and judges used straight staffs, rustics curved ones. The author of the Etymologicum Magnum says: "they called a staff orthon (straight)... and the judges used the curved one, the rustics." Hence also the shepherd's crook is sometimes called simply kampylē by the Greeks. Straight staffs seem also to have been called Persian: for Greek grammarians interpret Peripsō bakteria as orthon. Curved staffs were not very unlike the Roman lituus; so Greek teachers interpret lituus as kampylē bakteria, and Cicero calls it a curved staff gently bent at the top. But the staff of the Athenian judges had a distinctive and more elaborate form, which you will find described in more than one place in the commentators on Aristophanes and other ancient grammarians. The staffs of rustics in Italy were commonly made of blood-red twig. Pliny, book 23, speaking of that shrub: "Snakes and men shun the shrub, and rustics carry staffs made from it." But so much for this; for the staffs, their form, and their manifold use among the ancients, which we have observed in the light of many ancient writers, we will set forth more conveniently elsewhere, God willing.

units.la: αὐλίδιον παλαιστρικὸν κόνιν ἔχον. ] Periphrasis est κονιστεία [?]. De conisterio autem & puluere siue puluisculo palæstrico, res nota : non enim quiuis puluis ad palæstram, neque ad ceroma aut haphen aptus erat. Ideo refert Athenæus in duodecimo, Alexandrum in expeditione Indica, multa iumenta habuisse inter impedimenta, puluere palæstrico onusta. Verum de hoc puluere & varia eius utilitate præter Plinium, lege apud Lucianum, Περὶ γυμνασίων. Plutarchus de primo frigido, breuiter, ψύχῃ, inquit, τὰ [?] ἀθλητῶν ἡ κόνις σώματος, καὶ [?] καταδεύοντα τὰς ἱδρῶτας [?].
units.tr: "A wrestling-ground flask holding dust." Here is a periphrasis for konisteria (the dust-room). Concerning the koniste­rion and the dust, or powder, of the wrestling-ground, the matter is well known: not every dust was suitable for the palaestra or for the oil and the haphe. Hence Athenaeus in book twelve reports that Alexander, on his Indian expedition, had many beasts of burden among his baggage laden with wrestling-dust. But for more on this dust and its various uses, besides Pliny, read Lucian, On Gymnasia. Plutarch, in his On the Primary Cold, says briefly: "the dust of athletes cools the body and drinks up the sweat."

units.la: αὐλαίαν ἔχουσαν. ] Græci ζωνταὶ aulæa appellant. talia illa apud Virgilium Purpurea intexti tollunt aulæa Britanni.
units.tr: "Having a curtain." The Greeks call a curtain zōntai. Such are those "purple curtains woven, which the Britons raise," in Virgil.

units.la: καὶ τὰς [?] ἀξιῶν χέαν ἀεὶ ... ] Ita restituimus hunc locum, ex interdicto Vndevi. nam vox χέαν [?], quæ ab eruditis hominibus nullo suo merito miscella solum vertere coacta fuerat, afferenda omnino nobis ex antiquis editionibus fuit. Enimuero qui illam omittunt miserè totam sententiam labefactant ac destruunt: quam nos haud dubie expressam tibi lector exhibemus. An ignorat quisquam solitos olim diuites suas domos poëtis, atq; aliis ad recitationes & [?] commodare? hoc igitur est χέαν [?]. sic apud Iuuenalem, —at si dulcedine fama Succensus recites, Maculonus commodat ædes.
units.tr: "And he who thinks it worthy always to pour..." We have restored this passage from the edition of Undevi. For the word chean, which learned men, through no merit of their own, had forced to take refuge in the margins, had to be restored to us entirely from the old editions. Indeed, those who omit it wretchedly undermine and destroy the whole sense, which we, undoubtedly, set forth to you, reader, as expressed. Does anyone not know that the rich in former times used to lend their houses to poets and others for recitations? This, then, is chean. So in Juvenal: "but if, fired by the sweetness of fame, you recite, Maecenas lends his house."

units.la: Tacitus in dialogo de oratoribus, de recitationibus poëtarum loquens, ut sint qui dignentur audire, & nec id quidem gratis: nam & domum mutuatur & auditorium exstruit, & subsellia conducit, & libellos dispergit. Plinius epistolarum libro v i i i. Domum suam recitantibus præbet. Mox etiam legimus, [?] τῷ Θεωμένων. intelligit autem fortunatum aliquem è spectatoribus cuius esse locum illum in quo fit ὁ [illegible, ~8 letters] , fingit apud veritatis ignarum verus possessor. Cui bono? dicet aliquis: ac memini quaerere id à me virum doctum. Duplicem possum afferre causam huius facti. Altera ἀρέσκω, imò κόλακι pulchrè convenit. Intelligendum est enim ita hos sermones de aliquo ut diximus diuite & beato viro haberi, ut ipse eos possit exaudire: eum autem ostentatorem aliquem merum esse, & gloriosum, cuius ingenio iste se accommodat, eique supparasitatur: qualis describitur à facetissimo poëtarum Artotrogus initio Militis. Altera ratio est, quæ homini λυποδοξῶντι, qui laudis sui miserè cruciatur, prorsus quadrat. Est enim insolens quoddam ostentationis genus, quę sua sint manifestissimè, ea dicere alius esse. Estque à summo philosopho hæc ἀλαζονείας species in Nicomacheis haud prætermissa. Ait ille, indecenter ironia uti, & τὰ λίαν φαντά sibi derogare, ineptæ & putidæ cuiusdam esse ostentationis. Nam, inquit, ἡ ὑπερ-βολὴ, καὶ ἡ λίαν ἔλλειψις ἀλαζονικόν, qua sententia nihil verius, nihil certius. Clarum huius rei documentum in multis: qui eximiam quandam præ cæteris probitatis famam aucupantes, pauperes humilesque simulant: cum interea, si velo reducto propius eos intueatis, pleni sint immanis cuiusdam ambitionis & φιλαυτίας. hoc tantum à cæteris ambitiosis differentes, quòd ambitionem non rectâ sed peruersâ, ut Seneca ait, via sequuntur.
