Atque hæc planè est illa figura, qua ait idem secundo De beneficiis, quosdam reiicere quæ magis ad se volunt attrahere. Quintilianus libro x 1. cap. 1.
units.tr: Tacitus, in the dialogue On Orators, speaking of the recitations of poets: "so that there are those who deign to listen, and not even gratis: for one borrows a house and builds an auditorium, and hires benches, and scatters pamphlets." Pliny, in book eight of the letters: "he offers his house to those reciting." Next we read "to the spectators" (tō theōmenōn). He means some wealthy man among the spectators, whose is the place where the ... takes place; he pretends that the true possessor is one ignorant of the truth. To what end? someone will say; and I remember a learned man asking me this. I can give a twofold reason for this act. The first agrees beautifully with areskō, or rather with kolax (flatterer). For these speeches must be understood, as we said, to be made about some rich and fortunate man, so that he himself may be able to overhear them; and he is simply some showy and boastful man, to whose disposition this fellow adapts himself and plays the parasite to him: the sort described by the most witty of poets, Artotrogus, at the beginning of the Miles Gloriosus. The other reason is one that fits perfectly the man who is lypodoxōn, who wretchedly tortures himself for praise of himself. For there is a peculiar kind of ostentation: to say that things which are most manifestly one's own belong to someone else. And this species of boastfulness is not omitted by the greatest philosopher in the Nicomachean Ethics. He says that to use irony indecently, and to disparage oneself in excess (ta lian phaula), belongs to a foolish and putrid kind of ostentation. For, he says, excess and too much deficiency are boastful, a judgment than which nothing is truer or more certain. There is clear evidence of this in many: those who, eager for a certain extraordinary reputation for uprightness above others, pretend to be poor and humble; when, meanwhile, if you look at them more closely with the veil drawn back, they are full of some monstrous ambition and self-love. They differ from other ambitious men only in this, that, as Seneca says, they pursue ambition not by the straight but by a perverse way. And this is exactly that figure by which the same author says, in book two On Benefits, that some reject what they more want to attract to themselves. Quintilian, book eleven, chapter one.

units.la: Aperte gloriari nescio an sit magis tolerabile, vel ipsa vitij huius simplicitate, quàm illa iactatione peruersi, si abundans opibus pauperem se neget, nobilis obseruans, & potens infirmum, aut si se dissertus imperitum plane infantem vocet. Παλαιστρᾶν[?] certum est de loco hic esse accipiendum, vt Pars in gramineis exercet membra palaestris. Est autem commune poëtis, philosophis, sophistis, hoplomachis, harmonicis, atque aliis item, vt τὰ μελέται[?], sic etiam τὸ ἐπιδεικνύσθαι[?] habent enim quique eorum suas ἐπιδείξεις & exercitationes: quod notum est ex Græcis scriptoribus. Ὁπλομάχοι sunt, qui sub campidoctore veris armis certare discunt, aut ipsi qui docent: puto enim vtrunque hac voce significari. vide Platonem in Lachete. At vulgò inuentus non veris armis se exercebat: sed tudibus, aut pilis præpilatis, quæ dicuntur Græcis ἐσφαιρωμένα ἀκόντια. Xenophon libro secundo Ἀναβάσεως de Phalino quodam ita scribens, [illegible, ~20 letters] videtur innuere hoplomachos ea ætate fuisse appellatos, etiam eos qui tacti-ci Græcis proprie dicuntur. vide Vegetium.
units.tr: I do not know whether it is more tolerable to boast openly, which at least has the simplicity of the vice itself, or to practise that perverse kind of boasting: a man rich in resources who denies being wealthy, a nobleman who pretends to be humble, a powerful man who claims to be weak, or an eloquent man who calls himself quite ignorant, a mere infant. That Παλαιστρᾶν [palaistran] must certainly be taken here of a place, as in "Part of him exercises his limbs in the grassy palaestras." It is common to poets, philosophers, sophists, hoplomachs, musicians and others as well, that, just as they have τὰ μελέται [meletai, practices], so they also have τὸ ἐπιδεικνύσθαι [epideiknysthai, display]; each of them has his own epideixeis and exercises, as is known from the Greek writers. Ὁπλομάχοι [Hoplomachoi] are those who learn to fight with real arms under a drill-sergeant, or those who teach them; I think both meanings are signified by this word. See Plato in the Laches. But the common hoplomach did not practise with real arms, but with clubs, or with blunted javelins, which the Greeks call ἐσφαιρωμένα ἀκόντια [esphairōmena akontia]. Xenophon, in the second book of the Anabasis, writing of a certain Phalinus, seems to hint that in that age the hoplomachs were so called, even those who are properly called τακτικοί [taktikoi] by the Greeks. See Vegetius.

units.la: Ἡ δὲ ἀπόνοια ἐστιν [illegible, ~12 letters] τῶν ἔργων καὶ λό-γων. ] Definitio ista ἀπονοίας parum plena est nam cum discrimen latum sit inter ἀναιδωλίαν[?], de qua infrà est integrum caput, & ἀπὸ οἴας[?] nihil videtur in hac definitione, quod non conueniat etiam τῇ ἀναιδωλίᾳ. quid enim pudor aliud est quàm vitiosæ naturæ retinaculum, & vt aurigarum verbo vtar, sufflamen?Erit igitur pudor ἐχ ἀπορίας [?] ἔργων ἐ λόγῳ: impudentia verò ἀναισχυντία [?] eorundem. Est autem ἀπόνοια vt rem paulò pluribus explicemus, & quod ille ait, ἀμαθέστερον πως καὶ ἀφέστερον: est inquam ἀπόνοια, prauus quidam animi habitus, quo qui præditus est, omnis ab eo famæ pudor abest: omniqué honestatis ac bonæ existimationis cura penitus deposita ad quoduis facinus ac dedecus suscipiendum pronus est, propensusque. Proprium hoc homini ἀπολειπόμενον [?] est, primum vt non huic aut illi vitio sit deditus, sed omnibus: deinde vt non instinctu tantum naturæ improbè aut nequiter agat: sed quia turpitudine ipsa delectatur, & vitia sua, malaque, quod malorum vltimum est, amat. Quod enim, ait Seneca quarto De beneficiis, neminem adeò à naturali lege desciuisse, & hominem exuisse, vt animi culpa malus sit: dictum hoc, inquam, in homine ἀπολειπόμενῳ [?] claudere videtur; nam hic, etiam gratis malus est. Ideo dicebat auctor orationum contra Aristogitonem, ἀπόνοιαν esse morbum immedicabilem. Notum quid sit ἀπόνοια in re militari. Proprie sic vocatur non desperatio, sed is animi habitus qui ex desperatione induitur. Quamobrem inter ἀπόγνωσιν, & ἀπόνοιαν discrimen statuit. D. Chrysostomus non vno loco orationum suarum, inde est hoc vitiorum extremum appellatum: vel dicta est ἀπόνοια, quia penitus ἐκ τοῦ ἐξίστασθαι [?] ἔστι, vt placet quibusdam è veteribus. Ὑπόνοια [?] quod loco generis positum est in Theophrasti descriptione, non est genus, sed ἴδιόν τι τῆς ἀπονενοημένου. semper enim ἀπόνοιαν comitatur audacia: ideo auctores 7 λμαν & ἀπόνοιαν folent cóiungere. vt apud Iosephum libro 11. cótra Appionem. Plutarchum in Agesilao, & in Catone Vticensi,& in edicto Iuliani, quo Athanasium Alexandria pellit. & apud Demosthenem in ea πρὸς Μακάριον, Φλμπρος κα[?] Ἀπονενομένη[?]. In Actis synodi Ephesinae extat epistola,cuius initium est Οὐδὲν ἀπονοίας ἐν πλημμελήματι χαλεπώτερον· αὕτη γὰρ πάντας ὅσι τῶν ἀγεμών[?]. Sed non est praetermittendus locus insignis eius auctoris, qui orationes contra Aristogitonem (quae falsò, vt alibi disputamus, inter Demosthenicas circumferuntur) scripsit, vbi graphicè admodum quid ἀπόνοια sit, & quis homo ἀπονενομένος, orator describit. Sic ille, ὑχ ὁρᾶτε ὅτι ἡ φύσεως αὐτὴ, ὁ ἡ πολιτείας, ἡ λογισμὸς, οὐδ' αἰδὼς οὐδεμία, ἀλλ' ἀπόνοια ἡγεῖται, μᾶλλον δ' ὅλον ὅστιν ἀπόνοια, ἡ ζῶντα πολιτεία[?]· ἡ μέγιστον μὲν ὅστιν αὐτὴ τὴν ἔχοντι καλὸν[?], δ' ἡ δύσον ὁ ζ' χαλεπὸν πᾶσι, τῇ πόλει δ' ὁδ' ἀνέκλον. ὁ δ' ἀπονενομένος ἅπας, αὐτὸν μὴ προσέταξ, ὁ τῶν λογισμῶν σωθείσαν[?]. ἐν ἡ τὰ πραγμάτων ὁ τὰ [?]ἐὰν ἀρα σωθῇ, σωζεται[?]. Apud comicos praeclara extant hominum huiusmodi, hoc est, fingulari quadam improbitate & audacia praeditorum, qui patrimoniis fuis naufragi, vt rem facere poffint, per fas nefasque audacter ruunt, exempla. Talis apud Aristophanem in Nebulis Strepsiades, in Equitibus fartor ille impurus Agoracritus:tales etiam in Plauti & Terentij comœdiis lenones omnes. Porrò ἀπόιοια Latinis est audacia, vel audacia perdita, vt in illo Satyrici poetæ,
units.tr: The definition of ἀπόνοια [aponoia] given here, "apononia is ... of deeds and words," is rather incomplete. For although there is a wide difference between ἀναιδωλία [anaidōlia], about which there is a full chapter below, and ἀπὸ οἴας [apo oias], nothing in this definition seems to be lacking that does not also apply to shamelessness. For what is shame but a curb on a vicious nature, or, to use the charioteers' word, a drag-shoe? Shame, then, will be a restraint from disgraceful deeds and words, while impudence is the lack of the same. Apononia, to explain the matter at somewhat greater length, and in the author's words, is "somewhat more ignorant and remote": I say, apononia is a perverse habit of mind, possessed by someone from whom all sense of reputation is absent, who, having wholly cast off all concern for honour and good standing, is ready and inclined to undertake any crime or disgrace. This is peculiar to the man who is ἀπολειπόμενος [apoleipomenos]: first, that he is given not to this or that vice but to all; second, that he does wrong and acts wickedly not merely from the impulse of nature, but because he delights in baseness itself, and loves his vices and evils, which is the final evil. For what Seneca says in the fourth book of De beneficiis, that no one has so departed from the natural law and stripped off his humanity that he is bad through a fault of mind, seems to shut out the man who is ἀπολειπόμενος, for he is bad even without cause. That is why the author of the orations against Aristogiton said that apononia is an incurable disease. What apononia is in military matters is well known. Properly, it is not called despair, but that habit of mind which is put on from despair; hence he drew a distinction between ἀπόγνωσις [apognōsis] and ἀπόνοια. Chrysostom, in more than one place of his homilies, calls it the extreme of vices; or it is called ἀπόνοια because it is wholly ἐκ τοῦ ἐξίστασθαι [ek tou existasthai, from being beside oneself], as some of the ancients think. The word ὑπόνοια [hyponoia], which is put in the place of a genus in Theophrastus's description, is not a genus but a peculiar feature of the man who is ἀπονενοημένος [aponenoēmenos]; for audacity always accompanies apononia, which is why writers are accustomed to join λύσσα [lyssa, frenzy] and ἀπόνοια, as in Josephus, book 2 Against Apion; in Plutarch's Agesilaus and Cato the Younger; in the edict of Julian by which he drove Athanasius from Alexandria; and in Demosthenes, in the speech against Macarius. In the Acts of the Council of Ephesus there is a letter beginning, "Nothing is more grievous as a fault than apononia, for it ..." But the notable passage of that author who wrote the orations against Aristogiton (which, falsely, as we argue elsewhere, circulate among the Demosthenic speeches) must not be passed over, where the orator describes very vividly what apononia is and what sort of man the ἀπονενομένος is. He says: "Do you not see that it is not nature, nor the constitution, nor reason, nor any shame, but apononia that leads? Or rather, the whole life of such a man is apononia, which is for the one who has it the greatest evil, and for the state the most difficult of all, and for the city the most unbearable. The man who is ἀπονενομένος, if he is not restrained by reason, ... if he is saved, he is saved..." Among the comic writers there survive famous examples of men of this kind, that is, of those endowed with a peculiar wickedness and audacity, who, shipwrecked in their patrimonies, rush boldly through right and wrong in order to make money. Such is Strepsiades in Aristophanes' Clouds, and that filthy fellow Agoracritus in the Knights; and in the comedies of Plautus and Terence all the pimps are of this sort. Moreover, for the Latins apononia is audacia, or audacia perdita, as in that line of the satirical poet:

units.la: Budæus vacordiam Latinè dici posse putabat : mihi visa ea vox Græcæ vim non satis explere. Nam ἄνοια omnis, vaecordia est: quippe homo ἄνους caret corde, id est sapientia: unde sunt excors & vaecors, at ἀπόνοια aliud longè est. neque profectò sicut dixit Cicero in Pisonem, ô vaecors & amens: ita dixeris Græcè satis proprie ὦ ἀπονενοημένε ἢ ἀνόητε. Homo ἀπονενοημένος, quem desperatè malum possis Latinè dicere, Ciceroni est homo perditus, vel perditus & profligatus: aut etiam desperatus: ut cum desperatorum hominum flagitiosos græges dixit in Catilina: & alibi sæpe. Nam etsi proprie vox desperatus aliud sonat, tamen de eodem vsurpatur.
units.tr: Budaeus thought vaecordia could be used in Latin; but that word does not seem to me to express the force of the Greek fully. For every ἄνοια [anoia] is vaecordia, since a man who is ἄνους [anous] lacks heart, that is, wisdom; hence come excors and vaecors. But ἀπόνοια is something quite different; nor could one, in Greek, say quite properly ὦ ἀπονενοημένε ἢ ἀνόητε, as Cicero said in the speech against Piso, o vaecors and amens. A man who is ἀπονενοημένος, whom one could in Latin call desperately bad, is for Cicero homo perditus, or perditus et profligatus, or even desperatus, as when he spoke of desperatorum hominum flagitiosos greges in the Catilinarians, and often elsewhere. For although the word desperatus properly means something else, it is nonetheless used of the same thing.

units.la: Οἱ ὀμόσαι ἐχύ.] Rectissimè prima nota hominis perditi profligatíque hæc ponitur: hic siquidem è numero eorum est, qui ut dixit olim Pacvvius iusiurandum aliud nihil esse censent quàm mantile, quæ noxæ quotidianæ extergeantur. Talis apud Græcum comicum Strepsiades, quem ita alloquitur suus creditor in Nebulis,
units.tr: Οἱ ὀμόσαι ἐχύ. [hoi omosai echy] Quite rightly, this is set down as the first mark of the lost and profligate man; for he is indeed one of those who, as Pacuvius once said, think an oath is nothing but a napkin with which daily harms are wiped clean. Such a man is Strepsiades in the Greek comic poet, whom his creditor addresses thus in the Clouds:

units.la: Δα. Καὶ ταῦτ' ἐξελάσῃς ἀπομόσαι μοι θεούς, [?]Ἴν' ἂν κελεύσω σε; Στρ. Θεοὺς ποίους θεούς;
units.tr: Dα. And will you, to make me swear by the gods, if I order you to? Στρ. What gods, pray?

units.la: Δα. Τὸν Δία, τὸν Ἑρμῆν, τὸν Ποσειδῶ. Σφ. Νὴ ΔίαΚαὶ προσκαθεδεῖλω γ' ὥστ' ὀμόσαι τρισ[?]
units.tr: Dα. Zeus, Hermes, Poseidon. Σφ. Yes, by Zeus! And I'll swear by them three times if you like, sitting down right beside you.
Such is Ballio in the Latin comic poet.

units.la: Ca. Iurastin' te illam nulli venditurum nisi mihi?
units.tr: Ca. Did you swear that you would sell that girl to nobody but me?

units.la: Ba. Fateor. Ca. nempe conceptis verbis. Ba. etiam confultis quoque.
units.tr: Ba. I admit it. Ca. Indeed, in express words. Ba. And after consulting too.

units.la: Ca. Periurasti sceleste. Ba. at argentū intra condidi. Athenis qui facile iusiurandū suscipiebant, Ardetti vulgò à loco ubi iurare moris erat, appellabantur, Hesychius. Τοὺς ῥᾳδίως ὀμνύντας ... τοὺς ὅρκους ἰσχὺς ἀρδήττους ἐκάλουν. τότε δ' ὁ ἐν τῷ Ἰλισσῷ, ἰσχὺς Παναθη-ναϊκῶ [?] Ϛωαικὴ ϛαξις, ἐν ᾧ ὅρκος ἐποιοῦντο[?].
units.tr: Ca. You perjured yourself, you scoundrel! Ba. But I have hidden the money away. Those at Athens who swore oaths easily were commonly called Ardettians, from the place where it was customary to swear; Hesychius: "those who swore easily ... they called the oaths ardettians; but then the one by the Ilissus, the Panathenaic ..., the Stoic stoa, in which oaths were made."

units.la: τῷ ἤδει ἀγοραῖος τις.] Criticorum sanctio postulat vt scribamus ἀγέραιος τις. Ammonius, Ἀγο-ραῖος ἐὰν προπαροξυτόνως, σημαίνει τὸν ποιητὴν, τὸν ἐν ἀγορᾷ τεθραμμένον· ἐὰν ἢ προσθιαγωμένως σημαίνει τὸν ἐν ἀγορᾷ τιμώμενον. recte. est enim ἀγοραῖος & cognomen Iouis, Mercurij, Minervae & Dianae qui in foro colebantur. Recte etiam notat Suidas ἀγοραῖον dici diem quo lites disceptantur. ita omnino scribendum in Actis,cap. xix. ἀγόραιοι ἀγοραῖοι, non ἀγοραῖοι. & subaudiendum ἡμέραι. Glossarium vetus, Cum res agitatur, ἐπε ἡ ἀγόραιος ἔστιν[?]. Nam vt prolatae res dicuntur quando iustitium est, sic agi res, quando vt loquitur Demosthenes, αἱ δίκαι εἰσὶ[?]. Plinius Secundus in Epistolis, Eia tu cum proxime res agentur quoquo modo ad iudicandum veni. hinc apud Suetonium rerum actus, pro diebus iuridicis. Strabo libro xiii. de Romanis loquens, ἐτέρος, inquit, πρότον διέξαν τὰς δικοικὰς ἐν αἷς τὰς ἀγοραῖος ποιοῦντας ἢ τὰς δικαιοσύνας[?]. hoc est, vbi conuentus agunt & ius reddunt. Sed vt ad Theophrastum redeamus, homo ἀγόραιος est qui dies totos forum conterit: quemque oratores & comici appellant ἀγοραῖος περιστήματα: Latini veteres hominem ordinarium, teste Festo: vel subrostranum, vt in octauo epistolarum ad familiares: vel subbasilicanum, vt in Capreiicis,
units.tr: τῷ ἤδει ἀγοραῖός τις [tō ēdei agoraios tis]. The authority of the critics requires that we write ἀγέραιός τις [ageraios tis]. Ammonius: ἀγοραῖος, accented on the antepenult, signifies a poet, one brought up in the market-place; but with the accent on the penult it signifies one honoured in the market-place. Rightly so; for ἀγοραῖος is also an epithet of Jupiter, Mercury, Minerva and Diana, who were worshipped in the forum. Suidas also rightly notes that ἀγοραῖον is the name for the day on which lawsuits are decided. So in the Acts, chapter 19, one must certainly write ἀγοραῖοι ἡμέραι [agoraioi hēmerai], not ἀγοραῖοι, and ἡμέραι must be understood. An old glossary: Cum res agitatur, ἐπε ἡ ἀγόραιος ἔστιν. For just as prolatae res is said when there is a suspension of business, so agi res is said when, as Demosthenes puts it, the courts are sitting. Pliny the Younger in his Letters: Eia tu cum proxime res agentur quoquo modo ad iudicandum veni. Hence in Suetonius rerum actus for judicial days. Strabo, book 13, speaking of the Romans, says: "Then, he says, they first established the courts in which they held the market days or the days of justice." That is, when assemblies are held and justice is administered. But to return to Theophrastus: the ἀγόραιος man is one who wears out whole days in the forum, and whom orators and comic poets call ἀγοραῖος περίστημα [agoraios peristēma]; the old Latins called him hominem ordinarium, according to Festus, or subrostranum, as in the eighth book of the Letters to Friends, or subbasilicanum, as in the Caprenses:

units.la: Quorum odos subbasilicanos omnes abigit in forum. Glossarij auctor paullo aliter: Basiliciarius, Μαλακὸς ἀγοραῖος. Notum est in Basilicis iudicia Romę pro ferrum centum viralia celebrata fuisse. Idem auctor alibi, Tabellio, ἀγόραιος, νομικός. Alio autem loco lixa vertit ἀγορᾷ[?]. ne id quidem absurdè:est enim is qui quæstus caussa castra sequitur, tot enim modis vox ἀγορὰ accipitur.
units.tr: He drives all of these subbasilicani out into the forum. The author of the Glossary puts it a little differently: basiliciarius, a soft, effeminate frequenter of the forum [Μαλακὸς ἀγοραῖος]. It is well known that at Rome the centumviral courts were held in the basilicas. The same author elsewhere glosses tabellio as ἀγόραιος, a lawyer [νομικός]. Elsewhere again he renders lixa by ἀγορᾷ [ἀγορᾷ], and that is not even absurd, since a lixa is one who follows an army for profit, and the word ἀγορά is taken in so many senses.

units.la: κὴ ἀ:ἀσεσυρμένῳ[?]. ] Non rectè docti viri qui sic vertunt, Vestibus impudenter subductis. Nam aliud est ἀιασεσυρμένῳ[?], aliud ἀιτρυφῷ[?]: de qua voce dicemus infrà. At homo ἀιασεσυρμένῳ[?], id est, qui ἀτρυφὴς etiam dicebatur, teste Hefychio. extat ea vox apud Polybium libro quarto: & in extremo fragmento libri xvii. τυχὸν ὃ δὲ ... [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐν βίου ἀτρυφῆ. Idem significat apud M.Tullium,vox, purcus: qua notione accipi vox purcities debet illo Lucretij loco libri quinti,
units.tr: Learned men who render this as "with clothes shamelessly stripped off" are not right. The Greek words are different, and one is not the other; I shall speak below about the word ἀτρυφῷ. But a man of this kind, who was also called ἀτρυφής, is one who lives plainly, according to Hesychius. The word occurs in Polybius, book four, and at the end of a fragment of book seventeen, where the text reads "perhaps ... in a life that is not luxurious" [ἐν βίου ἀτρυφῆ]. In Cicero the word spurcus has the same meaning, and the word spurcities in the passage of Lucretius from book five should be understood in that sense:

units.la: Quidue superbia, spurcities, petulantia, quantasEfficiant clades? quid luxus desidiesque.
units.tr: "What pride, what filthiness, what wantonness, what great disasters do they produce? What luxury and idleness?"

units.la: ὀρχεῖσθαι ὑπὲρ τὴν κόρδακα.] Quantum fit ponderis in voce ὑφῶν, licet intelligere ex eo quod Demosthenes in secunda Olynthiaca pro argumento vitæ penitus dissolutæ sociorum Philippi, ait cos ubi largiùs poti fuerint, solitos cordacem saltare. Multo enim turpius si quis siccus cordacem saltet, quàm si madidus. Est autem cordax lasciuæ & comicæ saltationis genus: ideo ait ἐν κωμικῷ χορῷ. Aristophanes verò in Nebulis gloriatur in suis comœdiis huic saltationi nullum esse locum. Puto autem ad restim solitum cordacem saltari: nam Aristophanes pro κορδακίζειν dixit κόρδακα ἐλκυστήν. Iulianus & alij ἐλκεῖν κόρδακα.
units.tr: "To dance beyond the cordax" [ὀρχεῖσθαι ὑπὲρ τὴν κόρδακα]. One can see how much weight lies in the word ὑφῶν from what Demosthenes says in the second Olynthiac, using as an example the utterly dissolute life of Philip's allies: when they had drunk too freely, they were accustomed to dance the cordax. For it is far more shameful for a man to dance the cordax when sober than when drunk. The cordax is a kind of wanton, comic dance, and so he says "in a comic chorus" [ἐν κωμικῷ χορῷ]. Aristophanes, in the Clouds, boasts that there is no place for this dance in his comedies. I think, however, that the cordax was danced with a rope; Aristophanes used the phrase κόρδακα ἐλκυστήν ("drawn cordax") for κορδακίζειν, and Julian and others say ἐλκεῖν κόρδακα ("to draw the cordax").

units.la: καὶ προσωπεῖον ἔχων ἐν κωμικῷ χορῷ.] Falsi suspe[?]tam hanc lectionem habeo : puto enim decisse negationem, & ita legendum, προσωπεῖον ὡς ἔχει ἐν κ. χ. magis enim hoc modo perditissimi nebulonis describitur ingenium : nam etsi omnino turpe est scenicum histrionem agere : tamen qui personatus in scenam prodit, quodammodo sub persona latet, & pudori suo nonnihil consulit : non item qui sine persona. quare etiam Demosthenes in oratione de ementita legatione, Cerybionem quendam καζρᾱζον[?] appellat, ὅς, inquit, ἐν ταῖς πομπαῖς ἀνὰ τὰ προσωπεῖα κωμάζει. Apud Romanos, histriones si minus placerent, cogebantur in scena ponere personam. vide Festum in Personata fabula. Porro interpretes ita hunc locum verterant, quasi legeretur ἔχει. contra omnium codd. auctoritatem.
units.tr: "And wearing a mask in a comic chorus" [καὶ προσωπεῖον ἔχων ἐν κωμικῷ χορῷ]. I am suspicious of this reading, which I think is false. I believe a negation has dropped out, and that it should be read: "and with a mask, as he has it in a comic chorus" [προσωπεῖον ὡς ἔχει ἐν κ. χ.]. In this way the character of a utterly abandoned scoundrel is described more accurately: for although it is entirely shameful to act as a stage-player, the one who comes on stage in a mask lies to some extent hidden under the persona and spares his own shame somewhat; the one who appears without a mask does not. That is why Demosthenes, in his speech on the false embassy, calls a certain Cerybion a kazrazon [καζρᾱζον], saying, "who in the processions goes about dancing in masks" [ἀνὰ τὰ προσωπεῖα κωμάζει]. Among the Romans, if actors did not please, they were compelled to put on a mask on stage; see Festus under personata fabula. The translators had rendered this passage as though it read ἔχει ("has"), against the authority of all the manuscripts.

units.la: καὶ ἐν Θαυμάσι ὁ τῆς χαλκῆς ἐκλέγειν.) Inter ludicrarum artium artifices, & voluptatum ministros quibus olim veteres, fuere qui à Graecis dicti sunt Θαυματοποιοὶ à Latinis praestigiatores : quos Athenaeus inter Διονυσιακὰ Τεχνίτας recensetlib. duodecimo. Fuerunt autem variae & plane mirificae istorum artes quibus imperitorum feriebantur oculi, omnia quorum causas non nouere mirantium. Eius generis fuerunt mimi, ἀρχιμίμοι[?], cybistetae, petauristae, petaminarij, funambuli, neurospastae, item ἐγγαστρίμυθοι[?] siue ἐγγαστριλόγοι[?], & machinatores, de quibus dicemus σαῦ[?] aliquando, quae sunt nobis cum cura obseruata & annotata. Qui igitur has artes exercerent, Graeci eos Θαυματοποιοὺς vocabant, artemque eorum Θαυματοποιτικὴν, & spectacula huiusmodi praestigiarum atque offuciarum Θαύματα. Errant enim & qui Θαύματα[?] legi hic non θαύμαζα[?] volunt: & qui aliter hanc vocem interpretantur. Hesychius θαύμαζα[?], ἃ οἱ θαυματοποιοὶ ἐπιδείκνυνται, sic apud Dionem Chrysostomum, πολλοὺς[?] ἢ θαυματοποιοὺς θαύματα ἐπιδεικνύμενοι[?]: & apud Platonem cùm in septimo De Republica, tum in secundo De legibus, θαύματα ἐπιδεικνύμενοι[?]: denique sic semper accipienda illa verba ἐν θαύμασι[?]. in quibus passim errare interpretes etiam doctissimos observauimus, ut apud Athenæum non uno loco. neque aliter accipiendus locus Aristotelis libro secundo, De generatione animalium, vbi τὰ αὐξόμαζα τῆς θαυμάτων[?] commemorat: quæ αὐξόμαζα θαύματα[?] alio loco appellat: intelligit autem pegmata quædam per se surgentia, vel simulacra suapte sponte mobilia, quæ à neurospastis colligendæ pecuniæ gratia circumferebantur. Quod ait Theophrastus χαλκῆς ἐκλέγειν[?], pertinet ad mercedem quam prestigiatores isti à spectatoribus pro lucare exigebant: eam mercedem Græci, ut puto θαυματοποιόν[?], nuncupabant. est enim à θαυμάζω: eadem analogia quà διδακτρον[?] minerval à διδάσκω, μάντυρον[?] indicium siue indicinæ præmium, à μηνύω. & pro eodem ἐρετρον[?] ab ἐλέγχω apud Vlpianum. Sophron. φησὶ τὸ θαυματοποιὸν[?], κ' ἀπιδυσωμένης[?]. Hinc dicti sunt vulgò cùm hi tum alij agyrtæ, qui similibus artibus stipem in circulis corrogabant, χαλκολόγοι, Latinè æruscatores: pari in utraque lingua ratione: nam ut χαλκοῖ Græcis nominantur quiuis parui pretij nummi: sic Latinis æra. Martialis, Et centum aureolos sic velut æra rogat. & Hieronymus illa duo λεπτὰ[?] viduæ mulierculæ cuius fit in Euangelio mentio, æra interpretatur. Reperio & asculatores fuisse dictos, Glossarium vetus: χαλκολόγ@, nummularius, asculator: & alibi, ᾱsculator χαλκολόγ@. inde verbum asculor pro eo quod Theophrastus τὰς χαλκᾶς ἐκλέγὴν dixit. Glossarium, χαλκολογῶ, asculor. Apuleius τὰς χαλκᾶς, stipes æreas vocat in octauo Metamorphoseon: alibi, exiguam stipem. Ouidius 1. De ponte, stipis æra. & rectè in Glos-sario, κέρμα, ᾱs nam quid fit κέρμα Græcis notum est. Maximus Tyrius, δύο ὀβολούς. Hanc illi stipem a spectatoribus exigebant, postquam se quisque scf-sum receperat, ordines sedentium obambulantes. Ideo ait Theophrastus καθ᾽ ἕκαστον παρεῖναι. quæ verba male accepta sunt ab interpretibus. Lucianus in Asino, ἐπειδὴ ἡ καζακόλαν ὅτως ἑαυτὸς, ἐν τῇ ἡηκότων θεατῶν συνέλεγον ὀβολὸς ἐ δραχμάς. prorsus istis declarantur superiora Theophrasti. Idem Lucianus verbo ἐκλέγὴν vtitur alibi, vt Theophrastus hic, χαλκοῦ ὀβολὸν παρὰ τῆς καζαπλεόλων ἑκάστῳ ἐκλέγων. Hodie isti artifices solent ad fores aliquem collocare, cui necesse habet vnusquisque prius quàm spectatum admittatur, in antecessum aliquid pro lucare porrigere.
units.tr: "And in wonders the man of the bronze coins gathers" [καὶ ἐν Θαυμάσι ὁ τῆς χαλκῆς ἐκλέγειν]. Among the practitioners of comic arts and the purveyors of entertainments, whom the ancients used to employ, there were those whom the Greeks called thaumatopoioi (wonder-workers) and the Latins praestigiatores (conjurers); Athenaeus lists them among the Dionysiac artists in book twelve. Their skills were varied and quite astonishing, and they dazzled the eyes of the unskilled, since those who marvelled did not know the causes of what they saw. Of this kind were the mimes, archimimoi, cybistetae, petauristae, petaminarii, funambulists, neurospastae (puppeteers), and likewise the engastrimythoi or engastrilogoi (ventriloquists), and the machinators, about whom I shall perhaps speak some time, since I have observed and noted them with care. Those who practised these arts the Greeks called thaumatopoioi, their art thaumatopoiitikē, and such displays of tricks and illusions thaumata (wonders). Those too are wrong who want thaumata to be read here rather than thaumaza, and those who interpret this word otherwise. Hesychius glosses thaumaza as what the wonder-workers display; so in Dio Chrysostom, "displaying wonders, like the wonder-workers"; and in Plato, both in book seven of the Republic and book two of the Laws, "displaying wonders." In short, those words en thaumasi must always be understood in this sense, and I have noticed that even the most learned interpreters go astray here, as in Athenaeus in more than one place. Aristotle's passage in book two of the De generatione animalium, where he mentions "the growing wonders" (auxomata thaumaton), must be taken in the same way; elsewhere he calls these auxomata thaumata, and he means certain structures that rise up by themselves, or images that move of their own accord, which were carried about by the puppeteers to collect money. What Theophrastus means by "gathering the bronze coins" refers to the fee which these conjurers demanded from the spectators as their profit. The Greeks, I think, called this fee thaumatopoion, since it comes from thaumazō, by the same analogy by which didaktron (tuition fee) comes from didaskō, and mantyron (reward for information) from mēnyō; and in Ulpian eretron (a fee for proof) from elenchō. Sophron says ... "the thaumatopoion." From this, both these performers and others, the agyrtae, who gathered alms in circles by similar arts, were commonly called chalkologoi, in Latin aeruscatores (copper-collectors), with equal reasoning in both languages: as in Greek chalkoi is the name for any small coin, so in Latin aera. Martial: "and begs for a hundred gold coins as if they were bronze." Jerome also translates the two lepta of the poor widow in the Gospel as aera. I find that they were also called asculatores; an old glossary has chalkologos: "money-changer, asculator," and elsewhere "asculator: chalkologos." Hence the verb asculor corresponds to what Theophrastus called tas chalkas eklegein. The Glossary: chalkologō, asculor. Apuleius calls the chalkas "bronze alms" (stipes aereas) in book eight of the Metamorphoses, and elsewhere "a small alms." Ovid in the first book De Ponto says "the bronze of alms." The Glossary rightly renders kermα as as, for what kerma is is known to the Greeks. Maximus of Tyre says "two obols." This was the alms they demanded from the spectators, walking along the rows of those seated, after each had retired into himself. That is why Theophrastus says "to be present at each." The words have been misunderstood by the translators. Lucian in the Ass says: "since the ... thus, in the presence of the spectators, I collected an obol, not a drachma." Those words clarify Theophrastus' earlier statement. Lucian uses the verb eklegein elsewhere too, as Theophrastus does here: "collecting an obol of bronze from each of the spectators." Today these performers usually station someone at the door, to whom each person, before being admitted to the show, must hand over something in advance as a fee.

units.la: κἀ μάχαιραν [?] ] Telleram intelligit, quam aliquis acceperat a præstigiatoribus, ea lege, vt qui hoc symbolum quod arrabonis vim habebat, referret, gratis spectaret. De symbolis & contractibus per symbola, quam Aristoteles κείμενα [?] vocat, dicemus vti spero alias.
units.tr: "And the token" [κἀ μάχαιραν]. He means a ticket which someone had received from the conjurers on the condition that, when he returned this token, which had the force of a pledge, he would watch the show free of charge. I hope to discuss tokens, and contracts made by tokens (which Aristotle calls keimena), elsewhere.

units.la: καὶ περὶ [?] ἀξιῶσι.) In multis optimæ notæ codicibus vox ἀξίωσι non extat: quare ita pol-sumus vertere, Ac si quis tesseram afferat, duris enim sermonibus accipiet, ipse gratis spectans. Fortasse ita auctor [?]crip[?]erat. [?] μα. [?]Ωις τὸ σύμ. φέρονται καὶ ἀροῖκα Θεωρεῖν ἀξιοῦσι· αὐτὸς ἀροῖκα Θεωρῶν. vel, ἕτω ἀροῖ- κα αὐτὸς Θεωρεῖν. De istiusmodi librariorum peccatis sæpe quæsti sumus.
units.tr: "And ... they think fit" [καὶ περὶ ἀξιῶσι]. In many manuscripts of the best quality the word axiōsi is absent. So we may translate it: "and when someone brings a token, for they will receive it with harsh words, watching the show for nothing himself." Perhaps the author wrote something like this: "they think fit to watch for nothing." I have often inquired into mistakes of this sort made by copyists.

units.la: [?]ῆμος ὁ πανδοκεῖον.) Olim apud Græcos, sicut etiam hodie, vt audio, in quibusdam Italiæ locis, non multò erat honestior locus πανδοκ[?]εῖον sive taberna meretoria, quàm οἴκημα, hoc est, lenonis aut meretricis domus: & apud Hebræos eadem vox Zonah & meretricem significat & cauponam. nec multo aliter apud Latinos, qui τὸ πανδοκεῖον stabulum, & τὸν πανδοκέα stabularium dixerunt: meritricem autem prostibulum. Eò factum, vt viri quibus honestas curæ, æquè in cauponis ædibus conspici erubescerent, ac in lenonis: quod vel ex iis patet, quæ de Stratonico citharœdo refert Ælianus Variarum libro xiiii. capite xiiii. Sed & Isocrates, ἐν καπηλείῳ ait, φαγεῖν ἢ πιεῖν, εἰς οἰκίας [?]ἀνδρῶν [?]ἐξ[?]λθ[?]ε. vide Athenæum libro xiii. hunc ipsum Isocratis locum proferentem. Sed quam parum interfit lenocinium & caupona, declarat optime ius Rom. Nam ex Impp. constitutionibus domina cauponæ quæ vilius à marito solita haberi, soluitur lege Iulia, de adulteris.
units.tr: "Like the inn" [ὥσπερ ὁ πανδοκεῖον]. Formerly among the Greeks, as I am told is still the case today in certain parts of Italy, the place called pandokeion, an inn or brothel, was not much more respectable than a oikēma, that is, the house of a pimp or prostitute. Among the Hebrews the same word Zonah means both a prostitute and a innkeeper. Not much differently among the Latins, who called the pandokeion a stabulum and the innkeeper a stabularius, but a prostitute a prostibulum. As a result, men who cared about their reputation blushed to be seen in an inn no less than in a pimp's house. This is clear from what Aelian reports about the lyre-player Stratonicus in book fourteen of the Varia Historia, chapter fourteen. Isocrates too says, "to eat or drink in an inn" (en kapēleiō), "to go out of the houses of men." See Athenaeus, book thirteen, where he quotes this very passage of Isocrates. How little difference there is between pimping and innkeeping is shown very well by Roman law: by the constitutions of the emperors, a mistress of an inn, who was customarily held in lower esteem by her husband, is released from the Julian law on adultery.

units.la: κα[?] πορισ[?]ονται.) In edicto prætoris de iis qui notantur infamia, numeratur inter primos qui lenocinium fecerit. Vide & titulum. Codicis, De spectaculis scenicis & lenonibus.
units.tr: (κα... πορισ...ονται.) In the praetor's edict on those branded with infamy, he is listed first among those who have run a brothel (lenocinium). See also the title in the Code, On Theatrical Shows and Pimps.

units.la: Pag. 20. τελωνίσαι.) Quanta flagrarint olim apud Græcos & Iudæos inuidia vectigalium & tributorum conductores, nemo nescit. Ex omnibus Græcis videntur Oropij huic quæstui maxime fuisse
units.tr: Page 20. (to be a tax-farmer.) No one is unaware of how fiercely the Greeks and Jews once resented tax-farmers and tribute-collectors. Of all the Greeks, the people of Oropus seem to have been most devoted to this trade,

units.la: dediti : extat enim de iis veteris poetæ Xenonis elogium huiusmodi.
units.tr: for there survives an elegiac verse about them by the old poet Xenon, of this kind:

units.la: Πάντες τελῶναι, πάντες εἰσὶν ἁρπαγές, Κακὸν τέλος [?] Ὠρωπίοις.
units.tr: "All tax-collectors, all are robbers; an evil end to the Oropians." [Πάντες τελῶναι, πάντες εἰσὶν ἁρπαγές, Κακὸν τέλος Ὠρωπίοις.]

units.la: Apud Romanos etsi portitorum & coactorum magna semper vilitas vt alibi: Publicanis tamen inter honestos suus erat locus. quippe equites fuere splendidissimi. ideo toties & tam effusè publicanorum ordinem laudat M. Tullius. Quare τελώνας vertimus portitores, non publicanos, vsum vetustum auctorum secuti. Glossarium, portitor, τελώνης. Portorium τελωνεῖον. & sanè τελώνης proprie est qui vectigaliarius, & telonarius in Cod. Theodosiano. ἀλλὰ κηρύττειν.] Iuuenalis satyra septima.
units.tr: Among the Romans, though portitores and collectors were always held in low esteem, as elsewhere, the publicani had their own place among the honourable, for they were the most splendid of the knights. That is why Marcus Tullius so often and so lavishly praises the order of publicani. Therefore we render telônas as portitores, not publicani, following the old usage of the authors. Glossary: portitor, telônês [τελώνης]. Portorium, telôneion [τελωνεῖον]. Indeed telônês properly means one who collects vectigal, and telonarius in the Theodosian Code. (but to proclaim) Juvenal, satire seven.
"Nor did they think it foul for others, nor shameful"

units.la: Præcones fieri. & satyra tertia lenonum, præconum, & gladiatorum pueri eodem iure censentur. Verum tamen Horatius præconum ordinem & coactorum tuetur alibi propter patrem. Multa Cicero de præconibus in ea pro Quintio.
units.tr: to become heralds. And in Juvenal's third satire, the sons of pimps, heralds and gladiators are rated under the same law. Yet Horace elsewhere defends the order of heralds and collectors on account of his father. Cicero says much about heralds in his speech for Quinctius.

units.la: μαγειρῶν, κυβευτῶν.] M. Tullius, Officiorum libro primo sub finem, Minimèque [?] hæc probanda, quæ minister sunt voluptatum, cetarij, lanij, coqui, sartores, piscatores, vt ait Terentius: adde huc si placet unguentarios, saltatores, totumque ludum talarium. Eleganter Cicero tanquam εἰς μίαν, quod alunt, μύκονον [?] congessit plerasque omnes artes quæ a Romanis improbabantur. par eorundem Athenis vilitas, vt restantur scriptores Attici. Cetarij sunt ζειγοπῶλαι [?], vilissimum hominum genus Athenis: vt & salsamenta apud eos seruorum & pauperum cibus fuit, quod supra diximus. Inde apud Lucianum, θερμοπωλεῖν [?] τὰ ἀτοπίας, ἢ τὰ γεράμματα [?] δι-δάσκειν [?]. Manauit ab istis proverbium de homine obscuro & terrae filio: dicebant eum patre esse ortum qui cubito mungeretur: quod erat falsamentariorum proprium, ut ad Strabonem pluribus expositum. de coquis, & restatur Theophrastus hic, & habes de iis fusè apud Athenaeum. Fartores sunt ἀλλαντοπῶλαι [?] infimae sortis homines: vide Equites Aristophanis. Piscatores quo loco ab iisdem habebantur, declarat vetus proverbium, quod in Hesychij Glossis reperimus: Ἀσπὶς μὴ εἰς ἐπαχθείας, λαβεῖν ἢ μή [?]. sumtum est ex aliquo comico. monebat viros auctor adagionis, ut uxores ex ordine piscatorum ne caperent: etsi filias ut piscatoribus nuptum demus propter difficultates conditionum reperiendarum, concedit. ἐπαχθεῖς [?] sunt piscatores. Piscatoribus adiici debent aucupes & pomarij, atque omnis Tusci turba impia vici: ait Horatius Satyra tertia libri 1. De unguentarijs & saltatoribus, res notissima. Athenis olim lege Solonis cautum fuit, ne quis civis Atticus myrepsicam faceret. auctor Athenaeus libro xiii. ut minus mirum sit quod Seneca refert, fuisse aliquando unguentarios Lacedæmone pulsos. Postremò adiicit Cicero, ludum talarium, sicut & Theophrastus τὸ κυβευτήν [?]. vide superiùs titulum Codicis De alearum & aleatorum usu.
units.tr: (cooks, dice-players) Marcus Tullius, near the end of the first book of On Duties: "Nor are those things to be approved which are ministers of pleasures: fishmongers, butchers, cooks, tailors, fishermen, as Terence says; add, if you like, perfume-sellers, dancers, and the whole dice-game crowd." Cicero neatly gathered into one heap, as they say, nearly all the trades that the Romans disapproved of. There was the same cheapness of such men at Athens, as the Attic writers attest. Cetarii are salt-fish sellers [ζειγοπῶλαι], the lowest sort of men at Athens; salted fish was also the food of slaves and the poor, as we said above. Hence in Lucian, to sell hot ... things, or to teach ... letters. A proverb arose from these men about an obscure person, a son of the earth: they said he was born of a father who was milked with an elbow, which was the peculiar mark of the salt-fish sellers, as is explained at length on Strabo. On cooks, Theophrastus is restored here, and you have them fully treated in Athenaeus. Fartores, sausage-sellers [ἀλλαντοπῶλαι], were men of the lowest rank: see Aristophanes' Knights. How fishermen were regarded by the same people is shown by an old proverb found in the Glosses of Hesychius: "A shield, not for hateful things, to take or not." It was taken from some comic writer. The author of the saying warned men not to take wives from the order of fishermen, though he allows giving daughters in marriage to fishermen because of the difficulty of finding suitable matches. Epachtheis [ἐπαχθεῖς] are fishermen. To the fishermen should be added bird-catchers and orchard-keepers, "and the whole impious crowd of the Tuscan street," says Horace in the third satire of the first book. As for perfumers and dancers, the matter is very well known. At Athens of old, by the law of Solon, it was provided that no Athenian citizen should make perfumes. Athenaeus in book 13 is the authority, so it is less surprising that Seneca reports perfumers were once expelled from Lacedaemon. Finally, Cicero adds the dice-game, just as Theophrastus has the dice-player [τὸ κυβευτήν]. See above, under the title of the Code On the Use of Dice and Dice-Players.

units.la: τῶν μητέρα μὴ τρέφειν. ] Lege Solonis notabantur infamia qui parentes non alebant, aut tectum ad habitationem non præbebant: ut vel ex Æschine contra Timarchum constat. Non temere autem
units.tr: (those who do not support their mother) By the law of Solon, those who did not support their parents, or did not provide a dwelling-place to live in, were branded with infamy, as is clear even from Aeschines against Timarchus.

units.la: matrem potius dixit Theophrastus quàm patrem: latius enim patuit exhibendæ matris necessitas, quàm patris, quando & vulgò quæsitus mater necessariò fuit alenda: in patre non idem obseruatum: vide Plutarchum & Laërtium in Solone.
units.tr: Theophrastus was not without reason speaking of the mother rather than the father. The duty to support a mother extended more widely than that to support a father, since even a child of uncertain paternity had necessarily to support his mother. The same was not observed for the father. See Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius on Solon.

units.la: ἀπάτης ἐκ κλοπῆς[?] Arcesi[?], inquit, solet furti adde, & aliorum criminum. sic apud comicum Agoracritus perfectissimum ἀποφίας[?] exemplum id sibi nomen ait inditum, ex eo quod perpetuo alicuius criminis reus in iudicio volutaretur. Notabis κυνολοχίαν[?] in voce ἀπάγεσθαι[?]: nam ἀπάγω, in furto Atheniensi proprie dicebatur de furto, sicut de aliis criminibus: auctor Vlpianus in Demosthenem Πρὸς Ἀπατουρίου[?]. quamquam alij veteres quibus potius assentior, ἐνδείξιν[?] & ἀπάγω ita distinguunt, vt illa sit absentis delatio: hæc præsentis in ius abductio: quando aliquis manifesti criminis conuictus, in carcerem & ad vndecimuiros rapiebatur.
units.tr: (deceit from theft) Arcesi, he says, usually adds theft and other crimes. So in the comic poet, Agoracritus, the most perfect example, says that he was given that name because he was constantly rolling about in court as defendant on some charge. You will note the dog-like wordplay in the word "to be led away" (apagesthai): for apagô, in Athenian law, was properly said of theft, as of other crimes; the author Ulpian, on Demosthenes' speech Against Apaturius. Although other ancient writers, whom I prefer, distinguish endeixis from apagô, so that the former is the denunciation of an absent person and the latter the leading of a present one into court, when someone convicted of manifest crime was dragged off to prison and before the Eleven.

units.la: τὸ δεσμωτήριον πλεῖω χρῆν οἰκεῖν ἢ πλὴν αὐτῇ οἰκίᾳ[?].
units.tr: (it was better to dwell in the prison than in that house) A saying of Attic elegance; so in Cicero, "to live in prison."

units.la: Dictum venustatis Atticæ: sic apud Ciceronem habitare in carcere. Dinarchus Καὶ γὰρ ἀπὸ ἀττὲν ἄλλα ἕτερα δίκην ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ[?] ἐν ἀνδρὸς ἡν ἐξεῖ[?] loquitur de Aristogitone, quem propterea actor earum orationum contra Demosthenis vulgò tribuuntur, ὁ ἔχειν[?] in carcere appellat, & alteri opponit recens carcerem ingresso, & vt ipse loquitur, ὁ τοτεῖ[?]. Demosthenes in ea Timocratem Aristogeidrotioni obiicit, quòd pater eius Ἀνστρατίδης ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ ἀποθήσκειν[?]. Appio Claudio apud Liuium obiicitur pro magno crimine, quòd carcerem appellasset domicilium plebis Romanæ. Postremò ipsum etiam hominem improbum carcerem vocaiunt[?]. Lucilius, —carcer vix carcere dignus.
units.tr: Dinarchus, speaking of Aristogiton, whom for this reason the author of those speeches against Demosthenes is commonly credited with being, calls him "the one who holds" in prison, and sets him against another who had only recently entered the prison, and as he himself says, "the one who ..." Demosthenes in that speech charges Timocrates with saying that Aristogeiton's father, Antistratides, died in prison. Appius Claudius in Livy is charged as a great crime with having called the prison "the home of the Roman plebs." Lastly, they even call a wicked man himself a prison. Lucilius: "a prison scarcely worthy of the prison."

units.la: καὶ τὸς δ᾽ ἂν ἴῃ[?] δόξειε. ] Lego, ἡ ἑαυτὸ δ᾽ ἄν[?].
units.tr: (and how would he seem to go?) I would read: "how would he himself go?"

units.la: τῶν συστηκότων ὄχλος[?]. ] Hoc est, eorum qui coetus & concursus faciunt: quod capitale fuit Athenis. vide infrà ad caput περὶ λογοποιΐας[?].
units.tr: (a crowd of those who gather) That is, of those who form assemblies and gatherings, which was a capital offence at Athens. See below, at the chapter on gossip (perì logopoiias).

units.la: μεγάλῃ τῇ φωνῇ. ] Alta voce loqui suprà signum erat rusticitatis: alibi superbi & elati animi: sed addit hic Theophrastus, καὶ παρρησιαστικῶς[?], quae vocis appellatio, vel ex eo manavit, quòd multi nimia vocis intentione rami ces fregerunt: vel declaratur ea dictione vastus oris hiatus: sicut Aristoteles in secundo Historiarum, & tertio De partibus, ora canum, leonum, ac reliquorum καρχαρόδοντων[?] dicuntur esse διερρωγότα. Aristophanes in Equitibus Cleonem vocat καρχαρόδοντα, & mox ei vocem tribuit χαράδρας, propter asperitatem & inaequalitatem. Vide scholiasten: & ita etiam vocem παρρησίαν hic interpretari licet: vel est translatio à sensu tactus ad sensum auditus: nam quae sunt abscissa & abrupta, eadem aspera sunt. Apud Ciceronem inter vocis differentias sunt, fractum & scissum. fere autem fracta vox apud Latinos auctores dicitur de voce effœminata, aut eius liquido qui plasmate guttur mobile collinerit. Graeci σαθρὰν vt viderunt[?], & παρρησιώδη[?] scissam vocem nominant. Sed de omnibus vocis differentiis acutè vt omnia suminus[?] philosophus in libello Περὶ ἀκουστῶν[?].
units.tr: (in a loud voice) To speak in a loud voice was, as we said above, a sign of rusticity, and elsewhere of a proud and haughty spirit. But Theophrastus adds here "and boldly" (parrhêsiastikôs). This term for the voice may have come from many having broken their vocal cords through excessive straining, or the expression may describe a wide-gaping mouth, as Aristotle says in book 2 of the History of Animals and book 3 of On the Parts of Animals, that the mouths of dogs, lions and other sharp-toothed animals are said to be gaping (diërrhôgota). Aristophanes in the Knights calls Cleon sharp-toothed [καρχαρόδοντα], and soon gives him a voice of ravines [χαράδρας], for its roughness and unevenness. See the scholiast. So too the word parrhêsia can be understood here, either as a transfer from the sense of touch to that of hearing, for things that are cut and broken off are also rough. In Cicero, among the differences of voice are the "broken" and the "split." Among Latin authors a "broken voice" is usually said of an effeminate voice, or of one whose throat has been smeared with a soft plaster to make it mobile. The Greeks, as they saw, call a faulty voice sathra, and a split one parrhêsiôdê. But the philosopher treats all the differences of voice acutely, as he does everything, in his little book On Audible Things.

units.la: Pag. 21. ἡ ὅταν ἡ πανήγυρις[?]. ] Proprium hoc, vt initio dixi-mus, hominis ἀναιδείᾳ[?]: qui assiduis conuiciis ita depudere didicit, vt la tetur etiam insamia. Habuit hoc quoque impurus ille sæpe iam[?] à nobis commemoratus Aristogiton:quem quidem ait orator ea fuisse oris duritie, vt quæ alij taciti & in tenebris admitterent, quibus tale quid humani-tus usuveniret,ea ipse tantum non appensis sibi tin-tinnabulis patraret: quod est dicere palam & in omnium oculis. Sic ille, Καὶ ἃ τῇ ἀλλων τῇ ἡτ-χκοτων ἑκαστῳ ἀφοβητὶ ποιεῖ, ταῦθ᾽ ἅτ᾽ μονοῦν κ-δωρας ἐξαφανίζω διαπαρᾶ[?].
units.tr: Page 21. (or when the assembly ...) This is, as I said at the beginning, a characteristic of a man of shamelessness (anaideia), who through constant abuse has learned to be so brazen that he boasts even of infamy. That impure fellow, whom we have often mentioned before, Aristogiton, had this too. The orator says that he had such hardness of face that what others did timidly and in the shadows, and what might happen to humans, he did almost with bells hung on him, that is, openly and before everyone's eyes. So he says: "And what each of the others does fearlessly, these things I bring to light ..."

units.la: τὰς δ᾽ ἐξομνύσθαι[?]. ] Lego, ἢ τὰς μὴ ἐξομνύναι, ἔχων ἐχθρόν. ] Vasculum fuit in quo asseruabantur litium instrumenta, quæ in libris Græcorum Iurisconsultorum ἀρχαλίσματα vocantur. Erat autem echinus, vel testaceus, vel æneus, teste in Vespas Aristophanis scholiaste.
units.tr: (and to refuse to swear) I read: "or not to refuse the oath, having an enemy." It was a little vessel in which the instruments of lawsuits were kept, which in the books of the Greek jurists are called archalismata. It was a sea-urchin-shaped box, either of earthenware or bronze, according to the scholiast on Aristophanes' Wasps.

units.la: ὀρμαθὸν βιβλίων. ] Aristoteles apud Dionysium Halic. ἐσχάτως[?] βιβλίων. Iuuenalis de causidicis in forum venientibus:
units.tr: A string of books [ὀρμαθὸν βιβλίων]. Aristotle, as quoted by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, [a string of books]. Juvenal, on the lawyers who come into the forum:
—and, with a great bundle of little books, their companions.

units.la: καὶ τ᾽ ἀρχαμής[?].) Plane istud hominis est, non hominis. Nam cùm in genere fœnerari idem sit quot hominem occidere, vt Cato senior aiebat: & ὧν[?] ἐργάζεσθαι[?], vt Aristoteli placet: ac proinde faeneratores furibus peiores clues à veteribus Romanis fuerint existimati, vt probat idem Cato: quid obsecro te, existimandum est de eo qui fœnus id exerceat quod hîc commemoratur? Neque tamen putemus fingi hæc à Theophrasto: dixit enim ipse initio, ex iis quæ vulgo fierent, & in vsu apud homines essent, esse hoc à se scriptum conflatum. Imprimis animaduertenda est istorum techna, qui vt fœnus hoc horrendum minore cum inuidia poffint exercere, non folent grandem pecuniæ summam fimul eidem credere, neque in multos dies. Hi funt quos Græci ζκοῦ λύφυς dixerunt, Latini toculliones: qua voce vtitur M. Tullius ad Atticum. Cùm autem obolus fit fexta drachmæ pars, facile cuiuis æftimare, quale fit hoc fœnerandi genus quando drachma obolum femis quotidie parit. Fuit fanè maxima Athenis fœnerandi licentia. etfi enim vfitatus in ea ciuitate vfuræ modus erat, vt pro mina quot menfibus drachma penderetur: quæ eft centefima Romanorum vfura:tamen & binas centefimas,& ternas, ac quaternas folitas exigi non eft dubium. quippe cum iftiufmodi hominum improbitas, non folùm non coërceretur vllis legibus: fed etiam approbaretur veteri Solonis lege hac: Τὸ ἀργύεων ςάσιμον τῷ, ἐφ' ὑπόσον ἂν βέλη ὁ δανείζων. hoc eft, Ius esso seneratori pecuniam suam quantacunque vsura volet collocare. Sic enim Lysias hanc legem exponit. Τὸ ςάσιμον' inquit, τοῦτο δέιν, ὦ βέλτιςε, ὁ ζυγὸς ἰσάναι, ἀλλὰ τόκον ςφάτλεσθαι ἐπόζν ἂν βέλητας.
units.tr: And [καὶ τ᾽ ἀρχαμής]. This is plainly the mark of a man, or rather of something other than a man. For since lending at interest is the same as killing a man, as the elder Cato used to say, and since, as Aristotle holds, [ὧν ἐργάζεσθαι], and since the ancient Romans judged usurers worse citizens than thieves, as Cato also proves, what, I beg you, must we think of the man who practises the kind of usury mentioned here? Yet we should not suppose Theophrastus invented these things. He said at the outset that he had written of what was commonly done and was in use among people. Above all we should note the tricks of those who, so that they may practise this dreadful usury with less odium, do not usually lend a large sum to one person at once, nor for many days. These are the men the Greeks called [ζκοῦ λύφυς], and the Latins toculliones, a term Marcus Tullius uses in his letter to Atticus. An obol is the sixth part of a drachma, so anyone can easily work out what sort of lending this is when a drachma yields an obol and a half every day. Certainly the licence to lend at Athens was very great. For although the customary rate in that city was a drachma a month on a mina, which is the Roman centesima, there is no doubt that double, triple and quadruple centesimae were commonly exacted. The wickedness of such men was not only unchecked by any laws; it was even approved by this old law of Solon: [Τὸ ἀργύριον ... ἐφ᾽ ὑπόσον ἂν βούληται ὁ δανείζων]. That is: the lender shall have the right to place his money at whatever interest he wishes. Lysias explains this law thus: "That," he says, "is not a yoke, my good sir, but interest; the lender may exact as much as he wishes."

units.la: τέλα ἡμιωβόλια. ) Antiquum est Græcorum loquendi genus, τέλα ἡμιωβόλια, pro, obolus femis, vel fefquiobolus. Pollux, φίλον ὁ Ζῆς ἀρχαίοις ἐ τὸ ἐν ἥμισυ ζάλαῖον τέλα ἡμιλάλαῖον λέγεν. Ita sæ-pissimè cuiusuis aut mensuræ aut ponderis numeros antiqui scriptores præsertim Attici efferunt.sic apud Hippocratem legas τέλα ἡμίχοα, τέλα ἡμιώρια, τέλα τεμπλημόεια & τέσσαρα τεμπλημόεια: apud Pla-tonem τέλα ἡμιναῖα, sexto Legum: apud Xenophontem τέλα ἡμίσραχμα: apud Theophrastum in secundo Historiarum τέλα ἡμιτόδια: apud Athenæum libro quarto τρία ἡμιμέδιμνα [?] : & in Dioscoridis aliorumque medicorum libris sæpe. Sic Latini interdum : Martialis, Et thuris pyxides tres selibras [?] quod & nos in vernaculo nostro idiomate retinemus.
units.tr: The phrase τέλα ἡμιωβόλια [whole and half-obol] is an old Greek idiom meaning an obol and a half, or sesquiobol. Pollux says that the ancients, instead of saying [half a stater], said [whole half-stater]. In this way the ancient writers, especially the Attic ones, very often express the numbers of any measure or weight. So in Hippocrates you will find τέλα ἡμίχοα, τέλα ἡμιώρια, τέλα τεμπλημόεια and τέσσαρα τεμπλημόεια; in Plato, in the sixth book of the Laws, τέλα ἡμιναῖα; in Xenophon, τέλα ἡμίσραχμα; in Theophrastus, in the second book of the Histories, τέλα ἡμιτόδια; in Athenaeus, in the fourth book, τρία ἡμιμέδιμνα; and often in the books of Dioscorides and other physicians. The Latins too sometimes did so. Martial: and three boxes of incense, each of a pound and a half. We still keep this usage in our own vernacular.

units.la: Attici vero quàm delectarentur hoc loquendi genere, declarat Theophrastus, qui in libro περὶ ὀσμῶν [?] δύο ἡμιλίτρα [?] dicere maluit, quàm ἑκτέα. In Cod.Theod. sex semisque quàm tres siliquæ. Augustus in testamento ex parte dimidia & sextante quàm ex besse. Hinc illa sunt nomina composita, τριμιχεῖτ [?] apud eundem Theophrastum : & ἡμιχοῖνιξ [?]. item apud Xenophontem τρίμοιρον [?], sic etiam apud grammaticos dictus versus, qui duos pedes & partem a reliquo carmine quasi scissa & separata haber. Caue vero confundas loquendi hoc genus cum alio simili, quidem, sed significatione longè diuerso: Τέτρον ἡμισυ [?] enim quando dicunt Græci, non iam obolum semis, sed duos obolos semis volunt intelligi. Sic dixit Herodotus ἥλιον [?] pro eo quod est, pendens sex talenta cum dimidio, apud Dinarchum τρίτων ἡμιδραχμον [?], pro drachmis semis. vide Pollucem. Hoc quoque imitati sunt Latini veteres. Fuit enim veterum consuetudo, ait Varro, ut retro aere dicerentur, ita ut semis tertius, semis quartus pronunciarent. Inde est sestertius pes, pro duobus assibus semis, & duobus pedibus semis. & apud Plinium libro xvii. capite xi quinque semipes ex Græcis scriptoribus, quod dixerant τέμπρες ἡμιτάλαντον [?]: hoc est, quatuor pedes cum dimidio. Adi Priscianum, & Volusium Mætianum, qui hoc posterius loquendi genus diligenter explicauerunt. Nos autem ideo hic notauimus, vt ne similitudo duarum locutionum cuiquam imponeret. quo in errore doctissimos etiam viros versari videmus. Testis sit Demosthenes: in cuius orationibus quoties extat altera harum φράσεων, toties peccat eruditissimus Vuolfius. Nam quod in ea pro Androtione scribitur, ὡς Ἀποδράς ὠχεῖο, ἔχων τέτταρα ἡμιτάλαντον [?] duo talenta semis significat: non quatuor cum dimidio vt putauit interpres. sic debet hic etiam locus ex oratione ὑπὲρ Φορμίωνος ex-poni, ὡς ἀποδίδωσι πέντε ἡμιταλάντων καὶ ἑξακοσίων δραχμῶν. item iste ex ea πρὸς Νικοστράτην, sub initium, ἀπεξαλφάμην ἂν τῶν ἡμιμναίων ἄξια ἀποδοῦναι [?]. Postremò in oratione contra Theocrinem quæ ἐν δείξεις inscribitur, non aliter illa exponi debuere, ἐδόθη τρίτα ἡμιμναῖα τέτρῳ τῷ ἀδωροδοκήτῳ. Tot locis apud summum oratorem, extat loquendi hoc genus: in quibus omnibus lapsus est vir doctus, quum non obseruasset quid inter τρίτα ἡμιτάλαντα, & τρίτον ἡμιτάλαντον intercesset. Enimuero doctissimo viro facile ignosco, qui ἄλλως ἐν ἐξήλοις ἔνδ' ἀπωθεῖται φόρον: vapulet vero sciolus ille Græculus qui Vuolfium in errorem induxit. Ita enim annotatum reperies ad superiorem locum ex Androtiana, τὸ δὲ περὶ ἡμιτάλαντα, ἀντὶ τῶν τέτταρα [?] ἡμιτάλαντον ὡς τέτταρα καὶ τῶν σὰδμα ἐπὶ Ἡροδότῳ. Hæc ille: quæ omnia falsa esse & inepta ex superioribus liquet: quibus libet adhibere velut ἐν ἀπιστίαις, vt omnis omnino scrupulus eximatur, locum Ariftotelis insignem. Sic philosophus nono Historiarum. βλίττεται ὁ σφῶν [?] χοᾶ, ἢ τριῶν ἡμίχοα. τὰ δ' ἀδύνατα δύο χοᾶς, ἢ περὶ ἡμίχοα. τρίτα δ' χοᾶς ὀλίγα. Eximunt, inquit, ex uno apum alueari choemvnum, aut vnum cum dimidio.vel,bene vt agatur,choas binos, aut binos cum dimidio : raro ternos choas. Eat nunc iste opicus, & dicat πέντε ἡμίχοα εἶναι τέτταρα ἢ ἥμισυ[?]. Absit vero à nobis, vt hæc & alia huius farinæ, qualia nonnulla in illis scholiis obseruauimus, Vlpiano tribuamus.
units.tr: How much the Attic writers delighted in this way of speaking is shown by Theophrastus, who in his book On Odours preferred to say [two and a half litrae] rather than [six]. In the Theodosian Code it is six and a half rather than three siliquae. Augustus in his will says from half and a sixth part rather than from two-thirds. Hence come those compound words in the same Theophrastus, [τριμιχεῖτ], and [ἡμιχοῖνιξ]; likewise in Xenophon [τρίμοιρον]. So too grammarians call a verse that has two feet and a part of the rest of the line, as if cut and separated from it. But beware of confusing this way of speaking with another that is similar but very different in meaning. When the Greeks say [τέτρον ἡμισυ], they mean not an obol and a half but two obols and a half. So Herodotus said [ἥλιον] for weighing six talents and a half; in Dinarchus, [τρίτων ἡμιδραχμον] stands for drachmas and a half; see Pollux. The old Latins imitated this too. For, says Varro, it was the custom of the ancients to count backwards in money, so that they said "third half" and "fourth half". Hence the sestertius pes, for two asses and a half and two feet and a half. And in Pliny, book seventeen, chapter eleven, five semipes from Greek writers, which the Greeks had called [four talents and a half]: that is, four feet and a half. See Priscian and Volusius Maecianus, who explained this later usage carefully. I have noted it here so that the resemblance of the two expressions may not mislead anyone; we see even very learned men fall into this error. Demosthenes is witness: wherever the second of these phrases occurs in his orations, the most learned Wolf goes wrong. In the speech against Androtion, where it is written [he had four and a half talents], [ἔχων τέτταρα ἡμιτάλαντον], this means two and a half talents, not four and a half as the translator thought. So too the passage in the speech For Phormio should be explained: [he paid five and a half hundred drachmas]. Likewise that passage in the speech Against Nicostratus at the beginning: [I would have been able to pay the worth of the half-minas]. Finally, in the speech against Theocrines, entitled On Proof, that passage ought to be explained no differently: [three and a half minas were given to the incorruptible man]. This way of speaking occurs in so many places in that greatest orator, and the learned man has erred in all of them, since he did not notice the difference between [τρίτα ἡμιτάλαντα] and [τρίτον ἡμιτάλαντον]. I readily pardon the learned man, who, as the saying goes, shakes off the burden elsewhere; but that little Greekling who led Wolf into error deserves a whipping. For you will find this noted on the earlier passage from the Androtion: "the expression about the half-talents, instead of the four and a half talents, as four and [something] in Herodotus." So he writes, and all of this is false and foolish, as is clear from what has gone before. To remove every doubt, let us use, as it were, a decisive proof, the notable passage of Aristotle in the ninth book of the Histories: [the beekeeper takes from one hive a choe and a half, or from three a choe and a half; from two, a choe and a half, or a little less; and rarely three choes]. He says: they take from a single hive of bees one choe, or one and a half; or, if things go well, two choes, or two and a half: rarely three choes. Let that boor now go and say that five half-choes are four and a half. Far be it from us to attribute these and other errors of this sort, several of which we have noticed in those scholia, to Ulpian.

units.la: τῆς ἡμέρας προσπράξεσθαι[?].) Atticum est, ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰσπράξεσθαι[?]. non aliter fere Demosthenes caeterique scriptores de meliore nota. non ergo sunt audiendi qui εἰσπράξεσθαι iubent rescribi. Veteres & Græci & Latini sæpe eleganter simplicibus verbis pro compositis vtuntur : sic ergo πράσσω aliàs pro ἐμπράσσω, exigo : pro συμπράσσω. Pindarus Nemeonicis Πράσσει γὰρ ἔργῳ μὲν [?] βελτίων ἢ φράσει[?]. hoc est, συμπράσσει, σωτηρεῖ. Notabis pactionem de vsura in singulos dies : cuius extat etiam in Epidico Plauti exemplum.
units.tr: [τῆς ἡμέρας προσπράξεσθαι]. This is Attic usage for [εἰσπράξεσθαι], to exact. Demosthenes and the other writers of the better sort use it in much the same way. So those who bid us rewrite it as [εἰσπράξεσθαι] should not be heeded. The ancient Greeks and Latins often and elegantly use simple verbs for compound ones: thus [πράσσω] is sometimes used for [ἐμπράσσω], to exact, and for [συμπράσσω]. Pindar in the Nemean Odes: [for he is better in deed than in word], that is, he [συμπράσσει], he brings about salvation. You will note the agreement about interest by the day, of which there is also an example in Plautus's Epidicus.

units.la: Id adeo argentum ab danista apud Thebas fœnore:
units.tr: That silver, from the moneylender at Thebes, at interest:
Each day, a single silver mina, in coin.

units.la: Qui hanc vsuram exercebant, Græci eos ἡμερησί[?]ς vocabant, vt Laertius in Menippo.
units.tr: Those who practised this kind of usury were called by the Greeks [ἡμερησίους], by the day, as Laertius says in the life of Menippus.

units.la: Res hodie tocullionibus præsertim Iudæis non incognita.
units.tr: This practice is not unknown today, especially among Jewish money-lenders.

units.la: καὶ τὰς ὥρας διὰ τὴν ἐμπολήματος εἰς τὸ ἀ[?]ν ἐν ἐν.] Iam venimus ad locum longè elegantissimum, & ex iis vnum qui vetustatem libelli huius arguunt : cuius veram interpretationem prioribus interpretibus ne per somnium quidem in mentem venisse affirmare ausim : est enim & obscurior propter ignorationem priscorum morum:& nonnihil etiam corruptus : sed de re primùm : de verbis mox viderimus. Sciendum igitur, morem olim fuisse Athenis hominum vilium atque abiectorum qui in foro res venales habebant, vt quas pecunias ex venditione mercium suarum colligerent, eas in os & buccam conderent: maximè, credo, cum esset turba emturientium: tum enim, ne tempus sibi aperienda claudendáque crumena periret, vt quidque accipiebant numorum id statim in os coniiciebant. Sic erat istis os suum instar crumenæ, quam collo appensam istiusmodi homines apud Romanos gerere solitos fuisse, supra ex Plauto annotabamus. Propterea scribit Artemidorus in re somniorum maxillas indicare horrea : τὰς σταγόνας [?] inquit πρὸς ἀποθήκας [?] ἀπολλ[?]ων. Hoc est quod Theophrastus vocat εἰς γνάθον ἐκλέγειν, in maxillam colligere. nam ἐκλέγειν pro συλλέγειν positum, vt etiam paullo ante. Græci comici ἐγκάπτειν εἰς τὸ γνάθον eodem sensu dicunt. Alexis in Lebete describens venditorem ficorum, hominem impudentissimum,
units.tr: [καὶ τὰς ὥρας διὰ τὴν ἐμπολήματος εἰς τὸ ἀ[?]ν ἐν ἐν]. We now come to a passage far the most elegant, and one of those which prove the antiquity of this little book. I would not venture to say that the earlier interpreters ever even dreamed of its true meaning. It is obscure because of our ignorance of ancient customs, and somewhat corrupt as well. But let us first consider the matter, and later examine the words. We should know, then, that it was once the custom at Athens for common and low people who had goods for sale in the marketplace to put in their mouths and cheeks the money they collected from selling their wares, especially, I think, when there was a crowd of buyers. For then, so that no time was lost in opening and closing the purse, they threw into their mouths at once each coin as they received it. So their mouths served them as a purse, which, as I noted above from Plautus, such men among the Romans were accustomed to wear hung round the neck. Hence Artemidorus, in his book on dreams, says that the jaws signify storehouses: [collecting the drops] he says, [into storehouses]. This is what Theophrastus calls [εἰς γνάθον ἐκλέγειν], to gather into the jaw; for [ἐκλέγειν] is used for [συλλέγειν], as also a little earlier. The Greek comic poets say [ἐγκάπτειν εἰς τὸ γνάθον] in the same sense. Alexis, in The Kettle, describing a seller of figs, a most shameless fellow:

units.la: Εἶ' ὁ μὲν ἔδωκεν ὡς ὠιαυτ' ἀνηρπάζω, [?] Τιμᾷ. ὁδ' ἐγκάψας τὸ κέρμα εἰς τὸν γνάθον, [?] Εεἶνε ἀπίδοῖ, σῦκα πωλᾶν ὀμνύων. [?]
units.tr: "Then one gave me, as much as I could snatch up," says Timas. "He, stuffing the coin into his cheek, swore that he was selling figs" [Εἶ' ὁ μὲν ἔδωκεν ὡς ὠιαυτ' ἀνηρπάζω, Τιμᾷ. ὁδ' ἐγκάψας τὸ κέρμα εἰς τὸν γνάθον, ὀμνύων σῦκα πωλᾶν].

units.la: Sic apud Aristophanem, quem iure veteres critici τὸν Ἀττικῶν ἐδῶν διδάσκαλον [?] appellarunt, Philocleon ait cum traditâ tam sibi quam Lysistrato communis drachma fuisset (iudicibus enim binis, drachma merces dabatur) conuenisseque inter ipsos vt illam Lysistratus permutaret, & eius dimidium, hoc est, tres obolos, ipsi daret: ait inquam, se à sodali miserè deceptum fuisse: qui monetæ loco squamas mugilis piscis in manum sibi tradiderit: quas ipse imprudens tanquam probam monetam in os subitò immerfit. Verba poëtæ sunt,
units.tr: Philocleon says the same in Aristophanes, whom the ancient critics rightly called the teacher of Attic wit. When a drachma had been handed over, shared between himself and Lysistratus (two jurors being paid a drachma between them), they agreed that Lysistratus should exchange it and give him half, that is three obols. Philocleon says, I repeat, that he was cruelly cheated by his comrade, who, instead of coin, put fish-scales of the mullet into his hand. He himself, not noticing, plunged them straight into his mouth as if they were good money. These are the poet's words:

units.la: —δραχμὴν μετ' ἐμῆ λαβὼν,Ἑλθὼν, ἀιεκρμαλίζετ' ἐν τοῖς ἰχθύσι.Κ' ἄπήτ' ἐπέδηκε τρεῖς λοπίδας μοι κιςρέων.Κ' ἀγὼ ἑνέκαλ' ὀδολὸς γ' ὠμίλω λαβὼν. [?]
units.tr: "Taking the drachma with my share, he went off and tossed it among the fish. Then he gave me three scales of the mullet for my portion, and I, taking my obol with the crowd, ..." [δραχμὴν μετ' ἐμῆ λαβὼν, ἑλθὼν ἀνεκρμαλίζετ' ἐν τοῖς ἰχθύσι. κ' ἄπήτ' ἐπέδηκε τρεῖς λοπίδας μοι κιςρέων. κ' ἀγὼ ἑνέκαλ' ὀδολὸς γ' ὠμίλω λαβὼν.]

units.la: Scholiastes, πολλοῖς γὰρ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ σόμαλι φυ-λάττειν τὸ ἀργύριον Multis, inquit, moris eft, vt pecunias in ore cuftodiant. Idem poëta in Æolosicone, ὥσπερ λοιπὸν μόνον ἦν ἐν τῇ γνάθῳ γέντλαγ μοι. & in Anagyro, ἐν τῇ σόμαλι τρημιωσόλων ἔχων. Hodie mulieres moris eiufce veftigium retinent: multæ enim confueuerunt, maximè αἱ κομμωτρίαι, fiue ornatrices in ore aciculas habere: nam inde facilius ad vfum promuntur quàm ex aciario, fiue βελονοθή, aut c puluillis iis quos ad cuftodiendas aciculas folent fibi fabricari. Atqui hanc commoditatem magno fæpe conftare, exempla triftiffima illas debuerant docere. Quid quod etiam nummi in os recepti, nedum aciculæ, periculum aliquando veteribus crearunt? Nam apud Ariftophanem in Aubus Euelpis quidam eft, qui dum more Athenienfium miluum veris indicem prouolutus ad terram falutare parat, obolum quem forte in ore habebat, imprudens nec fine fummo periculo deglutit.
units.tr: The scholiast says: "For many have the habit of keeping money in the mouth. Many, he says, have the custom of keeping their money in their mouths." The same poet, in the Aeolosicon, says: "as if only the cheek remained for me to fill." And in the Anagyrus: "holding the coins in my mouth." Women today still keep a trace of this custom: many, and especially the <bl>hairdressers</bl>, are accustomed to keep needles in their mouths, since they can be drawn out more easily for use than from a needle-case or a bodkin-holder, or from the little cushions which they usually make for themselves to keep their needles in. Yet the very sad examples should have taught them that this convenience often carries a great cost. What of the fact that coins taken into the mouth, let alone needles, have sometimes put the ancients in danger? For in Aristophanes' Birds there is a man who, while he throws himself on the ground to greet the kite, as the Athenians do, the herald of spring, unthinkingly swallows the obol he happened to have in his mouth, and not without the gravest danger.

units.la: — ἐγὼ γοῶ, ait,Ἐκυλινδ́ψμὴν, ἵκλινον ἰδὼν· κἀξ ὑπὸ ὤν, ἀνα-χύχων [?]Οἴξολὸν κατεβρόχθισ. [?]
units.tr: "I," he says, "was rolling about, and seeing the kite, I gaped. And from beneath it, ..., I gulped down the obol." [ἐγὼ γοῶ, ἐκυλινδ́ψμὴν, ἵκλινον ἰδὼν· κἀξ ὑπὸ ὤν, ἀνα-χύχων οἴξολὸν κατεβρόχθισ.]

units.la: Ex his luce clarior mens auctoris hoc loco: fupereft vt de mendo quod hæc fententia continet, videamus. Non enim τόχυς rectè legitur: vt ex illis verbis ἀπὸ τῶν ἐμπαιζολυμαί[?], quiuis intelligat : sed vel ὀζολὸς[?] legendum, vel χαλκοῦς dicere, vel κέρμα[?], nisi longius ab edita lectione abesset. vel igitur, ὀζο-λὸς[?] scribendum, ut in superiore Alexidis loco : vel χαλκοῦς, ut in hoc Ariftophanis Concionantibus, —πωλῶν γὰρ βόστρυς[?] Μέσην ἀ̓ άνπα τὸν γνάθον χαλκῶν ἔχων[?].
units.tr: From these passages the author's meaning in this place is clear as daylight. It remains to examine the error which this sentence contains. For τόχυς is not correctly read, as anyone can see from the words that precede it; rather either ὀζολὸς should be read, or χαλκοῦς should be said, or κέρμα, unless the reading had been too far removed from the printed text. Either, then, ὀζολὸς should be written, as in the earlier passage of Alexis, or χαλκοῦς, as in this passage of Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae: "for selling curls... holding bronze coins in my cheek."

units.la: Scimus Græcū esse ἐκλέγειν τόκας[?]; ut in 1. Stromat. Clementis, τόκας ἐκλέγειν ὅτι χρήματα[?], sed hoc nihil ad istum locum. Fuit cum hoc referrem ad ἀπρολόγυς[?], vilissimum hominum genus Athenis. Sic enim vocabant Athenieses abiectissimos quosdam homines, imò hominum mendicabula, qui forum & Digma oberrantes, si quid è mercium oneribus, ut fit, excideret, id legebant, & vitam hoc quæstu sustentabant. Auctor Eustathius. Sed superiore interpretatione nihil verius, ne ea quidem quæ apud Sagram.
units.tr: We know that ἐκλέγειν is Greek for collecting taxes, as in the first book of the Stromateis of Clement: "to collect taxes, because they are money." But this has nothing to do with the present passage. I once referred this to the ἀπρολόγους, the most worthless class of men at Athens. For the Athenians called by this name certain most abject men, indeed beggars, who wandered about the market and the Dygma, and if anything fell from the loads of merchandise, as happens, they gathered it up and supported their lives by this trade. So says Eustathius. But the earlier interpretation is nothing if not truer, nor is even that which is found in Sagra.

units.la: Pag. 22. ἐργώδεις ἢ εἰσί.) Hoc est, δυσχερεῖς & φορτικοί. Malo sic quàm ut quidam, His semper est quod agant.
units.tr: Page 22. "ἐργώδεις ἢ εἰσί." That is, disagreeable and vulgar. I prefer this to the way some have rendered it, "They always have something to do."

units.la: καὶ φθεγγόμενοι μεγάλῃ τῇ φωνῇ. } Ecce iterum eandem notam de qua diximus paullo ante. apparet Theophrastum teneras aureis habuisse, & clamoribus importunis valde solitum offendi. Auctor Rhetoricorum ad Herennium in descriptione hominis impudentis hoc non neglexit, Tum vero, inquit, iste cœpit clamare voce ista, qua facile cuius rubores excire posset. Sed de hoc vitio plura Clemens Alex. Pædagog. lib. 11. cap. v11. Quintilianus lib. v1. cap. v. & alicubi Iustinus Martyr.
units.tr: "And speaking in a loud voice." Here again is the same mark we spoke of a little while ago. It appears that Theophrastus had sensitive ears and was much offended by unseemly clamour. The author of the Rhetorica ad Herennium, in his description of the impudent man, did not neglect this point: "Then indeed," he says, "he began to shout in a voice by which he could easily provoke anyone's blushes." But Clement of Alexandria says more about this vice in the Paedagogus, book 2, chapter 7; Quintilian in book 6, chapter 5; and Justin Martyr somewhere.

units.la: Hac dictum nobis ad caput περὶ ἀδολεσχίας. In Platonis Ὅροις ita definitur, λαλιά, ἐκρασία λόγου ἄλογ. Hominem λάλον, Latini veteres, linguacem, linguacem, linguacem, & locutuleium dixerunt. vocarunt & linguosum, vt Hieronymus sæpe. sic apud Græcos γλωσσώδης ἀνθρωπος, & ἀρόγλωσσος, vt cui sit lingua prominens. Vsus est Clemens elegantissima ea voce, quæ ei responder quod Francoceltæ dicimus, auoir la langue longue. Vorrò λαλιὰ in malam partem non semper accipitur, sed interdum pro familiari colloquio inter amicos, aut alios. Quare etiam λαλιᾶς præcepta prodita sunt à veteribus dicendi magistris. Menander rhetor, Τὸ τῆς λαλιᾶς εἶδος [?] ἀρτιμώσατον ἔσν ἀνδρεὶ ... Ἐσιφῖς [?] ... plura ibi lege. Extat & Aristidis oratio λαλιὰ inscripta.
units.tr: We have said this in relation to the chapter on περὶ ἀδολεσχίας. In Plato's Definitions it is defined thus: λαλιά, the excess of speech without reason. The older Latins called a λάλος man a linguax, lingulaca, or loquacula, and locutuleius. They also used linguosus, as Jerome often does. So among the Greeks we have γλωσσώδης ἄνθρωπος and ἀρόγλωσσος, as one whose tongue is prominent. Clement used that most elegant word which answers to what the French call avoir la langue longue. But λαλιά is not always taken in a bad sense; sometimes it means familiar conversation between friends or others. For this reason the ancient masters of rhetoric also handed down precepts on λαλιά. Menander the rhetorician: "The kind of λαλιά most suited to a man ... " Read more there. There is also an oration of Aristides entitled Λαλιά.

units.la: ἔτι ἄδεν λέγες.) Hoc solebant de iis vsurpare qui falsa aut quæ nihil ad rem essent loquerentur. Aristophanes Vespis τὰ αὐτὰ ἀδὲν λέγεις. & alibi sæpe, & in Platone passim. Alio sensu apud comicum positum obseruauimus τ. ἀ. [?] illud ἄδεν λέγει, non de verbis sed de re inutili: sicut hodie nos quoque loquimur de re quam improbamus. Ait autem Theophrastus ἀν ὁ, τοιοῦ, vt indicet locutuleios istos, non posse quamuis exigui temporis loquendi moram ferre. Ad hos pertinet non ad ἀδολέσχους locus Ciceronis primo Officiorum. Nec vero tanquam in possessionem suam venerit, excludat alios: sed cum reliquis in rebus, tum in sermone communi vicissitudine utendum putet. Similia Basilius in epistola quadam ad Gregorium.
units.tr: "ἔτι ἄδεν λέγες." They used to apply this to those who spoke falsehoods or things that had nothing to do with the matter. Aristophanes in the Wasps: "you say the same nothing." And elsewhere often, and throughout Plato. I have noted that the comic poet used it in another sense, ἄδεν λέγει, not of words but of a useless matter, just as we today also speak of a thing we disapprove of. Theophrastus says that such people, as he shows, cannot bear the delay of even the briefest time in conversation. To these, and not to the πολυλέσχοι, belongs the passage of Cicero in the first book of De Officiis: "Nor indeed should one, as if he had come into possession of it, shut others out; rather in other matters, and also in common conversation, he should think that there must be alternation." Basil says similar things in a certain letter to Gregory.

units.la: ἢ ἂν ἀχύη ἀντί, μαθήσεσθαι. [?] ) Tale illud fere Aristophanis in Avibus,
units.tr: "or, if he will be silent for a while, he will learn." Something very like this is in Aristophanes' Birds:

units.la: Pag. 23. ἀποξάλλει, εἶναις σὺ, μὴ ὀπλάδυ. [?] ) Praua distinctio hactenus veram huius loci sententiam infuscauit. Nam distinguendum est ἀποξάλλει, εἶναις, σὺ μὴ ὀπλάδυ. [?] Et εἶναις scribendum, non εἶπας. Est enim non verbum, sed participium, quo saepe vitatur Aristoteles. Prorsus id est quod vulgo excusationis gratia dicere solemus, quando verba facientem interloquimur, Sans interrompre vostre propos: vel, De vostre propos vous souvienne. Sic mox, εὖγε ὅτι μὴ ὑπείμνῆς, illud est quod dici solet, A propos de cela. eadem ratio illorum, καὶ ὁ παρέλιπον. nam qui illa verba loco suo mutant, & locum illum transpositione opus habere arbitrantur, nae illi toto, quod aiunt, cœlo errant. Elegantissimè sanè Theophrastus omnes loquendi ansas recensset, quas homines loquaces captare solent, ut cum aliquo saltem praetextu loquentem possint interpellare, & ut veteres loquebantur obacerare. In Sapientiae libro cum alia praeclarè, tum hoc junioribus nunquam obliviscendum, πρὶν ἢ ἀκοῦσαι μὴ ὑποκείνε, καὶ ἐν μέσῳ λόγων μὴ παρέμβαλλε ῥῆμα. Ne respondeas priusquam audieris, & in alterius sermonem verbum nullum interjce.
