units.tr: Pag. 23. "ἀποξάλλει, εἶναις σὺ, μὴ ὀπλάδυ" [ἀποξάλλει, εἶναις σὺ, μὴ ὀπλάδυ]. A faulty punctuation has hitherto obscured the true meaning of this passage. It should be punctuated thus: "ἀποξάλλει, εἶναις, σὺ μὴ ὀπλάδυ" [ἀποξάλλει, εἶναις, σὺ μὴ ὀπλάδυ]. And εἶναις should be written, not εἶπας. For it is not a verb but a participle, a form which Aristotle often avoids. It is exactly what we commonly say by way of apology when we break in on someone who is speaking: Sans interrompre vostre propos, or De vostre propos vous souvienne. So too shortly after, "εὖγε ὅτι μὴ ὑπείμνῆς" [εὖγε ὅτι μὴ ὑπείμνῆς], "well done that you did not mention it," is what is commonly said: A propos de cela. The same reasoning applies to "καὶ ὁ παρέλιπον" [καὶ ὁ παρέλιπον], "and what I left out." For those who move those words from their place and think that the passage needs transposition are, as they say, wholly wide of the mark. Theophrastus very elegantly lists all the openings for speech which talkative people are wont to seize, so that they may at least with some pretext interrupt the speaker, or, as the old writers put it, interject. In the book of Ecclesiasticus, among many other excellent sayings, this should never be forgotten by the young: "πρὶν ἢ ἀκοῦσαι μὴ ἀποκρίνου, καὶ ἐν μέσῳ λόγων μὴ παρεμβάλλε ῥῆμα" [πρὶν ἢ ἀκοῦσαι μὴ ἀποκρίνου, καὶ ἐν μέσῳ λόγων μὴ παρεμβάλλε ῥῆμα]: "Do not answer before you have heard, and do not put in any word in the middle of another's speech."

units.la: καὶ εἰς τὰ διδασκαλεῖα. ) Ne hoc quidem temerè ponit auctor: nam quod putet aliquis fuisse leue
units.tr: "καὶ εἰς τὰ διδασκαλεῖα" [καὶ εἰς τὰ διδασκαλεῖα]. The author does not put this in lightly either, for what someone might think a trifling matter

units.la: intrare in ludum literarium , id vero Athenis crimen capitale fuit. Lege enim Solonis poena capitis fuit conftituta, fi qui ludum literarium aut palæftram dum ibi erant difcipuli ingrederetur.quod cur à caftiffimo viro fuerit ita conftitutum , non eft difficile diuinare. Hanc igitur in legem committit ifte,& dum garrire cupit,fraudem capitalem admittit. Adi Æfchinem contra Timarchum. Sed videtur ei legi poftea derogatum, vel contraria lege , vel vfu ipfo & contraria confuetudine ; quod ex multis dialogorum Platonis locis licet intelligere. Vel Lyfidem vide.
units.tr: to enter a school was, at Athens, a capital crime. For by the law of Solon the penalty of death was laid down for anyone who entered a school or wrestling-ground while the pupils were there. It is not hard to guess why so chaste a man enacted it in this way. The fellow, then, who wants to chatter commits a capital offence under this law. See Aeschines against Timarchus. But it seems that this law was later repealed, either by a contrary law or by practice itself and contrary custom, as may be gathered from many passages in the dialogues of Plato. Or see the Lysis.

units.la: ἀρομαι δὲ ἐν Γοργίᾳ.] Scribendum προσμαρτυρῆσθαι[?] Attica confuetudine , pro fimplici μανθάνειν[?]. Sic apud Ariftophanem Vefpis.
units.tr: I would read the verb in Gorgias as προσμαρτυρῆσθαι [ἀρομαι δὲ ἐν Γοργίᾳ], an Attic usage in place of the plain μανθάνειν. So it is in Aristophanes' Wasps.

units.la: Τὶς παιδοτρίβαις καὶ διδασκάλοις.] Chiafmus eft: nam παιδοτρίβαι ad παλαίστρας refertur : διδάσκαλος ad διδασκαλεῖα. Æfchines in Timarchum , καὶ τὰς διδασκάλως τὰ διδασκαλεῖα, καὶ τὰς παιδοτρίβας τὰς παλαίστρας ἀνοίξειν[?]. Porrò παιδοτρίβης vertimus corporum exercitator , cum Latinis fcriptoribus : nam qui lanifta vertunt (in his eft vir eruditiffimus Demofthenis & Æfchinis interpres) ij neque Græcam neque Latinam vocem intellexerunt, Poffis & gymnafiarchum dicere.qua voce vfus & Cicero:γυμνασίαρχης αὐτὲ & παιδοτρίβης sæpe pro eodem ponuntur. vide Æfchinem. Item γυμνασίης & σωμασκιλὴς. Itaque Pythagoras quidam Laertio σωμασκιλὴς dicitur, Plinio exercitator ἀπλῶς.
units.tr: This is a chiasmus: παιδοτρίβαι refers to the palaestra, and διδάσκαλος to the schools (διδασκαλεῖα). Aeschines, against Timarchus: "the teachers will open the schools, and the trainers the wrestling-grounds" [καὶ τὰς διδασκάλως τὰ διδασκαλεῖα, καὶ τὰς παιδοτρίβας τὰς παλαίστρας ἀνοίξειν]. I translate παιδοτρίβης as "trainer of bodies", with the Latin writers. Those who render it "lanista" (in which group is the very learned translator of Demosthenes and Aeschines) understood neither the Greek nor the Latin word. One might also say gymnasiarch, a word Cicero used. γυμνασίαρχης and παιδοτρίβης are often used for the same thing; see Aeschines. Likewise γυμνασίης and σωμασκιλής. So Laertius calls a certain Pythagoras σωμασκιλής, while Pliny calls him simply exercitator.

units.la: Pag. 24. καὶ τὰς ἀπιέναι φάσκοντας.) Hoc etiam ἀδολέχη convenit : Horatius,
units.tr: Page 24. "And those who say they are going away" also suits the word ἀδολέχη. Horace:
"I made no reply. You wish, he said, to be gone, miserably;

units.la: Iamdudum video; sed nil agis: vsque tenebo, Perseguar.
units.tr: I have seen this for a long time, but you achieve nothing: I will hold on to you, I will pursue you."

units.la: τῷ ἐν Αεισοφῶντι ποτὲ ξυομένῳ τῇ ῥήτορι μά-χλῳ.) Notabis verborum traiectionem quae ambiguitatem parit: nam & cum μάχλῳ verba illa τῇ ῥήτορι iungi possunt: & cum Αεισοφῶντι iungi possunt: quod malo: & ita accipio τῇ ῥήτορι ξυομένῳ ποτὲ μάχλῳ. Traiectio est vt diximus. quod ἄῆμα mirum quàm sit frequens cum apud alios veteres Atticos tum imprimis apud Aristotelem, ex quo pauca animi causâ libet hic annotare. Historiarum libro tertio, de aorta vena loquens, ἀιρρώδης, inquit, ὅτι φλέψ, τὰ μὲν τελδλαῖα ἡ παντελῶς αὐτῆς. hoc est; τὰ μὲν τελδλαῖα αὐτῆς, ἡ παντελῶς. In quinto, de genere malacostracorum loquens, ὀχέϊεται ἡ ἀρχομένῳ πρὸς τῇ γῇ ἐαρ. pro ὀχέϊεται πρὸς τῇ γῇ ἀρχομένῳ ἐαρ. Eodem γίνεσθαι ἡ φάδοντες ἐν ἐν τῇ ἔαει τούτων, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ μεζωτάρῳ. In tertio De partibus τὰ μὲν ἄνω καὶ κάτω, ἐν ὅς μᾶλλον ὄντ ἄνω. elegantèr: sed obscuriuscule pro ἐν ὅς ἄνω μᾶλλον ὄντ. Item illud in eodem, τῷ γὰρ μᾶλλον ὄντ ἐξίστασθαι ἀκοσαι λεγόντων ἢ τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ κεφαλῷ ὡς ἀνθρώπων ἐπιγείσθαι τῇ ἀνθρώπων. & alibi locis sexcentis: sed & apud Ciceronem quoque similes traiectiones locis non paucis obseruare lector diligens poterit: quas videas sæpe doctos viros suis [illegible, ~12 letters] immutare. Verum ad rem. Ἐπ' Ἀεισοφῶντι non est, tempore Aristophontis, vt putarunt interpretes: sed id quod expressimus. Fuisse autem archontam Aristophontem anno tertio olympiadis centesimæ duodecimæ, certum ex Bibliotheca Diodori. Intelligit inclytam illam pugnâ ad Arbela pugnatam: quasi[?] etsi constat priore anno contigisse prætore non Aristophonte,sed Aristophane : nihilominus tamè vulgus Atheniensium anno illi, qui Aristophontem prætorem habuit , illam ascripsit : vel quia revera cædes Darij, in quo erat victoriæ summa, in annum illum incidit : sicut Arrianus ait : vel quia, vt disserè notat Diodorus , cùm eius victoriæ fama in Græciam pervenit,jam archon erat Aristophon: quod etiam Dionysius Halicarnasseus in epistola ad Ammæum docet. Aristophon verò iste qui fuerit, & cur oratorem illum appellet, vel mediocriter in historia Græca versati scire debent : vixit. n. Athenis æqualis Demostheni : ac pene in dicendi facultate par, si quidem ipsius Demosthenis testimonio stare volumus. Meminère locis pene infinitis & Demosthenes & Æschines : itémque Plutarchus, Athenæus, alij , quorum testimonia nihil attinet huc congerere. Hæc vera est, vt quidem censeo,istius loci interpretatiõ.Potest tamen etiam sine traiectione accipi: vt nimirum intelligatur nobilis illa controversia quæ fuit inter summinos[?] oratores Demosthenem & Æschinem : quod iudicium constat fuisse factum cum esset prætor Aristophon : quamuis multo ante fuisset postulatum: nam decem ipsis annis prius hanc multam Æschines à Ctesiphonte petierat Charonda magistratu. auctor Plutarchus. Hanc interpretationem si veram putarem , dicerem ϫῆ[?] ῥητόρων rescribi debere: nunc in priore & lectione & interpretatione acquiesco.
units.tr: Here the Greek has a hyperbaton, which produces the ambiguity. The words τῇ ῥήτορι can be joined with μάχλῳ, or with Ἀεισοφῶντι; I prefer the latter, and so I take it as τῇ ῥήτορι ξυομένῳ ποτὲ μάχλῳ. This hyperbaton, as I have said, is extremely common in the other early Attic writers, and above all in Aristotle, from whom I wish to note a few examples for interest. In the third book of the History of Animals, speaking of the aorta, he says ἀιρρώδης, ὅτι φλέψ, τὰ μὲν τελδλαῖα ἡ παντελῶς αὐτῆς, meaning τὰ μὲν τελδλαῖα αὐτῆς, ἡ παντελῶς. In the fifth book, speaking of the crustaceans, ὀχέϊεται ἡ ἀρχομένῳ πρὸς τῇ γῇ ἐαρ, for ὀχέϊεται πρὸς τῇ γῇ ἀρχομένῳ ἐαρ. In the same book, γίνεσθαι ἡ φάδοντες ἐν ἐν τῇ ἔαει τούτων, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ μεζωτάρῳ. In the third book On the Parts of Animals, τὰ μὲν ἄνω καὶ κάτω, ἐν ὅς μᾶλλον ὄντ ἄνω: elegantly, but rather obscurely, for ἐν ὅς ἄνω μᾶλλον ὄντ. Also that passage in the same book, τῷ γὰρ μᾶλλον ὄντ ἐξίστασθαι ἀκοσαι λεγόντων ἢ τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ κεφαλῷ ὡς ἀνθρώπων ἐπιγείσθαι τῇ ἀνθρώπων, and elsewhere in countless places. A careful reader may also observe similar transpositions in Cicero, in not a few places, which learned men often alter in their own copies. But to the point. Ἐπ' Ἀεισοφῶντι does not mean "in the time of Aristophon", as the interpreters have thought, but what I have expressed. It is certain from the Library of Diodorus that Aristophon was archon in the third year of the 112th Olympiad. He means that famous battle fought at Arbela; although it is agreed that it took place in the preceding year, when the praetor was not Aristophon but Aristophanes, nevertheless the Athenian crowd ascribed it to that year, the year in which Aristophon was praetor. Either because the slaughter of Darius, in which the chief point of the victory lay, really fell in that year, as Arrian says; or because, as Diodorus clearly notes, when the report of that victory reached Greece Aristophon was already archon, which Dionysius of Halicarnassus also shows in his letter to Ammaeus. Who this Aristophon was, and why he is called that orator, those moderately versed in Greek history ought to know: he lived at Athens, contemporary with Demosthenes, and nearly his equal in the art of speaking, if we wish to abide by Demosthenes' own testimony. Both Demosthenes and Aeschines, and likewise Plutarch, Athenaeus and others, mention him in almost countless places; there is no need to gather their testimonies here. This, as I think, is the true interpretation of that passage. It can nevertheless be taken without hyperbaton, so that it is understood as the famous dispute between the two greatest orators, Demosthenes and Aeschines. It is agreed that the trial took place while Aristophon was praetor, although it had been brought much earlier; for Aeschines had sought this fine from Ctesiphon ten years before, in the magistracy of Charondas, as Plutarch records. If I thought this interpretation the true one, I would say that ϫῆ[?] ῥητόρων ought to be rewritten; but as it is I rest content with the earlier reading and interpretation.

units.la: ἃ[?] μεταξὺ καταλιπόντες.] Μεταξὺ positum pro μεταξὺ λόγων, vel λέγοντα: aut etiam λεγομένων, vt in Luciani Philopseude, μεταξὺ λεγομένων ἀπιστῶν, ὠχύ-μλω[?].
units.tr: The word μεταξὺ is used for μεταξὺ λόγων, or λέγοντα, or even λεγομένων, as in Lucian's Philopseudes: μεταξὺ λεγομένων ἀπιστῶν.

units.la: Pag. 25. καὶ ὡς ἐν ὑγρῷ ἔζιν ἡ γλαῦξ[?].] A. Gellius de linguofis iftis, libro primo, Quorum lingua, ait, tam prodiga infrenisque fit, vt fluat semper effluétque collatione verborum teterrima: quod genus homines à Graecis significantissimo vocabulo λάλος appellatos. Ibidem ait importunos iftos locutores verbis humidis & lapsantibus diffluere. quae vim verborum Theophrasti aptissime exprimunt. Perfius paullo aliter cùm ait,
units.tr: Page 25. "And as the owl is in water." Aulus Gellius, in the first book, on those talkers: "Whose tongue is so profuse and unbridled that it always flows out in the most foul torrent of words; such men the Greeks called λάλοι, with a most expressive word." In the same place he says these tiresome talkers "flow away in moist and slippery words", which expresses the force of Theophrastus' words most aptly. Persius puts it somewhat differently:

units.la: —summa delumbe saliuaHoc natat in labris: & in vdo eft Maenas & Attin.
units.tr: "The thick spittle floats on the lips, and in the wet there are Maenas and Attis."
The comic poet who said it long ago put it well:

units.la: — ὡς γὰρ λάλοισιν ἐξ ἄκρηςἡ γλαῦξ ὡς ἂν τετευμένη[?].
units.tr: "For, as the owl is to chatterers, as if ..." (the rest of the line is corrupt in the text).

units.la: Genus porrò loquendi quo hîc Theophrastus vtitur, ἐν ὑγρῷ ἡ γλαῦξ, memini obseruare apud Orum Apollinem: vt apud Cedrenum ὑγρὸν γλαῦξ[?].
units.tr: I recall noting this kind of expression, "the owl in water", which Theophrastus uses here, in Horapollo; as in Cedrenus, "moist owl" [ὑγρὸν γλαῦξ].

units.la: τῆς χελιδόνων δόξειεν ἂν εἴη λαλίστερα[?].] Prouerbium eft, χελιδόνι λαλίστερα. Eft enim hirundo garrularum & κωτίλων auicularum: imò verò ἀλλ' μᾶλλον ἢ ἄλλη ὄρνις, inquit Arrianus libro primo. Alij tamen aliter prouerbium efferunt: vt τέτλα λαλίστερα: ficut apud Anacreontem. vel τευχόν λαλίστερα, vt notat Euftathius. vel etiam ἀνδρόν λαλίστερα: quò allusit Plautus Bacchidibus, initio. Alexis in Thrasone,
units.tr: "Chattier than the swallows." The proverb is χελιδόνι λαλίστερα, "chattier than a swallow", for the swallow is among the garrulous and chattering little birds; indeed, as Arrian says in the first book, it is more so than any other bird. Others, however, express the proverb differently, as τέττιξ λαλίστερα ("chattier than a cicada"), as in Anacreon; or τεῦχος, as Eustathius notes; or even ἀνδρόν, to which Plautus alluded at the beginning of the Bacchides. Alexis in Thrason:

units.la: — σὺ δ' ἐγὼ λαλισέρανΟὐ πώποτ' εἶδον, ὅτε κερκώσων γυναῖκαΟὐ κίτταν, ὡς ἀνδρόν, ἡ τευχόν, ἡ τέτλα[?].
units.tr: "But you, I have never seen you chattier when the women are weaving, not a swallow, not a cicada, not a ..."

units.la: extat hic locus apud Athenaeum, lib. quarto, fed mutilus. ita autem legendum vt scripsimus, ex membranis & veteribus grammaticis.
units.tr: This passage survives in Athenaeus, book four, but mutilated. It should be read as I have written it, from manuscripts and old grammarians.

units.la: ὥσαν αὐτὸν ἤδη καθεύδοντα[?] (&c.) Depravatum hunc locum ita (sed non nisi arbitrario iure) constituimus, ὥσαν αὐτὸν ἤδη καθεύδειν βακχυλίδα[?] κτλ., λέγοντα ἄτα λαλεῖν τι ἡμῖν. Est hoc garrulitatis cuiusdam summae indicium, si paterfamilias ferat aequo animo rogari se à suis pueris, (sive de liberis accipias, sive de vernulis) ut sibi somnum captantibus assideat, & fabellas narret: quo nimirum possit ipsis audientibus somnus obrepere. Enimvero vix dupondia[?] nutrix alumni sui paullo adultioris tales delicias[?] ferat. Atqui proprium hoc tamen illarum est munus: idque cum faciunt βαυκαλίζειν, vel βαυκαλᾶν Graecis dicuntur. Hesychius, βαυκαλᾶν, καλακοιμίζειν, τιθηλεῖν, παιδία μετ᾽ ᾠδῆς κοιμίζειν, dixe runt & βαυκᾶν pro eodem, ut & Eustathius & Hesychius docent. cum tamen apud Latinos aliud longè sit baubari, quod canibus proprie tribuitur. Hinc dictae καλακαυκαλίστις cantilenae nutricum, quibus cantandis somnum pueris conciliant: apud Athenaeum libro xiii. item ὑαύιον pro eodem. vide H. Fychium. Neniam Latinè possis dicere: veteres enim grammatici ad illud Horatii, Dicetur merito nox quoque nenia. naeniam interpretantur carmen soporiferum & somnolentum. Arnobius libro vii. somno occupari ut possint, lenes audienda sunt nenia. Apud Persium & ex Persio Hieronymum, lallare pueri dicuntur quos nutrix κατακαυκαλᾷ. Sic apud Graecos quoque, λάλα fuit παιδικὸν ἐπιφέρειν[?], ut apud Lucianum in Philopseude. Exemplum neniae istiusmodi habetur hoc in Theocriti Heraclisco, quod propter suauitatem ipsius non parcam ascribere. Ibi igitur mater cunas mouens ita gemellos suos καλλαυκαλᾶ[?].
units.tr: "As if he were already asleep" (etc.). I have restored this corrupt passage thus, though only by an arbitrary license: "as if he were already sleeping, ... Bacchylides, ... saying that they chatter something to us." It is a sure sign of extreme garrulity if a head of the household patiently bears being asked by his children (or by his household slaves) to sit beside them while they court sleep and tell stories, so that the listeners may steal into slumber. Indeed a nurse can scarcely bear such indulgences from her charge when he is somewhat older. Yet this is nevertheless their proper office, and when they perform it the Greeks say βαυκαλίζειν or βαυκαλᾶν. Hesychius glosses βαυκαλᾶν as καλακοιμίζειν, τιθηλεῖν, "to lull to sleep with song, to nurse"; they also said βαυκᾶν in the same sense, as Eustathius and Hesychius show. In Latin, however, baubari is quite different, a word properly applied to dogs. Hence the cradle-songs called καλακαυκαλίστις, with which nurses lull children to sleep; see Athenaeus, book 13. Likewise ὑαύιον is used in the same sense; see Hesychius. In Latin one may say nenia: the ancient grammarians, on Horace's line "night too will rightly be called a nenia", interpret nenia as a sleep-inducing and drowsy song. Arnobius, book 7: "to be lulled into sleep, they must hear gentle nenias." In Persius, and in Jerome after Persius, children are said to be lallare, which the nurse does when she κατακαυκαλᾷ them. So among the Greeks too, λάλα was a child's lullaby, as in Lucian's Philopseudes. An example of such a nenia is found in Theocritus' Heracliscus, which I will not hesitate to quote for its sweetness. There the mother, rocking the cradle, thus lulls her twins [καλλαυκαλᾶ]:

units.la: Εὕδετ' ἐμὰ βρέφεα γλυκερὸν ἡχὴ ἱέρσιμον ὕπνον[?], Εὕδετ' ἐμὰ ψυχά, δύ' ἀδελφιώ, ἄδ' ἔα τέκνα[?], Ὅλλοι ἀνύσουσιν[?], ἡ ὀλλοι ἀὼ ἴκοισι[?].
units.tr: Sleep, my babes, sweet slumber; sleep, my soul, my two little brothers, these children. They will bring rest, or they will come to you. [Εὕδετ' ἐμὰ βρέφεα γλυκερὸν ἡχὴ ἱέρσιμον ὕπνον, Εὕδετ' ἐμὰ ψυχά, δύ' ἀδελφιώ, ἄδ' ἔα τέκνα, Ὅλλοι ἀνύσουσιν, ἡ ὀλλοι ἀὼ ἴκοισι]

units.la: Meminere amplius harum cantilenarum, quibus vsæ olim nutrices, Quintilianus lib. 1. cap x. Ælianus in historiâ Animalium, Tertullianus & Nonius 111. Dionysiacorum.
units.tr: You will find more of these lullabies that nurses once used in Quintilian, book 1, chapter 10; Aelian in his History of Animals; Tertullian; and Nonius in book 3 of the Dionysiaca.

units.la: λαλεῖν τι ἡμῖν.) Debuerat dicere αὐτὰς: ita enim postulabant præcedentia: sed mutauit rationem orationis, sicut sæpe fit ab optimis scriptoribus. & est breuis quasi προτωποποιΐας, vel μιμήσεως species. Scholiastes Pindari, μεγαλύνειν τὸ λόγος solet appellare: Longinus λόγος μεγαλύνειν. eum vide.
units.tr: "to speak something to us." He ought to have written "to them," for the preceding words required it, but he changed the construction, as the best writers often do. It is a brief form of prosopopoeia, or of imitation. The scholiast on Pindar usually calls this μεγαλύνειν τὸ λόγος, and Longinus calls it λόγος μεγαλύνειν; see him.

units.la: Ἡ δὲ λογοποιία.) Vide ad caput ἀδολεσχίας. Nos famigeratorem Latinè dicimus: & hominem λογοποιόν, famigeratorem, vt in Trinummo Plautus. Is planè est quem vulgò appellamus forgeur de nouvelles. hoc est, nouorum rumorum, quos Demosthenes λόγος μαλακὸς vocat, fictores, siue, vt cum Plauto dicam, gerulifigulos. Sanè Impp. in extremo Codice gerulum nuntiorum appellant, qui noui aliquid nuntiat: isti autem non nuntiant tantùm, sed etiam fingunt: quare si placet gerulifigulî dicantur. Ammianus Marcellinus rumigerulos nuncupat. Seneca sermones gestare dixit pro λογοποιεῖν, epistola c x x i i i. Pessimum, ait, genus hominum videbatur qui verba gestarent. Sunt quidam qui vitia gestant. Demosthenes λόγος πλάτῃ [?] in Philippicis. Οἱ δ[?], inquit, λίσς πλάτωντες ἕκαστ@ [?] ἀξιερχόμεϑα [?]. Hoc porrò genus hominum multum suisse olim Athenis certissimum est: eius enim rei testem habemus omni exceptione maiorem D. Lucam in Actis, cui concinit, vt mox indicabimus, multis locis Demosthenes, testis & ipse locupletissimus. Notum est quod scribit Cæsar de veteribus Gallis super hoc nouorum rumorum aucupio. sed & Romanis vitium idem scriptores ipsorum obiiciunt: quorum princeps Iuuenalis, satyra v 1. de nobilibus mulieribus loquens:
units.tr: "Tale-bearing" (ἡ δὲ λογοποιία). See the note on the chapter on babbling (ἀδολεσχία). In Latin we call such a man a famigerator, and the Greek λογοποιός is the same, as Plautus uses famigerator in the Trinummus. He is exactly the man we commonly call a forgeur de nouvelles, that is, a maker of fresh rumours, whom Demosthenes calls a "soft talk" (λόγος μαλακός). Or, to use Plautus' word, they are gerulifigulos, carriers and fabricators. The emperors, at the end of the Code, call a bearer of news, one who reports something new, a gerulus nuntiorum; but these men do not merely report, they also invent, so they may fairly be called gerulifigulî. Ammianus Marcellinus names them rumigerulos. Seneca, in letter 123, used sermones gestare for λογοποιεῖν: "The worst kind of men," he says, "seemed to be those who carry words. There are some who carry vices." Demosthenes, in the Philippics, uses the phrase λόγος πλάτῃ. "Those who spread idle talk," he says, "we give ear to." That this kind of man was very common at Athens long ago is quite certain; for we have a witness above all exception, St Luke in the Acts, whom Demosthenes, himself a most abundant witness, supports in many places, as I shall point out shortly. It is well known what Caesar writes of the ancient Gauls, who hunted after new rumours in this way. But the same writers also charge the Romans with this fault, and the chief of them is Juvenal, who in Satire 6, speaking of noble women, says:
Instantem, he says, the Armenian king, and the Parthian comet
She is first to see, and she receives in the gates the fresh reports and rumours

units.la: Excipit ad portas : quosdam facit isse Niphaten
units.tr: Some she makes go off to Niphates

units.la: In populos, magnóque illic cuncta arua teneri
units.tr: among the peoples, and that there all the fields are held
by a flood, that cities totter, that lands sink down,

units.la: Quocunque in triuio, cuicunque est obuia narrat.
units.tr: she tells whatever she meets, at whatever crossroads, to whomever it is.

units.la: Pap. 2 5. κα[?]αλὼν τὸ ἦϑ@ [?]. Accipe hic τὸ ἦϑ@ vt sæpe apud Græcos, maximè apud Aristotelem pro eo quod Latinis est os vel vultus: quam vocem censuit M. Tullius Græcè dici non posse. Illi sanè pro eo dicunt sæpe ἦϑ@, aut τὸ ἴϑι προσωπα ἦϑ@, vel τὸ ἐπαυρομένον ἦϑ@. Inde illa apud Aristotelem in Physiognomonicis, καὶ τὰ ἤϑη φυσιογνωμονεῖν, & ἐκ τῶν ἐπαυρομένων ἤϑων. Plutarchus in Alexandro magis proprie τὰ ἀξι τῶν ὀψεων εἴδη, οἷς ἐμφαίνεται τὸ ἦϑ@. Sulpicor autem μεγαλὼν legendum, non καζαλών. Sic dixit Aristoteles in eodem eleganti libello, τὸ ἦϑ@ τὸ ἴϑι τῶ προσωπα μεγαλ-λέγε: λέξιν : quòd paullò antè dixerat, καὶ χρόνως[?] τινὰς τὰ ἤδη ἃ τὰ αὐτὰ ἀλλ' ἑτέρων ἔχειν. Contrarium est apud Plutarchum in Agide, καθιςάναι τὸ πρόσωπον : & in eiusdem Demetrio σωεσῶτι προσώπῳ προσιέναι[?]. Si cui magis arrideat vulgata lectio, καταζάλων[?], aut minima mutatione καταζάλλων τὸ ἦθος[?], erit mores suos & ingenium exprimens. id enim interdum est καταζάλλειν[?], proferre in medium & prodere. Inde λόγον καταζάλλειν[?] apud Plutarchum in Fabio. Darius in epistola ad Heraclitum, Καταζείληναι λόγον[?] ἐπὶ φύσεως. Scholiastes Pindari, πολλαὶ ἀεὶ τὰ Κινύρα καταζειζλωλίας[?] ἰσοεῖα. Sic apud Aristotelem, πολλοὶ καταζειζλωλίας λόγοι.
units.tr: "Pap. 2 5." Take τὸ ἦθος here as the Greeks often do, and especially Aristotle, for what the Latins call the face or countenance. M. Tullius thought this word could not be rendered in Greek. The Greeks often use ἦθος in this sense, or τὸ ἴδιον πρόσωπον ἦθος, or τὸ ἐπαυρόμενον ἦθος. Hence Aristotle's phrase in the Physiognomonics, "to read the character from the features" (καὶ τὰ ἤθη φυσιογνωμονεῖν), and "from the apparent characters" (ἐκ τῶν ἐπαυρομένων ἤθων). Plutarch in the Life of Alexander says more precisely "the forms of the appearance by which the character is shown" (τὰ ἀξιὰ τῶν ὄψεων εἴδη, οἷς ἐμφαίνεται τὸ ἦθος). I think μεγαλῶν should be read rather than καταζάλων. Aristotle used the same phrase in that elegant little book: "the character is shown by the face" (τὸ ἦθος τὸ ἴδιον τῷ πρόσωπα μεγαλύνει λέξιν), which he had said a little earlier, that some people have the same character but different faces. The opposite is found in Plutarch's Agis, "to compose the face" (καθιστάναι τὸ πρόσωπον), and in his Demetrius, "to approach with a composed face." If the vulgar reading καταζάλων pleases someone more, or with the smallest change καταζάλλων τὸ ἦθος, it will mean "expressing his manners and disposition." For καταζάλλειν sometimes means to bring forward and reveal. Hence λόγον καταζάλλειν in Plutarch's Fabius. Darius, in his letter to Heraclitus, has "to bring forth a word about nature" (καταζείληναι λόγον ἐπὶ φύσεως). A scholiast on Pindar: "many always bring out their Cinyra ..." (πολλαὶ ἀεὶ τὰ Κινύρα καταζειζλωλίας ἰσοεῖα). So in Aristotle, "many words of ..." (πολλοὶ καταζειζλωλίας λόγοι).

units.la: καὶ Θησέων ἐρωτᾶν. ] Varie exponi potest hic locus: estque similis illi Lucae in actis de Petro. καὶ Θηβαλῶν ἔκλαυε. de quo lege Theophylactum.
units.tr: "and to ask about Theseus" (καὶ Θησέων ἐρωτᾶν). This place can be explained in various ways, and it is like that passage of Luke in the Acts about Peter, "and he wept for Thebes" (καὶ Θηβαλῶν ἔκλαυε). On this see Theophylact.

units.la: μὴ λέγεταί τι χαμηρότερον. ] Diuus Lucas Actorum capite xvii. Ἀθηναῖοι δὲ πάντες, καὶ οἱ ἐπιδημοῦντες ξένοι εἰς οὐδὲν ἕτερον ηὐκαίρουν ἢ λέγειν τι καὶ ἀκούειν καινότερον. Hanc lenitatem suis ciuibus saepe exprobrat Demosthenes. In ea oratione qua respondet epistolae Philippi, Ἡμεῖς δ', inquit, εἰρήσεται δ' τ' ἀ-[?]λλ' ἀδὲν τοιοῦντες ἐνθάδε καθήμεθα, μέλλοντες ἀεὶ, ἢ ἀφιζόμεθα[?], ὁ πιωθανόμενοι[?] τῶν ἀγορὰν, ἐπὶ λέγειν κεώτερον. Similis querela in secunda Olynthiaca: item in tertia. Plutarchus Περὶ φιλαυτοφιλοσωμίας, οἱ πολυπράγμονες φιλοῦντες τὸ ἀρχαῖον, εἰς τὸ βῆμα καὶ τὸ ἀγορὰν καὶ τοὺς λιμένας ἀθρωπῶντ[?], μή τι καινόν; &c.
units.tr: "nothing is said too lowly." St Luke, Acts chapter 17: "All the Athenians and the strangers who lived there had no other leisure than to tell or to hear some newer thing." Demosthenes often reproaches his fellow citizens for this curiosity. In the speech in reply to Philip's letter he says: "We, however, sit here doing nothing, always intending to do something, or we go to the market and ask whether there is any newer thing." A similar complaint is in the second Olynthiac, and likewise in the third. Plutarch, in On Curiosity (Περὶ φιλαυτοφιλοσωμίας?), says: the busybodies, loving the old, go about to the platform, the market and the harbours, asking whether there is anything new, etc.

units.la: ἀωχῆσθ[?] καινῶν λόγων.) Vsitatius, καπαῖς λόγοις[?], vt apud Athenaeum in sexto, & Maximum Tyrium, atque alios: verùm ita magis Atticum. Plato De republica, libro primo, Εὐωχῷ τὰ λέξι, ἐφη, Σαρῥῶν. sic ἐςιὰν καινῶν λόγων ἐ σκέψεων [?], initio noni eiusdem operis. & cum tertio casu similiter, ἀμοφόρῖς ἐσιώυλῳ μάχας [?], apud Lycophronem. Affinis locutio cui respondet φαγεῖν ῥήματα apud Aristophanem in Gerytade, vt in Aulularia Plauti comedere sermonem. & τὰ λεγόμενα καταζήνη [?], quod vulgo solitum dici ait Chrysippus apud Galenum, libro tertio De dogmate Hippo. & Plat. & alia id genus multa.
units.tr: "fed on new words" (ἀωχῆσθ καινῶν λόγων). The more usual form is καπαῖς λόγοις, as in Athenaeus book 6, Maximus of Tyre, and others; but the phrase here is more Attic. Plato in the Republic, book 1, says "Feed on the words, said Sarpedon" (Εὐωχῷ τὰ λέξι, ἔφη, Σαρπηδών). So at the beginning of book 9 of the same work, "feeding on new words and considerations." Likewise with the dative, "feeding on the battle" (ἀμοφόρις ἐσιώυλῳ μάχας), in Lycophron. A similar expression is φαγεῖν ῥήματα in Aristophanes' Gerytades, as comedere sermonem in Plautus' Aulularia. And τὰ λεγόμενα καταζήνη is what Chrysippus, as quoted by Galen in book 3 of On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato, says is commonly said; and there are many other expressions of this kind.

units.la: χαὶ ἔςιν ἀπὸ ἡ ςραλιώτης.] Hic est mos mentientium, vt falsiloquiis suis, vel iureiurando fidem adstruant, vel testium quos nemo requirit laudatione, vel circunstantiarum adiectione. Quintilianus declamatione xv i i i. Necesse est contentiosius loquaris quod probare non possis: & affirmationem sumit ex homine quicquid non habet ex veritate. Eleganter Æschines de Demosthene loquens Περὶ παραπρεσβείας [?]. Hγεῖται ἡ inquit, ὡσπερ τὶ ἐλδηντας [?], τοῦ λόγων, ὅρκῳ καὶ ἀναχωρῶν ὀφθαλμῷ [?]· ἐ τὰ μὲν γενόμενα ὁ μόνον ὡς ἐςι λέγει [?]. ἀλλὰ ἐ τῷ ἡμέραν ὃν ἢ ὅπως ἐγένετο [?]. καὶ προσιθὲν τινὸς ὄνομα πλατάνου ὃς ἔτυχε ἀφαρὰν [?], μιμάσθαι ὡς τ' αλλὸν λέγονσα [?]. Sic scribendus est locus hic Æschinis elegantissimus: quo cum esse nihil queat apertius, miror interpretem doctiss. tam infeliciter hic esse versatum. Tale illud etiam capite vltimo, καὶ ἀποσιθεὶς τιθαν ἱκάσοις τούτων ὀνομαζε [?].
units.tr: "and there is from the lying-in-wait" (καὶ ἔστιν ἀπὸ ἡ ςραλιώτης). This is the habit of liars, who support their falsehoods either by swearing an oath, or by appealing to witnesses whom no one asks for, or by adding circumstances. Quintilian, declamation 18: "You must needs speak more contentiously about what you cannot prove; and whatever he does not have from truth, he takes from assertion." Aeschines speaks elegantly of Demosthenes in On the False Embassy: "He is led," he says, "as if by some ... of words, with an oath and turning away the eye; he does not say what happened as it was, but not on the day it happened, or how it happened. And adding the name of some plane tree that happened to be there, he imitates as though he were speaking of another." These words of Aeschines are the most elegant; they should be written thus, and since nothing can be clearer, I am surprised that so learned an interpreter should have gone so wrong here. Similar is that phrase in the last chapter, "and having set aside ... of these he names" (καὶ ἀποσιθεὶς τιθαν ἱκάσοις τούτων ὀνομαζε). [Sic.]

units.la: Λύκων ὁ ἐρλοάςῳ.) Puto ea aetate notum magis quam nobilem Athenis fuisse Lyconem istum: qui vel manceps erat & redemptor certarum rerum publico praestandarum: vel simpliciter artifex operas locare solitus. nam interdum ἐρσολάζω[?] est relatū, τῷ ἐρσοδότῃ[?]. & significat idem ac χειροτέχνης. Artemidorus libro primo ἀιδεὶ χειροτέχνη[?] ἀλαζόν' πολλῶν δ' ἀκούεται ἐρσοδοτής[?].
units.tr: "Lycon the hirer" (Λύκων ὁ ἐρλοάςῳ). I think this Lycon was known at Athens in that age more than he was noble; he was either a contractor and lessee of certain public works, or simply a craftsman accustomed to hire out his labour. For sometimes ἐργολαβέω is said of the one who takes the work from the employer (τῷ ἐργοδότῃ), and it means the same as χειροτέχνης, a manual worker. Artemidorus, book 1: "a manual worker, a boaster; but an employer (ἐργοδότης) is heard of by many."

units.la: αἱ μὲν οὖν ἀναφοραὶ τῆς λόγων θεαῦται εἰσι[?].) Λόγων ἀναφορὰ est auctoris laudatio à quo te audisse dicas: id enim est διαφέρειν. Plato in Apologia, εἰς ἀξιόλογων τ' λέγων ἀνοίσω. Alio sensu utitur hac voce idem Theophrastus,in libello De odoribus, cū ait, ἐν ἀμφοῖν ἢ φίλον ὡς ἀεὶ πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον ἐ τέλειον ὧ ἡμῖν ἡ ἀναφορὰ[?]· πᾶς γὰρ τέχνη σοχάζεται τῶν[?]. Sic emendamus hunc locum in vulgatis codicibus depravatum, neque à magno Turnebo restitutum.
units.tr: "The references of speeches are theatrical (αἱ μὲν οὖν ἀναφοραὶ τῆς λόγων θεαῦται εἰσι)." "Reference of speeches" (λόγων ἀναφορά) is the citing of an author from whom you say you have heard something, for that is what διαφέρειν means. Plato in the Apology: "I shall bring up (ἀνοίσω) something from worthy speakers." The same Theophrastus uses this word in a different sense in his little book On Odours, where he says: "in both of these there is a love of always going towards the better, not towards the perfect, which is our reference (ἀναφορά)..." For every art aims at ... Thus we correct this passage, which is corrupted in the printed copies, and which the great Turnebus did not restore.

units.la: Quis nescit vel tantillum in philosophia Aristotelis & Theophrasti versatus, bonis artibus finem duplicem esse propositum? ut vel emendent naturæ peccata:vel inchoatam illam & imperfectam adiuvent, atque perficiant?
units.tr: Who does not know, if he has even a little acquaintance with the philosophy of Aristotle and Theophrastus, that good arts have a double purpose: either to correct the faults of nature, or to help and perfect that which is begun but imperfect?

units.la: Pag. 27. ὧν ἀδελφὸν ἂν ἔχοι Φιλαδέλφου[?].) hoc est, quorum nomina nemini possint excidisse, vel esse incognita. Hæc sententia ferri potest: mihi tamen magis probabatur Φιλαδέλφου[?]: quod significat coarguere & reprehendere. Herodotus libro 11. ἐπιλαμβάνεται ἡ μήτηρ τῆς παιδός[?]. Francocelte, se prendre à quelcun. Igitur mens erit, solere τὸν λοξογράφον[?] eiusmodi auctores eorū quæ dicat laudare, quibuscum agere nemo possit, qui velit ipsos mendacii conuincere. Quomodo autem? quia vel fingit penitus suos auctores, vel ad quosdam refert ita ignobiles & paucis notos, ut etsi nomen scias, tamen ἔργον sit eos reperire. Sanè nihil æquè reformidant famigeratores isti, quàm ne vsque ab stirpe exquiratur auctoritas, unde quicque auditum dicant. quare hoc ne fieri possit, cauere diligenter solent. Οἱ ἀλαζόνες ὅταν τι ψεύδονται, ἀδεῖα[?] καὶ ἀλαζῶν πειρῶνται λέγειν, φοβούμενοι τὸν ἔλεγχον. appellat oratores ἀλαζόνες, homines mendaces & vanos: sic enim Atheniẹ́ses eam vocem vsurpabant, vt notat scholiastes Aristophanis: & ἀλαζονεύεσθαι[?] eisdem est mentiri.
units.tr: Page 27. ὧν ἀδελφὸν ἂν ἔχοι Φιλαδέλφου[?]: that is, whose names could never have slipped anyone's memory or be unknown. This sense may be put forward, but I myself preferred Φιλαδέλφου[?], which means to refute and rebuke. Herodotus, book 11: ἐπιλαμβάνεται ἡ μήτηρ τῆς παιδός[?], to take someone to task. The meaning, then, is that such a man, who praises the authorities for what he says, is one with whom no one could deal if he wished to prove them liars. How so? Either he invents his authorities altogether, or he refers to some so obscure and little known that, even if you know the name, it is a labour to find them. Certainly these rumour-mongers dread nothing so much as that the source of what they report should be traced right back to its origin. So they take careful pains that this cannot happen. Οἱ ἀλαζόνες ὅταν τι ψεύδονται, ἀδεῖα[?] καὶ ἀλαζῶν πειρῶνται λέγειν, φοβούμενοι τὸν ἔλεγχον [The boasters, when they tell a lie, try to speak with confidence and bravado, fearing refutation]. The orators call ἀλαζόνες men who are liars and vain; for so the Athenians used the word, as the scholiast on Aristophanes observes; and ἀλαζονεύεσθαι[?] means the same as to lie.

units.la: ] Etiam hic meminisse lectorem velim eius quod alibi diximus: quæcunque hoc libro continentur, ea non ficta esse ab auctore exempla: sed e vita quotidiana desumpta: & ex iis quæ vere facta dictáve essent, hunc librum esse concinnatum. Hoc posito iam pene annum illum inuenimus quo liber iste à Theophrasto est scriptus. Non enim dubitare debemus exempla illa falsorum rumorum quæ hoc capite habentur, illis temporibus esse accommodata, quibus hæc scribebantur. Quare statuamus audacter, non longe ab olympiade decimaquinta hæc scripta fuisse: quando necesse omnino est vt falsus hic rumor qui istis verbis continetur sub finem eius olympiadis fictus, & per Athenas sparsus ac disseminatus fuerit. Referendum enim istud est ad breue illud tempus quo Polysperchon regnum Macedoniæ, tanquam tutor regiæ sobolis, administrauit. Functus est eo munere primus post obitum Alexādri, Perdiccas: deinde Pitho & Arridæus, cum in Ægypto Perdiccas periisset: postea ad Antipatrum ea cura est delata, coactis Pithone & Arridæo sese administratione omni abdicare. Tandem post Antipatri obitum & cura illa siue tutela, & totius regni Macedonici summa ad Polysperchontem ex ordinatione Antipatri morientis peruenit. non sine magna Cafandri, qui fuit Antipatri filius, indignatione. unde illæ tantæ inter ipsum & Polysperchontem inimicitiæ: nec inimicitiæ solùm, sed bella etiam sæuissima: de quibus habes apud Iustinum, Orosium, imprimis verò Diodorum, libro duodevigesimo.
units.tr: Here too I would have the reader remember what I have said elsewhere: that the examples contained in this book are not invented by the author, but are taken from everyday life, and that the book was put together from things that were truly done or said. Granting this, we can now almost determine the year in which Theophrastus wrote this book. For we must not doubt that the examples of false rumours in this chapter were suited to the times in which they were written. Let us therefore boldly affirm that these things were written not long after the fifteenth Olympiad; for the false rumour contained in these words must necessarily have been invented near the end of that Olympiad and spread and circulated through Athens. It must be referred to that brief period in which Polysperchon governed the kingdom of Macedonia as guardian of the royal line. Perdiccas was the first to hold that office after the death of Alexander; then Pithon and Arrhidaeus, after Perdiccas had perished in Egypt; afterwards the charge was transferred to Antipater, Pithon and Arrhidaeus being compelled to give up all administration. Finally, after Antipater's death, both the guardianship and the supreme command of the whole Macedonian kingdom passed to Polysperchon by Antipater's dying arrangement, not without great indignation on the part of Cassander, Antipater's son. Hence those great enmities between him and Polysperchon, and not only enmities but the fiercest wars; of which you have an account in Justin, Orosius, and above all in Diodorus, book 18.

units.la: (ὁ βασιλεὺς[?].) Arrideus, Alexandri magni frater, homo ἀνόητος[?], nec minus tutoris quàm liberi Alexandri indigens. Regnauit in Macedonia annos sex & menses aliquot, estque de patris nomine, Philippus appellatus. De eodem accipienda, quæ Plutarchus narrat in Phocione extremo.
units.tr: (ὁ βασιλεὺς[?].) Arrhidaeus, brother of Alexander the Great, a man ἀνόητος[?] [without understanding], needing a guardian no less than Alexander's child did. He reigned in Macedonia six years and some months, and he was called Philip after his father's name. What Plutarch relates at the end of his Life of Phocion should be understood of this same man.
(καὶ πάντας[?] συμφωνεῖν.) It should be written πάντας[?] συμφωνεῖν.

units.la: καὶ πόλιν τὸν ζωμὸν γελοῖον[?]. ) Hæc est lectio quæ in veteribus membranis reperitur, ut docti homines testantur: at in recentioribus libris est φόνον pro ζωμόν. Valeat verò hîc vetus dictum, Quod antiquius, id melius. Vera enim lectio & germana est ζωμὸν non φόνον. Est autem translatio, è triuio quipem, imò è culina petita: sed quæ illi non malè conueniat, cuius hîc sustinet auctor personam: addo etiam quæ sordida sit potius quàm inepta: rem enim ipsam aptè sic satis exprimit. Sic dixit Latinus comicus fartum facere ex hostibus: translatione è culina itidem petita. Aristophanes [illegible, ~8 letters] ποιεῖν ἐκ τινός. Amat Theophraftus, sicut & comici eorum quos loquentes introducit, ineptias & inelegantes elegantias retinere. Profectò nisi ego vehementissimè fallor, vox ζωμὸς non est imperiti librarij partus, sed ingenuus ἀπὸ τῆς φωνῆς. Idem sentio de voce κλαδ[?] capite [illegible, ~6 letters] μικροφιλοτιμίας.
units.tr: καὶ πόλιν τὸν ζωμὸν γελοῖον[?].) This is the reading found in old manuscripts, as learned men attest; but in more recent books the reading is φόνον instead of ζωμόν. Let the old saying hold here: what is older is better. For the true and genuine reading is ζωμὸν, not φόνον. It is a figure taken from the street, indeed, or rather from the kitchen; yet it suits well enough the character whom the author here impersonates. I would add that it is coarse rather than foolish, for it expresses the thing itself aptly enough. So the Latin comic poet said to make hash of enemies, a figure likewise drawn from the kitchen. Aristophanes [illegible in the scan] ποιεῖν ἐκ τινός. Theophrastus, like the comic poets whose speakers he introduces, likes to retain such absurdities and inelegant elegances. Indeed, unless I am greatly mistaken, the word ζωμὸς is not the product of an ignorant copyist, but a native word derived from ἀπὸ τῆς φωνῆς. I think the same of the word κλαδ[?] at the beginning of [illegible] μικροφιλοτιμίας.

units.la: ᾧ ἐν Γίς ap. ) Demosthenes etiam τὰς ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς [?] προ magistratibus interdum dicit: vel ἐν τῇς π. nam utrumque vsurpat.
units.tr: ᾧ ἐν Γίς ap.) Demosthenes too sometimes says τὰς ἐπὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς [?] of magistrates, and sometimes ἐν τῇς π.; for he uses both.

units.la: Pag. 28. καὶ πάντα διξιῶν. ) Malim καὶ ταῦτα δ[?]. emendaumus autem quae sequuntur: & illud πῶς εἴωθε, interrogatiuè, ἐξ μὲν legimus, vt passim apud Atticos. cui simile est τὰς δοξὰς, quod & ipsum solet venuste interiici. Exempla passim obuia: vt mirum sit offendisse in tam plana via, & tam clara luce doctos homines. Est tamen vbi aliter haec verba collocentur, Themistius oratione nona, [illegible, ~8 letters]; [illegible, ~10 letters]; atque hoc minus est vsitatum.
units.tr: Page 28. καὶ πάντα διξιῶν.) I would prefer καὶ ταῦτα δ[?]. I emend the following words too; and I read ἐξ μὲν, and that πῶς εἴωθε is interrogative, as often in the Attic writers. Similar to this is τὰς δοξὰς, which is also customarily inserted with elegance. Examples are found everywhere, so it is remarkable that learned men should have stumbled on so plain a road and in such clear light. Yet there are places where these words are arranged otherwise: Themistius, in his ninth oration [illegible]; but this order is less usual.

units.la: πεδαύζω[?]) Scitum est enim illud Demosthenis apud Plutarchum, Μέγα ... [illegible, ~12 letters] Plurimum ad fidem momenti habet tenor, & ipsa dicentis actio. neque hoc praetermittunt dicendi magistri. Persius,
units.tr: πεδαύζω[?]) For that saying of Demosthenes in Plutarch is apt: Μέγα ... [illegible]. The tone and the very delivery of the speaker carry the greatest weight for belief, and the masters of rhetoric do not neglect this. Persius:
You will weep, you who wish to accuse me with a complaint.

units.la: ἐν[?] τὸ τῆς τύχης. ) interpretes videntur ἐνμὲν legisse: sed ἐν ἐν interrogatiuè legas, nihil erit cur hanc lectionem mutetur. Planudes Hegio Ca-preolus.
units.tr: ἐν[?] τὸ τῆς τύχης.) The translators seem to have read ἐνμὲν; but if you read ἐν ἐν as an interrogative, there is no reason to change this reading. Planudes, Hegio, Capreolus.

units.la: Sed [illegible, ~5 letters] fortuna humana sequi, atque ... Nam est illud Sophoclis, τύχη γὰρ [illegible, ~8 letters], & Terentij, O fortuna, vt nunquam perpetuò es bona.
units.tr: But [illegible] to follow human fortune, and ... For there is that saying of Sophocles, τύχη γὰρ [illegible], and that of Terence: O fortune, how you are never good for long.

units.la: ἀλλ' οὐ [illegible, ~6 letters]. Lego, ἐχωσιν[?] γὰρ [illegible, ~5 letters]. Est simile apud Sophoclem [illegible, ~10 letters], ἐν ἐν [illegible, ~4 letters] ἀνδ᾽ ὅσα ζῆλε [?] πεέφες.& Nafonis, Cernite sim qualis, qui modo talis eram. Valet hic locus ad excitádam miseri-cordiam mirum quantum: nihil enim est tam miserabile quàm ex beato miser. Marcus Tullius De inuentione primo, Primus locus est misericordiae per quem, quibus in bonis fuerit, & nunc quibus in malis sit ostenditur. Græci magistri ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων εὐξήσιν [?] vocant, & esse μέγιστον τόπον αὐξήσεως [?] docent. Tale illud in Menaechmis,
units.tr: ἀλλ' οὐ [illegible]. I read ἐχωσιν[?] γὰρ [illegible]. There is a similar passage in Sophocles [illegible], and in Ovid: Look upon what I am now, who was such a short while ago. This place is wonderfully useful for arousing pity, for nothing is so pitiable as a man going from happy to wretched. Marcus Tullius, On Invention, book 1: The first place of pity is shown by describing what good things a man once had and what evils he now suffers. The Greek masters call this ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων εὐξήσιν[?], the increase from contraries, and teach that it is μέγιστον τόπον αὐξήσεως[?], the greatest topic of amplification. Such is that line in the Menaechmi:

units.la: Heu hercle morbum acrem ac durum! dij vestram fidem,
units.tr: Good heavens, what a sharp and hard sickness! Gods, your faithfulness!

units.la: Vel hic qui insanit, quàm valuit paullo prius!
units.tr: Or this man who is mad, how strong he was a little while ago!

units.la: Cicero exul Attico, Possum obliuisci qui fuerim, non sentire qui sim? Græci hoc solent dicere ἐξ οἴων εἰς οἷα, quod alibi monebamus. Basilius magnus loquens de inuidia, χαὶ ἀθυμῶντι μᾶλλον ἢ συνδιαφέρεται, ὀδυρομένῳ ἢ συνδακρύει, χαὶ τὴν μεταβολὴν τῶν βίων ἐξ ἐπὶ εἰς οἷα μεταπίπτοντα καλουμένην. & sic alibi vir ille sanctissimus non semel. Apud Aristotelem tamen in Rhetoricis Iphicrates dicens ἐξ οἴων εἰς οἷα contrarium potius significabat: non enim misericordiam iis verbis captabat: sed laudes suas amplificabat, vt idem philosophus alio loco eiusdem operis declarat. quod hîc obiter dixisse liceat.
units.tr: Cicero, in exile, to Atticus: Can I forget what I was, and not feel what I am? The Greeks are accustomed to say ἐξ οἴων εἰς οἷα, which I have pointed out elsewhere. Basil the Great, speaking of envy: καὶ ἀθυμῶντι μᾶλλον ἢ συνδιαφέρεται, ὀδυρομένῳ ἢ συνδακρύει, καὶ τὴν μεταβολὴν τῶν βίων ἐξ ἐπὶ εἰς οἷα μεταπίπτοντα καλουμένην [it rejoices with the one who is downcast rather than sharing his distress, weeps with the one who laments, and... the change of lives called going from one state to another]; and so that most holy man elsewhere, not once. In Aristotle's Rhetoric, however, Iphicrates, speaking ἐξ οἴων εἰς οἷα, meant rather the opposite: for he was not seeking pity with those words, but magnifying his own praises, as the same philosopher declares in another place of the same work. This I may be allowed to note in passing.

units.la: τί πολὶ βασιλεύς λοιδορούμενοι.] Cum omnia nostra dicta, factaque ad certum aliquem finem referri debeant, miror, inquit Theophrastus, quid sit illud quò tendant οἱ λοιδορούμενοι. est autem nullus, honestus quidem, finis ipsis propositus: ideo Demosthenes, ἀνοήτως inquit οἱ λοιδορούμενοι. verissimè & prudentissimè. Tales enim sunt omnino illi λογοποιοί de quibus loquitur hîc Theophrastus, &
units.tr: τί πολὶ βασιλεύς λοιδορούμενοι.) Since all our words and deeds ought to be referred to some definite end, I wonder, says Theophrastus, what end those who revile one another are aiming at. In truth they have no honourable end set before them; therefore Demosthenes says that the revilers act ἀνοήτως [foolishly], most truly and most wisely. For such indeed are those λογοποιοί of whom Theophrastus speaks here, and

units.la: qui proprie sic dicuntur. Nam quibus λόγοιοι[?] teli instar est ad aliquid efficiendum: ij iam λόγοιοι[?] proprie dici non possunt, neque sine carere. Summos duces hoc vaframento saepe vsos legimus, vt didito aliquo rumore falso,& à se confiɗto, victoriam de hostibus reportarent. Vtuntur aliquando & mercatores simili fraude. Quare ait Lysias fieri solitum saepius Athenis, vt sitonas quo impunitius annonam flagellarent, falsa quaedam comminiscerentur, & in vulgus spargerent. ἅτω ὃ ἀσήμνοι[?], ait, τὰς συμφορὰς τὰς ὑμετέρας ὁρῶσιν, ὥστε τὰς μὲν πρότερον [illegible, ~12 letters] τὰς νεως ἐφθάρθαι τὰς ἐν τῇ Πόντῳ, ἢ [illegible, ~10 letters] Λακεδαιμονίων [illegible, ~8 letters] ἐκ[illegible, ~6 letters] συμπεπλῆρῶσθαι, ἢ τὰ ἐμπόρια κεκλεῖσθαι, ἢ τὰς [illegible, ~6 letters] μέλλειν ἀπορρήσθαι. De istis, & his similibus non sentit Theophrastus.
units.tr: those who are properly so called. For those who use λόγοιοι[?] as a weapon to bring something about cannot properly be called λόγοιοι, nor can they be without it. We read that the greatest generals often used this trick, spreading some false rumour that they had invented, so as to win the victory over their enemies. Merchants too sometimes use a similar fraud. So Lysias says that it was often the custom at Athens for the corn-dealers, so that they might sell grain with greater impunity, to invent certain falsehoods and spread them among the people. Thus, he says, the unclear men see your misfortunes, so that they say the ships were lost earlier in the Black Sea, or the Lacedaemonians had filled ..., or the markets were closed, or the ... were about to be cut off. Theophrastus does not mean such things, nor things like them. ἀλυσιτελῶς ἀπαλλάττεσθαι [to depart without profit].

units.la: ἀλυσιτελῶς ἀπαλλάττεσθαι.] Non solùm ἀλυσιτελῶς, sed etiam, vt arbitror, κερδαλεῶς. Exiftimo enim fuiffe nonnunquam Athenis in homines λοιδορουμένους publicè animaduerfum. Indicant non obscurè Plutarchi illa in extremo Nicia de eo qui primus per vrbem diffudit cladis Siculae nuncium, ὡς ὃ, inquit, ἐπωτώμενος παρ' ἂ ἀνθρώπων, ὥσπερ ἐν ὅσοις ἐκ φράζειν, δόξας λοιδορούμενος[?], καὶ ξαράττειν[?] τὴν πόλιν, εἰς τὸν προσχὼν κατελθεῖς, ἐσπέλασ ἀπολύσαι χρόνον.
units.tr: To depart unprofitably [ἀλυσιτελῶς ἀπαλλάττεσθαι]. Not only unprofitably [ἀλυσιτελῶς] but also, I think, shrewdly [κερδαλεῶς]. For I suppose that at Athens men who abused others were sometimes punished publicly. Plutarch's words at the end of the Life of Nicias make this plain, concerning the man who first spread the news of the Sicilian disaster through the city: when many people questioned him and he had nothing definite to say, he was seen to be abusing and disturbing the city, so he was taken to prison and kept there for a time.

units.la: πειρασθεὶς ποιήμονοι.) Sic supra, πειρασθεὶς τῆς ὀχλώσεως, in Περὶ Δικαιοσύνης. Inde dicuntur πειρασθεὶς, qui corona hominum cinguntur, vt apud Isocratem Σωφρονιστὴς πειρασθεὶς. Etymologici auctor, Πειρασθεῖ, πειρασθεῖς. ἐφ' οἷς ἂν τις ἀπὸ βλάβης ἀπόλλυσθαι.[?] Caeterum obserua mihi isto loco stultam hominis temeritatem: qui vt vitio naturae suae obsequatur,cœtum & concursum facere non veretur. Atqui constat legem Athenis fuisse quæ pœnam capitis in eos statuebat,qui hominum turbam ad se conuocassent. Auctor Seneca pater,quem vide libro 111. Controuersiarum , v 111. Hanc etiam puto caussam esse, cur & hîc & in simili loco capite [illegible, ~8 letters] tam citò dissipetur qui conuenerat globus hominum.
units.tr: Tried by the crowd [πειρασθεὶς ποιήμονοι]. Thus above, tried by the crowd [πειρασθεὶς τῆς ὀχλώσεως], in the book On Justice. Hence those are called πειρασθεῖς who are surrounded by a crowd of men, as in Isocrates' Sophronistes, πειρασθεὶς. The author of the Etymologicum has: πειρασθεῖς, those who are tried, of those who are in danger of perishing from harm. Meanwhile, observe in this place the foolish rashness of the man, who, in order to indulge the fault of his nature, does not hesitate to gather a crowd and a throng. Yet it is established that at Athens there was a law which laid the penalty of death on those who had summoned a crowd of men to themselves. The author is Seneca the Elder, whom see in Book 3 of the Controversies, declamation 8. I think this is also the reason why, here and in a similar passage, the crowd that had gathered is so quickly broken up.

units.la: τὰ ἱμάτια [illegible, ~8 letters]. Furto nimirum subrepta,à furibus balneariis:à quibus olim ne tum quidem recte caueri poterat, cum maximè cauebatur: tam multi erant, tam improbi. Propterea coacti veteres seruos habere qui vestes in balneis seruarent: Græci ἱματιοφύλακας vocant, Latini capsarios, vt apud Paulum Iurisconsultum. Motte pleĉtebantur apud Athenienses fures balnearij, si rei furtiuæ æstimatio erat ὑπὲρ δέκα δραχμάς, ait Demosthenes contra Iimocratem. vide Aristotelis Problemata, & Iurisconsultos.
units.tr: The clothes [τὰ ἱμάτια]. Snatched by theft, no doubt, by bath thieves; against whom in former times one could not be properly guarded even when the greatest care was taken, so many there were and so wicked. For this reason the ancients were compelled to keep slaves to look after clothes in the baths; the Greeks call them ἱματιοφύλακες, the Latins capsarii, as in Paulus the jurist. Bath thieves were punished by death at Athens if the value of the stolen goods was more than ten drachmas, says Demosthenes against Timocrates. See Aristotle's Problems and the jurists.

units.la: πεζομαχίαι καὶ ναυμαχίαι νικῶντες. Hoc est, νίκας λεῖοντες καὶ διαλύσιον, sicut apud Aristotelem multis locis, οἱ ψυχῶντες τὸν ἀέρα, pro eo quod est οἱ λέσ-τες τὸν ἀέρα [illegible, ~6 letters]. Sic dicuntur historici eos occidere quorum eadem narrant: quale illud est elegantissimè dictum à Plutarcho de Ctefia, qui Cyri interitum longa verborum ambage narrauerat, & quasi fabulam in varios actus distraxerat, Τοῦτ᾽ μὲν, inquit, ὁ Κτησίας λόγῳ, ὡς καθάπερ ἀμάξαι ξιφιδίῳ, μόλις ἀναφῶν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀνήρηκε. Planè miror lapsos hîc esse doctos homines tam fœdè. nam quis adeo in litteris hospes & peregrinus, cui non sint hoc loquendi genere tritæ aures?
units.tr: Winning land battles and sea battles [πεζομαχίαι καὶ ναυμαχίαι νικῶντες]. This means speaking of victories and dissolution [νίκας λέγοντες καὶ διαλύσιον], just as Aristotle says in many places those who chill the air [οἱ ψυχῶντες τὸν ἀέρα] for those who thin the air. Historians are said to destroy those whose deeds they relate in the same way. This is what Plutarch elegantly says of Ctesias, who had told of the death of Cyrus with a long roundabout of words and had split the story, as if it were a play, into various acts: Ctesias, with his words, as if with a little sword, having with difficulty raised the man, has killed him [Τοῦτ᾽ μὲν ὁ Κτησίας λόγῳ, ὡς καθάπερ ἀμάξαι ξιφιδίῳ, μόλις ἀναφῶν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀνήρηκε]. I am truly surprised that learned men have slipped here so shamefully. For who is so much a stranger and foreigner to letters that his ears are not familiar with this way of speaking?

units.la: Pag. 29. ἐρήμως δίκας ὠφλήκασι. ] Hoc ipsum notat Horatius in describtione garruli,
units.tr: Page 29. They lost their lawsuits by default [ἐρήμως δίκας ὠφλήκασι]. Horace notes this very thing in his description of the garrulous man:

units.la: —casu tunc respondere vadato Debebat, quod ni fecisset, perdere litem.
units.tr: —at that time he had to answer by a surety for the case, and if he had not done so, he would lose the suit.

units.la: nam ille mauult perdere litem quàm Horatium relinquere. Fuit autem eremodicii poena apud Athenienses grauissima. Nā si reus qui iudicio nō stiterat, absentiam suam excusare non posset, neque ad purgandam moram diem aduersario diceret (quod ἀντιλαχεῖν vel ἀντιτιμᾶσθαι τὸν μὴ ὄντα vocabatur), & intra decem dies erat praestandum: mille drachmae aduersario soluendae erant. quod si idem frustrari pergeret, locus erat τῇ ἐξελαύσει δίκῃ, vel potius γραφῇ, & multa publico pendenda.
units.tr: For he would rather lose the suit than leave Horace. The penalty for default was very severe at Athens. For if a defendant who had not appeared in court could not excuse his absence, and did not name a day to his opponent to clear the delay (which was called antilachein or antitimasthai ton me onta), and had to pay within ten days, a thousand drachmas had to be paid to the opponent. If he persisted in evading, there was the action of exclusion [ἐξούλης δίκη], or rather a public indictment [γραφή], and a fine to be paid to the public treasury.

units.la: εἰσὶ δ' οἱ καὶ πόλεις λόγῳ καὶ κράτῳ αἱρουῶτες, παρεδ[?]ήθη [?](ἂν.) Quid αἱρουῶτες? dicat aliquis intelligi extrinsecus χωρία vel πόλεις. Logi: & quidem Siculi, non Attici. Locus transpositione litterarum corruptus: & quidem iam olim: nam Palatinorum codicum lectio nihil edita melior est. Scribendum aio, εἰσὶ δ' οἱ ἢ πόλεις λόγῳ καὶ κράτῳ αἱρουῶτες. Sic Plautus Milite,
units.tr: There are some who take cities by word and by force [εἰσὶ δ' οἱ καὶ πόλεις λόγῳ καὶ κράτῳ αἱρούμενοι]. What of taking [αἱρούμενοι]? Someone may say that places or cities are understood from outside. The passage is corrupted by a transposition of letters, and this happened long ago; for the reading of the Palatine manuscripts is no better than what has been printed. I would write: "there are some who, either by word or by force, take cities." So Plautus in the Miles:

units.la: Postea cum magnifico milite, urbes verbis qui inermis capit, Conflixi.
units.tr: Afterwards I fought with the boastful soldier, who takes cities with words while unarmed.

units.la: Falluntur qui aliter futuram orationem Graecam putant. Hoc primum, iam illud καὶ κράτῳ αἱρεῖν πόλιν, est proprie quod ait Salustius, vi pugnandóque capere. nos Francocclte, d'assaut. Apud Plutarchum in Catone Uticensi, πόλις ἢ καταλαμβάνει ἀλώσιμος, urbs quæ munitior est, quàm ut capi inuasione murorum possit. Hefychius, καταλαμβάνει ἐλεῖν, τὸ ἐξ ἐφόλε, καὶ τὸ αἰφνίδιον. τὸ ἀψίδιον[?]. Deinde ἀποδειπνηθῆναι[?] non est, vt vulgò putant, domi cœnare: quod Martialis dixit elegantèr, affici domicœnio: non, sed cœnam perdere. Verbum est elegans & comicum: quod de eo dicitur, quo absente, vel præsente quidem, sed in garriédo occupato, cœna comesa est, & funus factum prandio, vt cum Peniculo Plautino, qui hanc calamitatem passus erat, loquar. Amphis vetus comicus vsus hoc vocabulo, vt notatum olim à doctissimo Athenæo, libro decimo: sic ille, Παραδεδειπνημένῳ ἢ ἔφησεν[?] Ἀμφὶς ἐν Πλάτῳ[?] ὕτως[?], Παραδεδειπνημένῳ, παῖδες, ἄλλα[?]. Hodie in editis Athenæi codicibus nullum ferè eius obseruationis apparet vestigium. nos hunc quoque locum cum aliis infinitis ex veteribus membranis emendauimus. Nam ille auctor eruditissimus multum aliquando nobis debiturus est, si dederit Deus, vt quæ in illum molimur, & pridem orsi sumus, perficere & detexere queamus. Affine est apud eundem Athenæum παροψωνεῖν.
units.tr: They are mistaken who think the Greek means otherwise. First, the phrase to take a city by force and strength [καὶ κράτῳ αἱρεῖν πόλιν] is what Sallust properly means by to take by force and fighting, vi pugnandoque capere; the French say d'assaut. In Plutarch's Cato of Utica, a city is described as one that is too well fortified to be taken by an assault on its walls [πόλις ... ἀλώσιμος]. Hesychius: to seize suddenly [καταλαμβάνει], which means from an ambush and by surprise. Next, ἀποδειπνηθῆναι does not mean, as is commonly thought, to dine at home; Martial elegantly said to be dined out (affici domicoenio), but the word means to lose one's dinner (cœnam perdere). It is an elegant and comic word, used of one who, while absent or even present but busy chattering, has his dinner eaten up and his supper turned into a funeral, as I would say with Plautus' Peniculus, who suffered this calamity. The old comic poet Amphis used this word, as the learned Athenaeus noted long ago in Book 10: Amphis in the Plato says, "having dined out, boys, ..." [Παραδεδειπνημένῳ]. In the printed editions of Athenaeus scarcely any trace of this observation appears today. We have emended this passage too, along with countless others, from old parchments. For that most learned author will owe us much, if God grants that we may complete and bring to light what we are working on and began long ago. Akin to this in the same Athenaeus is to buy side-dishes [παροψωνεῖν].
On the chapter Concerning Shamelessness [περὶ ἀναισχυντίας].

units.la: Ἡ ἀναισχυντία ἐστὶ καταφρόνησις δόξης αἰσχρᾶς ἕνεκα κέρδους. Aristoteles in Nicomacheis pudorem definiti ait, Φόβον τινὰ ἀδοξίας: & ἀναισχυντίαν esse τὸ μὴ αἰδεῖσθαι τὰ αἰσχρὰ πράττειν, nec multò se-cus in secundo Rhetoricorum. Theophrastus adiicit hoc amplius, αἰσχρῶν ἕνεκα κέρδους: non quò non sint aliæ occasiones cur impudens sit aliquis, sed quia hæc maximè vulgaris & quàm plurimis communis. Vulgus enim hominum rumorem parui faciunt, dum fit rumen qui impleant. veriffimeq; fummus vates Pindarus, αἰδῶς, ait, ὑποκρύφα κέρδεα κλέπτεται [?]. Plato in Ὅροις, ita: Αναιχυντία, ἐξις ἀν[?]χῆς [?]ἀποκοµικὴ ἀδοξίας, ἕνεκα κέρδους [?]: vide eiusdem Hipparchum.
units.tr: Shamelessness is contempt for a base reputation for the sake of gain [Ἡ ἀναισχυντία ἐστὶ καταφρόνησις δόξης αἰσχρᾶς ἕνεκα κέρδους]. In the Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle defines shame as a certain fear of disrepute [Φόβον τινὰ ἀδοξίας], and says that shamelessness is not being ashamed to do shameful things, and in the second book of the Rhetoric he says much the same. Theophrastus adds something more, "for the sake of base gain" [αἰσχρῶν ἕνεκα κέρδους]. He does not mean that there are no other occasions on which a man may be impudent, but that this is the most common and the one shared by the greatest number of people. For the mass of men make little of reputation, provided they can fill their bellies. And the most truthful of poets, Pindar, says that shame is secretly stolen away by gains [αἰδῶς ὑποκρύφα κέρδεα κλέπτεται]. Plato, in his Definitions, puts it thus: shamelessness is a state of mind ... of disrepute, for the sake of gain. See also his Hipparchus.

units.la: ὃν ἀποστρέφει [?]. ) cuius propterea confpectum, si micam pudoris haberet, quàm longissimè fugere debuit. Scitè & huic loco conuenientissimè Eustathius ad Iliadis [?] 1. ἀπαιδείας est χαρακτὴρ, τὸ τλῶν τὸν ἀδικοῦντα ἀπολέσαι [?] ἀνθρώπου [?]. Propterea illo loco de Agamemnone ait Achilles, — ἡδ' ἂν ἐμοίγε Τέλλαίν κυνὸς πρὸ ἐὼν εἰς ὤπα ἰδέσθαι.
units.tr: Whose sight, if he had any crumb of shame, he ought to avoid as far as possible. Eustathius, on the first book of the Iliad, very aptly fits this passage: impudence is the mark of one who bears to see the wrongdoer go unpunished [ἀπαιδείας ἐστὶ χαρακτήρ, τὸ τλῶν τὸν ἀδικοῦντα ἀπολέσαι]. For this reason Achilles says of Agamemnon, in that passage, that he would rather have the eyes of a dog than look upon him [ἡδ' ἂν ἐμοίγε ... κυνὸς ... εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι].

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters] τὸν ἀλλὰ ἀδικοῦντα, διὰ τῆς τρα[?]πέζης.) Moris fuit veteribus cùm ad conuiuium irent, feruum aliquem secum adducere, qui heros prandenti pone astaret, vel ad pedes, eiúsque praesto esset, si quid ille imperare vellet: Latini hos seruos vocant à pedibus, vel ad pedes. Solebant autem illis apophoreta à dominis tradi. Athenæus initio quarti, Καὶ ἕκαστον λαβὼν σὺν αὐτῷ τινάκι, τοῖς κατόπιν δι[?]δὲ πατσίν. mendosè enim ibi hodie τὰ ἔσωθεν legunt, & interpretantur. sic ibidem mox, ἐπεὶ δ' ὤκαυσεν [?] καὶ τὰ ἔδη [?] τοῖς δ' ἄλλοις. Lucianus Περὶ ἀπίστων, de philosopho qui è conuiuio domum redierat, ἀειμνῆ[?] πα[?]ρέλαβε τὰ κρέα ὁ τῆς παιδὸς καλόμενος ἐσωτὶ παρὰ δ' ὠδωκεί. Alias autem volente & auctore domino conuiuij haec auferebantur: vt in Cleopatrae conuiuio quod Plutarchus & Athenaeus describunt: & in eo Carani, apud Athenaeum quarti initio: & omnino in omnibus splendidioribus epulis, alias non tam vidente eo aut volente, quàm vel conniuente, vel insciō : quod rectè hīc Theophrastus inter hominis impudentis notas numerat. Lucilius libro secundo epigrammatum Graecorum, titulo In gluttones, Καὶ τραώξης ἐ(α πίντε λύχνοι Γάμε, καὶ τὰ ἰδιόντα [?] Οὐ ᾧ σὰ, τῇ ἢ πίεις, σανέα δίδως ὀπίσω. [?]
units.tr: ... but the one who does wrong, through the table. It was the custom among the ancients, when they went to a dinner party, to bring some slave with them who would stand behind the diner, or at his feet, and be at hand if he wished to give any order. The Latins call these slaves "from the feet" or "at the feet." Such slaves were usually given leftovers (apophoreta) by their masters. Athenaeus, at the start of the fourth book, says: "taking each man's share, with his own tray, for the attendants behind, at the feet" [Καὶ ἕκαστον λαβὼν σὺν αὐτῷ τινάκι, τοῖς κατόπιν δι' τοὺς πόδας]. The printed texts there wrongly read and interpret "the inner things" [τὰ ἔσωθεν]. Likewise, just afterward: "when he had burned ... and the ... to the others." Lucian, in On Those Who Disbelieve, speaks of a philosopher who came home from a dinner party, and his slave, called "the one at the feet," took the meat and gave it out. Sometimes these things were carried away with the host's will and approval, as at Cleopatra's banquet, which Plutarch and Athenaeus describe, and in the banquet of Carano in Athenaeus at the start of the fourth book; and generally at all the more lavish feasts. At other times they were taken away not so much with the host seeing and willing it, as with him conniving or unaware. Theophrastus rightly counts this among the marks of the impudent man. Lucilius, in the second book of the Greek Epigrams, under the heading "Against gluttons": "And you, though you have a lamp ... you give back the leftovers..."

units.la: Martialis, Omnia cum retro pueris obscenia tradas, Cur non mensa tibi ponitur a pedibus?
units.tr: Martial: "Since you pass all the obscene leftovers back to the boys behind you, why is no table set for you at the feet?"

units.la: Lucianus quoque in Lapithis, siue motosophorum convivio, Ὁρᾷς ὃ(ς) τῷ παιδὶ κατὰ τὴν ἐ ὅτι ὀρέγει, λαυθάνειν οἰσρῷυ(ς) τῆς ἀλλας, μεμνημένος τῆς μετ' αὐτόν. loquitur de gulosò quodam qui delibans ex iis quæ mensæ erat apposita gratissima quæque, clam aliis, ut sibi quidem videbatur, puero stanti à tergo omnia porrigebat. At iis quæ Theophrastus hîc describit, cautior est atque ingeniosior : palàm enim puero suo tradit quæ vult auferri, simulans se non ea fini dare, ut domum ad se ille ferat : sed ut iis ipse vescatur : in quo minor erat invidia. Ideo etiam τίμιοι eum appellat : quasi scilicet, non puerum suum & famulum alloqueretur : sed honestum aliquem virum, quem pro iure amicitiæ secum adduxisset : nam id quoque fieri solebat. atque hi sunt quos umbras vulgò vocarunt, & ex Plutarcho, Athenæo, & Latinis scriptoribus notum est. Horatius, — locus est vel pluribus umbris.
units.tr: Lucian also, in the Lapiths, or the dinner of the sophists: "You see how he hands to the boy behind him whatever he is reaching for, hoping to escape notice by the others, mindful of the one who comes after." He is speaking of a glutton who, nibbling from the most delicious items set on the table, secretly, as he thought, handed everything to the boy standing at his back. But the man whom Theophrastus describes here is more cautious and clever: he openly hands his boy what he wants carried away, pretending that he is not giving them to him, so that the boy may take them home to his master, but that he himself may eat them. In this the envy is less. That is why he also calls the boy "honoured" [τίμιοι]: as if he were not addressing his own slave and attendant, but some respectable man whom he had brought along by right of friendship, for that too was customary. These are the men that were commonly called "shadows," as is known from Plutarch, Athenaeus and the Latin writers. Horace: "there is room for even more shadows."

units.la: Εὐωχᾷ τίμιε. ]Τίμιε, hoc est, Domine: nam ut olim apud Romanos superiores dignitate ab inferioribus domini in congressionibus salutabãtur: sic apud veteres Atticos τίμιοι : declarat manifestò Theophrasti hic locus: sed & Euripides quoque Supplicibus,
units.tr: "Feast, honoured one" [Εὐωχᾷ τίμιε]. "Honoured one," that is, "Sir." For just as among the Romans, in greetings, inferiors in rank used to salute their superiors as "lords," so among the ancient Athenians the term was "honoured ones" [τίμιοι]. This passage of Theophrastus clearly shows it. Euripides too, in the Suppliants, says:
"But whoever meets misfortune is honoured as a man of worth [Ὅς δ' ἀτυχήσει Τίμιος γεραίρεται]."

units.la: & in Hecuba ait idem poëta, plerofque homines infolefcere: alium propter opes: alium ἐν πολίταις[?] Τίμιον κεκλημένον[?]. hoc est, quod dominus vulgò saluretur. Postea Romanos imitati sunt Græci, & sese inuicem salutarunt χαῖρε καὶ χαῖρε[?]: quæ vox deinde in χῶρ[?] degenerauit. nam ita citimæ ætatis scriptores.
units.tr: And in the Hecuba the same poet says that most men become arrogant, one because of wealth, another because he is called "honoured" among his fellow citizens [ἐν πολίταις Τίμιον κεκλημένον]. That is, "the master was commonly greeted." Afterward the Greeks imitated the Romans and greeted one another with "Hail and hail" [χαῖρε καὶ χαῖρε]; this word later degenerated into "chōr." So write the writers of the most recent age.

units.la: εἴ τι χρήσιμον αὐτῷ γέλοι[?].) Locus leuiter corruptus: scribendum enim χρήσιμον[?] : quomodo & legitur in quibusdam codicibus: & ratio omnino postulat, imò flagitat. χρήσιμος εἴ τινί[?], sest bene de aliquo mereri. Aristoteles in seprimo Eudemiorum, Διὸ δὲ οἱ ἐκείνως οἰόμενοι ἐγκαλεῖν, ἐὰν μὴ ὁμοίως εἰσὶ χρήσιμοι δ᾽ ἂν ποιῶσι[?], qui amicitiam inquit, vtilitate metiuntur, de amicis conqueri solent, si minus beneficiorum ab iis acceperunt, quàm ipsi in eos contulerint. Alciphron in epistolis, χρῆσει τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ἐν οἷς αὐτῇ χρησίμῃ φίλοντα[?], ἵν᾽ ὀνειδίζω[?]. Inde χρηστότης habitus ille dicitur, per quem propensi sumus ad bene omnibus faciendum. Andronicus definit ita, χρηστότης, ἕξις ἐκτάσεως δ᾽ ἁπλῆτικὴ[?].
units.tr: "If he might be of some use to him..." The passage is slightly corrupt, for "useful" [χρήσιμον] should be written, as it also is read in some manuscripts, and the sense absolutely demands it, indeed insists on it: "to be useful to someone" [χρήσιμος εἴ τινί], that is, to deserve well of someone. Aristotle, in the seventh book of the Eudemian Ethics: "Those who think that friendship is measured by usefulness are wont to complain of their friends if they have not conferred benefits on them to the same degree that they have conferred them" (he says that those who measure friendship by usefulness complain about friends if they have received fewer benefits from them than they themselves have conferred). Alciphron, in his Letters: "in other matters in which she is useful to him, loving..., so that I may reproach..." From this, that disposition is called goodness [χρηστότης], by which we are inclined to do good to all. Andronicus defines it thus: goodness is a habit of ... simple in its extension [χρηστότης, ἕξις ... ἁπλῆ].

units.la: μάλιστα μὲν χρέας, εἰ ἢ μὴ ὀρέων εἰς τὴν ζυγὸν ἐμβαλεῖν.] Vt hoc fit auctarium quoddam, vel suprapondium. Latini veteres mantisam vocabant. Lucillius,
units.tr: "Most of all meat, if not even to throw a little into the scales." This is a kind of addition or extra weight. The old Latins called it "mantisa." Lucilius: "the mantisa surpasses the side dishes." The Greeks called it ... as Polybius, in the eighth book at the beginning, reports through Athenaeus.

units.la: — mantisa obsonia vincit. Græci ἐαίδοσιν[?], vt Polybius apud Athenæum lib. VIII. initio.
units.tr: "Mantisa surpasses the side dishes." The Greeks [ἐαίδοσιν] ...

units.la: καὶ ξένοις ὁ αὐτὸς χρέα ἀπορᾶς[?].) Semper iudicauimus vocem χρέα esse corruptam: ac cum ξέαν[?] ex coniectura emendassemus, postea animaduertimus hanc etiam antiquorum manuscriptorum lectionem. Quare nihil certius quàm ita esse legendum. Quid esset apud Athenienses ξέαν ἀγοράζειν[?]. (Plutarch⁹ pro eo dixit θεωρηλίεια ἐπιμέδοντο[?] in Gracchis) quid item ξέαν καταλαμβάνειν[?] neminem puto qui ignoret: vide infrà ad caput περὶ βδελυρίας[?]. Iam verò nemini dubium est, quin ex vicinis populis magna frequentia Athenas ventitaret ad ludos spectandos: quæ turba omnis ferè ex veteri more apud amicos quibuscum ius hospitij esset, diuertebat: ideo ait, τοῖς ξένοις αὐτῆς[?].
units.tr: "And the same man bought meat for guests [καὶ ξένοις ὁ αὐτὸς χρέα ἀπορᾶς]." I have always judged the word "meat" [χρέα] to be corrupt, and when I had emended it by conjecture to "guest-meat" [ξέαν], I later noticed that this is also the reading of the old manuscripts. Therefore nothing is more certain than that this must be read. What "buying guest-meat" [ξέαν ἀγοράζειν] meant among the Athenians, I think no one fails to know. (Plutarch, in the Gracchi, for this said ... ) Likewise, what "to seize the guest-meat" [ξέαν καταλαμβάνειν] meant, I think no one is ignorant of; see below at the chapter Concerning Surliness [περὶ βδελυρίας]. Now indeed no one doubts that from neighbouring peoples a great crowd used to flock to Athens to watch the games, and nearly all of this crowd, according to ancient custom, lodged with friends with whom they had the right of hospitality. Therefore he says "for his guests" [τοῖς ξένοις αὐτῆς].

units.la: Pag. 31. ἀλλὰν ὁ καὶ τῆς εἰς τὸν ὑσεφ.[?]) Lego, ἀλλὰν ὁ καὶ τῆς υἱὸς εἰς τὸν ὑσεφαίαν[?]. Librarij vocum affinium τῆς & υἱὸς alteram omiserunt. Sensus est, Solitum impudentem istum quando cum redemtoribus theatri paciscitur de loco ad spectandum pro suis hospitibus, etiam sibi & suis domesticis consulere. Quomodo autem? de alieno nempe largiendo, fraudémque iis faciendo pro quibus apud theatropolas intercedit. sic fit, vt cum aliis omnibus pretio emta sit sedes in theatro, ipse gratis spectet: nec ipse tantùm: sed & liberi eius, & qui eos sequitur pædagogus. similes sordes infrà in descriptione τῷ θεάτρῳ[?]. Erant autem pleraque festa (quo tempore maximè spectacula exhiberi solita) plurium dierum: vt mirari nemo debeat, quod ait εἰς τὸν ὑσεφαίαν[?]: quod & ipsum plenum est venustatis Atticæ : est enim pro τῇ ὑστεραία[?]. Omnino constantet affirmamus hanc esse elegantissimi istius loci sententiam : prorsúsque desiderari vocem υἱός[?] : quod vel sequens mentio pædagogi euincit, nam adolescetes suis pædagogis comitati in theatrum veniebant. Suetonium lege in Augusto, capite xl i v.
units.tr: Page 31. "... also for his son, to the following day" [ἀλλὰν ὁ καὶ τῆς εἰς τὸν ὑσεφ.]. I read: "... also for his son, and the son's ... to the next day" [ἀλλὰν ὁ καὶ τῆς υἱὸς εἰς τὸν ὑσεφαίαν]. The copyists omitted one of the similar words, τῆς or υἱὸς. The sense is this: this habitual impudent man, when he bargains with the theatre contractors about a place to watch for his guests, also looks out for himself and his household. And how? Namely by spending what is not his own, and cheating those for whom he intercedes with the theatre-sellers. So it happens that, while everyone else has bought their seat in the theatre for a price, he watches for free: and not he alone, but also his children and the pedagogue who follows them. Similar meanness appears below in the description of the one who is at the theatre. Most festivals (at which spectacles were usually presented) lasted several days, so no one should wonder that he says "to the following day" [εἰς τὸν ὑσεφαίαν]: a phrase full of Attic elegance too, for it stands for "the next day" [τῇ ὑστεραία]. I firmly affirm that this is the meaning of this most elegant passage, and that the word "son" [υἱός] is certainly missing; the following mention of the pedagogue alone proves it, for young men came to the theatre accompanied by their pedagogues. Read Suetonius in Augustus, chapter 44.

units.la: καὶ ταῦτα χειρῶγες[?]. ) Ita est legendum : χειρῶγες inquam, non χειρῶγες[?], quasi esset à χειρ[?]. Etiámne hæc minuta viros doctos fefellisse?
units.tr: And these things [καὶ ταῦτα χειρῶγες]. Thus it must be read: cheirōges, I say, not cheirōges, as though it came from cheir. Could such trifles really have deceived learned men?

units.la: Ἀ̈νς[?] ὁ καὶ πρὸς τὰ χαλκεῖα τὰ ἐν τῷ βαλαν[?].) Pollux χαλκεῖα recenset inter instrumenta balnei. Sunt autem χαλκεῖα siue aena, vasa magna & oris vasti in quibus aqua balneorum calefiebat : sicuti in fundi instrumento Paulus Iurisconsultus aena numerat, in quibus aqua ad potandum calefit. Sed in aenis balneorum puto etiam oleum fuisse calefactum, & ita hîc accipiendum videtur. Elegans est apud Stobæum veteris scriptoris Teletis locus, vbi horum χαλκείων est mentio : quem ego etsi depravatus est adscribam. Loquitur ibi de homine Cynicæ sectæ. Εἰ ἀλείψασθαι χρείαν ἔχοι, εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὸ βαλανεῖον, τῇ λείῳ ἀλείψας[?]. καὶ βαδίζης ἐνίοτε πρὸς τὸ χαλκεῖον, τῷ [illegible, ~12 letters] τὰ χαλκεῖα, τῷ ὑὸν[?] εἰδὼν * [illegible, ~10 letters] ἀν ἐλαδίον, καθίζει ἡείσθα[?]. Si fiveret, inquit, vngi opus, balneum ingressus, strigmentis olei corpus vngebatur. nonnunquam etiam ad fornacem illam accedebat vbi sunt aena, & [illegible, ~8 letters] cum se oleo pauxillo perfidisset, sedens prandebat. Vitruuius in balnearum fabrica tria aena super hypocaustum vult componi, vnum caldarium, alterum tepidarium, tertium frigidarium. Aena appellat ille, non τὰ χαλκεῖα tantùm : sed etiam quas Plinius iunior in ea epistola qua Tusculanum suum descripsit, cellas nuncupat, & tres pariter commemorat, frigidariam, mediam, caldariam. Lucianus item in elegantissima balnei descriptione, has cellas οἴκας vocat sive oecos, nam ea voce sæpe Plinius & Vitruvius usi. Curtius edē ita usurpat pro oeco sive cella aut cubiculo Græcizans, non insolens. Aristides rhetor pro eodem ponit in hac re, οἶκον & δ᾿ἐξαρξυλίου. Tres autem oecos etiam Lucianus commemorat. τὸν μέγαν οἶκον ἔχοντα τρεῖς κολυμβήθρας: hæc est cella frigidaria: τὸν ἠρέμα χλιαινόμενον οἶκον: hæc tepidaria cella: τὸν ἔνδον [illegible, ~8 letters] θερμὰς πυίλας: hæc cella caldaria est. Fuit vero etiam quarta cella in quibusdam balneis, quam assam Cicero in epistola ad Q. Fratrem nominat. Et in dialogo Adriani imperatoris cum Epicteto quatuor diserte nominantur: prima tepidaria unctuaria: secunda, sudatoria: tertia assa: quarta, frigidaria. Aliter auctor Glossarij, Assa cella, ἀτιδρωτήριον [?], vult esse cellam sudatoriam. Porrò χαλκεῖα illa quorum usus ad calefaciendam aquam, Latini non aena tantum aut miliaria vocarunt: sed etiam scutra. Glossarium, Scutra, χαλκίον, alibi, Scutra λέβης. extat ea vox in Plauti Persa. dixerunt Latini & cucumam, Græci κυκύμιον, Arrianus in Epicteto libro III. δεῖ αὐτὸν κυκύμιον ἔχειν ὅπως τὸ θερμὸν ποιήσει. Fictiles fuisse cucumas scimus ex Marcellino Empirico. Remansit ea vox in usu in vernacula Gallorum lingua ut aliæ infinitæ. Ad hæc vasa respiciebat philosophus, cùm scriberet in libello De spiritu, τὰς φλέβας ἔχον πόρους ἐν αἷς τὸ θερμὸν ὅ, ὥσπερ ἐν χαλκείοις θερμαίνεται τὸ αἷμα. Fallitur enim doctus ille vir, qui obscurissimum eum libellum interpretans, χαλκεῖα hæc de ærariis officinis accepit. Similis error eorum qui superiorem Teletis locum sunt interpretati: nam etsi verum est, in officinis χαλκέων calfaciendi se caussa solitos pauperes conuenire, vel testibus Homero & Herodoto: nemo tamen non videat, qui locum attentius consideratit, de balneorum aënis ibi agi: vt taceam, quòd auctoris verba & loquendi ratio illorum interpretationem ferre non possunt. Illum verò Ariftotelis locum non parum illustrabunt quæ scribit Seneca Naturalium libro III. cap. XXIIII. de aqua per fistulas calefieri solita in draconibus & miliariis.
units.tr: Anēs [Ἀ̈νς] who also went to the cauldrons in the bath [πρὸς τὰ χαλκεῖα τὰ ἐν τῷ βαλαν]. Pollux lists cauldrons [χαλκεῖα] among the fittings of the bath. Now the cauldrons were either aena, large vessels with wide mouths in which the water of the baths was heated. So Paulus the jurist, in his treatise on the farm equipment, counts aena among the fittings in which water is heated for drinking. But I think oil was also heated in the bath cauldrons, and this seems to be the sense here. There is a fine passage in Stobaeus from the old writer Teles, where mention is made of these cauldrons. I shall quote it, though it is corrupt. He speaks there of a man of the Cynic sect.
