"If he needed to be anointed, he would go into the bath and, having anointed himself with the strigil [τῇ λείῳ ἀλείψας] ... and sometimes he would walk to the cauldron [πρὸς τὸ χαλκεῖον], [illegible] ... the cauldrons, [illegible] ... sitting down, he would dine." If he needed, he says, to be oiled, he would enter the bath, and his body would be anointed with scrapings of oil. Sometimes he would also approach that furnace where the aena are, and [illegible] after he had rubbed himself with a little oil, he would dine sitting down. Vitruvius, in his account of building baths, wants three aena to be set over the hypocaust: one hot (caldarium), another warm (tepidarium), and a third cold (frigidarium). He calls them aena, not merely τὰ χαλκεῖα; and Pliny the Younger, in that letter in which he describes his Tusculan villa, calls them cells (cellas), and likewise mentions three: cold, middle and hot. Lucian too, in his most elegant description of a bath, calls these cells οἴκας or oecos, for Pliny and Vitruvius often used that word. Curtius uses edē in the same way for oecus, or cell or bedroom, in a Graecizing manner, not unusually. The rhetorician Aristides, in this same matter, puts οἶκον for the same thing. Lucian also mentions three oeci: "the great room having three plunge-baths [τὸν μέγαν οἶκον ἔχοντα τρεῖς κολυμβήθρας]" is the cold cell; "the room gently warmed [τὸν ἠρέμα χλιαινόμενον οἶκον]" is the tepid cell; "the room inside with hot ... [τὸν ἔνδον ... θερμὰς πυίλας]" is the hot cell. In some baths there was also a fourth cell, which Cicero, in his letter to his brother Quintus, calls assam. And in the dialogue of the emperor Hadrian with Epictetus, four are expressly named: first the warm room for anointing, second the sweating room, third the assa, fourth the cold room. The author of the Glossary, on the other hand, explains Assa cella as the sweating room [ἀτιδρωτήριον]. Moreover, those cauldrons whose use was to heat water, the Latins called not only aena or miliaria, but also scutra. The Glossary has Scutra as χαλκίον, and elsewhere Scutra as λέβης. The word occurs in Plautus' Persa. The Latins also used cucumam, which the Greeks called κυκύμιον; Arrian, in Epictetus book III, has: "he must have a κυκύμιον so that it will make the water hot [δεῖ αὐτὸν κυκύμιον ἔχειν ὅπως τὸ θερμὸν ποιήσει]." We know from Marcellinus Empiricus that these cucumae were made of earthenware. The word has remained in use in the vernacular of the French, as have countless others. The philosopher had these vessels in mind when, in his little book On the Breath, he wrote that the veins have passages in which heat is kept, just as the blood is heated in cauldrons [τὰς φλέβας ἔχον πόρους ἐν αἷς τὸ θερμὸν ... ὥσπερ ἐν χαλκείοις θερμαίνεται τὸ αἷμα]. That learned man is mistaken, for in interpreting that very obscure little book he took these cauldrons to be the workshops of smiths. There is a similar error among those who have interpreted the earlier passage of Teles. For although it is true that poor men were accustomed to gather in the smiths' workshops to warm themselves, as Homer and Herodotus bear witness, yet no one who considers the passage more carefully can fail to see that it is about the bronze cauldrons of the baths; not to mention that the author's words and manner of speaking cannot bear that interpretation. Indeed, the passage of Aristotle will be much illuminated by what Seneca writes in Natural Questions book III, chapter 24, about water commonly heated through pipes in the dragons and cauldrons.

units.la: χὴ βάλας ἀρύταιναν.) Etiam Ἀρύταινα Iulius Pollux in supellectile balnearia refert: demiratus sum interpretes guttum vertisse. Sed ne alij quidem de hac voce (qua & Latini vsi sunt teste Festo & veteri Glossario & Iurisconsultis,) satis luculenter. Sic autem habe. Ἀρύταινα dicitur Græcis omne instrumentum cuius est vel in balneis, vel in culina, vel in mensa vsus ad hauriendum aliquid ex aliquo vase: est enim ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρύειν: vnde etiam ἀρυσήρ & ἀρυσίχις & ἀρυσιχῷ, tam significatione quàm origine cognatæ voces. Verùm quia multiplex est instrumenti huius vsus, Græci, (vt est admirabilis in ea lingua verborum copia) diuersas quasi species eius diuersis nominibus insigniuerunt. Nam illud, exépli caussa, quo puls hauriebatur, ἐτρύβυσις proprie vocatum: quo iusculum, ζωμήρυσις: quo vinum è cratere οἰνήρυσις. Erant autem & ἐτνήρυσις, & ζωμήρυσις, & οἰνήρυσις, excauata instrumenta cum manubrio. Sic Græci. Latini verò trullæ appellatione omnia hæc, vt opinio nostra est, sunt complexi.
units.tr: And βάλλας ἀρύταιναν [χὴ βάλας ἀρύταιναν]. Julius Pollux also mentions the arytaina among bath equipment; I have been surprised that the translators rendered it as "gutter." Nor have others explained this word (which the Latins also used, as witnessed by Festus, an old Glossary and the jurists) very clearly. But here is how it stands. The Greeks call arytaina any implement used in the bath, the kitchen or the table for drawing something out of a vessel: it comes from ἀρύειν, whence also ἀρυσήρ, ἀρυσίχις and ἀρυσιχῷ, words related both in meaning and origin. But since the use of this implement is manifold, the Greeks (for the Greek language has an admirable abundance of words) marked its various kinds with different names. For instance, the instrument with which porridge was drawn out was properly called ἐτρύβυσις; that for broth, ζωμήρυσις; that for wine from the mixing bowl, οἰνήρυσις. There were also ἐτνήρυσις, ζωμήρυσις and οἰνήρυσις, hollowed-out implements with a handle. So far the Greeks. The Latins, I think, embraced all of these under the name trulla.

units.la: Gloffatium, Ζωμάρυσρον, Trulla. appellat ζωμάρυσρον quam veteres Græci ζωμήρυον. Idem alibi, Trulla lignea, ζωμήρυος. Trullaria ζωμάρυσρον. vbi suspecta vox trullaria. Esse vero trullam etiam vas vinarium simile bacrioni (de quo Festus) constat. Horatius,
units.tr: The Glossarium has Gloffatium, Ζωμάρυσρον, and Trulla. It calls the ζωμάρυσρον what the old Greeks called ζωμήρυον. Elsewhere it has Trulla lignea, ζωμήρυος. Trullaria is ζωμάρυσρον, where the word trullaria is suspect. It is established that the trulla was also a wine vessel similar to the bacrion (on which see Festus). Horace:

units.la: Campana solitum trulla. & Cicero in Verrem. Non desunt quibus placeat hoc solùm aut propriè trullam significare: nos putamus arytænam omnem, generali significatione trullam fuisse appellatam: etsi non negamus sæpius tribui illi à scriptoribus τῆς οἰνηρύσεως significationem. Quod igitur in Amphitruone Plauti ait ille,
units.tr: from the Campanian ladle, as usual. And Cicero against Verres. There are those who think the word means only a ladle in the proper sense; but we believe that every arytaina was in general called a trulla, although we do not deny that writers often ascribed to it the sense of wine-drawing [οἰνηρύσεως]. Therefore, when Plautus says in the Amphitruo, as he does:

units.la: Lances detergam omneis, omneisque trullas hauriam, sic interpretamur, vt trullas omneis accipiamus ἀντὶ τῶ ταλάντου ἀρύταναν[?], siue trullarum omne genus, neque ad οἰνήρυον tantùm referimus, sed etiam ad reliquas trullas: puta, ἐτυρύσεις, ζωμηρυσ̈ς, & alias, si quæ erant aliæ. Notabis βάλλε ἀρύταναν, pro βάλλας ἀρύειν immersa arytæna haurire,
units.tr: I will wipe all the dishes and draw from all the ladles, we interpret it so that we take omneis trullas as the equivalent of the ladle [ἀντὶ τῶ ταλάντου ἀρύταναν], or every kind of ladle, and we refer it not only to the wine-ladle but also to the other ladles: that is, the broth-ladle, the porridge-ladle [ἐτυρύσεις, ζωμηρυσ̈ς], and any others there were. You will note βάλλε ἀρύταναν, used for βάλλας ἀρύειν, "to draw out by dipping in the ladle."

units.la: Οὐδένεια (Gr. χρείας[?].) Hæc est merces quam iste impudens balneatori pendit discedens. More Romano quadrantem illi debuit: nam quadrante pauperiores lauabant. Horatius.
units.tr: Oudeneia [Οὐδένεια] (Greek: χρείας). This is the fee which that shameless fellow paid the bath-keeper as he left. According to Roman custom he owed him a quadrans, for poorer people bathed for a quadrans.
—while you go to bathe for a quadrans, you will be king. Horace.
To give way to Silvanus the pig, to wash for a quadrans.

units.la: Et Seneca epistola I xxxvi I[?]. balneum vocat rem quadrantariam. At pueri balneaticum non dabant, ait Probus in illud Iuuenalis,
units.tr: And Seneca, Epistle 1 (xxxvi), calls the bath rem quadrantariam, "a quadrans affair." But boys did not pay the bath-fee, says Probus on the line of Juvenal:

units.la: Nec pueri credunt, nisi qui nondum ære lauantur. ars re familiaris moderatè utendi: parcissimum tamen hominem vocamus pusilli animi & contracti: cùm infinitum interest inter modum & angustias. Hæc alia sunt natura: sed effecit inopia sermonis, ut & hunc & illum parcum vocemus. volunt Seneca Græcam vocem μικρολόγος exprimere, cùm dixit hominem pusilli animi & contracti. eleganter: sed tamen ita possum etiam eum appellare, qui μικροπρεπὴς illis dicitur.
units.tr: Nor do boys believe, unless they have not yet washed for money. It is a matter of using one's means with moderation; yet we call a man who is very sparing "small-spirited and mean," though there is an infinite difference between thrift and meanness. These are different by nature, but poverty of language has caused us to call both this man and that one "sparing." They think Seneca in saying "small-spirited and mean" expresses the Greek word μικρολόγος, elegantly; yet I can also call by that name the one whom the Greeks call μικροπρεπής.

units.la: At homo parcus apud Græcos præsertim comicos non μικρολόγος solùm dicitur, sed etiam γλίσχρος, κιυξίζ, κυμινοχίμιζ[?], κυμινοπρίσης, siue ὁ [illegible, ~6 letters] καὶ κυμινον: item καρδαμογλύφος[?], κραδοφάγος, σφιγξ[?], ὠγιλῶ, ἰξὸς, κυκλογαλῶ, γλοιὸς, ξυμβρεπὴς[?], σκιφὸς & κνιπὸς, πευγόκι, πευσίζι, ῥυπαροκαυδαλῶ, vel vt alibi legitur, ῥυπαρόνδυλος: nec non λιμὸς, λιμοχίμιζ, συκοταρίσης, συκοφάσης, μυκὸς, & μυσάλμης: sunt & aliæ apud veteres grammaticos eorundem hominum appellationes, quæ mihi nunc in mentem non veniunt. Cæterùm vocem μικρολογία Aristoteles ad disputationes philosophorum aliquando transfert, & pro ἀκολουθία, vel λεπτολογία (minutiloquium possis vertere ex Tertulliano) vsurpat: vt in pulcherrimo loco qui sub finem primi Metaphysicorum habetur. Iuuenalis μικρολογίαν dixit minimas sordes, satyra x i i i i.
units.tr: But the sparing man, especially in the Greek comic writers, is called not only μικρολόγος, but also γλίσχρος, κιυξίζ, κυμινοχίμιζ, κυμινοπρίσης, or ὁ [illegible] καὶ κυμινον; likewise καρδαμογλύφος, κραδοφάγος, σφιγξ, ὠγιλῶ, ἰξὸς, κυκλογαλῶ, γλοιὸς, ξυμβρεπὴς, σκιφὸς and κνιπὸς, πευγόκι, πευσίζι, ῥυπαροκαυδαλῶ, or as elsewhere read, ῥυπαρόνδυλος; and also λιμὸς, λιμοχίμιζ, συκοταρίσης, συκοφάσης, μυκὸς and μυσάλμης. There are also other names for the same sort of men among the old grammarians, which do not come to mind now. Moreover, Aristotle sometimes transfers the word μικρολογία to the disputations of philosophers, using it for ἀκολουθία or λεπτολογία (one could render it minutiloquium from Tertullian), as in the most beautiful passage near the end of the first book of the Metaphysics. Juvenal called μικρολογία minimas sordes ("the smallest meannesses"), Satire 14.

units.la: Sunt quædam vitiorum elementa; hæc protinus silos Imbuit, & cogit minimas edissere sordes.
units.tr: There are certain elements of vice: they straightway steep the silly and compel them to unfold their smallest meannesses.

units.la: Apuleius sordem infinitam pro eodem. Cicero τὸν μικρολόγον parcum & restrictum solet appellare: sicut & apud quosdam Græcos σεισήια hac notione positum inuenias: Suetonius in Nerone, sordidum & deparcum: Plautus in Persa, triparcum: in Aulularia, parcè parcum, quo loco extat elegantissimus amœnissimúsque & χαρακτῷρ[?] character hominis tenacis & σμικρολόγος[?].
units.tr: Apuleius uses "infinite meanness" [sordem infinitam] in the same sense. Cicero usually calls the stingy man (τὸν μικρολόγον) "sparing and restricted" [parcum & restrictum]. You will also find the word σεισήια [seiseia] among some Greeks in this sense. Suetonius in Nero has "mean and miserly" [sordidum & deparcum]; Plautus in the Persa has "triply sparing" [triparcum], and in the Aulularia "sparing to the point of sparingness" [parcè parcum]. In that passage there is a most elegant and charming portrait of a tightfisted man, a character who is a smikrologos [σμικρολόγος].

units.la: τῷ ἀδιαφόρῳ[?].) Significat τὸ ἀδιάφορον[?] sumtum & impensam: atque adeo pecuniam: sic apud Aristotelem, non solùm in definitione χρημάτων[?]: sed etiam alibi saepe. estque istud vocabulum hoc sensu Polybio, Dionysio Halicarnasseo, & aliis quibusdam familiare. Sic accipiendum illud Ecclesiastici capite v i i. commate x x. Μὴ ἀλλάξῃς φίλον ἀδιαφόρου[?] χάριν[?] μηδὲ ἐν μηδὲ ἀδελφὸν γνήσιον ἐν χρυσίῳ[?] ὀφείλ[?]. hoc est, Ne commutes amicum vlla re siue pecunia. Ὁ νῦς[?]: Caue quicquam tanti æstimes, ut id amici iactura velis redimere. Ita exponendum esse hunc locum clarum est: & euincit altera pars istius commatis: quæ eôdem cum præcedenti pertinet: quod ferè perpetuum est, in hoc & Solomonis prouerbiorum libro. Quare errant grauiter, qui aliter aut interpretantur aut legunt. Legunt enim doctissimi viri ἀδιάφορα: quos etiam vetus interpres refellit. In eodem scriptore sic legitur capite x x v i i. χάεν ἀδιάφορα πολλοὶ ἡμαρτον· καὶ ὁ ζητῶν πλουτῆσαι ἀσπερίζει ὀφθαλμὸν αὐτῆ[?]. Nos hîc quoque eandem vocem censemus restituendam: & legimus χάεν διάφορα πολλοὶ ἡμαρτον[?] perspicuo & optimo sensu: & confirmat hanc nostram emendationem posterior pars commatis, ut ne dicam veteres sic legisse: qui tamen insipiam[?] male verterunt, at in omnibus quas vidi editionibus est ἀδιάφορα. In libris Maccabæorum extat locis aliquam multis vox διάφορα numero multitudinis, prorsus pro χρήματα: quod interpretes cùm non observassent, mirè se torserunt, & locos censuerunt emendandos, qui optimè habebant. Exemplum unum aut alterum proferemus, libro secundo, capite primo, χρὴ οἷς ἐχρεί̈ζεῖο ὁ βασι-λεὺς πολλὰ διάφορα ἐλάμβανε ἐ μελετῶν[?] hoc est, πολλὰ χρήματα[?]. capite tertio, ὥστε τὸ πλῆθος τῆς συ-φόρων ἀναςεθμῶν[?] εἶ). τῆς συ[?]. dixit, pro τῆ χρημά-των[?]. neque recte haec mutant quidam, magni meo iudicio viri: hoc uno minores, quod se maximos credunt, & omnia sibi φιλοκαιςῶς[?] ἂν licere in literis volunt.
units.tr: (…) It means expense and outlay, and so money. This is how Aristotle uses it, not only in his definition of wealth [χρημάτων] but also often elsewhere. Polybius, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and some others also use the word in this sense. The verse in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7, verse 20, must be understood the same way: "Do not exchange a friend for anything, nor a true brother for gold." That is, "Do not barter a friend for any thing, whether money or otherwise." The meaning is: take care that you do not value anything so highly that you would buy it at the cost of losing a friend. That this passage must be read this way is clear, and the second half of the verse proves it, since it belongs with the preceding clause, as is almost always the case in this book and in the Proverbs of Solomon. So those who either translate or read it otherwise are gravely mistaken. Very learned men read ἀδιάφορα [adiaphora, "indifferent things"], and even the old translator refutes them. In the same author, chapter 27, verse 2, it is read thus: "For the sake of ἀδιάφορα many have sinned, and he who seeks to be rich turns his eye away." I think the same word should be restored here too, and we read "for the sake of διάφορα [diaphora, goods] many have sinned", which gives a clear and excellent sense. The second half of the verse confirms this emendation, not to mention that the ancients read it so; yet the translators, who were unskilled, rendered it badly, and in all the editions I have seen it reads ἀδιάφορα. In the books of the Maccabees the plural διάφορα occurs in many places, quite simply in the sense of χρήματα [chremata, money]. The translators, not noticing this, twisted themselves into knots and thought these passages, which were perfectly sound, needed correcting. I will give one or two examples. In the second book, chapter 1, "where the king needed many διάφορα he took them, not thinking" — that is, many χρήματα. In chapter 3, "so that the multitude of the tax-payers…" the word is used for money. Some men, great in my judgment, but lesser in this one thing, change these readings badly; they think themselves very great and want to be allowed to do anything they please in literature.

units.la: Οἱ ... ἐν τῷ μὴ ἡμιωβόλιον ἀπαιτεῖν ὅτι τὸ οἰκίαν[?]. Fortasse ὅτι τῇ οἰκίᾳ[?]. Est autem horum verborum, quae esse integra praestare nolim, obscurus & in abdito latens sensus. An igitur ita exponendum? Solet cùm locatae à se domus pensionem, (ἐνοίκιον Graeci vocant) ab inquilino exigit, ita rigidus esse & acerbus exactor, ut si de integra summa absit vel semiobolus condonare id nolit, aut in proximum mensem differre eius solutionem. An referendum potius ad conuiuia veterum? Solebant illi collatis symbolis, coire apud aliquem amicorum, & in eius aedibus conuiuium agitare. Videtur ergo sordidus iste petere, ut aliquid sibi pro aedibus quas amicis commodat, soluatur. Sed cur dissimulem parum mihi de isto loco liquere? quem quidem, quoties lego, toties ad incitas redactum me sentio. Doctiores hoc vulnus sanent: ego herbam lubens merito dabo. In membranis quae seruantur in Palatina Bibliotheca, illustrissimi principis, scriptum est, ἐλθὼν ὅτι τῷ οἰκίαν[?]. optimè iudicio meo. Nam vox ἐλθὼν totius sententiae, nisi fallor, [?] eido est. Vult enim hominis μικρολόγου notam esse, quòd de menstrua pensione sesiduum obolum qui sibi debeatur, tanti faciat, ut eius exigendi gratia ad debitoris sui domum ipse veniat. Possumus de usura hoc interpretari quæ ex debita forte proficiscatur. Nam certum est fœnus menstruum pendi solitum. Sed non ipsi creditores exigebant: verùm seruos flagitatores mittebant, quos propterea μνιαίους ἀπαιτήλας [?] vocat Basilius. Possumus & de mercede conductæ domus accipere: nam & hoc certum, τὰ ἐνοίκια menstrua die pendi solita: cuius rei testes sunt, ut alios taceam, epigrammatarij poëtæ Græcorum.
units.tr: "…in not demanding a half-obol, because the house…" Perhaps the reading is ὅτι τῇ οἰκίᾳ [because of the house]. The meaning of these words, which I would not vouch are sound, is obscure and hidden. Should it be understood thus? When a man demands the rent (the Greeks call it ἐνοίκιον) of a house he has let to a tenant, he is such a rigid and harsh collector that if the full sum is short even by a half-obol, he will not forgo it, or will postpone its payment to the next month. Or should it rather refer to the banquets of the ancients? They used to gather at a friend's house with shared contributions and hold a feast in his home. So this miser seems to ask that he be paid something for the house he lends to his friends. But why should I hide that this passage is quite unclear to me? Whenever I read it, I feel I am reduced to a sorry state. Learned men may heal this wound; I will gladly give the herb, deservedly. In the manuscripts kept in the Palatine Library of the most illustrious prince, it is written ἐλθὼν ὅτι τῷ οἰκίαν [coming because of the house]; in my judgment this is best. For the word ἐλθὼν, unless I am mistaken, fits the whole sense. For it is meant to show that the man is a mikrologos, since he thinks a single obol owed to him out of the monthly rent so important that to collect it he comes to his debtor's house himself. We may take this of interest, perhaps arising from a debt, for it is certain that monthly interest was customarily paid. But the creditors themselves did not demand it; they sent slaves as collectors, whom Basil therefore calls "monthly demanders" [μνιαίους ἀπαιτήλας]. We may also take it of the hire of a rented house, for it is also certain that rents [τὰ ἐνοίκια] were customarily paid monthly. Greek epigrammatic poets are witnesses to this, to say nothing of others.

units.la: Memini tamen legere in Græcorum commentariis, solitos Athenienses τὰς μισθὰς καὶ τὰ ἐνοίκια καὶ τρυ(γ)νείας [?] ἢ μῆνα τελεῖν [?]. ἀειθμεῖν πόλις κύλικας ἔκας [?] τέσωκε [?]. ) Martialis lib. 1 x. in Charidemum.
units.tr: I remember, however, reading in the Greek commentaries that the Athenians used to pay wages, rents and… by the month. (The Greek is corrupt here.) Martial, book 10, on Charidemus.

units.la: Et numeras nostros adstricta fronte trientes, Tanquam de cella sit cadus iste tua.
units.tr: "And you count our trientes with a knitted brow, as if that jar were from your own cellar."

units.la: Fuit olim apud Athenienses in epulis publicis ei rei quidam præfectus, ut quoties quisque, & quomodo biberet obseruaret: eumque magistratum οἰνόσπλω [?] vocabant, vel ὀφθαλμόν. Athenæus libro decimo.
units.tr: Once among the Athenians at public feasts there was an official appointed for this purpose, whose task was to observe how often and how each man drank. This magistrate was called the oinospolos [οἰνόσπολος] or "eye." Athenaeus, book 10.

units.la: καὶ ἀπάρχεσθαι ἐλάχιστον τῇ Ἀφ. ] Mos antiquissimus, deos placare primitiis victus. Varro Manio, Quocirca oportet bonum ciuem legibus parere, & deos colere, in patellam dare, μικρὸν χρίας. Nota res eruditis.
units.tr: "And to offer the smallest first-fruits to Aphrodite." This is a most ancient custom, to placate the gods with first-fruits of food. Varro, in his Manius: "Therefore a good citizen ought to obey the laws and worship the gods, giving a little in a dish, a little incense." A familiar matter to scholars.

units.la: ἐὰν τις μικρὰ ἀριθμῷ λογίζεσθαι [?].) Λογίζεσθαι non est hic putare: sed imputare alicui, & expensum ferre. Loquitur enim Theophrastus de mandatario, vel negotiorum gestore, qui amici vel mandatoris nomine aliquid emerit. ita denique accipiendum, vt cum ait Ariftoteles in fecundo Oeconomicorum de Cleomene Alexandrino loquens, ἀποσείλας δέ [?] τινα ὅτι ἀγόρασμά τι, αἰσθόμενος, ὅτι ἐώνων τετύχηκε, ἀπὸ ᾧ μέλλῃ ἐκλελογισμένα λογίζεσθαι. Diuus Paulus etiam ἐλλογεῖν hoc sensu solet vsurpare. Appianus καταλογίζειν.
units.tr: "If someone reckons small things…" Here λογίζεσθαι does not mean to think, but to charge something to someone and enter it as an expense. Theophrastus is speaking of an agent or manager of business who has bought something in the name of a friend or principal. It must be understood as Aristotle does in book 2 of the Oeconomics, speaking of Cleomenes of Alexandria: having sent someone to buy something, and perceiving that he had bought it, he began to charge him with the sums to be reckoned. The divine Paul also commonly uses ἐλλογεῖν [ellogein] in this sense; Appian uses καταλογίζειν [katalogizein].

units.la: ἡ οἰκέτου χύτραν ἢ λοπάδα καταξαίνων.] Bellè hæc cōueniunt Athenienfibus: quos in rebus ita minutis & parui pretij mirè fuiffe attentos & follicitos, nequid sibi seruorum fraude periret, Ariftophanis fabulæ testantur. Nam in Ranis ait poëta plerosq; Athenienfium statim vbi domum fuerint ingressi, nihil antiquius habere, quàm vt seruos suos magno cum clamore appellent, & ab ipsis scifcitetur, quid olla factum esset, quid capite mænadis quæ forte fuerat è mensa sublata: quid paropside anno superiore empta: quid pridiano allio; quis denique de oleis deguftarit. Verba poëtæ,
units.tr: "…scraping a slave's pot or dish." These things fit the Athenians well. Aristophanes' plays show that they were wonderfully attentive and anxious about such small and cheap things, lest anything be lost to their slaves' fraud. For in the Frogs the poet says that most Athenians, as soon as they enter the house, think of nothing more urgent than calling their slaves with great shouting and asking them what had happened to the pot, what had become of the head of the mackerel that had been taken from the table, what had become of the little dish bought the year before, what of yesterday's garlic, and who finally had tasted the olives. The poet's words:

units.la: νυὶ γὰρ Ἀθη- ναίων ἅπας τις εἰσιὼν κέκραγε πρὸς τοὺς οἰκέτας, ζηλεῖ τε, πῶ 'στιν ἡ χύτρα; τίς τὼν κεφαλῶ ἀπεδήδοκε τῆς μαινίδος; τὸ ψυχλίον τὸ περύσινον τέθνηκέ μοι. πῶ τὸ σκόροδον τὸ χθεσινόν; τίς τῆς ἐλάας παρέσχηται;
units.tr: "For now every Athenian who enters shouts at his slaves, and demands: where is the pot? who has eaten the head of the mackerel? my little Persian dish is dead. Where is yesterday's garlic? Who has served up the olives?"

units.la: Scholiastes & Suidas aiunt esse hæc μικροφρεπείας δείγματα, indicia angusti animi. μικροφρέπειαν, accipiunt ἀντὶ μικρολογίας. Sic & alij scriptores, Hierocles, φησὶ χρημάτων ἀκαίρῳ εἰς μικροφρέπειαν δείγ-
units.tr: The scholiast and Suidas say these are signs of small-mindedness, indications of a narrow spirit. They take μικροφρέπεια [mikrophrepeia, pettiness] in place of μικρολογία [mikrologia]. So too other writers: Hierocles says that to spend money at the wrong time is a sign of pettiness.

units.la: Κάλαμοι[?] ex quarto Nichomacheorum discas quid fit μικροφερέπα[?]. ἀποβαλλούσης τείχαλκον.[?] Vide Iulium Pollucem.
units.tr: From book 4 of the Nicomachean Ethics you may learn what mikropreperia is. … Compare Julius Pollux.

units.la: Pag. 33. καὶ τὰς κιβωτούς.[?] Capsæ erant ad condendas vestes, Clemens Alexandrinus Pædag. lib. III. πῶς δὲ τὴν ἐσθῆτα[?] τὰς κιβωτοὺς; erant autem κιβωτοὶ ligneæ, κίσαι[?] è vimine. Abillis arcis dictus vicus Athenarum, vicus κιβωτίων[?], cuius meminit Plutarchus.
units.tr: "…and the chests." These were boxes for storing clothes; Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, asks how to keep clothes in chests. The chests were of wood, or woven of wicker. Abillis, the district of Athens called the quarter of the chest-makers, is mentioned by Plutarch.

units.la: καὶ ὃν ἐσαι.[?] Contrarium est quod de viro magno Peticle testantur historiæ: Eum quippe legimus, vt populum sibi conciliaret suorum agrorum macerias sustulisse: quò possent omnes quibuscunque effet libitum fructus ex arboribus decerpere.quod & alios factitasse qui liberales & esse & haberi volebant,eadem historia testis. vide Plutarchum in Pericle & Cimone.
units.tr: What the histories report of the great man Pericles is the opposite. We read that to win the people's favour he removed the hedges of his fields, so that anyone at all could pick the fruit from the trees. The same history witnesses that others too did this, who wanted to be and to be thought liberal. See Plutarch in the lives of Pericles and Cimon.

units.la: καὶ τὰς ὄρυς ὁ Θεόκριτος.[?] Olim soliti veteres, seruos sibi parare & in villis habere, quorum munus erat custodia finium. De Græcis constat vel ex idyllio Theocriti quo Augiæ κλήρῳ[?] describitur. Latini hos seruos faltuarios appellabant. Glossarium vetus, Saltarius ὀρεοφύλαξ[?]. in mendo & Græca vox & Latina cubat: lege, Saltuarius, ὀροφύλαξ[?]. Vlpianus lege xii. Dig. De instructo vel instrumento legato. Saltuarium autem Labeo quidem putat eum demum contineri, qui fructuum feruandorum gratia paratus sit: eum non, qui finium custodiendorum causa. Saltuariorum, vt vides, duo genera: alij fines custodiebant: de quibus sensit Glossarij auctor superiore loco: alij fructus. de his accipio quod in altero Glossario scribitur ὑλαυροφύλαξ[?], Saltuarius. Porrò termini moti, siue vt erat in lege Pompilij, exarati,(quod Græcis est τὰ ὁροθεσια ὁροϊλυφεῖν)quàm graue crimen fuerit, & diuina testantur iura & humana: quàm frequens, vel hic locus fit indicio.
units.tr: And Theocritus [mentions] the mountain-guards. In former times the ancients were accustomed to acquire slaves and keep them on their country estates, whose duty was to guard the boundaries. That this was so among the Greeks is clear from Theocritus' idyll describing the lot of Augeas. The Latins called these slaves saltuarii. An old glossary has "Saltarius" = oreophylax. The error lies in both the Greek and the Latin word; read "Saltuarius" and orophylax. Ulpian, in book 12 of the Digest, On instructed or bequeathed equipment: "Labeo thinks that a saltuarius is strictly one who is kept for the sake of guarding the produce, not one kept for the sake of guarding the boundaries." So, as you see, there were two kinds of saltuarii: some guarded the boundaries, which is what the author of the glossary meant in the passage above; others guarded the produce. It is of these that I take what another glossary has: hylauro-phylax, "Saltuarius." Moreover, that moving boundary-stones, or inscribing them as was done under the law of Pompilius (in Greek ta horothesia horoilyphein), is a grave crime, both divine and human law attest; how frequent it was, this very passage is evidence.

units.la: ὑπερπιμεῖαν πράξαι[?]. ] Oratores Græci hoc solent dicere τὸν ὑπερπίμπερον εἰσπράττειν. & erat Athenis grauissima eorum poena qui iudicatum non soluissent: scholiastes Aristophanis in Nebulas ait, in quadruplum solitos condemnari: aut si non habuerent in ære, luisse in corpore, & à creditoribus suis in neruo & compedibus habitos. Hos Græci ἐλκαλοσχελεῖς, Latini nexos vocabant.
units.tr: Hyperpimeian prasai ("to exact the excess"). Greek orators commonly say ton hyperpimpron eispragein. At Athens the most severe penalty was for those who did not pay a judgment. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Clouds says that such debtors were usually condemned to four times the sum, or, if they had no money, paid with their bodies, being held by their creditors in stocks and fetters. The Greeks called these elkaloscheleis, the Latins nexi.

units.la: ἢ τόκον τόκῳ.) Satius erat hanc notam referre inter ἀπροιας[?] notas: grauius enim istud, quàm vt μικρολόγῳ censeri debeat qui id faciat. Impp. Diocletianus & Maximianus lege x x.Cod. Ex quibus caulis infamia irrogatur: Improbum fœnus exercentibus & vsuras vsurarum illicitè exigentibus infamiæ macula irroganda est. Lucullus vt refert Plutarchus inter alias leges quibus improbitatem fœneratorum per Asiam grassantium coërcuit, hanc quoque tulit, vt qui vsuras cum forte coniunxisset, & fortes & vsuras amitteret. Fere tamen hoc iure veteres vsos legimus,vt vsura quæ exacto anno non soluebatur, sorti accederet, & deinceps fœnus parereť. anatocismum Græci Latiniquę nuncupant.
units.tr: "Or interest upon interest." It would have been better to list this mark among the signs of shamelessness, for it is a more serious thing than that the man who does it should be counted a petty person. The emperors Diocletian and Maximian, in law 20 of the Code, say: "Infamy is to be imposed on those who practise wicked usury and unlawfully exact usury upon usury." Lucullus, as Plutarch reports, among other laws by which he checked the wickedness of the moneylenders who ran riot through Asia, also passed this one: whoever had joined interest to principal would lose both the principal and the interest. Yet we read that the ancients generally observed this rule: interest not paid when the year was up was added to the principal, and thereafter bore interest. The Greeks and Latins alike call this anatocismus.

units.la: μικρὰ τὰ κρέα κόλας[?] σαβδεῖναι[?]. ] Plinius Epistolarum libro secundo, de sordido conuiuatore loquens, Vilia, inquit, & minuta ponebat conuiuis.
units.tr: "He served small and cheap meats." Pliny, in book 2 of his Letters, speaking of a stingy host, says: "He set before his guests cheap and meagre food."

units.la: ὀψωνῶν[?], μηδὲν προιαμένῳ εἰσελθεῖν[?]. ] Censen' de alio Theophrastum loqui, quàm de Euclione Plauti? quem locum vt hîc non ascribam, nihil suaue meritum est.
units.tr: Do you think Theophrastus is speaking of anyone other than Plautus' Euclio? I do not quote that passage here, since it deserves nothing pleasant.

units.la: Venio, ait ille, ad macellum : rogito pisces. indicant Caros : agninam caram, caram bubulam, Vitulinam, cetum, porcinam, cara omnia: Atque eo fuerunt cariora, as[?] non erat: Abeo illinc iratus, quoniam nihil est qui emam: Deinde egomet mecum cogitare inter vias Occepi, festo die si quid prodegeris, Profesto egere liceat, nisi peperceris.
units.tr: Plautus: "I come, he says, to the market and ask the price of fish. They point out that everything is dear: lamb dear, beef dear, veal dear, tunny dear, pork dear, all dear. And the dearer they were, the less money I had. So I go away from there in a rage, since there is nothing I can afford to buy. Then I began to reflect to myself on the way: if you spend something on a feast day, you may be able to go hungry on a working day, unless you have been sparing."

units.la: μήτε ἅλας χρωννύν[?].) Nimirum aceto : Sal & acetum olim, pauperiorum cibus, ut norunt jam & lippi & tonsores. Alexis χωμαλίζειν[?] sic accepit.
units.tr: Mēte halas chrōnnyein ("neither to salt [anything] with..."). Surely with vinegar: salt and vinegar were once the food of the poor, as even blear-eyed men and barbers know. Alexis understood it so.

units.la: Τὸ ψύμμα[?] Ἡπτολῆς[?] ἀρύθμως[?] διμένον[?]ὄξει σπαίῳ χωμαλίζας[?].

Latini, intingere. Cato, Brassicam crudam si edas, in acetum intingito. Persius, Tingit olus: & passim Cornelius Celsus. Recte igitur χωννύειν[?] conuenit, si ad ἅλας tantùm referas : si ad ea quæ sequuntur, non item. Nam quis tam amens, qui ellychnium saltem intingi & madefieri nolit? cymino quoque aut origano parum conuenire videtur, quorum vsus est in condimentis, vt docet Athenæus : nec multo melius sequentibus vocibus· ἁλὰς[?], κέμμαζ[?] & Συ-λήμμαζ[?]. Quare puto subesse hic mendam, desideraríque verba aliquot. Lego, μήτε ἅλας χωννύειν[?], ....... μήτε ἐλλύχνιον[?]. in lacuna desideratur tale quid, μήτε χὰν τινί[?], vel χορηγεῖν[?], fortasse tamen nihil deest: sed illud χωννύειν[?] ex deprauatione veræ lectionis est natum. Ita igitur legi potest, μήτε ἅλας χὰν τινὶ[?], μήτε ἐλλύχν[?]. Hoc posterius vt probabilius, sumus amplexi.
units.tr: The Latins say intingere ("to dip"). Cato: "If you eat raw cabbage, dip it in vinegar." Persius: "He dips the greens." And Cornelius Celsus everywhere. So chrōnnyein fits rightly if you refer it to salt only; if to what follows, it does not. For who is so mad as not to want even a wick dipped and soaked? Cumin and oregano also seem scarcely suited to it, since their use is in seasonings, as Athenaeus teaches; nor are the following words much better: halas, kemmaz and syllemmaz. So I suppose there is an error here and some words are missing. I read: "neither salt ... [to anyone], neither a wick." In the gap something like "to anyone" or "to supply" is missing, or perhaps nothing is missing and chrōnnyein arose from a corruption of the true reading. It might therefore be read: "neither salt to anyone, neither a wick." We have adopted the latter reading as the more probable.

units.la: μήτε ἐλλύχνιον[?].) Etiam ellychnia ad curam hominum μικρολόγων pertinebant. Itaque in Nebulis Aristophanis lamentatur auarus ille Strepsiades,& puerum tantum non verberat, quòd ellychnia lucernæ adhibuisset crassa nimis. Aliusin Vespis filium obiurgat, quòd stuppas non acu vel festuca, sed digito produxisset: ἡ ζεῦ, inquit, τὰς ἀλαΐς σπα-νίζοντ[?]. Iuuenalis,cuius dispenso & tempero filum.
units.tr: "Nor a wick." Wicks too were a concern of stingy people. So in Aristophanes' Clouds the miser Strepsiades laments and almost beats his boy because he had used wicks for the lamp that were too thick. In the Wasps another man scolds his son because he drew out the tow not with a needle or a straw but with his finger: "Heavens," he says, "you are sparing the wicks!" Juvenal: "whose thread I dole out and ration."

units.la: Pag. 34. μάτε Συλλήμα(τα). ) Scribendum Συλλήμα(τα). Sunt quæ alio nomine ψυχὰ dicuntur, hoc est, fruges ἐ-ψυσμέναι[?], siue fractæ saxo, vel molitæ. Latinis mole, vel liba. vide grammaticos. His solis antiquissimi homines deos sibi conciliabant, vt ait Ouidius in Fastis. quare cùm posterior ætas alia sumtuosiora sacrificia vsurpare coepisset, is honos antiquitati habitus, vt non solùm adolendas victimarum partes farre conspergerent, (de quo ritu poetæ interpretes Ouidius vx.Metamorph.& Dionysius Halicar. libro v 1 r. aliiúque) sed etiam post omnia, extremo loco tandem Συλλήμα tanquam offerumentum Deo gratissimum offerrent. Notat hunc ritum Porphyrius Περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων, lib. secundo, τὰ δ' ἀληλισμένα βίᾳ σιτοῦ τὸ πρόσθεν μακα-ρίτης ἀπόρξαντα τῆς ψευδείας προφῆς προσῶν εἰς τὴν τῆς θεοῦ, ὅτε ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἀρὸς τὰ τέλεα τοῦ Συν-λῶν, ὡς ψευδεῖον Συλλήμασι χρώμενα. Atque hoc proptiè ὑπὸ ὑπόδ ὑπ posterior ætas dixit, vt docet idem auctor, quia post alia sacrificia fiebat. Sed & Συλλή μα verbum est, quod significat Συλλήματα offerre. Porphyrius eodem libro de pauperis Docimi oblatio-ne loquens, ἐκ τῆς ἀρτιφευμένης πόρας τῆς ἀλφίτων ὀλί-γας δράκας ἱθυλλάζ. Constat autem ex historia pauperiorum sacrificia non alia ferè quàm ista fuisse.
units.tr: (p. 34) "Nor syllemata." Read syllemata. These are things called by another name psycha, that is, grains that have been crushed or broken by stone, or ground. In Latin they are mola or liba; see the grammarians. Ovid says in the Fasti that the most ancient men won the favour of the gods with these alone. Therefore, when a later age began to use more costly sacrifices, this honour was kept for antiquity: they not only sprinkled the parts of the victims to be burned with spelt (on this rite see the commentators on Ovid's Metamorphoses and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5), but also, at the end, as the final offering, they presented the syllema as a gift most pleasing to God. Porphyry notes this rite in book 2 of On Abstinence from Animal Food, where he speaks of the former practice, and of the offering of the poor man Docimus, who threw a few handfuls of meal into the fire. And the word syllema itself means "to offer syllemata." From history it is clear that the sacrifices of the poor were scarcely anything but these.

units.la: Theophrastus apud Stobæum, Τὸν ὃ μὴ οἰκεῖ[?] ἐν ἄσει. Σὺν τὸν ὅρκον ὅτι τὰ Διὸς τὰ ἀγοραῖα[?]· τὰν ὃ ἡ Θυ-σίαν τῆ ἐλαττόνων τῇ Θυλήμα[?].Diuites verò cùm alia sacrificabant, tum etiam loco Θυλημάτων thura, & alia id genus libamina in bustum arae iaciebant. in quo illud legimus obseruatum, vt summis digitis vel thura,vel frugeos offerrent. Porphyrius,φησιν, ἡ Πυθία τὸν Ερμιονέα κεκαρπῶσθαι, Θυσίαι τῆ ... ἐκ τὰ ἀπειδία ... ἐς τῶς ... δακτύλοις. Hieronymus, epistola prima, Non est tantum in eo seruitus, si quis duobus digitulis thura in bustum ara iaciat, aut haustum pateræ poculo fundat merum. propterea dicebat Lactantius de religione paganorum, nihil in ea se videre aliud quàm ritum ad solos digitos pertinentem. & Seneca pater negat eum cui praecisæ sint manus posse adorare: non solùm ritum hunc respiciens, sed alios qui fuêre à veteribus in re diuina facienda obseruati: de quibus fortasse aliàs. Atque hæc quia non ita vulgò nota videbantur, placuit paullo susius exponere.
units.tr: Theophrastus in Stobaeus: "The man who ... swears by Zeus ... the sacrifice of the lesser ... syllema." Rich people, when they offered other sacrifices, also cast incense and other such libations onto the altar's pyre instead of syllemata. In this, we read, it was the custom that they offered the incense or grain with the tips of their fingers. Porphyry says that the Pythia ... with the fingers. Jerome, in his first letter: "There is no great slavery in it if someone casts incense onto the altar's pyre with two little fingers, or pours a sip of wine from a cup." Hence Lactantius, in his work on the religion of the pagans, said that he saw in it nothing but a rite concerned with the fingers alone. And Seneca the Elder denies that a man whose hands have been cut off can worship: he has in mind not only this rite but other observances which the ancients kept in performing divine worship, of which perhaps more elsewhere. And since these matters seemed not so commonly known, I have chosen to explain them a little more fully.

units.la: ὅτι τὰ μικρὰ ... ... τὰ ἑαυτῶ. ] Præclarè philosophus in quinto De republica, si quis saluam velit Rempublicam, monet cauendum, ne quicquam omnino contra leges fiat: & addit, summa in primis cautione opus esse, in eo quod paruum videtur: nam id ni fiat, paullatim & latenter irrepere rerum omnium depravationem: vt necesse sit illam funditus tandem perire rempublicam. Sic pessundari domos locupletes paruis,sed frequentibus sumptibus.hoc enim decipi plerorumque mētem, dum sibi persuadent, nihil aut perpetuum illos sumptus esse nocituros, quorum sit vnusquisquc que paruus : contrarium tamen cuenire : minutas enim iftas impenfas magnum damnum tandem afferre, imò labem ac perniciem totius rei familiaris. ἀλλ' ἢ διὰ οἶα ὑπ' αὐτῷ, ὥσπερ ὁ σοφιστικὸς λόγος, Εἴ ἕκαστον μικρὸν, καὶ τὰ πράγματα τῶν μικρῶν, σύγκειται δ' ἐκ μικρῶν [?] inquit Aristoteles, ἢ διά. Par prudentia magni viri Demosthenis, cuius hæc ex quarta Philippica, pulcherrimè superiori Aristotelis loco concinunt.
units.tr: "That small things ... themselves" [ὅτι τὰ μικρὰ]. The philosopher admirably, in book 5 of the Republic, warns that if anyone wishes to keep the commonwealth safe, he must take care that nothing at all is done contrary to the laws; and he adds that the greatest caution is needed above all in what seems small. For unless this is done, the corruption of everything creeps in gradually and unnoticed, so that the commonwealth must at last perish utterly. Thus wealthy households are ruined by small but frequent expenses, because the minds of most people are deceived while they persuade themselves that these expenses, each of them small, will either do no harm or harm only for a time; yet the opposite happens, for these petty outlays in the end bring great loss, indeed ruin and destruction to the whole household. Aristotle's argument runs like this: if each thing is small, then things composed of small things are small. A similar prudence is shown by the great man Demosthenes, whose words from the fourth Philippic agree most beautifully with the passage of Aristotle cited above.

units.la: Η καθ' ἡμέραν ραςῶιν καὶ ραδυμία, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῆς ἰδίας βίος ἕτω ἑκάστης ἀπλῶς, ἐν τοῖς πόλεσιν, ἐν δὲ ἑκάστῳ τῶν ἀμελυμένων ποιεῖν τῶ αὐτοῦ ... ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς ... τῶν πραγμάτων ἀπαλλᾶ [?]. Quemadmodum, inquit, in privata vita, sic etiam in Republica, defidia & discordia quotidiana, non in singulis statim, ut quidque est neglectum, animadvertitur : sed in summa rerum tandem apparet. Sed & graviffimus auctor Plutarchus in vita Cæsaris monet, nullum vllius rei initium esse paruum exiftimandum, quod magnum ftatim fit reddĭtura affiduitas, licentiam & impunitatem ex fui contemtu nacta. Græcè melius, ὡς ἑνὸς ἐμίαν ἀρχὴν πράγματος ἡγεῖσθαι μικρὸν, ἥν ἔχω τοιοῦτ' μεγάλου τὸ ἐν- δελεχὲς, ἐκ τῆς καταφρονήσεως τὸ μὴ κωλυθῶσαι λαβὲ- ῶν. Sic ille locus Plutarchi legi & exponi debet. Hoc eft quod Aristoteles tot locis appellat, τὸ σμικρὸν μικρον.
units.tr: Daily negligence and sloth, as in private life, so in each thing generally, in cities, and in each of the neglected matters... As in private life, so too in the commonwealth, idleness and discord day by day are not noticed in each single thing as soon as it is neglected, but at last they appear in the sum of affairs. Plutarch, a most weighty author, in his Life of Caesar also warns that no beginning of anything should be thought small, because constant repetition soon makes it great, once licence and impunity have been gained from contempt. The Greek is better rendered: one should regard as small no beginning of a matter from which a lasting great thing arises, when it is not checked after contempt. That is how the passage of Plutarch should be read and explained. This is what Aristotle calls in so many places "the small in the small" [τὸ σμικρὸν μικρόν].

units.la: ἐλάττω τῷ μικρῶν τὰ ἱμάτια φορεῖν.) Fortaffe, τῷ μικρῷ. breuiores quàm ut femora penitus tegant. Sed & μικρῶν ferri poteft. Sic dixit Sappho, ἀνδρὸς μεγάλα πολὺ μείζων. Sic Synefius, τῷ ὀλίγων ἐλάττων. Sic Paufanias, ἀνδρὸς ὁ μείζων μεγάλα. Sic Appianus, οἱ τὰ μεγέθη μείζους τῶν μεγίστων ὑπάρχοντες. Poteft & μετρίων legi. Sic dixit Herodotus libro 11. [?]ἀνδρὸς μικρὸν μετρίων ἐλάσσονες ἀνδρῶν [?]. Quemadmodum autem veftis breuitas eft fordium argumentum, fic veftis ad talos demiffa vitæ delicatæ & diffolutæ, vt apud Platonem in Alcibiade priore [?]ἐλαχίστων ἰματίων [?] indicium [?]ἀξιόρητος[?]. inde illa Plutarchi in Alcibiade, [?]ἐσθῆτας τε καὶ ϑηλύτητας ἐσθῆτων ἀλουργῶν ἐλκομένων [?] δὲ ἀγορᾶς. Horatius, Cum bis ter vlnarum toga.
units.tr: "wearing garments shorter than the small ones." Perhaps it should be "the small one." Shorter than to cover the thighs fully. But "of the small ones" can also stand. Thus Sappho said of a man, far greater by much; thus Synesius, lesser than the few; thus Pausanias, the greater of the great men; thus Appian, those who are greater than the greatest in size. "Of moderate ones" may also be read. Thus Herodotus said in book 2 that the men were lesser than moderate men. Just as the shortness of a garment is a sign of squalor, so a garment hanging down to the ankles is a sign of a delicate and dissolute life, as in Plato's Alcibiades I, where the sign is of the least garments. Hence Plutarch's words in the Alcibiades about the purple robes trailing in the marketplace. Horace: with a toga of six yards.

units.la: Apud Dionem Calenus obiicit Ciceroni, quod μι[?]χρὰ σφυρῶν τῶν ἐσθῆτος σύγερ[?] & Cicero ipfe de Oppianico, Facite,inquit, vt non folitm mores eius, & arrogantiam, fed etiam vultum atque amictum, atque illam vfque ad talos demiffam purpuram recordemini. Seneca pater libro 11. Omnia à te vitia : quòd vnguento colorem madet, tuum eft : quòd laxior vfque in pedes tunica demittitur, tuum eft. Propterea breues veftes honores graues & δ' ἀραιότεροι geftabant. Horatius,
units.tr: In Dio, Calenus charges Cicero that ... of the ankles of his garments; and Cicero himself, on Oppianicus: Bring it about, he says, that you remember not only his habits and arrogance, but also his face and dress, and that purple hanging down to the ankles. Seneca the Elder, book 2: All faults are yours: that he soaks his complexion in perfume is your doing; that a tunic hangs looser down to the feet is your doing. For this reason men of grave honours wore short garments and more sparing ones. Horace:
And a scanty toga pretends to be Cato in appearance.

units.la: Εἴμι δ' ἐν ἀσκητά μέσας ὑπερφρύνω κνήμας. [?]
units.tr: "I walk about in a tunic, with my shins high-exposed."

units.la: καὶ ἐν ἀγορᾷ κεκορυμμένους. [?] Ariftophanes Nebulis,
units.tr: "and armed in the marketplace." Aristophanes in the Clouds:

units.la: Ait poëta homines tenaces præ fordibus nunquam caput totondiffe. Videntur effe contraria, ftrictim ad cutem vfque tonderi, & nunquam tonderi : funt tamen eiufdem hominis, & vt loquitur Ariftoteles,[illegible, ~10 letters]. Nam qui ad vnum tonderi vult, id fpectat, vt raro tonfwris opera indigeat, vitat, inquam, fumtus, non minus quàm ille alter. Ex his intelligi poteft, quæ ratio fit cur apud Ariftophanem philofophi modò tanquam [?]κομψῶς[?] irrideantur. rideantur : modò vt ἐν χρῷ κεκαρμένοι : vtrumque enim extremæ parsimoniæ est. à quibus fordidibus vt se ostenderent esse alienos homines venusti & elegantes, solebant quod Theophrastus capite quinto dicebat, πλῆς-άκις ὑποκείρεσθαι[?].
units.tr: The poet says that men stingy from squalor never had their heads shaved. These seem contrary, to be shaved close to the skin and never to be shaved; yet they belong to the same sort of man, and, as Aristotle puts it, [illegible]. For he who wishes to be shaved to the one length aims that he should seldom need the barber's work; he avoids expense, no less than the other man. From this it can be understood why in Aristophanes the philosophers are sometimes mocked as elegant [κομψῶς], sometimes as shaved close to the skin; for both belong to extreme parsimony. Men who wished to show that they were refined and elegant, and not of such squalor, used to do what Theophrastus in chapter five called shaving frequently [πλῆς-άκις ὑποκείρεσθαι].

units.la: τὸ μέζον τῆς ἡμέρας ὑπολυομένης.) Non semper veteres Græci calceati erant vt hodie nos fumus: multus enim fuit τῆς ἀνυποδησίας vsus. Spartanos quidem etiam lex Lycurgi coegit esse discalceatos, vt refert Xenophon in eorum politia. Athenienses quoque paullo qui essent in ratione vitæ astrictiores aut seueriores, non nisi necessario tempore, ad vitandum scilicet frigus, aut itinerum asperitates, calceis vtebantur, vide Plutarchum in Phocione: & ait idem auctor in vita Lycurgi oratoris, eum τὰς ἀναλκαίας tantum ἡμέρας calceos induisse. Oppianus etiam in venatoris institutione, iubet eum nudis pedibus ad venationem ire.
units.tr: "the middle of the day when the..." The ancient Greeks were not always shod as we are today, for going barefoot was common. The law of Lycurgus compelled the Spartans indeed to go unshod, as Xenophon reports in his account of their constitution. The Athenians too, if they were somewhat stricter or more severe in their way of life, used shoes only at necessary times, namely to ward off cold or the roughness of journeys; see Plutarch in the Phocion; and the same author says in the Life of the orator Lycurgus that he put on shoes only on the days of... Oppian too, in his instruction on hunting, bids the hunter go to the chase barefoot.

units.la: Κείνῳ δ᾽ ζῶσιν ἴχνη μίλεται δυσέρχεα θηρῶν[?].
units.tr: "For him the tracks of the beasts are hard to follow..."

units.la: Clemens Alexandrinus Pædagog. iii. libro ii. ἀνδρεῖ δ᾽ μάλα ἀρμόδιον, ἀνυποδησία[?]· πλὴν εἰ μὴ στρατιώταις[?]· καὶ γὰρ πως εἰκὺς τὸ ἀνυποδεῖσθαι τῷ ἐδάσθαι[?]. id est, Sine calceis esse viro admodum conuenit: parum enim à vincto differt cui pedes in calceis vincti. Nota est & Romani Catonis ἀνυποδησία. item Neronis: vide Suetonium capite quinquagesimo primo. Martialis vero libro xii. Cottam quendam ridet quòd excalceatus iret ad cœnam. Seneca quoque epistola lxxxvii. erubuisse se ait mulionem suum excalceatum non propter æstatem. Quod ait τὸ μέζον τῆς ἡμέρας, Atticum est, vt admonent veteres magistri.pro κῇ τῷ μεσημβείαν vel vt loquitur Diogenes Cynicus τὸ μέσῳ ἡμέραν. errant enim qui aliter accipiunt. Theocritus dicere solet τὸ μεσημβρινὸν, vel τὸ μεσημβρινὸν: & Lucianus De gymnasiis. τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτῆς ἔξει πολλῷ γλίσ. ) Nempe κονίαν, vel potius κιμωλίαν. Hoc Liuius dixit, cretam, siue album in vestimentum addere: Theophrastus in libro De lapidibus, γλῶ ἱματίζειν εἰς τὰ ἱμάτια. Erat olim duplex cretæ vsus in officina fullonum: alia sordes eluebantur: alia candorem nitoremque vesti parabant. Plinius, libro xxxv. cap. decimoseptimo.
units.tr: Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, chapter 11: "Going without shoes is very fitting for a man, unless he is a soldier; for in a way going barefoot resembles being bound." That is, to be without shoes is very suitable for a man: for he differs little from one whose feet are bound in shoes. The going barefoot of Cato the Censor is well known, and likewise that of Nero; see Suetonius, chapter 51. Martial, in book 12, mocks a certain Cotta because he went to dinner unshod. Seneca too, in epistle 87, says he blushed that his muleteer was barefoot, not because of the summer. As for the phrase "the middle of the day," it is Attic, as the old teachers remind us, in place of the phrase for midday, or as Diogenes the Cynic puts it, "the middle of the day." Those who take it otherwise are mistaken. Theocritus is accustomed to say the midday [τὸ μεσημβρινόν]. And Lucian, in On the Gymnasiums: "her garment will have much..." (a whitening). Here, of course, is meant [κονίαν], or rather chalk [κιμωλίαν]. Livy called this creta, adding chalk or white earth to a garment; Theophrastus in his book On Stones speaks of whitening garments [γῆ ἱματίζειν]. There was once a double use of chalk in the fullers' workshop: one kind washed away dirt, the other gave the clothes whiteness and sheen. Pliny, book 35, chapter 17.

units.la: ΟΥ χαλεπὸν δὲ ἔχει τῷ βδελυρίαν διορίσασθαι.) Negat Theophrastus difficile esse definire τὸ βδελυρίαν: nec sanè multum difficile est quid ille velit intelligere. Illud, puto, difficilius sit, vocem Latinam reperire quæ Græcæ respondeat. Non enim satis mihi facit vox obscœnitas: quoniam animaduertimus iocos ludósque qui hic recensentur, non omnes esse obscœnos, neque ea turpitudine infectos, quæ castas pudicásque aures solet offendere: vt erant illa quæ in Fescenninis versibus & Atellanis solebant vsurpari. Multa inquam hîc continentur, inhonesta illa quidem, sed sine obscœnitate & αἰσχρολογία: turpia tamen nihilominus & μύσεις ἄξια, quod proprie sonat vox βδελυρὸς. Ac notat scholiastes Aristophanis βδελυρὸς Athenis fuisse vocitatos homines infames, vt sunt lenones, & id genus : itémque τὸς ἀνελ[?]θέρες, hoc est, eos qui præ auaritia turpiffimis fordibus delectarentur : quod pulchrè facit ad multa quæ hic commorantur. Nos duabus dictionibus vocem ῥυπαρία[?] expreffimus obscœnitas & impuritas : fed visa est poftmodum vox impuritas vel fola non malè auctoris mentem exprimere : vt quidem apud comicos frequenter folet vsurpari.
units.tr: Theophrastus says that it is not hard to define bdelyria [βδελυρία]. It is not really very difficult to see what he means by it. I think it is harder to find a Latin word that answers to the Greek. The word obscenity does not satisfy me, because we notice that the jokes and pranks listed here are not all obscene, nor tainted with that filth which usually offends chaste and modest ears, such as the things that were used in the Fescennine verses and the Atellan farces. Much is included here that is indeed disreputable, but without obscenity or foul speech [αἰσχρολογία]; still, it is no less base and deserving of abomination [μύσεις ἄξια], which is what the word bdelyros [βδελυρὸς] properly means. The scholiast on Aristophanes notes that at Athens men of ill repute were called bdelyroi [βδελυροί], such as pimps and the like, and likewise the miserly, that is, those who out of greed took pleasure in the most shameful filth. This fits well with much that is discussed here. We rendered the word with two terms, obscenity and impurity, but afterwards the word impurity alone seemed to express the author's meaning well enough, as it is often used in the comic writers.

units.la: ἀνασυρπάμψω. ] Componens videlicet se, vel fimulans se componere ad κολλυβισ[?]τὴν, vel ad meiendum : nam is olim χεζητιώντων[?] (honos fit auribus) & micturientium mos & gestus. Dionyfius Halicarnaffeus, de Philonide Tarentino loquens, ἀνασυρπάμψω τῷ ἀναβοᾶλλω, & γυμαλίας ἑαυτὸν ὡς αἰχμὴν [?] ἐκλύναι, τῷ ὃ λέγεσθαι πρέπει ἂν ἀκαθαρσίαν [?] τῆς ἱερᾶς ἐδάφους τὰ πρόσωπα τῆς κατεσκευάσατε. & in eadem hiftoria alij, Galenus in exhortatione ad artes, οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς ὑδρίας φρυγάνων [?]ὑδρ, ἐπειδὴ ἂν μυκτὴρ[?] ἔχωσιν ὕδωρ, ἀνασυρπάμψοι προσωπεῖον[?]. & est in viris τὸ ἀνασυρπάμψω, quod in sequiore sexu varicitus stare, vt apud Apuleium. At οἱ χεζητιῶντες incoxare se etiam dicuntur: vnde est coffim χίζειν, quasi coxim. Vide Nonium.
units.tr: Anasyrpampso [ἀνασυρπάμψω]. Clearly he is arranging his clothes, or pretending to arrange himself for the purpose of the kollybistes [κολλυβιστής], or for urinating; for among the ancients this was the manner and gesture of men who were about to defecate (I apologise to modest ears) and of those who were urinating. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, speaking of Philonides of Tarentum, uses anasyrpampso [ἀνασυρπάμψω] for anaboallo [ἀναβοάλλω], and says that he shook himself like a fish, as is fitting, when he uncovered the parts of the body which he had covered. In the same story others have it too. Galen, in his exhortation on the arts, says that those who carry water from the jar, when they have water in their nostrils, anasyrpampsoi [ἀνασυρπάμψοι] their mask. The word anasyrpampso is used of men, while in women it means to stand with the legs apart, as in Apuleius. Those who are defecating are also said to incoxare, to draw up the thighs; hence the verb coxim [χίζειν], as if from coxa. See Nonius.

units.la: συεῖτλεν ὡς ἡδέως ἰσυρὰ σύμψον οἱ λοιποί. ] Exemplo sit Theophraftus quidam in Ariftophanis Vefpis:
units.tr: Syeitlen hos hedeos israa syrpsomon hoi loipoi [συεῖτλεν ὡς ἡδέως ἰσυρὰ σύμψον οἱ λοιποί]. As an example, take a certain Theophrastus in Aristophanes' Wasps:

units.la: Οἱ δ' ἀνεκρότησαν, πλὴν γε Θουφράσου μόνου,Οὕτω δ' ἠμύλλαινεν, ὡς δὴ δεξιός.
units.tr: "But they applauded, all except Theophrastus alone, and he whistled thus, as if he were clever" [Οἱ δ' ἀνεκρότησαν, πλὴν γε Θουφράσου μόνου, Οὕτω δ' ἠμύλλαινεν, ὡς δὴ δεξιός].

units.la: nam ἡμυλλαίνειν à rictu oris facta vox, idem est ac συεῖτλεν: quod significat sibilo siue paftoritia fiftula, vt loquitur Cicero, aliquem profequi : di-citur & κλώζειν, pro eodem, vt in ea contra Midiam. vide Hefychium, Harpocrationem, & Euftathium in ὀδυσ. δ'. Id eft, κλωσμοσυρίζειν vox elegantiffima apud Philonem.
units.tr: For hemyllainein [ἡμυλλαίνειν], a word formed from the movement of the mouth, is the same as syeitlen [συεῖτλεν], which means to accompany someone with a whistle or with a shepherd's pipe, as Cicero puts it. It is also said klozein [κλώζειν] in the same sense, as in his speech against Midias. See Hesychius, Harpocration, and Eustathius on the Odyssey delta. That is, klosmosyrizein [κλωσμοσυρίζειν] is a very elegant word in Philo.

units.la: ἀνακύλας ἐρυγεῖν.) Simile est quod notat Cicero in Antonio: Cui ructare turpe effet, is vomens, fructis efculentis, vinum redolentibus, gremium fuum, & totam tribunal implevit.
units.tr: Anakylas eryge‹i›n [ἀνακύλας ἐρυγεῖν]. Similar is what Cicero notes in the Antony: "The man for whom belching would be disgraceful vomited, filling his lap and the whole tribunal with food and wine-scented fluid."

units.la: Pag. 36. καὶ κάλεσαι.) Plautus Menaechmis, Certò hac mulier aut infana eft, aut ebria Meffenio, Hominem qua ignotum compellet me tam familiariter.
units.tr: Page 36. Kai kalesai [καὶ κάλεσαι]. Plautus in the Menaechmi: "Surely this woman is either mad or drunk, Messenio, since she addresses me so familiarly, a man she does not know."
Sadison de pou [σαδίσον δέ που]. I would rather read soi [σοί].

units.la: καὶ ὀψωνεῖν ἑαυτόν.) Scribe ἑαυτῷ. Vide suprà.
units.tr: Kai opsonein heauton [καὶ ὀψωνεῖν ἑαυτόν]. Write heautō [ἑαυτῷ]. See above.

units.la: καὶ σκωμμαλεῖν ὅτι ζῷα. ) Ridiculi causa, non ferio. Atqui hoc infulse rudere eft, non falsè ridendi occasionem praebere.
units.tr: Kai skommaleīn hoti zōa [καὶ σκωμμαλεῖν ὅτι ζῷα]. For the sake of ridicule, not seriously. Yet to offer an occasion for laughter that is not falsely ridiculous is a sign of a foolish man.

units.la: καὶ διηγεῖσθαι ἀρχὰς πρὸς κουρεῖον.] In tonstrinis iam olim male feriatorum hominum conciliabula celebrari solita.vndeeft κυρεῖ λαλιὰ dictum παροιμιακῶς à Polybio in tertia historia. Lysias in ea contra Pancleonem, ἤλθον ὅτι τὸ κυρεῖον τὸ ἀρχὰς τῆς Ἕρμᾶς, ἵνα οἱ Ἀτκελεῖς προσφοιτῶσι· Idem alibi, ἑκάστῳ ὑμῖν εἴθισαι προσφοιλᾶν, ὁ μὲν πρὸς μυροπώλιον· οἱ δὲ πρὸς κουρεῖον. Damnat hunc morem sanctissimus vir Clemens Alexandrinus, 1 1 1. libro Pædago. Μὴ ξύνω, αἰ μηδὲ οἱ ἀνδρες ὅτι τῆς κουρείων καὶ καταλεῖων ξεναγεῖν ἀδολεσχοῦντων σωμυλιοπυοι. Theophraftus vero nofter vt erat ingenio perurbano, tonstrinas appellitabat abstemia conuiuia, fiue ἄοινα συμπόσια, ὅ-τι τὸ λαλιὰν τῆς προσηγορίαν. Plutarchus. Adiicit auctor ἡ μυροπώλιον, quia vt tonstrinæ, ita & myropolia otiosis hominibus referta solebant esse. Sic Demosthenes in Aristogitonem, ἐδὲ προσφοιλᾷ πρός τι τῆς ἐν τῇ πόλει κουρείων ἢ μυροπωλ ἀ μυροπωλίων , & pasim.
units.tr: Kai diēgeisthai archas pros koureion [καὶ διηγεῖσθαι ἀρχὰς πρὸς κουρεῖον]. Already in antiquity the barbershops were places where idle men were wont to gather for talk. Hence the proverbial phrase kyreî lalia [κυρεῖ λαλιὰ], used by Polybius in his third book. Lysias in his speech against Pancleon says: "They came to the barbershop of Hermas, where the Athenians used to resort." And elsewhere: "It is your custom, each of you, to frequent either the perfume shop or the barbershop." The most holy Clement of Alexandria condemns this custom in the third book of his Paedagogus: "Let not men, who in the barbershops and perfumeries are led about with idle talk, babble..." Our author Theophrastus, being of a very urbane wit, called barbershops "teetotal banquets" or aoina symposia [ἄοινα συμπόσια], since they had the name of chatter [λαλιά]. Plutarch. The author adds the perfume shop, because, like barbershops, perfume shops too were usually full of idle men. So Demosthenes against Aristogiton: "Nor does he frequent any of the barbershops or perfume shops in the city," and so on throughout.

units.la: χαὶ οἰνοπωλῶν, κεκραμένον τὸν οἶνον.] Fraus pridem Miscere aquas vino: apud Tertullianum ex propheta Isaia. Hoc nomine malè audiebant Athenæ. Alexis comicus in Afoto, facetè qui id facerent excusat: negans sui compedij illos habere rationem: sed sanitatis ementium, vt ne possint mero potato morbi cauffam contrahere. Locus suauissimus est; quem ideo placuit apponere,
units.tr: "And wine-sellers, the wine being mixed." Adulterating wine with water was long ago called "mixing water with wine," a phrase Tertullian takes from the prophet Isaiah. Athens had a bad reputation for this. The comic writer Alexis, in his Asotus, wittily excuses those who did it: he says they took no account of their own profit, but of the health of the buyers, so that they could not contract illness from drinking undiluted wine. The passage is very charming, and I was glad to set it out here.

units.la: A. Κομψὸν γε τῦτ' ἔστιν παρ' ἡμῖν ὦ Σόλων Ἐν ταῖς Ἀθήναις, δεξιῶς δ' ἀρημένον.
units.tr: A. "This is a clever custom among us, Solon, in Athens, and a skilful thing to do."

units.la: Σ. Τὸ ποῖον; A. ἐν τοῖς συμποσίοις ἵν' ὑμῖν φίνετε Ἀκρατὸν ἢ γὰρ ῥᾳδίως πωλεῖν γὰρ Ἐν ταῖς ἀμάξαις ἐθίως κεκραμένον. Οὐχ ἵνα τί κερδαίνωσι; τὴν δ' ὠνεμένων Προνοοῦ μύροι, τὰ τὰς κεφαλὰς ὑγιεῖς ἔχειν.
units.tr: S. "What is it?" A. "To sell unmixed wine at the banquets, so that you may drink it; for it is easy to sell it mixed in the wagons. Will they not do it for the sake of profit? But care for the perfumes that you buy, so that your heads may be healthy."

units.la: Sed in venditione vini triplicem fere fraudem cauponum notant veteres: quod illud diluant, mangonizent, & falsa mensura vendant. Lucianus, οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἀποδιδόασι τὰ μαθήματα ὥσπερ οἱ κάπηλοι κεκαπηλευμένοι, καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ, & δολωθέντες & κακομεταχειρούντες.
units.tr: But the ancients note that in selling wine the wine-sellers commonly practised a threefold fraud: they watered it, adulterated it, and sold it by false measure. Lucian: "Philosophers sell their teachings like tavern-keepers who have been cheated and mistreated..."

units.la: χαὶ δὴ ἔιαν ἐνίκα.) Corruptissimum locum minima mutatione, sic emendandum censemus: καὶ ὅτι ἔιαν ἐνίκα ἂν δὲν ποριέσθαι ἐκ ἐῶν ὡς ἡμεῖς· ἐνίκα ἢ πρὸς ἀφιέσαν οἱ Σ. Imperiti homines cùm non possent legere illa ἐκ ἐῶν pepererunt nobis istud ἀτιῶν, quod huc nulla ratione quadrare potest. Iam supra diximus lucar Athenis pendi solitum ab iis qui locum in theatro habere vellent. cuius moris auctorem grammatici faciunt Periclem, quem aiunt primum fecisse ὡς τόπους ὠνητάς. Propterea viritim accipiebant de ærario certam pecuniam, vt haberent etiam pauperes vnde possent sumtum illum facere, & locum sibi ad spectandum emere, quod Θέαν ἀγοράζειν vocabant. Inde tam multa apud oratores Atticos, Demosthenem maximè, de pecunia theatro destinata. Hanc mercedem ei dabant qui hîc vocatur Θεατρώνης, apud Aristophanem Θεατροπώλης: non sunt enim vt prima fronte possint videri hæ duæ voces inter se relatæ, sed de eodem, etsi diuersa ratione, dicuntur. Θεατρώναι sunt, redemtores theatrorum, qui facienda & extruenda subita theatra conducebãt: constat enim veteres Athenienses spectasse ἀπὸ τῶν ἰχείων [?]. Iidem mox in extructo theatro sedes siue foros spectaturientibus vendebant, vnde dicti Θεατροπῶλαι, οἱ Θέαν ἀγοράζοντες, inquit Pollux. Demosthenes cum à quo sedes erat emenda, architectum appellat in ea pro Corona, & eius interpres vetus persæpe, propter eam quam exposuimus rationem. Duobus autem obolis spectabant Athenienses. Demosthenes pro Corona, ἀλλ' ἐν ταῖν δυοῖν ὀβολοῖν ἐθεώρουν ἄν [?]: vbi mirè turbat Græcus interpres, non raro nimis quàm impeditus dicam, an imperitus? Aristophanes Vespis,
units.tr: Kai dē ean enikā [καὶ δὴ ἔιαν ἐνίκα]. This badly corrupted passage, we think, can be emended with a very small change to read: "And indeed, if he won, he would procure from them what we did not give; he would send..." Unskilled men, unable to read the words ek eōn, produced for us the reading atiōn, which cannot fit here in any way. We have already said that at Athens a seat was commonly paid for by those who wished to have a place in the theatre. The grammarians ascribe the origin of this custom to Pericles, who they say first made the places purchasable. Therefore the citizens each received a fixed sum of money from the treasury, so that even the poor might have the means to pay the cost and buy themselves a place to watch, which they called theān agorazein [Θέαν ἀγοράζειν]. Hence the many references in the Attic orators, especially Demosthenes, to money set aside for the theatre. This fee was paid to the one called here theatrōnēs [Θεατρώνης], in Aristophanes theatropōlēs [Θεατροπώλης]. These two words, at first sight, may not seem related, but they are used of the same thing, though in different ways. The theatrōnai were the contractors of theatres, who undertook to build and erect temporary theatres; for it is known that the ancient Athenians watched from wooden structures. Afterwards the same men sold seats or benches in the built theatre to those wishing to watch, and so they were called theatropōlai [Θεατροπῶλαι], "those who buy the sight," as Pollux says. Demosthenes, when speaking of the one from whom the seat was to be bought, calls him an architect in the speech On the Crown, and his old interpreter very often does the same, for the reason we have explained. Athenians paid two obols to watch. Demosthenes in On the Crown: "But they watched for two obols" [ἀλλ' ἐν ταῖν δυοῖν ὀβολοῖν ἐθεώρουν ἄν]; here the Greek interpreter wonderfully confuses things, so that one may hardly say whether he is more unskilled or more hampered. Aristophanes in the Wasps:

units.la: Ἐγὼ δὲ τεθεώρηκα πώποτ' ἀδαμάς, Πελν ἐς Πάρον. καὶ ταῦτα δυ' ὀβολὼ φέρων.
units.tr: "I have once watched Adamas, when I was in Paros, and I paid two obols for it" [Ἐγὼ δὲ τεθεώρηκα πώποτ' ἀδαμάς, Πελν ἐς Πάρον. καὶ ταῦτα δυ' ὀβολὼ φέρων].

units.la: Scholiastes : Ἰχείοις θεωροῦντες, τὰς δύο ὀβολὰς παρεῖχον. Reperio tamen vnam aliquando drachmam dari solitam. Hesychius Δραχμὴ χαλαζῶς· ὅτι Διο-φάντου τὸ θεωρικὸν ἐχίζεσ δραχμή [?]. Vide primam Olynthiacam, & ibi Vlpianum. Porrò videntur hi theatrorum redemtores sub finem spectaculorum facile quemuis vel gratis soliti esse admittere: id enim Theophrastus isto loco manifestò innuit, τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἐφόδιον.] Qui publicè legati aliquò proficiscebantur, accipiebant ex ærario legatiuum. Marcellinus in Hermogenem, Νομῷ τὸν προπέμπειν [?] λαβόντα τὸ ἐφόδιον ἀχρὶ τῆς πεζῆς ἡμερῶν ἐξελθεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν πρεσβείαν. Legatiui modus fuit, duæ in singulos legationis dies drachmæ: quod etsi paruum videatur ad nostra tempora si referas: illis tamen temporibus magnum fuit. Indicio est Aristophanis iste locus Acharnensibus,
units.tr: The scholiast: "Watching from the wooden stands, they paid two obols." Yet I find that sometimes one drachma was customarily given. Hesychius: "Drachma: a chalazōs. Because the theoric fund of Diophantus [Διοφάντου τὸ θεωρικὸν] was one drachma." See the first Olynthiac and Ulpian there. Moreover, it seems these contractors of theatres were in the habit, towards the end of the shows, of easily admitting almost anyone, even for nothing; for Theophrastus clearly hints at this in that place: "the travelling money from the city" [τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἐφόδιον]. Those who set out publicly on embassies somewhere received from the treasury an allowance for the journey. Marcellinus, against Hermogenes: "Having received the travelling money by law, he was to set out on the embassy within the days of the journey." The rate of the travel allowance was two drachmas a day for each member of the embassy. Though this may seem a small sum compared with our own times, it was large in those days. Evidence for this is that passage of Aristophanes in the Acharnians,

units.la: Ἐπέμψαθ' ἡμᾶς ὡς βασιλέα τὸν μέγαν, Μισθὸν φέροντας δύο δραχμὰς τῆς ἡμέρας Ἐπ' Εὐθυμένης ἄρχοντος. Δι. οἴμοι τῆς δραχμῆς.
units.tr: "They sent us to the great king, carrying two drachmas' pay a day, in the archonship of Euthymenes." Dicaeopolis: "Oh, the drachma!" [Ἐπέμψαθ' ἡμᾶς ὡς βασιλέα τὸν μέγαν, Μισθὸν φέροντας δύο δραχμὰς τῆς ἡμέρας Ἐπ' Εὐθυμένης ἄρχοντος. Δι. οἴμοι τῆς δραχμῆς.]

units.la: Romanorum veterum non diuersa fuit frugalitas, qui Tyberio Graccho rem agenti publicam extra vrbem, sumtum diurnum assignarunt nouem obolorum: auctor Plutarchus. Hanc autem pecuniam, non tantùm ἐφόδιον, vt hic & apud Demosthenem, sed etiam πορεῖον vocabant. Auctor Etymologici, Πορεῖον, τὸ διδόμενον τοῖς πορευομένοις εἰς τὴν πρεσβείαν ὡς περὶ ἐφόδιον. Porro exemplum simile βδελυρίας in Pisone exagitat M. Tullius.
units.tr: The frugality of the early Romans was no different. When Tiberius Gracchus was carrying out a public commission outside the city, they assigned him a daily allowance of nine obols; the authority is Plutarch. This money was called not only ephodion, as here and in Demosthenes, but also poreion. The Etymologicum says: "Poreion: what is given to those travelling on an embassy, as an ephodion is." Cicero, in his speech against Piso, likewise castigates a similar example of baseness.

units.la: τῷ ἀχσλέϑῳ ἐπιθέναι μ. φορτίον.] Intelligit stragulam vestem, & alia instrumenta viæ, quæ olim moris fuit iter facientibus secum deferre. cuius rei passim exempla sunt in veterum monumentis. Has sarcinas quæ σφιγγαλίδεσμα [?] Græcis vocantur, Seneca, sagmi, vnus aliquis validus seruus ἀναφόρῳ sine æruminulis religatas gerebat. vnus, inquam: plurium enim opera in eam rem vti mollis & delicati nimis habebatur. quare Æ. Schines Demosthenis vitio vertit, quòd cum legatum sequerentur duo serui cum duabus farcinis : σωμηκολάθου ϑ, inquit, ἀνὴρ ἀνθρωποι δύο γρωματοδισματα φίρειν. videbatur enim hominis esse nimis mollis & effœminati tot rebus ad corporis cultum pertinentibus feruos onerare. Atque hoc ipsum in Romanis notat Seneca primo Naturalium quæstionum. Adeo, ait, omnia indiscreta sunt peruerfissimis artibus, vt quicquid mundus muliebris vocabatur, farcina viriles sint : minus dico : etiam militares. & Suetonius aliquot locis. Hunc seruum vocat Theophraftus ἀχολάθων, & ita Xenophon in tertio Commentariorum extremo, & alij. & fanè ἀχολάθη erat, quia onustus herum fuum fequebatur. Sciendum tamen proprie ἀχολα θος dici pueros qui viros nobiles & honoratos, honoris cauffa fequebantur. Hefychius, Αχολάθῳ, ὁ νεώτερος παῖς. Στράτων ὁ τὸ σῶμα. Atque hu-jufmodi elegantes pueros plures habere Athenis inuidiofum fuit:ac ne legibus quidem permiffum, vt teftatur Vlpianus in eam Demofthenis contra Midiam. Melius hoc fanè & caftius Athenienfes quàm Romani : quorum nota eft licentia effrenata, in alendis ornandifque pædagogiis: de quibus non repeto quæ funt à doctis hominibus obferuata. Eapropter fcribit Tatianus, Romanos folere παίδων ἀγέλας, ὥσπερ ἵππων φορβάδας σωαγεῖφιν. Similis querela Clementis de fui temporis hominibus, οἰνοχόων τε ὁμιλος ἀπεῖταφ' αὐτῶν, καὶ μίμα-λίων ὡραίων ἀγέλας, καθάπερ θερμάτων ὧν ἀμέλ-γοντας τὸ κάλλος. vt modò dicebamus: propterea sæpe eueniebat vt vnus ille qui duceretur, pondere iniquo oneraretur· quod genus iniquitatis, ita frequenter vsurpabatur ab Atheniensibus ætate Aristophanis, vt comici eorum temporum, non aliud argumentum sæpius in suis fabulis tractarint. In omnibus enim illorum comœdiis erat semper misellus aliquis seruus, qui onere pressus clamaret Θλίβομαι, vel Πιέζομαι. eam ob causam Aristophanes æquales suos comicos tanquam insubidos, ineptos, & eadem semper chorda oberrantes castigat, cum in Ranis, tum in parabasi illa elegantissima, quæ est in Pace: & tamen idem ipse poëta Pasiam similiter querentem inducit in Ranis. vide initium eius fabulæ.
units.tr: "To place a load upon the attendant." He means the rugs and other equipment for the road, which it was once customary for travellers to carry with them. There are examples of this everywhere in the ancient monuments. These bundles, which the Greeks call sphingalidesma, were carried by one strong slave, bound to a pack-frame with no extra straps. One, I say: for to use several men for the job was thought too soft and pampered. So Aeschines reproaches Demosthenes because, when two slaves with two bundles followed his embassy, he said: "a man of soft and effeminate habits, to load slaves with two such loads of things for the care of the body" [σωμηκολάθου ... ἀνὴρ ἀνθρωποι δύο γρωματοδισματα φίρειν]. For it seemed the mark of a man too soft and effeminate to burden slaves with so many things pertaining to the care of the body. Seneca notes this very thing among the Romans in the first book of his Natural Questions: "So completely," he says, "are all things confused by the most perverted arts, that whatever was called women's finery has become men's baggage: I say less, even soldiers'." Suetonius does so in several places. Theophrastus calls this slave akolathon, and so Xenophon at the end of the third book of his Memorabilia, and others. Indeed the akolathē was so called because, loaded down, he followed his master. It should be noted, however, that properly akolathos was the name for boys who followed noble and honoured men as a mark of honour. Hesychius: "Akolathos: the younger boy. Straton: the body." And to keep several such elegant boys was held in odium at Athens, and even the laws did not permit it, as Ulpian testifies in his commentary on Demosthenes against Meidias. Certainly the Athenians were better and more chaste in this than the Romans, whose unbridled licence in maintaining and adorning their pedagogues is notorious; I shall not repeat what learned men have observed about them. Therefore Tatian writes that the Romans were accustomed to keep "herds of boys, like mares in a herd" [παίδων ἀγέλας, ὥσπερ ἵππων φορβάδας σωαγεῖφιν]. Clement makes a similar complaint about the men of his own time: "a crowd of cupbearers around them, and herds of youthful mimes, like cattle whose beauty they milk" [οἰνοχόων τε ὅμιλος ... ἀγέλας, καθάπερ θερμάτων ὧν ἀμέλγοντας τὸ κάλλος]. As we were just saying, it therefore often happened that the one who was led along was burdened with an unfair weight. This kind of injustice was so frequently practised by the Athenians in the age of Aristophanes that the comic poets of that time scarcely treated any other theme more often in their plays. In all their comedies there was always some poor slave, crushed by his load, crying "I am squeezed!" or "I am pressed!" [Θλίβομαι, Πιέζομαι]. For this reason Aristophanes rebukes his fellow comic poets as dull, silly, and forever straying on the same string, both in the Frogs and in that most elegant parabasis in the Peace; and yet the same poet brings in Pasias, complaining in just the same way, in the Frogs. See the beginning of that play.

units.la: ἐλάχισα ὑπηλίδα τῆς ἱκανῷ.] Notabis ἐλάχισα pro ἐλάττω. Aristoteles tertio Topico. μᾶλλον γὰρ τὸ φερεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ αἰσθητῷ τίνι τῇ ὑπηδέου. τὸ δὲ ἑαυτὸν μᾶλλον τῆς γραμμῆς γραμμὴ ἢ σημείου μᾶλλον[?]. & hinc μάλισα pro μᾶλλον. Idem libro De sensu & sensili, χειρέστερα ἐχόμενα τῷ ἀλλων ζῴων τῷ αἰσθητῷ ταύτῃ. χειρέστερα dixit pro χείρω. Quare nihil opus emendatione, quod quibusdam videbatur.
units.tr: "Less than a sufficient..." You will note that elachisa is used for elatto. Aristotle in the third book of the Topics: "for the more ... is nearer to the perceptible than ..., and the line is more a line than the point is" [μᾶλλον γὰρ ...]. And hence malisa is used for mallon. The same author in the book On Sense and the Sensible: "the things that are next to the perceptible in other animals are worse" [χειρέστερα ...]. He said cheirestera for cheirō. Therefore there is no need for emendation, which some thought necessary.

units.la: Σαπρόν γὰρ τὸ ἔλαιον ἐπεί.] Σαπρὸν oleum est, τὸ παλαιωμένον, vetustate corruptum, ac rancidum, & cuius odorem nequeas perferre, vt ait Horatius. Græcis σαπρὸν proprié. Putre oleum dicere noluimus: qui præsertim didicissemus ab Aristotele τὰ λιπαρὰ magnam partem esse ἄπηκτα. Atticis autem σαπρὸν & ῥέον, siue νεαλὲς sæpe opponuntur: vbi ineptissime σαπρὸν putre reddideris, vt est à veteribus Græcis grammaticis obseruatum. Sic σαπρὸν εἶναι[?] interpretantur grammatici veteres, τὸν πρὸς πῷ τέ-λει ὑλώδη.
units.tr: "Rancid oil" [σαπρὸν γὰρ τὸ ἔλαιον]: sapron oil is oil that has grown old, corrupted by age and rancid, whose smell one cannot endure, as Horace says. The Greeks use sapron in its proper sense. We did not wish to say "putrid oil," particularly since we have learned from Aristotle that fatty substances are for the most part unfermented. But among the Attic writers sapron is often set against rheon or nealeson, and there it would be most absurd to render sapron as "putrid," as the ancient Greek grammarians have observed. Thus the ancient grammarians explain sapron einai as "what is woody towards its end" [τὸν πρὸς πῷ τέλει ὑλώδη].

units.la: καὶ τῆς ξεικομένων χαλκῶν. ] χαλκῆς accipe pro quibusdam parui pretij nummulis: quales Athenis fuere & χαλκοῖ, quos ἐραῖος ὀβολοὺς Plautus dixit: & κόλλυβοι & σίλαι, & κραταλλαι [?], quorum omnium mentio in comœdiis. Tales apud Romanos lupini, & plumbei illi nummi, de quibus apud Plautum & Martialem. Raro autem Athenienses æreos nummos cuderunt. vide Aristophanem Concionantibus, & eius scholia: necnon Athenæum libro xv. vbi de Dionysio, cui cognomen χαλκοῦς.
units.tr: "And of the coppers that are..." Take chalkē as some small coins of little value, such as there were at Athens, and the chalkoi, which Plautus called aereos obolos, as well as kollubi and silai and krataliai [?], all of which are mentioned in the comedies. Among the Romans such were the lupini and those leaden coins mentioned in Plautus and Martial. The Athenians, however, rarely struck bronze coins. See Aristophanes in the Ecclesiazusae and its scholia, and also Athenaeus book 15, where he speaks of Dionysius, who was surnamed Chalkous.

units.la: δεινὸς ἀπαιτῆσαι τὸ μέρος.) Αἰτεῖν positum & hic, & paullo ante pro μεταιτεῖν: id enim proprie μεταιτεῖν est. Aristophanes, Αἴτ' ἂν εἴτω τις ξένῳ, τύτων μεταιτεῖ τὸ μέρος. sic apud Demosthenem. Vel ἀπαιτεῖν accipe pro vehementius petere, & quasi flagitare: ab inuito denique per vim quodammodo extorquere tanquam debitum. Αἰτεῖν est poscere quod gratiæ apponatur acceptum. ἀπαιτεῖν, repetere quod sibi debeatur. Andocides orator, ἐὰν ὑμᾶς, εἰ μὴ βάλεσθε, αὐτῷ· εἰ ἡ μὴ βάλεσθε, ἀπαιτῶ.
units.tr: "Clever at demanding the share." Aiteein is used here, and a little before, for metaiteein, for that is properly what metaiteein means. Aristophanes: "Let someone ask a stranger for a share of these things" [Αἴτ' ἂν εἴτω τις ξένῳ, τύτων μεταιτεῖ τὸ μέρος]. Likewise in Demosthenes. Or take apaiteein in the sense of demanding more insistently, almost to exact, to extort by force, as it were, from an unwilling person, as though it were owed. Aiteein is to ask for what is received as a gift; apaiteein is to claim back what is owed to oneself.
