The orator Andocides: "if you do not put it to a vote, I shall... ; if you do not put it, I demand it" [ἐὰν ὑμᾶς, εἰ μὴ βάλεσθε ... ἀπαιτῶ].

units.la: κοινὸν εἰ) φίλας τὸν Ἑρμῆν.) Olim apud Græcos cùm duobus simul ambulantibus alter in via aliquid inuenerat, statim alter Κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς aiebat: partem rei inuentæ his verbis sibi vindicans. Hesychius, Κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς, παροιμία ὅτι τῆς κοινῆ τι δεινόν. Romani non multò aliter. Seneca epistola centesima & vigesima, Quoties aliquid inueni, non expecto donec dicas, In commune: ipse mihi dico. Lucianus in Votis vtriusque formulæ meminit: Κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς φασι, καὶ, Ἐς μέσον καταθεὶς φέρων τὸν πλοῦτον.
units.tr: "Hermes is common" [κοινὸς Ἑρμῆς]: Formerly among the Greeks, when two men were walking together and one found something on the road, the other immediately said "Common Hermes!", claiming a share of the find with these words. Hesychius: "Common Hermes: a proverb, meaning something is common property." The Romans did not do much differently. Seneca, letter 120: "Whenever I find something, I do not wait until you say 'into the common pool'; I say it to myself." Lucian in his Votive Offerings recalls both formulas: "Common Hermes, they say," and "putting the wealth into the middle and bringing it."

units.la: Affinis huic alia paroemia Graecorum, Σῦκον ἐφ' Ἑρμῇ [?], de qua Hesychius, & Eustathius in Odysseam ἡ. Notum est quid sit Ἑρμαῖον. Plato Charmide, Ἑρμαῖον, ἔφη, ὦ Σώκρατες, γεγονὸς ἂν εἴη ἡ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἀδένεια τῇ νεανίσκῳ, εἰ ἀναλκαδήσεταί, &c. In lucro, inquit, ponere debebit puer hic capitis morbum, si futurum est, ut per occasionem sanandi capitis, etiam mens sanetur. Interpres nouus etiam hic clara luce caecutiit. Sic etiam dicunt Ἑρμαῖα ποιεῖσθαί τι.
units.tr: A related Greek proverb is "a fig for Hermes" [Σῦκον ἐφ' Ἑρμῇ], which Hesychius and Eustathius on the Odyssey (book 8?) discuss. What a Hermaion is, is well known. Plato in the Charmides: "A Hermaion, Socrates, the boy's headache would have become, if he is to be cured..." etc. The sense: "This boy will have to count the headache as a gain, if it turns out that by the occasion of healing his head, his mind too is healed." The new translator has here too blundered in clear daylight. Thus they also say hermaia poieisthai ti, "to make a gain of something."

units.la: τὰ ὁ δὴ ζιαῦτα φεσί [?]. ) Lego, ὡρὸς ὁ δὴ τὰ ζιαῦτα, φάσί [?]. vel τὰ τε δὴ ζιαῦτα, ἐ φεσί [?]. hoc est: Eiusmodi homini, cùm haec conueniunt quae diximus, tum illa quae sequuntur. sic infra, capite ἀξὶ δυσχερείας [?].
units.tr: "Such things, indeed, they say" [τὰ ὁ δὴ ζιαῦτα φεσί]. I read: "to such a man, indeed, when these things agree which we have said, and also those which follow." So below, at the chapter "not at all unpleasant" [ἀξὶ δυσχερείας].

units.la: Φεσιδωνίῳ μέτρῳ τὸν πωύδακα ἐκκεκριμένῳ μετρεῖν [?].]
units.tr: "To measure out with a Phidonian measure the ... rejected" [Φεσιδωνίῳ μέτρῳ τὸν πωύδακα ἐκκεκριμένῳ μετρεῖν].

units.la: Mirificam lectionem. An vero quisquam ita parum iudicio valet, ut putet moribus eius qui hic describitur, hoc est, sordidissimi hominis & auaritia perditi, conuenire, ut suis famulis diaria metiatur mensurâ, non dicam quae pertusa sit, & perpluat: sed quae fundo omnino careat? id enim ista lectio egregia prae se fert. Cur non eadem opera credat aliquis aquam se cribro haurire posse, aut Danaidum πίθῳ continere? Sed res ipsa loquitur, nihil inquinatius ista lectione, nihil infrunitius esse posse. quod non esse ab interpretibus animaduersum, rem tam absurdam, tam ineptam, mirarer si quisquam esset qui non miraretur. Emendatio vero in promptu. Lege ἐγκεκρυμμένα [?], vel εἰσεκρυμμένα [?], aut εἰσεκρυμμένα [?]. nihil enim refert. Sensus ex versione apparet: nititur haec emendatio nostra, certissimis & γεωμετρικωτάτας rationibus. Est autem defœda quae istis verbis notatur auaritia. Non desunt hodieque qui simili artificio utantur, dum vel oleum vel vinum, vel alia vendunt, quæ mensura aut stannea aut ferrea mensurari solent. Id genus mensurarum videtur Theophrastus φειδώνια [?] μέτρα nuncupare: cùm enim ex varia materia cófici mensuræ soleant, non omnis profecto huius fraudis est capax: sed illa demum quæ malleo tractari, flecti, subigíque potis est. Talem igitur mensuram intelligit hoc loco Theophrastus, & Phidoniam appellat, cum vulgo Atheniensium sine dubio. quanquam eius appellationis hodie rationem explicare non possumus. Nam etsi & Strabo noster & veteres grammatici Φιδωνίων μέτρων mentionem faciunt: nihil tamen extare memini, quod hunc mihi locum satis explanet: nisi quis putet φιδώνιον μέτρον hîc dici mensuram illam, sive ἐλαυνρὸν ἀλγεῖον quod Athenis vocabatur φειδῶν, auctore Polluce. mihi quidem id non placet. Hoc igitur mittamus: illud teneamus, sic esse ut emendavi legendum. Pherecrates Ἀηρὸς [?], Λαβὲ μὴ τῆς χοίνικος τὸν σιωδακα εἰσέρχονται [?]. Non dubium ad eandem fraudem pertinere hunc Pherecratis locum. Iuuenalis,
units.tr: A most wonderful reading. Could anyone have so little judgment as to think it suits the character of the man described here, that is, a most sordid man ruined by avarice, to measure out daily rations for his servants with a measure that is not, I will not say pierced and leaking, but without any bottom at all? For that is what this excellent reading implies. Why should someone not equally believe he can draw water with a sieve, or hold water in the jar of the Danaids? But the thing speaks for itself: nothing can be more distorted than this reading, nothing more senseless. That the translators have not noticed this, I should marvel at such an absurd and foolish thing, if there were anyone who did not marvel. The emendation, however, is at hand. Read egkekrymmena, or eisekrymmena, or eisekrymmena; for it makes no difference. The sense is apparent from the translation. Our emendation rests on the most certain and most geometrical reasons. The avarice denoted by these words is shameful. Even today there are not lacking those who use a similar trick when they sell oil or wine or other goods that are customarily measured with tin or iron measures. Theophrastus seems to call this kind of measure phidōnia metra; for although measures are commonly made of various materials, not every kind is capable of this fraud, but only that which can be worked, bent, and shaped with a hammer. Theophrastus therefore means such a measure here, and calls it Phidonian, since it was doubtless common among the Athenians. Yet we cannot today explain the reason for that name. For although our Strabo and the ancient grammarians mention Phidonian measures, I do not recall anything extant that explains this passage to my satisfaction, unless someone thinks that phidōnion metron here means that measure, or the bronze vessel which at Athens was called pheidōn, on the authority of Pollux. This does not please me. Let us therefore set this aside and keep to this: it must be read as I have emended it. Pherecrates: "Take not the ... of the choinix" [Λαβὲ μὴ τῆς χοίνικος τὸν σιωδακα εἰσέρχονται]. There is no doubt that this passage of Pherecrates belongs to the same fraud. Juvenal:
"He punishes the stomachs of slaves with a meagre measure."

units.la: Similis Saluiani querela libro tertio. Seruis, inquit, etiam si stipendia usitata præstentur, consuetudini hæc magis quàm sufficientiæ satisfaciunt: & ita implent canonem, quod non explent satietatem. Εἰσκεκριμένα ἀλγεῖα [?], aut ἐγκεκριμένα Ciceroni dicuntur vasa collisa. fit enim collisione ἡ εἴσκρισις [?], sic vocat Hippocrates ἐντεταλασμένον [?] & ἐμπεταλασμένον ὀστέον [?], quod sit incussum, & ex collisione intro cesserit. Aliud est Ἀπόρρυσις [?]: quod de vasis dicitur per collisionem fraætis[?], aut quibus vel labrum vel ansa vel emblema fuerit excussum. Aristophanes Acharnensibus,
units.tr: A similar complaint is found in Salvian, book three. He says that even when slaves are given their usual allowance, this satisfies custom rather than need: they fill the measure but do not fill their hunger. Vessels that are dented or struck together are called by Cicero "eiskekrimena" or "enkekrimena" [εἰσκεκριμένα, ἐγκεκριμένα]. The dent comes from a blow, and Hippocrates calls such a bone "entetalasmenon" or "empetalasmenon" [ἐντεταλασμένον, ἐμπεταλασμένον], that is, struck in and sunk inward from the impact. "Apporrysis" [ἀπόρρυσις] is different: it is said of vessels broken by a knock, or from which the lip, handle or boss has been knocked off. Aristophanes, in the Acharnians:
"little cup, its lip knocked off" [Κολυλίσκιον, τὸ χεῖλος ἀποκεκρουσμένον]

units.la: Scholiastes exponit, ἀποκεκλασμένον. Legimus in hoc versu comici κολυλίσκιον, non ut vulgo κυλίσκιον, secuti auctoritatem Athenæi & Eustathij. In Athenæi codicibus ἀποκεκομμένον male legitur hodie ex glossa, pro ἀποκεκρυσμένον. Locus est libro vndecimo.
units.tr: The scholiast explains this as "broken off" [ἀποκεκλασμένον]. In this line of the comic poet we read "kolyliskion," not the usual "kyliskion," following the authority of Athenaeus and Eustathius. In the manuscripts of Athenaeus, "apokekommenon" is read today by mistake from a gloss, in place of "apokekrysmenon." The passage is in book eleven.

units.la: σφόδρα ἀποξῶν.) Oppidò quàm belle conveniunt hæc superioribus. Est enim σφόδρα ἀποξᾶν[?], hostorio cumulum diruere, & demere studiosè, quod mensuræ superest. Sic accipit Hesychius in ἀπομάκτρας[?]. & apud Pollucem libro quarto τὰ ὑ κάλεψημένα μέτρα[?], quibus non est dirutus radio cumulus. In vetere Glossario sic scriptum extat, ψηκτὸς μόδιος, Rasus. Lego ψηδς[?] : est enim ἀ ψάω. Dicitur & ἀπομάτλιν[?] : vnde apud Lucianum in πλοίῳ choenix ἀπομεμαγμένη[?] ; & apud Syracusanum poëtam, Οὐκ ἀλίγω μή μοι κινεὰν ἀπομάξης[?] quem locum ne pluribus nunc exponam non solū librorum, sed & otij inopia facit. raptim enim ista, & in itinere scribebamus. Inde ἀπόμαχλρα[?], siue ἀπόμαχλρον[?] radius. quod & ἀπόψηστρον[?], & ῥύχαγον[?] dixerunt. Reperio & ἀποληλίσον[?] in vetere Glossario inter interpretationes vocis ruplus, siue replus. de quo alias. Contrarium πῇ ἀπο-ψὴν[?] est κορυσσῆν[?]. Glossarium, κορυσσὸς μόδιῳ cumulatus. docte sanè. Hesychius Κορυσὸν[?], ἐπίμετρον. minus rectè ibi vulgò, κορυτόν[?]. Idem grammaticus κορύσσειν[?] paullò ante exponit αὐξῆν[?], amplificare, cumulare, quæ interpretatio convenit huic loco siu[?]ari in Pythionicis. βίον κορυσσέμου ὀρθοβούλοιο μυχα-[?]ραῖς. Opponitur etiam τῷ σφίσρα ἀπολαβὴν[?] verbum ἀλλὰ[?], quod grato debitori quadrat, qui nō eadem tantum, sed cumulatiore etiam mensura quod accepit vult reddere. D.Lucas capite sexto, μέτρον καλὸν, πεπιεσμένον, καὶ σεσαλευμένον, ὑπερεκχυννόμενον δώσουσιν εἰς τὸν κόλπον ὑμῶν.cuius loci singularis mihi semper & admirabilis visa est elegantia. Obseruauimus etiam apud poetas affinem huic vocem, ἀλάτλειν pro implere aliquid largiter: proprie tamen est mouere, concutere, idem quod ἀλλὰ. Leonidas poëta epigrammatarius in Anacreontem, Πρὸς Ἀναχρεόντα χρύσεον σεσαλαγμένον εἶναι Θέατο. En inquit, Anacreontem vino ita obrutum atque impletum, vt etiam redundet & diffluat. Hesychius, Σαλάξαι, καλλυσαι, κυνίκαι, perperam enim in vulgatis codicibus, καλαξήσαι. Macedonius libro sexto Graecorum epigrammatum,
units.tr: "scraping off thoroughly" [σφόδρα ἀποξῶν]. These words fit the earlier ones very well. "Sphodra apoxan" [σφόδρα ἀποξᾶν] means to pull down the heap with a strickle and carefully remove what is left over above the measure. Hesychius understands it so, under "apomaktras" [ἀπομάκτρας], and Pollux in book four speaks of measures "kalepsemena" [ὑ κάλεψημένα], from which the heap is not levelled off by the strickle. An old glossary has the entry "psektos modios, rasus" [ψηκτὸς μόδιος, Rasus]. I read "psēdos" [ψηδς], since it comes from "apsaō." There is also "apomatlein" [ἀπομάτλιν], whence in Lucian, in the Ship, a choenix is "apomemagmenē" [ἀπομεμαγμένη]; and in the Syracusan poet, "Not with a small measure, lest you scrape it off for me" [Οὐκ ἀλίγω μή μοι κινεὰν ἀπομάξης]. I will not explain that passage at length now, since lack of books and of leisure prevents it; I write these things hurriedly and on the road. From this comes "apomachlra" [ἀπόμαχλρα] or "apomachlron" [ἀπόμαχλρον], the strickle, which they also called "apopsēstron" [ἀπόψηστρον] and "rhychagon" [ῥύχαγον]. I also find "apoleliso" [ἀποληλίσον] in an old glossary among the explanations of the word "ruplus" or "replus," about which I will say more elsewhere. The opposite of this, "pē apo-psēn" [πῇ ἀπο-ψὴν], is "korysseīn" [κορυσσῆν]. The glossary has "korysos modios, heaped up," very learnedly indeed. Hesychius has "Korysos" [Κορυσὸν], "an addition," though the common text there wrongly reads "korython" [κορυτόν]. The same grammarian explains "korysseīn" [κορύσσειν] a little earlier as "auxein" [αὐξῆν], to increase, to heap up. That explanation suits this passage, where in the Pythionicae we find "bion korysseměnou orthoboulou mychaxais." The word "alla" [ἀλλὰ] is also set against "to sphisra apolabē" [τῷ σφίσρα ἀπολαβὴν], and it suits a grateful debtor, who wishes to repay not only the same amount he received but a heaped-up measure of it. St Luke, chapter six: "good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, they will give into your bosom" [μέτρον καλὸν, πεπιεσμένον, καὶ σεσαλευμένον, ὑπερεκχυννόμενον δώσουσιν εἰς τὸν κόλπον ὑμῶν]. I have always found the singular and admirable elegance of this passage striking. I have also noticed in the poets a word related to this, "salassein" [ἀλάτλειν], meaning to fill something abundantly; properly, however, it means to move or shake, the same as "alla." The epigrammatist Leonidas, on Anacreon: "Anacreon, shaken and filled with gold, they saw" [Πρὸς Ἀναχρεόντα χρύσεον σεσαλαγμένον εἶναι Θέατο]. "Behold," he says, "Anacreon so overwhelmed and filled with wine that it even overflows and runs away." Hesychius: "Salaxai, to be adorned, to be harmonised" [Σαλάξαι, καλλυσαι, κυνίκαι]; in the common manuscripts it is wrongly "kalaxēsai" [καλαξήσαι]. Macedonius, in book six of the Greek epigrams:

units.la: Κισσοκόμα Βρομίῳ σάτυρον σεσαλαγμένον εἶναι Ἀμπελοσφέρος ἀνὴρ ἀρθέ Ἀνακρέοντας.
units.tr: "Ivy-haired, the satyr shaken by Bromios; the wine-bearing man raised Anacreon" [Κισσοκόμα Βρομίῳ σάτυρον σεσαλαγμένον εἶναι Ἀμπελοσφέρος ἀνὴρ ἀρθέ Ἀνακρέοντας].

units.la: Ἐπιμελήσαντες φίλου ἔπι λαβεῖν ἀποδοῦναι.] Videntur hic voculae quaedam deesse, quas sine libris supplere non erat opis nostrae: ac ne officij quidem fortasse erat: diuinationis enim res est, non eruditionis, aut ingenij. Capiat igitur, qui volet, per me quidem coronam, & incipiat hic ariolari: nos Oedipi non sumus. Fuit cum legebamus ὑπερυφὸν τε σοφῆς φίλου τὶ λαβεῖν, ἀποδοῦναι. vt hic notetur duplex βδελυγεία istius. Altera, quod mutuo dans aliquid amico suo, pignus ab eo accipit: altera quod id ipsum pignus mox vendit, sicut facere solent difficiles & inhumani creditores, si debitum sua die
units.tr: "taking care to receive a friend's pledge and return it" [Ἐπιμελήσαντες φίλου ἔπι λαβεῖν ἀποδοῦναι]. Some small words seem to be missing here, which could not be supplied without the books, and perhaps it was not even my duty to supply them: this is a matter of divination, not of learning or wit. Let whoever wishes take the crown for guessing, and begin to conjecture here; I am no Oedipus. There was a time when I read "hyperyphon te sophēs philou ti labein, apodoūnai," so that the double baseness of the man is marked here: first, that when he lends something to a friend he takes a pledge from him; second, that he soon sells that very pledge, as hard and inhumane creditors are wont to do if the debt is not paid on its day.

units.la: hon fuerit solutum.Næ qui hunc locum primi deprauarunt, digni fuerunt, quibus pro hac noxia multæ prægnates infligerentur plagæ, cum hoc superdicto, Μὴ κακύργει τὰ [?]ῆς Μούσων.
units.tr: Those who first corrupted this passage deserved to be punished with many severe blows, along with the saying quoted above: "Do not wrong the things of the Muses" [Μὴ κακύργει τὰ τῆς Μούσων].

units.la: [?]ἐλλῶν τέτταρα δραχμὰς ἀποδιδόναι.] Apud Latinum comicum Dordalus leno in Persa sexaginta minas soluturus, duos numinos retinet: vt ille quidem ait, pro crumena: re autem vera, ea causa erat quam hîc Theophrastus notat. Propterea ait Toxilus,
units.tr: "to pay back four drachmas" [...ἐλλῶν τέτταρα δραχμὰς ἀποδιδόναι]. In the Latin comic poet, the pimp Dordalus in the Persa, about to pay sixty minae, keeps back two coins; as he says, this is for his purse, but in truth the reason was the one Theophrastus notes here. That is why Toxilus says:

units.la: Sine quæso quando leno 'st, nihil mirum facit.
units.tr: "Please, since he is a pimp, it is no wonder he does this."

units.la: [?]ἡ Φράτορας [?]ἑορτῶν.] Quemadmodum apud Romanos fuêre dies curiæ, vt Cicero vocat, hoc est, curialium conuiuia: ita etiâ apud Athenienses: fuitq; hoc χορηγίας vnum genus, è quamplurimis quæ in ea Republica fuerunt. Vide Harpocrationem in voce Ἐςιάτωρ, & Demosthenis orationem contra Midiam, & eius interpretes multis locis. Moris etiam fuit vt septima decimáue die postquam aliquis infans erat natus, celebrarentur eius nomina lia, & conuiuio exciperentur curiales: quò putet fortasse aliquis hæc pertinere, propter verba sequentia. verùmtamen poßit & ad priorem morem commodè referri.
units.tr: "the phratores of festivals" [Φράτορας ἑορτῶν]. Just as among the Romans there were days of the curia, as Cicero calls them, that is, feasts of the curiales, so too among the Athenians; and this was one kind of liturgy, among the very many that existed in that commonwealth. See Harpocration under the word "Eziatōr" [Ἐςιάτωρ], Demosthenes' speech against Meidias, and his commentators in many places. It was also customary that on the seventeenth day after a child was born, its name was celebrated and the curiales were received at a feast. Perhaps someone may think this refers to that custom, because of the words that follow; yet it could also be fitly referred to the earlier custom.

units.la: [?]ἡμίσῃ τῆς φρατρίας [?]ἀπονέμεσθαι.] Iam protulimus ex Aristophanis Ranis, Τίς τλῷ κεφαλῷ ἀπεδήσατο τῆς μανίδος; item τὰ τὸ σκόροδον τὸ χθεσινόν; τίς τῆς ἐλάας παρέσχε; vide ad superius caput. Plautus Persa,
units.tr: "to be assigned half of the phratry" [ἡμίσῃ τῆς φρατρίας ἀπονέμεσθαι]. We have already quoted from Aristophanes' Frogs: "Who wrapped his head in the mania's..."; likewise "the garlic of yesterday"; "who gave the olive?" See the note on the previous chapter. Plautus, Persa:

units.la: Nam id demum lepidum est, triparcos homines vetulos, avidos, aridos Bene admordere,qui salinum seruo obsignant cum sale.
units.tr: "For that is indeed charming: to bite well the thrifty, old, greedy, dried-up men, who seal the salt-cellar with salt for a slave."

units.la: Iuuenalis verò elegantissimè de sordido homine loquens, satyra decimaquarta.
units.tr: Juvenal, speaking most elegantly of a sordid man, in satire fourteen:

units.la: Ipse quoque esuriens, neque enim omnia sustinet vnam quam Mucida caerulei panis consumere frusta: Hesternum silitus medio seruare minutal Septembris: nec non differre in tempora cœna Alterius conchem, astiui [?] cum parte lacerti Signatam, vel dimidio, putrique siluro, Filaque sectiui numerata includere porri.
units.tr: "He himself, though hungry, for he does not endure to consume alone the one mouldy loaf of blue bread; he keeps the leftover scraps of yesterday's meal for the middle of September, and he postpones dinner to a later time: a piece of cold, salted ... of another's dish, a half-eaten sprat, and stuffs away the numbered threads of leek cut up."

units.la: Lucianus de quodam è cœna domum reuerso; [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀλαζὼν τὰ κρέα, ὁποῖα τῆς [?] ἐπιστήμης ἐξῶτι [?] ἐπιστελῶς, τὸ ἀ[?] ἐκείνῳ καθ' ἡσ[?].
units.tr: Lucian, of a man returning home from a dinner: "[illegible] boasting of the meats, such as ... of knowledge ... that thing ..."

units.la: Ἠμὲν οὖν ἀκαιρία.] Appellat Theophrastus ἀκαιρίαν, vitium ei virtuti oppositum, quæ εὐκαιρία vocatur, & ita à Platone definitur. Εὐκαιρία χρόνου ἐπίγνωσις, ἐν ᾧ [?] ταχὺ ἢ τεταγμένη: cui definitioni simillima est ἡ τῷ καιρῷ apud eundem. Καιρὸς est, inquit, ἐν ᾧ ἕκαστον φιλοτίμως [?] ταχεῖ ἢ πεποιημένον. Stoici non ἀκαιρίαν, sed εὐκαιρίαν, vt auctor est in Officiorum libris M. Tullius, hanc virtutem appellabant: ipse Tullius, ordinem rerum, & temporum opportunitatem, vel vno nomine modestiam. modestiæ enim nomine complectitur ille tam μετριότητα, quàm ἀκαιρίαν. duplicem namque facit modestiam: alteram in qua modus spectatur: ea est μετριότης: alteram, in qua ordinis conseruatio: ea est, vt diximus, Stoicorum ἀξία.neque dubium est Ciceronem duabus dictionibus fuisse vsurum, si potuisset, hoc est, si tulisset Latini sermonis paupertas.Modestiam hanc, siue ἀξίαν definiri ait ille à Stoicis, vt sit, scientia earum rerum quae aguntur aut dicuntur suo loco collocandarum.. recte sane & eleganter. Andronicus noster, sic: Εὐταξία, ἐμταξία καταχωρισμὸς πράξεως. ἢ, ἐχωρὶς τῆς καταχωρισμὸς πράξεων[?]. Non potuit rotundius vis Graecorum verborum exprimi, quàm vt fecit Cicero. Adiicit Andronicus & aliam definitionem, ἡ περὶ τὰς πράξεις ἐχωρὶς τὸ βέλτιον[?]. alludit horsum Tullius, Talis est igitur (ait) ordo actionum adhibendus, vt quemadmodum in oratione constanti, sic in vita omnia sint apta inter se & convenientia. Τὸ ἀκαιρίαν idem auctor infscientiam temporum eleganti[ssi]mè vertit. Importunitatem vero caue dixeris. In schida manu exarata reperi hanc ἀκαιρίας definitionem: Ἀκαιρία δὲ λείψις καιρῷ κατ' ἐπιθυμίαν προθυμία[?], τὸ ζηλούμενον.
units.tr: "Yes, then, tactlessness" [Ἠμὲν οὖν ἀκαιρία.] Theophrastus calls it ἀκαιρία, the vice opposed to the virtue called εὐκαιρία, and Plato defines that virtue thus: εὐκαιρία is the knowledge of the right time, in which something is done quickly or in due order [Εὐκαιρία χρόνου ἐπίγνωσις, ἐν ᾧ ταχὺ ἢ τεταγμένη]. The definition most like this one, from the same author, is his account of the opportune moment (τῷ καιρῷ). He says that καιρός is the time in which each thing is done eagerly and well made [Καιρὸς ... ἐν ᾧ ἕκαστον φιλοτίμως ... πεποιημένον]. As Tully reports in the books On Duties, the Stoics called this virtue not ἀκαιρία but εὐκαιρία. Tully himself calls it "the order of things and the fitness of times," or, in a single word, "modesty." For under the name of modesty he embraces both μετριότης and ἀκαιρία. He makes modesty twofold: one kind, in which measure is observed, is μετριότης; the other, in which order is kept, is, as we have said, the Stoic ἀξία. There is no doubt that Cicero would have used two words had the poverty of the Latin language allowed it. Tully says that the Stoics define this modesty, or ἀξία, as "the knowledge of placing in their proper position the things that are done or said," which is certainly correct and elegant. Our Andronicus puts it thus: εὐταξία is the orderly arrangement of action [ἐμταξία καταχωρισμὸς πράξεως]. Cicero could not have rendered the force of the Greek words more fully than he did. Andronicus also adds another definition, concerning actions, without what is better. Tully alludes to this when he says: "Such, then, is the order of actions to be observed, so that in life, as in a consistent speech, everything fits together and agrees." The same author rendered τὸ ἀκαιρίαν very elegantly as "ignorance of times." But do not call it "importunity." On a slip of paper in a hand I found this definition of ἀκαιρία: ἀκαιρία is the lack of the right time, an eagerness contrary to desire, the thing to be aimed at.

units.la: ἐσὶν ἐπιτάξις.) ] Nihil mutandum. Attici ἐπιλυχάνειν pro ἐπιλυχάνειν vsurpant. vt Plato sexto Legum. ergo etiam ἐπιτάξις pro ἐπιτάξις.
units.tr: "is a contrivance" [ἐσὶν ἐπιτάξις.] Nothing needs changing. The Attic writers use ἐπιλυχάνειν for ἐπιλυχνάειν, as Plato does in book six of the Laws. So also ἐπιτάξις may stand for the other form.

units.la: καὶ δίκλω ὠφελητικὸς εἰγύνς.] Hoc veteres Latini dixissent, Eum qui sponsionem exactus fuerit. Plautus, Quas sponsiones pronuper tu exactus es. Cicero: qui quod pro alio spopondisset, coactus fuerit dependere. At κελεύειν αὐτὸν ἀναδέχεσθαι est sponsum vocare. Horatius, Hic sponsum vocat, hic auditum scripta. Notum quid sit ἀναδέχεσθαι. inde ἀνάδοχος. Glossarium Pras, ἐγγυος ἀνάδοχος. alibi, Vades, ἐγγυοι, ἀνάδοχοι.
units.tr: "and useful in both ways" [καὶ δίκλω ὠφελητικὸς εἰγύνς.] The older Latins would have said, "one who has been compelled to give security for a promise." Plautus: "Those sponsions you have recently been made to pay." Cicero: one who, having stood surety for another, was forced to pay. But κελεύειν αὐτὸν ἀναδέχεσθαι is "to call him to be surety." Horace: "This man calls for the surety, that man for the written record." What ἀναδέχεσθαι means is well known, and hence ἀνάδοχος. The Glossary has, for Vas, ἐγγυος, ἀνάδοχος; elsewhere, for vades, ἐγγυοι, ἀνάδοχοι.

units.la: ἔστιν ὁ καὶ προσοιὴν ἐν ὠνητῷ[?].) Mos fuit Athenis, vt qui vellent aliquid vendere certorum hominum opera uterentur ad reperiendum emtorem. Eos homines Dinarchus & Ifæus, ait Pollux, προπράτορας vocarunt: Ariftophanes προπωλὰς[?]: Plato προπωλητὰς[?]. Hodie quoque multū illis mercatores vtūtur: vocanturq; vulgo Italico, vt opinor, vel Hifpanico nomine curfitatores. De iis accipiedus est iste locus: itemq; hic Platonis in duodecimo De legibus, vbi de fideiussoribus disputans, Ἐγὼ μὲν δή, inquit, ἡ ὁ προπωλῶν ὅτι τὰ μὲν ἐνδίκως πωλεῖν [?], ἡ καὶ μηδαμῶς ἀξιόχρεω. Ἐαὐτὸν δ᾽ ἔγω, ἐὰν ὁ προπωλῶν, καθάπερ ὁ ἀποδόμενος[?]. Fideiussor esto qui rem alienam vendit, eius qui non iure vendat, aut qui non sit futurus auctor idoneus. Tenetor ergo evictionem praestare, tam is qui rem alienam vendit, quàm is cuius res est. Statuit philosophus, vt ὁ προπράτωρ qui aliquid emendi cuipiam auctor fuerit, habeatur pro fideiussore: adeo vt si res emta fuerit ab emtore evicta, (vtpote quòd venditor parum bona fide cam possideret) liceat emtori cum proxeneta & parario in iudicio experiri, non secus ac cum eo cuius res esse tum dicebatur cum vaeniret[?]. Hæc mens Platonis. Romæ quoque vt Vlpianus docet, venditores aliquando fideiussorem interponebant. quem, ait ille, vulgò auctorem secundum vocabant. Glossarium, Secundus auctor, βεβαιωτής. Sic etiam per intercessorem æs alienum faciebant, vt indicat Seneca epistola cxx. & libro II. De beneficiis. meminit & libro III. vide epistolam Alciphronis: quæ incipit Μίγα ὦ, &c. & apud I C. de proxeneticis libro I. Pandectarum. ἀνίσαζαν ἐξ ἀρχῆς διδάσκω:] Sic capite sequenti, ὡς, ἐπαλγέλεσ ἀνασάς[?]. sumtum à more qui in concione & curia seruabatur: nam qui verba facturi erant, surgebant.
units.tr: "There is one who also... in buying" [ἔστιν ὁ καὶ προσοιὴν ἐν ὠνητῷ.] It was the custom at Athens that those who wished to sell something used certain men to find a buyer. Dinarchus and Isaeus, Pollux says, called these men προπράτορες; Aristophanes called them προπωλαί; Plato called them προπωληταί. Even today merchants much use them, and in Italian or Spanish, I think, they are commonly called cursitatores. This passage must be understood of them, and so must that of Plato in book twelve of the Laws, where, discussing sureties, he says: "I say, then, that the one who acts as προπωλῶν, whether he sells justly or even unjustly, must not be considered trustworthy." [Ἐγὼ μὲν δή ... ἡ ὁ προπωλῶν ... ἀξιόχρεω.] And I say that if the προπωλῶν is like the one who sold it... "Let him be a surety who sells another's property, for one who has no right to sell it, or who will not be a sound guarantor. Therefore the one who sells another's property must answer for eviction, just as the owner does." The philosopher lays down that the προπράτωρ, who has been the advisor of someone's purchase, is to be regarded as a surety, so that if the bought goods are taken from the buyer by eviction (since the seller held them without good faith), the buyer may sue the broker and the middleman in court, just as he could sue the one whose property it was at the time of sale. This is Plato's view. At Rome also, as Ulpian teaches, sellers sometimes put in a surety, whom, he says, they commonly called the "second warrantor." The Glossary has, for secundus auctor, βεβαιωτής. So too they made debts through an intercessor, as Seneca shows in letter 120 and in book two of On Benefits. He also mentions it in book three. See the letter of Alciphron that begins "Μίγα ὦ," etc., and in the jurist on brokers, in book one of the Pandects. "I teach from the beginning" [ἀνίσαζαν ἐξ ἀρχῆς διδάσκω:] Similarly in the following chapter, "as ... ἐπαλγέλεσ ἀνασάς," taken from the custom observed in assembly and senate, for those who were about to speak used to stand up.

units.la: καὶ Θύοντες καὶ ἀναλίσκοντες ἤκων.) Lege ὡς Θύοντες, hoc est, παρὰ Θύ. Iam ἀναλίσκω, non est simpliciter sumtus facere, vt putarunt interpretes: sed comedere atque epulari. Sic enim accipi illam vocem, vel ex vno Athenaeo notius esse potest, quàm vt moneri quisquam debeat. Sic & δαπανᾶν vsurpant. Xiphilinus de Vitellio, τὸ πλέον τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τῆς νυκτὸς ἐδαπάνα. idem in verbo consumere est apud Latinos.
units.tr: "and sacrificing and spending" [καὶ Θύοντες καὶ ἀναλίσκοντες ἤκων.] Read ὡς θύοντες, that is, "as those sacrificing." Now ἀναλίσκω does not simply mean "to spend," as the translators thought, but "to eat and feast." That this word has this sense can be known from Athenaeus alone, so well known that no one should need to be reminded. They also use δαπανᾶν in this way. Xiphilinus, on Vitellius: "he spent [ἐδαπάνα] the greater part of the day and night." The same usage of Latin consumere occurs as well.

units.la: τόμον ἀναλίσκων.) Ne hic quidem τὸ ἀναλίσκειν vsurpatam significationem retinet, quae est, repolscere rem suam: sed [?] ita accipi debet, vt in ἀναλίσκειν apud Euangelistam: vtque in ἀπεδίειν, & aliis accipi debere fusè docet Athenaeus. Notum est autem conuiuia rem sacram solita olim comitari: aut si conuiuium celebrare nollent, è victima partes ad amicos mittebant. Theocritus Bucoliastis, καὶ τὸ ὁ θύσας Ταῖς Νύμφαις, Μόρσωνι καλὸν χρέας αὐτικα ἐίμυον. Plautus Milite,
units.tr: "spending a portion" [τόμον ἀναλίσκων.] Here too ἀναλίσκειν does not keep its usual sense of demanding back one's own property, but must be understood as it is in the Evangelist, and as in ἀπεδίειν and elsewhere, as Athenaeus fully teaches. It is well known that feasts used to accompany sacred rites; or, if they did not wish to hold a feast, they sent parts of the victim to friends. The scholiast on Theocritus: "and he who sacrificed to the Nymphs, for Morson, immediately sent a fine piece of meat." Plautus in the Miles:

units.la: Sacrificant? dant inde partem maiorem mihi quàm sibi.
units.tr: "They are sacrificing? They give me a larger share than they keep for themselves."

units.la: καὶ παρὼν διαίτη συγκρύφν.] Intempestiua commemoratione iustorum alterius partis: quorum commemorandorum non id est tempus, sed id potius, quando apud iudicem res agitatur. Ibi enim stricto iuri, hic aequitati locus est. Peccatur igitur ab isto inscitia temporis. Hoc moneo, quia poterant haec videri ad ἐπιεικείαν, de qua capite sequenti, referenda.
units.tr: "and being present, shared a meal" [καὶ παρὼν διαίτη συγκρύφν.] An untimely recital of the merits of the other party. This is not the time for such recitals, but rather when the matter is being argued before a judge. For there strict law has its place, here equity. So the fault lies in ignorance of the right time. I point this out because these remarks might seem to belong to ἐπιεικεία, which is treated in the following chapter.

units.la: καὶ ὀρχησάμενος, ἀ.) Omnino ὀρχησάμενος legendum. Vt ait Cicero, saltatio, comes erat extrema conuiuij tempestiui: cum enim erant bene saturi, ac bene poti, tum ad saltandum animum appellebant. Supra nota erat Χαῤῥοίας, siccum, necdum madidum, saltare. Dion Chrysostomus in oratione ad Alexandrinos: Τὰς μὲν ἄλλως ἀνθρώπως ἡ μέθη πρὸς φιλίαν τρέπει καὶ ὄρχησιν παρ' ἡμῖν ἢ τ' ἐναντίον ὄξυν. ἡ δὲ φιλία μέθῳ ἐμποιεῖ ἢ ὄρχησιν. De saltandi studio antiquorum, Athenæus, Lucianus, Macrobius, alij.
units.tr: "and dancing" [καὶ ὀρχησάμενος, ἀ.] Clearly ὀρχησάμενος should be read. As Cicero says, dancing was the companion of the final part of a feast held at the right time: when the guests were well fed and well drunk, they then turned their minds to dancing. Earlier it was noted that to dance sober, not yet tipsy, was a Χαῤῥοίας [a thing of the Charrhoia]. Dio Chrysostom in his speech to the Alexandrians: "Drunkenness turns other men to friendship and dancing, but among us the opposite happens; friendship produces drunkenness or dancing." On the ancients' zeal for dancing, see Athenaeus, Lucian, Macrobius, and others.

units.la: De saltandi studio antiquorum, Athenæus, Lucianus, Macrobius, alij.
units.tr: On the ancients' zeal for dancing, see Athenaeus, Lucian, Macrobius, and others.
On the chapter concerning Obsequiousness (περὶ ἀρεσκείας).

units.la: ΑΜέλει ἀρεσκεία δέξειν ἂν ἕῃ.] Parum videtur vitium istud à blanditia de qua dictum supra differre: differt tamen. Blando enim homini, vt eum nobis definiit Theophrastus, scopus est propositus delectare omnes, nemini molestus esse, in sermonibus quotidianis omnium offensionem vitare. Hoc si assequitur homo blandus, habet ille tota quod mente petebat, estque eius voto abundè satisfactum. At is quem ἀρέσκον [?] Theophrastus hic vocat, magis ad naturā adulatoris accedit: habet sanè hoc cum illo commune, quod cum ossiciosus admodum videri cupiat, ineptam tamen eius rationem init. fine etiam ac scopo parum sæpe distant: vterque enim alius gratiam cupit, non virtutis amore, sed quia sic suis rationibus conducere existimat. Omnino paruo interuallo separantur hæc tria, adulatio, blanditia, & ἀρεσκεία. quæ est officium ab eo profectum in quo non est assectio sed affectatio, vt cum Tertulliano dicā. Hanc possis cum Cicerone, fictum officium, & simulatam vel ineptam sedulitatem dicere: possis & ambitionem, Latinissimè. Officium superuacuum dicere cum interpretibus non placuit. nam τὸ ἀχρεῖον[?] in hac voce non tam quod superuacaneum est & non necessarium notat, quàm id quod abundans est nimis & affluens & exsuperans, sicut in alia voce rectè explicat A. Gellius. Curiosum officium potius dixerim: ut loquitur Tertullianus etsi in alia re.
units.tr: "He would receive him with obsequiousness, if he were to come." [Μέλει ἀρεσκεία δέξειν ἂν ἕῃ.] This vice seems to differ little from the flattery of which I spoke above, yet it does differ. For the flatterer, as Theophrastus defines him for us, has as his aim to please everyone, to be a nuisance to no one, and in daily conversation to avoid giving offence to anyone. If the flatterer achieves this, he gets all that he sought in his mind, and his wish is amply satisfied. But the man whom Theophrastus here calls obsequious [ἀρέσκον] comes closer to the nature of the sycophant. He certainly has this in common with the flatterer, that while he wishes to seem very dutiful [ἀρεσκεία], he goes about it in a clumsy way. Their ends and aims, too, differ little, for each seeks another's favour, not from love of virtue, but because he thinks that in this way he will serve his own interests. These three, flattery, fawning and obsequiousness [ἀρεσκεία], are separated by only a small interval. It is dutifulness that proceeds from a source in which there is not real devotion but display, as I would put it with Tertullian. This one might call, with Cicero, a feigned service, and a pretended or clumsy eagerness; one might also call it ambition, which is most elegantly Latin. The translators did not like to call it superfluous service, for the Greek word ἀχρεῖον in this context denotes not so much what is superfluous and unnecessary as what is excessive, overflowing and exuberant, as Aulus Gellius rightly explains in another word. I would rather call it officious service, as Tertullian speaks, though in another matter.

units.la: ἐπαγγέλλασθαι[?] ἀναγκάς, ἀμὴ δωνίσεται.[?] ] Accidere multis solet ut rogati aliquid, cui praestando pares se non esse probè sciant, nihilominus tamen id in se recipiant, & operam suam prolixè polliceantur. sic miseri in laqueos ipsi se induunt, unde mox extricare se saluo pudore cum cupiant, nequeant. Eius rei duplex causa esse solet: vel quòd pudet multos imbecillitatem virium suarum, & pauperiem suam denudare: vel quòd ita nati sunt, ut denegare quicquam rogati non sustineant, impediente illos pudore quodam subrustico, & planè inepto, quem δυσωπίαν[?] vocant Graeci: de quo legat decori & honesti studiosa iuuentus pulcherrimum Plutarchi commentarium: reperiet multa quae ad ἀτελέρον[?] hunc pertineant. Hi sunt de quibus Seneca, Multos, inquit, liberales facit frontis imbecillitas. Neque aliena hinc illa Charini apud Terentium querela:
units.tr: "They promise what is necessary, but they will not perform it" [ἐπαγγέλλασθαι ἀναγκάς, ἀμὴ δωνίσεται]. It often happens to many people that when asked for something which they well know they are not equal to providing, they nevertheless take it upon themselves and promise their services lavishly. Thus wretches entangle themselves in snares, from which, though they soon wish to extricate themselves without loss of face, they cannot. This has a twofold cause: either many are ashamed to reveal the weakness of their powers and their poverty, or they are born so that they cannot bring themselves to refuse anything when asked, being held back by a certain rustic and altogether silly shame, which the Greeks call δυσωπία. On this, let the studious young men of honour and decency read Plutarch's most beautiful treatise; they will find many things pertaining to this lack of perfection. These are the people of whom Seneca speaks: "The weakness of the face makes many generous," he says. Nor is that complaint of Charinus in Terence foreign to this:

units.la: — id genus est, ait, hominum pessumumIn denegando modo queis pudor est paululum: Post vbi iam tempus est promissa perfici, Tum coacti necessario se aperiunt, & timent, Et tamen res cogit eos denegare. ἐν τινὶ σὰς ἐλεγχθῶσι.[?] ] Sensum, puto, expressimus: verba autem valde sunt depravata. Arbitror autem locum esse mutilum: ideoque non ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως[?], sed σφαλεραποφῆ[?] potius curandum. Ita igitur expleo, ἐν τινὶ σὰς, δ' ἐχνύφν ὡς ὑχ εἴοντε ἐλεγχθῶσι.[?] Si quis malit referre ad eum cui nulla probatio satisfacit, neque acquiescit iis quae omnes esse vera fatentur, ita erit legendum, ἐν τινὶ σὰς,δ' ἐχνύφν ὡς οἴοντε ἐλεγχθῶσι.[?] Molesti autem esse solent qui in re clara haerent: & à Latinis nodum in scirpo quaerere dicuntur. Lucilius. Nodum in scirpo insanè facere vulgus. Terentius.
units.tr: "— He is that sort of very worst of men, who only has a little shame in refusing; afterwards, when the time comes for what was promised to be performed, then, forced by necessity, they reveal themselves and are afraid, and yet the matter compels them to refuse." [ἐν τινὶ σὰς ἐλεγχθῶσι.] I think I have expressed the sense, but the words are badly corrupted. I think, moreover, that the passage is defective, and so it should be treated not by subtraction but rather by a plausible supplement. Thus I fill it out as follows: [ἐν τινὶ σὰς, δ' ἐχνύφν ὡς ὑχ εἴοντε ἐλεγχθῶσι]. If someone prefers to refer it to the man whom no proof satisfies, and who does not agree with things which everyone admits to be true, it should be read thus: [ἐν τινὶ σὰς, δ' ἐχνύφν ὡς οἴοντε ἐλεγχθῶσι]. Those who cling to a plain matter are usually troublesome, and among the Latins they are said to seek a knot in a rush. Lucilius: "The crowd is insanely making a knot in a rush." Terence:

units.la: At mihi vnus scrupulus etiam restat, qui me male habet. P. dignus es.
units.tr: "But for me one doubt still remains, which troubles me badly." P. "You deserve it."

units.la: Cum tua religione odium: nodum in scirpo quaris. Cicer. Æbutium cui personam hominis ἀφιλέργε[?] imponit, appellat cognitorem viduarum, defensorem nimium litigiosum concitum ad rixas.
units.tr: "With your scruples you hate; you seek a knot in a rush." Cicero. He calls Aebutius, to whom he gives the character of an unaffected man, "a guardian of widows, an overly litigious defender, eager for quarrels."

units.la: καὶ διεγείρειν τὰς μαχομένας.[?] ] Non damno hanc lectionem. optimè enim conuenit homini inepte officioso. Tales autem multi passim reperiuntur, qui contendentes amicos rixantésque suis acclamationibus, ἐν σαῦτ[?], accendant potius quàm vt eos diremtum eant, quod erat veri amici officium. Sed nec, διεγείρειν,[?] quod aliquando in mentem mihi venerat, penitus damno: vt nimirum intelligamus ineptum istum hominem cum aliquos videt inter se certantes, siue id verbis fiat, siue armis, (vtroque enim modo verbum μάχεσθαι[?] accipi potest) temerè se in eorum contentiones immiscere: quasi pacificaturus illos sit: cui tamen praestando auctor non sit futurus idoneus. Διεγείρειν[?] ergo erit certates inter fe dirimere : quomodo accepit Plato in nono De legibus.
units.tr: "and stirs up those who are fighting." [καὶ διεγείρειν τὰς μαχομένας]. I do not condemn this reading, for it agrees very well with a man who is clumsily officious. Many such people are to be found everywhere, who, when friends are contending and quarrelling, inflame them with their shouts, instead of going to separate them, which was the duty of a true friend. But I do not wholly condemn the word διεγείρειν, which had occurred to me at one time: so that we understand this silly man, when he sees some men contending with one another, whether by words or by arms (for the verb μάχεσθαι may be taken in either way), to thrust himself rashly into their quarrels, as though he were going to pacify them, though he will not be a suitable author of any peace. Διεγείρειν, then, will mean to settle disputes between them, as Plato understood it in the ninth book of the Laws.

units.la: μὴ δυνάσθαι ὁρᾶν ἢ προδιεῖσθαι.] Scribe οἱ, vel ἢ. passim ita peccatur. Cùm ait Theophrastus μὴ δυνάσθαι ὁρᾶν, scitè & venustè exprimit ἀγωνίαν æstúmque hominis in biuio hærentis. Oppianus poëta doctissimus Ἁλιευτικῶν libro tertio,
units.tr: "not being able to see or to foresee." [μὴ δυνάσθαι ὁρᾶν ἢ προδιεῖσθαι]. Write οἱ or ἢ; this error is made everywhere. When Theophrastus says μὴ δυνάσθαι ὁρᾶν, he expresses with elegance and grace the anxiety and agitation of a man hesitating at a crossroads. The poet Oppian, most learned, in the third book of his Halieutica:

units.la: κείνῳ ὡς ὅτε τειδοσι[?] πολυτρόπῳ κυμάτι[?]
units.tr: "to that one, as when the many-turning wave"; [κείνῳ ὡς ὅτε τειδοσι πολυτρόπῳ κυμάτι]

units.la: ἕσπ᾽ ἐφορμαίνων· κραδίην δέ οἱ ἀλλὰ λαίλαπι[?]
units.tr: "rushes upon him; but his heart, by the storm"; [ἕσπ᾽ ἐφορμαίνων· κραδίην δέ οἱ ἀλλὰ λαίλαπι]

units.la: ἀλλὰ δ᾽ ἐξιλερῷ ὑπαλλάλαν ἐς ὑδῶν ἐλθεῖν[?]
units.tr: "but by the tempest, being driven, it comes into the waters"; [ἀλλὰ δ᾽ ἐξιλερῷ ὑπαλλάλαν ἐς ὑδῶν ἐλθεῖν]

units.la: Πεπλαύνει δ᾽ ἱκάτερθε νόῳ δέ οἱ ἤτε χῶρα[?] Εἰλεῖται, μάλα δ᾽ ὀξὲ μῆς ὥρεξατο βυλῆς[?]. πότε μέλλει ᾄσεσθαι.)
units.tr: "rushes from both sides; and in his mind the place is turned about, and very sharply his desire was roused"; [Πεπλαύνει δ᾽ ἱκάτερθε νόῳ δέ οἱ ἤτε χῶρα Εἰλεῖται, μάλα δ᾽ ὀξὲ μῆς ὥρεξατο βυλῆς]. When is he about to sing?

units.la: Non tulit rex Antigonus ἀθυμίαν[?] istiusmodi, ne in filio quidem : à quo cùm esset aliquando interrogatus : Quando sumus castra moturi? respondens ille, Quid, inquit, vereris ne tubæ sonum vnus omnium non audias? Cæterùm videntur duces Atheniensium scripto soliti significare, quid opus facto, suis centurionibus & tribunis. Vide Suidam in πινάκιον.
units.tr: King Antigonus could not bear such irresolution, not even in his son; when he was once asked by him, "When are we going to move camp?" he replied, "Why are you afraid that you alone of all will not hear the sound of the trumpet?" Moreover, the Athenian generals seem to have been accustomed to signify in writing to their centurions and tribunes what needed to be done. See Suidas under πινάκιον.

units.la: τῷ πατρὶ εἰπεῖν.) Non quò matrem deferre aut accusare apud patrem velit : sed vt patrem admoneat tempus esse vt cubitum eat, ne fit matri iam cubanti imò iam dormire incipienti, longior expectatio molesta. Δωμάτιον est κοιτῶν, thalamus siue cubiculum, vbi erant lecti cubiculares diuersi à tricliniaribus. Plato 1 1 1. De republica, de Ioue loquens libidine inflammato, καὶ ὅπως ἐκπλαγεὶς ἰδόντα τὸν πρᾶον, ὥστε μηδ᾽ εἰς τὸ Δωμάτιον εἰσελθεῖν, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοῦ βλυσμένον χαμαὶ ξυγγενέσθαι. Ex illo loco Platonis apparet quare dicatur vxor maritum expectare ἐν τῷ δωματίῳ: & quanta sit filij ἀφεδρ[?]ας ista curare, & matri suæ pene dixerim lenocinari. Cæterum vocem δωμάτιον id significare quod diximus, cum sit indubitati iuris: (Hesychius diserte alicubi explicat κοιτῶν) observauimus tamen doctissimos viros sæpe hac illius notione non observata, grauiter peccare. vertere enim passim domus, aut nescio quid aliud, contra auctoris sui mentem. Exempla reperies in Plutarchi Catone, in eiusdem Cimone, item Alexandro, Cæsare, Catone Vticensi, Demetrio, Antonio, & aliis locis apud eundem magnum scriptorem: vbi fere semper offendunt interpretes: quod in rudiorum iuuenum gratiam, non in doctorum hominum contumeliam dictum sit.
units.tr: To the father, he says. Not that he wishes to report or accuse the mother before the father, but to remind him that it is time to go to bed, lest a long wait become tiresome for the mother, who is already lying down and beginning to fall asleep. Dōmation [δωμάτιον] is koitōn [κοιτῶν], a bedchamber or room, where there were bedchamber couches, different from the dining couches. In Plato's Republic, speaking of Zeus inflamed with lust, he says: "and how, struck with wonder at seeing the gentle one, so that he did not even go into the dōmation [δωμάτιον], but, gushing forth, lay with her on the ground [καὶ ὅπως ἐκπλαγεὶς ἰδόντα τὸν πρᾶον, ὥστε μηδ᾽ εἰς τὸ Δωμάτιον εἰσελθεῖν, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοῦ βλυσμένον χαμαὶ ξυγγενέσθαι]." From this passage of Plato it is clear why a wife is said to wait for her husband en tō dōmatiō [ἐν τῷ δωματίῳ], and how much the son's concern for such privy matters, and I might almost say his pandering to his mother, amounts to. Yet that the word dōmation means what we have said is beyond doubt (Hesychius explicitly explains it somewhere as koitōn [κοιτῶν]). Still, we have observed that very learned men, when they have not heeded this meaning, often err gravely. For they translate it everywhere as "house," or as something else entirely, against the intention of its author. You will find examples in Plutarch's Cato, in the same author's Cimon, likewise in Alexander, Caesar, Cato of Utica, Demetrius, Antony, and other passages of that great writer, where the translators almost always stumble. This is said for the benefit of younger and less experienced readers, not to insult learned men.

units.la: ὅπως μὴ δώσει οἶνον τῷ καλλωπιζομένῳ.) Placet quod docti viri excogitarunt, καλλωπιζομένῳ. videamus tamen num minore mutatione in integrum vulgata lectio queat restitui. Quid enim si ita scribamus? ὅπως μὴ τῷ δώσει οἶνον, καλλωπιζομένῳ, καὶ φιλῶς βλά. Τό δ' est, alicui, nempe ægroto: quem planius illa mox designant, τὸν κακῶς ἔχοντα. at καλλωπιζόμενον est, inepte si illi venditans. nam quia solus ex omnibus domesticis & amicis ægroti voluntati morem gerit, hoc iste suum in illū studium oftentat & venditat: homo præposterus, qui id sibi gratiæ apponi velit quod iusta reprehensione dignum sit. Ita posse accipi verbum καλλωπιζεσθαι, docti non negabunt. sic apud Plutarchum in Antonio, ἐγκαλλωπιζεσθαι ὡς αἰσχροῖς. ostentare tanquam pulchra, quæ sint turpia. Omnino istam vocem mordicus retinendam censeo: vel propter effatum Coi senis, qui in lib. Περὶ ἐντῆς vere & elegáter, ζητεῖ) ὁ νοσέων: inquit, ἡ καλλωπισμὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ συμφέρον. Verùm de hoc loco Theophrasti amplius cogitemus. At illud ἀ-ςεσιςαι [?] quod statim sequitur, nō est hortari aut inducere, vt doćti homines putant: sed quod Hippocrates μλεωείζειν [?] dicere solet, hoc est ægrotum in lećto iacentem attollere, & ita componere, vt possit commodè bibere.
units.tr: "so that he does not give wine to the one who is showing off." [ὅπως μὴ δώσει οἶνον τῷ καλλωπιζομένῳ]. The conjecture which learned men have devised, καλλωπιζομένῳ, pleases me. Let us see, however, whether the vulgar reading can be restored to its original form with a smaller change. For what if we write it thus: ὅπως μὴ τῷ δώσει οἶνον, καλλωπιζομένῳ, καὶ φιλῶς βλά? The τῷ means to someone, namely to the sick man, whom the following words designate more plainly as τὸν κακῶς ἔχοντα. But καλλωπιζόμενον means showing off clumsily, if he is making a display of himself to him. For since he alone of all the household and friends humours the sick man's will, he displays and parades this zeal of his towards him: a foolish person, who wishes to have credit for what deserves just reproach. That the verb καλλωπιζεσθαι can be understood in this way, learned men will not deny. Thus in Plutarch's Antony we find ἐγκαλλωπιζεσθαι ὡς αἰσχροῖς: to show off as beautiful things what are shameful. In general I think this word should be kept stubbornly, if only for the saying of the old man of Cos, who in his book On Decency rightly and elegantly says: the sick man seeks not display but what is advantageous. But let us think more about this passage of Theophrastus. As for the word ἀ-ςεσιςαι [?] which immediately follows, it does not mean to urge or to induce, as learned men think; rather it is what Hippocrates is accustomed to call μλεωείζειν [?], that is, to raise up a sick man lying in bed and arrange him so that he can drink comfortably.

units.la: καὶ γυναικὸς τελεσθησάσης. ) an τῆς ἰδίας? an τῆς τὲ πλησίον ἢ φίλῳ? vtroque enim modo possis accipere. Quanta fuerit veterum ἀφιερυχία [?] & ambitio in titulis cipporum, res ipsa indicat. Plato verò vt huic ambitioni stultæ, vt vocat Tertullianus: humanæ, vt Plinius, obuiam iret, legem hanc inter cæteras ferebat, Ne cui liceret tumulo cuiusquam longiorem quatuor versibus heroicis titulum inscribere. libro xii. De legibus.
units.tr: "And when his wife had been buried." Is this his own wife, or the wife of a neighbour or friend? Either sense is possible. How great the ancients' vanity and ambition were in the inscriptions on their tombstones is shown by the thing itself. Plato, to meet this foolish ambition, which Tertullian calls human, as Pliny does, enacted among his other laws this one: that no one may inscribe on anyone's tomb a title longer than four heroic verses. Book 12, Laws.

units.la: ὅτι καὶ ἀπότερον πολλάκις ὁμώμοκε. ] O hominem non solum πτεφεπρυον [?], sed planè vacui capitis, & vt ait Pindarus λάκων φρενῶν! Vult hîc iuriiurando quod adigitur fidem astruere, & ait sæpius iurasse se: non poterat melius probare quanto haberet neglećtui iurisiurandi religionem: quæ quidem in non iurando, aut quâ rarissimè iurádo maximè sita est. vix est enim, vt qui sæpe iuret, non interdū peieret. Quare optimo sanè cõsilio Theophrastus supra inter hominis perditi, profligatiq; notas hanc cũ primis numerabat, quod facilè & leues ob causas iuraret. Scite & eleganter Hierocles, Σέξτος [?], inquit, τὸν ὅρκον, τῷ μὴ προσεῖρως ἀντῷ καταχρῆσθαι, ἐν ἐθι-ςῆς ἀορκεῖν, ἐκ τῷ μὴ ἐθισθῶσι ὀμνύναι. Exemplũ huius stultitiæ in his versibus lepidissimi Menandri,
units.tr: "That he has often sworn to it before now." O the man, not only feather-brained but plainly empty of head, and, as Pindar says, hollow of mind! He wants the oath he is compelled to take to establish his credibility, and he says he has sworn often. He could not have proved better how far he neglected the sanctity of an oath, which consists chiefly in not swearing, or in swearing very rarely. For one who swears often will hardly fail sometimes to perjure himself. So with excellent judgement Theophrastus, above, counted this among the first marks of a worthless and abandoned man: that he swears easily and for trivial reasons. Hierocles says it neatly and elegantly: one should not use the oath carelessly, for by accustoming oneself to swear one comes to swear without need. An example of this folly is in these verses of Menander's, most charming:

units.la: Γλυκέρα τί κλαίεις; ὀμυνῶ [?] τὸν Δία Καὶ τῷ Ἀθηναῖν φιλάττῃ [?], ὁμωμοκώς Καὶ πρότερον ἤδη πολλάκις.
units.tr: "Glykera, why do you weep? I swear by Zeus and by Athena, [having sworn] many times before now." [Γλυκέρα τί κλαίεις; ὀμυνῶ τὸν Δία Καὶ τῷ Ἀθηναῖν φιλάττῃ, ὁμωμοκώς Καὶ πρότερον ἤδη πολλάκις.]
On the chapter concerning insensibility [περὶ ἀναισθησίας].

units.la: Ἔστι ὁ καὶ ἡ ἀναισθησία.) Est hoc vitium τῆς δυσ-ξυνοίας [?], neque ad mores proprie refertur : oppo-nitur enim ei virtuti δυσγνωμοσύνῃ [?], quam Græci ἀγχί-νοιαν, Latini, puto, folertiam appellant. quemadmodum autem stupiditatem definit Theophrastus tarditatem mentis, siue animi : sic Platoni in Char-mide definitur ἀγχίνοια ἐξύτης τις τῆς ψυχῆς [?] : de eadem habes apud Aristotelem, & in v I. Nicomacheorum, & in priore Posteriorum, & alibi : sed nolo praetermittere eiusdem definitionem quae est in libello Andronici, Ἀγχίνοιά, inquit, ἔστιν ἕξις ἐξ ἑαυτῆς τὸ καθῆκον ἐξεπιτελεῖν [?], καὶ καταζοχαζομένη τὴν διάνοιαν [?]. quae prorsus huic loco est accommodata. Suetonius in Claudio stuporem, de quo nostrer, μελεωείαν καὶ ἀλεξίφαν [?] elegantissime vocauit. Vulgo qui essent eiusmodi audiebant ἀσπλαγχνοι [?]. Galenus libro 111. De dogmate Hippocratis & Platonis, ἐς ἀν εἰς ἀναισθησίαν σαρκικὴν [?] ἀσπλαγχνους ὀνομάζεσθαι [?]. idem scribit & alibi. In sacris litteris & libris patrum ἀσπλαγχνία [?] idem est atque ἐλλείμων [?]. Est vero singulare ἀναισθησίας exemplum in eo qui afino vehens, cum plureis duceret, vnum sibi furto periisse quiritabatur, illum nempe cui insidebat. Est in ore vulgi fabula: Sed vt rem gestam narrat Galenus in libris De vsu partium. {Greek} ταύτῳ εἰσιέναι μέλλων. ] Dicitur εἰσιέναι τῷ δίκῳ[?], is qui admittitur ad caussam apud iudicem dicendam, siue coniiciendam, vt veteres loquebantur. Dicunt autem vtroque modo: & ὁ φεύγων, siue ὁ διώκων μέλλει εἰσιέναι τῷ δίκῳ ἢ γραφῇ[?]: & ἡ δίκη μέλλει εἰσιέναι: sic enim orator cum in ea Κατὰ Μει- δίαν[?]: tum in πρὸς Φορμίωνα.
units.tr: "This is the vice of dullness, and it is not properly referred to morals. For it is opposed to the virtue of quickness of wit, which the Greeks call ἀγχίνοια [agchinoia] and the Latins, I think, folertia. As Theophrastus defines stupidity as slowness of mind, or of spirit, so in Plato's Charmides quickness of wit is defined as a certain sharpness of the soul. You find the same in Aristotle, in book 6 of the Nicomachean Ethics, in the first book of the Posterior Analytics, and elsewhere. But I do not want to omit the definition of the same thing in the little book of Andronicus: quickness of wit, he says, is a disposition that of itself accomplishes what is fitting and quickly grasps the thought, which fits this passage exactly. Suetonius, in his life of Claudius, most elegantly calls the stupor of which our author speaks dullness and senselessness. Commonly those of this kind were called ἀσπλαγχνοι [asplanchnoi, without bowels]. Galen, in book 3 of On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato, says they are called ἀσπλαγχνοι because of their fleshly insensibility, and he writes the same elsewhere. In the sacred letters and the books of the Fathers, ἀσπλαγχνία [asplanchnia] means the same as ἐλλείμων [elleimon, lacking mercy]. There is a notable example of insensibility in the man who, riding on an ass and counting his party, complained that one of them had been lost by theft, namely the very man he was sitting on. It is a popular tale, but Galen relates the story in his books On the Use of the Parts." [ταύτῳ εἰσιέναι μέλλων.] "He is said to be going in to the court, [eisienai tō dikō], the one who is admitted to plead his case before the judge, or to be brought forward, as the ancients put it. They say it in both ways: the defendant or the prosecutor is about to go in to the court or to the indictment, and the suit is about to go in. So the orator says in his speech Against Meidias and in the one Against Phormion."

units.la: {Greek}[?] ] Lego Ἀπὸ Σάτυ[?]. Si nihil aut deest, aut corruptum hîc est, sensus erit huiusmodi. Solet iste stupidus ac stolidus, cum noctè tota se cibis supra modum onerauerit, posteaquam in theatrum venit, vino somnoque sepultus iacere: vix vt tandem euigilet, vt sero domum suam reuenire instituat, quo quidem in itinere sæpe accidat vt aberrans à foribus suis, & incautiùs ad vicini ædes accedens, à mutis custodibus qui ad vestibulum excubias agunt, mordeatur. Optimè autem concinit hoc ei quod modò dicebat, solitum τὸν ἀναίσθητον[?], in theatro dormientem solum relinqui. Θέατρον[?] est theatrum, aut alius locus in quo sederi vulgò ad spectandum solet: Θᾶκοι[?] enim sunt sedes & subsellia theatrorum. Latini vt notat Liuius [?]siros appellabant. iremque spectacula, cùm ipse Liuius tum alij: melius Græci θεωρεῖα: vide Hesychium in ἰχεῖον[?]. Atticum autem est, locum vbi multæ sessiones & θᾶκοι sint, appellare θᾶκον. Scholiastes Aristophanis in Nebulas, Θάκος καλεῖταί ὁ τόπος Ἀθήνησι ἔνθα πολλοὶ συνέρχονται τεθμένοι[?]. Sic alia loca vocabant Athenienses ab iis rebus quæ ibi multæ erant aut multum. Sic exempli causa ἔλαιον[?] vocabant vbi venale prostabat oleum. Menander, ἀγοράζω σε πρὸς ἔλαιον[?], μύρον myropolium. vt in Aristophanis Equitibus, & μειράκια, & ἐν τῷ μυρῷ καθήμενα. πεσσὸς, τὸ κυβεῖον, vbi calculis vel talis ludi folet: qui locus Ciceroni ludus talarius, Augusto apud Suetonium, forum aleatorium dicitur.Euripides Medea,
units.tr: "I read [Ἀπὸ Σάτυ]. If nothing is missing or corrupted here, the sense is as follows. This stupid and dull fellow, after he has stuffed himself with food beyond measure through the whole night, when he comes to the theatre lies down, buried in wine and sleep, and scarcely wakes up at last to set about going home late. On the way he often strays from his own door and, approaching a neighbour's house carelessly, is bitten by the dumb guards who keep watch in the vestibule. This agrees very well with what he said just before: that the insensible man is usually left alone asleep in the theatre. Theatron [θέατρον] is a theatre, or any other place where people usually sit to watch a show. For thakoi [θᾶκοι] are the seats and benches of theatres. As Livy notes, the Latins called them siros, and the shows spectacula, both he and others. The Greeks better call them theōreia; see Hesychius under icheion. It is Attic usage to call a place where there are many seats and thakoi a thakos. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Clouds says: 'Thakos is the name at Athens of the place where many gather who are seated.' So the Athenians named other places from the things that were there in great number. For example, they called the place where oil was sold for sale elaion [ἔλαιον]. Menander: 'I buy you by the oil [pros elaion] and by the perfume shop' (myropolion), as in Aristophanes' Knights, and meirakia, and 'sitting in the perfumer's' [ἐν τῷ μυρῷ καθήμενα]. Pessos [πεσσὸς] is the gaming house, where people usually play with pebbles or dice. Cicero calls this place a ludus talarius, Augustus in Suetonius calls it a forum aleatorium. Euripides in the Medea:"

units.la: Ἠκουσά τε λέγοντ' ὦ δοκῶν κλύειν Πεσσὸς προσελθὼν ἔνθα δὴ παλαιῖ, Θέασαι.
units.tr: "I have heard, as if I seemed to hear, a man talking, having come to the gaming house [pessos], where, long ago, you see [theasai]." [Ἠκουσά τε λέγοντ' ὦ δοκῶν κλύειν Πεσσὸς προσελθὼν ἔνθα δὴ παλαιῖ, Θέασαι.]

units.la: Scholiastes. Ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν τοῖς Γάμοις ὠνόμαζον τὰς τόπως. πεσσὸς γὰρ νῦν καλεῖ τὰς τόπως τῆς κυβείας, ὡς ἅλον καὶ μύρα ἔνθα τοῦτο συμβῆναι ἔξιν. Pollux quoque notat dixisse poëtas comicos εἰς τὸν οἶνον, εἰς τὸ ἅλον, εἰς τὸ ταλαιον, εἰς τὰς χύτρας, εἰς τὰ σπορόδα. & id genus alia. Ita debes accipere in hoc Alexidis loco apud Athenæum,
units.tr: "The scholiast: they named the places from the things in them. For pessos now means the place of dice-playing, as halon and myra mean the places where those things are sold. Pollux also notes that the comic poets said eis ton oinon, eis to halon, eis to talaion, eis tas chytras, eis ta sporeda, and other things of that kind. So you must understand this passage of Alexis in Athenaeus:"

units.la: Τοῖς ἰχθυοπώλαις ἐστὶν ἐληρμένον Ὃς φασι, χαλκῷ Καλλιμέδοντ' εἰκόνα Στῆσαι Παναθηναίοισιν ἐν τοῖς ἰχθύσι.
units.tr: "To the fishmongers it has been said, as they say, that Kallimedon [should be honoured] with a statue in bronze, set up at the Panathenaea among the fish."

units.la: fallunturque enim ibi interpretes, dum non animaduertunt dictum esse ἐν τοῖς ἰχθύσι. pro in foro piscario, qui locus Plutarcho in Hyperide ἰχθυοπώλις ἀγορὰ nominatur: sicut eidem in Timoleonte ἀγορὰ ὀψοπώλις dicitur quæ Attice ὄψον. Sic etiam accipiendum apud Aristotelem, in nono de historia animalium, capite xl i i i. vbi teredinem ait esse λίχνον ζῷον, & solitam aduolare πρὸς τὰ μαγειρεῖα καὶ τὰς ἰχθύας. hoc est, τὰ ἰχθυοπωλεῖα: sicut dixit Theophrastus capite v i. ἐφοδεύειν τὰ μαγειρεῖα, καὶ τὰ ἰχθυοπωλεῖα.
units.tr: "The interpreters go wrong there because they do not notice that en tois ichthysin means 'in the fish market' [in foro piscario]. Plutarch in his life of Hyperides calls this place the fish-market [ἰχθυοπώλις ἀγορά]. In the same way, in his Timoleon, he calls the market for cooked meat [ἀγορὰ ὀψοπώλις] what in Attic is opson. The same must be understood in Aristotle, book 9 of the History of Animals, chapter 43, where he says the woodworm is a greedy creature and is wont to fly to the cookshops [μαγειρεῖα] and the fishmongers' stalls [ἰχθύας], that is, the ichthyopōleia. Theophrastus, in chapter 6, similarly said: 'to haunt the cookshops and the fishmongers' stalls.'"

units.la: καὶ μὴ δύνασθαι ἀφεῖν. ) Notanda ista verba: quibus indicat se de eo intelligere qui non solùm quærat quod sit à se reconditum & certo loco positum: sed qui omnino nequeat reperire. quod sanè stuporis alicuius esse indicium fatendum est. Nam alioquin scimus hoc multis vsuenire, interdum etiam iis qui sint ἔτε φύης [?]ϑηδ[?] ἔτε νόσου, vt quod alicubi collocarint, statim inuenire non possint. Quanquam quid hoc mirum, si etiam liberorum, aut amicorum aut seruorum nostrorum nomina, quando vocare illos volumus, in mentem nobis non veniunt, sed in primoribus labris haerét? Imò ausim dicere vix quenquam esse cui non aliquando vsuenerit quod ille apud Plautum ait:
units.tr: "And not to be able to find it." These words must be noted: by them he indicates that he means one who not only looks for something he has put away and placed in a certain spot, but who cannot find it at all. This must certainly be admitted to be a sign of some stupidity. For otherwise we know that this happens to many people, sometimes even to those who are neither healthy nor ill, that they cannot immediately find what they have put somewhere. Yet what is so surprising about it, when we want to call our children, or friends, or slaves, and their names do not come to mind but stick on the tip of our lips? Indeed I would dare to say there is hardly anyone to whom it has not sometimes happened, as the character in Plautus says:
"That, he says, is wont to happen."

units.la: Quod in manu teneas atque oculo videat, id desideres.
units.tr: What you hold in your hand and see with your eye, you still go looking for.

units.la: Et sanè aliud est ἀγρυπνία, aliud ἀπροσεξία. Interdum, inquit Seneca, scimus aliquid, sed non attendimus. Idem, epistola LXXXI. Quibusdam euenit, vt quaedam scire se nesciant, quemadmodum quaerimus saepe eos quibuscum stamus. Proptereà dicebat Cyrus apud Xenophontem καλὸν [?] ἐν οἰκίᾳ ἐπιτηδεύματα ἔθνῳ [?]. Non dissimile est illud de quo quaerit in Problematis Alexander, διὰ τί εἰς τόπον τινὰ ἀπιόντες ἀναγκαίως, καταλαβόντες αὐτὸν ἀξιαίνουμεν [?]. Vide locum.
units.tr: "And indeed it is one thing to be sleepless, another to be inattentive. Sometimes, says Seneca, we know something but do not pay attention. The same, in letter 81: it happens to some that they do not know what they know, just as we often look for those we are standing with. That is why Cyrus in Xenophon said that it was a fine thing to practise [the arts] at home. Not unlike this is the question Alexander asks in the Problems: why, when we go somewhere necessarily and find someone there, do we pardon him [...]? See the passage."

units.la: ἵνα [?]ἀποθανόντες[?]. ) Nempe vt funeri operam det, sicut mos erat olim venire ad amicorum defunctorum πρόσθεσιν [?]. vnde est apud Isocratem, ἀποθανόντας ἐπὶ τὸ κῆδος [?]: apud Demosthenem, παρεῖναι τῇ πρόθεσει τῆς τετταρακοντάκτου [?]. Ea πρόσθεσις trium fere dierum erat: etsi lege Solonis vnus illi dies tantum praefinitus, postea sequebatur ἐκφορά [?]: efferebantur autem mortui ante solis ortum, verùm de his aliàs fortasse pluribus. δακρύσας, εἶπεν, Ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ.) Contrarium oportuit, Nollem factum, aut Molestè fero. Inepte igitur iste formulam vsurpat cuius vsus in re læta potius, vt cum ducenda vxor, aut aliud quid suscipitur. Nam tum solebant dicere Ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ, hoc est, Quod bene vertat, vel Quod sit felix & faustum, aut Felix hoc, vel denique Bonum factum. & apud Ciceronem ad Atticum libro vi 1. Bene eueniat, planè est Ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ, & quod dicit Persius, hoc bene sit: non Ἐσ[?] μὲν δ[?] quod affert Bosius ex Aristotelis testamento. id enim aliam vim habet. Dicebant etiam δ' ἀπάθως[?], cum aliquid facere instituebant, vt apud Lucianum qui è portu soluút. Moris etiam fuit veteribus, quicquid aggrederentur, Dei nomen inuocare, & veluti bonæ scæuæ gratia dicere inter initia Θεὸς Θεός. Annotant Hesychius & Eustathius ex veteribus criticis ad Ἰλιαδ. ρ. β. Porrò stuporis nō dissimilis exempla habes in Suetonij Claudio capite xxxix.
units.tr: "That he may have died": namely, so that he may attend the funeral, as it was once customary to come to the laying out (prothesis) of deceased friends. Hence in Isocrates: "to come to the funeral of those who have died"; in Demosthenes: "to be present at the prothesis on the fortieth day" [ἀποθανόντας ἐπὶ τὸ κῆδος; παρεῖναι τῇ πρόθεσει τῆς τετταρακοντάκτου]. This prothesis lasted about three days, although under Solon's law only one day was fixed for it. Afterwards came the ekphora, and the dead were carried out before sunrise. But perhaps this can be discussed at more length elsewhere. "Weeping, he said, 'May it turn out well'": the opposite would have been expected, such as "I wish it had not happened" or "I take it badly." So this man foolishly uses a formula whose proper place is on happy occasions, such as when a wife is to be taken or something else is undertaken. For then people would say "May it turn out well" [Ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ], that is, "May it go well," or "May this be happy and fortunate," or "Good luck to this," or finally "Well done." In Cicero to Atticus, book 6, letter 1, "bene eveniat" is plainly the same as Ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ, and so is what Persius says, "hoc bene sit." It is not the phrase Bosius cites from Aristotle's will, which has a different force. They also used to say a similar thing when they began to do something, as in Lucian, of those who set sail from harbour. It was also the custom of the ancients, whatever they undertook, to call on the name of God, and as a kind of good omen to say "God, God" at the beginning. Hesychius and Eustathius, citing the ancient critics, note this on Iliad ρ 2. Further examples of similar astonishment are found in Suetonius, Claudius, chapter 39.

units.la: μάρτυρας καλεῖν.] Tanquam videlicet flagitatum debitas pecunias iret: solebant enim illi testes secum adducere, vt si debitores inficias irent, aut caluerent, vt est in x i 1. præsto effet quem poffent antestati, & qui eum vnde petebatur, vocaret in ius, quod κλητῆρα dicebant Athenienses. vide Nebulas Aristophanis. Vel imitatur stultè eorum morem qui debitas pecunias soluunt: nam illi solebant ambitiosè multos bonæ suæ fidei testes adducere. Demosthenes eleganter in ea contra Phormionem, ὥσε δ' ἡμεῖς, inquit, πάντες, ὅτι δανείζονται μὲν μετ' ἄλλων μαρτύρων. ὡς γὰρ δ' ἀπέδοσαν, πολλοὺς παρέστησαν μάρτυρας ἵνα ὅτι δείξεις δ[?] ὀρθῶς ἢ περὶ τὰ συμβόλαια. καὶ προχάζειν.) Veteres & se & liberos suos cursu studiosè exercebant:vocabant autem προχον,tam genus hoc exercitationis (cuius varias species habes apud Platonem De legibus lib. v I I I) quàm locum ipsum. Aristophanes,
units.tr: "To call witnesses": as if, forsooth, he were going to demand debts that were owed. For those men used to bring witnesses with them, so that if debtors denied the debt or prevaricated, as in (?) x i 1, there would be someone present before whom they could call on him to testify, and who could summon the debtor to court; the Athenians called such a man a κλητήρ. See Aristophanes' Clouds. Or he foolishly imitates the custom of those who pay their debts, for they used to bring many witnesses of their good faith, to make a show of it. Demosthenes puts it neatly in his speech against Phormio: "We all know that they lend money with other witnesses present; but when they repaid, they brought forward many witnesses, so that it might be shown that they dealt rightly in their contracts." And "to run" (προχάζειν): the ancients trained themselves and their children in running with great care. They called the place for it a προχός, as well as the kind of exercise itself (of which you have various forms in Plato's Laws, book 8).

units.la: Βαδίζει μοι τὸ μεγάκιον ἀπὸ προχῶν. Euripides Medea 'Αλλ' οἷδε παῖδες ἐκ προχῶν πεπαυμένοι Σλέγχων. Vocabát & ἀρόχων:qua de voce plura alio loco ad lucem auctorum,faciente Deo.
units.tr: Aristophanes: "The big-bellied fellow walks away from the running-ground." Euripides, Medea: "But these boys, having ceased from the running-grounds..." They also called it ἀρόχων. I will say more about this word elsewhere, to shed light on the authors, God willing.

units.la: καὶ εἰς κόπτους ἐμβάλλειν.) Delendum censeo τὸ καὶ ante εἰς κ. Intelligendum est excedere istum in hac parte, neque modum feruare. Est enim legitimus modus & omnis exercitationis finis, lassitudo: inquit Seneca, epistola L xxxi I I I. Clemens Ale- xandrinus, ὡς πάνυς σπίων ἡγεῖσθαι ἄεισον, ὅταν τὸ ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον πονεῖν, καὶ κάκιτον, καὶ ποτώδες, καὶ νο- σωδες. Kónov accipe, non lassitudinem, sed fatigationem, & incommoda quae nimiam lassitudinem consequi solent, quae à medicis explicantur. Haec notare volui: nam alioquin laude dignum potius quàm reprehensione istius istud studium. Seneca De diuina prouidentia, Non vides quanto aliter patres, aliter matres indulgeant? Illi exercitari iubent liberos ad studia obeunda mature: feriatis quoque diebus non patiuntur esse otiosos: & sudorem illis, & interdum lacrymas excutiunt.Cauenda sane in educandis pueris lassitudo corporis: quae vt ait idem alibi, consumit quicquid in nobis est mite placidúmque, & acria concitat. quin eadem iuuenes[?] reddit fegniores: quam ob caussam ait Varro illos qui catulos educant, non pati eos defatigari.
units.tr: "And throwing themselves into the beating": I think the καί before εἰς κόπτους should be deleted. It must be understood that he goes too far in this respect and does not keep to measure. For the lawful measure and end of all exercise is weariness, as Seneca says in letter 83. Clement of Alexandria says that one should consider it very dangerous to labour beyond measure, since it is harmful, drinking-like, and unhealthy. Take κόπος not as mere weariness but as fatigue, and the troubles that excessive weariness usually brings, which doctors explain. I wished to note these points, for otherwise this zeal of his would deserve praise rather than blame. Seneca, On Divine Providence: "Do you not see how differently fathers and mothers indulge their children? The fathers order them to be trained early for their studies; they do not let them be idle even on holidays, and they squeeze out sweat and sometimes tears." Care must certainly be taken in bringing up boys not to tire their bodies, for, as the same Seneca says elsewhere, weariness consumes whatever is gentle and mild in us and stirs up what is harsh. Indeed it makes young men even more sluggish; for this reason Varro says that those who raise puppies do not let them be overtired.

units.la: καὶ ἐν ἀγῶσι.) Cur ista adliciuntur? An legendum ἐν ὑγρῷ. Nam vt ait Xenophon, τὰ ἱφθὰ πάντα μετ᾽ ὕδατος τὰ πλέϊστα ἐπιδέξασθαι. Nihil pronuntio.
units.tr: "And in contests": why are these words added? Or should we read "in moisture" (ἐν ὑγρῷ)? For as Xenophon says, all dry things take in most of their moisture from water. I pronounce nothing.

units.la: αὐτὸς φαχὴν ἔϕων.) Lego αὐτός. Nam etiam in hoc est stultitiæ argumentum, quod ipse ollam curat. Sic refert Plutarchus subsannatum fuisse Antagoram poëtam à rege Antigono, quum rex illum vi-disset γόγγον ἐϕονῶ, καὶ αὐτὸν τῷ λοιδὸρα σείοντα.
units.tr: "He himself, blowing on the pot": I read "he himself." For this too is evidence of his folly, that he himself tends the pot. So Plutarch reports that the poet Antagoras was mocked by King Antigonus, when the king saw him blowing on the fire and shaking the bellows himself.

units.la: ἡδύγε τῆ ἀσρων νομίζει.) Conclamatus locus, nisi meliores libri proferantur. nam quæ ab interpretibus afferuntur ad curationem huius defperantis vlceris, planè sunt omnia, quod ille ait, gerra germane, atque adepol lire lire.
units.tr: "It is pleasant to think of the stars": this is a desperate passage, unless better manuscripts are brought forward. For what the interpreters offer to heal this hopeless ulcer is plainly all of it just what he says: "gerra germane, atque adepol lire lire."

units.la: κῆ τὰς ἱερὰς πύλας.) Appellat ἱερὰς πύλας portam Sacram Athenarum, cuius meminit Plutarchus in Sylla, vbi ἱερὰν πύλην vocat. sed vsitatum est Græcis qui purius locuti sunt, vt portarum nomina numero multitudinis efferant, vt πύλαι Μελιτίδες eiusdem vrbis, & aliæ fexcentis locis apud veteres scriptores: idque Homerico ξίλῳ & imitatione, si veterum criticorum stamus sententia. Euftathius: Παυσανίας τὰς πύλας, καὶ ἐχὶ ἑκάστην ἐνικῶς πολλαὶ χάφεται τῷ παλαιῶν, ἀφῄσυμένη μέρη ὡς ἕδινεσ τὴν πύλην λέγει ὁ ποιητὴς, ἀλλὰ πύλας. Latini aliter vt notum est: quare non rectè Sacras portas, vulgò hic vertunt. An autem cerra aliqua fuit porta Athenis, per quam efferrentur mortui? Olim enim mortuos in plerisque ciuitatibus sepelire in vrbe fas non fuit. Romæ quidem disserte legibus XII. vetitum: quod ex Solonis axibus puto translatum. Fuit etiam Athenis in nomophylacio ianua vna quam χαρώνεσ θύραν vocabant, qua educebantur ad supplicium, qui capitis essent condemnati: vide Pollucem, & Græcos parœmiographos. Testatur etiam Plutarchus, in aliis vrbibus Græciæ, portam quandam sceleratam fuisse qua sontes, (nam extra pomœria, in reos animaduertere moris erat) ὡς θανάτῳ[?] ducerentur: ipse πύλας ἀποφράδας[?] vocat. Hinc est apud Plautum prouerbium, Extra portam ire, in Milite. Seneca pater, Controuersiarum libro primo, Dicendum est in puellam vehementer, non sordidè nec obscœnè. Sordidè Basilius qui dixit: Extra portam istam virginem. Respondet illis Græcorum, ἐς Μαχαδίαν[?], & ἐς κόμανας[?]. & ei quod est apud Tertullianum, Malum foras.
units.tr: "Through the sacred gates": he calls them the sacred gates, meaning the Sacred Gate of Athens, which Plutarch mentions in his Sulla, where he calls it "the sacred gate." But it was customary for Greeks who spoke more purely to express the names of gates in the plural, as with the Melitid Gates of the same city and in many other places in the ancient writers. This was done by Homeric usage and imitation, if we follow the opinion of the ancient critics. Eustathius says that Pausanias writes "the gates" and not the singular for each, since the poet says "gates" and not "gate," and many such plurals occur in the ancients. The Latins do otherwise, as is well known; so the Latin translators here wrongly render it "Sacred Gates." But was there some gate at Athens through which the dead were carried out? For long ago in most cities it was not lawful to bury within the city. At Rome the Twelve Tables expressly forbade it, which I think was carried over from Solon's axones. At Athens too there was a single door in the nomophylakion which they called the door of Charon, through which those condemned to capital punishment were led out to execution; see Pollux and the Greek writers of proverbs. Plutarch also testifies that in other cities of Greece there was a certain accursed gate through which the guilty were led to death, for it was customary to punish criminals outside the pomerium; he himself calls them "unlucky gates." Hence the proverb in Plautus' Miles, "to go outside the gate." The elder Seneca, in book 1 of the Controversies: "One must speak against the girl vehemently, not meanly or obscenely." Basil, who said "that virgin outside that gate," was mean. The Greek phrases "to Machaerodas" and "to the cemeteries" answer to these, and so does the saying in Tertullian, "Bad thing, out!"

units.la: ὡς τοὺς εἰπεῖν, Οἱ[?] ἐμοὶ καὶ οἱ ψοῖνοι.[?] Non est is horum verborum sensus quem putant interpretes: Non enim optat efferri è suis familiaribus, aut eius quem alloquitur, mortuos: quod non esset stuporis nota, sed nescio cuius immanitatis. Enimuero peccatum idem hîc, quod suprà in Ἀγαθῆι τύχῃ. Lingua enim tardam hominis mentem præcurrit. Cum igitur prouerbialis esset locutio de iis quorum copiam magnam indicare volebant, Tot esse quot sint in orco mortui: stupidus iste postquà audiit magnum esse mortuorum numerum, optat tantam sibi copiam, non mortuorum quidem, non: sed alius cuiusuis rei bonæ: puta, nummorum, vel modiorum tritici, aut nescio cuius: imò ipse quoque, qui est eius stupor, quid dicat aut optet, non satis scit. Apud Plautum in Pœnulo Agorastocles adolescens, insanorum more loqui incipiens, simile quid ait, Non hercle, inquit, mereram quantum Acheruntæ est mortuorum; neque quantum aquæ est in mari, neque nubes omnes quantum sunt.
units.tr: "As if to say, 'May my people and your people...'": the sense of these words is not what the interpreters think. He does not wish that the dead be carried out from his own family or from the family of the person he addresses; that would be a mark not of stupidity but of some monstrous savagery. Indeed the fault here is the same as above in "May it turn out well." For the tongue runs ahead of the slow mind of the man. Since the saying was proverbial for those whose great number people wished to indicate, "as many as are dead in Orcus," this dolt, having heard that the number of the dead is great, wishes for such a great abundance for himself: not of the dead, certainly not, but of some other good thing, say money, or bushels of wheat, or I know not what. Indeed he himself, being foolish, does not know well enough what he says or wishes. In Plautus' Poenulus the young man Agorastocles, beginning to talk like the insane, says something similar: "No, by Hercules, I would not have deserved as many as are dead in Acheron, nor as much as the water in the sea, nor as many clouds as there are."

units.la: Η[?]δὲ αὐθάδεια.) Pertinet hoc quoque vitium ad τὰς ὁμιλίας, vt capite secundo annotauimus. Sunt enim quidam ita odiosè sibi placentes, tantúmque sibi tribuentes, &,(quod fere coniunctum est) ita alios præ se despicientes, vt difficile sit admodum cum iis versari: fere enim omnibus contradicere solent, & suam mordicus in omni re sententiam tueri. Grauitatis scilicet nescio cuius opinionem & famam aucupantur: neque sciunt gravitatem morum eam demum probandam, quæ comitate & hilaritate frontis iuncta, condita & temperata fuerit.
