Hoc genus homines philosophus in Nicomachceis δυσκόλους & δυσεχίδας semper vocat: vbi elegantissimè incudi eos comparat, quæ cedere nescia malleum semper repercutit. Ait enim istos πρὸς πάντα ἀλλότριον, τὰ λυπηρὰ εἰδ', ὁ, τὴν φρονti-ζοντας. Virtutem autem huic vitio oppositam in Nicomachceis quidem φιλίαν semper vocat: nonnulla quodam modo φιλίαν vsurpans, vt ipse explicat: intelligi autem voluit eo vocabulo, morum facilitatem, & grauitatem decenti conditam lenitate. At in Magnis & Eudemiis σεμνότητα virtutem illam nuncupabat: sicut etiam facit Demosthenes in Erotico, vbi ait multos ὅτι σεμνότητι & αὐθάδεις fuisse habitos. Paullo alicer Plutarchus, qui Dionem ait Dionysio minori fuisse inuisum propter σεμνότητα, quam tyrāni adulatores ὑβριστὰς vocabant: & ἀπροσπαθείαν, quam ipsi αὐθάδειαν nuncupabant. Aristoteli verò id verbi videtur postea displicuisse : non enim de nihilo est,quod in accuratissimo opere mutauit, & φιλίαν dixit, voce praesertim ambigua,ut jam diximus.Sic etiam in iisdem libris malnit [?] Δυσκόλως & Δυσκολίας dicere quàm αὐθάδεις, ut in Magnis & Eudemiis. in Magnis verò etiam notationem nominis adiecerat: τὸ τρόπος [?], inquit, ἐκεῖνον [?] δὲ τὸ τρόπος κεῖ Ξ[?] ὁ δὲ αὐθάδης, αὐθάδης τὶς ἦν, ἀπὸ αὐτὸς τὸ αὐτῷ ἀρίστῳ. Latini hoc vitiū, modò superbiam modo arrogantiam, modò proteruitatem, modò pernicaciam, siue pertinaciam, sæpe ferocitatem, interdum truculentiam nominant. Hominibus autem αὐθάδεσιν opponuntur homines benigni & mansueti, quos auctor ad Herennium commodos & suì cognoscentes vocat: quod planè contrarium est τῇ αὐθαδείᾳ, cui Plato tribuit τὸ ἀχαρίστον [?] (inde est ἀπάνθρωπα in descriptione Theophrastea) in x 1 1. De legib. in 1 x. autem De republica, τὸ ἐφιλάνθρωπος [?] & τὸ λεοντῶδες: vbi αὐθάδειαν etiam δυσκολίαν vocat, sicut de Aristotele antè annotauimus. Idem Plato in Politico pulchrè τὸν αὐθάδη describit, ἀμαθῆ appellans, &c, qui nihil probet nisi quod sibi fuerit visum: quíque nunquam quenquam in consilium aut aduocet, aut admittat. Ac videtur Terentius eum locum Platonis in animo habuisse, cum faceret illa Mitionem dicere:
units.tr: Arrogance [αὐθάδεια].) This vice also belongs to social intercourse [τὰς ὁμιλίας], as we noted in the second chapter. For there are some who are so offensively pleased with themselves, who attribute so much to themselves and, what usually goes with it, so despise others in comparison, that it is very hard to live with them. They nearly always contradict everyone and stubbornly defend their own opinion in every matter. Clearly they are chasing after a reputation and opinion of some sort of gravity, and they do not realise that seriousness of character deserves approval only when it is joined with courtesy and a cheerful countenance, and seasoned and tempered by them. The philosopher in the Nicomachean Ethics always calls this sort of men unaccommodating [δυσκόλους] and difficult [δυσεχίδας]. There he aptly compares them to an anvil, which, unable to yield, keeps striking back the hammer. He says that they are always opposed to everything and find fault with all things that please others. He calls the virtue opposed to this vice friendliness [φιλίαν] in the Nicomachean Ethics, using the term in a somewhat special sense, as he himself explains; he wished it to mean ease of manners and gravity tempered with a becoming gentleness. But in the Magna Moralia and the Eudemian Ethics he named that virtue dignity [σεμνότητα], as Demosthenes also does in his Erotic Oration, where he says that many were considered dignified [σεμνότητι] and arrogant [αὐθάδεις]. Plutarch says something rather different: that Dion was hated by the younger Dionysius because of his dignity [σεμνότητα], which the tyrant's flatterers called insolence [ὑβριστὰς], and his unresponsiveness [ἀπροσπαθείαν], which they themselves called arrogance [αὐθάδειαν]. But Aristotle later seems to have been displeased with this word: it is not for nothing that in his most accurate work he changed it and called it friendliness [φιλίαν], especially since that word is ambiguous, as we have already said. So too in the same books he preferred to say unaccommodating [Δυσκόλως] and unaccommodation [Δυσκολίας] rather than arrogant [αὐθάδεις], as in the Magna Moralia and the Eudemian Ethics. In the Magna Moralia he had even added an explanation of the name: "the character [τρόπος]," he says, "... but the arrogant man [αὐθάδης] was a certain sort of man, from self [αὐτός] and pleasure [ἀρέσκω?]." Latin writers call this vice variously pride, arrogance, petulance, obstinacy or pertinacity, often ferocity, and sometimes truculence. Opposed to arrogant men are kind and gentle men, whom the author of the Ad Herennium calls agreeable and mindful of themselves [commodos & suì cognoscentes]; this is clearly the opposite of arrogance, to which Plato attributes the unfriendly [τὸ ἀχαρίστον] (hence the inhuman [ἀπάνθρωπα] in Theophrastus' description). In the eleventh book of the Laws and in the ninth of the Republic he speaks of the unfriendly [τὸ ἐφιλάνθρωπος?] and the lion-like [τὸ λεοντῶδες], where he also calls arrogance unaccommodation [δυσκολίαν], as we noted earlier concerning Aristotle. In the Politicus the same Plato describes the arrogant man admirably, calling him ignorant [ἀμαθῆ], and so on: one who approves nothing except what has seemed good to himself, and who never either asks anyone for counsel or admits anyone to it. Terence seems to have had this passage of Plato in mind when he made Micio say:

units.la: Homine imperito nunquam quicquam iniustius: Qui, nisi quod ipse facit, nihil rectum putat.
units.tr: "There is nothing more unjust than a man without learning: who thinks nothing right except what he himself does."
Euripides too, similarly, in the Medea:

units.la: Οὐδ᾽ ἄξιον, αἴτ᾽, ἵνα [?] τις αὐθάδης [?] ἢ ἐγώ [?], Πιερὸς πολίταις ἕξιν ἀμαθίας ὑπο [?].
units.tr: "Nor is it fitting, I say, that a man who is arrogant or I should be thought wise by the citizens of Corinth, having a wisdom that is ignorance."

units.la: Non multum diuersa est natura illius quem Graeci ἰδιογνώμονα [?], vel αὐτογνώμονα [?] dicunt, Cicero in Verrem, sui iuris & sententia.
units.tr: The nature of the man whom the Greeks call self-minded [ἰδιογνώμονα] or self-opinionated [αὐτογνώμονα] is not very different, Cicero says in the Verrines: "of his own right and opinion."

units.la: [illegible, ~4 letters] [?] ἐρωτηθεὶς. Superbum est, ait Cicero, non respondere, si habeas quod liqueat. Proprium sanè est hominibus grauitatis opinionem ineptè affectantibus, ut sint [?]ἀπροσποίητοι. De His Iuuenalis, Rarus sermo illis, & magna libido tacendi.
units.tr: [illegible] "Asked [ἐρωτηθεὶς]. It is haughty, says Cicero, not to reply when you have something clear to say." It is certainly characteristic of men who foolishly affect an appearance of gravity not to be unaffected. Juvenal speaks of them: "Rare is their speech, and great their desire for silence."

units.la: [?]Πράγματα μὴ μοι παρέχειν.) Hoc passim in ore hominibus superbis & reliquos fastidientibus. Plautus Truculento,
units.tr: "Do not give me trouble [Πράγματα μὴ μοι παρέχειν].") This phrase is everywhere on the lips of proud men who despise the rest. Plautus, in the Truculentus:

units.la: Quid hic vos agitis? P H. Ne me appella.
units.tr: "What are you doing here?" P. H. "Don't address me."

units.la: S T. Nimium sanis. P H. Sic sine.
units.tr: S. T. "Too sane for you." P. H. "Let it be so."

units.la: In Mostellaria Phanifcus de insolentia conferuorum conquerens, vbi, ait, aduorsum vt eant, vocantur hero, Non eo, Molestus ne sis. & iterum scena sequenti, & alibi. Quid quòd in Cafina formulam hanc ipsam Græculorum arrogantium vsurpauit poeta ingeniosissimus? Ibi Stalino herus & Olympio seruus, sed qui dominum suum nequissimè [illegible, ~10 letters] ludos faceret, ita loquuntur,
units.tr: In the Mostellaria, Phanisca complains of the insolence of fellow slaves: "when," he says, "they are told to go towards their master, they say, 'I won't go; don't be a nuisance.'" And again in the following scene, and elsewhere. What of the fact that in the Casina the most gifted poet also used this very formula of arrogant little Greeks? There Stalino is the master and Olympio the slave, who, most wickedly [illegible], makes a game of his master; they speak thus:

units.la: OL. [illegible, ~4 letters] odio es. ST. Mane vero quanquam fastidis. OL. Hei hei fœtet
units.tr: OL. [illegible] You are hateful to me. ST. Good morning, though you turn up your nose at me. OL. Phew, phew, it stinks!

units.la: Tuus mihi sermo. ST. quae res? Etiamne astus?
units.tr: ST. "What is it? Are you even being witty?"
"You are giving me trouble [Πράγματά μοι παρέχεις]."

units.la: [?]ἀλλ' ἐρωτᾷν, τί δείκνυσι;) Non potuit suas mercès magis laudare. Sic Parmeno apud Terentium,
units.tr: "But to ask what he is showing [ἀλλ' ἐρωτᾷν, τί δείκνυσι;]." He could not have praised his own wares more. So Parmeno in Terence:

units.la: Nunquid habes quod contemnas? quid tu autem Thrasò? Tacent: satis laudant.
units.tr: "Have you anything you may despise? What do you say, Thraso? They are silent: they praise enough."

units.la: vbi [?]τὸ ἔχειν, ἐστι, δεικτικὸς, vt etiam Donatus explicat. χαὶ τῖς τιμῶσι χαὶ ἀεμτιεσιν εἰς τὰς ἑορτάς.) Appa- ret subesse vlcus. Interpretes verò quos quidem vidi parum digné hinc fe expediunt. Scilicet τιμὰν, stipem colligere est. φὰ τῆς δαιμονίας! sed ad rem. Notat auctor in homine ἀυθάδεια conteintum diuini numinis, & religionis omnis: Ita enim feré comparatum videas vt qui erga homines superbi sint, etiam erga Deum insolescant, eumqúe colere parum curent: quod etiam Theophrastus in extremo capite alia nota indicat. Fuit autem olim diuini cultus pars, deorum festis solennibus interesse, & ea concelebrare. Quare, qui religiosiores erant, ij non festa tátùm vrbis in qua habitabant, religiosè obseruabant: sed ad alia quoque aliarum vrbium festa solennia cum muneribus accurrebant, vt etiam Platonis Leges docent. Atque hoc,etsi sine magnis sumtibus fieri non poterat, non tamen ea res illos deterrebat: sed cum Plautino Pleuside sibi persuadebant, Quod in diuinis rebus sumas, sapienti lucro est. Contrà verò iste factum eorum ridet: & quòd illi propterea boni aliquid à diis sperent, id quoque sceleratus scelerate ridet,& negat esse tanti: Magno, inquiens, vobis id bonum, si modo vllum vnquam futurum est, constabit. Sic autem lego, χαὶ τῆς τὸ θεῖον τιμῶσι, χαὶ π. Aut me omnia fallunt, aut rem acu tetigimus, & quod Græci αἰῶτ, αὐτὸν κήρυκα τὸν βατῆρα τῆς Σύρας. Pietatis apud Græcos præcipua censebantur argumenta, si sacra patria diligenter colerent, & dona ad aliarum vrbium deos mitterent. Vide Isocratem in Areopagitica: vbi verbum τίμησιν sic accipi debet vt hoc loco.
units.tr: where [τὸ ἔχειν] is a showing-off [δεικτικὸς], as Donatus also explains. [And they honour and ... at the festivals.] There seems to be a sore underneath. The interpreters whom I have seen extricate themselves from this in a rather unworthy way. Clearly honour [τιμὰν] means collecting an offering. Oh, by the goddess! But to the point. The author notes that arrogance in a man implies contempt for the divine power and for all religion. For you will generally find that those who are proud toward men also grow insolent toward God and take little care to worship him; Theophrastus also indicates this with another mark at the end of the chapter. In the past, part of divine worship was to attend the solemn festivals of the gods and to celebrate them. So the more religious did not merely observe carefully the festivals of their own city, but also hurried with gifts to the solemn festivals of other cities, as Plato's Laws also teach. Although this could not be done without great expense, that did not deter them; they persuaded themselves, as in Plautus' Pseudolus, "Whatever you spend on divine matters is a gain for the wise." The arrogant man, on the contrary, laughs at their conduct; and because they hope for some good from the gods on that account, the wicked man wickedly laughs at this too and says it is not worth so much: "This good," he says, "will cost you dearly, if it ever comes at all." I read the passage thus: [and they honour the divine, and ...]. Either I am quite mistaken, or we have hit the mark; and the Greek [αἰῶτ, αὐτὸν κήρυκα τὸν βατῆρα τῆς Σύρας]. Among the Greeks, the chief marks of piety were considered to be the diligent cult of one's own country's rites and the sending of gifts to the gods of other cities. See Isocrates' Areopagiticus, where the word τίμησιν must be understood as it is here.

units.la: ια αν ἐν ἂν χρώϊς διδόμενα[?]. Sententia quam ex his verbis elicimus par & similis est illi, quam hostis humani generis pronuntiat Iobi capite primo, cōmate 1 x. hoc tantum interest,quòd hîc diuini numinis in homines religiosos benignitas extenuatur: ibi sancti viri Iobi,pietas in Deum. argumentum quidem geminum planè est.
units.tr: "...[the things given in the ...]." The sense we draw from these words is equal and similar to that which the enemy of the human race pronounces in Job, chapter one, verse ten. The only difference is that here the benevolence of the divine power toward religious men is belittled, whereas there it is the piety of the holy man Job toward God. The argument is indeed twofold.

units.la: καὶ ἐκ ἔχων συγγνώμην[?]. ) Seneca De beneficiis, libro v 1. Quid est iniquius homine, qui eum odit,à quo in turba calcatus, aut respersus, aut quò nollet impulsus est ?
units.tr: "And not having forgiveness [καὶ ἐκ ἔχων συγγνώμην]." Seneca, On Benefits, book five: "What is more unjust than a man who hates the one by whom he was trampled in a crowd, or splashed, or pushed against his will?"

units.la: φίλῳ ὁ ἔρανον κελεύοντι ἐπεντευξεῖν[?]. Adeon' interpretes alias res egisse cum hunc pulcherrimum libellum verterent, ut vocem ἔρανον semper de symbolis conuiuarum acciperent? Atqui,contra quàm illi putant nusquam ita Theophraftum hac voce in hoc Χαρακτηρισμῷ esse vsum affirmamus. vbi quoties dictio ἔρανος occurrit, semper referri debet ad pulcherrimum & verè pium Græcorum morem pauperes amicos subleuandi. Fuit enim apud illos moribus receptum, vt cum aduersam fortunam passus esset aliquis, amicorum atque sodalium facultatibus subleuaretur: accipiebat enim ab iis pecuniæ aliquam summam, ea lege vt si Deus aliquando meliora daret, quantum illi erogatum esset, tantundem ipse restitueret. Hanc illi stipem collatitiam vocabant ἔρανον, & factum ipsum ἐρανίζειν respectu vt plurimùm accipientis, vel ἔρανος συλλέγοντ[?]ς dantis vero, ἔρανος εἰσφορά. Atque hoc fuit veluti medium quoddam genus inter id quod δάνειον creditúmque proprie dicitur, & stipem illam quotidianam quæ mendicis hominibus & ærusca-toribus toribus sine vlla recuperandi spe erogabatur. Ἑλλη-μοσωλῶ[?] Graeci illam stipem, non ἔπαρον vocarunt: etsi me non latet abusiue eos interdum vocabulum ἔπαρ[?] ita vsurpare. Huius moris apud Graecos scriptores passim fit mentio: apud Antiphontem gloriatur quidam se pecuniis suis non nisi honeste uti λαμπρῶς, inquit, χορηγοῦντες, πολλὰς ἐρανίζοντα, μεγάλας ὑπὲρ πολλῶν ἐνδυσας ἀποτίνοντα[?]: & paullo ante oftendit idem conferri solitum eranum siquis sententia iudicis, omnibus bonis suis fuisset evolutus: ἐξηγούμενος ἢ, ait, καὶ ληφθεὶς, καὶ ἔπαρον ἐπὶ τὴν φίλων συλλέξας, ἐπ᾽ ἂν εἰς τὰ ἔργα καὶ ἠλθον[?]. eundem morem tangit & Demosthenes in Midiana. & ex eiusdem oratione in Nicostratum constat pro captiuis amicis solitum dari ab amicis ἔρανον, ut esset unde se redimerent. Extant etiam pulcherrimi Philemonis antiqui poetae versiculi, ubi posteaquam varios casus recensuit quibus homines ad paupertatem redigi solent, subiicit.
units.tr: "To the friend who orders a contribution to be made [φίλῳ ὁ ἔρανον κελεύοντι ἐπεντευξεῖν]." Did the translators have so little else to do, when rendering this most beautiful little book, that they always took the word ἔρανον to mean the shares of dinner-guests? Yet, contrary to what they think, I affirm that Theophrastus nowhere uses the word in this sense in this Character. Wherever the word ἔρανος occurs, it must always be referred to the most beautiful and truly pious Greek custom of helping poor friends. For among them it was the accepted custom that when someone had suffered misfortune, he was helped by the resources of his friends and companions: he received from them some sum of money, on the condition that if God ever gave him better things, he would himself repay as much as had been contributed to him. They called this collected gift a contribution [ἔρανον], and the act itself erananizing [ἐρανίζειν], with reference mostly to the recipient, or a collected contribution [ἔρανος συλλέγοντ], with reference to the giver, a contribution-payment [ἔρανος εἰσφορά]. This was a kind of middle thing between what is properly called a loan [δάνειον] and creditum, and that daily alms which was given to beggars and mendicants without any hope of recovery. The Greeks did not call that alms a contribution [ἔπαρον], though I am not unaware that they sometimes use the word ἔπαρ in this loose way. Mention of this custom is made everywhere in Greek writers: in Antiphon a man boasts that he uses his money only honourably, "lavishly [λαμπρῶς] providing for the public liturgies, collecting many contributions and paying back great sums on behalf of many." A little before, he shows that the same contribution was usually collected if someone had been stripped of all his goods by a judge's sentence: "for," he says, "I was led out and taken, and collecting a contribution from my friends, I went to the work." Demosthenes in the Midian Oration touches on the same custom, and from his speech against Nicostratus it is clear that contributions were customarily given by friends on behalf of captive friends, so that there was something with which they could ransom themselves. There also survive some very fine verses of the ancient poet Philemon, where, after listing the various misfortunes by which men are commonly reduced to poverty, he adds:

units.la: Ἀλλ᾽ ἑταῖροι καὶ φίλοι (οἵ, καὶ σωνῆσθαι ἐν Δία, / Ἔρανον εἰσενεγκεῖν. ἐγὼ μὴ λαβεῖν τείραν φίλων[?]
units.tr: But comrades and friends (who, if they were saved in Zeus's ... , / bring in an eranos). I would not take a contribution from friends. [Ἀλλ᾽ ἑταῖροι καὶ φίλοι]

units.la: Εἰ δ᾽ μὴ, γνώσῃ σεαυτὸν (forrasse melius, αὐτὲς) ἄλλο μηδὲν, πάλιν σταίδ[?].
units.tr: If not, you will know yourself (perhaps better, "themselves") as nothing else; again ...

units.la: Pertinet ad hunc morem locus Aristotelis Physicae acroaseos libro 1 1. capite v. vbi hoc ponit exemplum eorum quae κατὰ τύχην accidunt, οἷς, ἕνεκα τῆς ἀπολαβεῖν τὸ ἀργύριον ἠλθεν ἂν κομιζομένης τὸν ἔρανον, εἰ ἤδει. Torquent verba philosophi interpretes Latini, nec certam interpretationem, ac ne lectionem quidem veram vident: quam ex Philopono protulimus: Illa verba ἠλθεν ἂν κομιζομένης τὸν ἔρανον significant, veniisset creditor ad debitorem suum cum ille ab amicis eranum, hoc est, pecuniam erani nomine collectam, auferret. Eodem censeo referendum & Plauti locum in Curculione, vbi ait leno in magno fuisse fe periculo ne argetum amitteret quod sibi argentarius debebat: eum enim inibi fuisse, vt cessione bonorum creditoribus suis satisfaceret: verùm postea amicos iuuisse ipsum, & dedisse vnde soluerct. Sic ille,
units.tr: To this custom belongs the passage of Aristotle in the Physics, Book 2, chapter 5, where he gives this example of things that happen by chance: a man who went to collect money owed to him would have come to his debtor, if he had known that the debtor was receiving an eranos. The Latin interpreters twist the philosopher's words, and they see neither a certain interpretation nor even the true reading, which we have brought forward from Philoponus. The words [ἠλθεν ἂν κομιζομένης τὸν ἔρανον] mean: the creditor would have come to his debtor while the debtor was carrying off the eranos from his friends, that is, the money collected under the name of an eranos. I think the passage of Plautus in the Curculio should be referred to the same custom, where the pimp says he was in great danger of losing the money which he owed to the banker. For the banker had been there so that he might satisfy his creditors by a surrender of goods; but afterwards his friends helped him and gave him the means to pay. So he says:

units.la: Postquam nihil fit, clamore hominem posco:ille in iis me vocat:
units.tr: Since nothing is done, I call the man by shouting; he calls me in to those men.

units.la: Pessimè metui ne mihi hodie apud prætorem soluerets
units.tr: I was very much afraid I would have to pay the money to you today before the praetor.
But the friends contributed; he pays the money from the house.

units.la: Sic enim lego, non compulerunt: Porrò autem videntur ea fini & apud Athenienses & in aliis Graecorum ciuitatibus instituta sodalitates quae communem arcam haberent, in quam quot mensibus certum quid à singulis penderetur, vt esset vnde iuuari possent qui ex illa sodalitate fortunam aduersam aliquo modo essent experti. Harpocration, Ἐρανιστὴς μισθοῦ κυρίως ἐστὶν ὁ τῶν ἐράνων μετέχων, ὁ τὴν φορὰν ἣν ἕκαστος μηνὸς καταβάλλειν, εἰσφέρων. Hos ἐρανιστὰς orator ἐράνους ἁπλῶς vocat. nisi malis referre ad δημοσίας ἐράνος: nam & in Rempublicam collatae pecuniae genus quoddam est ἔρανος. cuius saepe oratores meminere. Quemadmodum autem pensio ἐράνου fuit menstrua, ita & singulis mensibus lites disceptabantur, si quae forte inter sodales propter ἐράνους discordiae essent obortae. Harpocration, ἐμψοι [?], inquit, appellantur δίκαι αἱ τε ἐμπορικαὶ & αἱ ἐρανικαὶ meminit & Pollux. Neque dubium sicut erant δίκαι ἐρανικαὶ Athenis ita & ἐρανικὸς fuisse νόμος. Quare etiam apud Platonem in x 1.De legib. de istiusmodi eranis accipienda lex hæc est, non, ut vulgò faciunt de conuiuarum collectis. Verba Platonis sunt, Ἐράνων [?] ἢ πέζὸν [?] τὸν βουλόμενον ἐρανίζειν, εἶναι [?] φίλοις. ἐὰν δὲ τις διαφορὰ γίγνηται περὶ τῆς ἐρανιστέως, ὅτω παράτλῳ ὡς δίκων μηδενὶ περὶ τούτων μηδα-μῶς ἐξομένων. Lex est perutilis: Statuit Plato ut eranum ab amico exigere necessario tempore, in sua Republica ius sit & fas. quod ideò non prætermittendum in suis legibus putauit ille, quia non in omnibus ciuitatibus permissæ sunt olim huiusmodi ἑταιρεία. Apud Romanos quidem nihil tale * factitatum obseruauimus: quin potius exi⁠stimo vetitas istas sodalitates fuisse à Romanis in plerisque Græcorum ciuitatibus, postquam ad illos summa rerum peruenit. quare etiam Plinius Secundus epistola quadam Traianum consulit super libello ad eranos pertinente, sibi ab Amisenorum ciuitate oblato. Traianus verò respondens Amisenis quidem permittit eranos habere: eo facilius, inquit, si tali collatione non ad turbas & illicitos coetus, sed ad sustinendam tenuiorum inopiam utuntur. in cæteris vero ciuitatibus quæ Romanorum iure essent obstrictæ, rem huiusmodi vult prohiberi. Addit Plato, Si qua ex ea collectione controuersia inter amicos oriatur, nullam datum iri in sua Republica actionem eo nomine. quod aliter Athenis ut dixi obseruabatur: erat enim ibi locus ταῖς ἐρανικαῖς δίκαις. Sanè quin tenerentur qui huiusmodi collatione fuerant subleuati, reddere quod acceperant reparatis opibus, non potest ambigi: id enim diserťis verbis testatur Theophrastus capite περὶ μεταμελοιείας. & apud Lucianum Demosthenes ait, se multis amicis τὰς ἐφάρες σωσδιγαλύσας : hoc est sodales multos pro sua virili parte iuuisse in reddendis pecuniis quas ab amicis acceperant. Ex his intelligi potest quid ἐφάρον cùm hîc tum alibi Theophrastus vocet. Latini, vt diximus, rem ignorarunt : neque propriam vllam vocem habent huic rei:nec temere factum quòd & Plinius & Traianus vocem Græcam retinuerunt. Collationem aut collectam vertere potes: etsi alio sensu Marcus Tullius hac dictione vsus est.Plura de hac re ad Athenæum nobis obseruata.
units.tr: For so I read it, not "compulerunt." Moreover, it seems that in Athens and in other Greek cities there were established associations with a common fund, into which a set sum was paid by each member every month, so that there would be something from which those members who had met with some misfortune could be helped. Harpocration: "An eranistes, strictly speaking, is one who takes part in an eranos, that is, one who pays in the contribution which each person pays every month" [Ἐρανιστὴς μισθοῦ κυρίως ἐστὶν ὁ τῶν ἐράνων μετέχων, ὁ τὴν φορὰν ἣν ἕκαστος μηνὸς καταβάλλειν, εἰσφέρων]. The orator calls these eranistai simply "eranoi," unless you prefer to refer it to public eranoi, for a public collection of money for the state was also a kind of eranos, of which the orators often speak. Just as the payment of an eranos was monthly, so disputes were also settled every month, if any quarrel happened to arise among the members on account of the eranoi. Harpocration says that suits are called "commercial" (ἐμπορικαί) and "eranic" (ἐρανικαί), and Pollux also mentions them. There is no doubt that just as there were eranic suits (δίκαι ἐρανικαί) at Athens, so there was also an eranic law (ἐρανικὸς νόμος). Hence also in Plato, Laws x, this law must be understood of eranoi of this kind, not, as people commonly do, of the contributions of diners. Plato's words are: "Whoever wishes to make an eranos among friends, let it be permitted to him. If any dispute arises about the eranos-collection, let no one bring a suit about these matters in any way" [Ἐράνων ... ἢ πέζὸν ... τὸν βουλόμενον ἐρανίζειν, εἶναι φίλοις. ἐὰν δὲ τις διαφορὰ γίγνηται περὶ τῆς ἐρανιστέως, ὅτω παράτλῳ ὡς δίκων μηδενὶ περὶ τούτων μηδαμῶς ἐξομένων]. The law is very useful: Plato lays down that a man may, in his own commonwealth, demand his eranos from a friend at a necessary time, and he thought this should not be passed over in his laws, because such associations [ἑταιρεία] were not everywhere permitted in former times. Among the Romans, indeed, we have observed that nothing of this kind was practised; rather, I think that such associations were forbidden by the Romans in most Greek cities after supreme power came into their hands. Hence also Pliny the Younger, in a certain letter, consults Trajan about a petition concerning eranoi, presented to him by the city of Amisus. Trajan, in reply to the Amisenes, indeed allows them to have eranoi: "the more readily," he says, "if they use such a collection not for riots and unlawful gatherings, but for the relief of the poverty of the humbler sort." In the other cities, however, which were bound by Roman law, he wishes a thing of this kind to be prohibited. Plato adds that if any controversy arises among friends from such a collection, no action will be given in his commonwealth on that account; this was otherwise observed at Athens, as I said, for there was a place for eranic suits [ταῖς ἐρανικαῖς δίκαις]. That those who had been relieved by such a collection were bound to return what they had received, once their resources were restored, cannot be doubted; for Theophrastus testifies to this in plain words in the chapter on regret (περὶ μεταμελείας). And in Lucian, Demosthenes says that he had released many friends from their debts [τὰς ἐφάρες σωσδιγαλύσας], that is, that he had helped many friends, to the extent of his own means, in repaying the money they had received from friends. From these things it can be understood what Theophrastus calls ephares here and elsewhere. The Latins, as we have said, were ignorant of the matter, and they have no proper word for it; nor is it by chance that both Pliny and Trajan kept the Greek word. You may render it collatio or collecta, although Marcus Tullius used this word in another sense. More on this matter we have noted on Athenaeus.

units.la: ὅτι ἀπόλλυτι καὶ τῷ τὸ ἀργύριον. ] Hæ sunt voces eorum qui beneficium dare nescıunt.quò alludens ait Sapiens auctor Ecclesiastici cap. xxxix. Ἀπόλεσον ἀργύριον δι᾽ φίλον. Præclarè & ad hunc locum appositissimè Seneca De beneficiis libro v i. Sape beneficium manet nec debetur,si secuta est dantem poenitentia: [si miserum se dixit, quod dedisset:si cum daret suspirauit, vultum obduxit, perdere se credidit,non donare. Hic est quem panem lapidosum Fabius Verrucosus appellabat. Quanto melius qui dixit,
units.tr: "For you lose the money too." These are the words of those who do not know how to give a benefit; alluding to this, the wise author of Ecclesiasticus says, chapter 39: "Lose money for a friend." Seneca also, in his De beneficiis book 6, says very well and most aptly to this passage: "Often a benefit remains and is not owed, if repentance has followed the giver. [If he said he was wretched because he had given; if he sighed while giving, drew a long face, believed he was losing and not giving.]" This is the stony bread which Fabius Verrucosus used to call it. How much better was he who said,
"Desire to be loved." Clearly it should be written Σευοί, not Σευόν.

units.la: ἐν ἀπομένειν. ] Melius ἀπομεῖναι. imò verò mutato accentu & ἀπομένειν & ἀπομεῖναι scribendum est.
units.tr: "to remain behind." Better ἀπομεῖναι. Indeed, with the accent changed, both ἀπομένειν and ἀπομεῖναι should be written.

units.la: καὶ ὅτε ἄσαι, ὅτε φήσειν εἰπεῖν, ὅτε ἀρχήσασθαι ἐν ὀρχεῖσθαι. ] Scribendum hic quoque mutato accentu ἐρχῆσθαι. est enim modus optandi, vt loquuntur γραμματικῶν παίδες, non infinitiuus. Hæc autem eò pertinent quòd sicut diximus, istiusmodi homines graues seuerique, non comes videri volunt: cum re vera non gravitas ea fit, sed simulatio, fastus ac typhus, & vt eleganter Hierocles vocat, νόθους μυθο-λογίας. Notum autem veteres Græcos solitos vsurpare in suis conuiuiis quæ hic commemorantur. Cantabant enim vel scolium aliquod, vel odam aliquam, siue μέλος, aut aliquem ex poëta quopiam locum. Sic etiam apud antiquissimos Romanos fuerunt carmina quædam in epulis à singulis conuiuis cantitata de clarorum virorum laudibus, vt in Originibus scriptum reliquerat Cato. Saltatio sequebatur comes extrema conuiuij mensis remotis: non enim nisi bene poti vt bis supra dictum est, saltabant. Interpretes quid esset φησὶν εἰσάγειν assecuti non sunt: est autem, locum ex aliquo poëta recitare oblectationis gratia & ὀρχηστῆς χάριν : Id veteres factitabant aliàs quidem assa voce, quod est ᾄδειν : aliàs vero ad tibiam, vel aliud musicum organum: quod ψάλλειν Græci dicunt. & cantabant interdum quidem omnes confertim: interdum vero singuli per vices: quod eleganter vocat Clemens ἐν μέρει ἀποδόσεις τῆς ᾠδῆς. Exempla proferre non magis necesse est, quàm meridie lucernam accendere. Tantum dicam peccari sæpe ab interpretibus in ista voce: vt cum apud Platonem in x. De republica μακρὰ φησὶν Ἀντιγόνην ἐν ταῖς ἀδυρμοῖς, vertunt, contenta voce simulari. perperam! Plato enim de iis poëtis loquitur, qui lamentationes prælongas & multorum versuum heroibus tribuunt in suis poëmatis: qualis illa apud Sophoclem vere μακρὰ φήμης in Trachinus, quales item multæ in tragœdiis Euripidis præsertim: qui poëta reus iampridem hæret apud criticorum tribunal διὰ τὸ μακρὰς ἐπάγειν φύσεις ἤγεν διηγήσεις τοὺς συμφωνίας. propterea etiam, vt videtur, τὰς τραγῳδὰς per ludibrium τεταγμένως appellarunt. Male etiam iidem interpretes in septimo De legibus τινὰς ὅλας φύσεις, hoc est, integros poëtarum locos transtulerunt, scitè quædam dicta.
units.tr: "and when they sing, when they say they will speak, when they begin to dance." Here too the accent should be changed, to ἐρχῆσθαι; for it is the optative mood, as the teachers of grammar say, not the infinitive. These things pertain to this point, that, as I said, such men wish to seem grave and severe, not sociable, when in truth that gravity is not real but a pretence, arrogance and pride; and, as Hierocles elegantly calls it, "bastard fables." It is well known that the ancient Greeks were accustomed to use at their banquets the things mentioned here. For they sang either some drinking song, or some ode, whether a melody, or some passage from a poet. So also among the most ancient Romans there were certain songs sung at feasts by each guest in praise of famous men, as Cato left written in his Origines. Dancing followed as the last entertainment of the table, when the dishes had been removed; for, as has been said twice above, they danced only when well drunk. The interpreters have not understood what φησὶν εἰσάγειν means: it is to recite a passage from some poet for pleasure and for the sake of the dancer. The ancients did this sometimes with the voice alone, which is ᾄδειν; at other times with the flute or another musical instrument, which the Greeks call ψάλλειν. And sometimes they all sang together, sometimes each in turn, which Clement elegantly calls "the alternate delivery of the song." It is no more necessary to bring forward examples than to light a lamp at midday. I will only say that the interpreters often err over this word: for example, where Plato in Republic book 10 says "Antigone in her lamentations is long," they translate it, "imitated with a sustained voice." Wrongly! For Plato is speaking of those poets who give long laments, and many verses, to heroes in their poems: such as the famous long lament in Sophocles' Trachiniae, and likewise many in the tragedies of Euripides especially, a poet who has long been on trial before the tribunal of critics because he introduced long speeches and tedious narratives. Perhaps for this reason, as it seems, they called the tragedies by way of mockery "arranged." The same interpreters also translated badly, in the seventh book of the Laws, "some whole natures", that is, whole passages of poets, as "certain things said neatly."

units.la: A[?] Μίλες ἡ δεισιδαιμονία δέξειν τῇ δειλία πρὸς τὸ δαιμόνιον.] Alij sic definiunt, Δεισιδαιμονία ἐστὶ φόβος θεῶν καὶ δαιμόνων. Sed Theophrastus voce δαιμόνιον, & deos & dæmones complexus est, & quicquid diuinitatis esse particeps male sana putauit antiquitas. Δειλίαν accipe metum alium ab eo qui pios decet. Scitè enim Varro apud Augustinū dicebat, Deum à religioso vereri: à superstitioso timeri. Seneca dilutius epistola xlvii. Deo satis est quòd colitur, & amatur: Non potest amor cum timore misceri, Melius idem alibi, Religio deos colit: superstitio violat. Latius veteres, vt annotant Grammatici, metum pro religione, vel superstitione vsurparunt. Vide Nonium. Maximus Tyrius sermone iiii. pietatem à superstitione sic distinguit: εἰ δέ ἐστι, & ἀνθρώπου πρὸς θεὸν ὑπομιξία, ὁ μὲν ἀ σεβὴς φιλῶν θεῶν, ὁ δὲ δεισιδαίμων κόλαξ.
units.tr: Superstition is a cowardice before the divine [Μίλες ἡ δεισιδαιμονία δέξειν τῇ δειλία πρὸς τὸ δαιμόνιον]. Others define it thus: superstition is the fear of gods and demons [Δεισιδαιμονία ἐστὶ φόβος θεῶν καὶ δαιμόνων]. But Theophrastus, by the word daimonion, comprehends both gods and demons, and whatever else antiquity foolishly thought partook of divinity. Understand cowardice as a fear other than the kind that befits the pious. Varro, as Augustine reports, neatly said that God is revered by the religious man and feared by the superstitious. Seneca puts it more gently in Epistle 47: "It is enough for God that he is worshipped and loved; love cannot be mixed with fear." Elsewhere he puts it better: "Religion worships the gods; superstition violates them." The older writers, as the grammarians note, used the word fear more broadly for either religion or superstition. See Nonius. Maximus of Tyre, in discourse 4, distinguishes piety from superstition in this way: if there is any intercourse between man and God, the pious man loves the gods, but the superstitious man is a flatterer [ὁ μὲν εὐσεβὴς φιλῶν θεόν, ὁ δὲ δεισιδαίμων κόλαξ].

units.la: [?] ἀπονιψάμενος τὰς χεῖρας ἢ περιῤῥαντήριος ὑπὸ ἱερῶ.) Duplicem lauationem siue purificationem tangit: altera ad manus pertinet, altera ad totum corpus. Illa proprie χέρνιβ, hæc περιῤῥαντήρια[?] appellatur, fieri batque θαλλῶ, id est ramo felicis oliuæ, vt ait Virgilius. Vtriusque frequens apud Græcos mentio. Aqua vero lustralis qua aspergebantur, sic fiebat. Erat ad fores templi aquiminale quoddam magnum, quales ferè tinctorum cortinæ, (labrum Asconius nominat) in quod mergebant titionem ardentem ab ara sumtum, quando victima adoletur: eáque aqua omnes qui templum ingrediebantur sese aspergebant ipsi, aut à sacrificulis aspergebantur. Euripides Hercule furente:
units.tr: Having washed his hands, or having been sprinkled at the temple [ἀπονιψάμενος τὰς χεῖρας ἢ περιῤῥαντήριος ὑπὸ ἱερῶ]. He touches on a double washing or purification: one applies to the hands, the other to the whole body. The first is properly called chernips [χέρνιψ], the second perirrhanteria [περιῤῥαντήρια]. It was done with a thallos [θαλλός], that is, a branch of the fruitful olive, as Virgil says. Both are frequently mentioned among the Greeks. The lustral water with which they were sprinkled was prepared as follows. At the doors of the temple stood a large basin, much like the vats of dyers (Asconius calls it a labrum). Into this they dipped a burning brand taken from the altar when the victim was burned. With this water everyone entering the temple sprinkled himself, or was sprinkled by the attendant priests. Euripides, in the Hercules Furens:

units.la: Μέλλω δ' ἁλαδ' [illegible, ~14 letters] Εἰς χέρνιβ' ὡς βαλεῖν[?] Ἀλκμήνης γόνῳ.
units.tr: And I am about to throw salt [...] into the lustral water for the son of Alcmene [Μέλλω δ' ἁλαδ' [...] Εἰς χέρνιβ' ὡς βαλεῖν Ἀλκμήνης γόνῳ].

units.la: Athenæus quid sit, χέρνιψ, (vel vt ipse legi ait, χερνιβ) explicans, Ἐστιν, inquit, ὕδωρ εἰς ὃ ἀπέβαλον[?] ἐκ τῶν βωμῶν λαμβάνοντες[?], ἐφ' ᾧ τὴν θυσίαν ἐπετέλεσαν[?]. Nec solum in templis erat, περιῤῥαντήρια; sed etiam ad fores introitum, quorum sæpe meminerunt oratores Græci. Moris etiam fuit vt ad fores priuatarum ædium tantisper dum illæ funestæ essent, & dum fieret ἡ ἀρίζοης[?] eius quod[?] obierat, vas magnum statueretur, aqua lustrali plenum, quæ esset è domo non funesta allata: qua aqua sese quisque exiens aspergeret, qui exequias venerat. Idque vas siglinum fuit, & ἀρδάλου[?] proprie nuncupabatur: auctor Pollux libro octauo. Aristophani dicitur ὀσπακον[?]. Καὶ παράδη[?] τὸ σπακον[?] πρὸ τῆς θύρας. Hesychio ἴσφαξ[?] duobus locis. Non dissimilis ritus apud Romanos. Festus, funus prosecuti redeuntes ignem supergrediebantur aqua aspersi: quod purgationis genus vocabant suffitionem. Fuit & apud Iudæos similium lauationum & purificationum vsus: quas auctor Ecclefiaftici capite xxxiv. βασιλικὸς ἀπὸ νεκρῶν appellat.
units.tr: Athenaeus, explaining what a chernips [χέρνιψ] (or, as he himself says it should be read, chernib [χερνιβ]) is, says: "It is water into which they threw things taken from the altars, and over which they performed the sacrifice" [Ἐστιν ὕδωρ εἰς ὃ ἀπέβαλον ἐκ τῶν βωμῶν λαμβάνοντες, ἐφ' ᾧ τὴν θυσίαν ἐπετέλεσαν]. The perirrhanteria were not only in temples but also at the doorways of entrances, which the Greek orators often mention. There was also a custom that, at the doors of private houses while they remained in mourning, and while the funeral of the deceased was being prepared, a large vessel full of lustral water was set up. This water was brought from a house not in mourning, and everyone who had come to the funeral sprinkled himself with it as he left. The vessel was made of clay and was properly called ardalos [ἀρδάλος]; Pollux mentions it in book 8. In Aristophanes it is called ospakon [ὀσπακον], and the sprig is put before the door. Hesychius mentions isphax [ἴσφαξ] in two places. A similar rite existed among the Romans. Festus says that those returning from a funeral procession stepped over a fire after being sprinkled with water, and this kind of purification they called suffitio. Among the Jews too there was a similar use of washings and purifications, which the author of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 34, calls washing from the dead [ἀπὸ νεκρῶν].

units.la: Δάφνης εἰς τὸ στόμα λαβὼν.) Non leuis error est interpretum, qui ἀπὸ ἱερᾶς Δάφνης iunxerunt, & sacram laurum hic sunt commenti: quod profectò ferri non poterat. Dictum autem Δάφνης λαβὼν, vt ἄρτος φαγεῖν, & alia passim apud Atticos. Nos locum planius expressimus, & ita vertimus quasi esset scriptum Δάφνης στέφανα: eam enim vocem supplendam esse censemus. Scimus namque veteres in purgationibus, lauri foliis vti solitos. Clemens Alexandrinus in Protreptico, Καθαρσίων μεταλαμβάνε[?] Θεοσεβ[?]ῶν, ἡ Δάφνης στεφάνων, ἡ ταινιῶν τινῶν ἐλαίῳ [?] ἐξ ... πορφύρα[?] Τεπ[?]ικλα[?]ιων. Sic & Romani, vt ait Festus omnibus suffitionibus laurum adhibebant. Moris praeterea fuit Graecis baculum laureum prae manibus habere, tanquam ἀλεξίκακον φάρμακον, vt ait Suidas, quòd crederent lauro inesse vim quandam malum auerruncandi. Inde natum proverbium Δάφνη φυγῶν βακτηρίαν, cum quis negat se sibi ab alicuius insidiis metuere. Eodem etiam spectat quod obseruare aliquando meminimus, solitos Graecos pro foribus laurum statuere. auctor Hesychius in voce Κώμυνθα[?]. Quod ait Theophrastus laurum in os capi solitam à superstitiosis, nescio an huic similis superstitio sit quàm apud Hieronymum in Marcellae viduae epitaphio annotauimus. Sic ille, Nec mirum si in plateis & in foro rerum vcnalium fictus ariolus flultorum verberet nates & obtorto siste dentes mordentium quatiat. Nam ariolorum consuetudo fuit (colligi potest ex Seneca De vita beata) aurum gestare cum per vrbem incederent, quam fustem videtur Hieronymus vocare quia erat, credo, virga laurea. Hesychius, ἰδωτήεαν, ὁ φέρουσιν οἱ μάνλεις σιωπῶντες ἀπὸ δλάφης [?]. Sanè poëtæ dicuntur laurum mordere Iuuenali, & Cassandra ἀλεξιφράκη [?] à Lycophrone appellatur: quod quomodo critici explicêt non est obscurum.
units.tr: Taking laurel into his mouth [Δάφνης εἰς τὸ στόμα λαβὼν]. It is no slight error of the translators who joined from sacred laurel [ἀπὸ ἱερᾶς Δάφνης] and invented a sacred laurel here, which indeed could not be allowed. The phrase taking laurel [Δάφνης λαβὼν] is used like eating bread [ἄρτος φαγεῖν] and other expressions found everywhere among the Attic writers. We have expressed the sense more plainly, and translated as if it were written laurel wreaths [Δάφνης στέφανα], for we think that word must be supplied. We know that the ancients habitually used laurel leaves in purifications. Clement of Alexandria, in the Protrepticus, says that those who partake in the purifications of the pious use laurel wreaths or certain ribbons. Likewise the Romans, as Festus says, used laurel in every suffumigation. It was also the custom among the Greeks to carry a laurel staff in their hands as a remedy against evil (alexikakon pharmakon), as Suidas says, because they believed laurel had some power of averting harm. Hence the proverb Laurel, flee the staff [Δάφνη φυγῶν βακτηρίαν], used when someone denies that he fears another's plots. To the same point belongs what I remember observing at times, that the Greeks used to set laurel before their doors (Hesychius, under the word κώμυνθα, is the authority). As for Theophrastus' statement that the superstitious customarily put laurel into their mouths, I do not know whether this is like the superstition I noted in Jerome's epitaph for the widow Marcella: "Nor is it surprising if in the streets and in the forum a fake soothsayer beats the buttocks of fools and shakes the teeth of those who bite him with a twisted staff." For the custom of soothsayers, as can be gathered from Seneca's De vita beata, was to carry laurel when they walked through the city. Jerome seems to call it a cudgel because it was, I believe, a laurel rod. Hesychius glosses a word for what the seers carry in silence, made of laurel. Indeed, poets are said to bite laurel in Juvenal, and Cassandra is called alexiphrakē [ἀλεξιφράκη] by Lycophron; how the critics explain this is not obscure.

units.la: χαὶ τὸ ὀδὸν ἐαν ἀλεξιφράμη [?] γαλῆ. ) Fortasse ἀλεξιφράμη [?]. Ambigunt docti sitne γαλῆ mustela domestica an felis. Utrumque animal fuit olim inter ea quæ occursu suo auspicium facerent, quod Græci vocabant ἐνόδιον σύμβολον. De mustela habes apud Plautum in Sticho: de fele extat exemplum apud Terentium. Apud Athenienses autem γαλῆς transcursus dirimebat comitia, vt apparet ex Aristophanis Concionantibus. Artemidorus verò libro tertio, siue Ἐνοδίῳ non parum differre docet, fucritne γαλῆ visa accedens, an abiens: item agens aliquid gratum an contra: necnon, agerétne an pateretur.
units.tr: And if a weasel crosses the road [καὶ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐὰν ... γαλῆ]. Perhaps the word should be read as alexipharmakos [ἀλεξιφάρμακος]. Scholars dispute whether gale [γαλῆ] means the domestic weasel or the cat. Both animals were once among those whose meeting with a person made an omen, which the Greeks called enodion symbolon [ἐνόδιον σύμβολον]. You have the weasel in Plautus' Stichus; the cat appears in Terence. Among the Athenians, however, the crossing of a weasel broke up assemblies, as appears from Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae. Artemidorus, in his third book (or in his work On Roadside Omens [Ἐνόδιος]), teaches that it makes no small difference whether the weasel was seen coming toward one or going away, whether the person was doing something pleasant or the reverse, and whether he was acting or being acted upon.

units.la: Et quòd γαλῆ malum augurium faceret, inter alias hanc quoque caussam affert, quia fit voci ἴσο-ψηφῶ [?]. quod ita est: nam si vtriusque dictionis litteras ad calculum voces, redibit par summa x i ii. id autem est quod Græci intelligunt, cùm dicunt duo vocabula, aut duos versus esse ἰσόψηφα. Sed quid vetat ipsius Artemidori verba ascribere? Γαλῆ, inquit, γυναῖκα σημαίνει πανοῦργον ἢ κακόγεωνον, ἢ δίκλω. ἔσι γὰρ ἰσόψηφον δίκῃ ἢ γαλῆ. Διὰ γὰρ τῆς αὐτῆς συγκειτα γραμμάτων. ἢ Θάνατον, ὁ, τι γὰρ ἂν λαβῇ τὸς σίτει. ἢ ἐργασίας ἢ ὠφελείας. καλεῖται γὰρ πρός τινων κερδῶ, ἢ ἰλαεία. τὸ δ᾽ ἑτέρας ἔξεσι λαμβάνειν τούτων ἀπὸ τῆς βλέπεσθαι προσῆς ἢ ἀπωτίσθαι. παράτλησάν τι ἡδύ, ἢ ἀνδές. πάσχοντάν τι ἢ ἀρῶσαν. Ex his apparet γαλῆς conspectum non malum semper portendisse, sed aliquando etiam lucrum, aliquando gaudium ac lætitiam. Quid quod etiam purgandi vim quandam in hoc animali inesse crediderunt Athenienses ? qui propterea quando in concionem conueniebant circumferri felem iubebant: etatque[?] hoc purificationis & lustrationis certum genus. Aristophanes Concionantibus, ὁ ἀπεξιαρχὸς[?] ἀπεφιλὴν[?] τῷ γαλῷ[?]. Erat & canis interuentus, siue potius transcursus (Plutarchus Δεισιδαιμονίαν[?] vocat, Περὶ φιλαλήθειας[?]) inauspicatus: unde est apud Plautum, canina scæna.
units.tr: And because the weasel makes a bad omen, he gives among other reasons this one too: it is isopsephos [ἰσόψηφος] with another word. And this is so: for if you count up the letters of both words, the sums come out equal, and this is what the Greeks mean when they say that two words or two verses are isopsephoi. But why should I not quote Artemidorus' own words? "A weasel signifies a crafty or ill-natured woman, or a lawsuit (dikē), for gale is isopsephos with dikē, since both are composed of the same letters; or death, for it takes whatever it seizes; or work or profit, for by some it is called kerdo [κερδώ], gain. To take one of these things from seeing it approach or depart; to suffer something pleasant or the reverse; to act or to be acted upon." From these examples it appears that the sight of a weasel did not always portend evil, but sometimes also gain, and sometimes joy and gladness. Moreover, did the Athenians believe that this animal had some purifying power? That is why, when they came together in assembly, they ordered a cat to be carried around, a certain kind of purification and lustration. Aristophanes, in the Ecclesiazusae: "the herald [...] kissed the cat." There was also the crossing, or rather the passing, of a dog, regarded as inauspicious (Plutarch calls it a superstition in his work on the love of truth). Hence in Plautus we have canina scaena, the dog's scene.

units.la: ὡς ἀπεξιάθη τις.] Qui videlicet omen iuvat, & quod mali portendebat felis transcursus, id ipse iubeat.
units.tr: As someone went out [ὡς ἀπεξιάθη τις]. That is, he who helps the omen himself orders what the crossing of the cat portended as evil.

units.la: ἡ λίθος[?] ἀθεὰς[?] ὑπὲρ τῆς ἰδίας σφαλάσθη[?]. ] Ridere licet veterum stultitiam. Putarunt illi cum aliquod triste signum apparuisset, posse id facile eludi, & quod ostendebatur periculum effugi, si vel verbis, vel aliquo facto indicarent se omen non accipere, sed abominari. Verbis quidem, cum dicerent, Εἰς καλὸν[?] Gr. quæ abominandi formula frequens est apud utriusque linguæ scriptores. vnius Senecæ verba ponam ex consolatione ad Martiam: Quam non, si admoneatur ut de suis cogitet, tanquam dirum omen respuat, & in capita suinicorum[?] aut ipsius intempestiui monitoris abire illa iubeat? Re vero, aut facto aliquo detestabatur, id quod portendebat sinistrum aliquid infestantes. Cum enim vel avis inebra, vel aliud infaustum animal occurrisset, periculo se defunctos putabant, si id lapidibus periissent, & seruissent[?]. Augustinus libro 11. De doctrina Christiana, Plerunque tam superstitiosi sunt quidam, ut etiam canem qui medius interuenerit strire[?] audeant.
units.tr: To throw a stone for one's own safety [ἡ λίθος ἀθεὰς ὑπὲρ τῆς ἰδίας σφαλάσθη]. One may laugh at the foolishness of the ancients. They thought that when some dire sign had appeared, it could easily be evaded, and the danger that was threatened could be escaped if they indicated, either by words or by some deed, that they did not accept the omen but abhorred it. By words, indeed, when they said for good [Εἰς καλὸν]; this formula of abhorrence is common among writers in both languages. I will quote Seneca's words alone, from the Consolation to Marcia: "Who, if reminded to think of her own, does not spit at it as a dire omen, and bid those things go to the heads of the swine or of the ill-timed adviser himself?" By deed, they detested with some action what foreshadowed something sinister, and threatened it. For when a raven or some other unlucky animal had crossed their path, they believed they had escaped the danger if they had pelted it with stones and driven it off. Augustine, in book 2 of On Christian Doctrine: "Indeed, some people are so superstitious that they dare to beat a dog that has come between them."

units.la: Planissimè verò Dio Chrysostomus, oratione xxxiv. Ἀνὴρ Φρὺξ, inquit, ὅτι λίνυς[?] ἐξεδήξεν[?]· ὡς δὴ ἐπεδάτο τινα κορώνην[?], σιωνιτάμων[?] (οἱ γὰρ φρίς[?] τὰ ζῶντα δεινοὶ) λίθῳ βάλλει καὶ πως τυγχάνει αὐτῆς[?]· ἤδη, νομίζας εἰς ἐκείνην τετράφθαι τὸ χαλκόν[?].
units.tr: Dio Chrysostom, in his thirty-fourth oration, is quite plain on this: "A Phrygian man," he says, "when a weasel bit him, as though he had trodden on some crow (for the Phrygians are clever at handling living creatures), struck it with a stone and somehow hit it, and thought the bronze had turned toward that one." [Ἀνὴρ Φρὺξ, inquit, ὅτι λίνυς ἐξεδήξεν· ὡς δὴ ἐπεδάτο τινα κορώνην, σιωνιτάμων (οἱ γὰρ φρίς τὰ ζῶντα δεινοὶ) λίθῳ βάλλει καὶ πως τυγχάνει αὐτῆς· ἤδη, νομίζας εἰς ἐκείνην τετράφθαι τὸ χαλκόν.]

units.la: Hinc mos ille veterum notatus Apuleio Milesia tertia. Quid? (ait) quòd istas nocturnas anus cum penetrauerint larem quempiam, sollicitè prehensas foribus videmus adfigi: vt quod infaustis volatibus familiæ minantur exitium, luant cruciatibus. atque hoc scimus hodiéque à quibusdam obseruari. Simili igitur ratione iste quoque conspecta fele, tres lapides in ipsam iacit: vt nimirum quod malum videbatur portendi, id in ipsius felis caput reiicere se hoc facto testaretur. Nam vt Plinius ait, ostentorum vires in eorum erant potestate quibus ostendebantur: ac prout quæque essent accepta, ita valere illa arbitrabantur. Sic etiam oracula & vaticinationes eludi solitas legimus, cum apud alios historicos vtriusque linguæ persæpe, tum apud Suetonium in Lulio, capite lxix[?]. Ex his, & vera lectio istius loci intelligitur: (legendum enim ἰδεάλλη[?], non ἰδεάλζη[?]:) & verus etiam sensus perspicitur: à quo quantum docti viri deerrarint, nolo dicere: æquus lector facile æstimabit, & iudicabit. Ait autem τρὶς[?]: quia vt ex Plinio, Festo, aliisque notum, numerus impar Deo gratior. quare etiam in illis ἐπῳδαῖς[?], φυλακτηρίοις[?], & amuletis quibus suos libros. Marcellus & Alexander Trallianus, ipséque adeo Plinius referserunt, frequens is numerus. Porrò videntur Græci ad hanc similémue aliam trium lapidum superstitionem allusisse illo prouerbio, τρεῖς εἶσιν ἱκα-νοὶ πρὸς τὸν ἐκμάττειν λίθοι. qua adagione vsus Aristophanes: nec me fugit quomodo exponatur à veteribus: verùm ego arbitror olim fuisse aliter conceptum prouerbium: postea verò quæsita, vt fit, occasione ioci, ita coepisse efferri ab hominib. vrbanis. Ἐκμάττειν verbum esse huic rei accommodatissimum infra docemus. Notauimus & aliam in tribus lapidibus superstitionem veterum non minus ridendam. Columella libro De arboribus, capite xxiii. Mala Punica ne rumpantur in arbore remedio sunt lapides tres, si cum seres arborem, ad rądicem ipsam collocaueris. Simile est quod de scilla idem auctor adiicit. Palladius libro quarto, titulo x. Qui in scrobe deponit, si tres lapillos in ipsa radice constituat, prosidebit ne poma findantur. Ne illud quidem prætermittam τῆς φιλομμάτων χάεων. Olim si duos fratres simul ambulantes lapis saxúmve in via forte iacens diuisisset, ita vt medius inter fratres lapis reperiretur, ominosum id & infaustum habebatur. Refert Plutarchus Περὶ φιλαδελφίας.
units.tr: This custom of the ancients is noted by Apuleius in the third book of the Milesian Tales: "What of this? When those night-hags have entered some household, do we not see them, when they are caught, nailed anxiously to the doors, so that they pay with torments for the ruin they threaten to the household by their ill-omened flights? And we know that this is observed even today by some people." In the same way, then, that man, when he had seen the cat, threw three stones at it, so that by this act he would show that the evil which seemed to be portended was turned back upon the cat's own head. For, as Pliny says, the force of portents lay in the power of those to whom they were shown, and whatever each man took them to be, that was how they were thought to have effect. So too we read that oracles and prophecies were commonly mocked, both among other historians of either language, very often, and in Suetonius, in the Life of Julius, chapter 69. From these things the true reading of this passage is also understood (for one should read [ἰδεάλλη], not [ἰδεάλζη]), and its true sense is seen too. How far learned men have strayed from this I do not wish to say; a fair reader will easily judge and decide. He says [τρὶς], "three times," because, as is known from Pliny, Festus and others, an odd number is more pleasing to God. Hence also in those charms [ἐπῳδαῖς], protective amulets [φυλακτηρίοις] and amulets with which Marcellus, Alexander of Tralles and Pliny himself have recorded their books, this number is frequent. Moreover, the Greeks seem to have alluded to this superstition of three stones, or one like it, in that proverb: "There are three stones enough for rubbing out" [τρεῖς εἶσιν ἱκανοὶ πρὸς τὸν ἐκμάττειν λίθοι]. Aristophanes used this saying, and I am not unaware how the ancients explain it; but I think the proverb was once conceived differently, and afterwards, as happens, it was taken up on an occasion of jest and so began to be put about by witty people. That [ἐκμάττειν] is a word most suited to this matter, we show further on. We have also noted another superstition about three stones among the ancients, no less ridiculous. Columella, in his book On Trees, chapter 23: "Pomegranates will not split on the tree if you place three stones at the root itself when you plant the tree." Similar is what the same author adds about the squill. Palladius, book 4, title 10: "Whoever plants in a pit, if he places three little stones at the very root, will ensure that the fruit does not split." I will not omit this either, the [τῆς φιλομμάτων χάεων]: formerly, if a stone or rock lying by chance in the road had divided two brothers walking together, so that the stone was found in the middle between them, this was considered ominous and ill-omened. Plutarch relates it in his [Περὶ φιλαδελφίας].

units.la: καὶ ἐὰν ἴδῃ ἐν Θολῷ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ, ἱερὸν ἐπιφοράς.] Mendosam perspicuè lectionem docti viri sanant ὄψιν legentes, non Θολῷ: & afferunt appositè sanè locum Platonis è decimo De legibus. Mihi tamen placebat ὄψιν pro Θολῷ restitui: cuius coniecturæ nondum me pœnitet: atque adeo haud aliter à Theophrasto scriptum puto: qui cum paullò post ἐνυπνίων meminerit, vix est vt hic ὀλίγως mentionem fecerit. Non quò fugiat me ὄψιν & ἐνύπνιον subtiliter à veteribus criticis distingui: sed illam distinctionem nemo sanus hîc recipiet. Constat verò ex Ciceronis libris De diuinatione & multis aliis auctoribus, serpentem vidisse in aedibus aut in itinere, triste auspicium fuisse. Solebant autem loci in quibus monstra fuerant visa, religiosa fieri: ut in eo loco qui fulmine tactus esset observabant: quem locum Romani, ut notum est, bidental, quòd bidentibus ibi fieret, appellabant. notus est super hoc Artemidori locus: sed & Plutarchus in Pyrrho ait τὰ καταβαλλόμενα τῆς ἱερουροῖς ἀνέμβαλε μένσῃ χωρία[?]. Idem puto fuisse observatum in aliis locis ubi portenta visa fuissent. Hinc illa Platonis querela de superstitiosis hominibus, mulieribusque praesertim, quas ait levissimas ob causas, & pavores inanes, impelli solitas, ut aras & sacella diis statuerent: iam, inquit Plato, nullus locus iis vacet, nō domus ulla, nō vicus. Porrò serpentes fere per impluuiū è tectis descendebant in aedes, & ibi soliti conspici. Plautus Amphitruone, Devolant anguis subita deorsum in impluuium duo. Terentius Phormione, Anguis per impluuium decidit de tegulis. Vide Alexandrinum Clementem, Theodoretum in Θεραπ[?]. & Dionem. Eo igitur loco (non autem ubi videntur insomnia) ait auctor, sacella à sui temporis superstitiosis hominibus solita excitari. Iure Romano id non erat licitum: Fuit enim lex vetus tribunitia, quae vetaret iniussu plebis aedes, terram, aram consecrare. Auctor Cicero Pro domo sua ad pontifices.
units.tr: [καὶ ἐὰν ἴδῃ ἐν Θολῷ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ, ἱερὸν ἐπιφοράς.] Learned men clearly correct the faulty reading by reading [ὄψιν] instead of [Θολῷ], and they cite quite aptly a passage of Plato from the tenth book of the Laws. Yet I have been pleased to restore [ὄψιν] in place of [Θολῷ], and I do not yet regret this conjecture; I think Theophrastus wrote it no differently, for since he mentions [ἐνυπνίων] a little later, it is hardly likely that he would have mentioned it here in passing. Not that I am unaware that [ὄψιν] and [ἐνύπνιον] were subtly distinguished by the ancient critics, but no sensible person will accept that distinction here. It is clear, however, from Cicero's books On Divination and from many other authors, that seeing a serpent in the house or on the road was an ominous omen. Places where portents had been seen were regularly made sacred: as they observed in a place struck by lightning; this place the Romans, as is well known, called a bidental, because a sacrifice of two-year-old sheep [bidentibus] was made there. The passage of Artemidorus on this is well known, but Plutarch in the Life of Pyrrhus also says [τὰ καταβαλλόμενα τῆς ἱερουροῖς ἀνέμβαλε μένσῃ χωρία]. I think the same was observed in other places where portents had been seen. Hence comes Plato's complaint about superstitious men, and women especially, whom he says are customarily driven by the slightest causes and empty fears to set up altars and little shrines to the gods: "Now, says Plato, no place is free of them, no house, no village." Moreover, serpents commonly came down from the roofs into the house through the gutter, and were usually seen there. Plautus in the Amphitryon: "Two snakes suddenly drop down into the gutter from above." Terence in the Phormio: "A snake fell through the gutter from the tiles." See Clement of Alexandria, Theodoret in [Θεραπ] and Dio. So at this point (not where dreams are mentioned) the author says that shrines were customarily set up by superstitious men of his own time. By Roman law this was not permitted: for there was an old tribunician law forbidding anyone to consecrate a house, ground or altar without the order of the plebs. Cicero is the authority, in his speech Concerning His House, addressed to the pontiffs.

units.la: τῆς λιθαρῶν λίθων τῆς ἐν ταῖς ἀγειόδοις[?]. Legimus ἡγειόδοις[?], vel παρόδοις[?]: ut de iis lapidibus intelligamus qui in viis à viatoribus coli solebant: de iis Sibylla. Κὰν παρόδοισιν λίθων συγχώματα ταῦτα σύσθε[?], sed praestat legere τρίεδοις[?]: Nam aliud sunt ἑρμαικες[?], de quibus Sibylla sine dubio intelligit, ab vnctis lapidibus, qui in proverbium abierunt. Dicebant enim de homine superstitioso πάντα λίθον λιθαρβὸν ὑποσκυνεῖ[?]. Clemens Alexandrinus libro septimo Stromatum, οἱ αὐτοὶ ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνου ἐν ἀπολυτῷ λίθον, τὸ δὲ λεγόμενον, λιθαρὸν προσκυνοῦντες[?]. Meminit & Apuleius initio Floridorum, cuius locum apponam, quia insignis est: multa enim similia superstitionis exempla velut uno fasce completur. Neque enim iustius religiosam moram viatori obiecerit, aut ara floribus redimita, aut spelunca frondibus inumbrata, aut quercus cornibus onerata, aut fagus pellibus coronata, vel etiam colliculus spirmine consecratus, vel truncus domine effigiatus, vel cespes libamine humigatus, vel lapis unguine delibutus. Sed & alii multi unctorum lapidum meminere, quod pridem Turnebus in Aducersariis obseruauit. Quid quod etiam in sacra historia simile quid obseruauimus nos? Vide Genesios cap. vigesimum octauum, commate xviii. & caput xxxv. com. xiii.
units.tr: [τῆς λιθαρῶν λίθων τῆς ἐν ταῖς ἀγειόδοις.] We read [ἡγειόδοις] or [παρόδοις], so that we understand those stones which travellers used to worship on the roads; the Sibyl speaks of these: [Κὰν παρόδοισιν λίθων συγχώματα ταῦτα σύσθε], but it is better to read [τρίεδοις], for [ἑρμαικες] are something else, and the Sibyl undoubtedly means them, from anointed stones, which passed into a proverb. For they used to say of a superstitious man that he worships every stone [πάντα λίθον λιθαρβὸν ὑποσκυνεῖ]. Clement of Alexandria, in book seven of the Stromata: [οἱ αὐτοὶ ἀπ᾽ ἐκείνου ἐν ἀπολυτῷ λίθον, τὸ δὲ λεγόμενον, λιθαρὸν προσκυνοῦντες]. Apuleius also mentions it at the beginning of the Floridas, and I will set out his passage, because it is striking; for it fills out, as it were in a single bundle, many similar examples of superstition: "For no one could more justly object to a traveller a religious delay, whether an altar wreathed with flowers, or a cave shaded with leaves, or an oak loaded with horns, or a beech crowned with skins, or even a little hill consecrated with a sprinkling, or a tree trunk shaped into a likeness of a god, or a turf moistened with an offering of libation, or a stone anointed with oil." But many others too have mentioned anointed stones, as Turnebus observed long ago in his Adversaria. And what of the fact that we ourselves have observed something similar in sacred history? See Genesis chapter 28, verse 18, and chapter 35, verse 13.

units.la: καὶ ἐὰν μῦς Θύλακον ἀλφίτων ἀφέγη[?]. ] Etiam mures olim auspicium faciebant. Ausonius;
units.tr: [καὶ ἐὰν μῦς Θύλακον ἀλφίτων ἀφέγη.] And if a mouse gnaws through a sack of barley meal. Mice too once made auspices. Ausonius:
"What four-footed creature is joined to the auspices of the birds? The mouse."

units.la: Inprimis autem triste putabant, si quid mures arrosissent. Vide Ciceronem De diuinatione libro secundo. Plinius quoque libro octauo, capite lvii. idem annotat: addens, eos cum candidi prouenere lactum facere ostentum. Idem in soricibus obseruabatur: quorum occentu dirimi auspicia ibidem ait Plinius. Eleganter vero Augustinus De doctrina Christiana, libro 11. de superstitiosis loquens: Hinc sunt, ait, illa: cum vestis a soricibus roditur, plus timere suspicionem futuri mali, quàm præsens damnum dolere. Unde illud eleganter dictum est Catonis, qui cum esset consultus à quodam, qui sibi à soricibus erosas caligas diceret, respondit: non esse illud monstrum, sed vere monstrum habendum fuisse, si sorices à caligis roderentur. Græci auctores simillimum Bionis (nec scio an ita legendum sit etiam apud Augustinum) dictum referunt. Clemens, Τί ἡ ὃ Σωμα-τον[?] εἰ ὁ μῦς, φησὶν ὁ Βίων, τὸν Σύλακον διέτρεψαν, ἡ ὡς φάγῃ τῆς γὰ ἡν Σωματὸν[?], εἰ, ὥσπερ Ἀρκεσίλαος παίζων ἐπεχείρει, τὸν μιῶ ὁ Σύλαξ κατέφαγεν. Vide etiam Theodoretum. Θύλαξ[?] saccus est scorteus, vbi erat farina vel panis: nam etiam ἀρτοθήκῳ[?] hoc est, panarium, explicat Aristophanis scholiastes. Eiusmodi saccum secum ferebant quando ibant τὰ ἀλφίτα emtum: hoc est, farinam quæ in foro vænibat, quod ἀλφιτόπωλις ἀγορὰ appellabatur. Aristophanes Concionantibus,
units.tr: Above all they thought it ominous if mice had gnawed anything. See Cicero's On Divination, book two. Pliny too, in book eight, chapter 57, notes the same, adding that when they appeared white it was a sign of joy. The same was observed about shrews, by whose squeaking, Pliny says, auspices were disrupted in the same place. But Augustine, speaking of superstitious people in On Christian Doctrine, book two, says elegantly: "Hence come those cases where, when clothing is gnawed by mice, people fear the suspicion of future evil more than they grieve at the present loss. Hence the elegant saying of Cato, who, when consulted by a man who told him that his boots had been gnawed by mice, replied that this was not a portent, but that it would really have been a portent if mice had gnawed the boots." Greek authors report a saying very like this of Bion (nor do I know whether it should be read so in Augustine too). Clement: [Τί ἡ ὃ Σωμα-τον, εἰ ὁ μῦς, φησὶν ὁ Βίων, τὸν Σύλακον διέτρεψαν, ἡ ὡς φάγῃ τῆς γὰ ἡν Σωματὸν, εἰ, ὥσπερ Ἀρκεσίλαος παίζων ἐπεχείρει, τὸν μιῶ ὁ Σύλαξ κατέφαγεν.] See also Theodoret. [Θύλαξ] is a leather sack in which there was flour or bread; for the scholiast on Aristophanes also explains [ἀρτοθήκῳ], that is, a bread-box. People carried such a sack with them when they went to buy [τὰ ἀλφίτα], that is, the barley meal which was sold in the market, which was called the [ἀλφιτόπωλις ἀγορὰ]. Aristophanes in the Ecclesiazusae: [Κ᾽ ἀεὶτ᾽ ἐχώρουν εἰς ἀγορὰν ἐπ᾽ ἀλφίτα. Ἔπειθ᾽ ὑπ᾽ ἀχοῦ ἄρτί με τὸν θύλακον].

units.la: Κ᾽ ἀεὶτ᾽ ἐχώρουν εἰς ἀγορὰν ἐπ᾽ ἀλφίτα. Ἔπειθ᾽ ὑπ᾽ ἀχοῦ ἄρτί με τὸν θύλακον[?].
units.tr: "And they always went down to the market for barley-meal. Then, with a shout, he struck me on the bag..." [καὶ ἀεὶ ἐχώρουν εἰς ἀγορὰν ἐπ' ἀλφίτα. Ἔπειθ' ὑπ' ἀχοῦ ἄρτί με τὸν θύλακον]

units.la: Interpretes qui Θύλακον ἀλφίτων reticulum panis vertunt incogitantiæ magnæ se obligarunt & ταχιλίας. Reticulum enim panis apud Horatium & Iuvenalem est quod ὑρύαλον[?] Græci vocant. Hesychius, Τύρ[?]ακτον[?], σκὶ[?] καὶ ἀλεῖλον[?], ἐν ᾧ βάλλοι τὸν ἐρ-ῶν οἱ ἀρξάμενοι[?]. Glossarium, Reticulum, ὑρύαξ. Sed & ad alia his reticulis utebantur: unde est ὑρύαξ ὑφισμάτων[?] apud Athenæum lib. primo ex Aristophane: quem nimis inepte docti viri hactenus sunt interpretati. Aristophanes verò in
units.tr: Interpreters who render "bag of barley-meal" [θύλακον ἀλφίτων] as a bread-net have committed themselves to great thoughtlessness and error. For in Horace and Juvenal a bread-net is what the Greeks call ὑρύαλον. Hesychius glosses a similar word as a net in which one throws... and the glossary gives "reticulum, ὑρύαξ". But these nets were also used for other things, whence Athenaeus in book 1 quotes from Aristophanes the phrase ὑρύαξ ὑφισμάτων, which learned men have hitherto interpreted very foolishly. Aristophanes, in the Wasps, calls the Persians' breeches and trousers θυλάκας [bags].

units.la: Vespis Persarum braccas & anaxyridas θυλάκας dixit. Adeo autem familiare est muribus θυλάκας rodere, vt propterea θυλακοτρώγες à poetis appelleritur. Hesychius, θυλακοτρώγος, μῦς, οἱ ὁ ἀκεὶς.
units.tr: Since it is so customary for mice to gnaw bags, the poets have accordingly called them θυλακοτρώγες, bag-gnawers. Hesychius: θυλακοτρώγος, a mouse, ...

units.la: πρὸς τὸ, ἐξηγητήν ] Hoc est, ad portentorum interpretem, & divinum: qualis olim Athenis Lampon ὁ μάντις, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν dictus est ὁ ἐξηγητής. Multa de hoc apud comicum, & in historiis.
units.tr: "To the interpreter [ἐξηγητής]": that is, to the interpreter of portents and of divine matters, such as once at Athens was Lampon the seer, who was called "the Exegete" par excellence. Much about him is found in the comic poet and in the histories.

units.la: ἐνδέχεται τῷ σκυτοδέψῃ ἀποῤῥάψαι.) Lege fideiubente me ἀποῤῥάψαι: quod conuenientissimum verbum est cerdoni, & veteramentariorum sutorum quem σκυτοδέψην minùs proprie vocat ἀντὶ τῆς σκυτοτόμου, vel πισσοτόμου [?]. sic enim Athenis nominabantur. Iam ante diximus faccum de quo agitur, fuisse ex aluta aut corio: qualis erat, follis aut pafceolus apud Romanos. Scholiastes Aristophanis vocem σάκκον, vel vt alij legebant σάκκον, interpretatur ἐκ βυρσῶν [?] Ἀχείου, ὅπερ θυλάκον λέγομεν. Hesychius, θυλάκια, ἀσκοὶ δερματινοι. Graeci peram cynicorum solent vocare, vt Maximus Tyrius sermone xxxvii. ea pera fuit coriacea, quod certum est. Ideo Tatianus ait, loquens de cynicis, λέγοντες μὲν δεῖσθαι μηδὲν [?], ἡ ὁ τὸν Πρωτέα σκυτοδέψην μὲν χρῆζοντες δέγ [?] τῶν πήρας· ὑράσι ἡ δέξ. τὸ ἱμάτιον. Sanè vulgata lectio inepta est, neque huius fieri debet.
units.tr: "It is possible for the cobbler to stitch it [ἀποῤῥάψαι]." Read "fideiubente me ἀποῤῥάψαι", that is, "stitch up", a word most fitting for a cobbler and for the old-clothes sutors, whom he rather loosely calls σκυτοδέψης instead of σκυτοτόμος or πισσοτόμος; for so they were named at Athens. We said before that the bag in question was made of leather or hide, such as the follis or pelliceus among the Romans. The scholiast on Aristophanes explains the word σάκκον (or as others read it, σάκκον) as "made of the hides of Achaeus", which we call a θύλακος. Hesychius: θυλάκια, leather bags. The Greeks commonly call the Cynics' wallet πήρα, as Maximus of Tyre does in discourse 37; that wallet was certainly made of leather. So Tatian, speaking of the Cynics, says that they claim to need nothing, yet carry the wallet and the cloak. Certainly the vulgar reading is absurd and should not be followed.

units.la: ἀλλ' ἐκστρεπεῖς ἐκδύσασθαι.] Hoc verbum & exuendi, & excutiendi procul à se significationem habet: nec sunt audiendi qui referibunt ἐκλύσασθαι.
units.tr: "But to strip off [ἐκδύσασθαι]": this verb has the sense both of stripping off and of shaking out, far from oneself. Nor should we listen to those who prefer ἐκλύσασθαι (to wash off).

units.la: ἡ πύκνα ἡ τῶν οἰκίαν καθαιρεῖν.] Harum purgationum auctor & inuentor apud Graecos Epimenides, Laertius in vita, Λ[?] ἡ πρῶτος οἰκίας ἡ ἀχὴς καθύσαι [?]. meminit Dioscorides, & alij.
units.tr: The author and inventor of these purifications of the house among the Greeks was Epimenides, as Laertius says in his life; he was the first to cleanse houses. Dioscorides and others mention it.

units.la: χ̸ἢ ἔτε ὅπλίσωαι μνήματι.] Hesiodus. Μήτ' ἐπ' ἀνυπήσιοι καθίζειν (ὰ γὰρ ἄμεινον)[?] Παῖδα δ' ὑωδ' ἐκαλλιον, ὅ τ' ἀνὲρ ἀνήνορα ποιεῖ.[?]
units.tr: Hesiod: "Nor sit upon a tomb (for that is better)... a boy, and ... a man makes a man unmanly."

units.la: Nota sunt bustorum formidamina, & monumentorum terriculamenta. Hoc Romani maximè in Diali flamine obseruabant: nam ille locum in quo bustum esset nunquam ingrediebatur. A. Gellius lib. x. cap. x v.
units.tr: Here are the terrors of tombs and the bugbears of monuments. The Romans observed this especially in the Dialis flamen, for he never entered a place where there was a tomb. Aulus Gellius, book 10, chapter 15.

units.la: ἔτ' ἔπι νεκρὸν ἐλθεῖν.) Istud olim videtur in deorum ministris solitum obseruari: sanè apud Mosem hac lege summus sacerdos alligatur, Ne ad cadauera veniito: ne pro patre quidem suo aut matre se polluito. At apud Romanos Dialis flamen, cui tam multæ fuerant cæremoniæ impositæ, etsi mortuum attingere non poterat, funus tamen exequi non erat illi religio. vide A. Gellium. Lycurgi lege, vt Plutarchus ait, omnis huiusmodi circa mortuos superstitio fuit Lacedæmone sublata. Cæterum propter hanc causam, institutum olim fuit, vt indicia apponerentur foribus domus funestæ: ne videlicet, insciius aliquis ingrederetur, & se imprudens polluceret. De vase aquæ lustralis iam diximus: eodem spectabant capilli de ipsius defuncti capite secti, qui foribus appendi soliti. Euripides Alcestide, Πυλῶν πρόσθεν ἁ'χ ὅρῳ[?] πηγαῖον ὡς νομίζεταί[?] γε χέρνιβ' ὅπι φθιμένῳ πύλαις,[?] χαῖα τ' ἔτις ὅπι πρόσθυρα ζμαί-[?] ζ' ἀ δὴ νεκύων πέθεση πίλνει.[?]
units.tr: "Nor to come to a corpse": this seems to have been customarily observed among the ministers of the gods. Indeed, in Moses the high priest is bound by this law: he shall not come to dead bodies, nor defile himself even for his father or mother (Lev. 21). But among the Romans the Dialis flamen, though burdened with so many ceremonies, could not touch the dead, yet it was not against his religion to attend a funeral; see Aulus Gellius. By the law of Lycurgus, as Plutarch says, all such superstition about the dead was abolished at Sparta. Moreover, for this reason it was once the custom to hang signs on the doors of a house of mourning, so that no one might enter unknowingly and defile himself. We have already spoken of the vessel of lustral water; to the same purpose belonged the hair cut from the head of the dead person, which was customarily hung on the doors. Euripides in Alcestis: "Before the gates stands a vessel of water, as is customary for the dead, and a lock of hair cut off is set before the doors, as a sign that a dead person is there."

units.la: Apud Romanos cupressus domus funestæ faciebat indicium: quod ex Plinio & Seruio pridem doctis viris notum , notatumque.
units.tr: Among the Romans the cypress marked a house of mourning, as learned men have long known and noted from Pliny and Servius.

units.la: ἔτ' ἐπὶ λέγει.) Scribendum λέγῃ, vt ἠὸ[?]δὸ ἐπὶ νεκρόν. Hesychius, λέγῃ, ἐπ' οἷς τὰς νεκρὰς κοσμοῦσιν. Etiam Latini lectos vocant in quibus mortui collocabantur & efferebantur. Erit autem figura ἡ [?]ςΐγα Δηλοῖν[?], ἔτ' ὅτι νεκρὸν ἐλθεῖν[?], ἔτ' ὅτι λέγει[?], pro ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν νεκρῶν λέγει. & referendum ad ταφθ·σεως[?] solemnia. Sed est & alia lectio ἔτι λέγω. quam potius retineo.
units.tr: "Nor does he go to a bier [λέγῃ]": one should read λέγῃ, as in "to the dead". Hesychius: λέγῃ, the things with which the dead are adorned. The Latins also call "lecti" the couches on which the dead were laid out and carried forth. The construction will be: "nor to come to a corpse, nor (to go) to a bier", and it refers to the solemnities of burial. But there is also another reading, ἔτι λέγω, which I rather keep.

units.la: Τὰ τῆς Θεᾶς ὁ μέγαρα ζοίσματα[?]· Ἥτις βροτῶν μὲν ἐν τις ἀφλαγ[?] φόνῳ, ἡ δ' ἐξ ἀχειας[?], ἡ ιεραῖ θύῃ χερσίν, Βωμῷ προσείρηνδ[?] μυσαρὸν ὡς ἡγεμένη.
units.tr: "The halls of the goddess... whoever among mortals is stained with murder, or whoever with childbirth, or with a corpse, is held unclean, and approaching the altar with holy hands, is thought to pollute it."

units.la: ἢ ὅταν ἐνύπνιον ἴδῃ.) Notum est veteres cum triste aliquod insomnium viderant ἀποτροπιασμῶς χάριν sacra quaedam factitasse Aristophanes Ranis,
units.tr: "Or when he has seen a dream": it is known that the ancients, when they had seen some sad dream, performed certain sacred rites to avert its effects, as Aristophanes says in the Frogs:

units.la: Ἀλλά μοι ἀμφίσχολοι λύχνον ἀψάλε[?], Καλάσιον τ' ἐν πολυκτητῷ δρόσον ἄρατε, Θέρμητε δ' ὕδωρ Ὡς ἂν θεὸν ὀνείρων ἀπολύσω[?].
units.tr: "But light for me a lamp, and bring the Kalasian oil in a jar, and heat water, so that I may release myself from the god of dreams."

units.la: Amphora nunc petitur nigri cariosa falerni, Expiet vt somnos garrula saga tuos.
units.tr: "Now a jar of old, black Falernian wine is sought, so that some chattering old woman may expiate your dreams."

units.la: Sed in re nō obscura nō abutar, neque meo neque lectoris otio. Exempla passim apud tragicos.
units.tr: But I will not abuse your leisure or the reader's on a matter that is not obscure. Examples occur everywhere in the tragic poets.

units.la: τίνι θεῷ, ἢ τίνι θεᾷ.) Graeci vocant δαίμονας ἀποτρόπους: apud Romanos Iovi prodigiali fiebant sacra. Plautus Amphytrione,
units.tr: "To what god, or to what goddess": the Greeks call them averting daemons; among the Romans sacrifices were made to Jupiter of prodigies. Plautus, Amphitryon:

units.la: Sed mulier postquam experrecta es prodigiali Iovi Aut mola salsa hodie, aut thure comprecatam opor-tuit.
units.tr: "But since the woman woke up, she ought to have prayed to Jupiter of prodigies, with salted meal or with incense today."

units.la: Creditum etiam est à veteribus expiari somnia , si illa Soli narrassent. Euripides,
units.tr: The ancients also believed that dreams could be expiated if they were told to the Sun. Euripides:

units.la: Ἀ χαυνὰ δ᾽ ἴ̓ζει νὺξ φρυ[?]λα φάτ[?]ιμα[?]ζ[?],Λέξω πρὸς αἰθέρ, εἴτι δὴ τόδ᾽ ἐς ἀκο[?].
units.tr: "Dreams... the night brings... I shall speak to the aether, whether this is heard..."

units.la: Τοιαῦτα τ᾽ ς παρέν[?]Θ, νυνὶ ἡλίῳΔείκνυσι τ᾽ ἔναρ, ἔκλυον ἐξηγκυμένη.
units.tr: "Such things... now she shows the vision to the sun; I heard her, being..."

units.la: ὥσπερ τὰς Ὀρφεοτελέστας κ[?] μύσα τορδεδευ[?]ένα.) Orpheus in Græciam initiorum genus quoddam , vel teste Demosthene inuexit , quod Ὀρφικὰς τελετὰς vocabant, & qui illa docerent Orpheotelestas. Ait autem κ[?] μύσα , quia sub exitum cuiusque mensis videntur soliti initiari Athenienses. Habeo eius rei auctorem scholiasten Aristophanis qui testatur circa finem singulorum mensium fieri soliras τὰς μυστικὰς ἡμέρας. Proclus in Hesiodi commentariis auctor est, veteres operam simulatricibus dedisse die mensis xix. Atheniensibus , eos qui mysteriis istis & Eleusiniis essent initiati , diuinis in Orco fruiturum honoribus. Laërtius in Antisthene, & alij.
units.tr: "As the Orpheotelestae [Ὀρφεοτελεσταί]..." Orpheus introduced into Greece a kind of initiation, as Demosthenes attests, called the Orphic rites, and those who taught them were called Orpheotelestae. He says it is at the end of the month because the Athenians seem to have been usually initiated near the end of each month. I have as witness the scholiast on Aristophanes, who testifies that the mystic days were held near the end of each month. Proclus, in his commentaries on Hesiod, states that the ancients devoted their labour to the... on the nineteenth day of the month, and that the Athenians who were initiated into these mysteries and the Eleusinian ones would enjoy divine honours in the underworld. Laertius in his life of Antisthenes, and others.

units.la: ἢ δ᾽ ἐπὶ ταῖς περιόδοις ἀπελθὼν.] Imò δὴ τὰς περιόδους vt postulat Hellenissmi ratio : verùm arbitror maius vulnus subesse , & desiderari aliquod vocabulum, aut etiam fortasse plura. Notum autem in triuiis & compitis sacra Hecatæ olim fieri solita : eodem etiam moris fuit τὰ καθάρματα, & purgamenta vrbium proiicere. Eustathius, φασὶν ὅτι δίον ἐκάλουν ἱερεῖα τιθέντων Δὶ μειλιχίῳ ἐν τοῖς καθαρμοῖς θύουσι μαιμακτηρίων μείλιχος, ὥστε ἠνοῦ τὰ πομπαῖα ἐκβολὴ εἰς τὰς περιόδους ἐνίοτε. ea purgamenta etiam ὀξυθύμια appellata sunt: qua de voce & ritu hoc toto confule Harpocrationem. Atque hæc sacra cum peregissent, non ante domum redibant quàm & vestem & corpus aqua vel fluuiali, vel fontana purificassent. Porphyrius, Πάντες ἐν τέ-τῳ ὠμολόγῳ(ν) οἱ Θεολόγοι, ὡς ἄντε ἄτοκον ἐν ταῖς ἀπορροπαιοις θυσίαις τῇ θυομένῳ, καὶ καθαροῖς τε χρηστέον, μὴ γὰρ ἵνα τὶς εἰς ἄσυ, μηδ᾽ εἰς οἶκον ἴδιον, μὴ πρότερον ἐδήσῃ ἡ σώματ ποδαμοῖς ἡ πηγὴ ἀποκαθάρας. ἡ κεφαλῆς λούσθω. ) Colligi hinc posse videtur in triuiis fuisse ἀφραντίσια. potest tamen etiam aliter accipi.
