Ritum lauandi capitis in purificationibus exprimit Persius,
units.tr: "But going away at the circuits [περιόδοις]": rather, "δὴ τὰς περιόδους", as the rules of Greek idiom require; but I think a greater flaw lies beneath, and some word, or perhaps several, seems to be missing. It is known that sacrifices to Hecate were once customarily performed at crossroads and junctions; by the same custom they used to cast out the purgings and sweepings of cities. Eustathius: "They say that when they set up a sacrifice to Zeus Meilichios in purifications, they call the victim..." Such purgings are also called ὀξυθύμια; on this word and rite consult Harpocration throughout. And when they had completed these rites, they did not return home until they had purified both their clothing and their body with water, either from a river or from a spring. Porphyry: "All the theologians agree that in purifying sacrifices one must use pure things; for no one should enter a temple or his own house before he has washed his body in water from a spring, and washed his head." From this it may seem that washings were held at the crossroads; but it can also be understood otherwise. Persius expresses the rite of washing the head in purifications:

units.la: — Tiberino in gurgite mergis Mane caput bis, terque. & Iuuenalis Ter matutino Tiberi mergetur, & ipsis Vorticibus timidum caput abluet.
units.tr: "...dip your head three times in the Tiber's current in the morning." And Juvenal: "He will be dipped in the Tiber at morning, and will wash his fearful head in its very eddies."

units.la: σχίλλῃ ἢ σχύλακι κελάσαι αὐτὸν ἀφικαθάραι.) Tangit duplicem veterum confuetudinem expiandi lustrandiqué se. altera erat, circumaćta circa corpus scilla: altera catulo similiter circa corpus dućto. Hoc enim significat ἀφικαθάραι. De scilla, quòd expiandi vim crederetur habere, notum vel ex Plinio & medicorum libris. Artemidorus Ἐνοδίῳ. Ἡ σκίλλα καθάρσιον ἐν νεκρομάντει. Lucianus Ἐπισκοπεῖ τις. ἐκάθηρέ τί με, ἢ ἀπέμαξε, ἢ ἀφηγνίζει δαδὶ καὶ σκίλλῃ ἢ ἄλλοις πλέοσι. Dio Chrysostomus oratione XLVIII. ἀλλά μοι δοκεῖ ἀφικαθάρσεως τῷ ἀστρὶ μὴ σκίλλῃ μηδὲ ὑδάλις, ἀλλὰ πολὺ καθαρωτέρῳ χρήματι λόγῳ κοινῷ πράξειν. Plura Clemens Alexand. septimo Stromat. & Theocriti scholiastes in Thalysiis. De catulo, res minus vulgò, vt videtur, nota: quare etiam eius ritus ignoratione interpretes miris modis hunc locum depravarunt: in quo nihil erat prorsus mutandum. Nam verum est quod diximus, veteres catulo solitos lustrare se eum circumferentes circa corpus: eamque lustrationem vocabant περιστυλάκισμόν. Plutarchus in Κεφαλαίοις Romanorum institutorum: Τῷ δὲ κυνὶ πάντες, ὡς ἐπὶ εἴπεν, Ἕλληνες ἐχέω[?], ὃ, ἢ χρῶνται γε μέχρι νῦν ἔνιοι σφαγίῳ ἀρὸς τῆς καθαρμοῦ[?], ἢ περιμάτλεσι τῆς ὑγιασμὸς[?] δρομίνης, περιστυλάκισμὸν τὸ ζῶον[?] τῷ καθαρμῷ[?] καλοῦντες. Idem repetit in Romulo. Fuerunt & alij tum scillæ, tum catulorum in februationibus usus quos prudens omitto. Tyrones moneo pertinere ad hûc ritum verba legis 111.§. 3. D. Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis: quæ tamen alio referunt viri docti.
units.tr: "to have him purified with a squill or a dog" [σχίλλῃ ἢ σχύλακι κελάσαι αὐτὸν ἀφικαθάραι]. This touches on the ancients' twofold custom of expiating and purifying themselves. The first was to pass a squill around the body; the second was to lead a puppy around the body in the same way. This is what the word ἀφικαθάραι means. That the squill was thought to have the power of expiation is known even from Pliny and the medical books. Artemidorus, in Oneirocritica: "The squill is a purification in necromancy" [Ἡ σκίλλα καθάρσιον ἐν νεκρομάντει]. Lucian, in The Dream: "Someone purified me, or wiped me off, or cleansed me with a torch and a squill or other things" [ἐκάθηρέ τί με, ἢ ἀπέμαξε, ἢ ἀφηγνίζει δαδὶ καὶ σκίλλῃ ἢ ἄλλοις πλέοσι]. Dio Chrysostom, Oration 48: "But it seems to me that one who is to be purified from the stars should not do it with a squill or with a ..., but will act with a much purer thing, common reason" [ἀλλά μοι δοκεῖ ἀφικαθάρσεως τῷ ἀστρὶ μὴ σκίλλῃ μηδὲ ὑδάλις, ἀλλὰ πολὺ καθαρωτέρῳ χρήματι λόγῳ κοινῷ πράξειν]. More is found in Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 7, and in the scholiast on Theocritus, Idylls. The dog is a less commonly known matter, as it seems, and for this reason the interpreters, ignorant of its ritual, have mangled this passage in strange ways, though nothing at all needed changing. For it is true, as we have said, that the ancients were accustomed to purify themselves by carrying a dog around the body, and they called this lustration peristylakismos. Plutarch, in the Roman Questions: "All the Greeks, as it were, offer a dog [...] and some even now use it in purifications, or in the ... of the ... , calling the animal's circling around the one purified peristylakismos." He repeats the same in the Life of Romulus. There were also other uses, both of squill and of puppies, in the February purifications, which I prudently pass over. I advise beginners that the words of law 111, §3, D. Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis pertain to this rite, though learned men refer them elsewhere.

units.la: αὐτὸν περικαθάραι.] Significat hoc verbum applicare aliquid corpori, expiandi causa, idque in orbem ducere: quod & περιμάζαι dicitur: Latinis circumferre.
units.tr: "to purify around him" [αὐτὸν περικαθάραι]. This verb signifies applying something to the body for the sake of purification, and doing so in a circle; it is also called perimattein, which the Latins render circumferre.

units.la: Idem ter sacris pura circumtulit unda. Seruius;
units.tr: "The same, with a pure wave, carried him thrice round with sacred rites." Servius:
"Circumtulit means purgavit. It is an old word."

units.la: Plautus, Pro larnato[?] te circumferam: id est, purgabo, Nam lustratio à circumlatione dicta est vel tedæ vel sulphuris. Juvenalis,
units.tr: Plautus: "I will carry you around (circumferam), that is, I will purify you; for lustration was named from carrying around, either with a torch or with sulphur." Juvenal:

units.la: Rectè exprimit Seruius circumlationem illam quæ in lustrationibus fieri solebat. Similiter & urbes & agri lustrabantur, hostiis in orbem circumlatis. Polybius libro quarto de Mantinensibus, ἡ καθαρμὸν ἐποιήσαντο, ἢ σθάγια καὶ περιεμέχαν τῆς τε πόλεως κύκλῳ τῆς χώρας πάσης[?]. ideo Latinis ea sacra ambarvalia dicta. Atque hinc est, quòd τὸ περὶ fere in vocibus eò pertinentibus reperitur: ut in περιμάλλεσθαι[?], περιζύεσθαι[?], περιαγνίζειν[?], περιθεῖν[?] & περι-θείως[?], etsi Homerus ἴσδεσθαι[?] dixit. Sic & περιβάλλεσθαι[?] κάρφῳ[?] apud Aristotelem in sexto Historiarum, de lustratione gallinarum, quæ περιαπισμὸς[?] Plutarcho nuncupatur. Sed & ἀπομάττειν[?] eo sensu vsurparunt, vt Demosthenes Pro corona καθαίρων[?] τὰς τελετὰς, ἢ ἀπομάττων τὰ πηλῷ ἐν τῇ πόλει[?]. Sic accipiendum & in illo Callimachi, vt puto, versiculo, initio Athenæi.
units.tr: Servius rightly explains that carrying around which used to be done in lustrations. In the same way both cities and fields were lustrated, with victims carried around in a circle. Polybius, book 4, on the Mantineans: "they made a purification, and sacrificed, and carried the victims around the whole land of the city in a circle" [ἡ καθαρμὸν ἐποιήσαντο, ἢ σθάγια καὶ περιεμέχαν τῆς τε πόλεως κύκλῳ τῆς χώρας πάσης]. Hence the Latins called these rites ambarvalia. And from this it is that peri is found in almost all the words belonging here: as in perimallesthai, perizyesthai, periagnizein, perithein and peritheios, although Homer said isdesthai. So too periballesthai with a broom, in Aristotle's sixth book of Histories, on the lustration of hens, which Plutarch calls periapismos. But they also used apomattein in this sense, as Demosthenes in On the Crown says: "purifying the rites, or wiping off the mud in the city" [καθαίρων τὰς τελετὰς, ἢ ἀπομάττων τὰ πηλῷ ἐν τῇ πόλει]. It should be understood in this sense also in that verse of Callimachus, as I think, at the beginning of Athenaeus.

units.la: Τεῖς δ' ἀπομαξαμένοισι θεοὶ διδόασιν ἄμφορον[?]. quem locum non recte Erasmus, & alij aliorsum conati sunt trahere, cum ex hoc ritu fit explicandus. Hinc dictæ sunt mulierculæ illæ quarum hic Theophrastus meminit, ἀπομάττριαι[?], vt est apud Pollucem, vel ἀπομάττριαι[?], vt vocat eas Plutarchus De superstitione. Latinis piatrices, & simulatrices, vel potius simpulatrices, vide Festum. Talem fuisse ait Demosthenes Glaucotheam siue Empusam Æschinis matrem.
units.tr: "The gods give an amphora to those who have wiped themselves off" [Τεῖς δ' ἀπομαξαμένοισι θεοὶ διδόασιν ἄμφορον]. Erasmus and others have wrongly tried to draw this passage elsewhere, when it must be explained from this rite. Hence those little women of whom Theophrastus speaks here were called apomaktriai, as in Pollux, or apomattriai, as Plutarch calls them in On Superstition. In Latin they are piatrices and simulatrices, or rather simpulatrices; see Festus. Demosthenes says that Glaucothea or Empusa, the mother of Aeschines, was such a woman.

units.la: μαυσοὺς τε ἰδὼν ἢ ἐπίλησις[?]. Plautus Captiueis, Hegio hic homo rabiosus habitus est in Alide. Ne is tu quod istic fabulatur, aures tuas. Nam istic hajis[?] insectatus est domi matre & patre, Et idic isti qui putatur moribus interdum venit. Proin tu ab istoc procul recedas.
units.tr: "and seeing the madmen or the epilepsy" [μαυσοὺς τε ἰδὼν ἢ ἐπίλησις]. Plautus, Captivi: "Hegio here is thought a madman in Elis. Do not listen to what that fellow says there. For there he harassed his mother and father at home, and yet the one who is thought ... sometimes comes to such morals. So you should keep far away from him."

units.la: Suspicor etiam ob similem superstitionem factum, vt Akis rex Daunium infamiam simulantem procul à domo sua arceret: id enim videntur vltima verba eius capitis suadere. Locus est primo Samuelis, ca. xx 1. Similis sententia in Eumenidibus Varronis, Ἀπαγε[?] in diverticulum à domo nostra istam infamitatem.
units.tr: I suspect that, because of a similar superstition, King Achis also drove Daunius far from his house when he was feigning infamy; for the last words of that passage seem to suggest it. The place is 1 Samuel, chapter 20 or 21 (the text is printed as "ca. xx 1"). A similar saying is in Varro's Eumenides: "Begone to a side path from our house with that infamy."

units.la: Ἔστι τι ἢ [?] μεμψιμοιρία ] Iniustitiæ species quædam est & illiberalitatis hoc vitium: quod fere in calamitosis pauperibúsque, vel paupertatem simulantibus, & senibus reperitur. Nam vt felicitas superba, ita querula calamitas est eorum maxime qui è magnis aut mediocribus opibus ad inopiam sunt redacti: rectéque ille apud Terentium,
units.tr: "There is a certain μεμψιμοιρία." This vice is a kind of injustice and illiberality. It is found chiefly in the afflicted and the poor, in those who feign poverty, and in old men. For just as prosperity is proud, so misfortune is querulous, especially with those who have been reduced from great or middling wealth to want. Terence rightly says:

units.la: Omnes quibus res sunt minus secunda, magis sunt nescio quomodo
units.tr: "All those whose fortunes are less favourable are somehow more..."

units.la: Suspectiosi: ad contumeliam omnia accipiunt magis: Propter suam impotentiam se semper credunt neglgi. & alibi apud eundem poëtam querulus quidam senex, Me credo, ait, huic esse natum rei, ferundis miseris. Nihil autem interest facultatibus sit pauper aliquis, an animo, quæ sola demum paupertas verè misera est. Multa Seneca de hoc vitio variis locis: sed vnum notare sufficiet. Sic ille De tranquillitate vitæ libro 1.de amicorum delectu loquens. Præcipue tamen vitentur tristes, & omnia deplorantes, quibus nulla non causa in querelas placet. Constet illi licet fides & benevolentia, tranquillitati tamen inimicus est, comes perin. batus [?] & omnia gemens. Μεμψιμοιρίαν autem, querelam non querimoniam vertimus. nam etsi non fugeret nos bonos auctores promisceé his vocibus vti, monet tamen veterum grammaticorum auctoritas. Cornelius Fronto litterator, Querimonia certe rei est: Querela superuacua est. Itaque prior grauitatis est, posterior leuitatis. Glarij auctor, Querela, μέμψις ματαίαξ [?]. Querimonia, μέμψις. Vox ἐδομέν[?] fulpecta est,& sine damno sententiæ potest abesse. Habes apud Clementem Alex. Pædag. lib. III. & μέμψεως & μεμψιμοιρίας definitiones, quas prætermitto.
units.tr: "suspicious: they take everything more as an insult; because of their weakness they always think they are neglected." And elsewhere in the same poet, a querulous old man says: "I believe I was born for this, to bear miseries." It makes no difference whether a man is poor in resources or in spirit; only the latter is truly wretched poverty. Seneca treats this vice in many places, but one passage will suffice. In De tranquillitate animi, book 1, speaking of the choice of friends, he says: "Above all, the gloomy are to be avoided, those who deplore everything, for whom every cause finds a complaint. However faithful and kind he may be, he is an enemy to tranquillity, a companion of sorrow, who groans at everything." We have rendered μεμψιμοιρία as querela rather than querimonia. Although I would not deny that good authors use these words interchangeably, the authority of the old grammarians advises it. Cornelius Fronto the schoolmaster: "Querimonia certainly belongs to a matter; querela is superfluous. So the former belongs to gravity, the latter to levity." The glossary writer: "Querela, μέμψις ματαία. Querimonia, μέμψις." The word ... is suspect, and can be omitted without loss to the sense. In Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus book 3, you have definitions both of μέμψις and of μεμψιμοιρία, which I pass over.

units.la: Ἀποσείλαι[?] τῷ φίλῳ μεσίδα. ] Conuiuæ olim è conuiuio apophoreta referebant: de quo more suprà diximus: absentibus verò μεσίδες mittebantur. Plutarchus in Agelilao, ἔθυσεν ἀλαζόνια, ἐ διαιρῶν μεσίδας τοῖς φίλοις ἀπὸ τεθυμένων[?]. Idem auctor in Arati vita scribit Antigonum regem cum Corinthi sacra faceret, Arato Sicyonem misisse μεσίδας. Aristophanes Acharnensibus,
units.tr: "to send a portion to a friend" [Ἀποσείλαι τῷ φίλῳ μερίδα]. Formerly guests at a banquet carried away leftovers (apophoreta), a custom we have mentioned above; but portions (μερίδες) were sent to those who were absent. Plutarch, in the Agesilaus: "he sacrificed, distributing portions to his friends from the victims" [ἔθυσεν ... διαιρῶν μερίδας τοῖς φίλοις ἀπὸ τεθυμένων]. The same author, in the Life of Aratus, writes that King Antigonus, when he was performing sacred rites at Corinth, sent portions to Aratus at Sicyon. Aristophanes, in the Acharnians:

units.la: Ἐ σεμ̈λέ τίς Ὀι νυμφίῳ ταῦτ' χρέα[?]Ἐ ἡ ψ γέμων[?].
units.tr: [Greek verse, garbled in the scan; the sense is that someone should carry this to the bridegroom.]

units.la: Etiam Romanis mos fuit de mensa aliquid mittere amicis. imò verò etiam Iudæis aliisque gentibus Orientis eundem morem in vsu fuisse testantur litteræ sacræ priore Samuelis capite primo, Nehemiæ capite v i i i. & alibi.
units.tr: The Romans too had the custom of sending something from the table to friends. Indeed, the sacred letters attest that the Jews and other peoples of the East had the same custom in use: in the first chapter of 1 Samuel, in Nehemiah chapter 8, and elsewhere.

units.la: ἐ διότι ὅτι.] Quod vulgò fieri solet. Theognis,—ἐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ζεύς[?]ἐὼν ἴον πάντας ἀρδεύει, ἐπ' ἀνέχων[?].
units.tr: "and because" [ἐ διότι ὅτι]. This is commonly done. Theognis: "For Zeus waters all the flowers, holding..." [ἐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ζεὺς ... ἴον πάντας ἀρδεύει].

units.la: At hic iniquior etiam erga Iouem: quippe cui cum sit opportuna pluuia, nihilominus tamen de Ioue queritur, quod paullò serius quàm libitum ipsi fuisset pluat.
units.tr: But this man is even more unjust toward Jupiter, since rain is seasonable for him, and yet he complains of Jupiter because it rains a little later than he would have liked.

units.la: καὶ πρὸς ἀπάτορον ἄξιον.] Querela vsitata herorum, quòd nimio seruos emerint: quos propterea apud Plautum & Terentium male conciliatos vocant, hoc est, magno emtos. At istum miserum vilitas ipsa offendit. in quem iure illud vsurpauerit, ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ τὸν φάρυγγα [illegible, ~6 letters] τί δεῖ ἔτι πίνειν; χαὶ πολλά ἀ. ] Scrib. ἄτε πολλά ἀ.
units.tr: "and to the fatherless worthy" [καὶ πρὸς ἀπάτορον ἄξιον]. It is a common complaint of masters that they bought their slaves at too high a price; for this reason in Plautus and Terence such slaves are called male conciliati, that is, bought dearly. But this wretch is offended by cheapness itself. Over him one may rightly use that saying: "when the water [...] why should I still drink?" [ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ τὸν φάρυγγα ... τί δεῖ ἔτι πίνειν;] and "many..." [καὶ πολλά]. The text should read ἄτε πολλά.

units.la: ἐνθεὶς τῷ πολλῷ. ] Potest legi & ἐνθεὶς. Et sanè maius fuerit argumentum rei vili pretio emtæ, si emtor à venditore rogatus est vt eam emeret.
units.tr: "put in with much" [ἐνθεὶς τῷ πολλῷ]. It may also be read as ἐνθεὶς. And indeed it would be a stronger argument for a thing bought at a low price if the buyer had been asked by the seller to take it.

units.la: χαὶ ἀφὸς τὸν ἀγχιλαιζόμενον. ] Ait, ἀγχιλαιζόμενον, respiciens cupiditatem qua flagrare solent patres filios habendi potius quàm filias. Tale illud ἀγχιλαῖον apud Ariftophanem Thefmophoriazufis, λέων (Gi γέγονεν αὐτ' ἐκ[?] σὰν[?].
units.tr: And from the one being cuddled [ἀγχιλαιζόμενον]. He says ἀγχιλαιζόμενον, referring to the desire by which fathers are wont to burn for sons rather than daughters. Such is that ἀγχιλαῖον in Aristophanes' Thesmophoriazusae, [λέων γέγονεν...].

units.la: τῆς ὕσιας τὸ ἡμέτερον ἀτεσι. ] Terentius Heautontimor.
units.tr: Our property of the substance [τῆς οὐσίας τὸ ἡμέτερον]. Terence, Heautontimorumenos.
I know what you have done.

units.la: Sustulisti puellam scilicet.) Sy.Si sic factum est ἀληθῆ ἐρεῖς. ] q. d. quem tu beatum prædicas, verius miserum dixeris. sic querulus ille Horatianus Vulteius Menas,
units.tr: You have, of course, raised the girl. If it has been done so, you will speak truly [ἀληθῆ ἐρεῖς]. That is, the man you call happy you would more truly call wretched. So too that querulous Horatian, Vulteius Menas.

units.la: — pol me miserum patrone vocares Si velles, inquit, verum mihi dicere nomen.
units.tr: By Pollux, you would call me wretched, patron, if you wished, he says, to tell me my true name.

units.la: ἐ vixlw vixńσας. ] Errant interpretes in huius loci interpretatione: malè enim referunt alió quàm ad victoriā eius qui caussam obtinuit, & superior è iudicio discessit. quare etiam ἴvixlw vixńσας fcribēdum, non vixlw. familiare est Atticis ita loqui ἴvixlw vixῶν, vel ἠσπλαδέω ἴvixlw. Nam vixlw & ἡτῶν nō esse solùm πολέμῳ sed cuiufcunq; ἀσφίας vel vnicus in Lachete Platonis locus poterat docere. Male etiam iidem interpretes orationem cuius fit hîc mentio, ad ὈπὈφίας λόγας aut nescio quas viuentium laudationes referunt. quæ planè sunt ægrorum hominum fomnia. Quis nescit veteres Atheniensium oratores foliros orationes reis suam opem implorantibus scribere, quibus orationibus ipsi rei vrebantur in iudiciis? Tales sunt omnes fermè Lysiæ & Demosthenis quæ ad cauillas priuatorum pertinent:quod nec Cicero prætermittit & testatur Quintilianus non semel. Postremò δίκαια non sunt, laudes merito dicenda: sed continentia causarum & defensionis firmamenta. Terentius & Cicero iusta vocant.
units.tr: Having conquered, he conquered [ἐνίκων νικήσας]. Interpreters go wrong in explaining this passage, for they refer it to something other than the victory of the one who won the case, while the other departed from the court. For this reason one should write ἐνίκων νικήσας, not νικήσας alone. It is customary for the Attics to speak thus, [ἐνίκων νικῶν] or [ἠσπάλιεν ἐνίκων]. That νικᾶν and ἡττᾶσθαι are not used only of war but of any contest, the single passage in Plato's Laches could show. The same interpreters also wrongly refer the speech mentioned here to funeral orations [ἐπιτάφιοι λόγοι] or I know not what praises of the living. These are plainly the dreams of sick men. Who does not know that the ancient Athenian orators wrote speeches for defendants who implored their aid, and these speeches were then used by the defendants themselves in the courts? Nearly all of Lysias' and Demosthenes' speeches that concern the quarrels of private persons are of this kind, which Cicero does not overlook, and Quintilian attests more than once. Finally, these are not praises to be spoken deservedly, but the substance of cases and the firm grounds of defence. Terence and Cicero call them iusta, proper pleas.

units.la: ἐγκαλεῖν τῷ χρ. ] Quid censes facturum fuisse, si litem perdidisset? Atqui etiam damnator eo, oratori constat eloquentiæ officium si omni arte vsus est.
units.tr: What do you think he would have done had he lost the suit? Yet it is agreed that even the one who condemns, if he has used every art, performs the duty of the orator.

units.la: ἱλαρὸς ἔσ.[?] ] Lego ἱλαρὸς ἴσω. vt apud Terentium Hodie hilarum fac te. & Omitte nunc tristitiam tuam. Spectatur autem in vultu hilaritas, & opponitur proprie τῇ σκυθρωπότητι. Mox lege, ὅτε ἐλέι[?], non ὅτι. Sic in illo Theocriti χαίρῳ πως ὅτε τ' αἰδρας ἐρῶ τὴς μίτοτ' ὄτωπα[?].
units.tr: Cheerful, he was [ἱλαρὸς ἦν]. I read ἱλαρὸς ἴσω, as in Terence: "Today make yourself cheerful," and "Now put aside your sadness." Cheerfulness is seen in the face, and it is properly opposed to gloominess [σκυθρωπότης]. Next, read ὅτε ἐλεῖ, not ὅτι. So in that line of Theocritus: [χαίρω πως ὅτε...] "I rejoice somehow when..."
On the chapter Concerning Trust and Distrust [πίστεως ἀπιστίας]

units.la: Ἔστιν ἀμέλει ἀπιστία.[?] ] Huic contrarium vitium est, quam Græci ἀπιστίαν vocant, Latini credulitatem, quæ sæpe in fatuitatem vertit. In medio autem horum extremorum, virtus est quædam ἀ ὡ νμ[?], prudentiæ velut ἀπερρω[?], per quam & fidem iis habemus qui merentur: & eorum contra fidem suspectam habemus, qui erga alios repert⁠i sunt infideles. Semper enim infixum in animo noftro esse debet Ἐπιχαρίεῖν[?] illud, γνῶθι τῶς ἄλλῳ κι-νεῖσθαι[?]. itémque illud eiusdem poetæ Ciceroni fa-miliare. Νάρε, καὶ μέμνασο ἀπιστεῖν[?]· ἐ, ζῆα ταὐτα τῶν ἐρ⁠ι⁠ῶν[?]. hoc est, interprete Q. Cicerone, Nerui atque artus[?] sint sapientiae, NON TEMERE CREDERE. Extat in hanc sententiam praeclara oratio Dionis Chrysostomi, quam velim legatiuventus. Spectat eodem epistola x x 1 1. Plinij libro v 1. lectu & ipsa dignissima: nec minus elegans senis Ascraei effatum, Καὶ πίστις δ' ἀφ' ὑμῶς ἐ ἀπιστίας ὠλέ-ων ἀϊδρες[?].
units.tr: There is, of course, distrust [Ἔστιν ἀμέλει ἀπιστία]. Its contrary vice is what the Greeks call ἀπιστία and the Latins credulity, which often turns into foolishness. In the middle of these extremes there is a certain virtue, a kind of prudence, through which we give trust to those who deserve it, and we hold suspect the trust of those who have proved faithless to others. For that saying of the poet should always be fixed in our mind, "Know how the other is moved," and likewise that saying of the same poet, familiar to Cicero: [Νάρε, καὶ μέμνασο ἀπιστεῖν...], that is, in the translation of Q. Cicero, "The nerves and sinews of wisdom are: not to believe rashly." There is an excellent oration of Dio Chrysostom on this sentiment, which I would wish young people to read. Pliny's letter 22 bears on the same point, and his letter in Book 5, letter 1, is itself most worthy of reading. No less elegant is the saying of the old man of Ascra: [Καὶ πίστις δ' ἀφ' ὑμῶς...] "Trust too, along with distrust, destroys foolish men."

units.la: καὶ κ) σάδιον ἀειθμέιν[?]. ) Habes amplum in hunc locum commentarium Plauti Aululariam: vbi mirificissimè miserum senicem Euclionem illa auri aula inquietat. Itaque ait Staphylaeum decies dic vno extrudere omnes aedibus: vt nimirum solus thesaurum effodiat & nummos numeret. Sed ipsum poetam vide: est enim ingeniosissimus in illius infelicis ἀπιστίας describenda. Similia reperias apud Lucianum in Alcyone.
units.tr: And easily counted [καὶ εὔσταδιον ἀριθμεῖν]. You have an ample commentary on this passage in Plautus' Aulularia, where the wretched old man Euclio torments himself over his pot of gold. So he says that Staphyla should be told ten times to drive everyone out of the house, so that he alone may dig up the treasure and count the coins. But see the poet himself, for he is most ingenious in describing that wretched distrust. Similar things you will find in Lucian's Alcyon.

units.la: ἐ σκευωρίας τὸ κοιλιώχιον[?]. ) Non damno hanc lectionem: etsi alibi haec vox quod meminerim, haud mihi lecta. Fortasse tamen κωνόχιον scripserat auctor. Est autem κωνόχιον vas quoddam instar magni marsupij, seruandis vestibus, & aliis id genus rebus: sic dictum à pelle canina ex qua vel confici vel integi solebat, vt risus Latinorum. Meminere κωνόχυ Xenophon & Pollux non vno loco, itémque Eustathius, in ὀδυσσ. ε. Quid si etiam κυλικιόγιον scribamus? quam vocem pro κυλικεῖον legere alibi memini. Sed verius est, nihil esse mutandum. nam sic appellat, quas Iulius Pollux κεῖλιός. In eodem auctore κυρι. οδύσσ. legas pro panario vel ἐσεμαξ[?]-θαιν.
units.tr: The belly-pouch [κοιλιώχιον] in the matter of trickery. I do not condemn this reading, although, as far as I recall, I have not read this word elsewhere. Perhaps, however, the author wrote κωνόχιον. A κωνόχιον is a kind of vessel like a large purse, for keeping clothes and other such things, so called from the dog-skin from which it was made or covered. Xenophon and Pollux mention the κωνόχιον in more than one place, and so does Eustathius, on Odyssey ε. What if we should write κυλικιόγιον? I recall reading that word for κυλικεῖον elsewhere. But it is more correct to change nothing, for this is what Julius Pollux calls κεῖλιος. In the same author, in the Odyssey, you should read, in place of "pantry," [ἐσεμάξ...].
If the Euclio [εἰ ὁ μαχλός]. Plautine Euclio.

units.la: — occlude fis Fores[?] ambobus pessulis. εἰς τὴν Θύραν τὴν αὐλαίαν.) Puerilis sed frequens error, pro αὐλείαν. Apud veteres Θύρα αὐλεία, siue αὐλαῖα, perpetuò est idem cum πρωΐη Θύρα.
units.tr: "Bolt the door with both bolts," [εἰς τὴν θύραν τὴν αὐλαίαν]. This is a childish but common error for αὐλείαν. Among the ancients, θύρα αὐλεία or αὐλαῖα is always the same as the πρωΐη θύρα, the front door.

units.la: μὴ μαριφῶν ἀπαλλαγεῖν.) Supra ad caput De stupiditate.
units.tr: Not to be freed from the madman [μὴ μαινομένῳ ἀπαλλαγεῖν]. See above, at the chapter On Stupidity.

units.la: καὶ τὸ ἰμάτιον ἢ ἐκδωσι δ̓ ἰνός. ) Inepta lectio, & quem ex ca sensum interpretetur eliciunt, ineptus est, aut nullus potius. Dubio procul legendum est vt emendauimus ἐκδ̓ ἔναγ.quam voce supra eodem sensu vsurpauit: capite De superstitione. Scribendum etiam, ἢ ὧ τὰ βίλισα ἐργ. non ἡ ὡς τ. Est Atticismus tranflatitius, ἢ ὧ, pro ἡ ἐκείνῳ ὡς.
units.tr: And the cloak, or... [καὶ τὸ ἱμάτιον ἢ ἐκδῶσι]. The reading is inept, and those who try to draw a sense from it find either nothing or, rather, nothing sensible. Undoubtedly it should be read as we have emended, [ἐκδ̓ ἔναγ...], a word he used above in the same sense in the chapter On Superstition. One should also write [ἢ ὡς τὰ βέλτιστα ἐργ...], not [ἡ ὡς τ...]. It is a borrowed Atticism, ἢ ὡς, for ἡ ἐκείνῳ ὡς.

units.la: μάλισα μὴ ἀδύναι. ) Deesse aliquid luce meridiana clarius. Nos ex coniectura locum supplebamus in hanc sententiam, εἰ ἢ μὴ, δὲς ἀδύς ἀπαλλεῖν. Sed postea adducti sumus vt fermè crederemus, ita potius scripsisse Theophrastum, μάλισα μὴ ἀδύναι. εἰ δὲ μὴ, τὸν παῖδα κελεύειν ἀκολυθεῖν. nam quia sequuntur illa verba ἐ τὸν παῖδα ἢ ἀκολουθεῖ. puto hic idem esse mendum quod sexcentis locis obseruauimus, vt bis positae ab auctore voces locis vicinis, semel à librariis omitterentur. Similem ἀπιστίαν aut turpiorem etiam notat in diuitibus fui temporis Iuuenalis satyra quinta: vbi de illorum conuiuiis loquitur:
units.tr: Especially if he cannot... [μάλιστα μὴ ἀδύνατο...]. That something is missing is clearer than noonday. In conjecture we supplied the passage with this sense: "if not, he should be able to..." But afterwards we were led to believe almost, that Theophrastus wrote it thus: [μάλιστα μὲν μὴ δύναι. εἰ δὲ μή, τὸν παῖδα κελεύειν ἀκολουθεῖν]. For since the words [εἰ δὲ μὴ τὸν παῖδα ἢ ἀκολουθεῖ] follow, I think this is the same fault that we have observed in six hundred places, namely that words the author placed twice in nearby passages were once omitted by the copyists. Juvenal, in his fifth satire, notes a similar, or even more shameful, distrust among the rich of his own time, where he speaks of their banquets:

units.la: tibi non committitur aurum. Vel si quando datur, custos affixus ibidem, Qui numeret gemmas, vngues̃que obseruet acutos.
units.tr: Gold is not entrusted to you. Or if it is ever given, a guard stands fixed beside it, to count the gems and watch the sharp fingernails.

units.la: Quid si etiā sic legas, μὲ μὴ δύναι, εἰ ἢ μὴ, σ̓ιλες (vel σαθμίζες) δύναι. Nam profectò ita est, diligentiores & cautiores patresfamilias vasa argentea fi commodato alicui concedant, non illa tradunt prius priùs quàm illorum pondus accuratè explorauerint.
units.tr: What if you read it thus too: [μὴ δύναι, εἰ δὲ μή, σταθμίζειν (or σταθμίζειν) δύναι]? For truly it is so: more diligent and cautious heads of households, if they lend silver vessels to anyone, do not hand them over until they have carefully tested their weight.

units.la: καὶ τὸν παῖδα ὁ ἀκόλουθος.) Malim τὸν ἀκόλουθον, hoc est, puerum ἀκόλουθον, pedissequum, vel famulum itineris comitem. Sic dictum vt ἐρμάζων pro ἁρπάσης, διαζῶν pro δικαςὴς aliàque apud Atticos: quæ & Latini sunt imitati.
units.tr: And the boy, the attendant [καὶ τὸν παῖδα ὁ ἀκόλουθος]. I would rather read τὸν ἀκόλουθον, that is, a boy as attendant, a footman, or a servant who accompanies the journey. Words are so formed among the Attics: ἐρμάζων for ἁρπάζων, διαζῶν for δικαστής, and others, which the Latins too have imitated.

units.la: ὅπιςθεν μὴ βαδίζειν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐμπροσθεν.) Plautus Cur-culione.
units.tr: Not to walk behind but in front [ὄπισθεν μὴ βαδίζειν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔμπροσθεν]. Plautus, Curculio.

units.la: I tu pre virgo : non queo quod pone me est feruare. Idem Pseudolo,
units.tr: You go ahead, girl; I cannot keep what is behind me. The same in Pseudolus:

units.la: I puere pre : ne quisquam pertundat crumenam cautio est.
units.tr: Go ahead, boy; let no one pierce my purse, caution is the rule.

units.la: λέγεται πόσῳ.) Legimus ita hunc locum, & λέγοι, Πόσῳ, εἴπειν, Καλάθυ, ὃ ἡ χρ. inferta voce εἶπεῖν quæ manifestò desideratur. Πόσῳ autem verbum esse, non nomen censemus: éstque eo verbo vsus iterum capite vltimo. significat numerare, & rationem inire. Solent autem mercatores venditæ mercis summam conficere, quam in librum rationum conferant, præsens si pecunia non numeretur. Quod docti quidam viri emendant, & λογόντι τῇ ποσῷ, ne Græca quidem est oratio, nedum eo digna qui à diuinitate sermonis nomen inuenit: saltem dicerent ἐλλείπειν. sed ne sic quidem placet. Quod ait, ὃ σχολάζω [?], accipi debet de seruo flagitatore. Si legeretur Καλάθες pro κα̃λ̃ε̃, esset id, Solue nunc. quod Græci dicunt, αὐλίθεν καλλέαλλε. sed nihil necesse mutare, præsertim fine veteribus libris: quorum equidem hoc maximè loco optarim fieri mihi copiam. Non est autem dubium notari hîc diffidentiam mercatorum, quorum plerisque Verbum [?]ἀποίεσθαι sic esse accipiendum monemus etiam in Animadu. nostris ad Athenæum.co sensu & ἀποσκῖδναι vsurpabant. Vnde est ἀπόδοτος. Hermippus vetus comicus, vt ait Pollux, eum qui vinum de cupa sumserat, neque soluerat, ἀποδόξ[?] τὴν εἴρηκε, venustissimo ioco.
units.tr: It is said, "How much" [λέγεται πόσῳ]. We read this passage thus, and say, "How much? Say it" [Πόσῳ, εἰπεῖν]: "Kalathu" [Καλάθυ], which the Greek word [...] supports, with the word εἰπεῖν inserted, which is clearly missing. We think πόσῳ is a verb, not a noun, and the author used this verb again in the last chapter. It means to count up and reckon the account. Merchants usually work out the sum of goods sold, which they enter in the account book, when the money is not paid on the spot. Some learned men emend it to λογίζονται τῇ ποσῷ, but that is not even Greek, let alone worthy of one who found the name for language from divinity. At least they would say ἐλλείπειν, but even so it does not please. That he says [ὃ σχολάζω] should be understood of a slave who makes the demand. If Καλάθες were read for κα̃λ̃ε̃, it would mean "Pay now," which the Greeks say as [αὐλίθεν καλλέαλλε]. But there is no need to change anything, especially without old manuscripts, of which I would most of all wish to have access at this passage. There is no doubt that the distrust of merchants is being noted here. We advise that ἀποέσθαι be understood in this sense, as we also say in our notes on Athenaeus, and that ἀποσκίδναι was used in the same sense. Whence the word ἀπόδοτος. Hermippus, the old comic poet, as Pollux says, said of a man who had taken wine from the cask and not paid for it that he had [ἀποδόξ...], with a most charming jest.
On the chapter on ever-present surliness [ἀεὶ δυσχερείας].

units.la: Ταῦτα δὲ αὐτὰ συγγενῆ ἀρρωστήματα.) Appellat συγγενῆ quæ propriæ συγγενικὰ vt apud Plutarchum in Pericle: & paffim apud Galenum: qui non vno loco difputat contra fophiftas (fic enim appellat) qui dicebant ἡδὲν ἢ συγγενικὸν πάθος[?]. Sic συγγενῆ σημεῖα Ariftoteli quæ Straboni συγγενικά. Non funt autem συγγενῆ ἀρρωστήματα ingeniti morbi, vt docti viri vertunt: fed gentiles & auiti. Nam etfi fcio συγγενῆς interdum accipi pro σύμφυτος, ægrè tamen concefferim τόσον συγγενικῷ & σύμφυτον idem proprie fonare. Exiftimo enim proprie ῥύμφυτον νόσημα esse morbum qui ἀπὸ παιδὸς σωθῇ, ἢ συναιδρωθῇ, vt loquitur Hippocrates secundo prorrhetico. genitiuum morbum Latine dixerim: sicut dixit Ouidius genitiuam imaginem. Suetonius in Augusto genitiuas notas, hoc est σύμφυτα σημεῖα, non autem συγγενικά. Συγγενὴς enim vel συγγενικὸν est, quod à patre acceptum est, & vt hîc Theophrastus explicat cui pater aut auus ambóve fuerint obnoxij. Nam certum est morbos plerosque per successiones quasdam vt alia tradi. quin saepe accidit vt ex intervallo reddantur eaedem notae, iidem naevi morbíque in nepotibus, qui in filiis desiisse videbantur. Plutarchus De fera numinis vindicta Ἀκροχορδόρες, inquit, καὶ μελάσματα ἐ φακοὶ παλέρων ἐν παισὶν ἀφανιζόμενοι ἀνέκυψαν ὕστερον ἐν ἰψοῖς ἐ Ϙυλατρῖδος [?]. ἐλκὴ ἐχὴν ἐν τοῖς ἀιτικνημίοις.) Videtur haec ζυγέρια [?] frequentes per illa tempora Athenis fuisse: vt merito Theophrastus hanc notam nó praetermiserit. Nam etiam apud Aristophanem in Equitibus quo loco certant adulationis certamen Cleon & Agoracritus, sartor ille impurus pyxidem vnguenti pollicetur istiusmodi hominibus, quibus tibiarum vlcera sibi inungant. Haec sunt quae vocat Plinius tibiarum tetra vlcera, lib. xxi. 1. alibi tibiarum tadium, quod respondet voci Theophrasti ἀνδία. Ita affectos appellat ἀφροκνήμους [?] Dioscorides ἱξy' [?].
units.tr: These very diseases are συγγενῆ. He calls them συγγενῆ, which properly means hereditary (συγγενικά), as in Plutarch's Pericles, and often in Galen, who in more than one place argues against the sophists (so he calls them) who said that a disease was either ἡδὲν or συγγενικόν. So Aristotle's συγγενῆ σημεῖα are what Strabo calls συγγενικά. Nor are συγγενῆ ἀρρωστήματα ingeniti morbi (innate diseases), as learned men translate them, but gentiles & auiti (inherited from kin and grandparents). For although I know that συγγενής is sometimes taken to mean σύμφυτος, I could hardly concede that συγγενικός and σύμφυτος mean the same thing strictly. I think a σύμφυτον νόσημα properly means a disease that is contracted from childhood or sweated out together, as Hippocrates puts it in the second Prorrhetic. I would call it in Latin a genitive disease, as Ovid said genitiva imago. Suetonius in Augustus speaks of genitive marks, that is σύμφυτα σημεῖα, not συγγενικά. For συγγενής or συγγενικόν is what has been received from a father, and, as Theophrastus explains here, what a father or grandfather or both were liable to. For it is certain that most diseases are handed down through certain successions, as other things are. Indeed it often happens that the same marks and the same moles and diseases reappear after an interval in grandchildren, which seemed to have ceased in the children. Plutarch, in On the Delay of Divine Justice, says: "moles and freckles, which had disappeared in the children of the fathers, reappeared later in the offspring of their grandchildren…" ἕλκη on the shins [ἐλκὴ ἐν τοῖς ἀντικνημίοις]. These seem to have been common in Athens in those times, so Theophrastus rightly did not pass over this mark. For in Aristophanes' Knights, where Cleon and Agoracritus contend in a contest of flattery, the filthy tailor promises a box of ointment to such men, so that they may anoint their shin ulcers. These are what Pliny calls foul ulcers of the shins, book 21, and elsewhere the loathsomeness of the shins, which corresponds to Theophrastus' ἀνδία. Dioscorides calls those so afflicted ἀφροκνήμους.

units.la: Ἐγώ [?], inquit, κυλίχνιόν τε ἐ φάρμακον δίωμα [?], τὰν τοῖς ἀντικνημίοισιν ἐλκύδεια ἀξιαλείφῃ [?]. καὶ προσπλαῖσματα ἐν τοῖς ἀλλίλοις.] Sic vocat tubercula in manibus solita oriri, quae cutem non sinunt esse planam, sed asperam efficiunt: vnde etiam ἡ λέπρα nomen inuenit apud Graecos. Huius generis προσπλαίσματα[?] sunt ἀκροχορδόνες, μυρμηκίαι, δοθιῆνες[?], χοιράδες, & aliæ φυμάτων[?] species. Fuisse enim ἀνδρὲς[?] & δυσυιλίτες[?], qui haberent istiusmodi tubercula, etiam Horatius indicat,
units.tr: "I," he says, "[anoint] with a salve (?) for the shin ulcers…" and warts on the fingers [προσπλάσματα ἐν τοῖς δακτύλοις]. He calls by this name the little tubercles that commonly arise on the hands, which do not let the skin be smooth but make it rough; hence the Greeks also gave the name λέπρα (scaly disease). Of this kind are ἀκροχορδόνες, μυρμηκίαι, δοθιῆνες, χοιράδες, and other species of φύματα. That there were men with such tubercles, who were fastidious and unpleasant, Horace also indicates:

units.la: Qui ne tuberibus propriis offendat amicum Postulat, ignoscat verrucis illius.
units.tr: Since he asks that you not offend a friend with your own bumps, pardon the warts of that one.

units.la: Seneca, Papulas aberuant alienas, ipsi vlceribus obsiti. Possumus etiam paullò aliter προσπλαίσματα[?] ἐν τοῖς δακτύλοις[?] explicare: vt sint læsiones digitorum ex offensatione, hoc est ἐκ τῆς προσπλαίξης[?]: vt cum pes ad lapidem asperum offendit, & laceratur cutis, ac fit vulnus: aut cum ex pressura sanguis coit & corrumpitur. Sæpe enim accidit vt quæ ab initio neglecta sunt, magnum malum tandem afferant, ac nonnunquam integri membri perniciem: vbi semel διὰ[?] priùs vulnera mutarunt in καχοήθη[?] & ἀνίατα[?], & quæ medici Φηεωύματα[?] καὶ χειρώσεις[?] ἕλκη[?] ac τηλέφια[?] vocant, Plinius vlcera deperantia. Confirmat hanc interpretationem Pollux, qui notat digitorum χρύματα[?], hoc est læsiones ex offensione, προσπλαίσματα[?] appellari, ab Aristophane ἐπιπλασματα[?]. Et in libris medicorum προσπλασμα[?] est ἕλκος ἐκ τῆς προσπλάσεως. Idem fere προσπλάσματα[?]. de quo vide Eustathium.
units.tr: Seneca: They wander about pointing out the pimples of others, though themselves covered with sores. We could also explain προσπλάσματα ἐν τοῖς δακτύλοις somewhat differently: as injuries to the fingers from a knock, that is ἐκ τῆς προσπλάξεως, as when a foot strikes a rough stone and the skin is torn and a wound results; or when blood gathers from pressure and goes bad. For it often happens that things neglected at the start bring great evil in the end, and sometimes the ruin of a whole limb, when wounds that were at first simple have turned into malignant and incurable ones. Those that physicians call φηεώματα and χειρώσεις ulcers and τηλέφια, Pliny calls ulcers that spread. Pollux confirms this interpretation: he notes that injuries of the fingers from a blow are called προσπλάσματα, and Aristophanes calls them ἐπιπλάσματα. In medical books προσπλάσμα is an ulcer arising from the blow. Much the same is said of προσπλάσματα, on which see Eustathius.

units.la: τὰς μαχαίρας ϑηλυεράς[?] καὶ ἀλγεῖας[?] ἔχει[?]. Est figura ἐν ϛι ϙ ἀνδὶ[?]. ferinas & hirsutas alas habere, pro ferarum more hirsutas. Non temerè autem hæc dicit Theophrastus: inualuerat enim tunc temporis mos hic apud Athenienses, sanè ἀνδρεύς[?] & fœdus. Multi igitur quo magis viri fortes viderentur, & ab omni mollitie alieni, studuerunt hirsuti esse sub axillis. Nam quum in concionem venerant, in
units.tr: τὰς μασχάλας θηλυεράς καὶ ἀλγεινάς ἔχει (he has armpits that are female and painful?). This is a figure of speech: having wings (armpits) wild and hairy, hairy after the manner of wild beasts. Theophrastus does not say this at random: this custom had then taken hold among the Athenians, a manly and foul thing. So many, in order to seem the more manly and free of all softness, took care to be hairy under the armpits. For when they came to the assembly, at the voting, they bared that part, so that it could be seen by all when they had raised a hand or arm; and they counted it a credit to appear with that part of the side neglected and bristling with thick hair, and the whole flank rough.

units.la: Note: Greek forms in this page are read from a low-resolution scan; the Greek words marked [?] are uncertain. suffragiis ferendis, partem illam denudabant, vt posset ab omnibus, postquam manum vel brachium sustulerant, conspici. laudi autem ducebant videri habentes illam partem fruticante pilo neglectam, & totum latus horridum. Apud Ariftophanem Concionantibus mulier quædam indicare volens omnia fe fecisse per quæ latere in virorum cœtu posset, & pro viro haberi, sic infit,
units.tr: In casting their votes, they used to bare that part of the body, so that it could be seen by all once they had raised a hand or arm. They considered it a mark of distinction to appear with that part neglected, overgrown with bushy hair, and the whole side rough. In Aristophanes, a certain woman, wishing to show that she had done everything by which she could pass unnoticed in a gathering of men and be taken for a man, begins thus:

units.la: —πρῶτόν μὲν γ᾽ ἔγω τὰς μασχάλαςλόχμης ἀτυλέρας[?].
units.tr: —First of all, I pluck the armpits' thicket [πρῶτόν μὲν γ᾽ ἔγω τὰς μασχάλας λόχμης ἀτυλέρας].

units.la: Scholiaftes ibi, Ἐ[?]ρεῖλαν, inquit, τρίχας, ἵνα ἕως χρυσῶσι[?], ἀλοκῶσιν ἀνδρες[?]. Quod autem in ferendis suffragiis, quod χειροτονεῖν à sublatione manuum vocabant, latus nudarent, ex his apparet in eadem fabula,
units.tr: The scholiast there says: "[She] plucked the hairs so that, until ... the men ..." [ἐξείλαν τρίχας, ἵνα ἕως χρυσῶσι, ἀλοκῶσιν ἄνδρες]. That they used to bare the side in casting votes, which they called χειροτονεῖν [cheirotonein] from the raising of the hands, is clear from the same play:

units.la: Ἐκεῖνο δ᾽ ὃ πεφροντίκαμεν, ὅτῳ τρόπῳΤὰς χεῖρας αἴρειν μνημονεύομεν τότε.
units.tr: "That matter we considered, in what way we remember raising our hands then…"

units.la: Πρ. χαλεπὸν τὸ πρᾶγμα[?]. ὅμως ὁ χειροτονητέον[?].Ἐξωμισάσας τὸν ἕτερον βραχίονα[?].
units.tr: Pr.: "The thing is difficult. Nevertheless one must vote." …"lifting up the other arm…"

units.la: ἄχρι ὅτι πολὺ τῆς ἀλδρῶν[?]. ] Iuuenalis grandes alas appellat:
units.tr: "as far as much of the men's…" Juvenal calls them great wings:

units.la: Sed caput intactum buxo, naresque pilosasAdnotet, & grandes miretur Lelius alas.
units.tr: But he marks the head untouched by boxwood and the hairy nostrils, and Lelius marvels at the great wings.

units.la: Hispida membra quidem, & dura per brachia fetæ. Promittunt atrocem animum.
units.tr: Limbs indeed bristling, and hard through the arms, promise a fierce spirit.

units.la: Perfius, Hinc aliquis de gente hircofa centurionum.
units.tr: Persius: Hence someone of the goat-smelling race of centurions.

units.la: Constat verò apud Romanos sine vlla molitiei suspicione alas velli solitas: sed postea eò deliciarum ventum est, vt volsellis, pice, resina, & pumice brachia, crura, aliásque partes lævigarent: quam ad rem seruorum ministerio vtebantur, quos alipilos vel alipilarios vocarunt, Græci δρωπακισάς [?].
units.tr: It is certain that among the Romans armpits were commonly plucked without any suspicion of effeminacy; but later they came to such luxury that they smoothed arms, legs, and other parts with tweezers, pitch, resin, and pumice; for this purpose they used the services of slaves whom they called alipili or alipilarii, which the Greeks called ἀλοπακισταί.

units.la: τὰς ὀδόντας μέλανας, καὶ ἐξιομένας. ] Facetè dentes dixit ἐξιομένας, (Hippocrates & ἐξιομένας & βεβρω-μένας) cum potius iis conueniat vt fint ἐξίονλες [?].pari elegantia Symmachus, Rus, ait, quod folebat alere, nunc alitur. Plinius de fenè quodam, libro octauo epistolarum, Quinctiam (fœdum miferandúmque diEtu) dentes lauandos fricandósque prabebat. vbi fœdum miferandúmque, planè eft δυσχρές καὶ οἰκτρόν.
units.tr: "The teeth black and falling out" [τὰς ὀδόντας μέλανας, καὶ ἐξιομένας]. He wittily said "falling out" [ἐξιομένας] (Hippocrates uses both "falling out" [ἐξιομένας] and "eaten away" [βεβρωμένας]), though it would fit better to write "going out" [ἐξίοντες]. Symmachus, with equal elegance, says: "What used to nourish him is now itself nourished." Pliny, in the eighth book of his Letters, speaks of an old man: "Moreover (a foul and pitiable thing to tell) he offered his teeth to be washed and rubbed." Here "foul and pitiable" is plainly [δυσχρές καὶ οἰκτρόν] "disgusting and wretched".

units.la: καὶ τὰ Θιαῦτα. ] Simile illi capite Περὶ βδελυείας, τὰ ὃ δὲ Θιαῦτα, καὶ Φ. Hæc autem quæ sequuntur, etsi fœda sunt, & βδελυείας μεγὰ, alia tamen fœditate laborant, quàm præcedentia. Ideo videtur quodammodo à superioribus ea distinguere voluisse.
units.tr: "And such things" [καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα]. This is like the passage in the chapter On Disgustingness, "and such things" [τὰ δὲ τοιαῦτα], and then the letter Phi. The things that follow, though foul and of the same kind of disgust, suffer from a different foulness than those before. So he seems in some way to have wished to distinguish them from the earlier ones.

units.la: δύεν ἀρξάμυρ προσλαλεῖν.) Nihil mutauimus, libris non addicentibus. Notat iftum, cum facra facit lingua non fauere, quod factum oportuit, vt mox dicemus. Non difpliceat mihi fi ἐξίν legatur: Clemens Alexandr. Pædagogi libro 11. ᾱ̃αφ̓υ-λακλέον καὶ τὸ φθέγγεσθαι ὅ τι ἂν ἐξίονα ἄμα. ἀφειτης γὰ καὶ ἀτημῶν ἢ φωνὴ ᾱ̃ , πλήρεσ ζ̃ς γνάθοις ςεγοχω-ρυμένη.
units.tr: "Beginning to speak to" [ἄρξαμεν προσλαλεῖν]. I have changed nothing, as the books do not support it. He notes that such a man, when he performs sacred rites, does not keep his tongue favourable, which ought to have been done, as we shall say shortly. I would not object if "going out" [ἐξίν] were read. Clement of Alexandria, in the second book of the Paedagogus: "One must guard against even speaking whatever comes out at the same time. For the voice that comes from an unguarded and unrestrained mouth, full of spittle, is..."

units.la: καὶ Σποφίτιλν Ἀπὸ τὲ σόμαλ. ) Quid emittit? fputum nempe, hoc eft τὸν σιαλον : vnde σιαλόχυς iftos Græci vocitarunt. Hefychius, Σιαλόχυς, τὰς προσπαίσον ὁ σιαλον ἐν τῷ προσδέχεσθαι. extat & verbum σιαλοχίν apud Hippocratem 11 1.de morbis. Ab hoc vitio nomen inuenit olim Athenis Antimachus quidam Ψακὰς cognominatus: quia, inquit comici fcholiaftes, προσερρᾶνε τὰς σωομαλῶνες δλαλεγόμυρ. Iuuenalis,
units.tr: "And spitting out from the mouth" [καὶ σποφίτιλν ἀπὸ τὸ στόματος]. What does he eject? Spittle, that is [τὸν σίαλον]; hence the Greeks called such people "spitters" [σιαλόχυς]. Hesychius: "Sialochys: one who sprinkles spittle on those who receive him." The verb "to spit" [σιαλοχεῖν] also occurs in Hippocrates, Book 2 of the Diseases. From this vice a certain Antimachus at Athens was once nicknamed "Psakas", because, as the comic scholiast says, he sprinkled those who were speaking with spittle. Juvenal:

units.la: Tunc immensa catu sperant mendacia filles Conspuitúrque sinus.
units.tr: "Then the wretched girls hope for immense lies, and their bosoms are spat upon."

units.la: ἅμα πιεῖν, προσερπύζ.) Fortasse ἅμα τῷ πιεῖν, aut πίνων.
units.tr: "To drink at the same time, creeping forward." Perhaps "at the same time as drinking", or "while drinking".

units.la: ἐλαίῳ (Φαῶ[?]) ἐν βαλανείῳ λεξίθῳ[?]) Putà, oleo lucernario, quo infimæ fortis quidam se inungebant.
units.tr: "With oil in the bath" [ἐλαίῳ ἐν βαλανείῳ]. Think of lamp oil, with which the lowest sort of men anointed themselves.

units.la: —vngor oliuo, Non quo fraudatis immundus Natta lucernis. Iuuenalis in quinta, —at hic qui Pallidus offertur misero tibi caulis olebit Lucernam. illud enim vestibus[?] datur alueolis quod Canna Micipsarum prora subuexit acuta: Propter quod Romæ cum Bocchare nemo lauatur. Vngebantur pauperes & γλαύκῳ[?] hoc est, olei strigmentis, vt indicat locus Teletis quem supra protulimus.
units.tr: "I am anointed with olive oil, not like the filthy Natta with his cheated lamps." And Juvenal in the fifth satire: "But the pale cabbage that is offered to you, the lamp will make it smell..." For that is given in the vessels which the sharp prow of Micipsa's ship brought from Canna. For this reason nobody at Rome bathes with Bocchar. The poor were anointed, and [γλαύκῳ], that is, with scrapings of oil, as the passage of Teletes which we quoted above shows.

units.la: εἰς ἀγορὰν ἐξελθεῖν. ) In hoc est ἡ δυσχέρεια: nam veteribus in foro honestè vestiri moris erat: domi quod satis esset. aliud enim homini, aliud humanitati satis esse censebant, vt ait Varro. Inde est vestis alia domestica, siue οἰκιακή: alia forensis, siue εἰς ἀγορὰν προσερχομένων, Ciceroni ac Suetonio & Plutarcho in Sylla. Qui igitur fœdè vestiti in publicum prodirent, odio erant & irrisui, vt indicat Iuuenalis satyra III. De munditia in vestitu locus elegans Senecæ epistola XCIII. Munda vestis electio appetenda est hominis: Natura enim homo mundum & elegans animal est. Itaque non est bonum per se munda vestis, sed munda vestis electio: quia non in re bonum est, sed in electione: quia actiones nostræ honestæ sunt, non ipsa quæ aguntur. Quod de veste dixi, idem de corpore me existima dicere. εἰς ἀποθεωσκόντως τῆς μητρὸς ἐξελθόσης, βλασφημήσαι.) Vertunt, quum egreditur mater. sed ἐξελθόσης, dixit Theophrastus, non ἐξερχομένης. De eo loquitur qui matri adsit sacra facienti ex præcepto auguris. Fuere linguis olim in re sacra, vel maxima religionis pars erat. Fuebant autem linguis duobus modis: vel silentes: vel si loquerentur, male ominatis verbis parcentes. Itaque non solùm in templis præcones fauentiam imperabant, ut ex Plutarchi Theseo, Festo, & tragicis notum: sed etiam cum indicerentur feriae[?], populus per eosdem præcones monebatur, ut à litibus iurgiisque abstinerent, & ut loquitur Attius, ore obscœna dicta segregarent. quod & ait M. Tullius, & diserte præcipit Plato in undecimo Legum. cui legi non multum dissimilem Solonis legem Plutarchus in vita refert.
units.tr: "To go out into the market" [εἰς ἀγορὰν ἐξελθεῖν]. Here lies the offence: for it was the custom among the ancients to dress decently in the forum, while at home whatever was enough. For they thought one thing enough for a man and another enough for civility, as Varro says. Hence there is one domestic dress, or [οἰκιακή], and another for the forum, or [εἰς ἀγορὰν προσερχομένων], as Cicero, Suetonius and Plutarch in his Sulla say. Those, then, who came out in public foully dressed were hated and mocked, as Juvenal shows in Satire 3. On cleanliness in dress there is a fine passage in Seneca's Epistle 93: "A clean choice of clothing is to be sought by a man; for by nature man is a clean and elegant animal. So a clean garment is not good in itself, but the choice of a clean garment is: because it is not the thing that is good, but the choice; because our actions are honourable, not the things we do." What I have said of clothing, I think I am saying of the body too. [εἰς ἀποθεωσκόντως τῆς μητρὸς ἐξελθόσης, βλασφημῆσαι]. They translate it "when the mother goes out", but Theophrastus said "having gone out" [ἐξελθόσης], not "going out" [ἐξερχομένης]. He speaks of one who is present at his mother's sacrifice on the augur's instruction. In sacred matters the ancients kept silence, and this was the greatest part of religion. They kept silence in two ways: either by being quiet, or, if they spoke, by sparing words of ill omen. So not only in temples did the heralds order silence, as is known from Plutarch's Theseus, from Festus and the tragedians, but also when holidays were proclaimed, the people were warned by the same heralds to refrain from quarrels and brawling, and, as Attius puts it, to keep obscene words apart from the mouth. Marcus Tullius says the same, and Plato clearly prescribes it in the eleventh book of the Laws. Plutarch in his Life reports a law of Solon not very different from this law.

units.la: Græci ἐυφημεῖν[?] hoc dicunt: cui opponitur βλασφημεῖν[?], qua notione hic accipitur & sæpe apud Platonem. Plautus in Cafina benedicere dixit τὸ ἐυφημεῖν[?] vel ἐυφημεῖν[?] μετ' ἐυφημίας. At τὸ βλασφημεῖν eidem in Asinaria obscœnare dicitur: in Cafina omen alicui vituperare. Tunc autem plurimum videntur existimata nocere verba male ominata, quando à cognatis pronunciarentur. Plato septimo legum, Θυσίας [?]μένης καὶ ἱερῶν καθθέντων [?] νόμον, εἰ τῷ τίς φαμέν, ἰδίᾳ [?] προσχῶς τῆς βωμοῖς τε καὶ ἱεροῖς υἱὸς ἀ ἀδελφὸς βλασφημοῖ [?] ταλὰν βλασφημίαν, ἀρ ἐκ ἀν φαίμην ἀθυμίαν καὶ καλῶ ὅταν τ' μανίσιν πανεί τε καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀν οἰκείοις φθίνοιτο ἐχλθεῖς[?]. propterea ait Theophrastus τῆς μητρός.
units.tr: The Greeks call this "speaking auspiciously" [εὐφημεῖν], and its opposite is "to speak ill-omened" [βλασφημεῖν], which is the sense in which it is understood here and often in Plato. Plautus in the Casina used "to bless" for [εὐφημεῖν], or "to speak auspiciously with good omen". But in the Asinaria "to speak ill-omened" [βλασφημεῖν] is said of the same word as "to speak obscenely"; in the Casina it means to disparage someone with an ill omen. Words of ill omen seem then to have been thought most harmful when they were spoken by kinsmen. Plato, Laws 7: "When sacrifices are being offered and sacred rites are established by law, if anyone, whether a father, a mother, a brother, or a sister, should speak ill-omened words privately, in the presence of the altars and the sacred things..." Hence Theophrastus says "of the mother".

units.la: Porro quæ fuerint illa verba à quibus abstinendum esset in sacris, sciremus si pervenisset ad nos Suetonij liber cuius hodie superest solùm index De vocibus male ominatis. vide Artemidorum libro 1 1 1. capite xxxv111. Conftat fanè miram fuiffe veterum hac in re fuperftitionem :erant enim pene infinita,quæ nominare religio effet. Ac quoniam venit mihi in mentem loci cuiufdam Demofthenis,vbi eft talis ὀτλείας exemplum,quod doctiffimus eius interpres non animaduertit, obiter cum proferam & illuftrabo In ea contra Leptinem de veterum præmiis loquens, τότε μὲν, inquit, ἡ πόλις ἡμῶν, καὶ τῆς ἀπορίας, [?] χρημάτων, [?] τῶν ἄλλο διαφορά [?]. Δεῖ γὰρ ὅτῳ λέγειν, ὃ μὴ βλασφημεῖν. Eruditissimus Vvolfius βλασφημεῖν vertit conuiciari, non rectè profectò. nam hoc voluit Demofthenes, religionem effe fibi,dicere Rempublicam ἀτοπία :idque verbum à fe refpui propter ominis diritatem: ideo dicit ἀτοπώτερος quia dicere ἄτοπα non audebat, ἀτοπεῖ non poterat. Neque aliter fcholiorum Græcorum auctor interpretatur: quem cauffa non erat cur hic non fequeretur Vvolfius. Terentius,
units.tr: Moreover, we would know what those words were from which one had to abstain in sacred rites if the book of Suetonius had come down to us, of which today there survives only the index, On Words of Ill Omen. See Artemidorus, book 3, chapter 38. It is clear that the superstition of the ancients in this matter was remarkable, for there were almost countless things which religion forbade one to name. And since a passage of Demosthenes has come into my mind, where there is such an example of ill-omened speech, which his most learned commentator has not noticed, I shall quote and illustrate it in passing. In his speech against Leptines, speaking of the rewards of the ancients, he says: "Then our city, both through want of money and through the other differences..." For one must say what it is not allowed to speak ill-omened. The most learned Wolf translated [βλασφημεῖν] as "to revile", which is certainly not right. For Demosthenes meant that it was a religious scruple for him to say that the Republic was in an [ἀτοπία], an absurd condition; and he rejected that word because of the ominous harshness of it. So he says [ἀτοπώτερος] "more absurd", because he did not dare to say [ἄτοπα] "absurd things", and could not say [ἀτοπεῖ]. Nor does the author of the Greek scholia interpret it otherwise, and there was no reason why Wolf should not have followed him here. Terence:

units.la: Fide dem, rectè eft: nam non habere me religio eft dicere.
units.tr: "I give you my word, it is right: for it is a religious scruple for me to say that I have not..."

units.la: non ouum ouo magis fimile. Sic βλάσφημον εἰπεῖν apud eundem alibi.
units.tr: "No egg more like an egg." So elsewhere in the same author, [βλάσφημον εἰπεῖν] "to speak ill-omened".

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] Scribendum eft ἐκβαλεῖν τὸ πλεῖον. ficut apud Plutarchum in Craffo iii fimillima re, [?] ἐξεβάλλετο, [?] id quod vifum effe ait circunstantibus vere [?] & trifte. Hæc funt quæ Romani caduca auspicia vocabant. Feftus Caduca auspicia dicunt, cum aliquid in templo excidit, veluti virga è manu. Non hoc dicit Feftus (quod putat fummus Scaliger) tum demum caducum effe aufpicium; fi è manu flaminis commentaculum virga excidiset: sed quoties aliquid excidisset, puta spondeum vt hoc loco Theophrasti: aut victima, vel τὰ σωλάχνα, vt Crasso accidit. aut de capite sacrificantis vitta, quod de Syrhace canit Silius Italicus. Simile est quod notat Cicero De aruspicum responsis, ludos esse non rite factos, fi puer patrimus & matrimus tensam aut lorum omitteret. Meminerat iterum Festus huius superstitionis in voce silere, quantum ex iis quae supersunt licet coniicere.
units.tr: [illegible, about twelve letters] It should be written [ἐκβαλεῖν τὸ πλεῖον]. Likewise in Plutarch's Crassus, in a very similar matter, [ἐξεβάλλετο], which he says seemed to the bystanders truly sad and sorrowful. These are what the Romans called "falling auspices" [caduca auspicia]. Festus says: "They call them falling auspices when something falls in the temple, such as a staff from the hand." Festus does not say (as the great Scaliger thinks) that the omen is then only falling if the staff falls from the priest's hand; but whenever something fell, for instance a libation, as in this passage of Theophrastus, or a victim, or [τὰ σπλάγχνα], as happened to Crassus, or a fillet from the head of the sacrificer, as Silius Italicus sings of Syrhax. Similar is what Cicero notes in On the Responses of the Haruspices: that the games were not properly celebrated if a boy with a patrimus and matrimus should drop the rope or the thong. Festus again mentions this superstition under the word "to be silent", as far as one may conjecture from what survives.

units.la: ἀπελάσας ὁ βλάπτων ὑπὲρ τῆς τῷ.) Nihil hoc foedius, nihil spurcius: verùm praeterea notandum est, non δυσχέρειαν tantùm hic esse: sed etiam, vt sunt concatenata vitia, saltum, & conuiuarum contemtum. Olim enim in conuiuiis aut aliis congressionibus, procul spuere signum habebatur eminentiae. Plautus dixit magnificè conscreare: Quintilianus, clare exscreare. Sotades apud Stobaeum:
units.tr: "Having driven away the one who harms for the sake of..." [ἀπελάσας ὁ βλάπτων ὑπὲρ τῆς τῷ]. Nothing more foul, nothing more filthy. But it must further be noted that this is not only a matter of offensiveness, but also, as vices are linked together, of boastfulness and contempt for one's fellow diners. For in the old days, at banquets or other gatherings, to spit far off was regarded as a sign of eminence. Plautus said "to spit out magnificently" [magnificè conscreare]; Quintilian, "to spit out loudly" [clare exscreare]. Sotades in Stobaeus:

units.la: Εἰ δ' βασιλεὺς πέφυκας, ὡς ὄντες ἀνέχειν' Ἂν μακρὰ πύλης, φλεγμαίνει κραλῆ ἀξιοσῳ' Ἀνιδίματῆς, ταῦτα προ τε προβατικὸν ἔχεν.
units.tr: "But if you were born a king, as you seem to be, you hold the gate far off, and the head burns with a worthless fever. These things you possess before the cattle-like crowd." [Εἰ δ' βασιλεὺς πέφυκας, ὡς ὄντες ἀνέχειν' Ἂν μακρὰ πύλης, φλεγμαίνει κραλῆ ἀξιοσῳ' Ἀνιδίματῆς, ταῦτα προ τε προβατικὸν ἔχεν.]

units.la: Praeclarè verò Clemens Alexandrinus, de hoc ipso loquens 1 1. Paedagogi, ἐν ἐρωχίας δ' ἀξίας συμβολον, τὸ προδεῖναι τὶς ἡχοῖς ἐθέλειν, μὴ ἀχί ἀφαιρεῖν. Sic & plurimum tussire potentiorum erat tantum. Petronius, Secundum hanc formulam imperamus Eumolpo vt plurimum tussiat, vt fit solutioris stomachi, cibosque omnes palam damnet, loquatur aurum & argentum, fundi fque mendaces. Erant item argumenta potentiae cervices inflectere, & altum loqui, vt ex Plutarchi Pyrrho & Demosthene intelligitur.
units.tr: Clement of Alexandria speaks admirably about this very thing, in the Paedagogus: "To wish to spit forth in the presence of a superior is a sign of worth, not to take it away." [ἐν ἐρωχίας δ' ἀξίας συμβολον, τὸ προδεῖναι τὶς ἡχοῖς ἐθέλειν, μὴ ἀχί ἀφαιρεῖν.] So too, to cough a great deal was a mark only of the powerful. Petronius: "According to this formula we order Eumolpus to cough frequently, as happens with a rather loose stomach, and to condemn all foods openly, to talk of gold and silver, and of lying estates." There were also signs of power: to bend the neck and to speak haughtily, as is understood from Plutarch's Pyrrhus and Demosthenes.

units.la: Ἔστι ἡ ἀνδία.] Iam diximus ad caput superius. Parum autem differre δυσχέρειαν & ἀνδίαν, etiam ex eo discimus, quod Plato & Demosthenes saepe utramque vocem pro eodem vsurpant, quod à nobis est obseruatum. Sed & apud alios scriptores has voces saepe coniunctas leges: vt cum Isocrates in Æginetica, morbo Trasylochi tribuit δυσχέρειαν & ἀνδίαν simul: & cum exponunt veteres critici prouerbium ἀλλὰ δρυός. scribunt enim dici ἐπὶ τῶν δυσχερῶς καὶ ἀνδῶς ἐξιόντων. ὑστερον ἡ καλλιόν τι ἀρχόντων. Latissime sane vox ἀνδία patet, & quae saepe nihil aliud quàm ineptitudo, aut φιλοτιμίτης significat. Possis pro loco recte vertere insulsitatem, vel taedium, aut odium. quanquam Plautus & Terentius ipsum potius τὸν ἀνδῆ odium appellare solent. Plautus in Milite, incommoditatem dixit τῷ ἀνδίαν: vt contra tam apud ipsum quàm apud alios veteres ipsumque adeo M. Tullium, commodus est is qui opponitur τῷ ἀνδεῖ. cuius hominis habes graphicam descriptionem in Milite Plautina, scen. Cohibere intra lim. illo loco. Et ego amoris, &c. Notabis vocē ἀνδὴς & eum significare qui tedio est, & eum qui est fastidiosus. Nam ira quoque vsurparunt. Aristoteles Magnorum moralium, libro secundo, ὁ πλοῦτος πολὺς χρώμενος [?] ὑπερβάλλεται καὶ ἀνδεῖς ἐποίησεν. Diuitiarum accessio superbos & fastidiosos, morosque efficere solet. Par huic vox veterum Latinorum Tædulus. vide Festum.
units.tr: "It is ἀνδία." We have already spoken of this at the previous chapter. We learn from this that δυσχέρεια and ἀνδία differ little, because Plato and Demosthenes often use both words for the same thing, as I have observed. But in other writers you will also often find these words joined together: as when Isocrates, in the Aeginetica, assigns to the illness of Trasylochus both δυσχέρεια and ἀνδία at once; and when the ancient critics explain the proverb ἀλλὰ δρυός, for they write that it is said of those who go out with difficulty and ἀνδῶς, or of those who go out to something better of the magistrates. The word ἀνδία has a very wide range, and it often means nothing other than ineptitude or φιλοτιμία. You could rightly translate it, according to the place, as insipidity, or tedium, or hatred, although Plautus and Terence usually call the thing itself, the ἀνδής, hatred. In the Miles gloriosus Plautus called it inconvenience (ἀνδία); on the other hand, both in him and in other ancient writers, and indeed in Marcus Tullius himself, the one opposed to the ἀνδής is the agreeable (commodus) man. You have a vivid description of such a person in the Plautine Miles, in the scene at that place: Restrain yourself within the threshold, and then And I, of love, etc. You will notice that the word ἀνδής signifies both one who is a bore and one who is fastidious. For they also used it in this sense. Aristotle, in the second book of the Magna Moralia: "Wealth, when used in abundance, goes beyond measure and makes men arrogant and fastidious." The accession of riches usually makes men proud, fastidious and morose. A word of the ancient Latins similar to this is tædulus; see Festus.

units.la: [?]ἀναγκάζειν μέλλοντας, κωλύειν.) Non displiceret μειλίχῳ. Sensus erit: Solet retinere amicum qui iam nauim soluebat,& eius comites rogare, vt tantisper expectent donec aliquot cum illo suo amico spatia confecerit.
units.tr: "Those about to set out, hindering." Μειλίχῳ would not be displeasing. The sense will be: it is customary to keep back a friend who was already casting off the ship, and to ask his companions to wait a little while, until he has covered some distance with that friend.

units.la: μασσώμυλον σιτίζειν αὐτός. ) Infigniter lapsi sunt interpretes non animaduerso vnius literulae mendo. Legendum enim μασσώμυλος, non μασσώμυλον. Iam quod iidem μασσᾶσθαι interpretantur mammam fugere, puerilis est in re puerili error. Σιτίζειν dicuntur nutrices suos alumnos quando illis mansum ex ore suo cibum in os indunt: ipsi autem pueri λωυίζεσθαι. Aristophanes Equitibus.
units.tr: "He himself feeds the mass-sucker." The interpreters have slipped badly, not noticing a mistake of a single letter. For it should be read μασσώμυλος, not μασσώμυλον. As for their rendering of μασσᾶσθαι as "to flee the breast," it is a childish error about a childish matter. Nurses are said σιτίζειν their charges when they put chewed food from their own mouths into the infants' mouths; the children themselves are said λωυίζεσθαι. Aristophanes, in the Knights:

units.la: ΚΛ. Εσίσαμαι γὰρ αὐτὸν οἷς λωυίζεται.
units.tr: CLEON: For I see him being fed in the way that he is.

units.la: ΑΛ. Καθὼς περ αἳ τίτθαι σιτίζουσι κακῶς.
units.tr: SAUSAGE-SELLER: Just as the nurses feed them badly.

units.la: Μασσώμυλος γάρ, τὰ μὲν ὀλίγον ἐτιθεὶς.
units.tr: For he is a chewer-feeder, who gives only a little.
But he himself has swallowed that much over.

units.la: καὶ ἐπιζωοεῖσθαι ποιητικόν. ] Signate loquitur: Est enim proprie ἐπιζωοεῖσθαι, τὸ τοῖς παισὶ ἀρὸς ψυ-χαγωγίαν λέγειν τινά, cum infantibus nutricum more balbutire. Inde ad aliatransfertur, quoties pro duriore voce mollior vsurpatur & minimè odiosa. Cicero Attico, Video infinitum bellum,iunctum miserrima fuga, quam tu peregrinationem ἐπιζωοεῖζη. Accipitur & aliter.Sed hæc vulgò nota.Ποσπυζειν vox est ὀνομαζωσιν θεῖα pulchre ad imitationem eius qui voce blanditur, siue infanti siue equo. ponitur & pro manu blădiente permu'cere, siue χαῤῥίζειν.
units.tr: "And to be cooed over is a poetic word." He speaks precisely: ἐπιζωοεῖσθαι properly means to speak to children with a kind of soothing babble, as nurses babble with infants. From there it is transferred to other things whenever a gentler word is used for a harsher one and not in a hateful sense. Cicero to Atticus: "I see an endless war joined to the most wretched flight, which you soothingly call a journey" (ἐπιζωοεῖζη). It is also taken in another way, but these things are commonly known. ποσπυζειν [ποσπυζειν] is an onomatopoeic word, aptly imitating one who coaxes with the voice, whether an infant or a horse. It is also used for stroking with a caressing hand, or χαρίζειν.

units.la: καὶ ζωμὸς τὸ πεφρυμένον. ] Scribendum est, καὶ ζωμὸς τὸ πεφρυμένον, εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἐν τοῖς ἐπιχωρίμασιν αὐτοῦ μελαντέρα ἢ χολή. Est autem τι pro τινός. Intelligit ius nigrum,quod ἐξεσμα Λακωνικὸν à Grammaticis dicitur, quia plurimus eius vsus Lacedæmone : eratque hoc in eorum phiditiis coenæ caput,vt ait etiam Cicero : sed & aliæ gentes Græciæ eo vsæ. vide Athenæum.
units.tr: "And broth, the burnt." It should be written: "and broth, the burnt," saying that in his local dishes the bile is blacker. The τι stands for τινός. He means the black broth, which the grammarians call the Laconian ἔξεσμα, because it was used most at Lacedaemon; it was the chief dish of their common meals, as Cicero also says, but other peoples of Greece also used it. See Athenaeus.

units.la: ἐναντίον τῆς οἰκείων.) Quod tempus alios sermones postulabat. Peccat igitur inscitia temporis: éstque non solum ἀνδρῖς, sed etiam ἀκαιρῶς.
units.tr: "Contrary to the (time) of the household." This time demanded other conversation. The fault, therefore, is ignorance of time, and it is not only ungracious (ἀνδρῖς) but also untimely (ἀκαιρῶς).

units.la: ὅτι ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ ὅξι παρ' αὐτῷ λακκαῖον.) Etsi aliud est λάκκος, aliud ψυχρὸν, siue ὑδροψύχιον, hoc est, frigidarium : tamē,vt vides etiam λάκκοι à frigiditate cómendabantur.Macho poëta apud Atheneum.
units.tr: "That cold water and a pool are there with him." Although a λάκκος is one thing and cold water, or the ὑδροψύχιον, that is, a cold bath, is another, nevertheless, as you see, pools were also commended for their coolness. Macho the poet, in Athenaeus: [ὅτι ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ ὅξι παρ' αὐτῷ λακκαῖον.]

units.la: Νὴ τὸ Αθηναῖον & Ζεὺς ψυχρόν γ' ἔφη[?] Γνάθων' ἔχεις τὸν λάκκον ὁμολογούμενος.
units.tr: "By the Athenian... and Zeus, cold, said Gnathon. You have the pool, as you agree."

units.la: Frigida delectatos fuisse veteres Græcos constat: an calida vterentur quæ postea fuit in deliciis,quærit Pollux libro ix.
units.tr: It is established that the ancient Greeks enjoyed cold things. Whether they used warm baths, which later became fashionable, Pollux asks in book 9.

units.la: Δεῖξαι τὸν παράσιτον αὐτῷ σοῖος τις.) Suos enim parasitos ostentabant. Itaque ait ille in auctione parasitica apud comicum,
units.tr: "To show him his parasite, what sort he is." For they displayed their parasites. Hence that man says in the parasitic auction in the comic poet:

units.la: — nemo meliores dabit: Nullis melioresesse parasitos sinam.
units.tr: — no one will give better ones: I would not allow there to be better parasites than these.

units.la: ἐπὶ τὸ σολνείας. hoc est Super cœnam, vel inter cœnam. Plutarchus in Alexandro, ἐπαινέσαι κελευσθεὶς ἐπὶ τὸ σολνείᾳ Μακεδόνας ὁ Καλλισθένης. Plato in Conuiuio, ἐπὶ τῇ κύλικι λέγει. Vox ὅτι, vel παρέλκει, vel etiam fortasse tolli debet.
units.tr: "At the dinner," that is, over dinner, or during dinner. Plutarch in Alexander: "Callisthenes, being bidden to praise the Macedonians at dinner" (ἐπὶ τὸ σολνείᾳ). Plato in the Symposium: "he speaks over the cup" (ἐπὶ τῇ κύλικι). The word ὅτι, or παρέλκει, or perhaps even the whole phrase, ought to be removed.
On the chapter concerning petty ambition [περὶ μικροφιλοτιμίας].

units.la: Hδὲ[?] μικροφιλοτιμία.) Est hoc vnum è vitiis illis quæ circa τιμὴν καὶ ἀτιμίαν versantur: sunt enim non pauca,sed quæ fere nomine careāt. Aristoteles præcipua tantùm explicat, χαυνότητα [?] & μι-κροψυχίαν. istud autem vitium quod hoc capite describit Theophrastus, obiter tantū attingit in IIII. Nicomacheorum: quo loco ait eum qui sit μεγα-λόψυχος [?] & τὰς αὐτὰς τῆς τυχούσας [?] ὀλιγωρήσῃ [?] τιμῆς [?]. Nihil enim aliud est μικροφιλοτιμία, quàm cupiditas honoris siue laudis, vel, vt dicam melius, laudationis ἐπὶ μικροῖς, ob minuta quædam & parua. Atque hanc cupiditatem verissimè Theophrastus illiberalem iudicat. Neque verò vnicum est istorum hominum genus, sed duplex: sunt enim quidam φιλότιμοι, necessariò μικροφιλότιμοι: eos dico, qui vellent quidem laudem posse mereri alia ratione: sed quia inopes sunt & iis præsidiis destituuntur, quæ ad consequendos honores veros desiderantur: (ferè enim ἀμφὶ τιμὰς, vt ait Pindarus, μάρναται δαπάναι [?].) qua possunt ratione tentant innotescere, & vt laudentur, versentúrque in hominum ore efficere. Atqui satius erat, sua forte contentum, abstinere ab omni tali cupiditate. Hanc paupertatem ambitiosam vocat Iuuenalis. Alterum genus est eorum qui simul duobus morbis grauissimis tenentur, ambitione & auaritia. Hos vt honores affectent, impellit ambitio: vt non rectam viam insistant, sed sumtus maximè fugiant, facit auaritia. Μικροφιλοτιμίαν autem possis Latinè dicere ambitionem gloriæ ineptam & sordidam: vel ineptam & friuolam sicut A. Gellius ostentationem ineptam & friuolam dixit. & apud eundem, homo inepte gloriosus libro XIII. non longè abest ἀπὸ τῆς μικροφιλοτιμίας.
units.tr: This small-mindedness about honour (μικροφιλοτιμία) is one of those vices that concern τιμή and ἀτιμία [honour and dishonour]. There are not a few of them, but most have almost no name of their own. Aristotle explains only the chief ones, χαυνότης [vainglory] and μικροψυχία [pusillanimity]. The vice that Theophrastus describes in this chapter he touches on only in passing, in Book IV of the Nicomachean Ethics, where he says that the magnanimous man (μεγαλόψυχος) would disregard the same honours that ordinary people value. For μικροφιλοτιμία is nothing other than a desire for honour or praise, or, to put it more precisely, for praise over petty and trifling things (ἐπὶ μικροῖς). Theophrastus rightly judges this desire to be illiberal. Nor is there only one kind of such people, but two. There are some who are φιλότιμοι [lovers of honour] and so necessarily μικροφιλότιμοι [small-minded in their love of honour]. I mean those who would like to earn praise by some other means but, being poor and lacking the resources needed to win true honours, try by whatever means they can to make themselves known, to be praised, and to be talked about on people's lips. (For, as Pindar says, expense (δαπάνη) generally wrestles over honours.) Yet it would have been better to be content with one's lot and to abstain from every such desire. Juvenal calls this kind of poverty "ambitious poverty." The other kind is of those who are held at once by two very serious diseases, ambition and avarice. Ambition drives them to seek honours, and avarice makes them avoid expense above all, so that they do not take the straight road. Μικροφιλοτιμία you could render in Latin as a silly and mean-spirited ambition for glory, or silly and frivolous, as Aulus Gellius wrote ostentation that is silly and frivolous, and in the same author a man foolishly boastful (Book XIII) is not far from μικροφιλοτιμία.

units.la: καὶ τὸν υἱὸν Ξενοκράτους, ἀναλαμβάνων εἰς Δελφούς. ] Athenis fuit hic mos: Iuuenes comam alcbant ad annos pubertatis: tum à parentibus ad tribules adducebantur, vt comam tonderent, quæ μαλλὸς & κομὸς dicebatur. fere autem & Græci & Romani comam hanc primam alicui deo consecrabant: & cum illam alere se in eius honorem dicebant: rum vbi tonderentur, illam in eius Dei templo ponebant: cuius rei apud Pindarum, Æschylum, Festum, aliósque sunt testimonia. Ac videntur vulgo Athenienses Herculi consecrare soliti aut alicui alij deo cuius templum esset in vrbe. Hesychius: Ἀθήνησιν οἱ μέλλοντες ἐφηβεύειν πρὶν ἀποκεῖραι τὸν μαλλὸν, εἰσέφερον Ἡρακλεῖ μέτρον οἶνον, καὶ ἀπολυόμενοι τῆς σωφροσύνης ἐπεδήλουν τοῖς ... [?] οἰνισ[?]ήσια. Ita igitur vulgus: at qui supra vulgus existimari volebant, antiquo Atheniensium instituto, cuius meminit Plut. in Thefeo, comam filiorum suorum Apollini Pythio consecrabant, & quum tempus aduenerat Delphos suos filios adducebant, vt ibi comam deponerent. quod auctor vult esse μικροφιλοτιμίας indicium.
units.tr: "and the son of Xenocrates, when taking him up to Delphi" [καὶ τὸν υἱὸν Ξενοκράτους, ἀναλαμβάνων εἰς Δελφούς]. At Athens this was the custom. Young men let their hair grow until the age of puberty; then their parents brought them to the tribes to have their hair cut, which was called μαλλός or κομός. Generally both Greeks and Romans consecrated this first hair to some god, saying that they let it grow in his honour, and when it was cut they placed it in that god's temple. There are testimonies to this in Pindar, Aeschylus, Festus and others. The Athenians seem commonly to have consecrated it to Hercules, or to some other god whose temple was in the city. Hesychius: "At Athens, those about to become ephebi, before shearing their hair, brought a measure of wine to Hercules, and, released from restraint, they showed..." [Ἀθήνησιν οἱ μέλλοντες ἐφηβεύειν πρὶν ἀποκεῖραι τὸν μαλλὸν, εἰσέφερον Ἡρακλεῖ μέτρον οἶνον]. Thus the common people did it. But those who wished to be thought above the common people, following the ancient Athenian institution (which Plutarch mentions in his Theseus), consecrated the hair of their sons to Apollo Pythius, and when the time came they brought their sons to Delphi to lay down their hair there. The author takes this to be a sign of petty ambition.

units.la: Ὅτως ἀντὶ ὁ ἀκόλουθος Αἰθίοψ ἦς. Olim [?] & beati homines, puerorum Æthiopum ministerio vtebantur. Auctor ad Herennium describens oftentatorem ineptum, Et dicit in aurem, aut vt domi lectuli sternantur, aut ab anunculo rogetur Æthiops qui ad balnea veniat, asturconi locum ante ostium suum detur, aut aliquod fragile fulfa choragium gloriae comparetur. Athenaeus in descriptione conuiuij Cleopatrae, Λαμπαδηροφόρους παῖδας Αἰθίοπας [?]. Iuuenalis, — tibi pocula cursor / Getulus dabit, aut nigri manus ossea Mauri.
units.tr: "and the Ethiopian who was his attendant" [Ὅτως ἀντὶ ὁ ἀκόλουθος Αἰθίοψ ἦς]. Even in former times wealthy men used the services of Ethiopian boys. The author of the Ad Herennium, describing the ostentatious fool, writes: And he whispers in the ear, or has couches made up at home, or asks a friend for an Ethiopian to go with him to the baths, or has a place set aside before his door for an Asturian horse, or buys some fragile trinket as a stage-prop of glory. Athenaeus, in his description of Cleopatra's banquet, speaks of torch-bearing boys, Ethiopians [Λαμπαδηροφόρους παῖδας Αἰθίοπας]. Juvenal: "A Getulian runner will hand you the cups, or the bony hand of a black Moor."

units.la: Similiter mulieribus fuerunt suæ ex Æthiopia ancillulæ, vt est apud Terentium. Tibullus,
units.tr: In the same way women had their own little maidservants from Ethiopia, as in Terence. Tibullus:

units.la: Illi sint comites fusci quos India torret, Solis & admotis inficit ignis equis.
units.tr: Let dusky companions be hers, whom India scorches, and whom the fire of the sun, with its horses drawn close, darkens.

units.la: Et in epistola Leonti ad Lamiam apud Alciphronem nominantur Σερά́πονες;Σερά́παναξ, Ἰνδοί,Ἰνδαί[?]. Fuit etiam magnus vsus Afrorum nomenclatorum, quod ex Luciano colligimus, Περὶ τῶν ἐπὶ μισθῷ σ[?].
units.tr: And in the letter of Leontion to Lamia, in Alciphron, the names Serapon [Σεράπονες], Seranax [Σεράναξ], and Indians, male and female [Ἰνδοί, Ἰνδαί], are mentioned. There was also a great use of African nomenclators, as we gather from Lucian, in his treatise On Those Who Attend for Pay [Περὶ τῶν ἐπὶ μισθῷ].

units.la: Ꝯ ἀπονδὼς μὲν ἀργ[?]. ] Scribe ἀπονδώς[?]. Καννὸν[?] intelligo nûmum recens percussum & nouû. tales enim nummi veteribus & vsu tritis ac fordidis præferuntur. Tale illud in nono Apuleij demonstrat ei nouitate nimia candentes aureas. Hi sunt quos vocant nummos asperos, Seneca, Suetonius, Perfius, vt valde miratus sim nuper doctissimi viri sententiam, qui eam vocem ab origine Arabica repetit. verùm de eo aliàs pluribus.
