units.tr: "without a libation, indeed, ... silver" [ἀπονδὼς μὲν ἀργ]. Read ἀπονδώς. By kannon [καννὸν] I understand a coin newly struck and new, for such coins are preferred to old coins worn by use and dirty ones. Something like this is shown in Book IX of Apuleius, where he speaks of gold pieces gleaming with excessive newness. These are what they call nummi asperi, rough coins, in Seneca, Suetonius and Persius. So I was greatly surprised recently by the opinion of a very learned man who derives that word from an Arabic origin. But more on this elsewhere.

units.la: ἀπαλλαγῆς τῆς ἐπὶ ... ἀρσεπαράτ[?] ] Ita moris fuit apud Græcos, eam partem ædium (quæ ab ingredientibus prima conspicitur, aut à prætereuntibus, quando fores patent, quam ἐνώπια vocabant) omnibus modis ornare: ideo Homerus ἐνώπια παμ-φανόωσα dixit. Hefychius Ἐνώπια, τὰ καλλίκρῳ τῶ πυ-λῶν & φανόμενα μέρη, ἃ ἐκ διακόσμων ἕνεκα τῆ πεσείων[?]. Vide amplius Euftathium in Iliados rhapsodiam Θ, & in Odysseam. necnon Ælianum in epistolis. De Romanorum atriis & tablinis non est obscurum: at Græci atriis non vtebantur, si credimus Vitruuio: eum vide libro v 1. capite x. ἀναξαλόμενος ἢ Σομάτιον[?].) Cum tranfuehebantur equites Athenis, veste erant amicti purpurea & varia. Scholiastes Ariftophanis, ἐν πορφυρῖς & τωικίλοις ἱματίοις ἐπόμασον[?]. Eam veftem ξύσιδα vocabant. Ariftophanes Nebulis, Ὥσθ' οὐ, μέγας ὢν, ἀρμ' ἐλαύνης σφὸς πόλιν, Ὥσπερ Μεγακλέης ξυσιδ' ἔχων.
units.tr: "of the release from ... " [ἀπαλλαγῆς τῆς ἐπὶ]. This was the Greek custom: to adorn in every way that part of the house which is seen first by those who enter, or by passers-by when the doors stand open, and which they called ἐνώπια (the parts in front). So Homer said ἐνώπια παμφανόωσα, "gleaming in front." Hesychius: "Enopia: the parts of the gates that are beautiful and visible, which are set in order for show." See more in Eustathius on the rhapsody Θ of the Iliad and on the Odyssey, and also Aelian in his letters. That the Romans had atria and tablina is not unclear; but the Greeks, if we believe Vitruvius, did not use atria. See him in Book VI, chapter x. "Taking off ... " [ἀναξαλόμενος ἢ Σομάτιον].

units.la: Interpres, ξυσιλέγεται τὸ χροκωτὸν ἱμάτιον, ὁ οἱ ἀνὴ-χοι φορῶσι μίγει νῦν τομυρδίονες. Romæ quoq; equites trabeati erant in tranfuectione.
units.tr: "The commentator: ..." The commentator explains that the chroikōton himation, which the knights wear, is now mixed... Also at Rome the equites trabeati wore the trabea in the transvection (the parade of the knights).

units.la: ΚΑΑΔΟΣ ΜΕΑΙΤΑΙΟΣ.] Mirus vfus vocis κλὴ Ꮐ. Putet fortaffe aliquis refcribędum non procul ab editæ lećtionis veftigiis, ΚΥΝΟΣ ΜΕΑΙΤΑΙΟΥ, vel ΚΥΝΙΔΙΟΝ ΜΕΑΙΤΑΙΟΝ. Puto tamen verius effe quod fupra diximus, cum exponeremus illa ζωμὸν πολῶν γενόμεναι[?]. quæ ibi legantur. In poęta minus effet mirum:nam ob cognationem quæ eft inter plantarum genus, & ea quæ animalia proprie vocantur, non mirum plantarum appellationes ad homines aut alia animalia transferri: quod in vocibus ἐρι Ꮐ, ὀζ Ꮐ, μαχ Ꮐ, δάλ Ꮐ, ἀκριμων, ἔρπης, ςάχυς, paffim apud poetas licet obferuare. Ab eadem origine fuboles & propagatio tribuuntur animalibus.
units.tr: "KALLOS MEAITAIOS" [ΚΑΑΔΟΣ ΜΕΑΙΤΑΙΟΣ]. A strange use of the word. Someone might suspect that it should be rewritten, not far from the traces of the reading given, as KYNOS MEAITAIOY, or KYNIDION MEAITAION. But I think what I said above, when we explained those words [ζωμὸν πολῶν γενόμεναι] which are read there, is more correct. In a poet it would be less surprising: because of the kinship between the kind of plants and what are properly called animals, it is not surprising that the names of plants are transferred to men or other animals. This may be observed everywhere in the poets in such words as ἐρι-, ὀζ-, μαχ-, δάλ-, ἀκριμων, ἔρπης, σάχυς. From the same origin, offspring and propagation are attributed to animals.

units.la: ἐν τῷ Ασκληπιῷ.) Scribe vel fine ἐν, vel ἐν τῷ Ασκληπιεῖῳ. aut ἐν τῷ Ασκληπιείῳ. Erant duo Athenis templa Æsculapij: alterum in vrbe: alterum in Piræeo, vel Acharnis. notat comici fcholiaft.
units.tr: "in the Asklepieion" [ἐν τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ]. Write either without ἐν, or ἐν τῷ Ἀσκληπιεῖῳ, or ἐν τῷ Ἀσκληπιείῳ. There were two temples of Asclepius at Athens: one in the city, and another in the Piraeus or at Acharnae. The comic scholiast notes this.

units.la: τῆν ἐκτείσειν σεφανῶν Ꮐ ἀλλίζεσθαι ὅτ.[?] ) Scribe, ἐκτείσειν σε-φανῶν[?] Ꮐ ἀλλίζεσθαι ὅτ.
units.tr: "to have crowns ... " [τῆν ἐκτείσειν σεφανῶν]. Read ἐκτίσειν στεφάνων ... ἀλλάσσεσθαι ὅτι.

units.la: συνδιοκι(ζ ... τῶν ἐπὶ τῆν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τῶν ἔτ.[illegible, ~12 letters] Scribe τὰ ... τῶν.
units.tr: "... of those in the office ... " [συνδιοκι(ζ ... τῶν ἐπὶ τῆν ἀρχὴν]. Read τὰ ... τῶν.

units.la: Sic vocat ea quorum adminiftratio ad curam & officium prytanęorum pertinebat. Inter alia vnum hoc erat quod oportuit eos ἔπ' ἐκάςοῖς κοινῆ, vt eft in ea De falsa legatione. Solebant autem prytanei post rem diuinam factam populo renunciare, litafsint ne an non. Extat eius moris illustre exemplum in proœmiis Demosthenicis: quorum vnum est totum huic sacrorum renuntiationi accommodatum. Cum autem quater quoque prytaneatu (erat id spatium diernm xxxv. vel xxxvi, teste Harpocratione) populi concio celebraretur, fiebat vt puto quarta tantum concione hæc renunciatio. ait enim Pollux τῷ τετάρτῳ ἐκκλησίαν fuisse de rebus sacris & ad sacra pertinentibus.
units.tr: So he calls those matters whose administration belonged to the care and duty of the prytanes. Among other things, this was one thing they had to do jointly over each matter [ἔπ' ἐκάστοις κοινῆ], as in the speech On the False Embassy. The prytanes used to report to the people, after the sacrifice had been performed, whether the omens were favourable or not. There is a famous example of this custom in the prefaces of Demosthenes, one of which is entirely devoted to this report on the sacrifices. Since the people's assembly was held also four times during each prytany (this period lasted thirty-five or thirty-six days, according to Harpocration), I think this report was made only at the fourth assembly. For Pollux says that the fourth assembly [τῷ τετάρτῳ ἐκκλησίαν] was concerned with sacred matters and those pertaining to sacrifices.

units.la: καὶ σφαγιαζόμενοι λαμπρὸν ἱμάτιον.) Vt apud Romanos, sic etiam apud Athenienses qui rem diuinam facturi erant veste candida erant amicti. id enim est λευκὸν ἱμάτιον, non splendida vestis. Æschines de Demosthene, στεφανωσάμενος ἐν λευκῷ ἱματίῳ ἐσθῆτι λαβὼν, ἐξελθὼν [?] alij scriptores ἱερὰν ἐσθῆτα vocant. Porphyrius Περὶ ἀποχῆς [?] libro secundo, modò λαμπρὰν, modo λευκὴν: aliquando καθαρὰν, vt Latini pura vestimenta. Hanc ob causam solebant scurrae Attici si quis in publicum prodire candidatus confuesset, cum appellare ὁλολυγμόν, quasi tu dicas, perpetuò sacrificantem. Est enim ὁλολύζειν vox ad sacrorum cæremonias pertinens: neque aliter à vetustissimis scriptoribus vsurpatur, vt alibi annotauimus: idque certissimum est. Anaxandrides apud Athenæum libro sexto,
units.tr: "and sacrificing, wearing a bright cloak" [καὶ σφαγιαζόμενοι λαμπρὸν ἱμάτιον]. As among the Romans, so also among the Athenians those who were about to perform a sacrifice were clothed in white garments. For this is what λευκὸν ἱμάτιον means, not a splendid garment. Aeschines, of Demosthenes: "having crowned himself, taking up the white garment, going out..." Other writers call it ἱερὰν ἐσθῆτα, "sacred dress." Porphyry, in Book II of On Abstinence [Περὶ ἀποχῆς], calls it now bright (λαμπρὰν), now white (λευκὴν), and sometimes pure (καθαρὰν), as the Latins say pura vestimenta. For this reason, if anyone was accustomed to come before the public dressed in white as a candidate, the Attic buffoons used to call him ololygmos (ὁλολυγμόν), as if you were to say "one who is always sacrificing." For ὁλολύζειν is a word pertaining to the ceremonies of sacrifices, and the most ancient writers use it in no other sense, as I have noted elsewhere; and this is quite certain. Anaxandrides, in Athenaeus Book VI:

units.la: Ὑμεῖς γὰρ ἀλλήλους ἀεὶ χλιάζετε, Οἶδ' ἀκεῖσθ' ἂν μὴ γὰρ ἡ τις ἀπρεπὴς [?] Ἱερὸν γάμον καλεῖτ'· ἐὰν ἢ μικρὸν σανίλλως [?] Ἀνθρώπων, Σωλαμόν. λαμπρός τις ἐξ-ελίλυθεν; Ὀλολυμός ἐστ' ὅδ' ἦν. [?] Protulimus hunc veteris poëtæ locum, non tam vt auctorem nostrum illustraremus, quàm vt ipsum poëtam. Nam interpretis quidem postremorum verborum versio, planè est, (quod sine docti viri contumelia dictum sit) inepta:longè vero ineptior eiusdem annotatio. Risi suauiter cum illa legerem. Enimuero pauci obseruarunt quid proprie sit ἀλολύζειν: nec pauci ad eum scopulum offendunt.
units.tr: For you always make love to one another... [the Greek verse of the old poet is corrupt in the scan and cannot be restored with certainty]. I have brought forward this passage of the old poet not so much to illustrate our author as to illustrate the poet himself. The interpreter's version of the last words is plainly silly (I say this without meaning any insult to a learned man), and his annotation is far sillier still. I laughed heartily when I read it. Few have observed what ἀλολύζειν properly means, and not a few stumble on that rock.

units.la: Εὐριπίδης οἱ ἀρ.) Demosthenes in eo cuius modo meminimus proœmio, Ε[?]Ϋ[?]ΑΜ[?] τῷ Διὶ τῷ Σωτῆρι, ἐν τῇ Ἀθήνᾳ, ἐν τῇ Νίκῃ· ἐν γίνεσθαι καὶ ἐν σωτηρίᾳ τοῦδ' ἡμῖν τὰ ἱερά. Εὐ[?]Ϋ[?]ΑΜ[?] ἐν τῇ μυστηρίῳ τῆς Θεοῦ, ἐν τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι ἐν ἐπαλλισπερξ[?]μ[?]ν ἐν ταύτῃ.
units.tr: Euripides, ... Demosthenes, in the proem I have just mentioned: "To Zeus the Saviour, in Athens, in Victory; may these sacred rites be held for us in safety..." In the mystery of the goddess, in the temple of Apollo... [the rest of this Greek is too corrupt in the scan to be recovered].

units.la: ἡ ὑμεῖς ἰδίχεσθε τὰ ἀλλοδαπά.] Lege δίχεσθε. Demosthenes in fine eius proœmij, Δίχεσθε ἐν αὐτῷ τῆς Θεῶν διδόντων ἔλαδα. Quàm nihil intellexerint toto isto loco priores interpretes piget dicere.
units.tr: "...you are at odds over foreign matters." Read δίχεσθε. Demosthenes, at the end of that same proem: "You are divided among yourselves, while the gods give good things." It grieves me to say how little the earlier interpreters understood of this whole passage.
On the chapter On Illiberality [περὶ ἀνελευθερίας]

units.la: Ἡ ἀνελευθερία ἐστὶ σμικρότης τῆς περὶ φιλοτιμίας δα-πάνῃ ἔχει.) Nihil deprauatius, nihil infrunitius illa lectione: quae cum tàm male conueniat τῇ ἀνελευθερίᾳ, cuius definitione aut descriptionem saltem promittit, demirror doctissimos viros, & in philosophia apprime versatos mendum non suboluisse. Atqui illiberalitas neque ἀφιλοτιμία est simpliciter, hoc est, vt illi vertunt opulentia: neque recte δαπάνῃ ἔχειν dici potest: quare constat tam in eo quod generis locum obtinet, quàm in differentia vitium esse. At non sunt accuratæ Theophrasti definitiones in hoc libello, dicet aliquis: sanè fa-teor τὸ ἀχρεῖς[?] illas non habere: falsas tamen esse & ineptas, hoc verò nego tibi atque pernego. Vt igitur ineptias vitemus, sic legamus, Η ἀνελευθερία[?] ἐξ ἀξιοσίας τῆς ἀφιλοτιμίας[?] δαπάνλω φέγυα[?]. Nemo recti iudicij qui sit (quod impune dixisse liceat) de veritate huius lectionis dubitabit. Iam ergo nō est genus ἐλευθερία[?], sed ἀφιλοτιμίας ἀξιοσία[?]. neque differentia τὸ δαπάνλω ἔχειν[?]: sed τὸ φιλεῖν δαπάνλω[?]. Contra virtutis oppositae ἐλευθεριότητος[?], proprium docent esse philosophi τὸ ἀποβλέπειν[?] εἰς χρημάτων εἰς τὰ ἀναγκαῖα[?]. hoc est, facilem esse ad faciendos sumptus liberales. Est enim pecuniae usus duplex: alius ad sumptus necessarios, alius ad sumptus liberales, vt est apud M. Tullium. Ideo dicebat Plato in octavo De republica, τὰς φαυλῶς εἶναι φαύλας ἀντιγωνιστὰς ἢ τὴν ἐν τιμῆς ἢ ἄλλης φιλοτιμίας τῆς καλλίστης[?]. caussam nunc accipe, χρήματα τε καὶ ἐὐδοξίας ἕνεκα καὶ τῶν Θεάτων ἀγώνων ἀναλισκῇ[?]. Non alia aut interpretatione verba Theophrasti opus habent: aut confirmatione nostra emendatio.
units.tr: Illiberality is a shortness in the expense that concerns honour. Nothing is more corrupt than that reading, and nothing more senseless. It agrees so badly with illiberality, whose definition, or at least whose description, it promises, that I marvel that learned men, and those thoroughly versed in philosophy, did not suspect an error. Yet illiberality is not simply a want of ambition (ἀφιλοτιμία), that is, what they render as "wealth," nor can one properly say "to have expense" (δαπάνῃ ἔχειν). So it is clear that the error lies both in what holds the place of the genus and in the difference. But, someone will say, the definitions in this little book of Theophrastus are not exact. I grant indeed that they lack precision; but that they are false and senseless, this I deny to you and flatly deny. So, to avoid the absurdities, let us read it thus: "Illiberality is a lack of worth in the want of ambition, a meanness in expense." No one of sound judgement (and I may say this without fear of penalty) will doubt the truth of this reading. Thus the genus is not "liberality" but "worth in the want of ambition," and the difference is not "to have expense" but "to love expense" (τὸ φιλεῖν δαπάνῃ). Philosophers teach that the proper mark of the opposed virtue, liberality (ἐλευθεριότης), is to look to money for necessary things, that is, to be ready to make liberal outlays. For the use of money is twofold: one for necessary expenses, another for liberal ones, as Marcus Tullius says. Hence Plato, in book 8 of the Republic, said that those who spend their money on contests for honour or other fine ambition... Now hear the cause: money is spent for the sake of reputation and for the public games. The words of Theophrastus need no other explanation, and our emendation needs no other confirmation.

units.la: οἱ ... νικήσας τραγῳδὸς[?]. ) Scribe νικᾶς τραγῳδοῖς[?]. Alibi hunc locum explicabimus, & de hoc more multa dicemus. Notum autem tragœdiam Libero patri fuisse dicatam, vt Apollini comœdiam.
units.tr: "...the tragic poet who has conquered." Read νικᾷς τραγῳδοῖς. I will explain this passage elsewhere and say much about this custom. It is well known that tragedy was dedicated to the father Liber, as comedy was to Apollo.

units.la: ἢ ἐπιδίδοσαν ἐφορμένων[?]. ] Difficilibus Reip. temporibus solebant Athenienses pro virili parte quisque publicè pecunias erogare, ad sublevandam ærarij inopiam, quod ἐπιδιδόναι proprie dicebant, quasi dicat aliquis supra ordinaria munia aliquid amplius largiri. erant enim ordinariæ & legibus constitutæ λειτουργίαι. Cum igitur pecuniis opus erat, prytanei populum conuocabant: angustias Reip. exponebant: ad collationem quemque hortabantur. Tum surgebat vnusquisque ordine suo & loco: ac si quidem vellet aliquid conferre, id profitebatur & dicebat, Ἐπιδίδωμι ἐγὼ ζῶντον[?]. sin animus largiendi quicquam non esset, vel tacebant cum surrexerant,vel è concione clam se eripiebant.
units.tr: In difficult times for the commonwealth, the Athenians used to give money publicly, each man according to his means, to relieve the shortage in the treasury. They properly called this "giving over and above" (ἐπιδιδόναι), as if one were saying that someone bestowed something beyond the ordinary duties. For there were ordinary public services (λειτουργίαι) fixed by law. So when money was needed, the prytaneis summoned the people, laid out the straits of the commonwealth, and urged each man to contribute. Then each man rose in his turn and place, and if he wished to give something, he declared it and said, "I contribute, being alive." But if he had no mind to give anything, he either kept silent after rising, or slipped away secretly from the assembly.

units.la: quod vel ex isto loco clarum est. Athenæus libro xiii[?]. de Phoco Phocionis filio,homine luxu perdito, loquens: Ἐπιδόσεων δέ ποτε γινομένων, παρελθὼν δὲ αὐτὸς εἰς τὸ ἐκκλησίαν, ἔφη, Ἐπιδίδωμι κἀγώ· οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἀνεβόων, Εἰς ἀπολαυσιν. Sentiebat Phocus se velle conferre aliquid: populus verniliter nimis accepit Ἐπιδίδωμι, ea notione qua vsurpatur pro crescere,& in aliqua re proficere. In orationibus Græcorum oratorum sexcentis locis fit Ἐπιδόσεων istarum mentio.
units.tr: This is clear even from this passage. Athenaeus, book 13, speaking of Phocus, son of Phocion, a man ruined by luxury: "When contributions were once being made, he came forward himself into the assembly and said, 'I also contribute.' The Athenians cried out with one voice, 'For enjoyment!'" Phocus meant that he wished to give something; the people, in too rustic a way, took "I contribute" in the sense in which the word is used for growing and making progress in some matter. In the speeches of the Greek orators such contributions are mentioned in six hundred places.

units.la: ἐκ τῆς μέσης ἀπελθὼν.] Scribe ἀπελθὼν.
units.tr: "Having departed from the middle." Read ἀπελθών.

units.la: τῆς ἱερέως πλῶ τῆς ἱερέων.) Fortasse legendum, πλῶ τῆς ἱερέων ἢ ἱερῶν. hoc est, exceptis iis partibus quæ ad sacrificos & sacrificas pertinebant. Veteres enim deos precaturi,& viros & mulieres sacerdotes adhibebant. Plato, Legum quinto, εἴ ἱερῶν & ἱερεῶν ἀγαχῶν ἐπιμελουμένων ἐπὶ τῆς προθύρων ἕως ἐκ τῶν ἑτέρων ἐπιθυμίων[?].
units.tr: "...of the priest, except the priests." Perhaps one should read "except the parts of the priests or of the sacred things," that is, except those parts which pertained to the priests and priestesses. For the ancients, when about to pray to the gods, used both men and women as priests. Plato, in book 5 of the Laws, speaks of those who take care of the sacred things and priests at the doors...

units.la: τὰ ἱερὰ ἀπαλλαγῆς.) Quàm inhumanum Athenis hoc existimaretur, non potest melius declarari quàm Alexidis quodam loco: quem eò libentius proferam, quod videam hodie in editis Athenæi codicibus, qui illum laudauerat integros ferme duos versus desiderari. Nos igitur locum integrum ex veteribus codicibus apponemus. Sic Alexis,
units.tr: How inhuman this was thought at Athens cannot be shown better than by a certain passage of Alexis. I quote it the more gladly because I see that in the printed editions of Athenaeus, who cited him, nearly two whole verses are missing. So I shall set out the whole passage from old manuscripts. Thus Alexis:

units.la: Ἐπιδίδωμι ἐγὼ ζῶντον[?] : the Greek word in the first line is uncertain and marked [?].
Οὐδ᾽ ἐν Τειχάλλοις τῶν γ᾽ ἔχειν ἔννομα[?], Οὐ φασὶ τὴν δύναμιν[?] ὡς κεκλημένοις Δεῖξαντ᾽ ἰδεῖν τὸ δεῖπνον εἰς τὸ αὔριον Πωλεῖν, ἀδείπνοις ἅπερ ἐθνικ᾽ αὐτὸς ἰδεῖν[?].
units.tr: "Nor in Teichalla... of those who have, the lawful things... they do not say the power, as to those who have been invited, having shown the dinner for tomorrow, to sell, what they themselves saw, having no dinner."

units.la: τὰς δ᾽ ὁ δ᾽ [?] οἰκοσίτας ἐν τοῖς γάμοις μισθωσάμενοι.)

Mos fuit parcorum hominum cum nuptias celebrarent, opera & ministerio vti adiutorum atque adiutricum (sic vocat Plautus) οἰκοσίτων, hoc est, qui suo cibo ministrarent, vt Plautus loquitur: vel vt idem alibi, qui suo sumptu & cibo vescerentur. Crates Σωαγρισώσας fabula,
units.tr: It was the custom of stingy people, when they celebrated weddings, to use the labour and service of helpers, both men and women (so Plautus calls them), who were oikositai, that is, who supplied their own food, as Plautus puts it, or, as he says elsewhere, who ate at their own expense and from their own food. Crates, in his play Sōagrisōsas:

units.la: — ἀσεῖον τὸ μὴ Σωαγεῖν γυναῖκας μηδὲ δεῖπ᾽ ἰζειν ὄχλον, Ἀλλ᾽ οἰκοσίτας τὰς γάμους πεποιηκέναι.
units.tr: "...it is shameful not to bring women to the feast nor to seat a crowd there, but to have made the weddings with oikositai."

units.la: Scio aliter posse exponi γάμως οἰκοσίτας: sed quomodo hic recte accipiatur, nihil vetat. Plautus Casina, tangit morem illis versibus:
units.tr: I know that γάμους οἰκοσίτας can be explained otherwise, but nothing forbids taking it correctly here. Plautus, in the Casina, touches on this custom in those lines:

units.la: — Al. quin ædepol seruos, ancillas, domos Certum est omnes mittere ad te. ST. Eho nimium scite scitus es.
units.tr: "Al. Indeed, by Pollux, it is certain that I shall send all the slaves, maidservants and households to you." ST. "Hey, you are too cleverly clever."

units.la: Sed facito dum meminerit versus quos cantat Colax: cibo
units.tr: "But take care that he remembers the verses which Colax sings: ..."

units.la: Cum suo quisque facito uti veniant, quasi eant Sutrium. Item alibi. Menander οἰκόσιτον sponsum appellauit in Dactylo, qui parua aut nulla dote esset contentus: Οἰκόσιτον νυμφίον ὀλίγην δεόμενον προικός[?]. Plutarchus in Crasso, milites οἰκοσίτας qui sine stipendiis aliqui militarent.
units.tr: "Let each come with his own food, as if they were going to Sutrium." Likewise elsewhere. Menander called a bridegroom oikositos in the Dactylus, one who was content with a small dowry or none: "An oikositos bridegroom who needs little dowry." Plutarch, in the Life of Crassus, calls soldiers oikositai who served without pay.

units.la: καὶ τεμπαξών.) Cuiuis, puto, notum est ex oratoribus Graecis, quale genus λεπτογραφίας esset Athenis τὸ τεμπαξών: & veteres grammatici id ita diligenter explicant, vt videantur mihi (dicam liberè) parum in hac lingua exercitati qui hæc non intellexerunt. Vertimus autem , triremi quam instruxit præfectus ; non autem imperans quia omne imperium erat τὰ σφάλης , non τὰ ναυπάρχε,vti docent Atticæ historiæ, & ante omnes Demosthenes.
units.tr: I think it is known to anyone who reads the Greek orators what kind of fine-drawn trickery (λεπτογραφία) the tembaxōn was at Athens. The ancient grammarians explain it so carefully that they seem to me (I speak frankly) to have had little practice in this language if they did not understand it. We render it as the trireme which the captain (praefectus) fitted out, not as the one who commands; for the whole command was of the sphalēs, not of the naupēgos, as the Attic histories teach, and before all others Demosthenes.

units.la: Τὰ τῆς κυβερνήτης σρώματα ἐκ τῆς καταςρ.] De via- toriis cubilibus non repetam quæ supra diximus. Lego autem hîc, ὑπὲρ τῆς καταςρ. vel ὅτι. Lucianus in dialogo Mercurij & Charonis , τὸ μὲν ἐγχεις ἐπὶ τὰ καταςρώματα ἐκ ἐδείς. Nam super transtris dormiebant nautæ in naui , non sub transtris. Eustathius, ἤλον δ᾽ ὡς οἱ ναυλικοὶ ὅτι τῆς ἐνθίλων καταςρωμάτων κοιμῶνται. Trietarcho verò suus erat locus ad nauis puppim , vbi illi tabernaculum extrui solitum. Pollux , τὰ ἢ ἀεὶ τῷ φρύμναν ἀρίχονοι ἐύλα, ἀξιτόναια καλεῖται ἐκεῖ τε ἐ σκλωὴ ὀνομάζεται , τὰ ναυπύμβων σφάλης ἢ ναυπάρχω. Ibi ergo trierarchi in suis stragulis quiescere moris habebant : at illiberalis iste & sordidus promiscuè cum reliquis, in transtris cubat, & gubernatoris utitur stragulis: queq; solent esse vilia, & ut plurimum segestria, aut tegetes : proinde parū è trierarchi dignitate. Persius,
units.tr: "The bedding of the steersman from the..." On the sleeping places for voyages I shall not repeat what I said above. I read here "above the bedding" or "because of the bedding." Lucian, in the dialogue of Mercury and Charon: "You could not put your feet on the bedding." For the sailors slept on the deck-planks of the ship, above the benches, not beneath the benches. Eustathius: "I have learned that the sailors sleep on the bedding made of the benches." But the trierarch had his own place at the stern of the ship, where a tent was usually built for him. Pollux: "The wooden planks at the stern are called the aphlaston, and there the sleeping places are called... of the naval captain." There, therefore, the trierarchs were accustomed to rest on their own coverlets. But this illiberal and sordid man lies promiscuously with the rest on the benches and uses the steersman's coverlets, which are usually cheap, and mostly of rush mats or matting; so he is little worthy of the trierarch's dignity. Persius,

units.la: Tu mare transilias? tibi torta cannabe fultoCœna fit in transtro?
units.tr: "Can you leap over the sea? Is a dinner made for you on a bench, with a twisted cannabis mat as a cushion?"

units.la: Propterea Donatus τὰς φορμὰς , hoc est, tegetes & storeas, siue erones, quibus pauperes loco stragulorum & tapetium utuntur, stramen nauticum vocat. Alciphron epistola quadam, ὃ δ᾽ ἀντιχόμεν τῷ ξύλων τῆς ἁλιάδ ἐπὶ τε τῶν ξεινικῶν καὶ ἰφεσπίδων καὶ ἀλλαλίνεις· ὃ δ᾽ οἱός τε ἔφασκεν κέιτρη ὡς οἱ λοιποὶ δὴ τῷ καταςρωμάτων, τῷ ἐνίδα εἴμαι νομίζων. [?] λίξα τεραχύλέρα. ἐσθὴν μένειν.) Vtpote qui vestem forensem habeat vnicam : quod illiberale est planéque sordidum. Inde Ciceronis locus in Decianum quendam lepidissimus, in oratione pro L. Flacco, Ro-mam adiuenis:affers faciem nouam,nomen vetus,purpuram Tyriam, in qua tibi inuideo quod vnis vestimentis tandiu lautus es.
units.tr: For this reason Donatus calls the φορμάς, that is, rush mats and straw mats or coarse coverings, which the poor use in place of blankets and carpets, "nautical straw." In a certain letter Alciphron describes a man who, like the others, lies on the bare boards of the deck, thinking he has only one garment to wear. Such a man is illiberal and plainly squalid, since he owns only one outdoor garment. Hence Cicero's very witty passage against a certain Decianus, in the speech for Lucius Flaccus: "You have come to Rome. You bring a new face, an old name, Tyrian purple, and in this I envy you, that you have for so long been splendid in a single set of clothes."

units.la: ἀλλὰ μισθώσῃ εἰς τὰς ἐξόδας.] Iuuenalis satyra sexta in Romanis mulieribus hanc notat illiberalitatem simul & ambitionem,
units.tr: "But you let yourself out for hire at the outings." Juvenal, in Satire 6, marks this meanness and vanity in Roman women at the same time.

units.la: Vt spectet ludos conducit Ogulnia vestem, / Conducit comites, sellam, cervical, amicas, / Nutricem, & flauam cui det mandata puellam.
units.tr: "So that she may watch the games, Ogulnia hires a dress, hires companions, a chair, a cushion, female friends, a nurse, and a fair-haired girl to whom she gives her orders."

units.la: Demosthenes Midiæ exprobrat quòd cùm esset præfectus equitum, alieno equo in pompæ transuectione vsus fuisset. Ἐξόδως accipe vt in illo, χαλεπὴ γυναικῶν ἐξόδῳ, initio Lysistratæ. Raro olim matronæ pedem domo efferebát:nec in publicum nisi stiparæ gregibus ancillarum prodibant. Interdum ἐξόδῳ γυναικῶν dicitur de profectione ad ducendam pompam. vnde est apud Platonem in fine sexti De legibus, mulieb ris cuiusdam supplicij genus, μὴ μετέχειν τῆς ἐξόδων τῆς γυναικείων ἢ τιμῆς, ἢ τῆς εἰς τὰς γάμους, ἢ ἡλικίας παίδων φοιῆσεων. Lege Suidam in Αἰμιλία. Inde dictæ φιλέξοδοι γυναῖκες, quæ non sunt οἰκοποί & casariæ.
units.tr: Demosthenes reproaches Midias for using another man's horse when he rode in a procession as commander of the cavalry. Take ἐξόδως as in that line, "difficult for women to go out" [χαλεπὴ γυναικῶν ἐξόδῳ], at the beginning of the Lysistrata. In former times matrons rarely set foot outside their houses, and they came into public only surrounded by flocks of maidservants. Sometimes ἐξόδῳ γυναικῶν is said of setting out to lead a procession. Hence in Plato, at the end of the sixth book of the Laws, there is a kind of punishment for a woman: that she should not take part in women's processions, nor in honour, nor in weddings, nor in the rites of the children of her age group. Read Suidas under Αἰμιλία. From this are called φιλέξοδοι women, those who are not housekeepers and are not stay-at-homes.

units.la: καὶ τὰς κλίνας ἐκνοπήσαι.) Hefychius qui τὸ κορεῖν etiam φθειρίζειν exponit, videtur hoc voluisse docere, eam vocem à κόεις deducatam interdum accipi pro cimices occidere, vel cimicibus lectos purgare, quod cimicare Latinis dicitur, vt pulicare. Græci, φθειρίζειν. Atque hæc interpretatio locum hîc habere potest. Parmenio poëta ἐκχοεῖζειν[?] dixit in lepidissimo disticho:
units.tr: "and to clean out the beds." Hesychius, who explains κορεῖν also as φθειρίζειν, seems to want to teach that this word, derived from κόρεις, is sometimes taken to mean to kill bedbugs or to clean beds of bedbugs, "which in Latin is called cimicare, as pulicare is for fleas." The Greeks say φθειρίζειν. This explanation may well apply here. The poet Parmenio used ἐκχοεῖζειν in a very witty couplet:

units.la: ὅι κόεις ἄχει κόρα κορίζαντό μ᾿ ἀλλ᾿ ἐκορέσθων[?] Ἄχει κόρα καύλος τῆς κόεις ἐκχοείας[?]. καθεζούμενον ἀσπερχαῖ[?] τὸν τείχωα.[?] ) Non est in in eo nota illiberalitatis quod vestem inuertit: sed quod tritam & macularum plenam vestem gestat, quam postea in coetu honoratorum virorum (ita accipi debet illud καθεζούμενον) cogitur inuertere vt maculas ab oculis eorum submoueat quibus assidet: atque hoc saltem in isto laudandum: sicut contra in superioribus nota δυσχερείας erat, gestantem obsoletam & κηλίδων μεστὸν vestem, versari in oculis hominum. Hinc ortum est apud Graecos prouerbium, quod nos vt puto primi obseruauimus, τὰ καλὰ τείτεν ἔξω. Pindarus Pythionicarum tertio,
units.tr: Not a mark of illiberality is that he turns his garment inside out, but that he wears a worn garment full of stains, which afterwards, sitting among men of honour (this is how the word καθεζούμενον should be taken), he is compelled to turn so that he may remove the stains from the eyes of those beside whom he sits. At least this deserves praise in him. On the other hand, in the earlier case the mark was one of ill-temper: to go about in an old, stain-filled garment and to appear before people's eyes. Hence among the Greeks arose the proverb, which I think we were the first to observe, "keep your fine things outside" [τὰ καλὰ τείτεν ἔξω]. Pindar, in the third Pythian ode:

units.la: — τὰ μὲν ὧν ὃ Διωσάνδαι νήπιοι κόσμῳ φέρειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἀγαθοὶ, τὰ καλὰ πεί-λαντες ἔξω.
units.tr: "Of these things the foolish do not know how to bear the adornment, but the good, showing their fine things outside..."

units.la: Res aduersas inquit, nesciunt moderatè ferre stulti: at sciunt sapientes, quae pulchra sunt foras & in publicum vertentes: hoc est, cuiuis fortunae se accommodantes, & decenter ea vtentes: quae sunt aduersa dissimulantes. Miseriae enim, ait Q. Curtius, optimè ferunt qui abscondunt. Alio sensu dicere solet Seneca, bonos non fulgere extrinsecus, sed bona eorum introrsus esse obuersa. De diuina prouidentia, & epistola cxx. & alibi. Caeterum Pindaricum istud prouerbium vernacula nostra lingua hodieque agnoscit. Aliud autem ἀπέσπερ ἱμάτιον, aliud ἐκσπέφ[?]ν illud est ex parte inuertere: hoc totam vestem quasi deintegro reficere verfis pannis, & nouam illi faciem dare. Ariftophanes,
units.tr: "The foolish," he says, "do not know how to bear adversity with moderation, but the wise know how to turn their fine things outwards and into the open": that is, they adapt themselves to any fortune and use it becomingly, while concealing what is adverse. For, as Quintus Curtius says, "those who hide their miseries bear them best." In another sense Seneca is accustomed to say that good men do not shine outwardly, but that their goods are turned inward. See his discussion of divine providence and letter 120, and elsewhere. Moreover, our own vernacular language still recognises this Pindaric proverb today. But another phrase, ἀπέσπερ ἱμάτιον, differs from ἐκσπέφ(ν), which means to turn a garment inside out in part; the latter means to remake the whole garment, as it were from scratch, by changing the patches and giving it a new appearance. Aristophanes:

units.la: ἐκσπερξον ὡς τάχισα τὴς σαυτῆς πρόσωπος[?].
units.tr: "Turn your face outward as quickly as you can."

units.la: Scholiastes, ἀπὸ μεταφορᾶς τῆς ῥυσμένων ἰματίων κχ[?] ἐκσπειρομένων[?]· ἐκσπέλλᾳ ἢ ἱματίου, τὸ ἀλλάξαι τὸ πρὸς τὸ ἔτω μέρος ἔξω. Lucianus dixit ἀπέρχεσθαι τὸ τρίβων, in Alectryone, : ἀπέρχεται, ait, κοσμίως μάλα ἐχνμαλισμένον[?], ἀπλίσπολας τὸ τρίβων[?], ὡς ὅτι τὰ καθαρώτερα[?] ... quae verba Theophrasti locum explicant. Vox τρίβων, aliàs lacernam, aut pallium significat: aliàs tritam vsu & decorem veftem atque obfoletam. fic tamen vt aliud proprie fonet τρίβων, aliud ῥάκος. vide Euftathium.
units.tr: The scholiast: by metaphor from clothes that are worn out and turned inside out; ἐκσπέλλᾳ ἢ ἱματίου means to change the garment so that the other side is outward. Lucian said ἀπέρχεσθαι τὸ τρίβων, in the Cock (Alectryon): "he goes out very neatly dressed, having turned the worn cloak..." These words explain the passage of Theophrastus. The word τρίβων sometimes means a cloak or a mantle, and sometimes a garment worn and faded by use. Yet τρίβων properly means one thing and ῥάκος another. See Eustathius.

units.la: Ἀλαζονεία δόξειν ἔχει προσδοκία τινῶν ἀγαθῶν καὶ ἐπιλῶν[?]. ) Obfcurat hanc definitionem verbum ἀποσδοκία, in noua, ne dicam inufitata, fignificatione pofitum: accipitur enim non tam pro expectatione, vt vulgò folet, quàm pro excitatione expectationis: quod Græci ἀποσδοκίαν ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι[?] vel vno verbo ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι dicunt: Homerus ἐπαγγέλλω[?]. Latini promittere, vt in illo Iuuenalis,
units.tr: Boastfulness is "an expectation of certain goods and an arousing of hopes" [ἀλαζονεία δόξειν ἔχει προσδοκία τινῶν ἀγαθῶν καὶ ἐπιλῶν]. The definition is obscured by the word ἀποσδοκία, which is used in a new, if not indeed unusual, sense. It is taken not so much for "expectation," as it commonly is, but for the arousing of expectation. The Greeks express this as ἀποσδοκίαν ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι, or with the single verb ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι; Homer has ἐπαγγέλλω. The Latins use promittere, as in Juvenal's line, or spondere, as the same poet says of the boaster.

units.la: — dura per brachia feræ[?] Promittunt atrocem animum. vel spondere, vt cum ait idem de oftentatore, Spondet enim Tyrio stlataria purpura filo.
units.tr: "Through the hard arms of the beast they promise a fierce spirit." Or "For the stolen purple promises Tyrian thread."

units.la: denique idem fere eft ἀποσδοκία ifto loco ac ἀποσεισμός. Plato in Ὅροις, Ἀλαζονεία ἐξ προσκεῖσθαι ἀγαθῶν ἢ ἀγαθῶν τῆς μὴ ὑπαρχόντων. Ariftoteles adiicit hæc verba in Nicomacheis, ἀδόξης χάριν[?]. quæ particula necessariò addenda ad Platonis & Theophrasti definitiones : vt distinguamus ostentatorem qui mendacium suum refert ad inanem gloriam, ab eo qui lucrum aucupans, se suáque prædicat. nam id quoque hominum genus frequens est, vt ad caput primum notare meminimus. Notant grammatici Græci proprium esse Atticis,vt non gloriosum tantum, sed quemuis mendacem ἀλαζόνα appellent.
units.tr: Finally, in this passage ἀποσδοκία means nearly the same as ἀποσεισμός. Plato, in the Definitions, says that boastfulness is the claiming for oneself of goods that are absent or do not exist. Aristotle, in the Nicomachean Ethics, adds the words ἀδόξης χάριν [for the sake of empty glory]. This qualification must necessarily be added to the definitions of Plato and Theophrastus, so that we can distinguish the boaster who refers his pretence to empty glory from the one who, hunting for gain, advertises himself and his goods. That kind of man is also common, as we noted at the first chapter. Greek grammarians observe that it is peculiar to the Atticists to call not only a vainglorious man but any liar an ἀλαζών [boaster].

units.la: ἐν τῷ [illegible, ~20 letters]. Quid appellat ἀλαζονεύ-μα[?] non est dubium, publicum aliquem Athenarum locum intelligi, vbi conuentus fieri solebant. Quare arbitror locum esse corruptum,& lego Ἀρίσ-μαλι[?]. Digma appellabatur locus in Piraeo è re nomen habens. Ibi enim peregrini mercatores suarum mercium δείγματα & specimen producebant, ἐν τρυχλίῳ[?], credo, ἀσφορίας[?], vt alicubi Plutarchus ait. Itaque peregrinis hominibus fere erat ille locus refertus. Auctor scholiorum Aristophanis, Δείγμα τὸ [illegible, ~35 letters] quae postrema verba ita hanc emendationem confirmant, vt nihil supra. propterea enim ait Theophrastus [illegible, ~12 letters] ξένοις[?]. In antiquis libris lineola superducta nomina locorum propria solebant notari & distingui: qui mos postea neglectus multas saepe tenebras attulit. Exemplo sit, (& sunt infinita exempla) locus ille Platonis in Menexeno, vbi interpretes quòd legissent, ἐν τῇ σεαγίᾳ[?] perperam pro Σεαγίᾳ[?], turpiter lapsi sunt. quamquam Ficinus melius pudori suo consuluit omissis his verbis quæ non intelligebat: noui vero interpretes audacter iuxta & imperitè in hac clade verterunt.Intelligit Plato illos ccxcrii Lacedæmonios, quorum cxx. Spartani erant, qui expugnata tandem Sphacteria insula in potestatem Atheniensium venerunt, vt narrat Thucydides libro quarto. Sphacteriam autem infulam etiam Sphagiam dici solitam certum est: vel adi Stephanum Περὶ πόλεως. ὡς πολλὰ χρήματα αὐτῆς ἔσῃ ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ.) Scribe αὐτό. Pertinet hoc ad nauticum fœnus quod à multis exercebatur Athenis. Nemo autem ignorat quàm improbum & graue fuerit id fœnus, etiam legum concessu, vel Romanarum. vide Iurisconsultos. In orationibus Græcorum maximè Demosthenis plurima huius vsurae mentio, propter quam quod tantopere Demosthenem reprehendit Plutarchus, vereor vt ei sit satis æquus: damnat enim rem moribus legibúsque receptam & probatam. Sed apparet ex variis Plutarchi locis ipsum validissimè fœnus nauticum abhorruisse: quod in Catone Censorio appellat, τὸν μάλιστα διαβεβλημένον τῷ δανεισμόν.
units.tr: Of the word ἀλαζονεύμα [in the passage that is illegible in the scan] there is no doubt that it denotes some public place in Athens where people customarily gathered. I therefore think the text is corrupt, and I read it as [Ἀρίσ-μαλι]. The place was called Digma, and it had its name from the thing: in the Piraeus, foreign merchants there displayed samples (δείγματα) of their goods, I believe in a trychlion [ἐν τρυχλίῳ] of the asphoria [ἀσφορίας], as Plutarch says somewhere. So that place was usually crowded with foreigners. The scholiast on Aristophanes writes that Digma is [illegible], and these last words confirm this emendation, nothing more. For this reason Theophrastus says [illegible] to foreigners. In ancient books a short line drawn over proper names was customarily used to mark and distinguish them; this practice was later neglected and often brought much darkness. An example is that passage of Plato in the Menexenus, where the translators, reading ἐν τῇ σεαγίᾳ instead of Σεαγίᾳ, shamefully went wrong. Ficino, however, protected his own reputation better by omitting the words he did not understand; the newer translators boldly and ignorantly rendered them into this disaster. Plato means those 292 Lacedaemonians, of whom 120 were Spartiates, who at last, after the island of Sphacteria was taken, came into the power of the Athenians, as Thucydides relates in book four. It is certain that the island of Sphacteria was also commonly called Sphagia; see Stephanus, Περὶ πόλεως, "ὡς πολλὰ χρήματα αὐτῆς ἔσῃ ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ." Write αὐτό. This pertains to the maritime loan, which was widely practised at Athens. No one is unaware how wicked and burdensome that loan was, even where the laws permitted it, Roman laws included; see the jurists. In Greek orations, especially those of Demosthenes, there is very frequent mention of this usury. Plutarch reprehends Demosthenes greatly on account of it, and I fear he is not quite fair to him, for he condemns a practice received and approved by custom and law. Yet it appears from various passages in Plutarch that he himself strongly abhorred the maritime loan, which in his Cato the Censor he calls "the most infamous kind of lending" [τὸν μάλιστα διαβεβλημένον τῷ δανεισμόν].

units.la: (τῆς ἐργασίας τῆς δανειστικῆς.) Hoc quoque refero non ad fœnus ἐγγεον, sed ad nauticum: quam vocat Demosthenes τῷ ναυτικῷ ... θαλαττίαν ἐργασίαν.
units.tr: (of the lending business.) [τῆς ἐργασίας τῆς δανειστικῆς.] I refer this also not to interest on land [ἔγγειον] but to maritime loans, which Demosthenes calls the maritime business [τῷ ναυτικῷ ... θαλαττίαν ἐργασίαν].

units.la: ὡς μὴ Εὐάνδρῳ ἐσπατάλησε. Docti viri iam ante nos emendarunt μετ' Ἀλεξάνδρου quæ emendatio vera est & certa.
units.tr: (as he did not squander it on Euander) [ὡς μὴ Εὐάνδρῳ ἐσπατάλησε.] Learned men before us have already emended this to with Alexander [μετ' Ἀλεξάνδρου], and that emendation is true and certain.

units.la: περὶ δὲ Ἀλεξ[?]. Adnotata est in quibusdam codicibus altera lectio πεντακοσίων, pro περιτῶν, quæ ferri poterit, si referas ad tempus scriptæ epistolæ: alioquin sensus erit absurdus ob locorum interualla. Antipater hic ille est quem mors Demosthenis nobilitauit. Hunc ait Diodorus libro x i x. δοκεῖν γελοῖναι φρονιμώτερον τῆς ἐν Διωνυσίᾳ γελοίοτων[?].
units.tr: (but concerning Alex...) [περὶ δὲ Ἀλεξ[?].] Some manuscripts note another reading, five hundred [πεντακοσίων] in place of the surrounding [περιτῶν]. This could stand if you refer it to the time when the letter was written; otherwise the sense will be absurd because of the intervals between the places. This Antipater is the one whom the death of Demosthenes made famous. Diodorus, in book 19, says of him that he seemed more foolish than ridiculous, as compared with Dionysius [δοκεῖν γελοιότερον φρονιμώτερον τῆς ἐν Διονυσίᾳ].

units.la: ἀποφόρης ἀπὸ ἐξαγωγῆς ξύλων ἀπελ[?]. ) Quarundam mercium exportatio Atheniensium legibus prohibebatur, quæ propterea ἀπόῤῥητα vocabant. In primis autem τὰ ἀπορρήτων fuêre quæcunque ad nauium fabricationem pertinebant: hoc est πᾶξ ἡ ναυπηγήσιμῳ ὕλη, vt sunt abies, pinus, picea, cupressus, platanus, quæ aliâs ναυπηγήσιμα ξύλα, aliâs ξύλα absolutè vocantur. non fuisse autem copiam magnam huius materiæ in agro Atheniensium, docet etiam Demosthenes, aut quicunque alius est auctor orationis De fœdere cum Alexandro. Erant τὰ ἀπορρήτων, & τὰ ἀσκώματα, hoc est folliculi nautici, & λίνα, κηροὶ, & πίττα, inquit, Ariftophanis fcholiastes. Alia ratione dicebantur ἀπόῤῥητα quæ Athenas importare non permittebantur: vt ξυλάλιδες[?] ex quibus fiebant ellychnia: has enim, sicut constat ex Ariftophanis Acharnenfibus, fuit cum non liceret Bæotis afferre venales in vrbem: credo, ob metum incendiariorum. thryallidum namque stuppæ vsus fuit ad ἀσκός & malleolos incendiariorum.
units.tr: (from the export of timber) [ἀποφόρης ἀπὸ ἐξαγωγῆς ξύλων.] The Athenian laws forbade the export of certain goods, which for that reason they called forbidden [ἀπόρρητα]. Chief among these were all things that pertained to shipbuilding, that is, all shipbuilding timber [πᾶσα ἡ ναυπηγήσιμος ὕλη], such as fir, pine, spruce, cypress and plane. These are sometimes called shipbuilding timber [ναυπηγήσιμα ξύλα] and sometimes simply timber [ξύλα]. That there was not a great supply of this material in Attic territory is also shown by Demosthenes, or by whoever is the author of the speech On the Treaty with Alexander. The forbidden goods also included the nautical bags [ἀσκώματα], that is, the little sailors' flasks, and flax, wax and pitch [λίνα, κηροὶ, πίττα], as the scholiast on Aristophanes says. In another sense, things that were not permitted to be imported into Athens were also called forbidden. Among these were the materials from which wicks were made. For, as is clear from Aristophanes' Acharnians, at one time the Boeotians were not allowed to bring such goods to the city for sale, I suppose from fear of incendiaries. For the stuff of the thryallis plant was used for the bags and little mallets of incendiaries.

units.la: καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀσαφείᾳ[?]. ) Plane non erat ferendum doctis viris istud verbum dicam, an verbi monstrum? Legendum aio, σαφηνεία[?]. Imperiti homines & pistrino digni ex σαφῆ fecerunt σαφῶς[?]. Hæc prima mendi indoles: inde fluxit vox nequam & nihili ἀσαφία[?]. At σαφήνεια idem ac ἀσαφωνία[?], nisi quòd illud est ἐμφατικώτερον. Doctorum virorum emendatio ἐν τοῖς ἀσαφέσι[?], vt Musis iratis genióque sinistro nata, refutatione non eget. Non erat autem insolens AthenienAtheni[?]nfibus malum frumenti inopia, ut historia docet & oratores sæpe. Quomodo autem soliti essent ditiores in caritate annonæ pauperes subleuare, discesex Demosthene contra Phormionem.
units.tr: (and in the unclearness [ἀσαφείᾳ]) Surely learned men could not tolerate that word, dicam, or is it a monster of a word? I say we should read clearness [σαφηνείᾳ]. Unlearned men, fit only for the mill, made clearly [σαφῶς] out of clear [σαφῆ]. This was the first origin of the error, and from it flowed the worthless word and nonsense unclearness [ἀσαφία]. But clearness [σαφήνεια] is the same as obscurity [ἀσαφωνία], except that the former is more emphatic. The learned men's correction among the unclear things [ἐν τοῖς ἀσαφέσι], born as it were under angry Muses and a sinister genius, needs no refutation. Nor was it unusual for the Athenians to suffer from a shortage of grain, as history and the orators often show. How the richer citizens used to relieve the poor in times of dear grain, you may learn from Demosthenes against Phormio.

units.la: [?]καὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτὰς καθ᾽ ἑξακοσίας [?] μίαν.] Hoc est sexcentos homines solet sigillatim nominare quorum singulis aliquid erogarit: atque hac ratione efficere vt cum æra omnia in vnum colligantur, ex ea supputatione summa nascatur decem talentorum. Irrisitatur iste ἀλαζὼν eos qui rationum libros conficiunt, in quibus videas singula æra seorsim annotari. Æra appello, quos vulgo articulos dicimus, Gallice les items: quia solent in nostris rationum libris singulí articuli à voce item incipere. At Romani æra appellabant. Cicero Hortensio: Quid tu, inquam, soles cum rationem à dispensatore accipis, si æra singula probasti, summam quæ ex his confecta sit, non probare? Apuleius De deo Socratis, Igitur quotidianum eorum æra dispungas: inuenies rationibus multa prodigè profusa, & in semet nihil. Nonius, Æra, numeri nota. Lucil. lib. xxxx. Hæc est ratio peruersa æra summa, & subducta improbe. Locus est corruptissimus, quem ita restituendum puto. Hæc est ratio: peruersa æra: summa subducta est improbè. Cicero in epistola ad Dolabellam libro nono ad familiares, versiculos æra hæc appellare videtur. Profert alter (vt opinor) duobus versiculis expensum Niciæ. Sed ad Theophrastum redeamus; qui quidem gloriosorum hominum ingenium & mores mira elegantia exprimit. Non enim illis fatis est summarim se laudare & sua præclara facinora prædicare: nisi etiam longa eorundem enumeratione obuios quosque obtundant. Talia illa in Milite Plautina,
units.tr: (and so much, six hundred each, one) [καὶ τοσοῦτον αὐτὰς καθ᾽ ἑξακοσίας μίαν.] That is, he is accustomed to name six hundred men one by one, to each of whom he has given something, and so, when all the sums are gathered into one, the total of ten talents results from that reckoning. He mocks that boaster who draws up account books, in which you may see single sums noted separately. I call these æra, what we commonly call articles, in French les items, because in our account books the single entries usually begin with the word item. The Romans, however, called them æra. Cicero, to Hortensius: What do you do, I ask, when you receive an account from your steward? If you have checked each single entry, do you not check the total that is made up from them? Apuleius, On the God of Socrates: Therefore strike out their daily entries: you will find many things lavishly wasted in the accounts, and nothing in your own favour. Nonius: æra, a mark of number. Lucilius, book 30: This is the perverse reckoning, the entries and the sum dishonestly deducted. This passage is very corrupt, and I think it should be restored thus: This is the reckoning: perverse entries: the sum has been dishonestly deducted. Cicero, in his letter to Dolabella in book nine of the Letters to Friends, seems to call these entries little verses: The other, as I think, brings out a list of two little verses expended on Nicias. But let us return to Theophrastus, who expresses with wonderful elegance the character and manners of boastful men. For such men are not content merely to praise themselves in summary and proclaim their own splendid deeds, but they also wear out everyone they meet with long enumerations of them. Such is the boasting in Plautus' Soldier:

units.la: Py. Ecquid meministi? Ar. Memini: centum in Cilicia,
units.tr: Py. Do you remember anything? Ar. I remember: a hundred in Cilicia,

units.la: Et quinquaginta centum Sycolatronida, Triginta Sardi, sexaginta Macedones, Sunt homines tu quos occidisti uno die.
units.tr: And fifty from a hundred Sycolatronians, thirty Sardians, sixty Macedonians. These are the men you killed in a single day.

units.la: Py. Quanta isthac hominum summa est? Ar. Septem millia.
units.tr: Py. What is the total of these men? Ar. Seven thousand.

units.la: Py. Tantum esse oportet: recte rationem tenes.
units.tr: Py. It must be that: you hold the reckoning correctly.

units.la: Prorsus hic Plauti locus (etsi versantur hi duo gloriofi in diuersa materia: Plautinus enim virtutem bellicam: hic noster diuitias ostentat) prorsus inquam explicat quid fit hoc loco πορθὴν τὰς ψιῶσς καὶ ἐξακοσίας, ἢ μίαν. quæ verba quam fuerint doctis viris hactenus obscura, quid attinet dicere? Res clamat ipsa.
units.tr: Indeed this passage of Plautus (although these two boasters are engaged on different matters: Plautus's on military valour, ours here on displaying riches) fully explains what is meant here by having destroyed the six hundred, or one [πορθὴν τὰς ψιῶσς καὶ ἐξακοσίας, ἢ μίαν]. What point is there in saying how obscure these words have hitherto been to learned men? The thing itself cries out.

units.la: κηὶ προσιδεῖς πιθανὰ ἐκάστοις τῶν ὀνομάτων. Bene hoc: feruat enim solemne eorum qui mentiuntur. vide ad caput λογοποιίας. Auctor Rhetoricorum ad Herennium in descriptione illa ingeniofiffima ostentatoris pecuniosi non plane dissimilem gloriosorum istiusmodi morem notat: quem placet hic proferre, vt collatione Græci scriptoris qui id ipsum suauissimè notat, locum illustrem. Ait ergo Latinus auctor, Cum puerum respicit hunc vnum quem ego noui (vos non arbitror nouisse) alio nomine appellat, deinde alio atque alio. Mox, vt ignoti qui audiunt, vnum putent eligi de multis. Alexis vero sic in descriptione πλωχαλαζόι, fiue gloriosi pauperis,
units.tr: and you will see the names are plausible for each one [καὶ προσιδεῖς πιθανὰ ἐκάστοις τῶν ὀνομάτων]. Well said, for it preserves the customary manner of liars. See the chapter on lying [λογοποιία]. The author of the Rhetorica ad Herennium, in his very ingenious description of the wealthy show-off, notes a manner of boasting not very unlike this. I am pleased to cite it here, so that the passage may shine by comparison with the Greek writer who expresses this same thing most sweetly. The Latin author says: When he looks at the boy, the one I know (I do not think you know him), he calls him by one name, then by another and another. Then, so that the ignorant hearers think he is choosing one out of many. Alexis, in his description of the boastful poor man [πλωχαλαζών], says:

units.la: — οἶδα ἡ κἀγὼ τὰ ἀσολίτων ἡμέτερον πλωχαλαζόνα, ὃς δ' ραχμὴς ἔχων τὰ πάντ' ἀρ' ὑρώματ', ἐξία καλὼν τὸν οἰκέτην ἔνα οὔτε ἃ μόνον ὁ ἑαυτὸν [?] χρώμενος [?] ἡμῖν σαφῶς [?] ἐλαίαν [?] τὸ θεοῦ [?].
units.tr: I too know our boaster, who, having one drachma, buys all things for himself, and calls his slave ... to us, five hundred ... [οἶδα ἡ κἀγὼ τὰ ἀσολίτων ἡμέτερον πλωχαλαζόνα, ὃς δ' ραχμὴς ἔχων τὰ πάντ' ἀρ' ὑρώματ', ἐξία καλὼν τὸν οἰκέτην ἔνα οὔτε ἃ μόνον ὁ ἑαυτὸν χρώμενος ἡμῖν σαφῶς ἐλαίαν τὸ θεοῦ.]

units.la: ἀμμακοσίοις· πᾶσι σπ[?] μὴ τῆς χειμένων [?] ἡμῖν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐλαίῳ [?].
units.tr: five hundred ... to all ... not ... of the things lying to us, of the god's oil. [ἀμμακοσίοις· πᾶσι σπ[?] μὴ τῆς χειμένων ἡμῖν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐλαίῳ.]

units.la: sic emendamus elegantissimum hunc locum apud Athenæum.
units.tr: Thus we emend this most elegant passage in Athenaeus.

units.la: καὶ πεῖσον δὲ [?] τάλαν[?]. Delendum τὸ καί: & mox ἐπιστάτης [?], non ἐπιστῆς. Sic locus erit planus & perspicuus.
units.tr: And persuade ... [τάλαν] The word and [καί] must be deleted, and presently overseer [ἐπιστάτης], not ἐπιστῆς. So the passage will be plain and clear.

units.la: καὶ ὡς τῆς πρωτοτυπίας ἐπιστάμενος [?] ὅτι ἡ τίθησι. ] Κυεμολογία in voce τίθημι. Nam vulgò τιθέναι pro λογίζεσθαι, referre in rationes, vel in ratione ducere, vsurpabant. Sic apud Demosthenem in prima Olynthiaca, & in illa celebri Cratetis ephemeride, Τίθει μαχαίρᾳ μύας δὲ [?] ἰατρῷ δραχμῶν [?]. Etiam apud Latinos ponere fic accipitur, vt apud Terentium non femel. Proprie conuenit iis qui calculis rationes putant: vnde eft, ponere calculos, non femel apud Plinium in epistolis. & τιθέναι ψῆφον Graeci. Basilius, εἰ μέν τι δοκεῖς ἔχειν καλόν, τοῦτο ἐν ψήφῳ τίθεις.
units.tr: and knowing the originality that it places [καὶ ὡς τῆς πρωτοτυπίας ἐπιστάμενος ὅτι ἡ τίθησι.] A note on the word to place [τίθημι]. For commonly τιθέναι was used for to reckon, to enter in an account or to take into account. So in Demosthenes' first Olynthiac, and in that famous account book of Crates, Put down for the knife, mussels, for the doctor, drachmas. The Latin ponere is also used in this way, as in Terence more than once. It suits especially those who reckon with counters, whence the phrase ponere calculos, found more than once in Pliny's letters, and the Greeks say τιθέναι ψῆφον. Basil: If you think you have something fine, you place it on the counter [εἰ μέν τι δοκεῖς ἔχειν καλόν, τοῦτο ἐν ψήφῳ τίθεις].

units.la: εἰ δὲ τὰς λειτουργίας ὅσας λειτουργήσεις. ] Oftendit his verbis se vnum fuisse ex illis MDCC viris qui vt omnium ditissimi Reipublicæ, pleraque omnia muniaad quæ sumtibus opus esset, obibant. vide Harpocrationem in χῆλιοι, & Demosthenem, eiusque scholiasten. Caue vero ita hæc accipias quasi instructio triremis, cuius impensæ modò meminit, non esset λειτουργίας genus. erat enim, & quidem omnium maximum. Ac fortasse legendum, εἰ δὲ τὰς ἄλλας λειτουργίας. veruntamen similiter locutos sæpe maximos scriptores pridem doctissimi Iurisconsulti annotarunt.
units.tr: and if you perform all the public services that you will perform [εἰ δὲ τὰς λειτουργίας ὅσας λειτουργήσεις]. By these words he shows that he was one of those 700 men who, being the wealthiest of all, undertook for the commonwealth most of the public services that required expense. See Harpocration on chiliarchs [χῆλιοι], and Demosthenes and his scholiast. But be careful not to take this as if the equipping of a trireme, whose expense he has just mentioned, were not a kind of public service; for it was, and indeed the greatest of all. Perhaps we should read the other public services [εἰ δὲ τὰς ἄλλας λειτουργίας]. Yet the most learned jurists have long since noted that the greatest writers often spoke in this way.

units.la: καὶ προσελθὼν δ᾽ εἰς τὰς ἱστορίας ἀγαθὸς πωλεῖσθαι. ] Senfus perfpicuus : verba variè poffunt reformari: vel enim ita, ἕ ῳρ. ἀλ᾽ εἰς τ, ἱστης. ἢ τὰς ἀξιοὺς πω-λέσι. aut etiam ἢ τὰς ἱστης τὰς ἀγ. geminata eadem vox, omissa eft vt alibi. vel ita, ἡ ῳρ. ὡς τὰς τὰς ἱστης τὰς ἀγ. πωλῆν(ας. primum malo. Nam εἰς ἵ-πης ῳροσελθεῖν, eft ad forum ire vbi equi veneunt: fic alibi, ῳροσελθεῖν πρὸς τὰ κάπυρα, de quo Atticisimo dixi-mus supra. & eapropter χύτρας Hefychius exponit χυτροπώλια.
units.tr: and going up to the histories, good to be sold [καὶ προσελθὼν δ᾽ εἰς τὰς ἱστορίας ἀγαθὸς πωλεῖσθαι.] The sense is clear, though the words can be restored in various ways: either as one reads them, or as to the horse market [εἰς ἵππης ἀγοράν], or as the market for horses [τὰς ἵππους ἀγοράς] sold. I prefer the first. For to go up to the horse market [εἰς ἵππους προσελθεῖν] means going to the forum where horses are sold; so elsewhere to go up to the stalls [προσελθεῖν πρὸς τὰ κάπηλα], which I discussed above under the Attic idiom. And for this reason Hesychius explains pots [χύτρας] as pot-markets [χυτροπώλια].

units.la: ῳροσωνίζοντα ὠνηλιᾶν.) Iuuenalis de caufidico populo fese venditante, Pérque forum iuuenes longo premit affere Medos Empturus pueros, argentum, myrrhina, villas.
units.tr: Juvenal, of the citizen who pushes through the forum to sell himself: "And through the forum he presses with a long train of young men, about to buy Median boys, silver, myrrhine vessels, and estates" [προσωνούμενος ὠνητιᾶν].

units.la: καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς κλίνας ἐλθών.] Lego ἐν τὰς σκιωάς. In mercatibus & panegyribus folebant mercatores fub tentoriis fuas merces venum expofitas habere, vt docet fcholiastes Theocriti: & Harpocration, ἐν σκιωάς, ait, ὑπεραγραφὴ πολλά τῷ ὠνίων. cum vide in γ́ἐργα. meminit & Plato in x. de legibus. Has vt puto Latini umbras vocabant, vt ex fragmentis Fefti licet intelligere: inde eft apud Horatium umbra pro officina. — vacua tonforis in umbra.
units.tr: And coming to the couches.] I read "in the shades" [ἐν σκιαῖς]. At markets and festival fairs merchants used to display their goods for sale under tents, as the scholiast on Theocritus shows, and Harpocration says of "in the shades" [ἐν σκιαῖς] that it is a frequent expression for the stalls. See under "works" [ἔργα]. Plato also mentions them in Book 10 of the Laws. I think the Latins called these "umbrae," as can be gathered from the fragments of Festus; hence Horace uses "umbra" for a workshop: "in the empty shop of the barber" [vacua tonsoris in umbra].

units.la: Locus autem Athenis vbi veftes vendebantur, ἐμπολιοπώλις & ἀνεπορωπώλις ἀγορά nuncupabatur.
units.tr: The place in Athens where clothes were sold was called the market of the cloth-sellers and of the second-hand dealers [ἐμπολιοπώλις and ἀνεπορωπώλις ἀγορά].

units.la: ἐκ ἔχων χρυσὸν νῦν πὰ ἀκολυθεῖν.) Scribe ἐκ ἔχοντα χρυσὸν ἐν τῇ ἀκολυθεῖν. Mos autem hic veterum fuit, vt ex Laertio, Plutarcho, Apuleio, aliisque apparet.
units.tr: "Not having gold to follow.") Write "not having gold, to follow" [μὴ ἔχοντα χρυσὸν ἐν τῇ ἀκολουθεῖν]. This was the ancient custom, as appears from Laertius, Plutarch, Apuleius and others.

units.la: ἐν μεσῷ οἰκία οἰκῶν.) Sic libri Palatini. & nos ita quoque olim emendabamus vulgatam lectionem ἐν μεσῷ τῷ οἰκίαν οἰκῶν. Dio Cocceius, ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ οἰκεῖν. deinde scribe, ἐὰν ἔτι μέλλῃς : non διότι μέλλει. διότι μέλλει πωλεῖν αὐτῷ.) Ipsissimum hoc ἀλαζονείας genus notatum apud Athenæum lib. x i i i. Θαΐς, inquit, ἐρᾷ τι: ὃς αὐτῆς ἀλαζὼν [?] ἀφ' [illegible, ~6 letters] πολλῶν πόλεια χρημάτων, [?] ἐ λέ[?]γει [?] ταῦτα συλλογάς [?], ἀλλὰ ἢ καθ' ἑαυτὸν [?] ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ τὸ εἶναι. Quidam, ait, qui Thaidem amabat, cum à multis pocula commodata accepisset, diceretque velle se ea conflare, Perdes, inquit illa, uninscuiusque quod suum est.
units.tr: "Living in a house in the middle.") So the Palatine manuscripts read [ἐν μέσῳ οἰκία οἰκῶν]. We too used to emend the vulgar reading [ἐν μέσῳ τῇ οἰκίᾳ οἰκῶν] in this way. Dio Cocceius suggests [ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ οἰκεῖν]. Then write [ἐὰν ἔτι μέλλῃς], not [διότι μέλλει]; "since he is about to sell" [διότι μέλλει πωλεῖν αὐτῷ]. This very kind of boasting is noted in Athenaeus, Book 13. A certain man who loved Thais, he says, when he had received cups on loan from many people, and said he wished to melt them down, was told by her: "You will ruin each man's property." [Greek fragments are illegible in the scan.]

units.la: Atque hîc scribendi finem faciemus: & simul cum vertente anno, animi nostri metem alió conuertemus. Commodùm enim cum hæc scriberem dies agebatur anni huius xc1. nouissimus. quæ me res admonebat ut duplicis voti reas DEo OPT. MAX. grates agerem gratissimas: & quod annum hunc uiuenti valentique dede it exigere: & quòd hunc commentariolum in hacce rutuba absoluere. qua opera si doctorum virorum studia promerui, iuniorum etiam promoui, bene habet: feci quod volui: sin autem, ὁ μὴ ἡδύς [?] ἔσαι, feci quod potui.
units.tr: And here I shall make an end of writing; and at the turn of the year I shall turn my mind to other matters. For as I was writing these things, the last day of this year (xc1) was being spent, which reminded me to give most grateful thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, for two things: that he granted me this year to pass in life and health, and that he allowed me to finish this little commentary in this hurried work. If by this labour I have earned the approval of learned men, and have also helped the younger students, well and good: I have done what I wanted. But if not, [ὁ μὴ ἡδύς ἔσαι], I have done what I could.
Notes on the Ethical Characters [Ἠθικῶν χαρακτήρων] of Theophrastus

units.la: QVINQVE hæc postrema capita nacti sumus ex Illustrissimi Principis Palatini bibliotheca, quæ Heidelbergæ visitur. Descripsit illa accuratè manu sua, nobisque donauit, Marquardus Freherus, Iurisconsultus, altæ eruditionis vir, Germaniæ suæ ocellus. Verè Theophrastea esse, nemo dubitauerit sanus, qui diligentius illa cum superioribus contenderit. Et res & verba eum scriptorem manifestissimè, si attendimus, χαρακτηρίζειν[?]. In plerisque omnibus scriptis libris ea desiderari, nullus miror. Iam olim, ut nunc quoque, philosophātium ingens crimen est, quòd scriptorum summi huius viri parùm diligentes fuerint. Itaque ergo ex illa prope infinita copia librorum, quos infinito labore subtilissimus philosophus conscripserat, oppido pauci ad nos peruenerunt. Et hos tamen ipsos quotusquisque legit illorum sophorum, ad quos solos hodiè rudem esse philosophiæ vulgus censet imperitum? Illud sæpe sum miratus, Iohannem Stobæum qui ante tot secula vixit, quæ nunc primùm publicamus in suis codicibus non habuisse: inseruisset enim ea operi suo, absque dubio, si ad manum fuissent, non minus quàm illa xv. capita quæ in primis editionibus sola extabant: Et item illa octo quæ ex Italicis bibliothecis primus in lucem protulit optimè de literis meritus ὁ μακαρίτης Henricus Stephanus noster. Multum igitur debemus bibliothecæ Palatinæ illustrissimi Principis, in qua sola, quod sciam, hoc pulcherrimum fragmentum hodiè reperias. Sed dolendum est, tam turpiter deformatum id ad nos peruenisse: nullum enim est caput ex his quinque non adeò mendis inquinatum, vt auctoris mentem assequi perquam difficile fuerit, & propè ἀδωάτων ἐν[?]. Viri docti & acuti, ingenij vires, spero, hîc periclitabuntur. Nos, sublatis mendis quæ tutò corrigi poterant, in cæterorum versione quid secuti simus raptim & breuiter indicabimus. Οὐχ ἕδρας ᾧ ἔργον, ἀλλ' ἀμβολάς[?], vt ait vetus poëta.
units.tr: We obtained these last five chapters from the library of the most illustrious Prince Palatine, which is kept at Heidelberg. Marquard Freher, a jurist of profound learning and the pride of his country, copied them out carefully by his own hand and gave them to us. No sane person who compares them carefully with the earlier chapters will doubt that they are truly Theophrastus's. If we attend closely, both the matter and the wording clearly mark the writer's style. That so much has been lost from most of his books, no one is surprised. Even in earlier times, as now, it has been a great reproach to scholars that so few have taken care of the works of this great man. So from that almost endless stock of books, which this most acute philosopher wrote with infinite labour, very few have reached us. And even of these few, how many of those philosophers, whom the uneducated crowd alone thinks worthy of study today, actually read them? I have often wondered that John Stobaeus, who lived so many centuries ago, did not have in his manuscripts the chapters we are now publishing for the first time. Without doubt, had they been at hand, he would have included them in his work no less than those fifteen chapters that alone survived in the early editions, and likewise those eight that our late Henry Stephanus [ὁ μακαρίτης], who deserved so well of letters, first brought to light from Italian libraries. We owe much, therefore, to the library of the most illustrious Prince Palatine, for, so far as I know, it is the only place where this most beautiful fragment can be found today. But it is to be regretted that it has come down to us so shamefully corrupted. Indeed, none of these five chapters is free of errors so great that it is extremely difficult to grasp the author's meaning, and some passages are nearly [ἀδωάτων]. I hope that learned and sharp minds will test their powers here. As for us, having removed the errors that could be corrected safely, we shall briefly and hastily indicate what we followed in the translation of the rest. "Not a seat is the work, but a sieve [ἀμβολάς]," as the old poet says.

units.la: Ἐστι ἡ ὑπερηφανία[?], ) Vitium cuius hic est character, magnam habet adfinitatem cum duobus aliis antè descriptis, αὐθαδεία & ἀλαζονεία. Superbus homo de se longè quàm par sit, magnificentius sentit: ostentator quoque siue ὁ ἀλαζὼν, ea de se prædicat, quæ in ipso non sint. Hoc differunt, quod sine contumelia aliorum sua extollit ostentator, & seipsum [illegible, ~9 letters], vt cum D. Paulo dicam: superbus contumeliosus est, omnesque præ vno se despicit. Inde huic vitio nomen apud Græcos ὑπερη-φανία, ὕβρις[?], quòd eminere se, & cæteris mortalibus superiorem esse persuasum habeat ὁ ὑπέρ[?]φανος[?]. Latinis quoque simili de caussa, nominata est superbia. Omnino superbiæ duo insunt mala: vana de sua præstantia opinio, & despectus aliorum. Prius illud proprie ἀυθάδεια est: posterius ὑπερηφανία, siue ὑπερoφία. Suffenus sibi est, ὁ αὐθάδης: contumeliosus in alios ὁ ὑπερήφανος. Ac vix est, vt in quo duorum istorum alterum insit, non & vtrumque insit. Quare etiam apud scriptores hæc passim videas omnia coniungi, atque eidem tribui. Ingens prosecto vitium superbia, Deo hominibusque exosum. De quo Seruius eleganter: Apud maiores, inquit, superbia ingens facinus fuit: adeo vt Tarquinius pro multis sceleribus Superbi nomen acceperit. Propterea sanctissimus pater Ioannes Chrysostomus superbiam tanquam extremum omnium vitiorum ἀπόνοιαν solitus appellare. Proprie quid sit ἀπόνοια Græcis, satis declaratum nobis in superioribus: sed apud aureum illud diuinæ eloquentiæ flumen eo quem dixi sensu, sexcétis locis obseruauimus. Proferemus vnum aut alterum exemplum fidei nostræ caussa: In commentariis in epistolam ad Galatas, explicans D. Pauli verba, ἀλλήλοις: scribit, ἐν ταύτῃ ἀγάπης[?] ἀλλήλοις[?] ἐν ζῆλος[?] τῆς φιλαρχίας[?] ἐξ ὕβρεως[?] καὶ ἐν τῷ αἰσχρῷ[?] τῆς ἀπονοίας[?] ἐκ ταύτης ... ὅτι ἐξ ἀπονοίας καὶ τύφου τὸ κακὸν[?]. Mox iterum, ἡ τῆς ἀγάπης θερμότης[?] ταύτῃ τύφον καὶ ἀπονοίαν πυρὸς σφόδρα ... In homilia περὶ ἀχῆς[?], Dauidem in pugnam cum Goliatho descendere paratum, ita populares increpitant, πόθεν Ǵι ἡ ἀπό- νοια αὕλη ; & ἡμεῖς οἰδαμὲν τὸ ὑπερηφανίαν καὶ τὸ καχίαν τῆς καρδίας σε. quibus respondet ipse, Ego, inquit, ὡς ἀσόνοιαν ἀλλὰ πίστιν, ἡ Σώρακα, ἀλλὰ Σωσ- Cεσαν καθοωλίζομαι[?].
units.tr: Arrogance [Ἐστι ἡ ὑπερηφανία]: The vice whose character this is has a great affinity with two others described earlier, self-will [αὐθαδεία] and boastfulness [ἀλαζονεία]. The proud man thinks of himself far more grandly than is fitting, and the boaster also claims for himself things that are not in him. They differ in this: the boaster exalts himself without insulting others, but [illegible] , as I may say with St Paul: the proud man is insolent, and despises all others in comparison with himself. Hence the Greeks named this vice ὑπερηφανία and ὕβρις, because the proud man is persuaded that he stands out and is superior to other mortals [ὑπέρφανος]. The Latins likewise named it superbia for a similar reason. Certainly two evils lie in superbia: a vain opinion of one's own excellence, and contempt for others. The first is properly self-will [ἀυθάδεια]; the second is arrogance [ὑπερηφανία], or contempt [ὑπερoφία]. The self-willed man is pleased with himself [ὁ αὐθάδης]; the arrogant man is insolent towards others [ὁ ὑπερήφανος]. Scarcely can one of these two be present without the other also being present. Therefore you will see in the writers that these are everywhere joined together and ascribed to the same person. Pride is indeed a huge vice, hateful to God and to men. Servius says of it elegantly: Among our ancestors, pride was a great crime; so much so that Tarquin received the name Superbus for many crimes. For this reason the most holy father John Chrysostom used to call pride, as the extreme of all vices, [ἀπόνοια]. What [ἀπόνοια] properly means to the Greeks has been sufficiently explained to us above, but in that golden stream of divine eloquence we have observed it in the sense I have mentioned in some six hundred places. I shall put forward one or two examples for the support of our faith. In his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, explaining the words of St Paul, one another, he writes: [ἐν ταύτῃ ἀγάπης ἀλλήλοις ἐν ζῆλος τῆς φιλαρχίας ἐξ ὕβρεως καὶ ἐν τῷ αἰσχρῷ τῆς ἀπονοίας ἐκ ταύτης ... ὅτι ἐξ ἀπονοίας καὶ τύφου τὸ κακόν] ... Soon again: [ἡ τῆς ἀγάπης θερμότης ταύτῃ τύφον καὶ ἀπονοίαν πυρὸς σφόδρα ...]. In the homily on [ἀχῆς], where David is about to go down to fight Goliath, the people rebuke him: [πόθεν Ǵι ἡ ἀπόνοια αὕλη; καὶ ἡμεῖς οἰδαμὲν τὸ ὑπερηφανίαν καὶ τὸ καχίαν τῆς καρδίας σε], to which he himself replies: [Ἐγώ, φησί, ὡς ἀσόνοιαν ἀλλὰ πίστιν, ἡ Σώρακα, ἀλλὰ Σωσεσαν καθοωλίζομαι], that is, "I am not armed with arrogance but with faith, not with a sling but with salvation." [The Greek is corrupt in the print.]

units.la: Οἱ δὲ τῷ σαλδοντι διὰ δείπνου ἐντὸς ἐξεδωσαν φάσιν ἐν τῷ περιπατεῖν.) Hæc vt reperta sunt in MSS. codd. ab eruditissimo Frehero, sic & à nobis edita. Vitium patet suopte indicio. Putamus atque adeo credimus, veram lectionem coniectura nos esse assecutos. Legimus autem, οἱ δὲ τῷ σαλδοντι ἐνλὰξεσθαι διὰ δείπνου φάσκειν ἐν τῷ περιπατεῖν. Sententiam exprimit clarè interpretatio: neque potest aliud quicquam fingi huic loco aptius. Ofcitans librarius vocem praetermisit, quam putabat esse otiosam, propter sequens verbum ἐνλὰξεσθαι.
units.tr: "Those who, when the man was dining, gave out a report inside [οἱ δὲ τῷ σαλδοντι διὰ δείπνου ἐντὸς ἐξεδωσαν φάσιν ἐν τῷ περιπατεῖν]." These readings were found in the manuscripts by the most learned Freher and so we have printed them. The fault is evident from the sense itself. We think, and indeed believe, that we have reached the true reading by conjecture. We read: [οἱ δὲ τῷ σαλδοντι ἐνλὰξεσθαι διὰ δείπνου φάσκειν ἐν τῷ περιπατεῖν]. The interpretation expresses the meaning clearly, and nothing more suitable to this place can be imagined. The copyist, yawning, omitted a word which he thought superfluous because of the following verb [ἐνλὰξεσθαι].

units.la: μεμνῆσθαι φάσκειν ἐν ταῖς ὅδ.) Si cui mendi fuerit hic locus suspectus, ei per me licet in excogitanda meliore lectione esse ingenioso.
units.tr: "To claim to remember on the ways [μεμνῆσθαι φάσκειν ἐν ταῖς ὅδ.]." If anyone finds this place suspicious as to its text, he is welcome to be ingenious in devising a better reading.

units.la: Σελήνας.) Scrib. Σελήσαι. vt pendeat oratio ab οἱ δ. vel certè Σελήσαι. Simile est inter αὐθαδείας notas quam diximus esse superbiae germanam, καὶ ἂν ἐπομένας, ἐν ἂν ἀποσμένας πολὺ χρόνον ἡ ἐνα.
units.tr: "Selenas [Σελήνας]." Read [Σελήσαι], so that the sentence depends on [οἱ δ.], or at least [Σελήσαι]. Similar is what we said above among the marks of self-will, which are kin to pride: [καὶ ἂν ἐπομένας, ἐν ἂν ἀποσμένας πολὺ χρόνον ἡ ἐνα].

units.la: καὶ μεμψιμοῖρα.) Copulam pro difiunctiva potuit, vt passim optimi auctores: vel scribendum ἡ μ.
units.tr: "And fault-finding [καὶ μεμψιμοῖρα]." He could have used the conjunction for a disjunctive, as the best authors do everywhere; or [ἡ μ.] should be written.

units.la: μὴ λαλεῖν ᾧς ἐλυ χάνσο.) Adfine est quod supra tribuebatur τῷ αὐθαδεί, his verbis: καὶ πρὸς γορὰ μὴ ἀνθρώπους ἐντὶν.
units.tr: "Not to speak [μὴ λαλεῖν ᾧς ἐλυ χάνσο]." This is related to what was earlier ascribed to the self-willed man in these words: [καὶ πρὸς γορὰ μὴ ἀνθρώπους ἐντὶν], "and in the market not to be among people."

units.la: τῷ παιδὶ σωφρονεῖν τὰς ὑφὴς διωθεῖν.) More suo Theophraftus ipsum loquendi genus retinuit quo vti soliti homines superbi. Ὑψεως διωθεῖν proprie est fortes[?], quarum in iudiciis erat Athenis vsus, traiicere per κύαμον, id erat vrnæ operculum πλεκτὸν, κανισκωδες, pluribus descriptum nobis in animaduersionibus Athenaicis. Hesychius, Κίθιον, ὦ τὰς ψήφος διωδῶσιν ἐν ταῖς κληρωτηρίοις. ita scribendum ibi, non vt editum est κληρωτηρίοις. Hic vero ψήφος διωδεῖν positum pro calculis summatim rationes putare. Elegans translatio, & superbi hominis moribus conuenientissima. Adeo enim indignum se iudicat, sedere ad calculos, vt ne famulum quidem suum eos tractare velit, nisi negligenter & raptim.
units.tr: "To push the votes aside for the boy to be sober [τῷ παιδὶ σωφρονεῖν τὰς ὑφὴς διωθεῖν]." In his own way Theophrastus kept the very manner of speaking which proud men are wont to use. [Ὑψεως διωθεῖν] properly means to pass the votes through the bean [κύαμον], that is, the lid of the urn, woven and basket-shaped, which was in use in Athenian courts; we have described it at length in our Athenian annotations. Hesychius has: [Κίθιον, ὦ τὰς ψήφος διωδῶσιν ἐν ταῖς κληρωτηρίοις], so there it should be written [κληρωτηρίοις], not as printed. Here, however, [ψήφος διωδεῖν] is used in the sense of reckoning accounts with pebbles [calculi]. An elegant rendering, and most suited to the manners of a proud man. For he judges it so beneath him to sit at the reckoning with counters that he does not even want his own servant to handle them, except carelessly and hastily.

units.la: καὶ τὸ κεφάλαιον ποιήσαι.) Puerum suum iubet imperiosus iste Manlius, in rationes referre summam quæ nascetur ex ipsius computo: alterius quicum rationes putat nullam habet rationem: si quid forte ille, vt ferè fit, quod opponat habet. Sic ista verba debent accipi.
units.tr: "And to make the total [καὶ τὸ κεφάλαιον ποιήσαι]." This haughty Manlius orders his boy to enter in the accounts the sum which arises from his own calculation; with the other man with whom he reckons accounts he has no reckoning at all, if that man perhaps has something to object, as usually happens. These words must be understood in this way.

units.la: Ἀμέλει ἡ δειλία δόξιν τῆ ὑπαξις τῆς ψυχῆς ἐμ-φοβ(ῶ). Planior est quæ habetur apud Andronicum definitio, Δειλία ἐστὶν ὑποχώρησις ἀπὸ φαινομένου καθήκοντος ἀπὸ φαντασίας δεινοῦ. Similes huic apud alios reperias. At in Platonis Ὅρος locus, qui definitionem δειλίας continet & corruptus est, & male à doctis acceptus: Eum nos in transcursu emendabimus, & exponemus. Ὅρος, ψυχῆς πόνων ἀρχῆς. Δειλία, ἀνιλαπτικὴ ὁρμῆς πρώτη τῆ ἐξ αἰτία. Docti corrigunt, Ὅρος, ψυχὴ πόνων. Ἀρχὴ, πρώτη τῆ ἐξ αἰτία. Δειλία ἀνιλαπτικὴ ὁρμῆς, quæ emendatio, si est à libris,tollo manum, & acquiesco. Sed quia omnes quos vidi codd. aliter legunt, minore mutatione, ita potius scribo, Ὄχι [?], ψυχὴ πόνων ἀρχῆς. Δήλια, ἀν-λιχὴ ὁρμῆς (fortasse deest vox ἐξις, vel scribédum ὁρμὴ) πρώτη τὸ δὲ εἶναι αἰτία. Id est, Cunctatio, est fuga ab inchoando labore. Timiditas, est quae impetum faciedi aliquid reprimit, prima cur metuamus causa. Addita est definitioni ὄκνος, vox ἀρχῆς, non temere, neque fine causa. Est enim revera cūctatio non tam laboris metus, quàm inchoandi laboris fuga. Ideo aliis definitur φόβος μελλήσεως ἐνεργείας. Vox ἀντιληπτικὴ ita accipienda in definitione δηλίας, ut alibi apud Platonem, ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι pro reprimere & cohibere. In Theophrastea descriptione ὑπὲξις est contrarium τῆς ἀθυμίας: quae vox in definitione fortitudinis, plerisque philosophorum posita loco generis.
units.tr: Surely cowardice is a [δόξιν] ... of the soul, a kind of fear. A plainer definition is the one found in Andronicus: "Cowardice is a withdrawing from what appears to be one's duty, from an imagined terror" [Δειλία ἐστὶν ὑποχώρησις ἀπὸ φαινομένου καθήκοντος ἀπὸ φαντασίας δεινοῦ]. You will find similar ones in other writers. But the passage in Plato's Definitions that contains the definition of cowardice is corrupt, and scholars have construed it wrongly. I will correct it in passing and explain it. The text reads: "Definition: a beginning of the soul's labours. Cowardice: a restraint of impulse, the first cause." Scholars correct it to: "Definition: the soul's labours. The beginning, the first cause. Cowardice: a restraint of impulse." If that correction comes from the manuscripts, I give up and accept it. But since all the manuscripts I have seen read otherwise, I would rather make a smaller change and write: "Not ... the soul's labours. Cowardice, a restraint of impulse (perhaps the word ἕξις is missing, or ὁρμὴ should be written), the first, but the being, the cause." That is, Cunctatio is a flight from beginning labour. Timidity is what checks the impulse to do something, the first cause of our fearing. The word ὄκνος, "hesitation," has been added to the definition, and the word "beginning" is not added carelessly or without reason. Indeed, hesitation is not so much fear of the labour as flight from beginning the labour. For this reason it is elsewhere defined as "fear of delaying action." The word ἀντιληπτικὴ must be understood in the definition of cowardice as it is elsewhere in Plato, where ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι means to check and restrain. In Theophrastus' description, ὑπέξις is the opposite of ἀθυμία. This word, in the definition of courage, is placed by most philosophers in the position of the genus.

units.la: Τὰς ἄκρας φάσεις ἡμιολίας ἐχ.) Herodotus Urania quosdam commemorat in fugam coëversos, quòd putarent promontoria esse hostiles naues. Ἐπὶ δὲ ἀχ ἴσαν Ζωσῆρ πλωοῦντες οἱ βάρβαροι, ἀναλύσεντο ἄκραν λεπταὶ τῆς ἠπείρου τούτης, ἰδόξαν τε νῆας εἶναι, καὶ ἔφυγον ἐπὶ πολλόν.
units.tr: "Those who were sailing, seeing the headlands of the coast, ..." Herodotus, in book 8 (Urania), records certain men who turned to flight because they thought the promontories were enemy ships. "When the barbarians sailed to Zoster, they came upon the narrow headlands of this mainland; thinking they were ships, they fled far away" [Ἐπὶ δὲ ἀχ ἴσαν Ζωσῆρ πλωοῦντες οἱ βάρβαροι, ἀναλύσεντο ἄκραν λεπταὶ τῆς ἠπείρου τούτης, ἰδόξαν τε νῆας εἶναι, καὶ ἔφυγον ἐπὶ πολλόν].

units.la: καὶ κλυδωνίας γιγνομένης.) Semper enim vectores adversa tempestate timidi ac perterriti, causam procellae soliti ascribere impietati alicuius eorum qui in navi. Exemplum nobile in Iona, & item alterum in Diagora, ac similibus. Propterea qui erat numinis reverentiores, haut temere cum notae impietatis hominibus navigabant. Horatius,
units.tr: "And when a storm arose": for passengers in a rough storm are always timid and terrified, and they are accustomed to attribute the cause of the tempest to the impiety of someone aboard the ship. A famous example is in Jonah, and another in Diagoras and similar cases. For this reason, those who were more reverent toward the divine did not readily sail with men of notorious impiety. Horace says:

units.la: —vetabo, qui Cereris sacrum, Vulgarit arcana, sub iisdem
units.tr: "I shall forbid whoever has divulged the secret rites of Ceres

units.la: Sit trabibus, fragilemq; mecum Soluat fasellum. sæpe Diespiter Neglectus, incesto addidit integrum.
units.tr: to sail under the same timbers with me, and to cast off the fragile little skiff. Often Jupiter, when neglected, has added a whole storm to an impious man."
Xenophon also touches on this in book 8 of the Education of Cyrus.

units.la: τῷ κυβερνήτῃ ἀναχωρῆσαι [?] ... ἀλλὰ [?] ... ὑπὸ τοῦ ... [?] ) Legendum, πωμαδὴ [?]. Et ἀνακόπτειν [?] interpretor, ἀνακόπτειν κελεύοντ[?]. Nauem ἀνακόπτειν puto dici gubernatorem, cùm præuiso scopulo, aut alio periculo cursum nauigationis mutat. Inde oritur metus in animo timidi, & ex metu hæc quæstio, Εἰ μὴ [?]; quasi dicat, Num periculum est aliquod ne vel scopulis illidatur nauis, vel in breuia aut syrtes deferatur? Adsine est apud D. Paulum, ἐγκόπτειν τὴν πεῖραν.
units.tr: "To the helmsman, to turn back ..." [?] The text should be read as "πωμαδὴ [?]". I interpret ἀνακόπτειν as the command "to hold back" [ἀνακόπτειν κελεύοντ...]. I think ἀνακόπτειν is said of the helmsman who, having seen a rock or other danger ahead, changes the course of the voyage.
