From this arises fear in the mind of the timid man, and from that fear this question, "If ...?" as if he said: "Is there some danger that the ship will be dashed on the rocks, or driven onto shallows or sandbars?" A similar word is found in St Paul: ἐγκόπτειν τὴν πεῖραν [Gal. 5. "to hinder"].

units.la: καὶ τί δοκεῖ αὐτῷ τὰ τῆς θεοῦ.) Veteres nihil fecisse aut aggressos esse inauspicato,certum est:fuerte [?] autem modi fermè innumeri explorandæ Deum voluntatis, vt notum omnibus. Eò referenda sunt hæc verba.
units.tr: "And what does he think of the things of God?" It is certain that the ancients undertook nothing, nor began anything, without good omens; but there were almost countless ways of seeking out the will of God, as is well known to all. To these the following words refer.

units.la: καὶ ἐκδοὺς διδόναι τῷ ναυτῇ τὸν χιτῶνα.) Vestem exuit etiam interiorem, vt ad natandum sit paratior si frangatur nauis. χιτωνίσκῳ modò interiorem tunicam & ἐπίβρωκον significat, modò paruum, χιτῶνα, vt sagum: interdum operis subtilitas, & τὸ ὑπέρειον, & ἀνύφῳ ea voce declaratur. Sed hæc alibi nobis explicantur.
units.tr: "And giving his tunic to the sailor." He takes off even his inner garment, so as to be more ready to swim if the ship is wrecked. The word χιτωνίσκῳ sometimes denotes the inner tunic and ἐπίβρωκον, sometimes a small χιτών, like a sagum; sometimes it denotes the fineness of the work, and τὸ ὑπέρειον and ἀνύφῳ are explained by that word. But these matters are explained by us elsewhere.

units.la: καὶ σάλως [?] ... ) Cùm stetit vtraque acies, parans se ad pugnam, tum ille respectat de superiore loco, & hostem vbi sit quærit, simulans eum se inuenire non posse. Cæterùm characterem χαρακτῆρα hominis ad conspectum hostilium copiarum pauentis, habes apud eloquentissimum
units.tr: "And ... " When both lines have halted, preparing for battle, he looks back from the higher ground and asks where the enemy is, pretending that he cannot find him. You will find the portrait of a man terrified at the sight of the hostile forces, χαρακτῆρα, in the most eloquent writer [Synesius].

units.la: Synefium, epistola c 1 v. cuius initium, Τὰς αὐτὰς ἂν ἰδοις, &c. Lege sodes, & confer cum istis. κελ[?]δ́ν προσκοπεῖσθαι.) Malo κελ[?]δ' ὧν. προσφερόμενον τῇ φίλων.) Scribendum, vel προσ-φερόμενον ἐπὶ τῇ φ. vel προσφερομένων τ. φ. Est autem προσφέρεσθαι, ad tentorium deferre. Si esset προσφερόμενον, significaret ea vox, quem ex acie amici efferebant. πρὸς sæpe idem valet in compositione, atq; ἐκ. κ̀ρ̀ ... Legendum σαρρῆν[?]. ὡς κινδυνωδ[?]ῶς ... Lego ἵνα σέσωσε τ. φ. καὶ εἰσάγειν προς τὸν κα[?]. Ita verte, Atque eos (intelligit quoscunque obuios de pugna redeuntes) ad iacentem introducit, inquisiturus quinam sint illius tribules, quis populus, aut pagus. Notum quid δῆμ[?] Atheniensibus. Puto iam nihil deesse, neque corruptum esse : etsi fuit cùm aliter censerem.
units.tr: Synesius, letter 1, whose opening is "Τὰς αὐτὰς ἂν ἴδοις" [You would see the same things], etc. Please read it and compare it with those words. "κελ[?]δὼν προσκοπεῖσθαι" [...]. I prefer "κελ[?]δ' ὧν". "προσφερόμενον τῇ φίλων" [being carried to the friends]: it should be read either "προσφερόμενον ἐπὶ τῇ φ." or "προσφερομένων τ. φ." Now προσφέρεσθαι means to be carried to the tent; if it were προσφερόμενον, the word would mean "whom the friends carried out of the battle line." πρὸς often has the same force in composition as ἐκ. "κ̀ρ̀ ..." The reading should be "σαρρῆν[?]". "ὡς κινδυνωδ[?]ῶς ..." I read "ἵνα σέσωσε τ. φ. καὶ εἰσάγειν προς τὸν κα[?]". Translate thus: "And he brings in those (he means whoever they are that meet him returning from the battle) to the man lying down, to inquire who his tribesmen are, what people or village he belongs to." The word δῆμ[?] is well known to the Athenians. I think nothing is now missing, nor is the text corrupt, although at one time I thought otherwise.
On the chapter περὶ ὀλιγαρχίας [concerning oligarchy].

units.la: Δόξειν ἂν τῇ ἡ ὀλιγαρχία.) Quemadmodum Romæ duæ erant in Rep. sectæ, altera optimatium, altera eorum qui populares dici, haberiqué volebant: sic etiam Athenis. Cornelius Nepos in Phocione, cuius temporibus viuebat Theophrastus, Erant, inquit, eo tempore Athenis duæ factiones: quarum vna populi caussam agebat, altera optimatium. Populares scriptores Attici vocant τὰς δημοτικὰς: optimates, τὰς ὀλιγαρχικάς. Horum mentio passim in historia Attica, & apud oratores Græcos. Isocrates in ea de pace, ἐὰν πανσώμεθα δημοτικὰς μὲν νομίζοντες τῇ τὰς συνοφάντας ὀλιγαρχικὰς ἢ τὰς καλὰς καὶ αὐτὰς κα[?]ὶ ἀϑὺς [?]τῆς ἀνδρῶν. Intelligit igitur Theophraftus appellatione ὀλιγαρχίας, mores hominis, qui optimatium fectam fequitur. Defcriptio oligarchiæ ab auctore prodita corrupta eft. Legimus nos ita, φι-λαρχία τις ἰσχυρὰ κέρδους ἢ γλιχομένη, vel γλιχομένης, id eft, vehemens honorum cupiditas, in eo qui nullo ftudio lucri teneatur. Aliter ifta conftituere quiti non fumus.
units.tr: Δόξειν ἂν τῇ ἡ ὀλιγαρχία.) Just as at Rome there were two parties in the state, one of the optimates and one of those who wished to be called and regarded as popular, so too at Athens. Cornelius Nepos, in his life of Phocion, whose lifetime Theophrastus shared, says: "At that time there were two factions at Athens: one of which championed the cause of the people, the other that of the optimates." Attic writers call the popular party τὰς δημοτικὰς, and the optimates τὰς ὀλιγαρχικὰς. Mention of them occurs throughout Attic history and in the Greek orators. Isocrates, in his speech On the Peace, speaks of those who are thought popular and those who are thought oligarchic. Theophrastus therefore means by the name ὀλιγαρχία the character of a man who follows the party of the optimates. The description of oligarchy given by the author is corrupt. We read it thus: φιλαρχία τις ἰσχυρὰ κέρδους ἢ γλιχομένη [a strong love of rule, or a longing for gain], or γλιχομένης, that is, a vehement desire for honours, in a man who is held by no eagerness for gain. We have not dared to construct the text otherwise.

units.la: ὁ ἢ ὀλιγαρχ[?] θι.) Legendum, ὀλιγαρχικός.
units.tr: ὁ ἢ ὀλιγαρχ[?] θι.) Read ὀλιγαρχικός [oligarchikos].

units.la: οἱ[?] τὲ ϑ νῦμ βυλομένυ.) Et mutilus & corruptus eft hic locus. Nos vertimus quafi effet fcriptum, οἱ δὲ τῶν βουλομένων τινὰς [ ϑὲι αἱρεῖσϑαι ] τῶ ἀρ-χονῖι συνεπιμελη⊙μένυς παρὰ ταῦτης, παρελϑὼν, ὑπο-φῆναι ἑαυτόν.
units.tr: οἱ[?] τὲ ϑ νῦμ βυλομένυ.) This passage is both incomplete and corrupt. We have translated as though it had been written: οἱ δὲ τῶν βουλομένων τινὰς [θεὶ αἱρεῖσθαι] τῷ ἄρχοντι συνεπιμελουμένους παρὰ ταῦτης, παρελθὼν, ὑποφῆναι ἑαυτόν [but some of those who wish, … coming forward, to present himself].

units.la: Δεῖ αὐτὺς κ[?]αμί. ] Legi Οὐ ϑεῖ αὐτὺς κ.
units.tr: Δεῖ αὐτὺς κ[?]αμί.] I read Οὐ δεῖ αὐτοὺς κ[...] [they must not …].

units.la: Ϲϑεῖν τὰς Ϲϊϊτυς λόγυς. ] Lego σ.ἡ τ. λόγυς λέγων. Et accipio Ϲϑεῖν pro δ[?]ὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς Ϲϑεῖν, quomodo loqui amant Græci.
units.tr: Ϲϑεῖν τὰς Ϲϊϊτυς λόγυς.] I read σ[…]ἡ τ[…] λόγυς λέγων [speaking the words]. And I take σθεῖν to mean "to go through the marketplace" (διὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς σθεῖν), in the way the Greeks like to speak.

units.la: τὸν Θησέα φρῶν φήϛς. ] Lego, φρῶν αἴτιον φ. Malum illud cuius auctor primus dicitur fuiffe Thefeus,eft ἰϹμοιεία & equaliras inter ciues,quam primus ille Athenas inuexit, & fanxit. Lege Plutarchum, & optimatem ifta loqui memento: cui in ordinem cogi, & non αἰὲν ϑεισϑῆν ἐ ὑπείροχον ἐμμεναι ἄλλων, inftar mortis eft.
units.tr: τὸν Θησέα φρῶν φήϛς.] I read φρῶν αἴτιον φ[…]. The evil whose author is said to have been first Theseus is equality (ἰσομοιεία) and equal standing among citizens, which he first brought into Athens and established there. Read Plutarch, and remember that it is an optimate who speaks these words: to be brought into line, and not to be always the one set above others, is like death.

units.la: καὶ ϑιαῦξ ἕτερα.] Deeft verbum λέγειν.
units.tr: καὶ ϑιαῦξ ἕτερα.] The verb λέγειν is missing.
τὰς ὁμοιορόφως.] Write τὰς ὁμοιοτρόπως [tas homoiotropōs].
On the chapter ὡσὲ ὁμοιοϑίας [concerning homoiotheia].

units.la: Hδὲ ὁμοιοϑίας φ.] Appellat Theophraftus ὁμοιοϑίαν, non quòd proprie vox Græca fonat, seram institutionem, vel eruditionem, (vt vertit A. Gellius) sed vitium quoddam iis familiare qui sero sunt eruditi. Videmus enim naturaliter euenire, vt neque ij recte vtantur diuitiis qui magnis opibus non sunt innutriti: sed eas sero nacti, diuites nouitij, vt vocat Seneca, euaserunt: neque scientia, illi quibus sera contigit eruditio. Hoc genus vitij vocant Graeci ἀπειροκαλίαν vel ὀλιγμαθίαν. Prior appellatio naturam vitij declarat: posterior eius causam & ortum. Est enim verissimum quod disertissimus scriptor Agathias ait, τῆς ἀφρόσυνης [?] ἡ πάλαι συμβὰν ἀτυχίας τινὸς μετασχόντας, ὡς ἀπειροκαλίαν ἐκλιναι, καὶ τῷ ἀσωνίῳ καταπεπληχθαι [?]. Nasci ait Agathias ἀπειροκαλίαν ἐκ τῆς ἀσωνίας [?], id est, ex insolentia, siue ex eo quòd non sint assueti cultui meliori. Quare etiam Latini vitium sero institutorum, insolentiam aptissimo vocabulo nuncuparunt. Cicero Patro, ὀλιγμαθεῖς homines scis quam insolentes sint. Alibi apud eundem scriptorem infolentia idem est atque Agathiae, τὸ ἀσωνίης. De lege agraria contra Rullum, loquens de nouis Capuae colonis, Hi, inquit, ex summa egestate in eandem rerum abundantiam traducti, non solum copia, sed etiam insolentia commouebuntur. De hoc vitio A. Gellius libro x i. capite v i 1. Est adeo, inquit, id vitium plerumque serae eruditionis, quam Graeci ὀλιγμαθίαν appellant, vt quod nunquam (vel antequam) diceris, din ignoraueris, cum id scire aliquando coperis, magni facias quo in loco cumque, & quacunque in re dicere. Ab ea mente apud Lucianum in libro περὶ ὀρχήσεως, dicitur φιλολογία ἀπειροκαλῶ ἐ ὀλιγμαθίας.
units.tr: Hδὲ ὁμοιοϑίας φ.] Theophrastus calls it ὁμοιοθία, not because the Greek word properly means a late instruction or education (as A. Gellius renders it), but because it is a certain fault peculiar to those who were educated late. We see that it naturally happens that those who were not brought up with great wealth do not use riches rightly; having obtained them late, they become rich upstarts, as Seneca calls them, and they are no more skilled in knowledge than those to whom an education came late. This kind of fault the Greeks call ἀπειροκαλία or ὀλιγμαθία. The former name declares the nature of the fault; the latter its cause and origin. For it is most true what the very eloquent writer Agathias says: that those who have at some time been touched by some misfortune, as when they have come into [wealth?] late, incline to boorishness (ἀπειροκαλία) and are struck dumb by their lack of refinement. Agathias says that ἀπειροκαλία arises from ἀσωνία, that is, from insolence, or from the fact that they are not accustomed to better cultivation. For this reason the Latins also named the fault of late-learned people with the most fitting word, insolentia. Cicero, in the Patro: "You know how insolent men are who have learned late." Elsewhere in the same author, insolentia means the same as Agathias's τὸ ἀσωνίης. In his speech On the Agrarian Law against Rullus, speaking of the new colonists of Capua, Cicero says: "These, brought from the utmost want into the same abundance of goods, will be moved not only by plenty but also by insolence." A. Gellius, in book 11, chapter 7, writes about this fault: "This fault," he says, "is for the most part that of late education, which the Greeks call ὀλιγμαθία, so that whatever you have long been ignorant of, and only begin to know at some point, you value greatly, and you wish to speak of it in any place and on any occasion." In the same spirit, in Lucian's book On Dancing, the expression is φιλολογία ἀπειροκαλῶ ἐ ὀλιγμαθίας [a love of learning … of boorishness and late learning].

units.la: Τοῦτ᾽ ἂ ὧν πρὸς πάντ᾽ ἂ δ᾽ ὧν[?] ] Legendum, ταῦτ᾽ ἂ δ᾽ ὧν πρὸς πάν[?].
units.tr: Τοῦτ᾽ ἂ ὧν πρὸς πάντ᾽ ἂ δ᾽ ὧν[?].] Read ταῦτ᾽ ἃ δ᾽ ὧν πρὸς πάν[...] [these things, and of which, toward every ...].

units.la: ἅμα μελλῶν[?] ἀπαντᾶσθαι[?]. ] Non displicet hæc lectio: nam qui equo insident certos habent gestus quibus utuntur in salutandis obuiis, quando illos tanto honore non dignantur, ut propterea descendant. Hos gestus soliti tirones rei equestris doceri à suis magistris. Potest tamen vera esse coniectura nostra, qui aliquando existimauimus scribendum καλπάζεσθαι[?]. Notum est, inter ἀμίλλας equestres fuisse καλπάζων[?]. Unde est καλπάζειν[?], siue καλπάζεσθαι[?].
units.tr: ἅμα μελλῶν[?] ἀπαντᾶσθαι[?].] This reading does not displease me. For those who sit on horseback have fixed gestures which they use in greeting those they meet, when they do not think them worthy of such honour that they should dismount for them. Recruits in horsemanship were accustomed to be taught these gestures by their masters. Nevertheless, our conjecture may be true, since we once thought that καλπάζεσθαι [to gallop] should be written. It is known that among the equestrian contests there was a καλπάζων [galloping race]. Hence comes καλπάζειν or καλπάζεσθαι.

units.la: τῷ κεφαλῷ κατεσχύναι[?].) Legendum καταισχυνῶσι[?]. Homerus,
units.tr: "They would be put to shame with the head" [τῷ κεφαλῷ κατεσχύναι?]. Read "they will be put to shame" [καταισχυνῶσι]. Homer:
"...and he ... to the senseless one" [—χέλευν δ᾽ ἤχμυε φρὸς ἀφρονε?]

units.la: καὶ μακρὸν ἀπ᾽ ἐξ ἀνὰ[?] πα̃ς ἀνδρὸς[?].) Scribe καὶ πρὸς ἀνδρ[?].
units.tr: "And far from ... of every man" [καὶ μακρὸν ἀπ᾽ ἐξ ἀνὰ πα̃ς ἀνδρὸς?]. Write "and toward the man" [καὶ πρὸς ἀνδρ].

units.la: Genus exercitationis nobilium epheborum, & tironum: ut apud Romanos exercere se ad palum.
units.tr: A kind of exercise of noble youths and recruits, as among the Romans, to practise oneself at the post (palus).

units.la: καὶ ἅμα μαινόμενον παρ᾽ αὐτῷ.) Locus est vitij manifestus: vertimus quasi legissemus, καὶ ἅμα μ. παρ᾽ αὐτῷ, καὶ δ᾽ ἰσάσω[?] αὐτὸν, ὡς &c. nec videtur sententia absurda quam expressimus. Possis etiam pro παρ᾽ αὐτῷ scribere παρά τι ab aliquo.
units.tr: καὶ ἅμα μαινόμενον παρ᾽ αὐτῷ.) This is a clear place of corruption. We have translated as though we had read καὶ ἅμα μ[…] παρ᾽ αὐτῷ, καὶ δ᾽ ἰσάσω[?] αὐτὸν, ὡς &c. [and at the same time raving in his presence, and he will make him equal, as &c.], nor does the sense we have expressed seem absurd. One could also write παρά τι [from someone] instead of παρ᾽ αὐτῷ.
On the chapter περὶ κακολογίας [on abusive speech].

units.la: Ἔστι ἡ κακολογία ἀγὼν τῆς ψυχῆς εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐν λόγοις.) Habent hoc plerêque omnes isto libello comprehensæ descriptiones, ut vel subobscuræ sint, vel corruptæ, vel utrumque. Quid appellatur hîc obsecro ἀγὼν τῆς ψυχῆς? Putabam scribendum esse ἀγωνὶ τῆς ψ. hoc est institutio, siue inclinatio, & propenfio animi, fed muto fententiam, & ἀγωνα ἐν λόγοις interpretor ἀγωνολογίαν. qua dictione Galenus vtitur in libro De fectis ad eos qui initiantur. ἀνεπιχείρητον δ', inquit, τῷ δὴ τῷ ἀθλίων ἀγωνολογίαν φασίν. Sententia nihilominus eadem manet.
units.tr: "Abusive speech is a struggle of the soul towards the worse, in words" [Ἔστι ἡ κακολογία ἀγὼν τῆς ψυχῆς εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐν λόγοις]. Almost all the definitions contained in this little book are of this kind: they are either rather obscure, or corrupt, or both. What, I beg you, is meant here by "a struggle of the soul" [ἀγὼν τῆς ψυχῆς]? I thought it should be read as ἀγωνὶ τῆς ψ., that is, a disposition or inclination and bent of mind. But I change my view, and I take "a struggle in words" [ἀγὼν ἐν λόγοις] to mean ἀγωνολογία [a contest of words]. Galen uses this word in his book On the Sects, addressed to those who are being initiated: "They say," he writes, "that it is not to be undertaken by the wretched, the ἀγωνολογία [contest of words]." Nevertheless the sense remains the same.

units.la: ὁ δέσποινα τί ἔστι; [?] Ille quid eft? hæc interrogatio de vitæ genere quærit. ifta autem τίς ἔστι; [?] de natalibus.
units.tr: "ὁ δέσποινα τί ἔστι;" ["What is he?"] This question [Ille quid est?] asks about a way of life. But the other, "τίς ἔστι;" ["who is he?"], asks about birth.

units.la: ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῆς.[?] Sententia poftulat αὐτῆ.[?]
units.tr: "ὑπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῆς" ["by the soul itself"]. The sense requires αὐτῆ [to it, or to her].

units.la: ἐχρῆσθαι δ' ἐν ταῖς σφαιρώταις Σωσίσφατον.[?] Hoc ait: patrem huius feruum initio fuiffe, ac vocitari nomine Sofiam folitum: poftea parta libertate aut manumiffione, aut alia ratione, mutato nomine Sofiftratum dici cepiffe, eoque tempore facramento dixiffe, & inter milites effe verfatum: ferò tandem plenam libertatem effe confecutum, & in vnam tribuum, vnumque τῶν δήμων effe relatum. Legendum autem, ἐκ τῆς δ. ἐν non ἐπιδή.[?]
units.tr: "ἐχρῆσθαι δ' ἐν ταῖς σφαιρώταις Σωσίσφατον" ["And he used Sosisphatos among the sphairotai"]. His meaning is this: the father of this man was at first a slave, and was commonly called by the name Sophias. Afterwards, when he had gained his freedom, either by manumission or some other means, he began to be called Sosistratus under a changed name; at that time he took the oath, and served among the soldiers. Only late did he finally obtain full liberty and was enrolled in one of the tribes and in one of the demes. But the text should read ἐκ τῆς δ. ἐν, not ἐπιδή.

units.la: ἡ μήτηρ μήτηρ ἀγωνίς.[?] Id eft eius mater, quæ vulgo habetur pro nobili.
units.tr: "ἡ μήτηρ μήτηρ ἀγωνίς" ["the mother, mother, agonis"]. That is, his mother, who is commonly regarded as a woman of good family.

units.la: ἐν τῇ πατρίδι.[?] Hoc iste ait, obfcurè fignificans Threffas mulieres Athenis non effe nobiles, fed vel conditione feruas, vel genere vitæ meretrices. Certum eft peregrinarum mulierum Athenis, atque vbique fere locorum olim, fufpectam fuiffe pudicitiam, quamobrem in facris literis fæpe זָרָה vel זֹנָה hoc eft, mulier peregrina idem fonat ac fcortum. Sic effe hæc accipienda declarant quæ fequuntur.
units.tr: "ἐν τῇ πατρίδι" ["in the homeland"]. He says this obscurely, meaning that Thracian women at Athens were not of good family, but were either slaves by condition or prostitutes by way of life. It is certain that the chastity of foreign women at Athens, and almost everywhere else in former times, was suspect; for this reason in the sacred books זָרָה or זֹנָה [zarah or zonah], that is, a foreign woman, carries the same meaning as a harlot. That these words must be understood in this way is shown by what follows.

units.la: ἡ τῶν ἀλλαγῇ δ.[?] Verborum ἀλλαγή eft interrupta,quæ potest integrari hoc modo : [illegible, ~6 letters] [?] ὅτι [?] τᾶς [?] ἀιεξιῶν φησιν, αὐ. vel τὰ ὅτι τᾶ[?].
units.tr: "ἡ τῶν ἀλλαγῇ δ." ["the ... of exchange"]. The word ἀλλαγή is interrupted. It can be completed in this way: [illegible, about six letters] "that" [ὅτι], "of the" [τᾶς], "he says of the ... , αὐ." or "the things that ... of ...".

units.la: ἐκ τῆς ὁδῷ τῆς παιδίσκης ἀρπάζεσθαι.] Isto loquendi genere significat eam de qua loquitur, vilem fuisse copam, & publicæ libidinis victimam. Fere enim καπηλεῖα erant Ἀφροδίσια, vt ait Philostratus in epistola ad γυναῖκα καπηλίδα. Harum mos fuit miris illecebris, & vt loquitur Apuleius, tabernarijs blanditijs ad se prætereuntes allicere, quod venustissimè Theophrastus dixit ἀρπάζειν ἐκ τῆς ὁδὸς τῆς παιδίσκης. Suetonius in Nerone, capite xxvi 1. Quoties ostiam Tiberi deflueret, aut Baianum sinum prætəernauigaret, disposita per littora & ripas diuersoria tabernæ parabantur, insignes ganeæ, & matronarum institoria, copas imitantium, atque hinc inde orantium vt appelleret. Narrat & Xiphilinus ex Dione, Abitum τὰ τῆς καπηλίδων ἐργαζόμενον, cùm alia turpia fecisse multa, tum etiam τῆς παιδίσκης ἀδρᾶς καὶ κεκλασμένῃ τῇ φωνῇ προσελαλεῖσθαι. Ingeniosissimus poëtarum Virgilius omnes istiusmodi mulierum blanditias venustissimè expressit eo carmine quod Copa inscribitur. Porro secundùm vias solitas instrui popinas & diuersoria publica, testis Varro de re Rustica libro primo, cap. 11. & Suetonius Vitellio, capite xiii.
units.tr: "ἐκ τῆς ὁδῷ τῆς παιδίσκης ἀρπάζεσθαι" ["to be snatched from the road by the girl"]. By this way of speaking he means that the woman he is talking about was a cheap tavern-girl, a victim of public lust. For the kapēleia were commonly Aphrodisia, as Philostratus says in his letter to the innkeeper woman [γυναῖκα καπηλίδα]. Their custom was to lure passers-by with remarkable enticements, and, as Apuleius puts it, with tavern-keepers' flatteries; Theophrastus put this most elegantly as "to be snatched from the road by the girl" [ἀρπάζειν ἐκ τῆς ὁδὸς τῆς παιδίσκης]. Suetonius, in Nero, chapter 26: Whenever he was flowing down the Tiber to the mouth, or sailing past the Bay of Baiae, taverns and public inns were set up along the shores and banks, notorious brothels and houses of matrons who played at innkeeping, imitating the tavern-girls, and calling out from here and there for him to land. Xiphilinus also relates, from Dio, that Abitus, practising the trade of the tavern-woman, did many other shameful things, and also was addressed by the girl's pleasantly soft and broken voice [ἀδρᾶς καὶ κεκλασμένῃ τῇ φωνῇ]. The most gifted of poets, Virgil, expressed most elegantly all the blandishments of such women in the poem called The Tavern Girl [Copa]. Further, that taverns and public inns were customarily built beside the public roads is attested by Varro, On Agriculture, book 1, chapter 11, and by Suetonius, Vitellius, chapter 13.

units.la: ἀπάντων μεμισηκα.) Lege ἀπάντων μάλιστα μεμισηκα. τῇ Ποσειδῶνος ἡμέρᾳ.) Verti, Pofideone mense. Legi nempe τῇ τῆς Ποσειδεῶνος ἡμέρᾳ : vel τῆς ἡμέρας. hoc perinde valet ac si diceret, cùm iam maximè friget. nam Pofideon vltimus fuit mensis autumnalis in anno Attico, Decembri nostro & Ianuario ex parte respondens, vel teste Plutarcho. Quod ait τῇ ἡμέρᾳ in numero vnitatis, puto intelligi Kalendas eius menfis, Neptuno facrum diem, lautis epulis & Θεσμοφοριαῖς[?] folitum celebrari. Quare etiam librorum fcripturam non cenfeo mutandam, quæ habet Ποσειδῶν ὢν ϑ[?], nam ita fatis declaratur primus dies menfis Pofideonis, vel quicunque alius eius menfis dies fuit folemnibus Neptuni infignis.
units.tr: "ἀπάντων μεμισηκα" ["I hate all of them"]. Read ἀπάντων μάλιστα μεμισηκα ["I hate most of all"]. "On the day of Poseidon" [τῇ Ποσειδῶνος ἡμέρᾳ]: I translated this as "in the month of Poseidon." I read rather τῇ τῆς Ποσειδεῶνος ἡμέρᾳ, or τῆς ἡμέρας; this amounts to saying "when it is now at its coldest." For Poseidon was the last month of autumn in the Attic year, corresponding partly to our December and January, as Plutarch testifies. What he says, τῇ ἡμέρᾳ in the singular, I think means the Kalends of that month, a day sacred to Neptune, customarily celebrated with lavish feasts and Thesmophoria. For this reason I do not think the reading of the books should be changed, which has Ποσειδῶν ὢν ϑ [Poseidon being the 8th? ...]; for in this way the first day of the month of Poseidon, or whatever other day of that month was marked by the festivals of Neptune, is sufficiently made clear.

units.la: Δεινὸς ᾧ τῇ ἀναςάν[?] & εἰ ταῖς[?] .] Legi, ᾧ εἰ τῇ ἀνα- ςάς κακῶς (vel κακα) εἰπεῖν. Sic alibi accipitur, τὸ ἀνασάς. vt capite ᾧ ἀπεχθ[?]. οἴ & ἐκαλυσεν ᾧ ἀνασάς ἀ μὴ δ[?]ωνιστῆ. Ferri poteft & alrera lectio ἀναςάνῳ[?] , quam ita exponemus. Solet cum aliis fedens, de eo qui furrexit (vel verba factutus, vel difceffurus) male loqui.
units.tr: "Δεινὸς ᾧ τῇ ἀναςάν [Deinos ... ] & εἰ ταῖς [and if in the ...]." I read "ᾧ εἰ τῇ ἀνα- ςάς κακῶς (or κακα) εἰπεῖν," meaning "to speak ill of one who has risen." So it is understood elsewhere, τὸ ἀνασάς, as in the chapter "ᾧ ἀπεχθ[?]," and "οἴ & ἐκαλυσεν ᾧ ἀνασάς ἀ μὴ δ[?]ωνιστῆ." The other reading, ἀναςάνῳ [?], may also be carried, which we shall explain thus: he who sits among others is accustomed to speak ill of the one who has risen (or who has begun to speak, or who is about to leave).

units.tr: "καὶ ᾧ εἰ τῆ τελεσάτηκότων κακῶς λέγεν" ["and to speak ill of the dead"]. This is not only a fault against good morals, but also against the written law and the laws of the Athenians. For there was a law of Solon: "not to speak ill of the dead" [τὸν τεθνηκότα κακῶς μὴ ἀγορεύειν]. So much for this. In the Palatine books there followed two headings, but only headings, thus
